IMHO, far and away the best game in the Hack & Slash genre for non hardcore gamers (those who don't like the imbalance/xp penalties from death in PoE).
The music creates the same feel the score from Diablo 2. It does a great job of setting the mood.
The game itself is much like D2, 3 skills trees per class and ability to assign points to attributes every level that impacts what gear you can use and when.
The combat on normal absolutely nails down the fun of mowing through hordes of enemies with your special abilities. Elite difficulty is too much of a kite/grindfest for my tastes but others may enjoy it.
The endgame is well handled imo. You have the choice of starting a NG+ or running maps. Maps have random bonuses/penalties to keep them interesting but they tend to be a little long for my tastes (3-4 different levels in the map).
While I dislike Runic not including respec potions, that's easily fixed by tons of mods.
Speaking of mods, this game has amazing support for them. There are several mods adding new classes and pets. There's stuff to tweak drop rates, skill point gains, add tiered passive skills, and almost anything else you can think of. For people who don't mind a higher mob spawn rate for more champion mobs, I highly recommend the Synergies mod. It changes a lot of the spawn/drop rates of vanilla while adding new gear, classes, focus specific enchanters, and a whole new zone with boss mobs for level 100+ characters.

Anyone familiar with the Diablo series should know what to expect with a game like Torchlight 2. It's an action RPG with less focus on the story and more focus on beating the crap out of hordes of enemies.
The Good: I liked the idea of having a pet that can go sell stuff or buy stuff back at town while you keep dungeon crawling. That is something that should have been in this genre of game a long time ago. The graphics were fairly good for a game of this genre. I had no real issues with online play and no disconnects either. However, it does use it's own lobby system, so if you're buying this a few years after it's out the online multiplayer may be trickier.
The Bad/Ugly: The classes are rather shallow in this game. They're all really just different ways of dealing damage. I didn't feel like there was really any synergy between the classes. There were no real support ablities other than some self-buffs. The engineer has a healing bot, but other than that there isn't really any way to heal other teamates. Speaking of the engineer, played right, he/she does a lot more damage than the other classes. I was expecting more with the abilities, like in some of the older RPGs where different classes had different roles. In this game class just determines which type of damage you do more or less. As I said above I wasn't expecting an amazing story with this type of game, but this one was rather bland. It felt like World of Warcraft at times (and not in a good way), but with only 4 people.
Summary: It is an okay game, but definitely could have been better. It's fun if you have friends to play coop with, but I wouldn't play it singleplayer.
Note: Yes I do realize it has lots of workshop content, but I'm rating the game as is, not with as many mods as it takes to fix it to my liking.

Numba Deluxe has three game modes. Two of the modes in the game, Classic and Timeless, are a bit lacking. Both of them start as incredibly simple matching games. They both slowly increase in complexity as you play, but it takes maybe thirty minutes to an hour of agonizingly slow progression for the games to become complicated enough to be interesting. With no save or skip functions to let you avoid the many tedious early levels, these modes just aren't very fun.
Puzzle mode is much better than the others, though. Puzzle mode has 84 puzzles that increase in difficulty as you go along. Most of the early puzzles are very straightforward and easy. Eventually it starts throwing out some brain burners, though. I'm fairly average at puzzles, and it took me about three hours to beat all of them. Unlike the other modes, the game remembers which puzzles you've already completed, so you can always jump back in wherever you last took a break.
Overall, I found the game to be worth buying for fans of puzzle games. There's not much replayability due to two modes being subpar and the other consisting of pre-made puzzles, but there's still enough game here to be worthwhile at the low price point.

The games that offer real time strategies with contemporary military units are only a few and they are generally unexceptional so you can imagine my excitement for the Wargame series. Red Dragon's timeframe expands from 1975 to 1991 and has over 1600 air/land/naval units from 17 countries. The units have been modeled with realism in mind and they even have fuel and ammo counters that you need to manage during a fight.
Campaign mode might get a bit repetitive because sometimes you play the same map with the same units repeatedly. You can also manage troop compositions and deployment at a strategic level before fights but it's pretty light. Besides the five campaigns you also have multiplayer and skirmish mode. Even though the idea and its implementation are good, the game failed to really engage me.

At time of writing I'm only 21 hours in, but I think I've got the gist of it.
The TL;DR version is that this is a pretty solid game. In fact, even if it was released as 'complete' in its current state, it would be a pretty solid game for an indie developer.  There are many hours of playability here.
The Longer version...
It's pure sandbox. You mine with your mining lasers, you salvage with your salvaging beams, and you shoot bad guys with your shooty things.  You build your ship using various metals - which you tend to find in asteroid fields.  The closer you get to the galactic core, the better the metals you'll find.
Ship building is easy enough. Think "Space Engineers" lite. You place the blocks, but you don't need to 'craft' them with tools. As long as you've got the metal you need, you can just size them, rotate them, and place them.  Mostly this makes for pretty blocky designs - but I suspect that there will be a lot more block options as the game develops.
When you're building your ship, you need to consider your primary engine, thruster placement, armour, and power generation. Later on you get shields, storage batteries, and so forth.  You can place your weapons/turrets anywhere, but you can only fit a certain number without upgrading your internal components with found parts.
Graphically it's a mixed bag.  The blocky nature of the ships can be a bit off-putting, but the game will run on a sponge, let alone a half-decent computer. Cranking everything up to maximum settings can make for some very nice and atmospheric moments - with nicely rendered/shadowy starships attacking out of a combination of sun/mist... or enough incoming fire to make you think you've been caught in a fireworks display.
You fly with WASD and mouse. Your turrets can rotate quite a lot, but realistically, they'll be facing more or less forwards.
Ranges are short. I've not seen a gun fire further than about 5km at this point.  Mining tends to be well under 1km, which tends to have you cosying up to asteroids in some pretty dense fields.
Each sector - and there are thousands of randomly generated sectors - will have jump-gates, various stations, NPC ships of various types, and asteroids. There are occasional anomalies. You can also 'warp' without requiring gates, though the power-drain is enormous.  There are also plenty of empty sectors, so if you push away from the beaten track, it can be awkward finding a useful sector again. Some sectors are pirate strong-holds, some have bosses in, some are just nice and benign.
You can complete missions in certain sectors. There are lots of factions for you to help or hinder, and your reputation with them will change depending on what you do.   Pirates will often randomly jump in and start attacking ships in the sector, and you can either join in, defeat them, or avoid them and watch the battle from afar while you continue mining.
You can also run fleets of ships, with mining ships, combat ships, fighters, salvagers, etc, all following your commands. I haven't played with this too much, but it seems pretty powerful - though the path-finding of your AI ships in asteroid fields is poor at best.
The main problem with this game is that it's quite addictive. Building your ship, upgrading your ship, and exploring new sectors can take more hours than you expect, and this is honestly one of the best Early Access games I've played in a very long time.
It's not without faults.
THE BAD  (And bearing in mind that this is an Early Access game)
==============================================
I see that some people are having problems running it. I haven't encountered any kind of problem.
Pathfinding is not brilliant. Ships in asteroid fields tend to just drive straight into asteroids and sit there looking confused.
There's not enough feedback regarding damage to your own ship. You can see bits flying off, and there are status bars, but it can be hard to see where damage is coming from, how bad it is, and whether you should be running away or whether you can tank it for a while.
Aiming can be a bit awkward. Because your ship might be off to one side in 3rd person view, if you're close to a target, getting your shots to land can be frustrating.  At range, it's not a problem.
Not enough aesthetic options for ship creation.
Some kind of optional story/quest line would be nice... just to fill the gaps or provide a bit of structure if you feel you need it.
THE GOOD
========
It's nice and easy to get to grips with, right from the outset. It doesn't bog you down with too much detail, but you always feel like there's something to do.
It's an awful lot of fun sawing bits of enemy spacecraft, taking out their guns or thrusters, and cutting them apart with salvaging beams.
Difficulty progression seems relatively well balanced - perhaps a little on the easy side at default settings. Consider cranking it up a bit.
Just when you think you've seen it all, some new anomaly or sector-type turns up - or you can build a fighter-bay or install shields.  The game will always find something to keep you going.
It's just so much fun.
In short, I'm loving the game, and if I didn't have to go to work in the morning, I'd be playing it until the wee-small hours tonight.

Batman Arkham Origins Blackgate is a lot like playing a 2D Metroid game, but with Batman, which is awesome. It makes sense that it should have a bit of a Metroid flavor since many of the people who worked on this game also worked on the Metroid Prime games. You explore Blackgate Prison trying to take down Penguin, Black Mask, and The Joker while collecting gadgets, armor upgrades, and much more. The combat is a simplified version of the system from the other Arkham games. In this game you just punch,counter, and do takedowns and it feels surprisingly good. The combination of good combat, great exploration, and excellent setting have made for a fantastic game which I've had trouble putting down. The bottom-line is if you like Batman, Metroid, or both then buy it.

This had a lot of potential. Batman in a true 2/2.5D metroidvania game? Sounds awesome.
Sadly, the execution is severly lacking.
The controls are controller snappingly frustrating and unresponsive even at best. There is no jump button, for example, yet there are things for you to jump over, namely, spike strips on the floor. You CAN double tap the action button and roll, and sometimes that will get you over the spikes, but this only works about 25% of the time.
The combat against regular enemies is just button mashing, much like the other Arkham games. Only here, you don't even choose which targets to attack, you just spam melee and occasionally stun or jump over someone.
The bosses are horrid, and the main reason why I can't recommend this game. They are super scripted, multi phase fights with no check points. The problem comes from the controls being what they are, which makes what would be decent fights into brutally difficult excercises in frustration.
The map is a piece of crap. It's fixed angle, but room layouts are completely arbitrary and don't follow the map in logical ways.
The rest is kind of meh. Decent music. Graphics aren't bad considering they came from a portable. Voice acting is...passable. And the collecting is alright, from what I got into. I quit when I got to the penguin because he's impossibly hard for no good reason.
Why can we not have good metroidvania games made these days? It can't be THAT hard.

Review for single player campaign:
I got this game for free when purchasing a new graphics card. I left it a while as I had played the second game a little at a friend's house and wasn't in a rush for it. When the time came to play it I found the start of the game quite exciting and it rapidly gained my interest as I sunk the first few hours into the game.
The story line I found kind of generic but interesting enough. No real relatable characters or depth. This however was not the point of the game at least in my opinion. The kill camera for perfectly aimed shots was fun at first but by the time I had reached the half way point in the game I had turned them off completely. The game play however was enthralling throughout the campaign. I spent hours on a mission taking it as slowly as possible and trying to be "the perfect sniper", crawling through the grass on my stomach trying to reach the next point of cover to scope out a target area. Making my way around the map working out the best position for attacks and covering my rifle fire with ambient noises. When there were none, sneaking into the area and executing people from behind. I had a lot of fun.
Overall if you are looking for a first/third person shooter with stealth aspects and at least some level of control in choosing how you went about your objectives this could be the game for you. If you are looking for a sandbox environment you will be disappointed, while not having a linear game play progression style most areas only give you a couple of options on where to stage an attack from with only a couple of combat styles for those few choices. 7/10

I was a big fan of AA series, was playing America's Army since the firs version of 1.1+, then stick almost till the end of it, through AA:Operations and so on. I was playing America's Army III a lot too, al though it was far away from a good game in terms of implementation and quality.
America's Army: Proving Grounds was really good in closed beta, how ever it did looked like another cheep free to play game at first glance, but that impresion was only at the beginning. The game mechanics were mooth and there were no problems or major bugs, witch was really surprising knowing the long history of rusty and bugy frame of it's predesessors.
The open beta and launch was also fun, but there was a problem that developers, in my opinion, didn't know where to go with the meta of the game and were trying to pick from devided community of "new players" and the "old veterans" of AA:O. Again in my opinion,  the game in the end had shifted to fast paced CS like environment and lost it's charm and originality in the process, witch I find a real shame.
I played this game over 1000 raw hours, cince I am a fan of AA and am still the opinion that America's Army (the 1st game) was the best online tactical team shooter of all times. I played the firs game over 2000 hours.
The main issue for me, that AA:PB lost is it's tactical element, since maps begant to be more crampt and big open maps were not considered animore. Allowing rapid movement and fire, it all was redused to a fast paced duels instead of a planning and tactical aproach that it had in the beginning. The operation time had reduesed segnificantly in the process instead of 10-8 minutes it became 6-4 or even less.
Another interesting and unique thing witch I and a lot of other players found really cool  was lost in a process. Earlier when planting a bomb was introduesed to the game, the team that had to prevent the plant could recover the bomb from an eliminated solgier and disarm it on spot. In other words there was a lot of thing you had to keep in mind. The location of the bomb carrier, and seroundings along the plant zone. The assault team with the bomb needed to split in two teams, one would safe keep the bomb and another would try to prob the plant zones for resistence. The deffending team also could split in to several teams in order to form a deffence and prepare flanking manuvers. Spotting and reporting a bomb carier to your team was a big help. This was almost like VIP mission, where VIP was a bomb and if you lost it and enemy team destroyed it or disarmed it in the process you lose.
I still hope that the good old AA will reemerged some day in a new tytle, but for now, if you are in a favore of tactical team play shooter, sadly this game is not for you.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a game.
It is a game about trading, where you buy products for cheap where they are in bulk, then sell them for high prices where there are few of them.
It is a game about politics, where you ask lords if they need tasks done, and you earn favour by doing them.
It is a medieval tournament simulator, where you bet on yourself to win in a ~7 stage tournament.
It is a medieval peasant/knight/slave/baron simulator (pw) where you mine/chop wood/fight enemies/help knights/lord over groups of people.
It is a napoleonic-era fighting game with an active community where you fight with muskets and swords against real people/bots.
It is an archer simulator, where you snipe enemies off from a distance.
Finally, it is a open world medival mercenary/lord/baron/king simulator where you command troops from a size of 1-500, recruiting peasants, training them into warriors, knights and archers who help you conquer castles, villages and towns as you try to either reunite the land under: an existing faction, a claimant to a thone or your own banner.
Honestly one of my favorite games of all time. Can't wait for Bannerlord!

PLAYS LIKE JUST CAUSE NOT RED FACTION I
You start off as Alec Mason who goes to Mars to join his brother Daniel to start a new life on Mars as miners. Unfortunately your brother dies on the first mission to the new oppressive EDF regime of Mars and like Parker before you lead the Red Faction on a revolution to freedom. However this is done rather poorly as you have to revolutionize Mars one sector at a time; of 6 sectors. You do this through several types of Red Faction missions:Assault, House Arrest, Transporter, Convoy, Courier, Guerrilla Raid, Heavy Metal, and Collateral Damage. You can also progress by destroying propaganda, ammo depots, guard stations, and industrial complexes causing more people to believe in your cause. However, of all those missions Heavy Metal and Collateral Damage are the best since you get a heavy weapon or mayhem inducing vehicle to destoy all in your path which are the funnest parts of the game. Despite that it takes a long time to liberate each sector and will force you to play all the mission types at least twice.
The combined dry atmosphere of mars (ha-ha) and the sometimes vacant music and sound design can make a boring experience. That along with the uninteresting story and main character can make this game a real grind to just get to the next section or sector. However the fully destrucible buildings in this game and explosive weapons at your disposal (satchel charges mostly) make fighting the enemy a goofy experience when you can kill people with falling debris or make them ragdoll 1000 ft in the air.
There is a small upgrade system which gives your character new gadgets or weapons but most of these take a backseat to the satchel charges as kill groups of enemies and destroy buildings. Also if you increase the difficultly it can increase the cost of how much SALVAGE you need to upgrade. And like the previous Red Factions the difficulty increase = how many bullets can an enemy soak up.
All in all an okay game but there are better alternatives.
If you do get this game play your own music, upgrade satchel charges all the way, get the jetpack, and bob and weave your way to destroying everything with just your charges and hammer.

What do you get when you mix Minecraft, Space Engineers, Eve Online and Elite Dangerous together? You get this mind bogging amazement of a game! This game certianly has a ton of potential to become something even greater than what it already is and I really hope that it does.
Pros:
* Nearly limitless and incredibly diverse ship building (you're quite literally only limited by your imagination, ore collection and credit balance.
* Dynamic damage is freaking awesome and makes for sometimes unpredictable outcomes during combat
* You can actually build and control a fleet of ships! This game actually does have a bit of RTS built into it.
* Beautifully rendered environments
* Players can immerse themselves in the more complex aspects of the game such as ship statistics (much like in Eve Online).
Cons:
* The game can quickly become overwhelming for players who aren't used to space sims or 6DOF style combat and manuevering.
* The UI becomes a bit overwhelming at times (it has tons of things that are targeted that populate your screen, much like Eve Online).
* Currently (at the time of this written review) the game is pretty basic and barebones, but it has a ton of potential. For what it has in it already, it's actually surprisingly good.
My suggestions for the developer:
* This game totally needs a dedicated MMO server of some kind
* Mod support. I'm pretty sure there are players out there who want to mod the ever living snot out of this game.
* Landing on planets (eventually) and planetary vehicles.
A satisfyingly simple space game with a pretty good soundtrack.

A must play for fans of space games and those who enjoy piloting starcraft. Imagine kerbal but with warfare and fancy space lasers and easier exploration. This is an excellent game of superior quality. It comes with quite a few routes pre-insalled and all of them have excellent graphics. The DLC is available to buy directly from the Steam store and is installed into the game automatically for you. Most of the negative reviews on this game are moaning about the cost of DLC, and not the game in general. Well they should have checked the price of DLC before they bought the game, shouldn't they? I kind of agree that the DLC is expensive for what you get, but when you think about it, a whole new route is like just like buying a whole new train simulator. The best time to get DLC are when sales are on. Be patient and wait, becuase they come frequently. The only one downside to the game that I have noticed so far, is that Dovetail Games are cutting down on the number of routes and trains, that you get preinstalled with the game, when buying the Standard Edition. In the original RailWorks game you got about 8 routes and a heap of different trains. And the actual price of the game was cheaper than now. Thesedays, you only get 3 routes and about 6 trains. So they are really cutting down on your value for money. The only way get their real money is by people buying DLC. So in conclusion, I really recommend that you buy this game because it has excellent graphics and you will have plenty of fun playing it without having to buy any DLC.

So I finally got the pleasure of downloading the 1.4GB update to TS2016. I went to load my custom consist with SD70s on Union Pacific's Sherman Hill, one of my favourite routes. I haven't read into it enough to know whether or not this is supposed to be a beta, I hope it is because this new version is just awful. Instead of background music you only hear the continuous winter wind blowing on the menu screens from the introduction video. Exciting. There's no loading bar or screens to showcase recently released routes/trains as there was in the past, you get to stare at a black screen for several seconds/minutes and hope your desired route/scenario is still loading. The SD70 which was my favourite locomotive for being one of few with excellent audio, has been 'improved' to now sound nothing like a train. Rolling stock over the tracks sounds are even more terrible. On top of it all, the stupid brake decrease glitch - which I first discovered driving Soldier Summit's SD40-2 which requires you to spam the decrease button to shut the brakes off - has now also plagued my beloved SD70.
This is an embarrassment. Not only for Dovetail, but for me, having spent so much money on this. They've even seemed to have taken a step backwards as far as optimization goes, as this is now the only game I play where I can't achieve 60FPS (I don't even know if I'm getting 30) with an i5 and a GTX970 ACX2.0 on a 1440p monitor. If you haven't already, I highly suggest you do not update and resume playing TS2015. In my eyes, after this update, this game has fallen to "shovelware" (Google it if you don't know what that means) like quality. I'm not a person to rant, but this is an abomination. I pity the folks who have spent even more than I have on Dovetail's now even ♥♥♥♥♥ier DLCs. If I'm off my wagon and this is supposed to be some kind of Beta (Alpha??) or if there's other routes that have seen real improvements, please let me know. I'd like to have some sort of hope that the Train Sim I've enjoyed in the past has some potential to be playable again.
As far as the "All the DLC would cost over $3,000, that's stupid!" I don't really see the point of complaining about that, you certainly don't need to purchase more than a couple routes to enjoy the game. With that said, paying $44 CAD for a route I expect it to not have the poor optimization and bugs that they have. Even on sale they still cost too much for what they are. This wouldn't be the case if they worked like they should and didn't have any issues - these things you don't learn about until after you've spent your money. So yes, folks are right to complain about the price because most of them don't see how bad the routes are until after thay've made the purchase.
The icing on the cake is the beautiful video they have showcasing the UP Turbine, which features absolutely no in-game footage. Their beautiful In-Detail videos on YouTube and screenshots are appealing, but hide the truth about how horrible this game is/has become.
In conclusion, I'm disappointed to say that this update has officially killed the game for me. The sheer amount of bugs, glitches, and scenery issues would be tolerable if the game cost $10 and DLCs cost $5, but the state that Dovetail has released this game and at the pricepoint it and the DLCs, in addition to the ways that they advertise the game as mentioned above, is more than wrong, it's immoral. I do not recommend anyone spends any money on this game and supports these people for what they are doing.

When I say that wargame is one of the most disappointing games I have ever played, I mean it as a complement (sort of). It has every kind of military hardware a military geek could possibly want (except the US is nerfed for "balance" reasons, whereas artillery is not... more on that later). Want your own wing of FA-18 hornets? Done. Want a batallation of M1A1 abrams tanks? Done too. Seal teams in chinooks? Check. Apache helicopters? Check and check (except they suck in comparison to world in conflict).
The UI is terrible. It took me dozens of hours to figure out you can rotate the field of view. The siren that notifies you when your troops are under attack - it will drive you insane it's so annoying (but barely if at all actually communicates what troops are under attack and where). There is some (very tiny) amount of 3D-ness to the environments, but since the UI is so terrible you can't zoom in properly and see it, leaving you mystified why your tanks can't shoot a unit clearly in view. And when you try to zoom out to see the whole battlefield? you'll do it one tick too much or too fast and go into a useless megamap. Understanding all the weird, nuanced crap in this game is like I imagine trying to play PSO in japanese. The learning curve is steep, to put it mildly, and there are few if any resources to learn (reddit is actually the best place, although their players are bigger stackers than just about anyone in this game's "community"). The deck system (units you use are "cards" in a "deck") is interesting once you understand it, but it's like a brick wall for new players, and the built-in decks are beyond useless. The biggest improvement a player will make in their game is using a good deck.
The single player would be fantastic, with a number of realistic alternate reality conflicts centered in East Asia... except the AI only knows one strategy - spam. It turns every engagement into a kind of tower defense against endless, mindless AI spam. This occurs irrespective of what kind of unit the AI is using - helicopters? spammed. bomber aircraft? spammed. ships? spammed again. tanks? spammed obviously. infantry? you guessed it - spammed. It knows where all your units are and what they are. These systems actually make the AI in most strategy games look incredible by comparison.
Because of the futility of the campaign, multiplayer is the only thing worth doing. The problem with multiplayer is the "community". In Wargame:RD it's more common to see 10 people with >1000 hours each playing against 10 people with <200 hours combined than it is to see a balanced match. This results in a variety of problems that cause this game to be unplayable. Stacking breeds more stacking - >90% of people get tired of being stacked against and decide to stack themselves. Because of the learning curve, it's easy for someone mildly better to easily defeat an opponent, so 10v10 where every player on one team is significantly better than everyone on the other are a joke. Rather than ending these games quickly, the stackers will toy with their opponents to rack up pretty kill lists, etc. These people also love to abuse artillery because, when properly micromanaged, artillery is completely uncounterable.
This "metagame" leads to a scenario where periodically there is a steam sale, lots of people buy the game, and these people serve as the fodder for children with low self-esteem to beat up on in their stacks until they stop playing shortly thereafter. There will be another steam sale in a few months, and the cycle repeats. Anyone who stays has likely embraced the cancerous stacker meta, and the problem only worsens with time.
So in light of these glaring problems, they're releasing more nations and map packs as DLC! They do so rather than fixing the problems that have plagued this game for years - bad AI in single player and no matchmaking that REQUIRES players to play balanced matches. To their credit, they finally patched one of the most abusive things in the game - shooting helicopters with artillery. A small improvement but too little too late.
Note ranked matchmaking exists, but that is mostly top tier players smurfing. The VAST majority of the multiplayer player base (>99% of people) are playing in stacked 10v10 lobbies in unranked (either intentionally as stackers, or unwittingly as noobs, or the rare massochists (0.001% of people) like me who play against stacks intentionally and lose virtually every game).
I love the wargame series. I loved Red Dragon a lot more when I could actually play it with my friends. Please release the Mac update soon...

This is the first game I've played that I've been really, really conflicted about.
Pros: Graphically impressive, very complex tactics, amazing level of detail in unit design (including visibility, perception, armor, range, damage, etc. etc.). Probably the closest thing to real-time realism on the market right now.
Cons: Extremely steep learning curve, zillions of units and game mechanics to learn, and the developers didn't support it with a tutorial. The fan community has brought up various resources to help, but general feeling is that to get a proper designer tutorial, you'll be looking at buying the first game, European Escalation.
The game is very complex, which means it'll take time even for those familiar with the older games in the series to pick it up. (First game EE was purely land, second game AirLand Battle introduced aircraft, this game introduces naval units.)
I'm fairly experienced with other historical RTSes (although none are as realistic as this one) and I found the learning curve for RD unworkable with the limited time available to me. I put eight hours in-game, trying out guides and putting what I'd learned from fan manuals into practice: my victory or defeat still feels entirely arbitrary. [Update: this is because the guides deal with playing against humans, but the AI uses several pathfinding shortcuts which give it several important differences from human performance - it has omniscient line-of-sight so concealment doesn't work against it, and it has "human wave" mentality for dealing with chokepoints.]
The fan community has been great, and if you have a lot of time and attention to put into this game, it may be the game for you. Likewise, if you don't mind buying the first game and working through that as a prelude to playing this one. Folks who find analysis to be fun in its own right, or who are detail oriented, may enjoy this game too.
I found the time demands of learning the game to be too heavy. I disapprove of the designer's decision to essentially shortchange new players by removing the tutorial on the assumption that they'll have played the prior games. The fan support is very heartening, but it seems to reinforce the designer's laziness so they can get away with it. The designer should include solo-play tutorial support in ALL titles in the series, not just the first few titles. This sales model of "expecting people to buy your earlier games before they can play your later games" was already proven unworkable with the Wizardry series way back in the 1980s. Eugen should know better.
There's all the hallmarks of a good game in here, provided you can devote the very significant time and focus requirements to crack the shell, either by doing online mentorship with the fans, or by buying the previous titles in the series. However, in all honesty, it didn't work out for me and I couldn't recommend it in good conscience.

After reading a lot of the negative reviews on here, I will just say that I'm glad I decided to buy this game anyway. I ended up enjoying it quite a bit. I think a lot of the negative views of this game center around a couple things:
1. This is not a platformer nor a brawler. If you go into this game thinking it will be like its fully 3D Arkham bretheren, you will be greatly disappointed. However, if you go into this game knowing and expecting it to be more like a classic Metroid game, then you will be okay. Blackgate was clearly meant to be more about Batman as a detective and a puzzle solver than about Batman the asskicker.
2. The controls could be better. But again, I think this is more about expectations. If you think it's going to be a precise brawler like its bigger brothers, you'll hate it. It's meant to be a slower-paced, puzzle-solving and exploration game truly in the same vein as something like Metroid (minus the shooting). I was put off at first, but once I got used to the pacing I started to enjoy the game a lot (Metroid/Zelda-style games are my personal favorite).
There are other minor quibbles, such as it having a confusing map, and less-than-stellar combat, but overall it is a good game. If you like Batman and/or Metroid, you'll likely enjoy this game. Don't buy it if you want a platformer or brawler.

One of my favourite games from this year. Rogue-like randomly generated platformer. Brutally difficult, but fair. You learn through your deaths, and you WILL die a lot, and you will have to restart a lot, as death is permanent. But you will learn. And you will get better.
Three main modes - Adventure, Daily Challenge, and Death Match. Adventure is the main mode you will be playing, usually alone, though you can play up to 4 player local co-op. In adventure the goal is to grab as much loot (gold, gems, etc) and make it to the end of each level without dying (often mundanely to a basic enemy or killing yourself by accidentally throwing a rock into a wall and having it rebound and kill you Q_Q). There're leaderboards to compare you with your friends and with the rest of the world, so you can see who you're better than and who's better than you.
Daily Challenge is similar to adventure, but everybody plays the same randomly-generated adventure. You only get once chance, and if you die, you're done, no trying again until the next day. The daily also has a leaderboard and is a good way to challenge yourself once you're good at the game.
Deathmatch is just that, a multiplayer deathmatch with your friends. It can only be played locally, but it's a ton of fun.
If you're looking for a platformer which'll keep you challenged for hours and hours, and provide near endless replayability, this is the game for you. I strongly, strongly recommend it.

In a nutshell:
A very good game, which combines From the Depths, Terratech, Minecraft, No Man's Sky, Space Engineers, X the space simulator in a multiplayer environment, dedicated servers available to Windows and Linux.
This in-development game makes an enjoyable, complicated experience derived from it's simple mechanics.

As it is tested by us, here are the steps and info I've hunted together for a stable gameplay:
The mechanics will repair, altough slowly your unbroken parts - patience or money. :D
Mine 5000 iron and 1000 titanium or try, before building the first ship. Make battery, generator and integrity field from titanium.
You will need a lot of energy for engines, jumpdrive, turrets, and upgrade modules!
Mine more iron and you can sell that for credits.
Get a lot of crew, some functions can be overpopulated for bonuses.
You can set them to autopay salaries, and autoassign.
Do not fear!
On death, your turrets, upgrades, money, and building materials are kept, and you get a new mining drone at a friendly place nearby.
Your ship will be lost, it's cost will be refunded, if you've got insurance.
Turrets and upgrades in the destroyed ship also will. be lost.
Your wreckage may remain there.
Join in combat on your preferred side, after winning, clean up the rare parts of the wreckage with salvage cannons.
Yes, the little mouse icon above some weapon groups can be right clicked.
Bigger blocks have more HP, and other bonuses may apply.
Intergrity field causes blocks in range seemingly have ten times their HP considering is it breaking off. The leftover damage applies to all blocks, and to your overall HP.
The bigger is your ship, the more turret(civilian/military) and upgrade slots it will have.
Examine the builder interface with scrunity - there is 3 axis mirror mode, it's just in a dropdown list. ;)
You can exit and enter your ship by pressing T, if nothing/ship is selected.
This way you can build more ships, stations and mines on claimed big asteroids (with crew, and captain), telling them what to do.
If you are experiencing freezes, consider starting a dedicated server (just for singleplay, too).

I really, really want to like this game. The core puzzle gameplay is solid. The game itself, though, is riddled with small annoyances and dull spots that make me want to quit playing.
The puzzle element of the game is to select adjacent blocks such that a pattern is formed. This can be an addition or multiplication pattern or just the same number. This is a solid idea. There are also special blocks that change between turns, which help change up things. This part of the game is fun.
The way it presents the puzzle is faulty. All the number blocks look the same at a glance, without slight colorations or details besides the numbers themselves to distinguish themselves easily. This makes determining what numbers are what much more difficult to do quickly. I think it would have been better if the numbers themselves were dice dots instead, since the game is about pattern finding.
When you select blocks for your pattern, it doesn't show the path, which makes back-tracking harder to do.
Additionally, there are ice blocks and fire blocks that have an effect after a certain number of turns but no indication how close it is to that turn. The only way to know is to memorize which is annoying when blocks move naturally and impossible after doing the scramble action.
The sound effect that plays when you make a successful pattern sounds terribly out of tune and is not pleasant to listen too. This is a problem because you are going to make a lot of patterns one after the other, and at times in quick succession which will cause the sound effect to overlap producing a worse sound. The sound doesn't have weight to it either. Other games have blocks that crash or pop or something else that feels satisfying.
There are three modes: classic, endless, and puzzle. Classic is timed rounds that use preselected numbers on blocks and types of blocks. This is quite solid. Only frustration is reading every number quickly (as said above), which becomes a chokepoint when racing the clock. Endless mode is the same mechanics slowly being rolled out, but there is no way to actually lose except for your own boredom. Puzzle mode would be enjoyable if you could skip ahead to the more difficult puzzles. (Personally) I found the first puzzles trivial and tedious to do.
Overall, I wish the development of this game was higher quality. If you can overlook the faults, try it. Otherwise, avoid being annoyed by this game.

There are three modes: classic, endless, and puzzle. It's fun in short bursts as a way to zone out and kill a bit of time. Numba Deluxe is a casual puzzle game in which you highlight groups of number by type (eg. 1 1 1 1), order (1 2 3 4), addition (1 3 5 7) or multiplication (1 2 4 8), causing them to disappear and numbers from above to fall. There are three modes: Classic, Timeless, and Puzzle. I bought this for the puzzle mode, in which I've spent about 95% of my playing time, so that's what I'm reviewing.
This is very much a game of what you see is what you get: watch the video on the store page and you'll know whether this is your type of game or not. That might be kind of lazy of me to say in a review, but it's true ;)  Visuals are clean but unspectacular, music is cheery but non-descript--there are no bells and whistles here. The same background is used throughout all the menus/games, the same sound effect is used every.single.time. you clear blocks (and you will hear it a LOT).
That said, is the gameplay itself solid? I would say so. The puzzles, in which you must clear all the blocks from the level, are generally on the easy side so far (I'm at level 60-something out of 84, in about 1.5 hours), but once in a while there's some curveballs thrown your way via different block types to keep it varied. (eg. a fire block needs to fall on an ice block to melt it).
However, so far it's a good thing that levels are easy, because the puzzles appear sequentially, and there's no way to skip to a different puzzle without solving the one you're on.  The scoring system seems rather pointless as well, as every time you restart the game you begin at 0, and there's no score recorded for individual puzzles, so the highscore table is really just a matter of how long you played rather than how well/fast you solved the puzzles (there's also no timer, btw).
On a technical note, there are no resolution options.
I realize I'm sounding rather negative, but that's only because I'm mentioning things that are small annoyances.  The positives are all in the video: it's a simple, straightforward game that can be easily picked up and sometimes makes you put on your thinking cap. I have no regrets about my $3.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a game.
It is a game about trading, where you buy products for cheap where they are in bulk, then sell them for high prices where there are few of them.
It is a game about politics, where you ask lords if they need tasks done, and you earn favour by doing them.
It is a medieval tournament simulator, where you bet on yourself to win in a ~7 stage tournament.
It is a medieval peasant/knight/slave/baron simulator (pw) where you mine/chop wood/fight enemies/help knights/lord over groups of people.
It is a napoleonic-era fighting game with an active community where you fight with muskets and swords against real people/bots.
It is an archer simulator, where you snipe enemies off from a distance.
Finally, it is a open world medival mercenary/lord/baron/king simulator where you command troops from a size of 1-500, recruiting peasants, training them into warriors, knights and archers who help you conquer castles, villages and towns as you try to either reunite the land under: an existing faction, a claimant to a thone or your own banner.

Doesn't sound like the game for you? Stay away. Still interested, and read on...
Blackgate is definitely a game with a lot of problems, but if you can get past them, you'll still enjoy the game:
*Incredibly easy to get lost and the map is of very little help until you have played through enough to just about have the area memorized anyway. Prepare to spend vast swaths of time trying to figure out how to get back into "that one place you feel like you just came from."
*Really annoying method of discovering secrets, by stopping, and physically scanning every nook and cranny of the room. Really breaks up the pacing of the game, and you don't feel like you were outsmarted when you miss a secret. You just feel like you were too impatient to spend the extra time scanning that remote area.
*Voice acting is pretty sub-par. The same voice actors are back (except Black Mask for some reason) from Arkham Origins, but it's clear that something was different about the directing in this one. It just doesn't sound real. Everything is forced.
*High Definition "Delux Edition" makes it obvious that most character mouths and faces aren't actually animated.
*Story is not all that interesting, and only the final cutscenes of the game really add anything of value to the Arkhamverse.
*Combat feels less refined than the regular Arkham games. Very easy to miss an attack that past experience tells you ought to hit.
Pros:
*The animated cutscenes are kind of cool, even if they couldn't afford to do a full-on cartoon animation.
*Collecting Batsuits is fun. Who doesn't like to play dress-up?
*Picking up a new gadget is extra-rewarding because it means you're able to get into new areas.
*Achievements incentivise repeat playthroughs.
*Graphically it's not that bad considering it was originally a handheld game.
*It's the Goddamn Batman.

A mostly good game with some serious issues.
For the most part, this is a fun take on the Arkham games. You feel like Batman, and the combat has a similar free-flowing mechanic from the "big" games (although it IS different). The gadgets also all work as they should.
However, this game suffers from not knowing if it wants to be 2D, or 3D. Let me explain. The game is a 2D sidescroller: you move on a certain path, and always go left to right. But here they got creative, and added multiple routes that can make you change direction, for example by entering a vent. And this leads to very confused navigation.
The in-game map is nearly useless. Because Batman changes direction automatically while moving, you need to constantly check on the map where you are now headed, and since it is drawn on an angle to begin with, with overlapping segments, you WILL get lost.
I also got stuck multiple times. There are moments where the plot forces you go go to a certain area which ends in a blocked door, because you do not have the proper gadget yet, and it expects you to find the one spot in several screens that can be bombed to create an opening.
Remember how in e.g. Zelda any wall that can be bombed is marked with cracks? Not in this game. You must enter inspection mode, and literally sweep the entire screen of multiple rooms in the hope of finding the one spot which is "structurally weak", so you can progress.
The story is weak. You have three opponents, one opponent-slash-ally, and then they suddenly throw in Solomon Grundy... for a single fight, with no build-up whatsoever. The only reason Grundy seems to be thrown in is to emulate the Killer Croc fight from the first Arkham game.
I like the graphics, at their best they look very much like the big games. But the cutscenes are done in a highly distorted comic style, which really don't fit the look of the rest of the game. They would have been a lot better if they had been done in-engine, there are a number of "cinematic" scenes that are done this way and those look pretty amazing.
And while the voice acting is top notch, there is no lip sync whatsover: characters either "talk" in the cutscenes, which are little more than moving comic panels, or in-game, where their mouths never move.
Pick this up if you like Arkham Origins and want more, but skip it if you're not a huge fan of the game series. If this were a numeric review, I'd give it a 6//10.

I finished up Arkham Origins and lucked into a really cheap copy of AO: Blackgate at roughly the same time. Blackgate is a 2.5D side-scrolling beat-'em-up with a few puzzles thrown in. The story is told through motion-comic-style cutscenes with full voice-acting and it revolves around riots that take place at Blackgate sometime apparently not long after the events of Origins. Black Mask, Penguin, and Joker have all taken control of a section of the prison and Batman has to go in and rescue hostages and take down the bad guys in his inimitable Batman way.
Sadly, the gameplay itself is sorely lacking. Armature Studios made an effort to translate the Arkham series' signature free-flow combat to a 2.5D game but it doesn't quite work. As you see from the image below, the game is fond of tossing upwards of 5-8 opponents at Batman simultaneously; this level of opposition is non-problematic in the regular Arkham games because Batman is free to move around at will and target any of his opponents at any time. Here, the Darkknight Detective's movements are restricted to left and right and the game determines his target based on which enemy happens to be closest and in the direction he's currently facing. This makes tactically targeting specific enemies needlessly difficult, especially when facing knife- or stun-baton-wielding foes, which require certain actions to eliminate. In small groups the regular villains aren't too difficult to handle, but when the game presents you with multiple groups of antagonists at once, things can get hairy.
However, the boss fights are the epitome of everything that you hate about the concept of "boss fight" in a game. Some of them, like Black Mask and Bronze Tiger, are pretty straightforward, but the Penguin, Joker, and Catwoman battles get progressively more irritating as you fight through multiple stages that require very specific attack strategies to defeat. I actually quit the game before finishing the Catwoman fight because for some absurd reason the counters don't work the same way in this conflict as they do in the rest of the game; the second and third stages of this fight require you to counter her attacks before you can go on the offensive, and because the controls for countering appear to be virtually unresponsive in this fight, I gave up after 9-10 attempts. Maybe if you're more dexterous than me, you'll have better luck.
The other aspects of the game are merely okay. The game includes a detective mode, like its big brothers, so Batman can scan the environment for ways to get around and collectibles. There are suit pieces that can be collected and different Batsuits can confer bonuses. For example, the "Beware the Batman" suit that you get by having an Arkham Origins save on your computer provides a 50% armor bonus against gunfire. A Blackest Night suit (grants invulnerability to most forms of damage) is available by collecting the pieces in-game (you'll have to get about 95% of the way through the game to get all of the pieces so it's not game-breaking) and another (Zero Year) that you get from having a WBID login. You can only collect one of the other suits per playthrough, depending on the order in which you defeat the game's bosses. There are also detective cases to solve, which essentially involves going everywhere it's possible to go and scanning all areas with your Detective Vision until you find all of the clues associated with a specific case (these just basically provide a minimal amount of additional insight into the villains' activities just before or during the events of the game). You'll spend a lot of time doing Armature's version of the crypto-sequencer, which means matching a sequence of three numbers until you get the correct combination to unlock a door or device.
You won't be able to get every collectible in each area the first time you go through it because, as in the other Arkham games, some require you to have access to gadgets that you have to acquire as you progress through the story. That's not so unusual, but navigating through the different areas of the prison using the in-game map is quite a chore because it often appears that you can head in a particular direction, only to come across a dead end or switchback and the maps are really just cleverly-constructed labyrinths. At least a few hours of my playtime I can probably chalk up to wandering around the cell blocks and industrial areas, trying to reach an exit or some other specific landmark that was gratuitously problematic to locate.
Everything looks good here and the voice-acting is first-rate, so there are no issues on the presentation side, but in the final analysis, this game is remarkably inferior to its full-fledged, 3D brethren. The action is mediocre, the puzzles aren't really puzzles at all, the boss fights are infuriating, and the story is really the only interesting thing about it. I spent about 19 hours playing but if you're the kind of OCD person who needs to get every achievement, you'll have to play three times so you could easily get the same amount of mileage out of this as you did from Arkham Origins. By then you'll probably wish you'd never heard of Batman, let alone this particular game.

If you can't get enough of Batman even after having been disappointed by the "big" Origins game, you still might want to consider Blackgate.
Despite its handheld origin this is a good looking game that offers something different. The Metroid-inspired 2D gameplay lends itself great to the Dark Knight. Although the combat suffers a bit from the lost 3rd dimension and doesn't feel quite as accurate and responsive anymore.
The full potential might not be reached, but this roughly 10 hour trip to Blackgate prison (much longer if you plan to collect everything) is still worth taking. Especially if you are a fan of the ever so popular Metroidvania-style. Or simply to get a more complete picture of the whole Arkham story arc.

I don't regret getting this, but I can't rightly recommend it to anyone. It's basically the same formula as Arkham Asylum/City/Origins, but stuffed in a 2.5D game. Where Origins was still good fun even though it felt a bit like the B team had a go at making a Batman game, this game felt like it had the C team work on it.
The combat is unsatisfying due to the difficulty in targeting a specific enemy when 3 are lined up along the same height on the screen, which is especially annoying for enemies you need to stun or vault over. It's also hard to keep combos going, since the limited sight range might have you guessing if an offscreen enemy is up yet to recieve a beatdown, or you'll just whiff in place.
The map is the most confusing mess I've seen for a game map yet; it's an angled top-down view which is blown up in places and connected with dotted lines. Sometimes areas overlap by being above or behind each other, and it's really not clear what's going on on the map.
Detective vision has had a downgrade, and now requires dragging a large cursor over the screen to find interesting things, and then waiting for them to scan. Batman can't move while this goes on. It gets very boring after a few screens.
There's an explosive gel launcher, which is a better version of the explosive gel spray. In everything else, it's an extremely stripped down version of any of the Arkham games. The story isn't interesting, the cutscenes are (almost) motionless drawings, and the graphics are worse than Arkham Asylum. Visually recognizable pieces of the world that need a specific gadget to interact with need to be scanned first, no matter how many times you've opened/wrecked exactly the same thing. Bosses frequently introduce new game mechanics that aren't explained. The 2.5D movement makes the whole game feel very constrained, and especially the stealth gameplay suffers for it.
On the plus side, it can occasionally look nice, art-direction wise, and there's plenty to explore.

If Steam had a "alright" rating then I would apply this to this game instantly. If you're expecting a 2d version of the Arkham games by Rocksteady or WB Montreal, you're going to be disappointed. The combat has been limited to punching, stunning, and evading. No takedowns or insane combo's here, the fighting is anemic compared to the other Arkham titles and isn't the core of the game. This is a major plus due to the fact that this game is a Metroidvania type of game with the cape crusader. The graphics are better than the previous portable literation but that is not saying much, some textures are muddy, or stretched out and this is especially true during fights when you see prison inmates look like they have melted Crayola marks as tattoos on their arm when the camera zooms in. Furthermore the map used to find clues is horrendous, it makes finding certain items at times hair pulling or impossible until you look online to see where it is ( EX: Crowbar that is needed for a case). On the positive the game is enjoyable if you like going around the environment collecting things , finding upgrades , Batman suits (Zombie Suit is worth the hunt!), and so forth. Stardust Vanguards is a good game. For the price presented it is beyond a value purchase, it’s clear a lot of blood, sweat, and tears went into the making of this game. For what I bought the game at (around 70 cents) it’s near robbery. Buy this game.
Now with that out of the way I will go into so pros and cons along with some constructive criticism.
Pros:
The stylization of the game is downright phenomenal. The visuals work together perfectly and what you need to see is clearly displayed on the screen. It also has great and stylized UI elements such as the bounty element that appears above players when they’ve been doing well. Besides being functional, the sprites perfectly mimic the Gundam esc space opera shows, with big mechs, huge fleets, and all kinds of lasers!
To add to the visual aspect, the game has a great soundtrack and equally great effects. The soundtrack is lots of fun to listen to. It captures the overly dramatic space opera feel. The voice overs and sound effects work just as well. Making you feel like you’ve just taken control of your own mech, complete with plucky young pilots or snotty imperial soldiers!
The gameplay is solid. It is fun to fly around in your mech, shoot at the enemy ships, and duel other players. The controls on keyboard leave something to be desired, but they work well enough that they don’t hinder the game. The controls on the remote are ideal and work perfectly in that case.
The ability to summon ships is a great idea as it adds lot of entertaining chaos to the scene, not only this but because enemy AI give you points to summon ships it keeps the battle in a constant back and forth, making sure there is not a single moment where you can just hoard points in a corner.
Cons:
Despite all these good things Stardust Vanguards lacks two major things that hold it back from being a legendary game that everyone should own, variety and online multiplayer. Remember the game is already pretty complete as it is, these feature would just make the game one for the record books.
In Stardust Vanguards what you see is what you get, with the only unlockables being maps and a few game modes. Even with a good amount of map variety, there is still little to explore when it comes to mechanics. No customization, no leveling up, no different loadouts. Everyone gets the same mech with a different color and the same fleet with different colors. Even something simple like being able to create a custom pilot profile that tracks your stats would have gone a long way to helping this game with that problem.  Being able to choose different fighting styles (maybe a mech that has no bullets but summons more ships) would have sealed the deal.
The different game modes are refreshing and the space ball one is a lot of fun, but with so few options to shake up your playstyle there needs to be more modes to make up for that. The modes they have are good but not enough.
Now onto multiplayer. As the game stands, it only has couch multiplayer, with no option to connect online with other players, even through LAN. The developers have commented on this saying that it is beyond the scope of what they can achieve while still maintaining their desired game experience and vision for what the game should be (
)  This is completely understandable and I’m glad they are uncompromising when it comes to gameplay experience, but no multiplayer is still a disappointment, as being able to play with people online would increase the games overall value tremendously. Multiplayer becomes doubly necessary when you consider the very few single player options given. If the game had a short single player campaign or more interesting single player game modes, the lack of connectivity could be easily overlooked, but as it stands the game does not and it suffers for it.
Conclusion:
Despite the things it lacks, I recommend this game whole heartedly. It is good fun for the price, and goes on dirt cheap sales frequently, and has more content and polish than a good portion of games at the same price. If you want a cheap, fun, but well-made couch game to play with your friends this is it.

I played this game when it first came out, tried the show, didn't get hooked on either.
I returned to it a few months ago, and it felt much better than I had remembered it. It just feels like a hugely refreshing departure from other MMOs I've played (LOTRO, STO, WOW, Guild Wars 2, DCUO, TSW, SWTOR).  Here's where it stands apart:
1. Real player agency, in terms of skill, vs. the rule-based mechanics of most MMOs.  You can always get slightly better with your aiming and tactics, as in any FPS, and the game rewards you for it.  It just feels better waiting for you to reload while running for cover than waiting for your skills to refresh while you stand there.
2. One of the better told stories in an MMO.  The writing, staging, and VO work of the character interactions make storytelling in LOTRO, STO and GW2 look like puppet shows.  The only MMO that holds a candle to it is TSW.  I might say SWTOR too if their stories weren't so badly written and full of cookie-cutter animations.
3. Generous business model.  The only money I've had to put into this is for inventory.  I've never felt like I was being held back in terms of capabilties, as long as I took time to understand the upgrade systems.  Sure, there are a few things you'll miss out on, but none of it is gameplay content, and none of it is required to enjoy the game.
4. Best vehicles ever.  Seriously, after playing this, it's SO hard to go back to LOTRO's horses, SWTOR's pokey "speeders", or anything else.  Defiance is so confident in giving the players speed, it feels like they solved some technical problem that no other MMO has figured out.
The only downside I can think of is that after 2 hours or so in any given session, the sameness of gameplay and enemies creeps in. It's true what they say.  But I quit and come back in a day or two, and I'm having a blast all over again.

This game reminds me of when I was in grade school.
When I was in 3rd-4th grade I made all A's in my classes. The classes weren't that hard and everyone thought that I was this super smart genius child. As I got older, my grades began to drop as the classes got harder.
"What's wrong with you?"
"You're so smart! You should be doing so much better than this!"
I had built up a reputation of being so smart that when I got to something that challenged me, everyone assumed that I wasnt trying to do well.
I feel that Defiance suffers from a similar problem.
There's your tldr
Defiance suffers from the same problem that other Trion Worlds games suffers from. Much like ArcheAge, another F2P MMO released by Trion, I really, really like this game, but i just can't bring myself to say that this is a game that everyone should play. Obviously, I have some serious love/hate issues with Defiance. To better illustrate this, let me point out some pros and cons.
+Excellent gunplay - I seriously feel that the gunplay in Defiance is one of the most solid gunplay     experiences I've played with in other MMO shooter games. Obviously this is an open world game, so dont compare this to COD, but considering all the effort that was put elsewhere, The combat in Defiance is an excellent experience.
+BALANCE - I feel that creating a balanced game in an MMO setting is arguably one of the hardest things a developer can do, and as with the aformentioned ArcheAge, no matter what happens, there will always be one specific class that can outperform the other classes (ie. Archers in ArcheAge). However, what Defiance did, and i feel that more devs should do this, was that all abilities are available to be unlocked, regardless of any specifications put into your character. This is through the EGO system (basically exp). As your EGO rises, you can purchase new perks and abilities, and eventually unlock all abilities available to everyone, however you can only use 1 ability at a time.
+Great Storytelling - For those of you who maybe didnt play Defiance when it first launched, Defiance was actually a tie-in to a televison show on SyFy by the same name. The concept was pretty cool (in my opinion at least). As events unfolded in the show, events in the game would occur, and vice versa. so obviously, the writers of Defiance (the show) wanted to deliver an experience that would be engaging to the players of Defiance (the game). As such, the entire story of Defiance (the game) was developed in close conjunction with the writers of the show, and well, they arent professional writers if they were bad. Also, the show that the game originally launched with has since stopped airing, or has gone so far under the radar that I can no longer find it on any current tv network and I think that's kinda funny.
-Pay-to-Play(?) - So I actually bought Defiance when there was still a $10 price tag on it and honestly
I kinda regret doing that. Since I did that the game has gone F2P and has seen a resurgence in player activity, BUT Trion still needs to generate revenue somehow. Trion has released several DLC packs for Defiance as tie-ins for events that happened in the aforementioned televison show, such as the Castithan Charge pack which allows players to play as the Castithan race. Normally this wouldn't really be a problem if it weren't for the Gunslinger Trials and the 7th Legion packs. This problem does extend to the other packs, but I think that the Gunslinger trials and 7th legions packs are the worst. The problem is that, like in other MMO's you can recieve weapon loot from fallen enemies, BUT you can also recieve weapons from the DLC packs. However, YOU CANNOT USE THESE WEAPONS UNLESS YOU PAY FOR THEM. This is a huge problem if you love a great loot system like I do, because you can hoard all these weapons that are considerably better than the weapons you currently have, but if you dont pay actual real-world money, you cant use these weapons. I've seriously wanted to buy the packs just to get access to those weapons, but I refuse to spend more money on an F2P game to get access to weapons that I can get in the base game
-Lack of direction - IDK if this is the right way to phrase this, but despite all the effort put into the story, I dont really care about it. I like to play a game that challenges me, and the best way i usually think of to find a challenge is to move on to the next area with tougher enemies. Apparently you shouldnt do this, because it can ruin some of the story, but like I said, I appreciate the extensive work put into the story, but I just dont find it super interesting.
So, to summarize the points that I made, I really do think that Defiance is a fun game, but it suffers from a problem that Trion has had yet to fix in this game or in many of their other games.
However, this game is F2P now, so take my advise with a grain of salt.
Play this game
Form your own opinion
If you really like it, give in to Trion's iron grip on your wallet and buy the Season Pass for some extra fun.
Overall I'd give this game a 6/10
I really want to like this game, but there's just so much in the way of this game being great.

This game is not what it seems to be.
From looking at the screenshots, it would seem to be a good looking train sim, that provides an authentic train driving experience, using highly detailed models of real locations and real trains.
Unfortunately, and as much as I wanted to enjoy this game, I have found it to be a great dissapointment.
First of all, the game engine is a mess.  Sure, the graphics look good when you turn everything up, but even if your computer was built by NASA you won't be able to, because it will kill your FPS.
So, turning the graphics down to acheive a reasonable FPS means that there are artifacts and graphical glitches... shadows that continuously "catch up" a few feet in front of your train for example.
However, even when using minimal graphics setup, the game is FULL of bugs, glitches and other problems that make it extremely frustrating to use.
But it's worth pressing on because of the authentic "feel" of the trains, right? WRONG. The trains in this sim are trains that I have been on thousands of times, when commuting from Brighton to London, for example. This sim fails to model the sounds and operating methods of these trains.
For a game that is supposed to allow you to control trains, there is an astonishing amount of difficulty in setting up your controls. They have gone out of their way to make this game frustrating to use and difficult to control.
Also, forget about gameplay. This sim is strictly about driving your train, with many scenarios requiring you to perform tedious "shunting" tasks to assemble your train, a task made even more tedious by the games lack of user friendly options. The various scenarios are almost ALL BROKEN and have not been fixed by the publisher.
The publisher of this game charges a fortune for all the DLC, and it's broken, they don't fix things after it's released.
Instead, they rely on the "community" to add more workshop content for the game, which is completely ridiculous, like something a child would think of.
So, I am not recommending this game, unless you are looking for false promises and an un- authentic train sim.

When this game first came out I had high hopes for it. Over the years of playing it, the game has devolved. I have played the German side from the beginning. Reto, the game devs, have made the game very unbalanced. German weaponry has gradually gotten worse and worse. To the point that the revolutionary weapon known as the Sturmgewehr (STG 44) is nothing more than an anti aircraft gun after firing 3 bullets or more. It has more kickback than a BAR. The smoke that comes out of it is immediately blinding as if the Germans only used black gunpowder. It's like throwing a smoke grenade, within 3 bullets you can't see anything. It doesn't matter because the gun is pointing at the sky after the first 3 rounds anyway. Meanwhile all allied weaponry is extremely easy to use, have very little smoke and very little kickback no matter what gun you use. One of the most ridiculous things about the game is that the allies run around with panzerfausts as if they manufactured them. The Russians have the PTRD and it will one shot any infantry, does NOT need to be fired from the prone position and will rip to shreds any and all light tanks. One of the "features" of this game is that you can name your guns. One of the most over powered guns of the alllies is the M1/M2. Rate of fire, ease of use, accuracy, little smoke, you name it, it has it. Common names that people I've seen with this gun are "yes, I know it's OP" and "don't you wish your stg44 could be like this" Sick of the game after many years of play. Recommend it to no one unless you like being on the unbalanced allied side and enjoy and unfair advantage.

The game is extremely fun. Destroying anything you want is always a good time. The weapons are great and the game has a very distinct design to it.
Only real problem is the main campaign. The first 2 acts are really good, some missions are better than others, but it's great. Very enjoyable. However I recently completed the game fully and I realized how quickly the game falls apart by the third act. A new chapter kind of opens up where the main characters decide to ally with another faction and it seems like the game could really use this for more missions and story telling. But there's honestly about 3 more missions and about 2 cutscenes from the introduction of this new chapter to the end of the game.
I was really disappointed. The game makes such a big deal about this giant machine coming to kill eveyrone and the fact you're siding with another faction but the game just kind of wraps up when the conflict is at its peak. It almost felt rushed. I was really caught off guard with how quickly everything came to an end when the game and characters kept reminding me how big of a deal it is that we join forces to stop this huge giant spaceship that could kill everyone on Mars for the entire third act. I won't spoil it but you'll see what I mean when the final battle takes place.
Despite all the issues I had with the end of the campaign it's still a solid game. There's plenty to do besides the campaign and most if not all of it involves blowing stuff up and it's highly addicting. The destruction physics are great and as I said before the weapons you use are both creative and really fun to use. Although it's a shame they only give you 4 slots for every weapon in the game because I found myself literally never using some of the weapons I bought for the entire game because other weapons took priority over them. Which is a shame.
Either way, this game is very good. The positives definitely outweigh the negatives and there's plenty to do if you get bored. Solid.

The only noteworthy thing that RF:G has going for it, and that you should have any interest in, is its destruction system. As fun as it is (even today), it does not make this game worth "full price" ($20US), nor does it make it worth playing all the way through. To be honest, once you've got your hands on the tricked out rocket launcher and have had a few spins wreaking havoc in a mech, you've really seen all there is to this game.
The missions are dime a dozen, being repeatedly copied and pasted throughout with next to no exciting set pieces or unique concepts to make them memorable or give them substantial variety. The gameworld is very uninteresting and is a visually monotonous blur of red, grey and brown; seriously lacking flair in its landscape or manmade structures. The story is an absolute eye-roller, it is so unpleasantly familiar; far too cliche and predictable for it to be worth your time seeing it through. I will give credit where it's due for the very decent soundtrack and decent weapon line-up, but as a sum of its parts the game is highly mediocre. Destruction is not enough to make the rest of the game somehow magically good.

Torchlight 2 is an amazing sequel to the first and a true dungeon loot crawler that easily rivals if not succeeds in many areas of it's highest competitors like Blizzards Diablo 3.
Gameplay carries many of the standardizations one comes to expect in their dungeon crawlers, so there won't be many surprises in terms of controls, UI, etc. The addition of a pet companion is one of the most stand-out additions, and you'll learn to love that little "thing" (whatever you choose) quickly, if only for the Send-Home ability to sell off your crap loot.
In terms of a sequel, the open environments are a positive addition to just the downward mine from the first. You'll get a clear sense or progression and variation in your environmental visuals and enemies. The basic formula hasn't been altered severely but certainly feels refined, especially when it comes to your inventory. Sorting is now done with ease!
There is easily 10's of hours worth of gameplay to be done and with some extra additions as the end, that replayability further increases. My only major complaint with the game is there has/seeming will be no expansions, DLC or anything Developer generated to continue onwards. This means once you've beaten the main game you're pretty well done with it, which is more saddening than anything.
Nevertheless, this is a game you shouldn't miss if you like a good ol' click spam fun time in a dugneon with lots of unque, very well presented, pieces of loot.

If you are looking for a game that mimics Diablo and Diablo II. I would recommend this. Hours of fun exploring, character building, and the game is moddable!
Much like the original Diablo, the dungeons are randomly generated, as is most of the weapons and armor, so there is plenty of replay value.
Unlike the original Diablo, you cannot restart your game from the beginning with everything your character is holding at any point during your questing. You can only restart your game with everything after completing the final quest (New Game+)
You can trade items between characters utilizing the Shared Stash Box. If you find an Item that isn't for your current character, but would be perfect for another character, you can put it in the Shared Stash Box and your other character can retrieve it.
Diablo 3? Who? A very deep game that will give you hours of fun with lots of quests and bosses. Totally recomended.
