Spark is a horizontal side scrolling bullet-hell shoot’em up game, unlike others in the genre where you have one single weapon, upgrades or weapon pickups, Spark brings a unique concept of giving you four different coloured shots, they each have different movement speeds and damage as well as heat.
When the different coloured shots collide they explode into patterns that spread out in various patterns and can also leave weaker bullets behind that can be hit too resulting in longer chains being created, as such you can turn two simple straight forward shots into a triple shot.
You can also do Super-Combos which generate static mine-like bullets in specific layouts based on the combo used, when these are triggered they set off a certain chain of sparks that are more advanced than causing two kinetic bullets to touch as they result in a larger area or coverage and provides you with more angles of attack this means, so instead of being able to only shoot forwards you can have reactions that send a number of bullets behind you.
Chains and super-combos must be used tactically as shots generate heat, this limits how much you can fire within an amount of time. Attacking too much causes you to become exhausted and requires you to wait for a full cool down before you can attack again thus putting you at risk from being overrun. The higher the tier of bullet used the more sparks and damage you can do but can quickly overheat.
You will be rewarded more for focusing on combos by having your score multiplier increased; keeping combos active results in you gaining more points. Being hit resets your multiplier.
There are three game modes and using them effectively and avoiding being hit will put you higher on the leader boards.
The first mode is Conquest, where you will be fighting against a long waves of attacks and bosses. You must make it all the way through with your starting lives as death results in starting from the beginning.
The second mode is Survival, In which you fight against an endless stream of enemies, you can also pick up active abilities to help you for a limited amount of time.
The third mode is puzzles, you will need to destroy fixed targets using the different sparks to navigate around walls and objects as you’re unable to move forwards. Here you start with 60 seconds and you gain 10 seconds for completing each puzzle of which there are 20 of.
All three modes have an arcade feel to it due to you needing to start from the beginning if you die or run out of time and leaving you fight for the online high-scores.
Recomended for anyone that loves shoot'em ups and a good arcade style challange.
The developers have been very active with the community, listening to all feedback fixing bugs and making changes to the game. A demo of the game is available,

Batman Arkham Origins Blackgate is an interesting Batman game. It does things a bit different than the newer Batman games. If I had to make a comparison Arkham Asylum would be closest as far as the gameplay is concerned, because this one also plays like a Metroidvania game, except that you play it on a 2.5D pane this time. So the camera will shift to other angles depending on your location. And because of this the controls aren't as tight as they could be. Remember the older Resident Evil games with their stiff movements ? Sometimes you have to move a certain way but have no clue how to move your analog stick; the game doesn't recognize the obvious, natural move you'd normally make and therefore you unintentionally go back and forth sometimes. Infuriating and frustrating.
Another thing that also bothered me, in this day and age, was the lack of lip syncing. I can't think of many other games that don't have this feature nowadays. I know it's supposed to be some sort of budget Batman game, but come on, they could've easily used the models from the other games and downgraded them. Sloppy.
The game itself is, praise the Lord, pretty good. It works like any other Metroidvania game. I've told you a dozen times about what a Metroidvania game is all about so I hope you remembered it or else look it up somewhere.
The 'detective mode' is a feature that was pretty cool, because you have to scan the environments for clues. Find enough of these clues and you'll solve the case. These clues aren't shown on your map so you have to basically scan everything you see. It would've been nice if you could scan on the move instead of having to stand still but that's just me nitpicking I guess.
The boss fights are also nice; some of them are easy, other ones are a bit more difficult.
Because the game uses several maps instead of one big map like many other Metroidvania games navigation is sometimes hard. Near the end of the game you have to move between all 4 maps regularly and one mission in particular makes you backtrack through several of these environments. The downside is that you can't easily teleport. It wouldn't fit the game, I agree, but surely they could've come up with something. You can only leave a map at the beginning and at the end, and there's no way in between. The map is hard to read so you'll probably get lost every now and then. The fact that you can move into several directions doesn't help either. Unnecessary if you ask me.
The game is lengthy, and will take you about 7-12 hours, depending on what you what to collect. That's just right for a game like this.
The graphics haven't been upgraded because the characters still have blurry textures. But it still looks nice in motion. Just don't expect the graphics from the previous Batman games.
Batman Arkham Origins Blackgate is a fun game, but unfortunately not without its flaws. And despite these flaws it definitely deserves a chance.

Not going to discuss DLC. If you want it, get it. The game should only be judged for what it is, and likewise with the DLC. I am also not going to comment on the multiplayer aspect, just because I haven't tried it and don't really want to. It looks like there are always a few games going strong, but overall it is not very busy.
+ Game length is pretty good, and open missions bring some replayability.
+ Purist sniping is rewarding and not overly complicated. Likewise, if you want aim-assist, you still feel badass
+ Looks pretty good aside from zoom blurring
+ AI, sniping realism, and UI assistance options are independently customizable. Although there are only three settings for each, nothing in-depth
+ Stealth system is good and works fine for what it is, "but"
+/- Not very realistic. Stealth, AI, and many mechanics are too video game-y. As serious as the game takes itself (super gruffy mcsniper man gotta save arfica or whoever it was), it is not a realistic stealth game, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing unless you don't like that. The sniping alone may be realistic, though. I don't know, I'm not a sniper. But it emulates it well, at least. bullet drop, wind speed, yadda yadda. actually no yadda yadda, that's it I think.
- Poor weapon variety (four sniper rifles in a sniping game?)
- I mentioned AI is too video game-y, but I think it is so in a bad way.
SE3 is a pretty good recommendation for someone who is interested in a stealth and/or sniping game that is easy to get into and easy to enjoy. It has become a little more accessible than SE2 (and like pop music compared to the first game being like black metal), but improves on the framework a LOT. My first playthrough alone is/was almost 20 hours, but the map design is pretty well done and you should be able to replay the game a couple of times and it will still feel like a different experience, especially if you practice different play styles (run and gun, booby trapped house of horror, cat and mouse, pure stealth, etc). I think there are like 8 missions in all? 8 to 10.
There is nothing fancy about the stealth. It is simple and works (mostly). No parkour, pseudo-platforming, or anything remarkable. It is sight and sound-based. You crouch, go prone, hide in grass, shadows, or behind something. Instant kill enemies from behind, shoot em with a silenced pistol, take them out with a trap, or mask your shot with environmental noise. The automatic cover system is pretty seamless and I don't think it has ever frustrated me in the least. Very well implemented. I'm kind of disappointed there is no over-cover silent kill. If a guy was leaning up against a short wall and you were behind him: nope. sorry. You can hide and scurry off, and the enemy will stay pinned down assuming you are still active in your previous location (you'll see a ghost of your character, signifying you can relocate).
The AI regularly switches between omniscient and brain-dead. I think that is very, very bad, but I enjoy the game regardless, and personally it's more comical and inexcusable. An enemy will hear you running in an underground bunker beneath them...but they won't see you kill a guy right in front of them 50 meters out. They will hear you walking on a roof above them and go investigate with weapons ready... even though one of their buddies was just walking around up there before I killed him undetected. They will hear you running a couple of blocks away...but they won't hear the guy who just got shot through the helmet grunt and slump to the ground five feet to the side of them. They won't be alerted by explosive traps that go off outside of combat unless they are very close.
Some of the other mechanics in the game bothered me at first, too, but I quickly got over it. Sound masking makes some sense, but that logic isn't applicable to every situation. I can certainly understand shooting undetected when a plane passes low overhead, but not when some piece of machinery grunts and your gun is clearly much louder and sounds completely different (Like a gun, you know what I mean?). The sound masking is in relation to YOUR position, and never the enemy's. So when a loud noise happens near them, they will still hear you shooting just fine. Oh, and the AI will never ever see nor hear your bullet hit anybody or anything, no matter how close it is and even if it is in their field of vision.
A couple bugs, but overall the game is very stable. One problem, a HUGE problem at some points, is that loading into a game will make a noise at your location. I don't know if it spawns you slightly above the ground and it's a dropping noise, or what. But it actually "broke" my mission once when I had an objective where I could NOT be detected because yaknow I was eavesdropping on something important. I saved on a platform above the conversation, and when I loaded into it again after messing something up, I alerted them with every single attempt. Not cool.
Zooming in with your rifle or binoculars will make many foreground or background areas quite blurry until you aim at them and clear them up. I thought it was intentional at first, but it really looks like annoying texture bugs to me. Unsure if there is a fix for this. Might be.
I've discussed the cons a lot (I think that is most important to get out of the way) and my comments on the AI may turn you away. But I still recommend giving this game a shot if you can get it on sale. The mechanics, despite having a logic of their own, all work together very well and make the game tense and exciting. It's fun as hell to scout a location, lay out traps, plan your encounter out, and see how it goes.

Game does not live up to the hype, the price, or the title. Should be called "Pistol Elite III", because you are going to spend most of your time with that beautifully modelled sniper rifle slung on your back, while you sneak around with a silenced pistol shooting drone AI in the back of the head from 20 feet. Alternately, you can have even less fun with the "takedown" mechanic, aka sneak up on the guy and stab him. How sneaking around head-shotting people with a pistol and stabbing guys in the back came to be the dominant mechanics in a "sniper" game is rather beyond my ability to comprehend, but there it is, for what it's worth, which is approximately nothing.
I've only played on authentic level so I don't know about all the aids, but I will say that the developers have made a decent attempt at recreating real-world ballistic physics. It is not perfect, by any means, and seems to incorporate some random elements that are difficult to explain and rather puzzling. I can see that weapon ranges, bullet drop etc have had to be scaled to fit the rather puny maps, because consoles could never handle the size of maps that would be necessary in order to accomodate realistic weapon ranges.
Yes, it's very DLC heavy. I bought it on some super sale and got the whole works relatively cheaply, and still feel ripped off. Either way, you shouldnt be paying extra to get a few decent rifles in what is trying to pass itself off as a sniper game. Smells like a money grab when content that should have shipped with the game comes out as day one DLC.
There are other oddities that make this game much less than it appears to be. I've often shot guys square in the chest with a high-powered sniper rifle, seen the blood fly, and a few seconds later, they shake it off like a wet dog and they are good to go. I'm not sure what that's all about, but you'd think getting shot in the chest would actually hurt at least a little bit, or at least knock the wind out of a guy. Also questionable are such things as knocking out a Tiger tank by shooting it in the muffler with a rifle, but whatever.
The developer appears to have abandoned this game already, probably out of embarrassment, so don't count on any tech support or answers to your emails. ( see forum post Random Crashing)

The bottom line is that this game fails absolutely in delivering the goods as far as being a sniper game. Avorion is an interesting and rather promising indie title.
The build system, while somewhat frustratingly unintuitive at times, is also by far one of the most powerful I've seen in a sandbox game. It contains your typical mirror-mode options, however you (to my knowledge) cannot adjust the position of the mirror plane. Blocks can be stretched to practically any shape/size you want, with their relevant stats and material costs being adjusted according. The slider for the snap-grid spacing allows for the easy, uniform placement of objects (such as turrets), or incredibly fine-tuned positioning (to make sure something's in
the right spot), and anything in between.
The sorting of inventory (particularly ship equipment like turrets) desperately needs more options. Given the sheer number of different turrets and upgrades I quickly accumulated, it became rather frustrating to find the right (or best) one to use, since I couldn't tell it to sort or filter them by type, quality, material, etc.
The flight model appears fall somewhere between arcade and sim. It's newtonian-based, but feels like they took shortcuts with the physics simulations. Collisions can and do react oddly/unexpectedly at times.
The graphics are fairly simplistic. The tradeoff is this means you can get a very large amount of ships on screen. The customizability of block shapes and procedural generation of ship designs means you
see a lot of variety. However, at least in my universe, the procedural algorithm seems overly fond of creating very long "stick" ships. There are supposed to be multiple "templates" for the procedural generation, and the thematic differences between ships of these different templates
noticable, but the AI seems particularly fond of what I've dubbed the "stick" designs.
Multiplayer is done directly through steam (so none of that pesky port-forwarding business was necessary). While hosting a co-op game with a friend he did report the occasional lag spike, but the issue didn't seem prevalent regardless of whether we were mining or in combat, in the same system or halfway across the galaxy from each other.
I would recommend picking up Avorion during a sale or closer to "full" release if you're a fan of the genre. There are still some planned features missing (such as boarding/capturing ships), and the balancing of various game aspects still need tweaking (Hostile alien ships have jumped in. Pirates are attacking the sector. Another faction has invaded the sector. Pirates have - Slow down! We're still killing the
three invasion fleets!)

Of course, being Early Access, the game can run into a few problems, such as crashing, slight lag spikes, graphical glitches, variety of bugs and the sort. However, the developer of this game is not only working hard on fixing these problems (and doing a great job), but is quite active with the community, taking in ideas, and working with it to improve the game. I, like many others, have been stung multiple times from Early Access games before, whether due to non-completion, or abandonment, or false advertisement, this game has already lived up to, and exceeded expectations.

On a more serious note, this is an incredible game. It will take you about 4 hours to complete, but it will be one of those impossibly memorable videogame experiences that are few and far between. The basic premise of the game is that two brothers set out on an adventure to find a cure for their father's disease, who is very ill and will not make it without it. The twist here is that you control both characters at the same time, so if you are using a controller (and you really should be), each thumbstick will control a brother. This seems weird at first, but quickly everything fits and it starts to feel very natural so if hearing about that made you anxious, do not be. The game controls perfectly well.
The more important thing here is that the adventure that these two brothers embark on is as exciting as it is perilous, and as the stakes are slowly raised it becomes more and more fascinating. The scenery in the game is a joy to look at, and the score accompanies the key moments in a very special way. The puzzles that you need to solve to progress through the story are not necessarily hard, but they make the world believable and feel like they just fit perfectly.
All in all, I cannot recommend this game enough. I enjoyed every bit of it and sincerely hope that more people get to play this game. The devs really outdid themselves with Brothers. Not much else to say other than download and play it already!!! Haha.

An extremely fun and decently challenging puzzle game with the real surprise being the story that can be told from a few characters speaking gibberish.
The simultaneous dual character control is a fun take on your standard platformer puzzle game. Most of the puzzles are intuitive and won't leave you stumped for too long. The difficulty comes down to the player's ability to coordinate two characters rather than intense problem solving.
But by far and away, the real gem of this game is the story. As all the characters speak an unintelligible language (think the Sims language), you are largely left to pick up context clues as to what they are saying to one another. While jarring at first, this is a wonderful design idea that allows the player to use his or her own imagination to fill in the gaps. The story that develops between the two brothers is still largely constructed by the narritive laid out by the game designers, but the player is left to dream up the finer details. Despite the language barrier, the universal feelings from events shine through, and by the end of the game the player has been on a rollercoaster ride of emotions, least of which are the frustrations of actual gameplay.
I would highly reccomend the purchase and playthrough of this game.

This is a gamepad-friendly third-person shooter, that takes a lot of influence from games like Borderlands. Enemies tend to be bullet-spongy in this open-world RPG. You'll have access to your own vehicle after a short while, and you can purchase more than one.
Your character's armor and weapons can be modded by buying parts with money you made from selling loot, or by stripping parts off of the weapons of fallen enemies.  Weapons vary all the way from healing tools to multi-grenade-lobbing doomsday devices.  You'll always be on the lookout for better stats.  This is the functional predecessor to games like The Division, but you will run into players everywhere, and random group instances are aplenty. You don't necessarily need to roll with anyone else. You will bump into other people, and you're on the same side, so the tendency is to help one another. You don't make dialog choices, and some quests are text-based, but the game really feels alive, despite the fact that the story NPCs kinda always just sit in the same spot.
This game has so much amazing free content, I bought a $5 hat for my character from the cash shop just to support the developers. The cash shop sells nothing but vanity items and minor boosters. The boosters will not necessarily make you better than your friends, you'll just gain a little more XP for an hour or something like that.  There is honestly so little reason to spend money, the game is so full already, I honestly don't know how their business model works. This is one of the best F2P TPS MMORPGs out there. It's free, so if you think I'm wrong, who cares? Try it!

This quest system is not made for party play. I got into a party with my friend and we would talk to the same person at the same time in the story and get different quests. We tried this with several different NPCs and not once did we get the same quest.
If you want a Borderlands ripoff with a fun start and an infuriating massive ramp in diffuculty; then this is the game for you.

If you're looking for a fun addition to the Batman franchise, I'd recommend it. If you're looking for a good platformer, hold off on it. For now.
adds a good story upon Arkham Origins' original one that will keep any Batman-fan interrested to the end. However, in terms of gameplay, it's not too good. Not for a Batman game nor a platformer.
The Good:
· An interresting story that takes place after Arkham Origins and before Arkham Asylum, set mostly in Blackgate Prison.
· Fun and different take on the Arkham storyline. With drawn comicbook-esque cinematics and 2.5D gameplay it offers an entirely different way of playing as Batman. Using Batman's gadgets in 2D is surprisingly entertaining.
· Collectibles give fans a reason to return to the game after completion, albeit very linear. That being said...
The Bad:
· ... the game plays a bit
linear for an Arkham game. The combat and platforming feel a bit too stiff and at points even forced. The series is known for, among others, its Free Flow combat system. Don't expect to see Free Flow combat here. There
combat in the game that looks a little bit like the combat in Arkham Asylum, but it plays stiff and clunky.
· Confusing and overly-guided platforming combined with reasonably frustrating stealth gameplay will definately take some getting used to (for example, Batman will switch from one platform in the foreground to another platform in the background using the Batclaw and there is no option to look around while in vents).
The Ugly:
· For a port its pretty reasonable, with smoothened egdes and overall a slightly better quality but characters will still feel stiff and the environments at times a bit repetetive or downright boring.
Final Verdict:
is a fun game to play through if you're a big Batman fan, but platformer-lovers won't really find anything new or surprisingly interresting. Are you interrested in the game for its story, or are you looking for the series' innovative gameplay? That question is one this review answers.

Train Simulator series is somewhat awesome. Despite problems, it is the best all-round rail sim I have come across. Like many simulators though it is a hodge-podge of legacy systems held together with duct tape and fencing wire. Still I love it warts and all.
This years package is a great selection of what the sim has to offer, playing to the strengths of the three geographical areas covered. Each presents it's own difficulties; American big iron dragging insanely long trains over mountains, complex difficult to master German transport tech, the finely balanced driving style required of British heritage steam. Each is different and atmospheric enough for casual play, and on full-realism presents a unique challenge which gives a great sense of achievement upon mastery.
Simulators aren't for everyone, as they don't have the moment to moment excitement of most games. But if you enjoy the mastery aspect of simulators at all you are sure to get some value out of TS2016. An interest in trains is not required, because the trains in this package are so full of character that you can grow to love them from the game alone.

This is a rage-inducing, puzzle platformer that brings on the frustration for all the wrong reasons. As the store page description will tell you about the game, you play as Squishy, a child pig who wants to reunite with his family in heaven, and needs to kill himself over and over to fulfill his deal with the devil. The concept is pretty unique and the first few levels shows this idea in full, where you must figure out how to get yourself killed in each stage...
Each stage that wants you to die, at least, and this is one of the biggest issues with the game: it lacks consistancy in concept. Sprawled throughout the game's many levels are challenges were the idea is to NOT die, which defeats the purpose of the game's core concept, and these challenges range from racing a knock-off angry bird, to simply reaching the end of a very long stage, so that you can aquire a key to advance. Failure in completing the sequence required to finish the level will force you to restart the stage, be it by your own mistake or because of terrible RNG (random number generation for those who don't know).
To add to the game's inconsistancy, there are boss fights in which you must also survive, but if for whatever reason you need to stop playing before you actually defeat the boss, you must replay the entire stage that leads up to that boss before you can get another crack at them, which can be painful when going for achievements tied to them, like slaying them on higher difficulties. The difficulty system is used exclusively for the bosses, in no way can you change the difficulty of the other levels or the game in general. The only thing I can see that the difficulty does is increase the number of objects a boss throws at you, and how more punishing the RNG gets with those objects, as beyond the first boss (which was kind enough to show you where a box was gonna fall), you get no indicator on where they'll land.
The various platforming required in the game, regardless of how inconsistent the concept gets, is sluggish and bugged, where landing from a high enough platform will seem to stun you for half a second, preventing you from jumping again (which can lead to a forced restart on the stages not letting you die). On top of bugged jumps, sometimes you can jump at a wall and get stuck there, as though you were pushing against a crate, but fortunately moving in the opposite direction of said wall will let you fall back down. There are also various moving platforms in the game, and they conjure up mobility bonuses and penalties, based on when you try to jump off them, assuming the speed of the platform hasn't simply caused it to move out from under your own feet!
The game revels in trolling you with cheap gimmicks that is not shared between all levels, like wrapping the screen when you walk to the left to come out on the very right side of the level, or preventing you from quiting the game to solve a puzzle that seemingly has no solution (alt+F4 still works, but still, what the hell, developers!?). In addition to the trolling gimmicks, every world contains a secret hat shop level you can gain access to that, until you have essentially beaten the game 100% with bosses slain on insane difficulty, does nothing and prevents you from using vanity items on Squishy.
This game will stump you, it will frustrate you, and you will not want to continue playing. If this game was only puzzles that stuck to the game's concept, perhaps it would be worth picking up, but no, that is not the case.

Albeit Early Access and not yet finished, Avorion is definitely worth its price for anyone who likes sandbox and space games.
Fans of X, Freelancer and StarMade, and maybe even fans of Elite, Space Rangers and Space Engineers might want to keep it on their wishlist/watchlist.
The game is a sandbox, open-ended game with a basic story and a little lore behind it. The ability to quickly put some blocks together to make a ship and be ready for intense combat is really awesome, which makes it the most quick-action quick-fun  space game I can remember - space-themed games are usually extremely time consuming, but an hour or two in Avorion can already bring good fun.
Coming from someone who already played StarMade and Space Engineers, it really is a relief.
It has an economy and different job postings found on space stations. You can also build your own space stations and manufacture your goods, supplying your own stations.
You can have a fleet of mining ships, or mine yourself and sell to stations (including your own). You can have a military fleet, or set up ships to guard locations or escort yourself.
Automated Trading ships are currently not implemented, except for AI-faction ships.
Of course, you can skip empire-building entirely, and play the game as a lone mercenary, trader, warrior, explorer..the flexibility of that and the respective rewards for each playstyle are really cool, even at an early state.
You can customize your ship by building it out of different materials, as well as equipping it with different System Upgrades and Turrets - this is simple yet extremely versatile.
The same can be said about the in-game ship editor: REALLY easy to learn, but with a decent number of features that will make building much easier.
There's currently not a huge amount of story and lore content - expected from most space-themed games but, weirdly enough, not expected at all from sandbox games - which I really hope to see more of one day.
There's multiplayer! Which is amazing to finally have a game of this kind and scope to play cooperatively. Props to the developer, honestly.
Even though I haven't bumped into many bugs, the one or two issues I bumped into (server crashes that causes rollbacks in your position and CTDs in rare, insane overcrowded sectors) are extremely frustrating - and currently being investigated and fixed by the developers.
In this regard, it's much more polished (considering its scope) than many other Early Access titles.
Since Avorion is still in development, I cannot simply fully recommend it. There's important features that feel halfway done that I'd still wait to see its final implementation.
But you should definitely

Like Shmups like R-Type, Gradius, or Ikaruga? Then play Defiance, it's a 3rd person Shmup with a pretty decent single player experience and great pve events. Giant bosses, tons of weapons and equipment to upgrade your ship...I mean character, very, very fast "twitch" style gameplay.
Only other game that I can think of that is similar is Firefall, and Motocross Madness....

This has everything that I wish more games had. It has variety, creativity, beauty, and a story you can actually care about. The only problem this game has is occasionally stiff animation, and a very short length (though it may have felt redundant if they had made it any longer.)
If you are like me, and have been itching for a good 3D platformer for a while, this game will more than satisfy.
(Additionally, I should point out that this is not a game for kids. Things get pretty dark half-way in.)

I just played and beat Brothers: A tale of two sons by Starbreeze studios. Big budget studios need to take notice. THIS is how you make the player care about your game, and story. Through provoking use of music, tone of voice, and the environment around you. The characters never spoke a word of any language i could understand, but i had no issues understanding the story, their emotions, or any other element of the game. And i'm also not afraid to admit that i cried like a little baby near the end.
This was one of the best gaming experiences i have had in a very long time. In a gaming world filled with sequels, big budget IPs, and single gimmick over hyped games, this is exactly the type of game design we need to revitalize the gaming industry.
TLDR; 10/10 Would cry like a baby again

First of all english is not my mother tongue. This is my opinion/review that i am sharing is based in my experience in playing wargame in the single player campaings and Ai battles, i have and played all wargame titles of them.
The most important aspect is that wargame its a game of patience and strategy.I am saying this, because thinking that sending a convoy made of tanks,ifvs and chopper cover is not going to work very well in most ocassions, you have to decide how you are gonig to play it, like focus on using armor and crush your opponent early on or focus on using chopper by making lighting strikes, and so on. Find a way that you are comfortable and you like it and keep using it, expect to loose a lot of troops until you dominate the game, expect more if you are new to the wargame franchise.
This game is based in reality so expect moral, fuel,ammo,repairs,range and reconissence which is an aspect of the game that you have to be good if not excellent at, because with no recon your units can't see the target until it's faring on you or are close enought .

Now to the pros
You could say that red dragon is the second wargame( airland battle) with navy combat, asia focus and a better singleplayer, the singleplayer of red dragon is: you choose a campaing, you'll be taken to a map and high ranking officer you tell you the situation and how long you have in turns to win the campaing, just like a open world game you have complete freedom to win the campaing in any way you want, block the enemy retreat, surround the enemy, make beach landings, airdrops.
About the navy combat, is true that it's not the best and the developers could have worked more , but it's fun and realist like today naval battles are fougth with(misseils,torpedos and ciws), there are no 19 and 20 century gun battles and stuff.
Acess to a lot of nations armies and units a lot of details
Graphics and mechanics are good
Gameplay is nice but there could be more options in formations and  behavior.
The cons
The balance between nations armies are another topic that migth complicate, like the sweden army is balanced so it can face the soviet army in simple words, but all games(exclusively the strategy ones, save a few ones) have this issue we like or not. For a realistic game this con weighs a lot.
The time limit battles that happens in both the single and multiplayer, the multiplayer limit is understandable but the singleplayer sometimes it gives the nerves mainly if you want to try something different or use that unit or because in order to win the battle you have to get a high ponctuantion to get victory nor a draw.

After a few minutes testing I must say this proggy looks very good to me but also veryveryvery useless.
First its called "professional" but it looks like it can't handle vectors. (correct me, if I am wrong, please!)
But we want to produce some real graphics, don't we?! So we dont work in pixels but vectors.
It can export as gif - nice. Photoshop can do too and we even have more control of the single frames there. Plus we would have a lil problem with the alpha transparences and the limited colors in gif, no?!
So we would have to use png (IF it is png24 as I hopefully assume). But then png does not contain animations. And again, we can build png also in photoshop with more control over the pixels.
So, if we have to build single bodyparts and have to render them down to pixels anyway for use in spriter, then why to use spriter at all and not the proggy we already used to pixel them (latest since smartobjects seem to work halfway correctly in ps, finally)?
To make them look nice in higher resolutions we also would need some REALLY big images. ...as gif??? ...as png??? No wonder every little 5 minute game is a full GB strong nowadays. :P
Only useful thing in spriter I could find (but did not try) was the export as spritesheet. I guess its relaxed if you have to build sheets with 20 frames per direction. For little 4x4 sheets it seems too much work compared to the small result to me.
Don't get me wrong: It works fine (beside the first crash after 2 minutes) and is easy to use. I like it. But I simply see no point in using it, beside big spritesheets.
Feel free to leave a comment, if you have something it IS useful for.
I am not an artist but I used it for quite a while :)

TLDNR: I Bloody love Stardust Vanguards very much.
Let me start off by saying I really love Stardust Vanguards a lot. Stardust Vanguards is a great Local multiplayer game, but unfortunately no online multiplayer. It has some of the most fun 4 player craziness. The deathmatch is a lot of fun. Especially when you unlock the custom deathmatch. I had a friend over and we played deathmatch with infinite bullets, full reinforcement points, and the maximum amount of pirate encounters. There was so much happening on screen that it was hard to keep track of it all. It was still a ton of fun, me and my friend were just laughing and having a great time. Then we moved onto conquest mode. The mode was alright though nothing too special. It was your average king of the hill style game mode. Now that is out of the way let us move onto what I feel is the main event. SPAAAAAAACE BALL, yeah that is right Space Ball. In my opinion this was the most fun and fast gamemode. Me and my friend started it up and were greeted with a map with lots of walls, a ball in the middle, and a base on each side. We at first thought we were supposed to kick the ball into the other teams base, but it turns out that was not the idea of the game. It turned out were were supposed the get the ball back to our base using our swords, boost, and bodies to move the ball around. The ball almost never went where we wanted it to. It would rather just ricochet all over every wall, only sometimes hitting into our base. Sometimes we accidentally got it in the other  persons goal. We played about 6 rounds of Space Ball before trying out the Co-Op part of the game. The Co-Op was your standered survive for as many waves as possible without losing all your lives.

Cons-

I spotted this on the store feed and after watching a couple of youtube gameplay vids, decided to give it a go. I'm So pleased I did as this has to be one of the best sandbox titles I've ever jumped into.
The game has a superbly polished feel to it already.. a stunning good title, drawing on the best elements of titles like the X series and Freelancer, adding in a starship building system that is simple to use, but with a sense of depth and complexity that will satisfy even a Kerbals fan and mixing it all together in a single player or multiplayer mode that plays beautifully.
20 hours in and I'm pottering around in a ship based on the Battlestar Galactica (created and designed in creative mode and then imported in to a standard game).
Gameplay is as simple or as complex as you care to make it.. Like Elite, what you do is completely up to you.. trading is easy to do (but not so easy to master), missions are available at most stations.. ranging from trade runs to pirate hunts, with random missions popping up through radio chatter. Upgrading your ship is as easy as adding more "blocks", but balancing your ships energy needs, crew requirements and flight stablillity rewards some careful thinking and planning. New gear drops from ships fought (and wrecks salvaged) like candy from a Piñata and puts a real buzz on looting the battlefield once your done fighting.
When the Early Access info states "Avorion already has a lot of features, but it's still lacking some content.".. I can't help but wonder what the hell else they can cram into an already polished and content rich title.. and I'm drooling in anticipation to find out.

I recommend this game to anyone who likes stealth gameplay and/or third person action.  I found it highly enjoyable and well worth the price, a big improvement over the first and second titles.
The good:
The game looks great.  Polished visuals throughout.
A wide range of difficulty options and optional objectives lets you make the game as hard as you like.
More than long enough, especially with the DLC.
Open-ish gameplay with optional objectives, collectibles, and a little bit of upgrading and customization.
Historically accurate (mostly) settings and hardware.
A gruesome bullet cam which can be turned up, down, or off in frequency and grotesque-ness.
The bad:
Barely any story, and not much in the way of good storytelling.
A stealth system which is tempting to exploit, running away from the place from which you last shot to get "stealthed," then going right back to shoot again.
Despite a wide range of weapons, there is a clear winner in each category (primary, secondary, sidearm), regardless of playstyle.  For example, there's no reason to use any of the non-suppressed sidearms.

I loved this game initially. A series of poor decisions on R*'s part has led me to come to a place of great disdain and ambivalence towards this game and my more recent sessions. Each average update, if you don't wish to grind (and some players simply do not have the hours to to so), would cost around $100 to purchase and access completely unrestricted all of the content. Never mind the larger more involved updates where single items cost as much as the largest "Shark Card". Assuming an average total DLC cost of around $120 (averaging ALL DLCs regardless of size), and also assuming that you as a player are only interested in a mere HALF of the content of that DLC, that still comes to around $60 PER DLC to experience the content relevant to your interests. That's enough to buy the game again, each time a medium to large DLC is released. That's hundreds of dollars of DLC over the life of this game. Bear in mind these are VERY generously low estimates, and in truth, some cost more than this. 'Ah', but you say, 'I've gotten 750+ hours out of this game'. True. But that additional $60 is no guarantee of additional hours of enjoyment, not to mention to grind to get the content would mean MORE playtime. In essence, you pay NOT to play your game.
Okay; So you have your $380 worth of DLC from about 4.5 updates, plus the $30-60 you paid for the game. Now you have the challenge of enjoying it while dealing with the toxic community of this game. 'Well just play in a friends only session' you say. Well, see, many of the activities of the past two years are restricted to Open sessions, so for much of the content that may not even be an option. 'Okay, well use that trick where you hold alt+enter to get into an open session alone and invite your friends after that. That has worked since the game was launched on PC, right?' Good point! Except R* patched that this month for seemingly no real good reason, other than to force you to deal with the awful community and consolidate the smaller more spread out lobbies, thus making it seem like the population is stronger than ever. Okay, okay, so you managed to get into an open lobby, your friends all connected with none of the trademark R* connectivity issues, and everyone else in the lobby are fairly decent agreeable people, and you're actually having fun trying out new content, doing missions, and making good memories with friends, we've all had those moments. But then here comes Johnny F*ckwit who stole mom's credit card and bought a hack tool, come to be a d*ck for the sake of being a d*ck because he's a dried up sad lonely husk of a human and he's set on ruining it for everyone else. Now you're being teleported, ragdolled, set on fire, blown up, having your inventory or cash wiped, garages wiped, being immobilized, getting killed by an invincible demigod, or even having your game outright crashed. Now the fun is suddenly over, and frustration ensues. You all report him and votekick him, but somehow he's still here being a d*ck, and either way, your decent lobby has fallen apart and the last hour or so of trying to get to said decent lobby has just been wasted. 1 month later, R* finally reviews the reports against Johnny F*ckwit and bans the account. Then he buys another copy, and goes right back to being a d*ck. Rinse, repeat.
Okay, so maybe the modder in your lobby actually isn't a jerk, he's trying to give R* the middle finger, he's giving away money and cars that aren't normally obtainable and generally being okay. Awesome! Except, R* detects that, because clearly their focus is on modded money, as this denies them Shark Card revenue, and not on modders that ruin others' experiences. Well, now they have either stripped your cash, possibly to less than you had before the modder gave you money you may not have even asked for, OR they reset your progress, weapons, cars, level, properties, and given you a warning, OR they have temporarily banned you for a week to a month. OR ALL 3. Great. (OR just plain perma-banned you.) Now you've been smugly punished for something you may not have even asked for. You may have even lost some of your genuinely hard earned or outright paid for content. Welp, better buy some more shark cards right!?
In agitated, hastily typed summary: Do not buy this game until these criticisms have been addressed in some way. Possibly not even then. If you feel you still stand to gain some solid entertainment from this title, as it IS rather fun at times, or it WAS at least, please do not spend more than $30-$40 total on your GTAV/O experience. You have nothing to gain. The community is mostly shoot on sight hostile, friends are typically a must, assuming you can connect to them, the DLC items become more expensive with each update, despite grind revenue not scaling at the same rate, and modders, unfair bans, and totally absent support are the ever-present reality of this title. I had a lot of fun with it initially. I still can from time to time. But more often than not, as of late, my experience has been one of mostly defeated frustration. Please do not support this company.

Let me start by saying that TS2015 is the best simulator (most beautiful/realistic) I have played. I do recommend it, but there are lots of challenges for the user which I think need to be warned about. I personally do not regret purchasing DLC, but they aren't cheap, so DLC is not a negative to me. Now to the negatives - there are many - though to be fair to Dovetail I think most of my problems are with Steam, not them. I don't like steam very much - never have. Steam to me, is like a virus that contaminates your PC (like a common cold in people), and over time you learn to live with it.

Problem 1: disabling automatic updates. Someone has removed that option. I have tried to set to only allow updates when game runs, as I always run steam in off-line mode, but this doesn't work very well either. Whatever I do, everytime I take steam online I am forced to update a new patch. I believe if you have a game that you are happy with, you should be able to choose whether you want to install the latest patch. Steam, like Stalin, doesn't allow you this freedom. I am in the crazy position right now where I have a perfectly good copy of TS2015 with lots of paid DLC, and I cannot take steam online, or it will automatically update it to TS2016 - I don't want TS2016. Seems I am going to get it anyway. Not happy.
Problem 2: Dump file save error. Although I have a good working copy of TS2015 52.2A, never have any errors running it, the scenario editor is another story. I used to get this crash error alot, but now the editor works 9 times out of 10. Every once in a while I get this error.
Problem 3: I wish Dovetail had just launched a seperate 2016 game and allowed users to stick with a working copy of TS2015 which won't convert itself to 2016 everytime you take it online. From what I can see about the latest update - it seems to have caused more damage than good. The reason I don't want 2016 update is simply this. I have just bought a new fast laptop, and TS2015 runs very fast on it on high graphic settings. I am fully expecting that some addon, some graphic addition effect in 2016 will make the game run slower on my new PC. I just want to stick with an older version. Anyways that is my review. Great game, but it has its challenges. Be warned. Right now I have a working version of a game that I can't take online, without getting an update I don't want, which seems to have disabled the game. Its crazy.
Problem 4: Steam. Running steam offline - it is a very painfull and frustrating experience. Invariably something goes wrong, and you have to connect steam online again. I can't see why if you have set up games on it which you are happy with, ie they work, you should be forced to accept updates. Updating steam client I understand. But forcing updates of games ( with all the problems that entails) is mean spirited. Sometimes an update will do more damage than good. Updates should always be handled with caution.
One last thing: for new users or those who don't know, it is a shame that the steam launch setting (found under main properties tab) is not better advertised, to change the in-cab views when playing - it makes an enormous difference. I recommend using the setting for a view that shows you all the controls when driving.
-SetFOV=85

Well, at the beginning of the year I came up with the resolution to make a video game. Like many noob game makers out there, I opted for RPG Maker which seemed like the easiest method to make one. But I didn't like the basic elements it offered, including sprites and overall animations. I wanted to do something by myself. Something unique. I turned to Spriter. It looked good and it seemed like it worked. I always write long reviews and this one won't be an exception, but for the TL;DR people: It works for RPG Maker and it's a good software.
First, the presentation. It's not perfect. You pretty much entirely depend on tutorials if you want to get started. The software itself is not very friendly if you are a beginner. The video tutorials are on Youtube. I don't think that part was well done right from the start. First of all, perhaps it would have been easier to simply make tutorial "bubbles" pop up inside the software for your first time. Or maybe you could have just put a few tiny demonstration videos within the software, or have things highlighted to guide you. Something, anything. Well, no, it's pretty much all on Youtube. And the tutorials on Youtube, sure they teach you how to use the software, but man... No hate for the guy who made the videos, I know you're doing your best, but you should have given this task for someone who knew how to make tutorials. The videos have terrible audio (quality of a built-in laptop mic) and are unnecessary long. It shouldn't take more than 30 minutes to explain how to do a walking animation when, about 10 hours through the software, I managed to make a decent walking animation in under 20 minutes myself. The guy looses himself in his explanations so often, it requires a lot of patience not to skip the thing.
But that's one of the only negative things I have to say about it. The second issue I have is the lack of buttons. The interface is lacking in content. Some of the core manipulations you can do in Spriter don't have an icon to click on. The software often relies on keyboard shortcuts. But this is not a RTS game. This is a software. Where you frequently have to use your mouse or ( in my case ) tablet. This is a relatively simple software and yet you can make an efficient toolbox like in drawing programs such as GIMP or Photoshop? Erm...
Once you forget about those two problems and you learn how to make animations, however, Spriter works like a charm. It allows you to make animations easily and quickly. It does most of the work. To put it simple, you make the beginning of your animation and then the end and Spriter connects both ends. Of course, you can also make more complex animations as well. I really like the various export options at my disposal. You can choose how many frames, the speed of your animation and a few more things. Despite the negative part of my review, I can't honestly give it a thumbs down since it does the job it's made to do. One disappointment I have, however, is that you must rely on another software to actually draw the sprites. To me, it seems like a missed opportunity. Perhaps some people are scared of venturing in animation because they think it's too hard for them. Maybe they could've sold more if they would've introduced Spriter as an animation AND drawing software. I certainly believe that would be interesting. I, myself, would love to be able to rely on a single software instead of jumping from one to another.
I know they're making a Spriter 2. I'm really looking forward to this upcoming software and I'm pretty sure that the issues I've mentionned are already in the devs' notebook.

It's decent for what it is.  A lot of game engines come with the ability to create cut-out animations within them, such as Unity3D and Godot, but Spriter offers a more complete package over that if you need it.  Of course, it's irreplaceable for those engines or frameworks which don't offer any tools to manipulate animations, although I feel that Spline is an even more impressive package--nonetheless, Spline's complete package is several times more expensive than Spriter is, and though it does come with certain features that really polish the animations produced (IMO important to free yourself of that flash/tween feel of cheap animation as is, unfortunately, largely showcased in Spriter's example videos), the price point can be a big problem for indies in particular.
Spriter is by no means a bad piece of software and if you really feel that your engine's animator is simply inadequate, and you are certain you want to go the cut-out animation route, I'd give it a go.  But first consider your options: smaller sprites (e.g. pixel art) can be very easily hand-drawn animated due to their small file size, and the result of that can look much better than tweening; however, very large sprites (particularly if you're building your game for the inevitable upgrade to 4K resolutions) cannot be easily animated in this manner due to limitations of graphical memory: just one fully-animated character made in this way can take up hundreds of megabytes of memory if not more.  This is where cut-out animation is most appropriate: what would've taken a ton of memory to store frames of animation now takes just the cut-outs and some very small bits of data to store the animation itself.  Greatly more efficient than having tons of giant sprite sheets!
OTOH, if you are making pixel art, esp. with just a few frames of animations e.g. classic top-down RPG characters, Spriter (and all other 2D animation software) is complete overkill: creating a texture file, showing a grid in your favorite image software, and lining up your handful of animations properly is trivial, and requires no special software--not even poorly-featured in-engine animators are necessary to swap out a texture atlas.  Spriter can help this problem by exporting a sprite sheet, but do you want to spend 60$ for such an easily performed task?  It may not be worth it in this case.
There's also the problem of engines not supporting Spriter data.  Because the Spriter data does not really change, it's up to the engines themselves to take care of importing Spriter animations, whether this comes from the engine officially or some community add-on which can handle it.  Certainly Unity3D has some support for this (don't know for certain but it wouldn't surprise me if they did), but this can also be a pithole that's hard to get around: if there's a more obscure engine you're using which doesn't support Spriter, you'll need to write some compatability yourself or resort to exporting sprite sheets, which defeats a major advantage of cut-out animation while still leaving you with the problems of cut-out animation.  For example, I was using Toon Boom Harmony for a while to make animations for a Unity3D game, and the official Harmony support for Unity was actually broken and pretty much abandoned by the time I got to it.  So all that was left was either exporting to sprite sheet or trying to assemble the cut-out in Unity and animating it in there, which, again, defeats the purpose.  It's a common problem that you should be wary of.
Furthermore, if you are planning to create cut-out animations, you could also consider DragonBones, a free and open-source 2D animator which does much of the same.  Again, you should be wary of the aforementioned problem: poor support of external tools can be a pain to deal with.  I'm not certain if DragonBones is better or worse than Spriter, but given it's free you won't lose anything but time and energy checking it out.  In my experience it isn't as polished as paid alternatives but it's nonetheless functional.  Also, if you're making pixel art, there is software specially designed for animating that, such as Aseprite, and offers a lot more control over your animations than Spriter does, given that Spriter is not an image-creation tool, just an animation tool.
I got this piece of software from a Humble Bundle some time ago (i.e. got it on the cheap) but don't find myself using it very often.  Godot has a good-enough animator which has some basic bone functionality.  I could combine it with hand-drawn animation to make a kind of hybrid method, as showcased in some of Spriter's example animations.  And of course it's in-engine supported so I never have to worry about some compatbility breaking; also I have greater control over what can be animated outside of the sprites themselves, which is something Spriter is unlikely to support at any point in time--this would mean that, even with Spriter, you would still need to interact with your engine's animator.  I'm not missing very much by not using Spriter.  Of course, if you were using something like MonoGame or LOVE where you have no in-engine tools to assist development, it'd make a lot more sense to drop 60$ on an advanced piece of 2D animation software, though there's still the question to compatibility for Spriter data.
In short: If you're not planning on using large cut-outs to keep your game's graphical memory low, it may not be worthwhile to use Spriter, or any other 2D animation software which focuses on tweening for that matter.  Hand-drawn animation from a competent artist will virtually always be preferred to tweening by your audience.  Pixel art is better animated in software designed for pixel art.  Your engine may be enough to produce animations of this caliber.  Consider your alternatives.

It's like a 4-way bullet hell game in space.
You pilot your Totally-Not-a-Gundam around the screen and try to kill all your friends.
Everything is a one-hit-kill, but you can reflect projectiles with your blade or use a Super Smash Bros. -style bubble shield to block. Alternatively, there's a little dash you can use to dodge or close in on an enemy.
The game gets really interesting when players collect "RP", because spending RP lets players call in units from offscreen. The more RP a player spends at once, the more units spawn in that wave, even spawning large cruisers with fighter complements when the player uses a full RP meter.
Every minute or two, special events happen. These are typically pirate attacks, where tons of NPC ships flood the map and try to kill *everybody*. There are also VIP targets of opportunity and bounties set on players who are doing really well. This keeps everyone on their toes and shifts the balance of power around enough that nobody ever really feels safe.
If you get tired of killing your friends, you can try your hand at the survival mode, which pits the four of you against increasingly-difficult waves of pirates and severely limits your ability to call in support. Alternatively, you can play Space Ball, where two teams compete to smack the Space Ball into a goal zone, much like air hockey or foosball.
It's great as a local co-op game, but at the time of this writing there's no online component. If you can't get anyone to play this with you locally, the only thing you can really play is the survival mode. It's not enough content for a solo player to really carry the game. Be warned that my recommendation comes ONLY with the assumption that you have enough people to play local co-op with, or a future update adding some form of online multiplayer.

First of all, this is a very under rated quality game. Massive battles, wide variety of strategies and units, good single player experience (though the computer does cheat) and a multiplayer experience that deserves to be in the professional gaming leagues. This is an absolute gem of a game for any strategy game player.
One of the great aspects about the game is that it makes losing troops very difficult for me, but just like real war, sometimes you have to push your troops in order to take an objective even though you know you'll take losses. As a commander, it is your job to make those losses worth the effort.
While I am mostly praising this game, there are some big drawbacks that can potentially be patched with a hotfix.
#1 There are several hidden stats in the game. Units with silenced weapons are not clearly marked and neither are units with auto-loaders. In the forums it has been stated that there will be a stat indicating auto-loaders with a proper description if I remember right, so this is likely to be fixed in the future but I wonder if they will reveal all the hidden stats and abilities in a clear defining manor.
#2 The multiplayer community can be quite toxic. For a game that focuses on its multiplayer aspect, it is the biggest detriment to the game since you will have people who leave the game just because their initial push failed or even if they lose one unit. This often causes a cascade effect where people leave  one after another and while there are bonuses for the remaining team members and it is quite possible for the remaining members to win on their own, it often means that there are too many fronts for so few people to deal with and there is nothing that can be done. In addition to this, team killing is a potential problem. Luckily the team killing problem is rare, but when you're waiting in a lobby for a 10v10 map for about half an hour just to begin, it is quite disheartening when one of your team mates decides to bomb the spawning location killing most of the allied troops then proceed to bomb all of the supply bases and command vehicles before leaving.
#3 Artillery is very prevelant and there are few counters. This is somewhat a reality of war that I mostly don't mind in this game, but this is bad in a few ways. One of which is that it just becomes an annoyance when you're constantly getting spammed by arty even when you take little to no losses since it often isn't used properly. Another way is that you'll often have team mates on your own team that don't know how to use artillery properly, then they waste all of their supplies achieving almost nothing, and then they start taking from allied supplies which deprives front line troops with repairs, ammo, and fuel. The final way that the artillery spam is a bad thing is because people neglect to mark the locations they are sending artillery shells (or bombing runs from airplanes) and thus there becomes friendly fire issues.
My suggestion for avoiding the pit falls that somewhat plague this game is to manage to get some friends in the game that you know are reliable, or even better yet, bring friends with you to buy the game and play with you. It's the best way to play and provides a lot of enjoyment for anyone who can work together as a team.

There was a period of time in the early to mid 2000s where I worried that games were getting too easy. Too much hand-holding, too much tutorial, not enoough trusting in the player. As I branched out into the indie scene, and games like Demon's Souls and Binding of Isaac were becoming immensely popular, I realized that brutally hard, yet fair games, still have an audience. Spelunky is the ultimate version of this concept. You play as one of many explorers, and you dive into a randomely generated labyrinth of cave formations, complete with monsters and items and shops and alien spaceships. Where the brilliance comes in is how fragile the player initially seems. You always start with four hearts, and being hit by an enemy takes one, while being punctured by an arrow takes two, and falling on spikes is instant death. So you die and restart, and the process repeats.
But then Spelunky clicks with you. You see patterns in the randomness, and you start to learn things like animation priority and enemy attack patterns. Once you have conquered the randomness, the game becomes about progressing. In the beginning, you're overwhelmed by what seems like cheap deaths. By the time you get good, you just want to get a little further. You KNOW every death is your fault, and you're always going to smash on that "Quick Restart" button and dive back in. It's as pure as game design gets. The loop of try, fail, and repeat. That's what video games are. You never want to stop because you KNOW there's something cool on the next floor, and you KNOW you can go a little further into these mysterious, random acts of chaos.
Spelunky's a pretty rad game.

Spelunky is a fantastic game. It is frustrating, surprisingly dense and difficult to beat for the first time, but is incredibly rewarding to learn to play. The controls are what I like about the game so much. They feel very fluid with a controller and after some practice, you amaze yourself by how quick you get and how well you can judge jumps / throws.
I've put ~15 hours into Spelunky and love it. I bought it at the same time as Black Flag and Spelunky has gotten way more play time from me. If you enjoyed other roguelikes such as Don't Starve, The Binding of Issac and Rogue Legacy, this should be a no-brainer for you. If you're new to the Roguelike genre, Spelunky's smooth controls make it a great place to start.
There are multiple character unlocks and items to be found, which add some content for people who like to unlock things in games.
The only downside that I have found with Spelunky is the lack of online multiplayer. You can have local multiplayer up to 4 players, which seems very fun, but I would like to be able to play online with friends, since I live pretty far away from my gaming friends. Spelunky just won't be a game that we play multiplayer on, but will be the game to occupy all of my time when they aren't online.
I can't recommend this game enough. If you pay full price like I did, you won't feel like you threw money away. If you can catch it on a sale (Winter sale has it at $3.74, a steal!) it is definitely worth buying.

This game is fun for several reasons.
First of all, don't expect a realistic simulation of BEING a sniper. The realism is mainly present in the shooting physics - it doesn't really simulate how snipers actually operate because that probably wouldn't be as fun as what this game provides.
The best feature, in my opinion, is the consistently fun and non-frustrating gameplay, which persists despite difficult-to-master mechanics. This comes from the nice save system and forgiving stealth mechanics. Being able to quick-save really changes the fun of this game, in my opinion. Instead of what happens in other stealth games where you make a mistake, everyone gets alerted, then you have to open up a menu, sit through a long loading screen, and start at the beginning of the level, you get an quick-save button which saves while you continue playing, so you can always save before you try something risky and just focus on the fun sniping mechanics and visuals. Also, one of the other problems that can happen in a lot of stealth games is that it's hard to keep track of your surroundings, so somebody might see you but you won't realize it until it's too late. This game provides subtle audio-cues and less subtle visual cues to let you know when you are about to be spotted.
You might think that the aforementioned features make the game too easy or too simple, but I think it just lets you focus on what this game does best - being stealthy and sniping people.
If you really like sniping in other FPS games (the feel of precision and power), you'll definitely like this game because it focuses on that one aspect of FPS. If you're concerned about having to spend more time sneaking around than shooting, you're in luck because even though you might alert everyone and have them go aggressive, you can still clear levels just by running and gunning and shooting everyone in sight.
So, overall, I think this game is pretty fun.

I loved this game initially. A series of poor decisions on R*'s part has led me to come to a place of great disdain and ambivalence towards this game and my more recent sessions. Each average update, if you don't wish to grind (and some players simply do not have the hours to to so), would cost around $100 to purchase and access completely unrestricted all of the content. Never mind the larger more involved updates where single items cost as much as the largest "Shark Card". Assuming an average total DLC cost of around $120 (averaging ALL DLCs regardless of size), and also assuming that you as a player are only interested in a mere HALF of the content of that DLC, that still comes to around $60 PER DLC to experience the content relevant to your interests. That's enough to buy the game again, each time a medium to large DLC is released. That's hundreds of dollars of DLC over the life of this game. Bear in mind these are VERY generously low estimates, and in truth, some cost more than this. 'Ah', but you say, 'I've gotten 750+ hours out of this game'. True. But that additional $60 is no guarantee of additional hours of enjoyment, not to mention to grind to get the content would mean MORE playtime. In essence, you pay NOT to play your game.
Okay; So you have your $380 worth of DLC from about 4.5 updates, plus the $30-60 you paid for the game. Now you have the challenge of enjoying it while dealing with the toxic community of this game. 'Well just play in a friends only session' you say. Well, see, many of the activities of the past two years are restricted to Open sessions, so for much of the content that may not even be an option. 'Okay, well use that trick where you hold alt+enter to get into an open session alone and invite your friends after that. That has worked since the game was launched on PC, right?' Good point! Except R* patched that this month for seemingly no real good reason, other than to force you to deal with the awful community and consolidate the smaller more spread out lobbies, thus making it seem like the population is stronger than ever. Okay, okay, so you managed to get into an open lobby, your friends all connected with none of the trademark R* connectivity issues, and everyone else in the lobby are fairly decent agreeable people, and you're actually having fun trying out new content, doing missions, and making good memories with friends, we've all had those moments. But then here comes Johnny F*ckwit who stole mom's credit card and bought a hack tool, come to be a d*ck for the sake of being a d*ck because he's a dried up sad lonely husk of a human and he's set on ruining it for everyone else. Now you're being teleported, ragdolled, set on fire, blown up, having your inventory or cash wiped, garages wiped, being immobilized, getting killed by an invincible demigod, or even having your game outright crashed. Now the fun is suddenly over, and frustration ensues. You all report him and votekick him, but somehow he's still here being a d*ck, and either way, your decent lobby has fallen apart and the last hour or so of trying to get to said decent lobby has just been wasted. 1 month later, R* finally reviews the reports against Johnny F*ckwit and bans the account. Then he buys another copy, and goes right back to being a d*ck. Rinse, repeat.
Okay, so maybe the modder in your lobby actually isn't a jerk, he's trying to give R* the middle finger, he's giving away money and cars that aren't normally obtainable and generally being okay. Awesome! Except, R* detects that, because clearly their focus is on modded money, as this denies them Shark Card revenue, and not on modders that ruin others' experiences. Well, now they have either stripped your cash, possibly to less than you had before the modder gave you money you may not have even asked for, OR they reset your progress, weapons, cars, level, properties, and given you a warning, OR they have temporarily banned you for a week to a month. I completed Super Hexagon, Super Meat Boy, 1001 Spikes etc. So I do feel somewhat qualified to point out these supposedly “flaws” as the average gamer I am.
Most of the bosses are pretty much purely RNG based with a very low amount of positioning yourself out of danger's way. Too often i find myself in situations where death simply was unavoidable. It happens so frequently that it makes me wonder if that was supposed to be this game's gimmick?
Now, I’m not strictly talking about the Insane bosses I would also like to point out the at times unresponsive controls which lead me to fall into a pit or to leap over a platform because the moving platform I jumped from gave me too much momentum. This can get very frustrating and random obstacles like the sand pits in level 2-8 with no apparent purpose suddenly starts to make sense, they were put there to make backtracking take even longer and the player’s experience so much worse at other times it is the weird level design that gets me (yes I’m looking at you level 2-4 with awkward jump you had to make which apparently is “skill based”) or subtle hints like “Gur nafjre vf sbhe naq fvk” which I’m sure has a logical explanation to it that I’m just too stupid to translate, only problem is that the text disappears after 5 seconds and no, there’s no way for you to go up to the sign and read what it said again as it would in any normal game, you have to exit the level to read it again.

This is the ONLY game I've seen that combines RPG elements, Open World elements, Management elements, and a few RTS elements. Need proof? Okay.
RPG Elements: You play a character. Simple enough, yeh? You choose the background, if it's male or female, where it came from, etc. You level up, get stronger, find loot, etc. Pretty self explanatory.
Open World Elements: You have a HUGE sand box to play in. And that's just the basic vanilla game. Six unique factions across an expansive continent, each with their own specific biomes. Some of the DLC/Mods have even larger maps that venture into reality and are truly mind boggling.
Management Elements (Spoilers): Your character has a party to manage, a warband if you will. You have to make sure they're fed, happy, willing to fight for you, and you can upgrade them to stronger levels in the troop tree. Investments are also possible if you address a town's guild master whom you can purchase land from and start a business.
RTS elements (Spoilers): [spoilers]If you perchance become a Marshal or even a Ruler, you can order your vassals or fellow vassals into combat to assist you or even send them on missions.[/spoilers]
All in all, this is a fantastic game that I definitely recommend.

The most in-depth strategy game I've ever played.
Eugen deserves some felicitations for the ambition manifested by this game and its engine. Despite the learning cliff, this game strikes the right balance between predictability and replayability. The UI is deceptively simple, and the complexity of the game owes more to tactics than any other single element. There is no base-building mechanic or resource collection to speak of here; all the units are at your fingertips right from the start, ensuring intensity from the beginning of each game.
This is not an easy game to learn. Each unit has hard counters, many of which will not occupy the same price bracket. Tanks get a special mention not as invincible death machines, but simply as counters to enemy armour, which are themselves vulnerable to all kinds of threats, ranging from infantry to ATGMs to airstrikes. There is no unit that cannot be killed in one hit by another, far less expensive one. This means that Wargame can also be highly frustratinng at times. It also means that the ability to predict where your opponent is going to place their units is a skill to be valued. Coupled with a unique recon mechanic that completely eschews LOS bubbles and fog of war, this makes each round surprisingly tense. In many cases the only thing telling you whether a treeline contains an enemy squad or not will be your instinct. Expect to spend the better part of 50 games figuring out the basics. Watch replays or you will find yourself going up against and losing to the same formations again and again.
Playing a match of Wargame is like conducting a symphony. Miscalculating maneuvers by mere seconds can mean you'll be picked apart. But when it all comes together- it's exhilerating, and there is nothing like it.

Wargame, is a really fun and casual game, if you love Stragey Commanding Games, then this is the game for you! It really triggers your mind off to think about where to deploy vehicle assets, platoons, etc, but then again, as well is a casual game for a sit down and relax gaming moment.
