Stardust Vanguards is a fantastic game for local play.
(Note that there is NO ONLINE MULTIPLAYER, only local co-op & local multiplayer)
There are quite a few "local multiplayer only" games on Steam these days, and if you like those sorts of games, you will like this game!
The singelplayer consist of Wave Survival with 4 difficulties and it's really challenging. But it can get a little bit monotonous in the long run. But the multiplayer is where the game shines, it's fast, hectic, tactical, skill-based and very good for trash talking with your friends.
The game could do with some minor polishing though. I'll list pros and cons below.
Pros:
Rewards tactical and skilled players.
Punishes button-mashers.
Fantastic with some friends.
Plays well on keyboard. (though a controller is recommended)
Good selection of game modes for multiplayer.
Good selection of maps.
Sound effects are great.
Cons:
Somewhat monotonous singelplayer in the long run.
Menu transitions can be really slow and annoying.
The game quits to the main menu after each finished match.
The game doesn't teach you all the mechanics.
UI lacks information regarding remaining shield time and thruster heat build-up.
The music is nothing special, though that is a highly subjective opinion.
TL;DR - Got friends and controllers? Buy it!

(Note: I've only played the single-player portion to any significant degree)
Although it's perhaps a little light on content for the price (especially for solo players), Stardust Vangaurds oozes style and boasts a rocking soundtrack to duke it out with friends to. With a few minor balancing tweaks in Co-op (keeping Reinforce points between waves to discourage just blowing them all constantly, always reloading bullets at wave-halfway marks rather than only if you're empty, allied ships sticking around rather than puttering off randomly) and perhaps some cheesy pixel style cutscenes, this would be almost perfect. Happy to see Zanrai coming out swinging with the first release.

**********Give Away and Video Review*************
_________________________________________________________
Where do I even begin with Stadust Vanguards? The cool music and sounds? The fast paced gameplay? The well balanced and awesome multiplayer? To put it quite simply, Stardust Vanguards is amazing. Very seldom does a game come around that immediately grabs you in and feel this awesome.
I'll go ahead and start with the sounds of the game which are a nice mix of original sci-fi sounds and a very well orchestrated mix old school bit music. While slicing and gunning your way through other players and AI combatants you'll hear lightsabre like hums, a mass of blips as you rain down attacks with your blaster. When events or cool combos are unleashed an announcer ques in with exciting energy, and overall the sound FX are engaging enough to let you know they're there, without being distracting or annoying. The music as well has this cool classic arcade feel that sounds familiar yet unique. It sounds like a mixture of various soundtracks from Gundam mixed with  tones akin to Streetfighter, Dragonball Z, and Ape Escape.
Like the sound, the graphics and presentation do a great job as well. The game is presented in 16-bit graphics and they sure pack a lot of animation and detail to make it look fluid and nice. If you like old school graphics then you won't have any complaints here. Even with each player unleashing their fleets and duking it out on screen the frame rate remains steady. Each pilot is color coded, and their caricatures and features have a good level of difference in menus and in game head shots. The models themselves appear to be the same other than the color differences which is probably for the best to avoid advantages in size and features. A cool animation that occurs when fighting is the clash system. Whenever two players swing swords at one another they will clash with a large blip bursting from the point of action. When an enemy is destroyed they explode in a large blast leaving a plume of smoke in their wake. It really makes the fights look impressive and gives a good sense of power. Overall the graphics do the job very well and it doesn't feel like upping to 3D models would enhance the game in any way.
Moving onto gameplay, which is not only the most important factor for any game, but also the best part about this game. To describe this game in one word, "Fun". This game is pure, unrelenting fun. Myself and other members of the team were all amazed with just how great and intuitive it actually felt through it's different stages and modes. With friends is definitely how this game should be played. You'll banter and cheer eachother  as the b attle rages on, and in our experience even if we lost, it was gripping to watch the remainder of each battle. The controls are great with or without a controller and come fairly naturally with very little practice. You'll quickly rise and fall from the lead position and have a blast doing so. In one very redeeming moment I personally was on the losing end of life count and behind on wins but even then I was able to fight back and claim the match. The game feels intense and fast paced while still allowing you to focus. When someone unleashes a storm of missiles, you can slash a few back with your sword before making an attempt to escape. Colliding swords while boosting into each other results in a massive knock back forcing both people into opposite directions. You can try to swing your sword like a madman and get lucky, but if you watch your opponents moves and look to parry and follow up, you're almost assured the kill. While the battle rages on, pirates will constantly invade the battleground and force players to make the decision to keep fighting one another or to team up against the pirates instead. If you live long enough you can call in your own support fleet that acts much like the pirates. This makes for some very interesting actions and can lead to aggressive sneak attacks and betrayal. After unlocking custom mode though you can choose to turn the pirates off along with many other different settings. Ultimately you can make the game play like you want it to.
Don't mistake this praise of multiplayer for a bad single player experience. In single player you have the same speed and action but against waves of pirate ships. There are three different difficulties as well as a endurance mode that goes until you die whilst ramping up the difficulty each wave. The single player is very fun much like the multipayer and has a rewarding sense of accomplishment as you push on. It never seemed like the game was overly difficult or broken; if I died, it was my mistake, and my obstacle to overcome. The more you play, the better you get, and really shows that a level of skill is hardened s you go along.
In conclusion, I couldn't be more impressed. If I had any complaints, it's the lack of a "replay" button after each battle, and no online gameplay. But with the easy and brief menu, and fantastic local play this is easily overlooked. The game exceeds on every level and really pushes the scale in it's entertainment value. Every element of this game just radiates the amount of care put into crafting such a gem. And when I heard that the dev team consisted of only a two man group from the steam greenlight program, I was absolutely shocked. Stardust Vanguards is one of the best games I have ever played and it is with that, I'm giving it an A+. With fantastic gameplay, awesome music, cool graphics, and an unrelenting amount of fun, Stardust Vanguards is a game that every gamer should pick up and enjoy with friends. Avorion is what I expected to play when I first signed up with EVE Online (sans the MMO-verse, of course). I'm a tiny pilot in a large galaxy, and I'm tasked with making my to, I think, the center of the galaxy. To make it, there, though, I need a bigger and better ship--and, to get that ship, I need to mine, trade, merc, or pirate my way to success. So I buzz around asteroids and I train my mining lasers on them, and I pop out some iron and some titanium, but then some pirates pop into my system and swoop down onto me. I toggle my machine guns, pop them all into a wreck, after which I have the satisfaction of turning on my salvage laser, and slicing through what's left of their ship.
I cut their ship in two. Down the center. It's a small thing, but it was wonderful.
Later on, while hopping from sector to sector, I found myself in the middle of some... fleet battle?... for control of this area of space. I picked a side and pew-pew-pew'd with them. At the end of it, I had the satisfaction of cleaning the meat of the bones from each wrecked ship. Just slicing them apart. Didn't need the iron. So I simply cut that away and went for the titanitum.
In any case, it's still... Early Access or whatever, and me and my friends experience some crashing on multiplayer, but it's a wonderful little title so far.

I loved this game initially. A series of poor decisions on R*'s part has led me to come to a place of great disdain and ambivalence towards this game and my more recent sessions. Each average update, if you don't wish to grind (and some players simply do not have the hours to to so), would cost around $100 to purchase and access completely unrestricted all of the content. Never mind the larger more involved updates where single items cost as much as the largest "Shark Card". Assuming an average total DLC cost of around $120 (averaging ALL DLCs regardless of size), and also assuming that you as a player are only interested in a mere HALF of the content of that DLC, that still comes to around $60 PER DLC to experience the content relevant to your interests. That's enough to buy the game again, each time a medium to large DLC is released. That's hundreds of dollars of DLC over the life of this game. Bear in mind these are VERY generously low estimates, and in truth, some cost more than this. 'Ah', but you say, 'I've gotten 750+ hours out of this game'. True. But that additional $60 is no guarantee of additional hours of enjoyment, not to mention to grind to get the content would mean MORE playtime. In essence, you pay NOT to play your game.
Okay; So you have your $380 worth of DLC from about 4.5 updates, plus the $30-60 you paid for the game. Now you have the challenge of enjoying it while dealing with the toxic community of this game. 'Well just play in a friends only session' you say. Well, see, many of the activities of the past two years are restricted to Open sessions, so for much of the content that may not even be an option. 'Okay, well use that trick where you hold alt+enter to get into an open session alone and invite your friends after that. That has worked since the game was launched on PC, right?' Good point! Except R* patched that this month for seemingly no real good reason, other than to force you to deal with the awful community and consolidate the smaller more spread out lobbies, thus making it seem like the population is stronger than ever. Okay, okay, so you managed to get into an open lobby, your friends all connected with none of the trademark R* connectivity issues, and everyone else in the lobby are fairly decent agreeable people, and you're actually having fun trying out new content, doing missions, and making good memories with friends, we've all had those moments. But then here comes Johnny F*ckwit who stole mom's credit card and bought a hack tool, come to be a d*ck for the sake of being a d*ck because he's a dried up sad lonely husk of a human and he's set on ruining it for everyone else. Now you're being teleported, ragdolled, set on fire, blown up, having your inventory or cash wiped, garages wiped, being immobilized, getting killed by an invincible demigod, or even having your game outright crashed. Now the fun is suddenly over, and frustration ensues. You all report him and votekick him, but somehow he's still here being a d*ck, and either way, your decent lobby has fallen apart and the last hour or so of trying to get to said decent lobby has just been wasted. 1 month later, R* finally reviews the reports against Johnny F*ckwit and bans the account. Then he buys another copy, and goes right back to being a d*ck. Rinse, repeat.
Okay, so maybe the modder in your lobby actually isn't a jerk, he's trying to give R* the middle finger, he's giving away money and cars that aren't normally obtainable and generally being okay. Awesome! Except, R* detects that, because clearly their focus is on modded money, as this denies them Shark Card revenue, and not on modders that ruin others' experiences. Well, now they have either stripped your cash, possibly to less than you had before the modder gave you money you may not have even asked for, OR they reset your progress, weapons, cars, level, properties, and given you a warning, OR they have temporarily banned you for a week to a month. OR ALL 3. Great. (OR just plain perma-banned you.) Now you've been smugly punished for something you may not have even asked for. You may have even lost some of your genuinely hard earned or outright paid for content. Welp, better buy some more shark cards right!?
In agitated, hastily typed summary: Do not buy this game until these criticisms have been addressed in some way. Possibly not even then. If you feel you still stand to gain some solid entertainment from this title, as it IS rather fun at times, or it WAS at least, please do not spend more than $30-$40 total on your GTAV/O experience. You have nothing to gain. The community is mostly shoot on sight hostile, friends are typically a must, assuming you can connect to them, the DLC items become more expensive with each update, despite grind revenue not scaling at the same rate, and modders, unfair bans, and totally absent support are the ever-present reality of this title. I had a lot of fun with it initially. I still can from time to time. But more often than not, as of late, my experience has been one of mostly defeated frustration. Please do not support this company.

Mars: Where everything is made from Styrofoam and Pritstick. It was nice to revisit this game. Destruction is still really fun 8 years later, but the game doesn't really have a lot going for it otherwise. Apart from the ability to blow every building into tiny little pieces, it's a fairly basic, generic, and rather bland open world game, both mechanically and thematically. Missions really lack excitement too, which goes for most of the side missions as well.
Still, it can be a pretty fun game too. The destruction physics and the primal pleasure of setting it all in motion is entertaining enough to carry the game through its duration. Just don't go into it expecting anything you can really sink your teeth into and immerse yourself in. It's an amusing time waster at best, that you should probably switch onto Easy difficulty and just go on Thor-inspired rampages with your Mjölnir replica.

As a soldier in the Army, I can say this does not bode true to how the average 11B works...
This is a game designed for SpecOps/SpecFor elements like the Green Berets, Navy SEALs, MARSOC, or Rangers... The 11B doesn't do this kind of work.
If the Devs wanted to provided a great game for regular infantry operations, they should have expanded the play style and design, making grand campaigns like ArmA over a wide expanse of an AO, maybe even utilizing real time AO's in Afghanistan and Iraq with similar mission parameters...
Or they could've done that, but made a ranking board or something similar to For Honor, where OpFor and Coalition/US forces are fighting for control of zones and sectors of a particular country, and in so doing, multiplayer games determine the flow of the battlefield...
But this? This isn't remotely anywhere near what we do in the Army, even for training or real time operations... This is Police and SpecFor operations...
They took the game and small team ops from Counter Strike and Rainbow Six, utilized the realism in Arma (simplified for easier access and more casual play), and provided Call of Duty sized maps that are about as confusing as a Battlefield map in full swing...
I am not angry... I'm just disappointed and wished they could've done better to the true nature of the average 11B and the Army in general...

I bought this game on the release day, after someone recommended it to me.
I expected the classic 'early access' title with 2-3 hours of fun and then putting it back in the shelf.
When i started the game I was greeted by a clean main menu, and started a single player universe (all procedural generated) and went through the tutorial, which made many things easier, but left some things out, for example how to turn slanted blocks or that you have to hire trained captains to let AI drive your ship.
I got my ship up and running (it was a terrible dinghy, but i liked it) and mined some iron i went towards the middle of the galaxy to find that 'Avorion' material and be done with the game. Then i got distracted. Horribly. Instead of just flying to the center, i have built a fleet of mining and warships, and stop for long times each sector to get everything done that can be done. There are random events and distress calls.
In this game you can do almost everything (like in Freelancer, just with building your own ships), it even has a top down tactical view for when you command a fleet in battle. You can do trading, mining, scavenging, fight pirates or become one.
And this is not even finished. I really enjoy the game, and look forward to what's to come.

This is my review of SNOW, an Early Access game about skis.
The game is very hard to review without being picky, it's good and bad.

-The game was fun and was very in depth,

Cons:
-Multiplayer was slow and clunky,

-Graphics settings are low by default, I had to do alot of tweaking to make it run,
-No walk mode, I can't take in my surroundings while I am slipping around can I?
Overall, I would recommend this game but not until loads of errors are ironed out of the game.

The game overall is very fun indeed and the PC version is the one to get, provided your computer can run it. There's a lot to like, and sure it may not be the best in the series for some users but it's a game I liked quite a lot. (Although IV is my fav.)
However, the structure of GTA: Online and recent actions by Take-Two prevent me from recommending this game.
Any "free" dlc added to the game is only accessable via the Online mode, none of it is added to singleplayer. This content must be bought with in game currency which requires the user to either waste hours grinding away or to submit to Take Two and purchase Shark Cards.
Recent comments from Strauss Zelnick, CEO of Take-Two, stating that he feels that the publisher is "undermonetising" its userbase really do not do the sentiment towards this game and the publisher any favours. Essentially any player who is not yet buying shark cards are seen as unchopped wood or a cow yet to be milked by him.
Finally, the C&D towards OpenIV, a program that has existed for years and allowed for singleplayer mods across many games made by Rockstar's studios is the nail in the coffin. Rockstar and T2 can beat about the bush and blatantly lie to news outlets and us users but the fact that this specific tool was targeted at this particular time does appear to be T2's way of preventing single player users from enjoying content otherwise hidden behind Shark Card paywalls.
Play the game, by all means. Just do it in a way that involves Take Two not gaining any income.
TL;DR:
T2 want the entire userbase of GTA V to be buying shark cards, their actions and recent dialogue to the public clearly demonstrate this. The games industry is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and this is par for the course for this sort of thing but it still shouldn't be supported. Don't give them your money.

This is what SPAZ2 should have been like. Honestly.
I did not like SPAZ2 and ended up refunding it. SPAZ2 for me didn't capture game magic like SPAZ did.
Avorion pretty much manages to do that, capture that game magic that hooks you.
It is Early Access though, which shows as some minor glitches and design oversights.
Two glitches I've come across: derpy trader AI getting stuck with it's pathing in front of trading stations and sometimes stations dont get docking bay because they are made through RNG.
Design oversight: Stations don't do business with you if you have too many weapons on your ship, meaning you have to strip off your weapons EACH TIME you want to do business with a station (hire crew and sometimes trade upgrades/turrets, though sometimes latter one works even with weapons). This is really annoying.
But I'll give developer benefit of the doubt, this has just come to Early Access and say this game will be at least polished upon.
TL;DR: If you liked SPAZ1 and were not really impressed with SPAZ2 (or even if you were) I'd recommend this for you. However, if this game doesn't get improved upon, I might re-review this game and think again.

If you try to protect yourself with bombs from giant spiders, shop keepers will think you are a terrorist and kill you faster than you can even blink with their shotguns. If you try to pick up golden treasures that make booby traps activate, it will destroy any shops nearby and will cause them to kill you again as you are always a "terrorist". If you anger one shop keeper, they will forever kill you in every level you advance to. If you die, everything resets and you go back to level 1 like nothing happened..except your countless deaths of course. The weapon they give you is a whip that can reach about 2 milimeters in front of you, so be prepared to get hit by bats constantly. I did that, and it can still handle a fairly high load of units, but at a certain point the framerate will tank. combat is rather clunky, you cannot control your units, they just march forward, shoot whoever is closest in range, and continue on, or they sit in one spot, and shoot whoever is closest.
Base building is finicky as all hell. Building a big wall is a pain as you try and move your block over the right spot for it to be ontop of another, and one or two pixels off it might place on the ground instead. There is no delete button, so you have to click one of the soldier types to unselect the block, then click the block to select that individual block, and rinse and repeat until done deleting. Same for units.

I have little to no artistic talent, and was waiting on my graphics artist to simply animate some bending branches for a long time as other priorities came first. Eventually I decided to attempt animating them myelf using the static images she'd given me, and with a bit of photoshop chopping and the use of Spriter Pro I got the results I wanted.
There's definitely a lot of room for improvement on the software, primarily in the interface, but it has proven incredibly useful to me and I would highly recommend it.

Decent tool if you want to create some quick, easy, animations. Just make sure you understand one thing: this tool is for creating 2D VECTOR animation, not pixel.
Other than that it is pretty good. You can select any anchor area for an object so that it will rotate around that point (good for limb movement) and set it to all objects. You have hierarchical layering, multiple animations per entity, all sorts of nice goodies.
The only downside to this tool is that, on a few occasions, it crashed on me (so save OFTEN) as well as the export process, which could use some improvement.
TL;DR: look it up on youtube.

This product is AMAZING. I found it extremely easy to get used to. It helped me bring my lame game art to life with ease, which, in turn, allowed me to better my skills at making said game art. Even though I only scratched the surface of its abilities, I was able to do many things with the program. I would definitely recommend this to other gamemaking hobbyists.

It's a simple program. It's relatively cheap, it's fast, and it's easy. For a novice like me, spriter is easy to use and does what I need it to.
I'm too new to this kind of thing to really compare the software's capabilities to other programs on the market, so if you are a professional, look for some more informed reviews.

I'm using Spriter Pro to animate characters for a school project. It doesn't take long to learn, and you can create some really nice animations with it. And it does make some decent pixel art out of them, they don't turn all blurry and such. Looks nice and crisp.
This software  is great for Game Development, and even full on animations like youtube videos.

I bought this game at the begining of December and I knew what I was getting into. I knew of the rage I would have and how much work I needed to put into it. I expected what most people expected. But what I didn't expect to get out of the game was a moral.... a very deep one. But let me explain it all and trust me, there is a lot to explain. Look at what you climb over and what you experience, you experience climbing over everyday objects and not so regular environments. If you notice in real life these items sometimes cause you pain. Your computer has an 8 hour update that you need to wait through, you don't notice a lump or fold in the rug and trip over it, you stub your toe on a table, chair, or wall, your door hinge has an annoying squeek that won't go away. But these are examples of how the objects effect you physically, how would objects affect you emotionlly? Let's say you have a traumatic event where you could have changed the outcome but didn't or you have any of the starting over incidents from the begining of the game. You look upon those events and those events are engraved in your memory and you will remember them at different times in your life, and thats what I think the world built around you in Getting Over It With Bennett Foddy represents, someones mind. A mine can be described as a mess of thoughts and memories but it is not just a mess, but an organized one. Notice how places in Getting over it are segmented into parts but are still jumbled up and unorganized in some ways, this is the reason why I think the place you "Get Over" is actually someones mind made into a world. But that was just a side point that I wanted to talk about before getting to the main point. My main point is how everyone who buys this game plays and how different each one is. When you look around the web, you notice the same thing from every video you watch. A slow buildup of rage until they can't take it and give up forever or pursue onwards hoping for the victory of "Getting Over It". You also notice speedruns online where people finish the game in under 3 minutes, there good at it because they trained at it until finally figuring out the best actions to take in the game. But when people see these people play the game they think " This looks easy now, all I have to do is do what he does and I will be good to go!" Only... It dosen't work like that. The way how you play isn't determined by someone elses skills and accomplishments. You need to figure out those problems on your own. It's like cheating on a test, even though someone else shows you the solution you can't ever be sure if it is right until it is tested. But there was one thing that I though of that went off like a bombshell in my brain when I realized the true story and message this game was trying to tell. If we take my last point about everyones accomplishments being different notice how I phrased the task of "Getting Over It" as a "Problem?" well this is why. When people see those people do the game in 3 minutes they think they can copy what they did... but they can't because THERE play style and THERE tasks depend on THEMSELF, not others because they have there own PROBLEMS. listen to the title of this game again "Getting Over It" do you know what you do when you mistakes you GET OVER IT and move on. I can make a connection with that name to the gameplay. Let's say you fall off the steep mountain before the church and go all the way back to the begining and you don't know what to do with your emotions of anger or sadness. but guess what, you complaining about it won't help you so you GET OVER IT and move on. That statment is the moral of Getting Over It you continue on even when you make mistakes. But it goes deeper into my final point of this review. When you make a mistake, even big ones you get over it and LEARN from it. That aspect of learning is what we use to "Get Over It" in fact with this we can figure out what "it" in "Getting Over It" means. Players of this game learn from falling and failing that they learn what to do and what not to do and with that new information we can get over our mistakes and move on. Using all of are knowlage learned we will eventually "Get Over It". So what we are getting over in the title "Getting Over It" is our past mistakes. We make bad mistakes and nobody is perfect and get it all correct on there first try. So when you get over your problems and past mistakes, you will truely succeed and move on, and you thought when you bought this 8 dollar rage game that a moral that goes that deep would never be there in the first place. Merry Christmas and thank you to all of the creators of "Getting Over It" for giving us the moral to never think about a mistake for to long and to learn from it and move on. -The True One

Pretty much all of my game time was during their multi-year Open Beta, during which I had obtained nearly all of the Achievements. This is one of the few FPS games that requires a rather realistic approach to fire fights, whether it's CQC or open battle fields. Cover is your friend, mounting to cover for a stable & secure firing position (with ability to duck while maintaining cover lock) is your lover, and suppressive fire is your god.
Grenades and allies flanking your target/adversary are also great. So is walking/crouching to maintain stealth, unless you like giving away your position by running in full battle-rattle.
I don't have a list of Pro/Con to give, namely because I haven't actively played in a while since release. I probably have <5hrs play time since official release, though it did handle pretty much the same as when I lived in OB.
All I can say is, if you want to play an FPS that isn't some bullethell nonsense where it's all about taking 19 bullets while you put 20 into your opponent, full of spawn-camping tea-bagging scrubs, then I would definitely recommend this.

This is what Starmade meant to be, but couldn't do.
I just watched a rival faction warp in a fleet of ships and start attacking the system I was in, escalating into a 15-minute dogfight with the defenders calling in reinforcement and eventually winning. I was in awe of the fight, the aftermath, and the faction's war. Sifting through the broken wreckage with my tiny scavenger...it felt real.
Avorion is a 3D procedural exploration, combat, and trading game set in space. There is a nearly endless list of things you can do, and an amazing amount of content. The game is beautiful, with a blocky, colorful art style which heavily reminds me of the graphics of pre-2006 EVE Online. But unlike the older game it reminds me of, this has 21st century polish to the art style, and despite the classic look never feels old.
And speaking of polished, this is one of the best optimized games I have ever seen. I know I run this on a very high end machine, but literally nothing ever drops me below 60 FPS. Even more than 25 AI in full combat in a system with thousands of things floating around it. It's a common problem with games that feature so many objects to have lag spikes and glitchy movement. This game has none of that, and moves fluidly.
Glitches are practical nonexistent. I played for 12 hours in two days, and as of writing this I have not encountered a single major glitch. Nuff said.
The world feels fleshed out and real; there are conflicts, and some story. The galaxy you play in is huge. The progression your goal takes time and you can't just skip everything and win anyway. There is both a progression of materials, with you gaining more and more strong equipment as you go, and loot tiers for those items, with greater rewards for your harder work.
The game has a fully functioning loot system for ship parts you can take from destroyed enemies, a full 100+ items commodities system for trading, and a plethora of items and weapons. I have hundreds and am still finding new things constantly. The physical ship building is not done with items, and rather is done completely custom by you. It costs money  and raw materials and you can make any parts your heart desires.
The building features a somewhat unique solution to age old design limits: unlocked scaling. You take a material, and scale it to whatever size you need. Other games have parts at certain sizes, but this game lets you custom make them at nearly anything you could need. Their functionality is then based on that custom size. So if you made a 3x3x3 shield generator, it wouldn't be as powerful as a 3x3x9 shield generator. This keeps everything fair while still allowing huge freedom of design.
The building is only part of the game though, and after more than 10 hours of play I have only needed to make three ships. Combat is a main part of the game, and is very fun. Combat is fast-paced and with nutonian physics requires some thought. Equal fights are won with skill and strategy. Enemies are hugely varied, just like the weapons at your disposal to dispatch them. Pick sides and draw conclusions about who to shoot, or be a pirate and shoot everyone because it's fun! <3
Now for the few breif downsides of this game:
>The UI could do with some love.
>I would like a bloom intensity option in the settings. Some of my ships can get annoyingly bright with large amounts of  white Titanium thrusters.
>It's a 0.10 Beta.
Think about that last one for a second... all of this and the game is A F***ING 0.10 BETA. No part of this game feels like it's one-tenth the way done. This is an early access game the same way Besiege is an early access game. A fleshed out, well-made, heavily polished, fun game. Future content is coming, and the devs are working closely with people.
To long, didn't read version:
Buy it, it's f***ing awesome. It's like a 3D version of Reassembly, and just as addictive. Worth the price, devs are awesome, game is huge.
9/10 now, 10/10 when it's complete.
And one last footnote about the soundtrack. The game uses a soundtrack featuring a lot of music from Machinimasound (Look them up on YouTube). It was beyond amazing to hear songs I already liked and listened to included in a game. So far I have heard and identified the songs Anomaly Detected, Exigence and Hyperdrive. There are probably more. (And whoever picked Hyperdrive, you sir, need a high-five.)

I am travelling the stars. Mapping out the galaxy, taking note of good places to start up. I end up finding a hidden mass signature. Thinking nothing of it, I investigate anyway. I find nothing but an empty asteroid field. Preparing to jump back on track, I see a large object peeking from an asteroid. I moved to check it out, carelessly. I mean, who's gonna mess with my Trinium corvette in a far part of the galaxy? I move towards the object, and it puzzles me. It seems close by, but moving closer, it's distance seems to be fixed. Finally making it, the thing would make a planet look like a pebble (exaggerating a bit). It had holes big enough for me to fit my ship in, quite easily. I looked everywhere inside. It could have been the Death Star for all I knew. Filled with crew quarters, pillars connecting various walls, huge hallways, and fighter hangers. I eventually made it to the center of the ship-station-thing. The center was a ball of sorts. It looked to be just an oversized Hyperspace Core. Eventually, I decided to leave, as there was nothing of interest other than the aesthetically pleasing station. Finding my way out (not sure why I didnt just jump from the inside), I come back into view of the not-so-empty asteroid field. I press the jump button, but it doesnt go through? Could the station have a functioning jammer? Doubtful, it was still labelled as Wreckage. Perplexed of the situation, a small ship comes into view. Prepared to fight, I start approaching. This little iron/titanium ship just made a huge mistake. I approach the ship, but it runs. I give chase, being faster than the little guy. He uses asteroids as cover but I don't fire just yet. He boosts his way clear of the asteroids and I'm just behind him. This is it. All of a sudden, a ship jumps into view, right in front of him. Not a ship. A behemoth. It moves slowly, but dwarfs me. It has more guns than the average American. I turn and run, back to the remnants of the mega station. The station, being bigger than this baby behemoth, provides plenty of cover. But now I'm trapped. There is no escape. Jumping is not possible. And leaving will result in death. The only thing I can do is wait. Wait to die. Now, here I am, waiting for my aggressors to find me, as they slowly chip away the heavy armour of this monstrousity. This graveyard. My new home. For eternity.

Sniper Elite 3 is a rich, deeply entertaining third-person shooter that is sure to please even the most demanding gamers. Unlike many franchises, Sniper Elite continues to get better with each sequel while expanding on its original recipe for success. Naturally the graphics are much improved, but overall gameplay and concepts core to the game have also received major upgrades.
The much-loved "Kill Cam" is back and better than ever, giving gamers a rush of adrenaline and satisfaction after a successful target elimination in true sniper fashion. The stealth component of the game is also better than either of its predecessors and can play a vital role in a mission's success depending on the gamer's style of play. Replay value is extremely high for this game with the inclusion of steam achievements, co-op play and several options for multiplayer.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game personally and while I do recommend this game to those who enjoy action/adventure games,  I feel it is important to inform you that the game is not without its flaws and let-downs. as well. The awesome graphics come at a price. Those who are running older systems may experience lag or crashes due to the high CPU and RAM usage. I would strongly suggest passing on this game if your system does not meet the minimum system requirements listed by the publisher. Also, expect a few minor bugs, typically associated with troop ai and steam achievements. And most disappointing of all, while claiming to be a "sniper" game and containing some aspects that suggest that it is, most often you will find yourself armed with a silenced pistol or sneaking up behind enemies for hand-to-hand kills if you choose to play missions in a stealthy manner.
Overall, this is a very fun game and will give you many hours of enjoyment, especially if you pick up the extra DLC missions as well. However, I would only recommend picking this game up when it is on sale due to the reasons listed above and knowing that the base game only comes with eight missions for the single player campaign. In my opinion it is way over-priced ($49.99 USD) for a game that is over 8 months old on Steam and is also available on XBox 360, PS3, and PS4 which means finding a used copy for a console at a much cheaper price can easily be done.
The Sniper Elite series continues to improve and its success and popularity are growing. This is definitely one to keep an eye on and I hope to see a Sniper Elite 4 in the near future> For an action/stealth war game it is still only average in my opinion. It is dressed up nicely and a lot of fun but let's face it, there is still a lot that can be done to enrich the quality of this game. Camoflauge serves absolutely no purpose, enemies all have eagle eyes and can instantly spot you from several hundred yards away when even slightly out of cover, and for a game who's own namesake emphasizes the "sniper" concept, this game falls way short in actually delivering upon that in much of the mission objectives. It plays out as more of a commando or special forces type of game than an actual sniper game. All of that being said, I still recommend this game to all those who enjoy third-person shooters. Its that good!

Ah Spelunky - all that you are lacking is an Indiana Jones soundtrack ;)

Spelunky is a platform game set in an ever-changing underground maze. There is lots to keep you entertained and even more to kill you over and over again. And thats were you notice how addictive the game is - because you keep on coming back for more punishment. Always edging a bit closer. Always discovering something new.
The environment is fully destructable - so you always have a number of options. Having said that - time is always of the essence so its reflex time galore when the going gets tough.
One of the other wonderful thing about the game is the amount of "mishaps" one can easily fall prey to. Ever blasted yourself of a ledge thanks to the use of a shotgun? Boulder Trap sprung and shopkeeper out to teach you the shotgun macarena?
If you have played Spelunky before - this game has updated graphics and a few new surprises.
For those of you who havent - give it a go - we all need a little bit of adventure in our lives ;)

If you're looking for a few hours of chill, visually satisfying classic Hidden Object / Point & Click game, House of 1,000 Doors is for you. It's perfect for what it is — relaxing and simple fun.
The game is very beautiful to look at; sometimes Hidden Object games tend to look a bit mix-and-match but the art in this one is just lovely. The puzzles were quite easy (only one or two required more thinking) but not particularly boring, so I enjoyed them too.
My biggest issue by far is with the writing — it's incredibly weak especially when compared to the visual side of the game. The language used was usually simple and clunky and took something away from the atmosphere (It didn't help that the voice acting was also uninspiring at best). Overall the story was inconsistent and utterly uninteresting; each of the 'cases' had some juicy elements but they were wasted on hasty conclusions and unintentional humor. Now, this wasn't a huge issue for me since I was really playing the game for other reasons, but I really wish they would have put more effort into writing.
Overall; a fun & relaxing experience, can recommend for the fans of the genre.

No one talks about the long term support and updates we've seen over the years.  I purchased this in 2012.  Every year they give an update to the core engine and all your DLC rolls over. The gameplay is roughly what you'd expect. Just like setting soldiers up as a kid, and that's cool.
Thing is, you don't control your troops once you kick off the battle, at all. You have a toggle switch that you use when you're placing units, that is set to either 'offense' (walk towards the enemy base) or 'defense' (stand and wait). Now this is when you're PLACING units. So don't put your units down and then hit the toggle switch.
So there's one button. That's it. And it's buggy. After the first wave of enemy troops is wiped out, you get to rebuild and add more troops and so on. Then the second wave kicks off, where you get all of the troops from the first wave, you kill them all, then another wave of troops shows up without a break on your end. When the second wave hits, all of your troops default to 'offense', walk all over your fortifications, crushing them, and proceed to get shot to pieces.
Ordinarily I wouldn't be this bothered over a bug. But there's only ONE BUTTON AND TWO SETTINGS FOR IT. That's all you can do strategically as a player. So how does that not work right?
It's like, guys, you had one job.
AFAIK Wooden Battles is not in early access. So if even something that basic doesn't work properly, that you can uncover in 5 minutes of play, then what other issues are waiting for me? And how much effort will be made to fix them, given the game is complete? I don't know, but I'm not paying money to find out.

A good little puzzle game. Only took 9 hours to finish and is on the easy side, but it was enjoyable with nice aesthetics and sound, and interesting little short stories (it's almost like a ghost tale anthology.) It's not a scary game, but there is still enough of a supernatural theme to get your Halloween on.
It's not just a hidden object game, there are many types of puzzles, but where it shines is that it actually has well thought out level design. It's strung together in a more cohesive way than most games in this genre. There are also nice subtle intuitive hints, it's less about trying random things than it is about paying attention and exploring.

Play as Kate Reed, who receives a strange message regarding the veracity of the spiritual world. Kate being an author in the supernatural field couldn't lose the opportunity to see a real ghost with her own eyes. Things eventually turn to the
. A mysterious house that appears and disappears out of nowhere, leaving no trace or indication where the next stop will be.
It's up to Kate to uncover the real mystery behind this ghostly house, and discover her family spiritual past!
offers a tremendous concept for a ghost story, where a House with 1,000 Doors appears always at an unknown location, containing the trapped spirits of those who died with unfinished business, or are in too much pain to move on. The Player controlling Kate (which gave me a huge Dana Scully vibe) must free those spirits and at the same time gather information about her linked past, and relatives who were always connected to spirituality.
The game executes this concept really well, and leaves the player with a pretty cool story-plot to unveil and enjoy the 3D cutscenes that are actually pretty good visually.
Unfortunately the resolutions are locked to outdated ones, and the visuals are affected by it, stretching the image and losing overall quality. This being an Hidden Object Game surely could benefit from a resolution of 1280x720 as the bare minimum, this was released in 2014 after all!
probably developed this game using an old engine.
If weren't for such technical issues, this first chapter of
could easily be praised by its visuals, as they are very interesting, distinct and magical, varying from spooky hallways to snowy abandon houses. This adventure makes the player to travel through different times as well, and thus giving a much wider variety of interesting places to explore.
Although this game is named after 1000 doors, you can't go through all of them obviously, but the game still lets you explore quite a bit, with impressive detailed rooms, atmospherically perfect to give you the appropriate mood in each scene.
Hidden Object Scenes are included, but not as much as you would expect, making this more of an adventure. If the traditional and simplistic HoS are not enough, you can also search for objects connected through different dimensions.
The puzzles are also present, but slightly complex or difficult, which is great for new players or anyone looking for a simple and fun adventure without feeling the need to skip puzzles. Some of these puzzles are original and are very suitable for the story, others are jut plain generic we've seen dozens of times!
The Collector's Edition offers a Strategy Guide that may come in hand, and an extra chapter in the story, that focus more on the family side of the main character, as well as events such as the story of Kate's grandmother's, who started a spiritual journey, and therefore giving the player more answers. New areas are also available with new objectives to complete.
Overall
is a really good game that everyone who enjoys a ghostly adventure should try it, but keep in mind the poor resolutions.

Spelunky is a platform game set in an ever-changing underground maze. There is lots to keep you entertained and even more to kill you over and over again. And thats were you notice how addictive the game is - because you keep on coming back for more punishment. Always edging a bit closer. Always discovering something new.

I had never played a Sniper Elite game before so I had begun playing this game without knowing what to expect. Besides a barrage of sniping. The graphics in this game exceeds my expectation, the game truly delivers outstanding textures and effects that make the whole gaming experience more pleasureable and more enjoyable. I really enjoyed the bullet cam feature. It delivers a satisfying vibe along with every kill you perform. Though quite repetitive. Luckily, there is an option to lower the occurrences or even disable the feature. The missions are also quite repetitive. You'll find yourself performing the same objectives over and over again. The game is also rather short. There are only eight missions in total. Though each one of them can be made up of a long duration of time if you decide to take the stealth approach. Otherwise, you can blaze through each mission rather quickly if you decide to battle without the element of surprise. Another major problem is the spawning of enemies. Enemies would randomly spawn every time you fail. The enemies also tend to "camouflage" themselces by almost "merging" each other. Making the player to acknowledge that only one enemy is present. Overall, the story was great and in-depth and was well worth my time. The game isn't entirely bad. But I wouldn't recommend it either.

I've played through this game once as a marksman and once as a sniper elite. A little better than the 2nd game, but, some things I've noticed:
The character movement in here is sub-par (especially with the main sniper character, Carl Fairburne). Did they even have a motion capture team? It didn't look like it. Either he doesn't even move, or he moves too much when you lightly press a button.
The camera angle is also messed up. Sometimes, you need to shoot at an enemy on the right side of your screen, but the camera shows the left side, and blocks the right side, so you just have to shoot blindly.
There are plenty of invisible walls. Just from moving around, there are things that block your path, whether they're big or small things. My bullet seems to hit an invisible wall whenever I shoot at some faraway enemy. This is especially frustrating when shooting enemy snipers. They can shoot you, but you can't shoot them because of some invisible wall! I got so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off playing this game, that I pounded on my keyboard and broke one of the little feet!
Some of the times, I can not shoot from cover. If there is a low wall in front of me, I'll hit that instead of the enemy.
And if the enemy is right in front of you, like one foot away, the "fire" button suddenly gets disabled, and you can't shoot at all.
I can only sometimes vault over obstacles too. If it's not written into the game code, then I can't vault over a few, simple sandbags to get away from an enemy.
The music crescendoes at inappropriate times, so you'd think you got discovered by the enemy already.
Enemies can discover you whenever they get near you, even if you're in cover.
The main character totally sucks at hand-to-hand combat. Sure, you can sneak up behind an enemy and knife him, but, if you're already discovered, enemies can always block your fight moves.
And why is your suppressed pistol so inefficient at taking out the enemy, that you always need to shoot him with a headshot? If you shoot his torso, you need about 5 shots to kill him, even though he's 5 feet away. Same goes for your sniper rifle (at further range, of course); either one headshot or 2-3 body shots. And I don't think it's because of body armor. The artist didn't draw body armor on anyone in the game. The guns in this game sucks♥♥♥♥♥ totally not realistic.

The majority of Hidden Object games are pretty formulaic: make some progress, reach a dead end, find a spot where you look for a variety of items in a cluttered but well-drawn image, use at least one of the items to solve a puzzle, and repeat until you win the game. It's a casual experience that still feels rather rewarding at times, but for those that aren't a fan of the genre, why choose House of 1000 Doors over others? To start with, this game has a variety of environments to keep things interesting instead of just being stuck in a spooky house, thanks to the Doors (though there's not actually 1000 of them in this game). The plot has some supernatural elements, but doesn't feature any imagery that might scare younger players away. And the puzzles, while not all that challenging (especially if you choose to use hints), were still engaging enough to hold my interest.  The default price is a tad high, even for a "Collector's Edition", and especially since this game AND two of its sequels can be found in the "House of Snark 6-in-1 Bundle" (though there may be some quality issues and glitches with that pack). The operation of AWS and TPWS which are integral parts of driving trains are either missing or integrated incorrectly. AWS magnets at signals often don't even register. Obviously it has to be basic so it can be played by people of varying degrees of knowledge but there isn’t even an option to play a realistic mode.
The routes are never updated; the signals are mostly in the wrong place and act in un-characteristic ways. Platforms lengths, scenery, junctions are generally works of fiction. Train Simulator. It's a promising title isn't it if you love trains and want to be a train driver but otherwise can't, but behind this title, there is a game that although great for it's time, looks so cartoony and sterile with no sense of real-world immersion, and it is more of a game than a simulator, but what realistically what much else can you do with a train simualtor? This isn't FSX, you apply throttle and brake, but there's no real challenge to the game. Train driving is a very responsible job with roles more than just driving a train, but you don't get more than that in this simulator. Some random train faults or signal failures or something would be nice. Or even follow World of Subways with a character to walk about.
Passenger AI in this game is a disaster. They have the IQ of a teaspoon when they walk off the platform onto the tracks whilst somehow defying the laws of gravity in the process, and showing no care that a speeding train (or slowing one) is heading for them. Though let's face it, you wouldn't care if the train was just gonna go through you and not leave you with even a scratch. I mean it would be grim to include it, and this isn't Grand Theft Auto, so we can let the lack of an effect slide. It wouldn't be good advertising to show the windscreen wipers smearing blood on the front train window would it?
The trains themselves are for the most part nice, and the newer more interactive ones with realistic features such as lights on the front not affecting the lights on the back (you could drive with headlights on at both ends if you so wish, unless I am very wrong). But the sounds are also a disaster, I mean gaining access to depots is very difficult, and if we spent long enough waiting for access, DTG would lose customers cause of the demand for new DLC. Let's just say either waiting ages or forever for a train, or one with atrocious sounds. Whichever suits you best.
Routes are the best things in this game without a doubt, because despite the complex tools that most people aren't even bothered to make an attempt to get use to or understand, the outcome is very nice if done properly. In terms of detail and accuracy, routes are the strong point, because the quality assurance is vital in order to make profit. Some routes dominate others, but nowadays they're just getting too small or have too little trains. Germans have it worse, I mean why build something like Munich Augsburg at about 60km when you can build up to about 200km of railway? Time and money of course, but if there is any investors pumping money into DTG to do stuff like this, then by golly they are not paying them enough.
There is a route builder and scenario creator in this game, and this is probably the only time you will get something truly different. Unfortunately, most people decide "this is too complex" after spending five minutes trying to figure out how you make a train station or even put a train on the track. The tools are complex, but when you get use to them and become aware of them, then it's a nice little thing to do. Whoever thinks it needs to be simplified, try chatting to Network Rail telling them how hard you find it setting out cetenary wires which are created automatically in game without the need to get smelted iron for the overhead wires, and all the engineering plans and precision. Thought not, let's proceed.
Price of DLC is, like most people think, overpriced. Now everyone blames DTG for this, but I think it's Steam who set the price, and I do think this is unfair to pin the blame on DTG. I mean if a tube of Pringles is cheaper in Asda (or Walmart if you're an American reader) than it is in Tesco, clearly the crisp makers themselves aren't setting the prices, cause the one's selling need some cash as well. Unfortunately, unless you're well off and willing to spend a lot of money (which I have, but I'm quite the tight-wad) then you'll have to wait for Steam sales, cause otherwise you might need to have a word with your bank manager for spending over £2000 on Train Simulator DLC.
So overall, it's an alright game, but I wouldn't recommend it. Maybe I would've recommended it when it first came out, or even a few years after, but we're nearly in 2016, and with the UE4 version coming very soon, all the energy should really be put into that, kind of taking into account some of my points such as a playable character, less cartoony and more organic (something like dirt and grime and that, I mean this is UE4), more advanced trains with realistic interactivity, longer routes, and maybe more to do than just drive trains. I mean that should be the primary thing, but if every journey is the same, which for a real train driver it isn't cause anything can happen, then you're gonna get bored REAL FAST if you, like me, have no life and have spent around 1000 hours on the game in total already.
Final score... 5.5/10 (good, but really needs improvement).

The respawn points for which have recently been re-done need another look at. Also the removal of the majority of the health crates from cpature points makes taking damage while killing someone often fatal for the next firefight.
I have played an american para for a while now and generally use the carbine now I was a bit miffed when I realised that the auto fire conversion wasnt available for the para despite having every other one available to them (but understood why considering they get the johnson LMG.... eventually). Espeically as you often come up against the german FG42 which simply outmatches (at close and medium range) the carbine.
This led me to gettinng so frustrated with german paras all using the same weapon and utterly annihalating me everytime I would even get close to the capture point (and sometimes before id even landed) that I switched back to infantry to have a go with the BAR it was upon doing so that spawn point issue became apparent.
Now the system works well in cities beacuse it generally gives you a close option to where the fight is plus there is plenty of cover around, but where it really falls short is on large open maps where by the fight is so far away from the spawn option that by the time you've walked there its allready been swarmed with enemies or completely captured leading to another long walk to the next one or a quick death follwed by another even longer walk. Even using a vehicle can sometimes result in the same scenario.
To Illustrate my final point im going to use an example of a particular match:
Forward airfield - Germany vs America.
Germany have tanks and para's in large numbers against us having a load of infantry and a few tanks and para's of our own.
America is attacking germany defending. Doing well at first got upto the bridge which is when it completely turned round. The spawn point for the capture point immediatly after the bridge is directly on the centre of the bridge (for vehicles or infantry). To put the icing on the cake own paras then starting blaming the infantry because we couldnt defend our points whereby most of us where just simply trying to ge there.

Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy is an interesting kind of game that let me experience something which i don't often experience; Loss and Frustration. Not because i'm extremely intelligent and can handle any situation perfectly, but because i never risk anything. I just can't, being safe is just something i infinitely prefer more.
After watching a few people play this game i was pretty impressed, Bennett Foddy has created a game which perfectly encapsulates pure frustration and loss. Many games have frustration. But not many games have frustration appear from loss - especially to this magnitude.
The only time i'd ever really experienced so much frustration with a game was when my save on Dark Souls 2 got corrupted. About 500 hours of progress gone in a second. It's safe to say i hid that game away for a while. It was genuinely rage inducing having lost so much progress due to one small wall of text on my screen.
After about 13 minutes of progress with this game, i was climbing relatively steadily, when suddenly one small mismovement with my hand sent me plummeting straight down that mountain, to the very beginning. I wasn't infuriated, but i wasn't happy. And once again, Bennett Foddy reassured me to continue to progress to the steady, calming sounds of piano music. It's fine. All is good. You'll make it back up that mountain, and this time you'll double your progress.
This game taught me something. It's alright to fail. It's alright to make a massive slip up - whether it was your own fault or simply the world's fault - and end up plummeting back down to rock bottom. There's nothing wrong with that. But it's important that you dig your feet - or in this case your hammer - back into that ground and start climbing that mountain yet again. And one day, you'll reach the peak.
And i think that's a pretty good message to be taught, y'know? One that i think we can all learn.
I recommend it.

Ok to start this review off, Im just going to say i have much more than 4 hours of game play. For some reason this game doesnt count offline hours (had to play offline because of crud Australian internet). It doesnt even give you acheivements when you are offline but thats to be forgiven. Ive played atleast 30+ hours and know what this game is like. Every detail in this game so far is just amazing. I know the ships and asteroids arent the best they can be but the environments are amazing. I could stare at the planets all day lol. Anyways lets actully start writing a review instead of just droning on about random stuff xD
So first of all, this game is a spacey ship and fleet building game where you explore a near limitless galaxy, collecting different tiers of resources and getting more powerful as you go along. The closer you are to the center of the galaxy, the better the resources you find, but the enemies also get more difficult as you get closer to the center. Almost everything you find is procedurally (Randomly) generated which gives this game an awesome unique feel to it
Pro's:
+The ability to play offline singleplayer!!!! woo
+The fact that everything is procedurally generated. Its amazing. Ill go into more detail soon
+Multiplayer with friends or just online in general
+Ability to build your own ships and fleet, then combat RTS (Real time strategy) style or just normal 3rd person control style.
+The detail put into so many things. The physics of the game for example
+The galaxy is gigantic
+There are a large number of factions in game with different ship colors and designs, traits (smart, dumb, forgiving) who you can either make your enemy or ally. You can choose to rob cargo vessels and sell their items at smugglers dens. So you pretty much are able to be a pirate if you want to.
+Crew management
+Procedural modules and turrets with rarity and unique stats. So just like shoot and loot games like borderlands where the weapons are generated with different stats
+Even ships and stations are procedurally generated... Theres literally something new everywhere you go..
+You can construct your own space stations
+Everything. This is my favorite game and will be for a long time
Cons: (Because every review cant just be one sided)
-I was playing for a very long time and logged off on my singleplayer galaxy, and when i came back on the next day my ship was gone :( my 13 hours of work ship i rebuilt after losing my first one to asteroid collision. Bugs are to be expected and i have reported it
-Maybe the asteroids i suppose how they are just shapes pasted together but that isnt too bad of a problem. I dont mind it xD
-The video requirements too. It isnt a problem for me most of the time, but in large battles i get some bad FPS lag
-Oh and speaking of lag, sometimes i get some singleplayer server lag too, where everything is unresponsive. No damage numbers appear at all and ships just seem to spin out of control until it fixes its self and everything snaps back in place
To be honest the cons dont really effect me at all because this is such a great game and its still being developed. Its an early access game and these things dont bother me. With my ship dissapearing, it kind of bothered me a little. I dont even get the insurance that was on the ship. But the game is so fun that i dont even mind rebuilding
Ok im going to go into a bit more detail about things now so those of you who are still reading, you get to hear the amazing parts of the game now, that i find awesome.
Procedural generation: So earlier you heard me mention that i had awful Australian wifi. Because everything in this game is procedurally generated, the game barely takes away any of your data!! the game to download was about 200mb and it has so much more content than a 200mb game. Everything you encounter is generated in game. You're basically downloading a 200mb almost infinite universe generator. It would probably take real months to explore every single grid square of the galaxy.
Amazing detail: The physics in this game are awesome. The way thrusters work is cool as heck. Also weapons provide recoil too. If you have no power in your engines and thrusters and shoot a weapon on your ship, you will be pushed in the opposite directing of which you are firing
Anyways i should probably stop adding stuff to the pro's section before this review gets too long lol. I definitely reccomend people buy this game, and if you dont like your first few hours after buying this game you always have the option to refund. But i highly reccomend against that xD it really depends on what sort of games you like. I have been looking for a game like this for a long time and I am happy that i finally found it. I look forward to changes in the future, even though i wouldnt mind even if this game didnt change. But the developers of the game are working hard to add new features and fix any bugs you may encounter.
10/10

Alright, I am at 7.9 hours in, and despite getting rocked by the ai repeatedly, and forgetting to insure my ship. I am enjoying myself.
A little grindy early on it would seem, but so far I would reccomend the game to freelancer fans, it isn't quite up to that standard really, but for an alpha it seems close.

Long story short, I recommend this game in that if it keeps moving forward from where it started it will be very good but right now it’s definitely got some issues.
---
Being early access there are definitely a boatload of things that need to be tweaked. For example: the resource and ship progression. The starting resource (iron) is plentiful and very easy to come by. It’s also comically weak and doesn’t support the creation of energy blocks, which are needed for any kind of ship with more than basic capabilities. However, titanium (the next level) is really hard to come by in large quantities, which forces the player to roam into areas too advanced for their craft, and dying is perma-death for their ship.
Additionally, the pacing of building a ship is a bit off. It takes no time at all to quickly out class the resources and tech available to you. You’ll find that you have this “huge” ship with odds and ends stuck here and there, but can only pop three or four turrets on it and those turrets are wimpy. So you wander through this limbo time where the resources needed to advance are sparse and in dangerous territory, your ship is large and a bit cumbersome, your jump drives are really short range so you’re forced to follow pre-determined waygates, and your weaponry is paltry. So far that’s where I’ve spent about 6 of my current 10 hours of game play.
Next, quests and game play progression points are pretty rare and far-between. Besides the initial very basic tutorial nothing is explained and it’s left up to the player to figure it out, which is not a bad thing but this relatively simple game is laced with some complexity that makes connecting concept A and B a little difficult from time to time. Mate that with the fact that most message boards are empty and the game turns mostly in to flying in circles upgrading your ship arbitrarily with no real task in mind beyond the narrative that you create for yourself.
Also, the building mode itself could use some work. The camera has a fixed focus point that it pivots around, which can be moved, but it involves selecting the refocus option and then picking what block you want it to focus on. This makes it difficult to do on-the-fly fine tuning to your design since finding the correct camera angle can be a bit wonky. Next, there is no way to select a block and then move it. You can only place and delete. So if you put a turret on your ship, then decide you want it in a different spot, you have to first delete it then go grab it from your inventory again and re-place it. Also, selecting a block does not tell you what it is – is that turret you’re about to delete the good one or the one you want to swap out? Is that block a cargo bay or heavy armor since they look the same?
Finally, the UI leaves something to be desired. There is a lot of information that can be cumbersome to come by. For example: comparing the guns currently equipped on your ship to those in your inventory. In order to see what guns are currently active on your ship, you need to be in the “Ship” menu (hotkey P), but to see the guns in your inventory you need to be in the building mode and have the extended blocks menu open. Now, both can be opened at the same time, but it’s still a little frustrating that you have to open both just to see if what you picked up is better than what you have.
Another example of a UI that needs work is the station menu. In order to switch menus you need to completely leave the station, then re-dock (a simple task since you’re not moving), which means you need to re-“watch” (it’s scrolling text) the welcome dialog each time you want to switch from the message board to the resource sales tab to the upgrades tab. It’s not huge but it definitely adds time which can be annoying.
All-in-all the game is in a great starting spot. There is nothing massively broken or in a spot that can’t be fixed, it’ll just take time. So if you like space exploration games (think the X universe), show your support and give it a go.

TL:DR - Great game even in early access. It's full of features and depth. Great visuals for a voxel based game. Intersting diversity in factions and ships. Huge galaxy. Replayability.
Now that i've put about 10 hours into the game I feel I can leave a decent review. I don't review many games but this little gem is a great game. I am generally pretty wary of early access games after buying some that turned out to be piles of crap or devs gave up. This game, however, has surpassed my expectations. It has a lot of depth for such a simple seeming game. The galaxy is full of factions that interact with each other and you. Your relations to these factions are dependent upon your actions. Attack one and your relations deteriorate. Help them fight pirates or aliens and your relations improve. There are a slew of different stations that sell many different things including building you a randomly generated ship (if you want to go that route instead of build one). You can also mine for materials, salvage wrecked ships, explore and claim large meteors and then turn around and found a mine of your own or sell the meteor to a faction for a good chunk of change and reputation. There seems to be an underlying storyline here as well that is intriguing that I haven't delved into much.
Overall, this game has managed to keep me planted in my chair for hours on end..and this is no small feat.
Kudos to the devs for putting the attention to detail in this.

Well, I can't say that I am "all happy" with the game - so I'll try to give you some of the pro's and con's. I also have to say that I have only played "campaign" on intermediate difficulty level up to mission 6 so far:
Pros:
- good graphics, good physical effects (wind, noise etc)
- good choice of contemporary weapons with even more choice from DLCs
Con:
- it's not an open world. You can't climb rocks or get on top of some ridges/roofs if it's not "planned" by the producers.
- the enemies are very predictable e.g. the guards follow their routine tracks, only leave them when alert. There is no backup of enemies - if you kill all in an area, you can walk openly across the squares and guards from another area will stay in their designated places (as long they don't see you). And if you are used to other games like BF3 and use your weapons well (booby traps aso) - it's not too hard do kill! NOTE: that goes at least for intermediate difficulty!
- the game in this difficulty is very predictable in general: if you find e.g. an anti tank weapon - you can be sure you will need it quite soon!
Conclusion: if you like sniper games AND the WW2 flair - you will appreciate the graphics. If you need a real challenge, you may be rather disappointed by above limitations.

If you like sniping and crouching this is your game!
You can spend a long time hiding and collect info about patterns and positions of the enemy, as well as finding ammo and collectibles before even starting the elimination. What I really like is that you can choose not to kill everyone you see, but go in stealthy and focus on the objective at hand - if you are patient and skilled.
It has more or less (dependent of what you compare with) all elements of stealth, such as using masking sounds and hiding bodies as well as close take downs with hands and knife. Shoot search lights, jam power generators, and incapacitate wehicles beforethey even know you are there. Become a "ghost"!
You get to see where you hit bodies in animated slow motion. That is pretty cool, but might be somewhat irritating when you know that multiple enemies might be on your tail and you want to speed up things. However, the game actually let you be quick with a extremely good recollection of "where you were" when firing.
The different missions are expanding in length as you advance, but in the end you feel that there should have been a few more. You can replay with increased difficulty and that is something that I find appealing. No assistance in aiming and increased level of permanent death as resources and your life gets more precious.
I give this game a rewarding 8 of 10, and the last 2 is missing because I lack a few more missions and the ability to choose if you want to attack during night OR day. You are stuck with current time at hand. I also lack a "real" pistol with silencer (Better rate of fire) , but you will learn to use the provided one, which is true to  what was actually used by assassins during WWII.

*EDIT* Minor amendments after Episode 18 of my show.
I guess it's time for me to write a proper review of this game now.
To cut to the chase, I think that Train Simulator 2016 is one of the worse video games I've played in my life. Bearing in mind, I've played Sonic 06, Megaman & Bass, Spyro: Enter The Dragonfly just no name a few. TS2016 doesn't even qualify for the "So bad it's good" tier or even the visualy pleasing tier and has been simply getting worse and worse every year. Some of the problems I have with this game are as follows:
- Appauling opimization on high end computers. I've heard reports of people with GTX 960s having various issues with this game.
- No DX12 support or DX11 support.
- No Rebinable controls. In 2015.
- Most of the features, such as Career Mode, serve no purpose. The XP points you recieve do bugger all at the end of the day. Unlike in Pokemon, Final Fantasy or Chrono Trigger where XP points actually help you grow stronger in the game.
- Unrealistic physics.
- A very unstable engine. One could say you have a 50/50 chance of the game crashing whilst driving.
- Terrible loading times.
- Lack of respect for the source material for trains and routes (Great Western Mainline, North London Line and London To Brighton are good examples of this.)
- The game's downright INSULTING model for DLC. No, seriously, it's one of the worst. The company shove out DLC on a very frequent basis. Trains most of the time have unrealistic physics, sounds, consist formations and a lack of features. Routes are usually short, linear and offer the player to drive on...about 1 or 2 full services. Again, unacceptable for the money they're charging.

I think its only fair to edit and write a fresh review of this game and here is why I am now recommend it to those that want to play a train simulator on their computer and thus drive a train from their desktop PC (or an armchair for a gaming laptop). Good Points
- The game comes with a good selection of routes and trains to get you started
- Exceptional Amount Of Add-ons From Steam & Third Party Developers
- Game Runs Stable On Most Medium And High End Gaming PC's
Bad Points
- The game is prone to crashing on PC's with less than 8GB of RAM (I speak from experience)
- The DLC can be expensive for some budgets
- User-created content for the Steam Workshop is only compatible with the Assets available from Steam only (except for the Just Trains Class 60 Advanced Pack)
Overall Rating: 8/10.

It perfectly encapsulates the difficulties faced by true battlefield commadners; do you take forces from your flank to support your center and risk losing the flank, or do you leave everything and wait while reinforcements are called in and risk losing the center? Do you send in units to spot a forest that you know holds enemy forces so the tanks and infantry can shoot them, but risk losing the spotting unit, or do you make the enemy come to you? How are you going to resupply your units? A helicopter is faster than trucks or boats, but can be shot down by AA.
Overall a very fun and interesting game, with vast quantities of units to shoose from, both new and old, tried and true and prototypes.
