Overall, an extremely satisfying ARPG experience that will leave you wanting more. There's a reason this game has received many awards and such great reviews. If you haven't played TL2 yet, you need to. Here's a nitty-gritty breakdown review for those interested:
Pros
+ Great aesthetic (cartoony, mixed with beautiful skill effects)
+ LOTS of loot (plenty of upgrades are dropped while leveling)
+ Interesting classes (each class has a distinctive feel with several playstyles/viable builds)
+ Active modding community (just check out the Steam workshop page...)
+ Environment visuals, audio FX, music, etc. creates a solid gameplay experience
+ Pet system (allows for second inventory, buying necessities w/o going to town, etc.)
So-so
~ Storyline (enough to keep you interested)
~ Character build variety (much less variety than PoE, but akin to Diablo 2)
~ Low skill ceiling (this could be a negative or positive... may be nice for players new to ARPGs)
Cons
- Low multiplayer/online population (if playing solo, this will not be a negative)
- Minimal endgame compared to competitors (D3 and PoE will keep you playing longer)
- Hardcore ARPG fans will create characters and builds that end out feeling Godmode (difficulty does not scale very well even in the hardest, end-game zones) ... Note that I have played just over 100 hours. This game is AWESOME!!
I would like to start off by squashing the negative reviews.
Negative review type 1:  This game throws the new player into the middle of a dogfight, getting your first ship blown up during the tutorial.
- The galaxy is procedurally generated.  Which means, yes, there may be an invasion of pirates during your first go of the game.  There are 2 ways to get around this.  First way is, simply stay close to the stations in the starting sector that are guarded by friendly ships.  They will protect you.  The second is, just start a new game.  Once you learn the ropes, even starting in the middle of a pirate invasion, you will be able to survive with the newb ship you are granted.  Just stay with the game and you will have fun.
Negative review type 2:  The ships are blocky and they look like bricks in space.  Everything is chunky and blocky.  Graphics are bad.
-  The graphics are just fine.  Chunky ships are due to players who spend 20 minutes in the game and don't even take the time to adjust the parameters of the blocks they place on their ship.  The ship building system is actually very flexible, more on this later.
Negative review type 3:  This game is too big/vast, too much to do, it's overwhelming.
-  Seriously?  Giving a game a negative review because it's TOO BIG?  Grow up.  This is exactly what a game SHOULD be, vast, large, lots to do.  Give your head a shake.
Negative review type 4:  The game crashes, there are bugs.
-  It hasn't crashed on my system, not once.  And I have a low-medium end computer.  The difference with me and you is, my computer is virus free, my graphics drivers are up to date.  Everything is up to date.  I run regular virus/malware scans on my computer.  Try combofix/malwarebytes/c-cleaner/windows defender before thumbs downing this game because you can't figure out how to keep your computer up to speed.  The hardware req's for this game are minimal.
Negative review type 5:  All you ever do in this game is mine.
-  Yes, for the first bit, you are going to have to collect a large amount of iron to build your first capable ship.  There are stations that will buy your iron to pad your wallet as well.  It's important to go hunting for your first roid of titanium as quickly as possible so you can build energy generators and batteries, as well as hull hardeners.  The combat in this game once you hit this early-game milestone is amazing.  My ship just sits there soaking up damage with these items installed.  You can put these items on any type of ship you build.  So to say the combat is lacking, maybe try giving the game more than 5 minutes.  This isn't CoD in space.  You don't drop into the map and start capping your enemies.  This game isn't build on instant gratification.  You need to *work* towards your goal and at first, yes, some grinding is required.  But get past this and start building some capable ships, and the game opens up to you.
And now for my review:
This game is AMAZING!!   Did I say that already?  It's because it's true.  I typically play a game for 30 hours before I write a review, but I can feel within the first 10 hours of gameplay that this one is going to keep me coming back for a very long time.  I can see myself spending hundreds if not thousands of hours playing this one.  The ship building system is simple, not complicated, there are options for your build style.
To give you an idea, think of it this way.  Think minecraft.  If you spend 1 stack of materials building a hut, guess what.  You are going to get a blocky build.  And that's kindof the way it is with this game.  Except that even if you decide to place just a handful of blocks to build your first couple of ships, you have vast options.  You can resize the blocks any way you like.  Want your object long and thin?  You can do that.  Tall and chunky?  You can do that.  Thin, large, up, down, wide, narrow, you can change ALL of these options *on the fly* when building your ships.  You can also save your ships to the template manager, so all you need to do when founding a new ship is pull up that template and poof, you have a pre-built ship, ready to roll.
Now if you spend a large amount of resources building a ship, you are going to get a thing of beauty.  You can build your ship however you want.  You aren't limited to just "blocks".  Like I said, the more resources you use, the larger your ship is, and the larger your ship is, the more intricate your design will be.  You may not get hard curves on your ship, but pretty close.
The mission system in this game is really cool.  You will get random broadcasts for help every now and then, which you will have to largely ignore for the first while until you explore your instance of the galaxy enough to reveal some of the jump gates, and until you get some of the end game materials to build hyperdrive blocks which extend your jump range.  There are also stations which offer missions as well.  You can also just fly to a random sector and start attacking the enemies present there, and in doing so you will increase your standings towards the faction that owns that sector.
This game allows you to build your own stations, which are easy to do.  It also allows you to build multiple ships.  I haven't gotten to the fleet management portion of the game yet so I can't say how easy or difficult it is to manage your fleets and stations but I'm sure it's either there, or will be there.
There is a vast system of trade in this game.  Every station sells resources, the resources that it produces.  It will then buy resources, the resources it needs for production.  If the station runs out of its needed resources, it will adjust the buy price of the needed resources to high, so that you are more likely to sell what you have to that station.  It's a very solid system, and looks much like the X3 titles.  I'm not sure how automated traders work, as I haven't gotten to that portion of things yet, so I can't review that.
In general this is a real mix of minecraft and X3.  It's simple enough to build ships yet it's a very powerful system.  The way the core mechanics works is amazing.  Also, the playable area is VAST, and yet there are several ways of getting around, from jump gates to jump drives.  All in all there are thousands of sectors to explore, many hidden objects, upgrades to the ship, and so many different things to do.  I highly recommend this game.

I’ve recently got my mom to start playing Hidden Objects Games (HOGs for short) – which means I’ve been inadvertently playing them right along with her. Steam (and more importantly, bundle sites) are so flooded with the damned things that I’ve got dozens in my account without ever making a conscious effort.
So I might as well do a month-long writeup of the HOGs that I’ve got.
(We just don’t know)
Is that a daft question? I mean, they’re just this:
Right? At least, that's what I kinda assumed. Finding a bunch of hidden objects is right there in the name of the genre. Well… not really.
HOGs like "House of a Thousand doors" are basically all about a set of arbitrary obstacles, overcome by “special keys”, gathered through lite adventure game puzzles, arbitrary “real” puzzles of the sort you might find in a puzzle book for 4th graders, and relatively fairly few scattered hidden object hunts. Check out this screen:
I'm going to need to find a pendulum for the clock, a record for the player, a way to put out the fire, a spring for the door, weights for the cales, some thing or another for the creepy hands-clock thing on the right, and an axe to murder the guy drinking the coffee (I don't need the coffee, but his tie has a button needed to complete a puzzle later on).
Some of these objects can be found in hidden objects mini-games like the one above. Some just hang out in new screens you access. Some are acquired after completing a basic mosaic / numbers substitution / item rearranging / maze completion puzzles. Still others (and this is really fun) show up on totally unrelated screens after you've completed an arbitrary number of puzzles. Thankfully, you have a big old recharging
in the corner of the screen, telling you what to do and where to go next. You can easily play through the game with only a very vague understanding of what's going on, why you're here, what you're doing and where you're supposed to go next, merely hammering the hint button in order to progress further.
House of 1000 Doors: Family Secrets Collector's Edition (As an aside, every single HOG on steam is "Something of something: Subtitle here". I think there's a law and a regulatory commission) is literally the first HOG I ever played, and pretty much formed the standard for the rest - incoherent plot, semi-decent puzzles, interactive map (though you have to dig around a bit to use it) and a fairly fast "hint" button. All standard HOG features I came to expect in later games.
Obviously I'm reviewing this game first because the haunted thing fits the the whole October Halloween theme. I mean,  look at how horrified this very good actress is about
.
Seriously though, despite the fact that most HOGs fashion themselves in some trappings of Gothic horror - haunted mansions and spooky portals and creepy statues and other fuss - they're not exactly twitch stream jumpscare material. "Horrors of the Deep" isn't contending with SOMA, "Weird Park" is probably not as scary as...The Park, and Spooky Town Terrors aren't particularly spooky or terrifying. I suppose a generic horror-ish setting provides a good background for the detective / medium / writer (generally the protagonist is one of the three, if not all three at once) to investigate.
But I mostly introduced this game to my mom first because it had a semi-sane and heavily tutorialized introduction to the adventure-game-lite logic on which these games operate. Let me break it down for you, because I was genuinely dumbfounded by how it progressed.
The heroine receives a package, which you must cut open with a handy KNIFE. Inside is a a wind-up automatic typewriter (which were apparently a thing back in the 1920's?) with a message for you. USE the KEY on the typwriter to wind it up. No paper, and the typewriter ribbon is depleted of ink. OPEN the CUPBOARD, to recover a sheet of paper and some ink. Place the ribbon in the ink slot - you now need TWEEZERS to remove it without getting your hands dirty.
you're going to use your Golden Quill award as a key to your jewelry case, which contains your tweezers inside. Because it's never too early to introduce batshit adventure game logic.
The typewriter types out an invitation to a seance. When you arrive there, you don't speak to anyone (in fact, you don't even see anyone's face, just a bunch of hands reaching towards a crystal ball) and immediately start trying to figure out how to cut the power line leading to the ball. Once you do, a ghost of your dear departed granny appears. Having manifested your medium abilities (?) you are instructed to enter the House of 1000 doors - a spooky teleporting mansion that's about to show up next to the statue of Liberty - and uncover its secrets in order to exonerate your granny from some unspecified crimes she was accused of. The entire freaking intro had absolutely nothing to do with anything - granny could just as well had manifested in your cozy suburban home, with nothing of substance lost.
So whenever you see a review praising a HOGs storyline, treat it with a bit of caution. In the House trilogy, at least, the plots are scattershot bits and pieces, as arbitrary and interchangeable as the obstacles in your way. Maybe the game makers are operating in the Square-Enix "[s]cutscenes[/s] game screens first, plot later"  style.
The one thing that could have been unique about this game is the setting, but even that is a bit of a wash: Despite being set in the “House of 1000 doors” that can teleport to between space and time, and is full of inter-dimensional portals that the heroine is curiously incurious about, 90% of the game takes place in the same locale. Creepy mansion, creepy basement, creepy shed, short interlude for a creepy ghost train, creepy attic. Same old.
In terms of ease of use / help for casual players / my mom (because as a hardcore gamer, I naturally never had to resort to such measures) the game has an in-built walkthrough, a semi-hidden map that tells you which screens have something for you to do, and the big pulsing
recharges fairly fast and doesn't get used up if the hint is "go to different screen". (These are actually all fairly regular HOG features, just particularly well implemented. On the same note, whenever you need something to progress, the game is remarkably clear about what you need - another virtue that should be common enough, but still good to have)
So, not bad as an introduction, not really that brilliant either. Then again, I'm not a HOG connoisseur, so I'm sure the game is great / terrible by a set of measures I'm not familiar with. Pretty much every HOG you'll find on steam will have a "Very Positive" aggregate score, with the exception of a few stinkers which merit a "mixed" due to being literally impossible to play, so praise in reviews should be treated with a bit of caution.

Please note the fact that this review is BEFORE they add snowboards and other things.
Graphics:
If it isn't a gorgeous looking town in the distance then its the high resolution characters and incredible lighting.
Though i think that they could have done the single player crowds better with maybe a bit of A.I put in.
Game Engine/Feeling:
This is NOT an arcade ski game, in fact it is hard to say what type of ski game it is. I mean that in the game has points of Realism and moments of extreme glitchy hilarity. I do not know if the limitations of the engine was to blame for issues within the games physics for instance - Bouncing, no way to slide around without jumping, grinding feels like two magnetic fields opposing one another, or rocks that instantly kill you even if you are going VERY slow when you hit them.
What you do in the game:
Singleplayer has "Events" including things like time trials, freestyle, downhill (get to the bottom of the hill) and more.
Though it is fun to do these missions I think they need to change a few things.
- No instant restart if you fail the event (You have to mash "A" to get back to the top and it forces a timer you can skip instead of just letting you go instantly)
- Giving you another mission as a reward is not okay, that would be like cleaning your house and then being told to clean another house.
-Not enough credits as a reward each level ( At least give us 10 credits a level )
Multiplayer Does not have any missions or events to do with friends but lets you free roam and fast travel ( once you have found the place) to points on the HUGE map.
-Instant respawing in multiplayer helps ALOT
-Speeding down the hills and exploring the map is super fun with a friend
-Not being able to be in a party with friends makes it slightly rough around the edges to find your friend.
The menu and Micro-transactions:
-I can not praise this game enough for not shoving micro-transactions in your face and keeping them as an Extra Rather than a necessity. The micro-transactions in the game are JUST clothing and Drones that do the exact same thing as each other with no pay to win to be seen.
- The menu is clean and easy to navigate with a mouse or a controller (please don't play the game with a keyboard its just not as good)
Things they could add and or remove:
-More multiplayer maps, objectives and gamemodes
-Better physics and a better tutorial for showing you how to do tricks and such
- More items/objects as level up rewards
-Ragdoll physics in the multiplayer
-No -15 points for not landing tricks perfectly
-Personal servers for friends and allowing you to do  Events.
-A voice chat system for the game (not needed but would be nice to have in the game
-Steam Pictures on clothing

This game was somewhat similar to Lost Vikings in the sense that one player controls multiple characters to solve various puzzles. Here, though, you control two characters simultaneously, which I found neat. The controls are nothing too complicated, since all you really do is control each character with a different analogue stick and interaction button, and maybe move the camera if you want. As such, the game won't try and force a ton of tutorials on you, like most games nowadays, which is great for pacing purposes. The game's camera also positions itself appropriately for the different puzzles you encounter in the game, so that you can typically get an idea of what you are supposed to do and where you are supposed to go.
Story-wise, A Tale of Two Sons is pretty much about two brothers on a journey to find some magic water (I think it's magic, anyway...) to help cure their father of some sickness. This water is apparently very far away, so the boys have to put themselves in danger in various situations in order to obtain this water, and grand adventure ensues. Also, the younger brother is aquaphobic, which comes into play in some puzzles. It's a pretty basic story, for the most part, but the game does a pretty good job of developing the story and characters without much use of language. Characters are very emotive as they talk in their fictional language to each other, so even though you don't really understand what they are saying, you get how they are feeling or what they are trying to convey.
A Tale of Two Sons is also very visually appealing. Much of the game is pretty much about awing the player with the scenery. In fact, given that the automatic camera does its job quite well on its own, one would think the main purpose of the user-controlled camera would be to view all different angles of the scenery.
One of the only flaws I could find with this game is that it's a bit on the short side. I beat it in about two hours, and spent maybe an extra hour or so getting achievements I missed the first time. For the most part, you'll get most or all of the achievements the first time, since the game makes it very visible what divergent paths there are in your journey, and pretty much all these divergent paths lead to some sort of event that will get you an achievement. Of course, games like this tend to be on the short side, so it's not a big deal.
Another flaw I found was that the game occasionally glitched up in some areas. In particular, one of puzzle involved having a troll (?) character chase one of the brothers, but for some reason, that troll stopped moving at all, even when I was right in front of him. In another case, after climbing a ledge, one of the brothers somehow got stuck at the very end of the ledge, and there was nothing I could do to free him from that state. These glitches forced me to start over from an earlier checkpoint, which was a bit annoying. However, since checkpoints are reasonably spread out, these were only minor annoyances.
Overall, I would definitely recommend playing this game at least once. I'm not sure if I would have bought it at $15, which was its original price I saw it at, but at the $3 I bought it with, I felt it was worth the price.

Well, I think this is my first review ever that I have written on Steam. If you look at my time with Spriter, you can say I know what I am talking about with around 270 hours as of yet. Now this is going to be a little hard to give thumbs down to, but I have my reasons.
The best thing about Spriter is the price, you cant get another animating software this cheap ,except dragon bones which is free and this is where the problem comes in. Spriter is severely lacking in features. The most obvious one is meshing or free form deformation (if you don`t know what they mean, google it!). There is an alpha version of FFD in the app right now but it is very buggy and not that flexible. This alone sets Spriter back too much in my opinion.
And then comes numerous small limitations and weaknesses which add up and makes things even worse:
-Cant color the bones which makes it hard to discern them while animating.
-No good reliable plug in for exporting PSD files to Spriter (there is a community made one, but it is a bit buggy).
-Inability to mass-move the key frames and to change the distance (time) between them. It has to be done one by one.
-Bones need to be named manually, it would be much better if they were named after the image they are assigned to. Overall setting up the sprite takes way too long.
-Lack of various visual guides, this is very  crucial.
-Moving or rotating the bones are basically in the same mode, so for rotating the mouse has to be placed on the tip of the bone, for moving anywhere else on the bone works. This can be a pain in the neck as too often bone will rotate when they are meant to be moved and vice versa.
Spriter has its up sides of course, like how easy it is to attach new bones and images to an already made animation which is a huge time saver, the skinning works pretty good, the ability ot change the pivot points on images is awesome...
BUT, overall from my limited knowledge of Dragon Bones, Spriter does not have that many advantages over Dragon Bones, which makes it a hard sell. What is more disheartening is that Spriter is almost as old as Spine, and both were kickstarted about the same time and yet, Spine has gone to be the best animating software out there(Creature seems to be a good contender for Spine) while Spriter is still struggling with some basic stuff. I am afraid the gap between Spriter and Spine/Creature will get wider and wider. So when Spriter finally gets FFD, Spine/Creature will already have some new feature and so the cycles will continue. There has been talks about the devs doing Spriter 2 which will be a free upgrade for the owners of Spriter, but it remains to be seen how good it will turn out to be.
In the end, with a heavy heart I have to give this a thumbs down...I will get back to re-review when and if new features are added.
Update 1: With the latest version of Spriter, a few of the bugs I had has been fixed, I updated the review to reflect this.

I previously gave a positive review score but after playing this game for a considerable amount of time I have come to the conclusion that this isn't just a bad game but also one of the worst open-world games of all time. Here are the reasons:
- Artificially inflated difficulty. This game is easy and the enemies are cannon-fodder. So, how do you make this game challenging? Do you make the enemies smart, more tactical and passive-aggressive like the excellent AI of GTA V? Or, like every generic open-world game developer does, do you make the AI spawn in hundreds of number and write a single line of code telling it to beeline straight to the player's position? You can guess what the developer of this game went with.
- The guns are bad. This game's guns are ineffective and not fun to use at all. The only weapon that is good is the C4 explosive which you an detonate on your own after it sticks to a surface. Other weapons like the rocket-launcher, the electric gun, the grinder and other generic rifles are just plain bad and poorly designed. In this game, throughout, the only three weapons I always used were the hammer, C4 and pulse rifle which obliterates enemies in a single-hit.
- The story is the most generic you will ever see. Just skip through the cutscenes and trust me you will miss absolutely nothing. In fact, you can already guess what this game's story is and you will be right.
- What takes the cake in being the most poorly designed are the side activities. You have a game which relies on explosions so the side activities should be fun, right? Wrong! This game's side activities are poorly made and restrict you in several unfair ways. As a result, you don't have that much fun causing explosions. The best example of poorly designed side activities in this game are the DEMOLITION MASTERS side activity. It is the most poorly designed I have ever come across on. It's supposed to be some kind of puzzle side activity. However, it relies on hit and miss and can be completed on trial basis and pure luck. That is how I got through these atrocious and poorly designed side activities. And the side activities in the expansion pack are even worse.
- There is no marker or indication for collectibles on the map. This is bad because even if I start consulting a guide for collectibles, it is still a mess as I have collected some of them and so sometimes I would go to certain areas and start searching for a collectible only to realize after a while that I got it a long time ago. A simple indicator system that shows collectibles on the map should've been implemented. At the end of the game, I had so much scrap that I could've bought such a system from the vendor even for really high prices. But I guess if a developer is already too lazy to make a good or even a mid-tier decent game, asking this would be too much.

Well, talk about a late review. I've had this game for a long time, but after revisiting it I decided I should leave my two cents.

I'll say one thing right away. This game is flawed. Very flawed. The progression is a bit wonky, some of the challenges feel untested, the physics can be a bit odd and the difficulty can go from dying without knowing why to winning in a matter of seconds within a replay of the same mission. The story is bland, characters are bland, graphics are decent, but a bit flat. Normally it'd be nothing to write home about.

But there's a reason I came back to the game. Because it feels like 'Let the player have some bloody fun' was the first line in the design document. And that's far too rare these days.

It puts you down on a planet with the hammer of the Gods and a ton of explosives and your goal is to wreck just about everything. That's the story as far as I'm concerned; I'm liberating buildings from their foundations. And sure, I could fight enemies with boring machine guns and shotguns. Or I could attach explosives to their faces. Getting bored? Then here's a lightning gun. And a rocket launcher. And a saw blade gun. And a jet pack. And we'll just leave these mining robots, tanks and portable black holes laying around if the mood strikes you. Dying? Who cares? This is not a game to play seriously. This is a game to fart around in. Really, my main criticism is that it could've allowed more of that. Scrap all of the floaty racing challenges or, heaven forbid, -escort missions-. The game is good at breaking things and it should've fully embraced it. I'd want more upgrades to buy, more buildings to tear down, more salvage to... Salvage. I'd want weapons to go up to Ratchet & Clank levels of silly. I want armour that lets me shrug off tank rounds and upgrades that let me suplex the tank in revenge. No such thing as overkill. Let’s get Crazy!

Still, the destruction physics sadly remain relatively unique, even after all these years and, as mentioned, there are already quite a few fun toys in the game. So if you're looking to blow off some steam and you find the game on sale, I can recommend it. In short, the game is a puddle. Not very deep, but sometimes it can be fun to stomp around in. And possibly ruin someone's day.

The concept is very simple: you build spaceships and do whatever you want. The concept is simple, but the plethora of missions, factions, materials, goods and equipment in the game forces the player to plan ahead with some kind of overall strategy. You can pick from a buffet: mining, trade, questing, treasure hunting, looting, piracy, rescue, salvaging and even policing. Put whatever you want on your plate with the singular intention of making your empire fat.
If you're the enterprising type you will have a vast network of intergalactic trading posts, mobile merchants, producers and buyers to work with. Trading is a good way of improving relations with a faction. If you're the industrial type you can mine or salvage materials and/or equipment, either to sell or to use it yourself.
Battles are engaging, but be aware that the game physics oblige by Newton's second law of motion (almost), meaning the ships behave as if they were in space (almost). Something you don't see in a lot of games or movies/tv, but it adds a lot of strategy to the military gameplay when you have to consider inertia. Ships can be controlled directly by the player or commanded from a safe distance.
And as always, for my Linux peeps out there: yes, the games works nicely, even on arch. :)
EDIT: server games are pretty laggy, but doable if not so many players online.

"Here I am in the cursed house that is tormented by the angry ghosts, fearing for my life as I walk through its surprisingly pleasant and inviting corridors. I've stumbled upon a dine-room with a large table filled with all manner of food, surrounded by an ominous sculpture that keeps flashing its winking skeletal face at me... I think it’s trying to invite me on a date. The table is filled with exquisite food and wine, along with a gun, a whip, puzzle box, garter-belt, a horseshoe and... what kind of a dinner was this! There is even a dynamite sitting on a chair, what's a dynamite doing in a ghost house? This clearly makes no sense!!!... And... and.. there is a GOLD BAR under the table... I...uh... having problems to understand... are they wealthy, suicidal ghosts or... ooooh, shiny!"
This sum up my first impressions as I started playing House of 1000 Doors: confusion and frustration due to its internal inconsistencies. It wants to be a horror game, but most of the time plays like an easy-Sunday drama. It wants to be an adventure game with proper story and intriguing puzzles, and it also wants to be a by-the-numbers hidden object game. Most of the times these extremes clash against each other instead of working together, but somewhere along the way all of the game's elements balance out, and you get a hidden object puzzle game with intriguing collection of stories, pleasant look, decent traditional puzzles and rather well done cutscenes. The best parts are the short ghost stories that you encounter while you traverse the house and try to solve them, as they are creepy and unusual. They would make good Twilight Zone episodes easily!
There are some major downsides as well, biggest one coming from me not being convinced yet in the allure of hidden object games. I've played only one before House of 1000 Doors and didn't really like it. One of the biggest problems that game had, which also rears its ugly head in House of 1000 Doors is the repeating nature of side-trekking puzzles that force you to solve them more than once, and the story connected crucial inventory items that are popping up in the most illogical places and times, which is a death knell for the traditional adventure games.  While the visual look is rather nice, it is wildly inconsistent, producing next to zero horror atmosphere this game was clearly reaching for. Music is too chirpy and inappropriate in conveying a proper dark mood, In-game animations are bad, and the same goes for the voice acting. Some of the puzzles are unnecessarily complex and fiddly, but they are pale shadows to the puzzle masochism that Black Dahlia had.
But somehow, when you reach the end of this relatively short game, creepy and fairly original ghost stories that you meet along the way stay in your mind, leaving you with an overall positive experience. So yeah, House of 1000 Doors gets a pass for being an okay game, but the verdict for the value of the entire hidden object genre still hangs in the air. Maybe, if I encounter a few more of similarly good games in this genre, my cynical heart will mellow.

In the Keep first you must find a scroll that indicates the elements required to cast a spell. Placement of elements on your spellbook, a 5x5 grid, is like a puzzle. One element may be used in multiple spells so arrange them to maximize the number of spells that you can fit on the grid.
Melee unfortunately does not work as well as magic, at least not for me. Swiping the screen with your mouse is not an exact science- ever tried to draw a straight line with a mouse? Which is what is required to make a sword stroke in The Keep. My charactor, who has roughly equal Strength, Stamina, and Intelligence stats, runs out of stamina very quickly during melee, so spells, which are influenced by Intelligence, are my bread and butter.

A simple, surprisingly fun dungeon crawler with a nice magic system.
It suffers from a few usability mistakes - there is just one save slot, you cannot rebind keys and the keys are not even listed in the game anywhere.
But other than that if you like dungeon crawlers, try this one. It's short, sweet and simple
Go for a magic build.

There's an age old saying that applies to this game - Keep it simple, stupid. At every turn the designers found unnecessarily convoluted ways to program how combat and magic works, making for the most awkward playthrough.

The game has an interesting spell system where you arrange magic runes on a checkerboard and then draw lines over these runes to cast spells. It works fairly well and allows some creativity on how you place the runes to make certain spell combination work.
Combat is real time, you draw lines which attack specific parts of the target, depending where they were drawn. By attacking, you get combo points which let you execute a combo by drawing a more complicated line.
You only have one save file which gets automatically overwritten every time you save the game. The biggest problem with that is that the game has still some potentially game breaking bugs (e. g. key items disappearing) which can leave your game in an unusable state. In this case you would have to start over which is not acceptable.
While not overly ambitious, this is a solid entry in the dungeon crawler with grid movement genre. It doesn't overstay it's welcome, sometimes less is more. With 10 levels, it has the right amount of content to explore its mechanics in full without getting boring. Even though games like these have often very similar looking dungeon levels, it's mixed up enough here that there is enough variety to carry it through to the end.
Recommended if you get it for a good price.

I originally down voted this game after playing the demo, because of the clunky "mouse swiping" battle system, but I had to get it on sale for $3.74! I cannot complain.  I just played for almost an hour and didn't even know that much time had passed. I like it much better after minimizing all the windows that can be on screen at once. I didn't know you could do that when playing the demo.  It sure helps gameplay immersion! The nicest feature is the ability to save the game at anytime!
You do not create a character. You start out as a male character and cannot even name him. When you level up, there are only 3 stats you can increase. Strength, Intelligence and Dexterity. You get 3 points to distribute per level gained. I wish these features were different and somewhat ruin the game in areas, but this is a hand-held port. Oh well...
The battle mechanics are clunky, that's for sure. Weapon combat is not as bad if you minimize the windows, but it seems you must have a window open to cast spells.  Either way, it is a clunky design. So far I have only had to fight one or two enemies at a time, so it's not frantic or frustrating at all.  Combat consists of holding down the left mouse button and swiping the mouse across the enemies, low, medium or high, then letting go of the mouse button to initiate the attack.  Provided you have stamina for weapon based attacks and mana for spells. More on this later. It's kind of lame, but fighting isn't the only thing in this game.
It has decent graphics, but sounds are kind of basic. To me, it looks like the environments are nicer than the enemy models and animations aren't that great.  The lighting is good and sets a nice creepy atmosphere. The magic system is kind of cool. You place ruins that you find across a grid in the correct order found on scrolls, then you have to swipe the mouse across them to cast spells.  Again, provided you have the mana to cast the spells. It works, but is just as clunky as weapon based combat and you must have the spell window open, which takes up a good portion of the lower right-hand portion of the screen.
Gameplay is realtime, but seems slow, so the clunky combat isn't frustrating. It sure feels a lot like a single character version of the old Dungeon Master game, accept with newer features.  Like stacking potions and other stuff, much better graphics & sound of course, etc. There is a story and it flows well with the game. At the end of each level, it gives you stats and shows you if you killed all the enemies and found all the secrets. You can choose to not progress and go back to kill the rest of the enemies and/or search out any unfound secrets. There are pressure plates with rocks to hold them down and small buttons on walls to reveals secret areas. Spike pits and fireball traps, etc. Seems like the old Dungeon Master game was a huge influence.
I recommend this to dungeon crawlers looking for something with a touch of nostalgia, but also a different feel to it than other games in the same genre.

A fasinating game, but can be frustrating at times. We tend to think of modern stealth games as having silenced sniper rifles, melee kills that always suceed and sexy gadgets. That's not this game... the technology was just not there. The goal is to take a shot whenever you can and then relocate. It's a game of cat and mouse. Enemies will hear your actions, but often do not know where it's coming from unless you take repeated shots from the same location. Causing explosions are available to you, but it's the same story. All, in all, play this game if you're a fan of Splinter Cell, consider yourself an intelligent person who likes to set up each shot and get out of a pickle when it goes bad, or just want to see an xray view of testicles/brains/hearts/lungs/kidneys being torn apart. The developers appear to have made the decision to leave out the word Nazi or any Nazi symbols, which I found strange, but I can understand why they did. Overall, I'd recommend this game to a friend.
+You feel pretty darn smart when you do the highest difficulty and take that perfect shot.
+ Do I kill all of the nazi's in the level? Of course, they're nazis...
+It's a pretty, pretty game when you have a nice rig.
-You don't have a spotter that travels with you. Maybe that hasn't been invented yet...
-For a game that is focused on physics, I found myself shooting into walls or corners when I was clearly scoped on the target. Not often, but it happened.
-Enemies on elite difficulty can take a chest shot from the most powerful non-dlc rifle and not go down. What? They're wearing a t-shirt and mailman shorts.
-Very limted weaponry choices without buying the DLC. Four rifles, four secondaries.
-I can carry a rocket launcher and it sticks up over crates I'm hiding behind. Whatev.
Again, play it, enjoy it. It's a game worth playing, but don't go looking for a full Splinter Cell or Call of Duty experience.

I'll say one thing right away. This game is flawed. Very flawed. The progression is a bit wonky, some of the challenges feel untested, the physics can be a bit odd and the difficulty can go from dying without knowing why to winning in a matter of seconds within a replay of the same mission. The story is bland, characters are bland, graphics are decent, but a bit flat. Normally it'd be nothing to write home about.

But there's a reason I came back to the game. Because it feels like 'Let the player have some bloody fun' was the first line in the design document. And that's far too rare these days.

It puts you down on a planet with the hammer of the Gods and a ton of explosives and your goal is to wreck just about everything. That's the story as far as I'm concerned; I'm liberating buildings from their foundations. And sure, I could fight enemies with boring machine guns and shotguns. Or I could attach explosives to their faces. Getting bored? Then here's a lightning gun. And a rocket launcher. And a saw blade gun. And a jet pack. And we'll just leave these mining robots, tanks and portable black holes laying around if the mood strikes you. Dying? Who cares? Have a minor penalty that you can correct in a small-sized destruction and/or murder spree and get back at it.

This is not a game to play seriously. This is a game to fart around in. Really, my main criticism is that it could've allowed more of that. Scrap all of the floaty racing challenges or, heaven forbid, -escort missions-. The game is good at breaking things and it should've fully embraced it. I'd want more upgrades to buy, more buildings to tear down, more salvage to... Salvage. I'd want weapons to go up to Ratchet & Clank levels of silly. I want armour that lets me shrug off tank rounds and upgrades that let me suplex the tank in revenge. No such thing as overkill. Let’s get Crazy!

Still, the destruction physics sadly remain relatively unique, even after all these years and, as mentioned, there are already quite a few fun toys in the game. So if you're looking to blow off some steam and you find the game on sale, I can recommend it. In short, the game is a puddle. Not very deep, but sometimes it can be fun to stomp around in. And possibly ruin someone's day.

Having said that, if you like HOGs, Family Secrets is a typical example of the genre and doesn't do anything badly, just don't expect any surprises.

A game for those of us that either can't afford to go skiing or just can't be bothered.
SNOW features realistic mountains and courses that you can shred all day long for no cost at all, you begin the game with the basics including: a pair of skis, a coat, a hat, etc. and more is available for purchase through the store with a currency that can be bought with your steam wallet or unlocked through gaining levels (a feat completed through performing tricks and doing events and challenges on the mountains) but at the end of the day is only cosmetic and has no physical impact whatsoever.
The control scheme in SNOW is similar to other popular winter sports games: W to accelerate, S to brake, A & D to steer, then you use Spacebar to jump and the Directional Buttons to spin and can use a combination of the buttons previously mentioned to combo tricks (some alternate features of buttons such as grabbing the board have not been mentioned in this review for timesake).
As SNOW progresses both snowboards and skimobiles will be available to use if that strikes your fancy rather than the currently only available skis.
Overall the game is not fully finished and not all features are available to the player (hence Early Access) but the game is in a stable state currently with a fully open mountain to explore, giving you optional drop points and locations to find, along with many unique events and challenges such as getting down a precarious mountain range in a quick time to earn experience points and bragging rights over time scores.
SNOW is easy to learn and hard to master, offering many people an experience of skiing that may get you to try the real thing with the best part being: Its Free!

A good addition to the series but a few flaws hold it back from being the crowning achievement it could have been.
Depending on the map played, sometimes the craters that appear from heavy shelling will appear to exist in a layer of dirt that exists a few feet below the transparent ground that used to be there before.  Normally it isn't even noticable but if you zoom in a lot on areas that get heavily bombarded you will see problems.  This was not a problem in ALB and hopefully might get patched in the next major update.
The game is the first in the series to let you set up AI players to use your own custom-made decks, which means you can create target-practice decks or simulate historical or hypothetical engagements (well... sort of, heh).
The addition of new units really changes the gameplay mechanics, as enemy AA defenses will rely far less on easily-vulnerable radar guidance systems.  Also, although you get a few more units per card than in past titles, the maps are much larger and can really punish you for losing certain units.  These arguments are all illustrated best in the AH-64D Longbow, which is the US's endgame glass cannon capable of turning a match completely around... or being a large waste of points never to return (you get 1 or 2 per deck, period).
A very fun title which is also relevant enough to get denial-of-service attacks from the North Koreans on a monthly basis.  The game also automatically logs you into the chat room where you can see them taunt our capitalist way of life.

The Keep could flippantly be described as Legend of Grimrock Lite. It's a first-person, grid-based dungeon crawler with a single character and real-time combat. If you're looking for Might & Magic-style turn-based combat, you have the wrong game. The DNA on this one goes back to Dungeon Master.
The Keep is a decent length, you could likely finish it in under 10 hours unless you're looking for all the secrets. You can add another hour or two to that by forgetting to hit Quicksave (F5, by the way) and having to replay the whole freaking level over again if you get killed, because there's no autosave. That's not recommended unless you know some really creative swear words. Anyway, the game has a predictable story about crystals corrupting stuff, which would be unremarkable were it not for the scenery-chewing, Shakespearean voice actor reading it out. The in-game voice acting comes from the pizza delivery guy and is less impressive, but fortunately there's not much of it beyond reading signs and the occasional non-interactive exchanges with other characters. The art, which probably looked great on the 3DS, is a bit dated here. There's also not much texture variety between levels, so I hope you like rock walls with minimal decoration. At least it makes secrets easy to spot. Beware, at least two secrets are essential to progression, although most of them involve spotting barely-concealed buttons on walls. Still, I've done my share of searching for the more elusive ones.
You only play a single character, and although there are RPG elements in terms of leveling up and finding loot, it's pretty basic stuff. The first half of the game is essentially linear, with every new piece of loot obviously replacing something older. Near the end you start to get more difficult choices about which things to keep, depending on how you want to play your character. Realistically though, you are going to end up with a combined fighter / mage. Those are the only two options, and there's not much incentive to specialise.
The combat system is a bit more interesting. Melee involves swiping across a 3x3 grid to attack different zones of your enemy, which are supposed to have varying defences. Every few successful hits you'll get a highlighted combo for bonus damage, this is further influenced by what weapon you're using. The timing takes a bit of getting used to, it feels sluggish at first especially if you naively swipe the enemy instead of using the combat grid, but it works quite well if you don't rush it. The magic system is better; you will find a number of runes and have to arrange them on a grid, casting the spell by dragging through them in the correct order. You find scrolls which reveal spells, although it's possible to guess a few too. At first this is straightforward, but later on as the options stack up you have to put some thought into how you arrange the runes to give yourself easy access to your favourite spells, and near the end you'll have to make difficult choices because there's no optimal arrangement of runes. I quite enjoyed rejiggering my spellbook every so often.
Make sure you read the manual (right click on the game in your Steam list). The in-game tutorial is pretty basic, and doesn't tell you any of the shortcut keys which are - frankly - pretty much essential. There are no customisation options in-game, but you can set some basic detail levels and set key bindings in the launcher. My favourite key, F, switches between melee and magic combat grids, good to know if you want to survive later combat encounters.
I have to say I enjoyed it quite a bit, except those times when I lost my progress. Be warned, you only get a single save slot. Do not, for example, mistakenly click on "Restart Level" instead of "Load game", thinking you can say "Oh deary me, what a clumsy oaf" before hitting "Load game" instead, because you'll find it has gone. Then you won't say "Oh deary me", trust me. You'll say --CENSORED-- instead, which tends to frighten the dog.
Overall? It's no Legend of Grimrock, but it's an entertaining gridder that doesn't outstay its welcome.

Sniper Elite 3 gives the player control over a military sniper situated in Africa during WWII. Its a third-person shooter with open world stages, allowing the player freedom to approach his objectives in any way he chooses how. The AI in this game can be really difficult and unforgiving. Therefore, the player must be really careful and observant to reach his objectives or eliminating his targets with careful planning and strategy. Unlike most shooter games, this isn't the kind of shooter game where you can rush through your targets and win the mission easily. The character set in this game is very vulnerable to damage and you cant really depend too much on your sidearms to overcome dangerous scenarios if you alert the enemy. The stealth maneuvers isnt as efficient as you would expect which is why being very, VERY careful is the best strategy to adapt while playing this game. Time is also another factor to be aware of for Sniper Elite 3. Even though there are only 8 missions to complete this game, the time you have to spend on each level will probably take up at least half of your afternoon (if you wish to be entirely discreet getting your tasks done) which is how the game is meant to be played. Basically, players will have to adapt the strong patience of a real sniper, adding anticipation and thrill before firing each shot to your enemies with your sniper rifle.
The graphics and visuals in Sniper Elite III is excellent and satisfying. Compared to its predecessors, the developers of this game has improved the game's 'signature' sniper killcam, abling the player to view their bullet trajectory coursing through their victim's internal body with amazing detail. It is very stunning!
Apart from the best elements Sniper Elite III has to offer, there are a few things that hinder this game from perfection. Firstly, the AI behaviour isnt very dynamic as expected like in most games in today's generation of video games. There are often times when hiding the bodies doesnt have to be a necessity and even if the player alerted the area, the AI can be very static and predictable. Give it another minute and they will pretend nothing happened and return to their patrol routes. Second, the lacking of stealth maneuvers/tactics can make this game's experience unreasonably frustrating and annoying but maybe thats just my own personal opinion since I've been exposed to many stealth assassination games before this. Basically, stick to the old-school stealth mechanics when you play this game. I wouldnt want to consider mentioning the lack of story and background for this game because it doesnt really matter at all since the Sniper Elite franchise is meant to be a WWII sniper-simulator so lets just throw that out the window.
As much realism Sniper Elite III has to offer, these issues above unfortunately pushes this game back a few steps but that doesnt mean its entirely bad! This game will keep the players hot in their seat. It is a very fun game to play with and the visual effects will never bore you. In conclusion...

If any developer or studio wants to see a master-class in how to make another sequel - they should contact Rebellion. Sniper Elite 3 is one of those rare games that not only improves over it predecessor visually - but adds so much more to the proven central mechanics of the previous game.
The beauty at the core of SE3 (and to a lesser extent, in SE2) - is the way the game allows players to approach the mission in the best way they see fit. In the current climate of COD and BF games - going Rambo is commonplace - and that same mentality can be applied to SE3. However, it is vastly more rewarding to use your brain first, followed by your trigger finger (button!) second.
I despise stealth games as the norm. The tip-toeing around from map to map and making sure that the first two pixels of your characters' shoe are not seen in the daylight without bringing on instant-death. But play SE3 on its default difficulty of Marksman - and the game balance appears just right. You get a challenge if you alert the guards and quickly have to scurry to a fall-back location. But you also don't suffer from one-shot kills against you. It's this semi-realistic approach that makes you push-on under tension of being spotted, but without the constant fear of being killed from an unknown sniper from several hundred metres away.
However, if this isn't hardcore enough for you - ramp up the difficulty to suicidal levels with the Custom Difficulty option - including the function that disables any saved games.
That latter part is a statement in itself. Play SE3 as its meant to be played and you can easily spend 2 to 3 hours on a single mission. The planning, the thought processes, the noise cover, the creeping forward - all mix wonderfully into an absorbing and immersive experience. Your character genuinely comes across as being all alone behind enemy lines. Forget the off-map support. Forget having a squad for backup. This is you against a yet-unknown enemy force - with a sprinkling of optional objectives thrown in. That said, the game, as per SE2, can be played in co-op mode, should you so wish.
I generally don't like reviewing games until I have completed them - but SE3 is a prominent exception. Rebellion has enhanced a winning formula even more - and this game is one to simply savour and enjoy. The fact that I'm now going to cut this review short, so that I can jump back into my saved progress of SE3 must count for something!
Rebellion - I don't know what you can pull off for SE4 - but you've set yourself a VERY high benchmark to surpass. Well done.

Sniper Elite 3, along with the past franchise is a unique style of game virtually uncomparable to any other FPS on the market.  Within the games amazing visual enviroment, super realistic ballistic control and it's jaw dropping tactical gameplay, SE3 is by far one of the most Fantastic shooters i have ever played... EVER.
ENVIROMENT
Sure it's one thing for a game to have "pretty trees" or "moving clouds", but all of those bells and whisles are a fraction of what the game in it self has to offer the player.  Not only do you get to see the ever changing weather in the enviroment, but it will also effect you down to the tiny aspect during the gameplay.  SE3 was evolved how weather can effect how the player can react in its gameplay and its vast ideas of survivability.
THE BALLISTIC BLUES.
Alright, i'll be honest here...  I was ♥♥♥♥ING FLOORED how much comes into play when shooting a rifle.  Sure Sure, other games have simulated similar things such as Wind, Blood Pressure and breathing patterns, this is not what i am boasting on SE3 being the "first".  In person, i have never shot a gun before as country laws prohibit them for personal use, although i know in most countries ownership of them is normal so bare with me on this part :P.  Before i just thought, you point, squeeze the trigger, all said and done. Yet SE3 has taught me more than just being "trigger happy" and to consider much more than just WHO i'm going to shoot.  I was playing on the difficulty Sniper Elite so almost everything effected the Velocity of the traveling bullet, which was a huge eye opener seeing as how i could barely hit the 100 yard target.  God forbid if people think this game is comparable to Counter Strike or any generic shooter such as that i strongly advice you to NOT try and Flick scope with an AWP :P.  The gameplay is relentless and will make you think twice about launching bullets wildly toward your enemies.
BOOM, HEADSHOT.
Speaking of lobbing bullets towards your enemies, If there is one thing this game and other games like SOCOM have taught me, is that sometimes taking the shot is not in your best interest.  YOU DO NOT POSSESS INHUMAN STRENGTHS AND ABILITIES.  You can't just run into a gun toating armies with your eyes closed and hope to rid the world of evil, its just not how it works, PERIOD.  BULLETS INDEED OUCH, so to speak.  Now think about this, you have one Target you need to kill and search at the back of a camp filled with dilapidated buildings which is filled with 5 to 8 others, ( that you can see).  Would getting into a heated gun fight with limited ammo seem like a decent idea?  Probably not.  Tactics come in, watching where they patrol, following them, stealth killing them; its not just about having a large rifle.  Although i will admit that when you watch the bullet cam and you see a Rifling round whizzing through the air in slow motion as it shatters the skull and exits out the back of the head in a gruesome execution, is pretty ♥♥♥♥in' sweet.  Doesn't justify the intensity of careful gameplay you need to make just to not get filled with hot searing led.
TWO IS A TEAM
the CO-OP play.. my god.  I thought it was going to be horrible, buggy and down right stupid.  But i will admit it was probably one of the most hardest/fun CO-OP experiences i've had in the longest time.  You really need to connect on way more than a gaming level.  Not a "oh i'll go that way you go this way" kind of deal, you literally need to work as a team to help each other observe, seek out and eliminate if you want this to work out for the both of you. Also when one player goes down you have the chance to Revive them, they kinda get a "last stand" sort of thing, alot like Borderlands or Call of Duty, except you don't stand back up if you kill someone in it.  So your CO-OP player really shouldn't wander too far away from you.  When it comes to CO-OP play i STRONGLY RECOMMEND its done over a Voice program, I.E -- Skype, Ventrilo, Teamspeak etc.  Or to just play together locally, because the more communication you two have will make it worth your while in the long run.
CASTING THE FIRST STONE
Okay you caught me, i haven't played the game for too long i get it.  But i am just shocked and impressed with the quality and depth to the game. It is definetly a game in which i could see myself trying to get all the acheivements too or beating it on all difficulties. Yet who knows, i'm just a girl from the "Gun free" country of Ireland, but i love what i have seen so far :).  And others who play or would like to play, just add me!  Would always love a second gun in the mix! :)

Original review:
I can't make up my mind about this game. It gets a lot of things wrong, and feels quite contrived. But, I do enjoy sniping, and you get to do plenty of it.
My gripes:
This is essentially a console game at heart. 3rd person. Obligatory XP to unlock ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t ranks and custom loadouts (have to be like CoD, right?).
YOU CANNOT USE THE MOUSE AND KEYBOARD IF YOU HAVE A GAMEPAD PLUGGED IN. You must unplug it.
No jump button; you can only scale ledges the level designers say you can scale, or jump gaps they say you can jump. Lots of invisible walls stopping you from reaching nice shooting positions. It could be a lot worse than it is, but lots of areas feel very artificially constrained. Again, you have to bear in mind that this is a console game, and somewhat dumbed down.
The camera is always over your right shoulder. This makes taking left turns around cover much riskier.
The bullet slowmo x-ray kill cam is stupid, but fortunately it can be disabled.
Even on the hardest difficulty, the game still plays audio cues to tell you when the enemy is and isn't hunting you. You can disable all other hand-holdy crap (like the minimap), but not that.
Even on the hardest difficulty, officers you have to kill are marked with a star on your HUD. That you can see all the time. So you can use that to see when they're going to pop out from cover.
Positional audio doesn't quite seem to work. I can't hear anything from my rear speakers. Worse, it's hard to gauge how far away the enemy is by the sound of their voices. They're invariably further away than they sound.
Get a high score at the rifle range for the honour of being able to purchase DLC rifles! Oh joy to the world! I get to shell out for stupid camo on my WW2 rifle. The Krauts will be so jealous!
Minor gripes:
Hollywood physics. Guys practically do backflips after getting shot, instead of crumpling like dead weight. Cars explode when you shoot the gas tank.
What is an American soldier doing attached to a British unit anyway? And why is he carrying a Garand? Where is he going to find ammunition for that from the British supply chain?
It's WW2. Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog, not Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta.
Despite being a sniper, and the weapons loadout skewed towards sniping (you can only carry one mag of SMG rounds, but plenty of rifle ammo), the game basically casts you as infiltrator/commando.
How does Our Hero escape Tobruk after it falls in the first mission? Everyone in Tobruk was captured when the city fell. My granddad spent five years in POW camps after being captured when Tobruk was taken. Granted, my granddad was a medic and not a super sniper, but where exactly was Our Hero supposed to have evacuated to?
For all my whinging, at the end of the day, I like sniping and so I like this game. If you can put up with the above, get this game.

Who needs medical school when you have Surgeon Simulator?

Surgeon Simulator is one of these short joke games where the core of the gameplay is the hilarity that stems from overcoming intentionally awkward controls and buggy physics. You play as a newbie surgeon - or to be more precise, a clearly disembodied hand - who has to successfully complete various surgeries despite being clumsy as all hell.
Don't look for any kind of anatomical accuracy or realism in this game - ripping off the patient's organs and throwing them on the ground just to get to the one organ that needs replacement is a regular practice in the game, and the mission is considered completed if you manage to throw the new organ onto the spot where it's supposed to be. Even if said organ falls out immediately afterwards while the game merrily displays the success screen (which clearly suggests that the patient wasn't going to survive one way or another). The only thing you have to worry about regarding the patient is making sure that the blood level doesn't reach zero. And yes, you can still finish the mission even if the patient is left with as little as 1 ml of blood. This game exists to be a source of dark humor, not to be realistic.
You are given plenty of tools to accomplish various tasks and it's only up to you to decide what is going to be useful. Obligatory scalpels, various saws for cutting bones, drugs that either slow down or speed up the blood flow, and even axes, hammers and drills. Many of them, more often than not, are going to be only a hindrance in your desperate efforts, blocking your way to the actually important tools, bumping into the patient and making him lose blood, or even getting you high. And that's just the beginning.
As I mentioned, the game isn't very long; there is 9 levels total, plus 2 hidden, and the exact time it will take you to complete them for the first time will vary depending on how badly you'll be initially doing. There are 3 kinds of surgeries in 3 kinds of environments, so at some point you'll end up in a situation where, for example, you have to do a brain transplant in an ambulance that rides on a bumpy road, with the objects jumping up at random and the back door opening from time to time. Probably the funniest moment you are going to see in this game is successfully completing said surgery and then watching as the brain you just put in the patient's head falls out right away and ends up on the floor or even on the road. The mission is still accomplished, so who cares!
Surgeon Simulator is the kind of game that you either just can't stand, or love coming back to it despite how badly it frustrates you. And yes, after the initial hilarity wears off and you get better at playing it, you'll most likely start seeing the game's frustrating elements more and more. Probably the biggest one of them is how it can be a pain in the butt to actually grab things; there's NO indication whether you actually grabbed the damn object or not, usually resulting in you spending some time on the ritual of pressing the buttons to grab something and then raising the hand to see if you actually grabbed it.
Another problem is that the game gives you next to no information on how various things work. There is no tutorial at all; the only thing you get is the info on how to control the hand, which is displayed on the computer in the main menu (and the said menu uses the exact same hand mechanics as well, to make matters even better). The rest you either have to figure out yourself (most likely failing numerous times before you successfully complete a surgery at least once) or just Google things up. The game DOES give tips on certain things, but that's only AFTER you completed a surgery, and only if you figure out that you can put floppy disks into the computer in the main menu. And let me tell you, doing so can be frustratingly hard as well, since the computer will only accept them if they're perfectly aligned.
In the end, Surgeon Simulator is a little curiosity that some people will like, and some people will hate. My recommendation is to first play the demo provided by the creators of the game and see how well you'll do in it. If you'll end up loving the absurdity of the game, then I think you'll like the full game as well. But if you'll instead end up getting frustrated and/or freaking out over the patient dying, then I think you're better off giving up on this one.

I might write a more lengthy review when I've got the time, but basically it comes down to: it's amazing.
How is this being developed by one guy? It's everthing I wished games like Space Engineers was. It runs very well for me. It gives me exactly the kind of freedom I was looking for in space game. What you build is what you get. Want a small and nimble ship with low cost and capability? You can build it. Want a massive freighter that steers like a brick, but hauls like an oz? You can build it. Just consider you need to crew to run it, enough power to move it and plenty of firepower to fight off pesky pirates that might suddenly warp into the sector your're in.

Freelancer + X3 + Minecraft/Space Engineers = Avorion.

Perhaps what No Man's Sky should've been? Except you can't land on planets. But that doesn't matter. :P
Start in a tiny drone, mine minerals, sell some of them for cash, use the rest to build your own ship (which doesn't have to be blocky if you're creative enough!) - Or alternatively, buy a pre-made one in-game, or import one from a friend. Hire and manage your crew. Trade goods between sectors/factions, or fight pirates and sell their loot. Explore a procedurally generated galaxy, do simple quests, find treasure, and better materials and weapons to upgrade your ship - Or even command a whole fleet of your own ships.
Incredibly fun game, with co-op/multiplayer, too. :)
I'm liking it a lot - Most of my playtime has been spent importing and rebuilding some ships which I designed in other voxel games, and it's been nice to actually have a reason to do PvE things with them afterwards, which those games didn't have.
Bear in mind it's a little buggy at the moment, and some of the features seem overly complicated, but that's to be expected considering it's early access, so perhaps wait a bit and check on this title later if that's an issue for you. Also something to note is that the PvE is basic (with hidden depth), and some of the quests can be hard to find and then get a bit grindy - Although it's not the only thing that the game does, so you can't really expect more than that. It's a very great game otherwise. :)

I really recommend this game (along with the rest of the House of 1000 Doors games, which only seem to improve as the series goes on)! Though the voice acting can be a bit wonky/robotic at times, I think the main plot point of this game (there is a house that appears at certain places/times because there are souls who haven't found peace) is intriguing and super interesting. I love the visuals, the music is amazing, and while you're kind of alone with your thoughts most of the time, I think it really adds to how melancholic and sad this game truly is. It has a lot of the basics of a HOG but also pairs it with a fascinating and immersive storyline.
I do have two complaints, though:
1. Functional fixedness in this game drives me CRAZY. I know how ridiculous this sounds, but sometimes the game requires a very specific object for a task when you already have something in your inventory that could just as easily complete what needs to be done (for example, using a knife vs scissors to cut something). I know it's because the game is super expansive and if you could complete every task using a select few objects, it would be boring, but it still can be irritating at times.
2. This seems to be a pattern with most of the games this company puts out, but the ending is extremely rushed. Not only that, but the last door/portal you enter is extremely out of place in comparison to the other storylines. I don't know what it is about this company and their need to insert magic/demons/weird sci-fi elements ONLY at the tail-end of a great story, but that's what happens here, and it's a little sad, because the rest of the storylines are so beautifully thought out. The fourth and final portal is so short in comparison it feels tacked on.
That being said, if you purchase the CE, there is a phenomenal additional chapter to play which totally (IMO) makes up for the quickness of the final door. You get to learn more about Kate's family/why and how she's tied to the House (and also how it works), and it's on par with the melancholy of the earlier plotlines.
I really enjoyed this game and really recommend it, simply because the storylines are so fascinating (if you ignore when they randomly add magical elements), it has a longer gameplay than most HOG, and the environments are expansive and beautifully rendered.

Even after a couple of hours it's easy to recommend SpriterPro. The interface is simple yet complex enough to create detailed, varied animations, the export function work well, and the learning curve seems relatively low- I'm a hobby spriter and I can see a lot of use for this tool. I was looking for an animation tool that allows the export of sprite sheets, and man did I get a good deal at the current 75% off discount.
In all honesty, though, the price IS a bit high to buy SpriterPro just "playing around with it" at full price. If you're into game design and want a catch-all tool for your animations, you can't really do wrong with this software. But if you just want to toy around with some animations, wait for a sale/discount.
In both cases though, the sheer functionality is pretty damn worth it.

Spriter Pro makes it extremely easy to put together animated sprites literally in minutes (assuming you already have the graphical assets). At first, the interface isn't particularly intuitive, but track down the "getting started" video on YouTube and you'll be up and running in no time flat. I have practically no graphical talent (Dammit, Jim! I'm a programmer, not a graphical artist!), but my first experiment right out of the gate was an animated tank with rotating turret, recoiling gun, and smoke effects that's on par with Command & Conquer tanks (yes, I had decent assets to play with).

polished, and has a bunch of very mature runtimes for a pletorah of engines. Our teams graphics artist has Spine, but we couldn't afford a second license, which is why I went ahead and gave Spriter a try.

Let me start by saying I actually like this game.
It's fun to play, and you can spend hours and hours in it without getting bored. At least, if this is your thing. This is not a fast-paced shooter. It's a game simulating trains. Obviously.
However, despite me liking this game, there are some serious reasons why I would NOT recommend it.
First of all, the basic game is already quite expensive. You can have some fun with what comes with it by default. But a little more would never hurt. When you're done with the vanilla content, and turn to DLC's, things get really expensive, really fast.
The amount of DLC available is huge, and I applaud that. But the prices for these packs are not just high, they are exhuberant. In my opinion, the prices are at least three times what they should be at most.
A very, very big downside that shows itself in this DLC library, is that much of this DLC was made for older versions and weaker PC's, and has never been brought up to modern standards. But it's still sold at the same very high prices.
So you end up with a large library, but of very varying quality, especially in the visual department.
Another downside is that it's hard to tell how realistic or how deeply simulated a given locomotive is. Some require quite a bit of study, others are hardly more than visual skins over a very simple simulation. Again, hard to tell the difference beforehand.
And another problem I have encountered, is that even old, well known problems never get patched.
So, my advice?
If you like trains, and there's a sale going that will get you this game at -75% or so, by all means go for it. I did.
But at full price? I'd stay away if I were you. There's better things you can do with your hard earned cash.

I have owned this game on Steam for about four years, I think.  Been awhile anyway.  I have enjoyed it, although every year when they update, the experience has tended to deteriorate as apparent inefficiencies and bugs are introduced.   It's fun if you enjoy train simulators and is probably the best on the market from that perspective.
Yes, there is a lot of DLC, and yes getting it all would cost a small fortune.  This really hasn't affected me a great deal since it is still far cheaper than the model trains and accessories I collect.  There is absolutel no requirement to buy any DLC to enjoy the game as intended.  DLC is just an expansion, much like a new set of tracks and models is an expansion to a model rail display.
That said, I do not recommend this game to new players.  As noted, its quality is getting worse.  Support is essentially non-existent.  The community can be toxic.  It's not fun anymore.
With the release of 2016, I can no longer play any part of the game except the part where you fill out a marketing survey.  Every route is a blackscreen, and the game eventually gives up and crashes.  I am too tired to fight a battle with ignorant techs and seemingly intentionally unhelpful support people so I can do something I should find relaxing.   That's not relaxing; it's infurating, and I am done.
So, uninstall it is, and I'll consider my experiences an expensive lesson in how not to carry on your train hobby once your model set has become too large for your living space.
