To be honest, there's not *that* much to *do* in the game at this point. It depends very much on your own inventiveness and enthusiasm. Much like X3 and games of that nature, to be fair. I'd say this game is best explained as a blend between Reassembly and X3.
You have the casual gameplay and easy build mechanics of Reassembly (but with some Starmade thrown in), with an open universe with freighters, stations and territory like in X3. In fact, some stations are even extremely similar to in X3 with nearly identical names and icons (Cattle Farms, Crystal Farms, Satellite Factories etc).
You'll have a ton of X3 nostalgia while exploring this galaxy, thats for sure. Not in a bad way at all, mind you.
You can fly around and trade, fight, explore, do bulletin board missions of delivering cargo or attacking baddies.
Factions have positive or negative attitudes with you that govern which territories and fleets are friendly or hostile to you.
In some ways it is a bit too quick and easy to swing this, as even a single bullet hitting your ally will instantly give you a "-5 rep with Outer Space Mongrels, HOW COULD YOU!?"
While simply selling a single start-of-game module you cant use due to not having the energy supply yet (such as the radar upgrade you start with), will net you +700 rep with that faction and instantly make you best allies for life.
So it is very much like X3, but sped up to reduce tedium and grind, in some ways perhaps a bit too fast.
But thats where the Reassembly influences come in, with shipbuilding (and stationbuilding) being extremely well designed and with all the UI tools you could need. This isnt one of those early access games where you have to whine on the forums and wait for 3 months just to get a simple Mirroring option in the game. It pretty much has everything well thought out from the start.
Frankly it has the makings of a brilliant game, X3 and Reassembly / Starmade in one. What more could one want?
Worth mentioning is that it is extremely optimized, and even with everything cranked up to max and 4x Supersampling (native in the ingame options menu, something even AAA games dont do sometimes), it runs at hundreds of frames per second. Perhaps as might be expected, but considering the number of ships and blocks in high detail ships and stations, with hundreds of particles flying around during combat, it's very impressive indeed.
You can quite literally make a huge scale 1:1 Imperial Star Destroyer if you got the patience and talent, and it will most likely run at acceptable framerates. The question is if the AI factions have been set up to dynamically evolve and grow to match the players advances. It would be quite unfortunate if, after hundreds of hours of play once you accumulate resources for huge dreadnoughts you built, if the AI factions still only had corvettes and minor ships that couldnt stand a chance.
Hopefully the devs considered this and did NOT add a limit to the AI ship size, obviously needing to be weighted to not surpass the player too much.
It manages to make a simple block-style aesthetic look very beautiful and dynamic, due to each block having dynamic textures with emissive windows, glow details, or even reflections (if you enable that in the options menu) that can cause quite spectacular reflection effects from glass materials and titanium armor, reflecting the planets, skyboxes and lights and blocks surrounding it at the right angles.
Heck i angled some black glass near my glow-blocks just for that reason, to have the light catch the glass in just the right angle.
One thing that should be noted is that the colors to paint your parts with is quite limited. There are a strange abundance of yellows and blues, but only 2 real *reds* and not really any white whites or black blacks. The best you get is a light grey (with an overly extravagant sports car salesman name such as "Ad Astra Eternius Magnificus White", instead of just "Light Gray").
It'd be nicer with a more traditional RGB spread of colors and hues, perhaps even just a color wheel to fine tune it yourself.
All in all it's a great game with huge potential, if they can add more tangible long-term gameplay and consequences for your actions. You CAN make your own stations and fleets and claim territory (i believe). But in some sense it feels a bit empty like you're just dropped in the middle of a huge sandbox of nameless faceless generated factions and areas.
This is where X3 has the upper hand, due to its distinct factions and history / behavior of each faction. Unique weapons, products, goods, ships etc.
Granted the factions here have unique styles of ships too, but with lack of artistically designed unique PARTS for those, they all tend to drift towards the "big heap of greebles and blocks" category. A huge multiplayer server with player-designed things might alleviate this, or perhaps some workshop support for player-made "ship layouts" for the AI's to use or something, with dynamic greebling built off that, somehow. Would be much nicer.

You ever play Karoshi Suicide Salaryman? It's a series of free flash puzzle platformers where the goal is to jump into spikes or drop a box on your head, since the objective of the game is actually to kill yourself! It's a neat little game, with several bite-size levels to keep you satisfied the way Warioware does. The graphics aren't great and feel like they're fresh out of those way-too-edgy late 90s flash videos, but they're serviceable and do their job. I have fond memories of those games, so when I saw this game was on sale for just over a freakin' quarter and was mechanically similar, I figured why not.
Graphics and soundtrack are the only things this game does better than the Karoshi Suicide Salaryman series. Credit where credit is due, it's a pretty good-looking game. It isn't pandering to the retro aesthetic that so many pixelated modern games do, and I appreciate that. There's also a fair amount of effort put into this game, and a substantial amount of levels for the price. There's even a speedrun mode, which is nice to have even if I'd never use it.
Unfortunately, that doesn't change the fact that playing this game is a chore. The controls are archaic - you press up to jump instead of having a dedicated jump button separate from your movement buttons. It's a little thing but you get thrown off every once in a while. It's difficult, and not in the way a game like Dark Souls or Castlevania is difficult. Think I Wanna Be The Guy or something that's unfairly hard in an attempt to artificially extend the playtime.
The gameplay feels similarly dated, as there are no checkpoints. If the levels were shorter, this wouldn't be a problem, but far too often you'll accidentally screw up later in the level, so you'll hit the R button (which you have to find out on your own) only to find yourself back at the beginning, and have to slog through a puzzle you already know how to do but don't move quick enough to do so without getting frustrated.
The price doesn't save a game from not being fun. I know it might seem unfair to keep comparing this to a different game, but I cannot emphasize enough how much better the Karoshi series is at nearly everything Squishy the Suicidal Pig attempts. From the treatment of an inherently messed up subject matter to having to temporarily avoid killing yourself, every single thing in Squishy the Suicidal Pig feels like it's been done better before, and for free.
The one comfort is I've already sold the cards I got from wasting my time on this and gotten my money back.

Video:
Overview:  Flying Tigers:  Shadows over China is similar to Ace Combat. This is not a game like Il-2 Sturmovik. It is a action flying game set against the backdrop of defending China during WW2. It also features a clever mix of arcade and sim controls.  As this takes place in the Pacific Theater of Operations, it is strictly American, British, Russian/Chinese, and Japanese aircraft.
Music/Sound:   The sound effects and music are great.  I don't know too much about airplane engine noises, but they sound really good, the machine guns have a weighty sound to them, and the Soundtrack is just hands down, fantastic.
Gameplay:  This is a arcade flight game very similar to Ace Combat, but with slower, and less manueverable planes because of the time period.  You have the choice of detailed Cockpit flying, or traditional third-person cameras, and you can swap between them easily during play.  The game is incredibly breathtaking in it's graphics and presentation.  There are 12 missions in total, including the Tutorial, with 2 difficulty settings(Casual and Normal).  Missions vary from dog fighting to bombing runs.  The missions themselves are rather short, between 5 and 15 minutes.
There are four modes to singleplayer, Campaign, Dogfight, Challenges, and Free Flight.  The Campaign is the main game, Dogfight allows you customize your experience to shoot down AI, Challenges are little mini-missions with leaderboards, and Free Flight lets you pick any plane and any map to just fly around and relax in.
Controls:  The controls are responsive and intuitive, sensitivity is one of those things you will have to adjust.  The game can be played with mouse and keyboard, a controller, or a flight stick, and each method has fully rebindable keys.  This reviewer used an Xbox One Controller.
TLDR:
+Great overall Presentation
+Simple, responsive, and fully rebindable controls
+Detailed Cockpits
+WW2 on a front not often seen
+Free Flight
=More Arcade than Sim
=Soundtrack is amazing, but sometimes a little cheesy
=Fuel and Ammo are limitless
-Performance issues when running the game on Cinematic settings
-Sim only really changes pitch & roll
-A lot of exagerated explosions
-Have to return to the "Press Start" screen to exit

Spelunky is a game where everything it sets out to do feels accomplished, and then some.  The randomly generated level layouts are always possible to navigate, and allows for varying levels of challenge all within a single stage.
Speaking of challenge, Spelunky has a
of it.  However the challenge is never done in a way to where it's unfair.  If you ignore the occasional damsel spawning in front of a spike trap, or a guy with a projectile being a couple feet away from you at the start of the level.
Spelunky does "risk versus reward" extremely well.  The better the payoff, the more difficult a task will be to accomplish.  Using your best judgement, taking things slowly, and really thinking about the risks involved with every tasks are musts if you hope to beat the game even once.
Though it only has a few stages, Spelunky offers countless hours of gameplay.  The only thing I wish the game offered is online multiplayer, but the single player experience is more than enough to make Spelunky an almost flawless game.
If you enjoy platformers, or just a good challenge, I would highly recommend Spelunky.

Graphics: 42/100
-The game was not nearly as graphic as I thought it could be.  There was no graphic violence and no graphic novels.  I have not reached 100% completion but I have yet to find any infographics either.  If this turns out to be untrue I will update my review.
Essence: 72.5/100
-I had a lot of internal debate about this one but ultimately found it to be a fair score.  I frankly didn't think that there was enough to justify giving it a 73, but felt that a 72 really didn't reflect the quality of the end product that was presented.  I know I could receive a lot of hate for this score but I didn't see any other option.  In the end, I went with 72.5 as I am told that it is middle point in between the two numbers.  If this turns out to be false I will update my review.
Overall (unweighted): 74.375/100
-This is the overall score obtained by averaging out all previous categories.  However, as any competent reviewer knows, the notion that each category is equally important is naive and lacks nuance.  Therefore this score should be completely disregarded.
Overall (weighted): 80.582983289/100
-The large number of decimal places should stand testament to the accuracy and legitimacy of this score.  We weighted playability as being 70% as important as replayability but 120% the importance of Graphics, while essence was 83% as important as playability, making it 60.59% as important as replayability, which just felt right.  However, this left Graphics at a roughly a 1:1.714 ratio with essence, which felt too much, so we adjusted by throwing in the unweighted overall score at a 1:2 ratio with playability.  It only felt fair.
So should you buy this game?
-It depends.  Personally, I myself have a policy of not buying anything that rates lower than a 80.58298329, unless it is on sale by a percentage equal to the inverse proportion of the amount by which it falls under this score.  The reasoning behind this should be obvious.

Not as surprising or magical as the first one, but I did like it a lot, especially since the thing you spend the most time doing was specifically nostalgic for me. Mini-games are a mixed bag, but a few are great, and none were that hard, so it's a good trip to the zoo.

What I was expecting from this game was not what I ended up getting, but that's okay as the end result was immensely enjoyable. Glittermitten Grove mixes a whole bunch of ideas that probably wouldn't be too enjoyable outside of - say - a flash game, but are infinitely interesting and creative all the same. And that's ultimately what will draw you to it. Will you awkwardly manuever a sword for the hundredth time through a landscape you have difficulty remembering to find the next secret? To get to the next challenge whatever it may be? Most of the time it'll be yes, but the absolute bizarreness of Glittermitten Grove makes it difficult to predict ahead of time.
So basically, if you're ready to experience these bizarre concepts and test your mettle against a bunch of different puzzles, then you'll like Glittermitten. If you're unsure, you can wait for a sale.

I bought this game expecting a fun and wild ride with Frog Fractions 2 reminiscent of the first, instead I received an unstable fairy game hiding an incredibly aggravating ASCII world. I am very disappointed with how everything turned out.
The fairy portion of the game provides a very relaxed experience where you're trying to grow a fairy village as the overseer. The fairies will perform tasks on their own as you blast your way deep into the earth, prioritize which resources to collect (food, wood, crystals, sparkles), grow your trees, and build structures to support your growing population. You can increase the speed of the game to hurry things along if you don't want to wait around too much.
My only problems with Glittermitten Grove (fairy portion) were its proneness to crash after a half hour or so and that the fairies were unable to gather crystals that were too deep underground. The latter made progression difficult when I had a horde of 30-40 crystals just sitting there, taunting me.
Now Frog Fractions 2 (the game accessed through a secret door(s) in Glittermitten Grove) has good and bad parts. The mini-games were excellent and appropriately silly and weird. Some of the other meta aspects were funny too and subvert your expectations.
On the other hand, navigating the ASCII overworld and solving its puzzles made me frustrated to the point of stopping due to the unpleasantness of movement. The sword that constantly blocks you from quickly going down paths because you must rotate it in a way with Q and W where it doesn’t make you two spots wide or two spots tall. The skates also function in a way where they work with you or sometimes send you backwards or in other directions you didn’t intend, usually because of the sword or some other obstacle.
It just felt like one long battle against incessant annoyances to reach the funny and good parts. I was hoping for a smooth, interesting delivery of humor and quirks, but sadly sighing when thinking about the game is all I have now.
Glittermitten Grove seems like the better overall experience despite its problems, but Frog Fractions 2 does contain interesting things that are worth seeing such as those excellent and varied mini-games. However, I don’t know if playing it is the best choice. I cannot recommend this game.

Genuinely one of the worst games I've ever played. You waste an hour on a mediocre strategy game to get to the real game, which turns out to be a stupid, clunky, intentionally bad ascii rpg with occasional kind of okay but kind of underdeveloped minigames. TXT World is the worst part for sure though I just hated every second I spent in that part of the game. It's slow and tedious, it's ugly to look at, and it thinks it's so god damn clever but it's not. It's not clever. Even the minigames aren't that clever. Spaxris requires you to do this slot machine thing and then trivia just to start the game and it's just a useless barrier to entry. The moment that made me quit is the minigame that requires you to plug in a microphone and sing. I do have a microphone. I don't feel like it should be a necessity to play though & if I didn't have one I'd just be permanently unable to do this piece of content, I guess? It's inexcusably stupid either way. I think what bothers me the most is how smug the game tries to act when really its time has long passed. There's a minigame that fuses flappy bird and cookie clicker - like three years after the entire craze surrounding either of them. On the topic of Glittermitten:
It's a nice little simulator game, with a unique mechanic of having to manage light to make sure all of your trees are getting enough to grow. It doesn't get fleshed out a whole lot on account of just being a framing game and you can "beat" it in something like two hours tops, so if your sole interest is this portion of the game you may want to wait for it to go down to like $5-$10 before buying.

8.8/10
On the topic of Frog Fractions:
While TXT World lacks the weird sort of cohesion Frog Fractions 1 had with the story of the frog going on all sorts of adventures, it still does a great job of capturing the same sense of humor as the original, with plenty of funny dialogue throughout, and a number of points where it satirizes old tropes in game design, some intentionally bad, but does so well enough as to not be frustrating.
The main world has a number of clever puzzles, though at times it's easy to forget what area you need to backtrack to after getting a new powerup, especially since by memory at least one area requires you quit and re-enter the game so as to drop a powerup you previously needed.
The minigames share the funny designs and solid comedy of the original FF, but for as many of the little joke games there are, they now have games that actually have quite a bit of thought and even replayability to them. Me and my friends found the weird turn-based Tron game fun enough that we're honestly considering it as an entry for our next LAN.
Overall it's definitely a different sort of experience than the original Frog Fractions was, it's still a genuinely fun and entertaining experience that fans of the first should still find plenty entertainment out of. Though again, if you're -only- interested in this and won't get any enjoyment out of Glittermitten, you may want for the game to be on sale a bit.

As simulators go, this is a rather good one. As train simulators go, this is an excellent one. I definitely feel like I am at the helm of a large, powerful locoomotive when playing this game. The interiors are great, and the trains look great in terms of visuals. Sounds are quite good -- I know people complain about this aspect but I am not sure why. As a train enthusiast but not an actual employee of the RR, the sounds seem good to me. Maybe if you are an actual conductor or something, you would notice discrepancies but I do not.
Much has been made, pro and con, about the Career mode.  I was a little on the fence about this game because I like career modes in most sim games and this one seemed fairly superficial. And it is... it's just a track of your points in each scenario. Levels are meaningless. Consequently I thought I wouldn't like it.
But you know what? I really do enjoy it. Each scenario, when played 'perfectly' can yield 1,000 points. And I have really enjoyed myself trying to get as close to 1,000 as I can come. In most scenarios, even the 'green bar' (easy) ones, this is very difficult to do. I have only gotten 1,000 two or three times. But it is great fun to try, and it adds to the replayability. I utterly failed one scenario and then got a low score and tried again and got an 800+... and that was a good feeling.
On the other hand with this game the DLC is just insane. I might not have bought it at all, but for a great summer sale deal that included the base game plus a bunch of DLC for less than the price of the base game. This is definitely one to put on your wish list and wait for sales.
That said I have had many hours of fun (something like 18 and counting) on this game and it has slowly edged out other simulators like Euro Truck 2 and Farming Simulator 15 in my gaming schedule.
Pros:
+ Great sound and visuals
+ Feels like you are really driving a train
+ Each train drives a bit differently, making them unique and interesting
+ Each scenario has its own challenges
+ Lots of great tutorials to get you started
Cons:
- DLC is insanely expensive -- really for what you get in them they should be half the price they actually are.
- Some scenarios blindside you with speed limits for which there is no advance warning... Your map says speed limit is 60, so you go 60, and suddenly you are massively docked points because secretly it is a 20 mph limit. This just seems like it is done to bust players' chops.
- Very long load times for some scenarios
- On certain maps there is noticeable lag every few seconds where the screen freezes and then jumps ahead.
Overall, the pros outweigh the cons, so if you can get this puppy on sale and you like trains and/or simulators, it is well worth it and will provide you many hours of enjoyment.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons combines simple mechanics, memorable gameplay, and a beautiful story to result in one of my favorite games of all time. The game is short (seeing as I bought it yesterday night) but it is dense with nothing superfluous and, like a good book, I can see myself playing it again and again to renew the experience.
The game has you take control of, as the title suggests, two brothers. The trick is that you literally control both brothers simultaneously. Now, although the page might say that a controller is needed, it actually isn't - I beat the game with my keyboard. It was a little tricky, but it didn't hinder my experience at all.
The storytelling in this game is masterful and the game, although perhaps not as graphically impressive as some other games, it certainly is aesthetically astounding. The attention to little details, the differences in how the different characters move, the world around them, the shadows, the footprints, they all add to the immersive experience that is Brothers. Even the sidequests for achievements only helped the game to make a stronger impact on me.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a story, a game that will linger with them. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons will give you a story of love, life, and growing up like no other.
Edit: Years later, this game is still memorable, and I think on it fondly. Perhaps when the magic completely fades, I'll have the chance to play and re-experience it all over again.

Hey you!
I see you going "Eh, another Early-Access game..."
The term "indie game" actually rings really negatively in my ears.
Those recent "Indie Developers" are usually getting absolutely crushed by feature-creep.
They tend to use an existing engine for a quick moneygrab, suffer from their inexperience a lot and get nothing done.
Avorion is different.
Its not a stunning game at first glance, unlike other games (Ark Survival Evolved, Space Engineers, etc.), but the advantage of keeping it simple, not making HUGE promises, is that it's not going to be threatened to fail.
(Havent seen any of them deliver the insane promises either. Atleast not in a pleasant way.)
Factorio and Rimworld are examples of "Indie Developer Early-Access" done right.
They kept it simple, they got a solid game.

Sniper Elite 3 is a fun game and an improvement on its predecessor in almost every way. Levels are a lot bigger and more open, campaign is longer, graphics are better, stealth is improved and feels more viable, rifle customization has been added, and everything you do gives you xp so that you gain ranks regardless of if you touch multiplayer or not.
If you're looking for an amazing story with great writing and voice acting you will want to look elsewhere. Enemy AI can be questionable as well. I never had a problem with bugs and glitches, but people have reported them so that may be something to keep in mind. There is a lack of weapons in this one compared to the previous entry, but especially with the addition of weapon customization that isn't something that bothered me much. These games have never really been about weapon variety anyway.
Ranking up gives you unlocks and basically just adds a sense of progression beyond that of completing a mission. This is not some earth-shattering addition, but it is welcomed.
The new difficulty, Authentic, is highly punishing. Not only is it very hard, but if you die, you restart the level from the beginning. And these levels are not short. If you crave a challenge, you will not be disappointed.
On the other end of the spectrum you have Cadet difficulty which is almost
easy. Bullet drop and wind is removed and enemy AI is considerably dumbed down. If you feel like Call of Duty-ing your way through the game then this is the difficulty for you.
The game is optimized well and the controls are pretty much unchanged from Elite V2, which is not a bad thing. This is definitely not some lame console port.
The abundant dlc is something to be aware of as well. The game felt fine enough to me without any of it, but it is there.
I don't know that the game is worth paying full price for, but if you can get it on sale for a good price I doubt you will regret it.

Sniper Elite 3 is a worthy successor of Sniper Elite V2. It has a lot of fun stealth/sniping elements, and the hit boxes works well. The x-ray bullet time cam when you snipe someone never gets old. Graphics are decent and the game doesn't feel TOO much console damaged, although things like the weapon and gear selection clearly was designed with console in mind, along with how you move around the map.
The AI is as stupid as ANY sneak/sniping game. "Oh my friend died! ALERT!!!" 2 minutes later... "Probably nothing, let's go back to patrolling."
I very much enjoyed being able to pickup and hide bodies and being able to mask your shots by using other noises to snipe silently, without a silencer.
Overall, this is one of the better sniping games out there. If you enjoy stealth and sniping, give this one a chance.

And with apologies, the review:
So what was that all about, you ask?  I just disrespected a small chunk of your time and insulted your intelligence for my arbitrary punishments.  And that's just horrible.  As you might expect, this is a metaphor for Squishy the Suicidal Pig's gameplay.  Let's look:
Okay, so a puzzle platformer about a pig who has made a bet with the devil that's left him with a bunch of extra lives and the challenge is to burn them all up to earn a "Get Out of Hell Free" card.  That's a premise that's got a ton of charm and potential.  I'm guessing it's that premise that's drawn you in for a closer look.  I expected some free-form puzzling that poked fun at the platforming genre where deaths are easy and so often cheap.
Unfortunately, no.  It's not that.  It's just another "ragequit"-pandering frustration platformer, schizophrenically mixed with some janky pseudo physics and guess-what-the-designer-is-thinking puzzles.  But make no mistake.  Squishy isn't bad for not being the game I would have liked.  If you've got the platforms and the fireballs, I'll dodge 'em.  And you desperately need a better HVAC guy.  Point is: like the contents of several shot glasses, hard can be fun.  Although in both cases, if I end up falling into a pit, it had better be because of my own miscalculations in what I can handle.
This is not the case with Squishy.  Arbitrary is really the watchword for this game.  To tie it to the platforming: on the levels where it switches for no particular reason to a "not die" level, sometimes there are checkpoints.  The checkpoints only work once and then you restart the whole level.  Why?  Arbitrary punishment! To prove that you're willing to put in the man hours and really prove that you've nailed the level up until the brand new mechanic that will definitely kill you a half dozen times before you can possibly suss out a feel for it.  Or perhaps the developer just thought you'd be really pleased with seeing your indistinct hit box in action as you die from a deadly pendulum coming somewhat near your sprite.  Time for a side-scrolling shooter level!  Wait.  What?
I'm sure I could easily point out a dozen more examples of peculiar and unfair design, but ultimately Squishy breaks the two rules anybody out to make a precision platformer needs to put in big black text on a stark white background and set as their desktop wallpaper until the end of time:
1.  You must hold your game to the same standard of precision you demand from the player.
You want super responsive jumping that isn't competing with other animations. A sense of weight and speed is also welcome if you're going to ask the player to pass within a hair's breadth of hazards. The hit boxes must not extend outside the visible sprite.  And even then that's the minimum.  One pixel of toe touching a hazard should probably be forgiven.   Look at how bullet-hell shooters do it by only making the player's center mass vulnerable.  (Now look at what you've done, Squishy: you've got me calling bullet-hell shooters sensible)
2.  The player is going to fail a lot.  Respect their time and get them back in the action quickly.
Put a checkpoint after a lengthy segment and don't make it a limited use thing.  Really, we're supposed to be making fun of the idea of a limited resource representing your number of tries, right Squishy?  If the player dies after something like that, the only thing you're challenging is their patience.  To its credit, Squishy does have a dedicated "reload the level" button that helps with this, but any good will gained from that is instantly lost with every boss that has to waste around 10 seconds of my time with its unskippable intro dialogue every single time I restart.  Don't do that.  Especially don't do that if your boss is hard enough you might be dead in less than that amount of time.  And double-extra don't do that if it's a throwaway line that does nothing to characterize the boss outside of a generic bad-guy line.  Thanks, I think I got that much from them being the level boss and/or the devil.
Better yet, forget the wallpaper thing.  Tattoo these on yourself in mirror-writing Memento style so you never lose sight of your redemption.
So now that my mighty tirade against Squishy's platforming has thundered across the primeval plains devouring lesser megafauna, let's ask: could Squishy be saved from a negative review by clever puzzling, a strong visual aesthetic, or its narrative elements?  Nope.
Back to the word arbitrary that I seem to be hung up on; Squishy's puzzles are that.  Most of the puzzles are variants on get-box-in-air-and-get-crushed-by-it, but almost all the others are one-off tricks where you have to discover some completely unsignposted rule.  There's one level where you jump and don't fall, another where you have to try and wrap around the level, and one where you have to seemingly glitch your way through a fan that blows you upwards, just to name a few.  Oh, and there's blue and orange portals in some levels.  Because of course there are.
Can we please stop paying homage to Portal in our puzzle games?  I know every game would like to strive for the same level of wit, character, and solid design, but if you had those things in spades, then the ref would only hold you back.
On that note, the whole Squishy the Pig, deal with the pig devil, etc narrative that drew you in really doesn't go beyond just that much as a framing device at the beginning and end.  Don't expect to see Squishy or any of the antagonists portrayed beyond one or two sentences a pop.  Of course, I've been platforming since the dawn of the 90s so I can accept a back-of-the-box type story.  Still, strong character can save an otherwise mediocre game, especially if it proves a draw in the first place.
The art style's a bit of a mixed bag.  The game is pleasantly colorful and some of the sprites are appealing.  Squishy's idle animation does make him look nervous and sweaty, for instance.  But then you've got a slew of boxes and platforms and buttons that look very MS Painty.  The art's not going to carry this one, but it's not offensive overall.
What is a bit offensive is how buggy the game is.  During my first run through - before the latest patch - I found the exterminator's bonanza, but even during a quick refresher run of a couple levels before this review I got stuck in a wall, missing assets stopped me from beating a level, and the final boss looped forever outside of my reach.  Now, the dev is passionate enough about the game to keep patching it, but then again, should it be on sale on Steam if it still needs that much work?
Of course, if you're just getting this game because it goes on sale for less money than you'll get for selling the digital trading cards then Squishy will live up to all your desires! And why did you read this review anyway?  10/10, etc
But yeah, it is cheap this one.  I guess as one last point in its favor before the damning post: it's not like it will cost you much to try.  Mostly your time.  And that's the big reason why I can't thumb this one up:  it's just too damn smug about wasting my time when it can't see fit to fix its own issues.  That's what all that fooling with you up top was about.
Again, sorry about that.  I actually think you are discerning and very smart for reading my review.

Why I recommend this game:
-It's free, definitely not p2w.
-There is no "class". It is all based on what weapon you decide to use.
-You can join in a 'boss' fight with others with no party or any hindrance to others.
-Mobs are scaled to your 'ego rating' or level, so they level up with you.
-When others join, mobs are also powered up to give a challenge.
-There are plenty of 'pursuits' or achievements to try and attain.
-Fast travelling (teleporting) to towns is free, and can be done in combat or not.
-There is a self-revive which refreshes itself after a while, and others can revive you. If not it only costs a little money to be resurrected at the last checkpoint you activated.
Why I don't recommend this game:
-Gameplay may be boring after some time, grinding map events for exp but the same goes for most other mmos
-Inventory is very limited and there is no bank, Only 35 slots whether you equip items or not (Expansion requires cash)
-Bugs or glitches are not uncommon.
-Your 'ego rating' or level grows pretty fast so you have to upgrade to a new weapon often.
-Weapons are of random drop, all types and rarity. Unless buying from a 'supplies' vendor, theres no guarantee to what weapon you might get from bosses.
-Some weapons are DLC locked, you can get them but they cannot be equipped.
Endless fun, and no matter how unfair it feels you just keep on playing it.

Glittermitten Grove is a fun "city" building sim that puts you in charge of building a home for faeries in a forest. The concept is simple enough, but the detail is where it shines and where it falls short, though I would be quick to say that it shines more than not.
Faeries need homes to sleep in and food to eat. All of the faery buildings must be built in trees, and nothing can be built outside of the current sight radius. This limits building options at first, though you will quickly realize that trees grow on their own, allowing more prime building locations and allowing "sight orbs" or torches to be built, increasing your effective building space.
Building is not so simple as just throwing a building onto a tree, however. Many projects will require wood, meaning that a balance must be struck between which trees and branches to keep for building upon and which to cut down for use in woodwork. When a structure is built on a tree, its weight will cause the branch to lean realistically, meaning that if a large home is built on a dainty limb, there is danger of the branch snapping and the home being lost as it smashes on the ground. Other dangers include causing a tree to lean over another plant, stealing its sunlight and killing it.
The last layer of complexity in the game comes from the interactions you have with spells: besides food and wood, there are crystals and sparkles, which are both essentially useful in casting spells. The first "spell" allows any seeds that are found to be planted, allowing players to reforest areas if they make mistakes in tending to their trees or perhaps planting a tree that produces fruit instead of providing a large amount of building space. The second spell allows fireworks to be shot into the ground as a sort of mining explosion, allowing crystals and treasure chests to be pulled from the ground by adventurous faeries.
The fireworks spell is more complex than I would have expected it to be; a firework requires at least two (and at most three) types of patterns to be selected. A firework can be a combination of a a few different types of shots: straight firing rockets, a cone shaped blast, an advancing cone, a full semicircle blast, or a 360 degree explosion. Messing around with the different combinations you can make out of this (two straight shots just goes straight, a straight and a cone makes a long cone, etc) is simple and pure fun on its own. I found myself hoping my faeries would build torches underground faster so that I could see where the next crystals were and try out a new firework combination in getting to them.
There's plenty of space to explore underground, but unfortunately little to find. In the same merit, it's possible to grow trees up into the sky. The third spell in the player's repertoire is a fertiliser spell, allowing more controlled growth of a tree's specific branches. This adds more depth to the aforementioned building struggles and gives more agency over how to solve the problems of overcrowding trees and deforestation by lumbering.
Glittermitten Grove is a lot of fun, and I mean that. There are secrets within it that are excellent too, but no one needs a review of that part, as it's an adventure best taken with ones own opinions clean.
I'd like to see Glittermitten with a bit more depth to it. Making more use of the fireworks, having more to explore and find within the depths and the sky that builds up the grove, and just having more to be able to play and experience than the somewhat small size of the map would take the game to a higher level of quality. There's a bit of a stringent requirement on how far can be seen as well. Sight orbs become more expsensive as more are built, which leads to a sort of feedback loop which feels nice at first ("More vision, I can build in more trees, yay!") and gets less satisfying as time goes on ("The trees are too big, they need like three sight orbs, and even then I can't see to the right or left if I've focused on being able to see up the tree!"). Some upgrades to structures would improve this, I feel, and make digging for crsytals (or whatever upgrades might be tied to) more satisfying in the reward aspect. An upgrade for sight orbs that allows you to see everything to the ground in a cone from the orb would be great, for instance. Put one at the top of a tree and be able to build all in it!
Glittermitten is a solid game that could be made better. For the secrets in it, $20 seems very reasonable, but if Glittermitten Grove could be released as a standalone it would be hard to market for much at its current state, which is a shame, because it's very fun for a little while. I'd recommend it based on the base game alone, a solid amount of fun for the price of a movie ticket with some popcorn and drink.

Last Played: March 2014
PROS: + Everything, from character models to environments, is beautiful and the artistic direction is cohesive
+ Refreshingly, shows rather than tells a story
CONS: - Start to finish beatable in less than three hours
- Cranking elevators is so non-intuitive you may get stuck
REVIEW: Got this game on Steam sale for $5 and for this price, it is a bargain. The world looks and feels like a Grimm brothers’ fairy tale, where you skip from totally different backdrop to backdrop, though this is positive as well as negative. On the positive side the game’s artistic flavor never compromises the feel of ordinary characters in a supernatural and fantastic realm. Consistent with the Grimm story type however, is the “skipping” travel between areas where the protagonist has suddenly come to a completely different area with a completely different (and wholly unexplained) backstory. Whether you like this brand of storytelling or not is a personal preference, but I applaud the developers for having the guts to do what they wanted to do, exquisitely showing a rather simple story (there is not so much as a single written word or line of dialogue in the whole game, excepting menus and a control prompt or two).
On the complaints side, I do have to gripe that the game feels quite short, in fact having never played this game before most should be able to beat this in a single sitting if they choose. This raises some questions about value-for-money. Personally, I am of the opinion that if you can get this for less than the cost of a movie ticket where you live, you’ll get more entertainment out of this than whatever you could have seen there, but that’s just me. It certainly compares favorably with paying $60 for a trashy and forgettable 3-hour Call of Duty campaign, since you’ll actually remember what happened more than 10 minutes after you are done. No bugs to speak of, and controls are mostly fluid, but I do have one specific complaint: crank shafts in this game may be intuitive to some, but I tried every control scheme I could think of, and after five minutes stuck at the beginning of the game became convinced that I had a bug that was preventing me from moving on. Not so-when I looked up the supposed bug it turned out I just had to rotate the control sticks. However, a single counter-clockwise arrow could have saved me a few minutes of frustration and would have been trivially simple to include. Still, a fantastic experience, and I’d buy it again if I didn’t already own it.

Let me just state this upfront: Red Faction Guerilla is a great deal of fun most of the time.  This should likely come as no surprise to anyone familiar with the developer’s (Volition) most famous (and ridiculously fun and absurd) series, Saints Row.  That being said, Guerilla is far from a perfect game and definitely shows its age in some respects.
But first, the positives.  Like I said before, there is a lot of fun to be had in Guerilla and this is due in large part to the Geo-Mod system the game employs which essentially allows for you tear down damn near every structure in the game, brick by brick.  There’s an extremely visceral amount of fun to be had simply roaming around the Martian landscape plowing through buildings or bashing away at a building with your trusty sledgehammer before hearing that telltale creak that signifies a building is about to come crashing down all around you and scrambling to get out of the way of the debris.  Additionally, the system can even take on a bit of a puzzle like aspect as you try to find the most efficient manner of bringing a building down with your remote charges or rocket launcher.
From a technical aspect, the game is also well optimized for most any PC.  I tested the game on a mid-range laptop (8 GB RAM, i5 processor, and integrated graphics card) and it ran with very few problems (there were a few frame rate hiccups here and there when the destruction started to get really crazy but even still it was absolutely playable) on low to medium settings.  When I moved over to my desktop though (i7, 16 GB RAM, with a GeForce GT 730) I was able to get silky smooth performance at higher settings.  For what it’s worth, I’ve also played Guerilla on my 360 and while performance there was closer to what I saw on my laptop, I would still recommend it on that system to anyone who asked.
Unfortunately, a lot of what’s surrounding the actual gameplay in Guerilla leaves a fair bit to be desired.  The story of the game is utterly forgettable and extremely self-serious which is quite disappointing, especially in light of what Volition would ultimately go on to do in the Saints Row series.  I honestly couldn’t tell you the name of more than two or three characters in Guerilla and to say that the characters who are present in the game lack definition would be putting things lightly.  The Witcher 3 this game is not but then again not every game has to be.
What’s a bigger issue though, is that the game is unfortunately afflicted with an issue present in a lot of open world games in that there simply isn’t a lot there to make the world feel alive.  Much of the time you’ll simply be driving between the different “Guerilla Actions” (essentially side quests and events) or EDF (the game’s primary villain) bases looking for more targets to destroy with little points of interest in between.  Furthermore, I found the actual combat present in the game to be frustrating at times as there’s a surprisingly low ammo ceiling for the weapons you can carry and Alec Mason (the game’s protagonist) proved to be somewhat fragile in terms of survivability.  There is a cover system present in the game, but it’s laughably simple at best and actually detrimental to your play at worst as you can pretty easily get stuck to walls and find yourself swarmed with EDF goons in pretty short order.  I typically found it a lot easier to instead just get in whatever vehicle I could find and ram through as many enemies as I could before actually getting out and engaging in a direct fire fight.
That being said though, I would still recommend this game purely based on the amount of fun there is to be had with the destructibility of the environment.  Just know before going in that there are some gameplay frustrations that you’ll have to push through and that there really isn’t anything waiting for you at the end in terms of a satisfying narrative. Guerilla is one of those game’s you should play for exactly as long as you’re still having fun blowing stuff up and then feeling fine dropping once that loses its luster.

I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game. It's a Diablo-esque hack n' slash RPG at its finest.
PROS:
The game is extremely system-friendly, even low-end computers can run it and there are a myriad of settings to tweak to meet your system requirements. It's not exactly a graphically stunning game, but I like the art style of the game.
The gameplay, while simple, should be nearly exactly what you'd expect from a game like this: clearing dungeons, slaughtering hordes of enemies, and collecting tons and tons of loot. There's nearly constant inventory management, as one should find themselves constantly comparing their equipment with loot drops, sending their pets off to market to sell off junk and buy potions, and handling gems and artifacts to socket into weapons, armor, and accessories.
There's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in this game. You just kill everything that looks at you funny and loot their broken, eviscerated corpses.
Each playthrough on a typical vanilla game would last about a good 20 hours. It's a good length- it's not so short as to feel like I got cheated out of my money, and it's not so long that it wears out its welcome. The amount of character variety, EXTENSIVE mod support, multiplayer action, and just seeing the randomized loot offers great replay value.
CONS:
The plot is pathetic. There's next to no lore in the game and characters only exist to give you random fetch quests or prattle about ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that nobody cares for. The plot is about as cookie-cutter as you can get: evil thing comes to threaten the land and you go kill it. There's next to no characterization or real life in the setting. The quests can feel kind of dull, they're just one fetch quest after the other. The game in some ways is too forgiving. The only penalty for dying is being sent back a bit and losing some money. It's really not much of a setback at all and dying just feels like I'm wasting my time moreso than anything else. Being able to send your pet to market to buy stuff is cool and convenient... but there's plenty of potions out in the environment. It's not so much too easy as too forgiving. The challenge is there on higher difficulties, of course, but it's nothing like Diablo in terms of difficulty.
It's an extremely solid game all-in-all, and a worthy spiritual successor to Diablo. Highly reccommended for people who love randomized loot and hack n' slash gameplay. The huge amount of support the devs have given to modders is certainly a bonus.

If I ever had to recommend a slower, extremely complex, real-time tactics game to anyone, this would be my first and strongest suggestion hands down.  Impeccable balancing of units coincides with well-designed maps in a strong PvP experience.  It's certainly not flashy, but it is mostly realistic.  Single player is there, but hardly the focus of development and not where the real fun lies.
It's almost difficult to sum up what makes this so interesting.  The combination of crafting your own army (making a "deck"), the massively large amount of different numbers and units to take into consideration, the real time tactics of managing so many different things at once to be effective, all of that together (and more) at once makes it special when you end up succeeding with something you created along with the strategies you're employing.
If there is one thing to note, however, is that this game is -not- new player friendly.  It's difficult to understand and grasp many aspects of the game, and I was lucky enough to be liberally assisted by a very skilled friend who wanted me to play (starting with its predecessor, Airland Battle).  Dedication and skill is needed to get full satisfaction out of it, but it holds a high replay value and deep and varied combat mechanics to dabble in if you can get into it.

I recieved this game by backing the Kickstarter. (very early acess review)
So far it is a wonderful game, but I have not made it very far yet.
The combat is great although a little simple so far.
The ship building is limited only by your imagination and resources.

There is a lot of information on the HUD. So much so that it can be hard to find which information im looking for. There is no numerical indicator of your own speed, just a bar. Also, I have a ship system that scans for valuables, but it wont tell me where they actually are.
Sometimes the loot drops from a destroyed ship are much stronger or weaker then I would expect. For example a ship that probably cost around 50k dropped a half mil ship system in my first 20 mins of playing that made most other costs trivial to me.
It is early access, so I am not worried about this long term. Twice it has frozen. Each one lasting around 30 seconds, after which it resumes with no problems.
As far as I have seen, the flight physics are perfect. I love that you have to think about building reverse thrusters into your ship to break. I love that when you turn it keeps your original vector and speed. It makes it all feel very real.
So far, my experince with combat has been rather simple, it's just point and hold. However you can make it more complex by aiming at specific components on the enemy ship, such as engines, weapons, or shield generators. As I get more ships and fighter, it will certainly become more complicated also.

As simulators go, this is a rather good one. As train simulators go, this is an excellent one. I definitely feel like I am at the helm of a large, powerful locoomotive when playing this game. The interiors are great, and the trains look great in terms of visuals. Sounds are quite good -- I know people complain about this aspect but I am not sure why. As a train enthusiast but not an actual employee of the RR, the sounds seem good to me. Maybe if you are an actual conductor or something, you would notice discrepancies but I do not.
Much has been made, pro and con, about the Career mode.  I was a little on the fence about this game because I like career modes in most sim games and this one seemed fairly superficial. And it is... it's just a track of your points in each scenario. Levels are meaningless. Consequently I thought I wouldn't like it.
But you know what? I really do enjoy it. Each scenario, when played 'perfectly' can yield 1,000 points. And I have really enjoyed myself trying to get as close to 1,000 as I can come. In most scenarios, even the 'green bar' (easy) ones, this is very difficult to do. I have only gotten 1,000 two or three times. But it is great fun to try, and it adds to the replayability. I utterly failed one scenario and then got a low score and tried again and got an 800+... and that was a good feeling.
On the other hand with this game the DLC is just insane. I might not have bought it at all, but for a great summer sale deal that included the base game plus a bunch of DLC for less than the price of the base game. This is definitely one to put on your wish list and wait for sales.
That said I have had many hours of fun (something like 18 and counting) on this game and it has slowly edged out other simulators like Euro Truck 2 and Farming Simulator 15 in my gaming schedule.
Pros:
+ Great sound and visuals
+ Feels like you are really driving a train
+ Each train drives a bit differently, making them unique and interesting
+ Each scenario has its own challenges
+ Lots of great tutorials to get you started
Cons:
- DLC is insanely expensive -- really for what you get in them they should be half the price they actually are.

This game gives me a lot of mixed feelings. It was the first game I bought on Steam when it was called Railworks, and that was back in 2011. Lots of routes and trains, plenty of scenarios, and decent graphics and controls.
Now, it's an overpriced train sim with almost $5k worth of DLC with ok graphics and little content.
Three routes? Seriously? That's enough already to make people have second thoughts about this game. Even if they do get it, if they want more to play around with they have to buy more routes. At this point I would assume someone would just stop playing overall, because just look at the prices. $39.99 for a mediocre route with a few new engines and stock? Bull****. Utter bull****.
I mean, it would be better off if they lowered the prices for what they're giving you, but obviously they aren't listening after a few years of people telling them the same thing over and over.
Now, there are good things about this sim. It's way better than any other train sim out there, with decent graphics and pretty good controls. The physics can be a bit weird sometimes (cars moving away from the engine when you go to couple up to them, or when a train derails it spasms and has no weight at all), but its usually well done, especially the wheel slip. The engines/stock is pretty well modeled, but bridges, buildings, people, pretty much everything else, is nothing special. Major stations looking kinda nice though, and the routes are pretty accurate to their real-life counterparts.
The workshop is nothing to write home about, but it has some great fan-made scenarios and routes (If you have the DLC to play them). If you want more routes to play with, go to the workshop and download the Hedborough North and other classic routes to mess with.
Overall, this game is worth it if you are a rail fan looking for a good sim to play with, who also has the money for the WAY overpriced DLC they have to offer. If you don't have the money, just wait for the steam sales and you can get a few things for an ok price.
If you are someone just looking for a fun train game to pass the time, don't spend you're money on this. Go buy Mini Metro, it's like $5.00.

This isn't a great game by any means. The cover system shows its age; it's useless. The running/jumping/driving physics are early sandbox wonky which is embarrassing even for this game's 2009 release (and don't tell me it's because it's Martian gravity because if that's what they were going for, it's even worse). But sledgehammering the brains out of hundreds of faceless facist soldiers and blowing buildings to high hell is fun. The destruction physics are still pretty darn entertaining. Each sector has its goals, and it's rewarding in a completionist sort of way to run through the objectives and free Mars through "guerrilla" tactics.
There's a lot of nice science fiction literature references in the game, which I found surprising when I first played this game back in 2009, but don't expect anything exceptional in the story. Grab on sale to try it out. The beginning is slow, but once you pass the first area, you start to become an invincible god of destruction with better and better weaponry.

The previous version required a player to sit through training courses in order to utilize certain roles. Like you couldn't be a medic without going through a class and then doing some more hands on training. You couldn't play on a special forces map without doing a midnight hike without being spotted and taking a test on what image looked like a specific type of military vehicle or equipment. Training courses still exist, but they only help you to unlock different sighting devices or paint for your equipment.
Still, not a bad game at all though.

Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China: Quite an impressive little game set in the China Burma India Theater of the second World War.
Simple straight forward Arcade air combat,so no need to compare it to other games like the IL2 series and WarThunder.
FT:SOC reminds me more of Secret Weapons Over Normandy with its gameplay,and thats a good thing..
Its fun,entertaining,a little bit challenging at times and the voice acting adds to the enjoyment of playing.
Of note the game has been optimised for the use of TrackIR,so without it you only get  lateral views of your 3/6 & 9 o'clock.
The details of the scenery are outstanding on cinematic settings,although the colour saturation is a bit harsh and  distracting.
A couple of things I'd like to see implemented later would be the ability freely change to the gunners position and to be able to use flaps.Also To be able to look around without the need for the aformentioned TrackIR.
Right now the biggest let down is the complete lack of players on the multiplayer servers,but thats no fault of the game itself.
Overall  Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China is a fun,satisfying little gem set in a mostly overlooked theatre of war aimed at those who enjoy air-combat games,be it casual players or seasoned veterans.

Pretty fun game if you have an interest in larger scale military strategy, with a combined arms approach rather than just spamming your high cost tank. Alot of units have their utility, so cheaper units are not always directly inferior and have their use - aswell as cheaper units will give you more numbers. If you have for example a 180 cost tank, you will only get 1 or 2, where as a 90 point tank will give you maybe 8 or 7, allowing you to capitalize on numbers at a cost of a more powerful unit.
Not too easy to learn, so it's good to have a friend who is good at the game to teach you the ins and outs.
Alot of people complain about balance and there is a balance issue in certain places with the game. Depending on who you are, this is either a good or bad thing:  You may like a game balanced away from realism to make it slightly more 'fair', or you may prefer that the game lets both sides/individual nations have their strong and weak points.
Personally, I prefer to play against an enemy and in the lobby see what nation they are playing as, to know what their strong points and weak points are in terms of units, to help devise a plan to counteract that. I prefer to play a game where I have to think to nullify the enemies advantage, than have everything completely balanced.
At the end of the day, superior tactics will win games over just good units - Adapt and overcome. This sort of thing comes apparent when a team of 1980s North Korea beats a cocky well rounded BLU team. I've seen it happen, and no, it really isn't easy, but if you can outplan your enemy, you'll have positive kill/loss ratios in any match.
If at the end of the day you really just can't get a grip on the game but are willing to learn, theres an entire 200 page 'red dragon for dummies' guide that can teach you everything you need to know, although you really just need to in most cases think realistically about things.
It's a hard to game learn but a very good RTS.

I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game. It's a Diablo-esque hack n' slash RPG at its finest.
PROS:
The game is extremely system-friendly, even low-end computers can run it and there are a myriad of settings to tweak to meet your system requirements. It's not exactly a graphically stunning game, but I like the art style of the game.
The gameplay, while simple, should be nearly exactly what you'd expect from a game like this: clearing dungeons, slaughtering hordes of enemies, and collecting tons and tons of loot. There's nearly constant inventory management, as one should find themselves constantly comparing their equipment with loot drops, sending their pets off to market to sell off junk and buy potions, and handling gems and artifacts to socket into weapons, armor, and accessories.
There's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in this game. You just kill everything that looks at you funny and loot their broken, eviscerated corpses.
Each playthrough on a typical vanilla game would last about a good 20 hours. It's a good length- it's not so short as to feel like I got cheated out of my money, and it's not so long that it wears out its welcome. The amount of character variety, EXTENSIVE mod support, multiplayer action, and just seeing the randomized loot offers great replay value.
CONS:
The plot is pathetic. There's next to no lore in the game and characters only exist to give you random fetch quests or prattle about ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that nobody cares for. The plot is about as cookie-cutter as you can get: evil thing comes to threaten the land and you go kill it. There's next to no characterization or real life in the setting. The quests can feel kind of dull, they're just one fetch quest after the other. The game in some ways is too forgiving. The only penalty for dying is being sent back a bit and losing some money. It's really not much of a setback at all and dying just feels like I'm wasting my time moreso than anything else. Being able to send your pet to market to buy stuff is cool and convenient... but there's plenty of potions out in the environment. It's not so much too easy as too forgiving. The challenge is there on higher difficulties, of course, but it's nothing like Diablo in terms of difficulty.
It's an extremely solid game all-in-all, and a worthy spiritual successor to Diablo. Highly reccommended for people who love randomized loot and hack n' slash gameplay. The huge amount of support the devs have given to modders is certainly a bonus.

Honestly while I have had like 3 good times in GTA Online, and the game has an FPS mode that is really immersive thanks to some really well designed first person animations and a complete change in subtle control scheme to make it work great, the game is an unbalanced mess. It's got very high production value, you can see the budget that was put into this game before your very eyes, and there are some neat, fun touches in the single player campaign like Michael calling you when you rocket his house as trevor, but none of that matters when the game itself is actually quite boring.
I thought about not leaving a review since steam only has upvotes and downvotes because this game is a solid 5/10. Like, flashy visuals, good character acting and large amounts of high tier development technology are appreciated and do contribute to making a game better but they still ultimately don't make a good game since they're all surface level quality. Just because you have a lot of things to do in a campaign doesn't mean they're all fun. In fact I think all of the animation budget they put into the game has actually affected the gameplay, since despite good somewhat punchy firearm sound design weapons feel floaty to use likely as compensation for the fact that there is a delay for turning thanks to the animation and controls focusing on realism first and responsive gameplay second. This is alleviated by going first person mode for the most part, but still very noticeable.
In reality GTAV is somewhat of a slog. GTA Online seems deliberately grindy to get you to buy shark cards. The community is the worst one you'll ever see at times. The game gets old fast. But I could still leave a thumbs up despite all of that, were it not for mods being outlawed. This sets a dangerous precedent that should never be put in place.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone, like, not just because of this recent business with mods (That's a contributing factor though), but because the game seems to get worse with every update. There's more and more things, more and more controversies keep happening (for once not over the content but ♥♥♥♥♥♥ business practices, which is hilariously ironic because typically in the GTA series the opposite has been true; Ballad of Gay Tony and Lost & Damned for GTA 4 used to be prime examples of how to do DLC right.) and it all keeps making this game seemingly worse instead of better. Don't buy this. The PC port was appreciated even if it was 2 years late, but appreciating something doesn't mean you can't be critical of it.

I will start off saying most of my game knowledge will be from GTA Online, but I have watched the entire single player campaign twice and confident enough to state an opinion on the game. The game always had a great cinematic feel to the game and pointed out some great discoveries through satirical context and the personality of every living (and perhaps brutally murdered) citizen in Los Santos. As odd as this might sound, I've always been curious of any player's end result at the end of the main campaign where it records everything you've accomplished; typically of carnal pleasure and kill quotas.
I enjoy through observation and I will use that as an opportunity to get to my real point. This game, (online especially) has amazing memories that you, the player, achieve through your actions, where one day you're fist fighting on a moving bus with another player, to then immediately transition to that same player screaming in agony as a heist's escape plane shreds them from head to toe after you fought off an entire prison complex's security force. Eventually though, as free content flowed into the ocean of code for GTA, the creativity in most players dropped, one end because a grind would ensue that many people just simply do not have time for, another end because something as taboo as -ONLINE- modding suddenly is the only excuse to play the game. Due to some news at the time of this post, Rockstar and Two Star are at considerable fault for allowing something of that scale to remain untouched as long as it did, and caused honest reviews and thorough critique to overwhelmingly cease, the community preferring to put a game they had enough passion for to comment on burn to the ground, and anyone new to GTA should invest time in videos released between 2015-2016, both singleplayer and online.
This game is not for people who prefer a much more casual form of entertainment through the online platform, but the original content of the singleplayer is absolutely amazing and price efficient for that content alone. Bring your light-hearted humor and darkside to the life of crime today.

The easiest way to sum up Spelunky is to call it Indiana Jones:  The videogame.  There are other games with similar premise (La-Mulana, for instance) but none that quite capture the sense of whimsy and danger, the risk/reward appeal, of diving into the unknown in the hopes of finding glorious riches.
I don't think I have ever been less enraged getting the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of me by a game.  I can't pinpoint why exactly, but dying in Spelunky doesn't cause the outrage most games do.  Perhaps because, like Dark Souls, most of your deaths will be a result of user error and not cheesiness.  If an obstacle seems particularly challenging, look harder.  There's usually a trick to getting past hard parts and traps.
Your starting loadout of bombs and rope are a lot more useful than they first appear.  In most of your early runs, you will fail to utilize these affectively due to magpie syndrome.  However, it will quickly become apparent that your health is your most valuable resource.  You'll become a lot more stingy with your hearts than you are with your equipment.  I know this seems self explanatory, but it is very easy to have a great run end because you got lazy and missed the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bat or the hidden arrow trap.
I say "great run" because, like many mainstays in the (ugh) rogue-like genre, you will gather items and powerups that can give you an edge.  Most of these are bought, some of them are found, but all of them are a godsend.  Small things, like being able to scale sheer walls insead of having to use one of your hooks, increase your chances of survival by much more than it would seem on the outside looking in.
After a good 5 or 6 hours of Spelunky, I'm still a little undecided on how I feel about it.  It's not really the type of game that you'll sit and grind on for hours, it's more of a pick up and play type thing.  It requires a lot of attention, so your time with the game will likely turn into a quality over quantity affair.  It is very challenging, but not intensely so.  Advancing in the game requires strong attention to very minute details, but rarely will you feel an abundance of pressure.  These seemingly conflicting concepts are very much the heart of Spelunky, and it deserves a look if only to experience it's unique flavor.

Brothers: A Tale of Two sons checks off a lot of boxes on my list of things that make a great game: innovative gameplay, great storytelling, gorgeous visuals and a good soundtrack.
Controlling both brothers at once is this game's biggest novelty and one that I never tired of in my 3.4 hours with it. One aspect of controlling both that I didn't anticipate is that it aids in making you as the player feel more connected to both of them. Each brother also has a unique personality that shows up in what gameplay actions each one can and can't take. For example, the older brother can boost the younger one up to the top of a tall ledge and then the younger one can drop down a rope. Even in optional environmental interactions (like blowing into a huge horn) each boy has a different response.
The inclusion of these little details reminds me of the sense of childlike wonder that Studio Ghibli (Hayao Miyazaki) movies do so well to turn the ordinary into the extraordinary. It's incredible to me how clear of a story and how rich of a world the developers were able to get across entirely nonverbally. There are voices in the game but it is all in a very simplistic, fictional language. Their meaning is conveyed sufficiently through voice tone and body language. The world itself tells its own story and made me feel like I knew plenty of the lore surrounding it, again, all without words.
It certainly helps that a game so focused on visual storytelling also has great art design. There are numerous benches throughout the game that you can direct the boys to sit on. When you do the camera pans out to show off some impressive vistas. In most games I couldn't be bothered to go sit on a bench yet here I made it a point to seek out each one. The soundtrack packs an emotional punch during major scenes but can be very quiet or absent during others.
With so much positive to say about the game I do have a few negatives. There are a few points where the gameplay gets repetitive. For example you'll climb up numerous cliffs, nets, root balls, etc. and none are particularly challenging or exciting. In general though, they do a pretty good job of changing things up as the game progresses. I also encountered a bug in the PC version of the game where two elevator cranks you'll encounter in the game operate VERY slowly. We're talking roughly 2 minutes for the first one and 3 minutes for the second before you can continue on with the game. You cannot bypass these. Finally, I wasn't much of a fan of the overall tragic tone of the game. I don't mind dark themes but I like them to have a purpose for being a downer besides trying to be different or to tack extra emotional impact to a scene. This is perhaps an area where the nonverbal storytelling is a weakness because I couldn't discern enough purpose to warrant Brothers' somber tone.

I truly forgot how friggin fun this game is, it was one of the first game's I ever played to have full crazy building leveling destruction in true red faction tradition of having stupid amounts of destruction, like how in RF1 you could tunnel for miles through walls with explosives, 2 was about the same with some more/less in some areas, and then this came out eons later and blew my mind, It still holds up as an awesome game and the whole series is worth the money to me having grown up in love with the Red Faction.

I tend to call this game the last great destructible scenery game. Red faction since its inception has given players enormous freedom in blowing open walls to make new paths, blowing up bridges to drop things, etc. Red faction Guerrilla is the pinnacle of this system, with a truly beastly amount of freedom to destroy. Car bombing a building into a tiny pile of rubble is totally possible. The fact that the game has this system but does not force you to use it means that players can just as easily go in tactically on a mission despite all the explosive possibilities. You can blow the entire block up to kill a target, or blow a hole in the roof and blast him. Vehicles are not left out of this and can be used to destroy things just as easily as a det charge.
In terms of story, it really is not bad at all, nothing groundbreaking, but the fact it ties into the old games and still stands out with cool themes of its own (Such as the awesomely dressed raider faction) makes it a pleasure to find in a game that could easily have shipped with a cookie cutter story.
The weapon selection is extravagant and awesome, with precision deconstruction weapons like the nano rifle, and massive ordinance like the thermobaric rocket that can level blocks.
While the game in large part is totally badass, there are some pitfalls. The inability to redo main missions is bad to find in an open world game, though theres alot of side missions that can be replayed, that does not excuse the inability to redo missions.
Along the same lines, if you destroy many landmarks, those landmarks do not come back, ever. Blow up the biggest coolest bridge in the game and thats it, never again. Many buildings do respawn, especially ones used in side missions, but the many that do not are a sad one time bit of fun that will never be again.
So overall, red faction guerrilla is a game with a fantastic destruction system, above any other game to come out before or since. Blow everything up, deconstruct your enemies bunkers, bridges, and tanks. Sneak in, blow your way out. use vehicles as disguises, wrecking balls, or escape methods. Work with the reistance. This game is a great example of an open world game made right, but with the downfalls of diminished replayability due to being unable to replay missions or regenerate the environment.
