First here is the official website for the game where you can get yourself some great screen savers...
The game was developed by these people...
And you can clearly see by the size of the picture they use to advertise this game in comparison to all the other games they have helped with how proud they are of this masterpiece. This is also because the true inspiration and vision of the game came from a famous Swedish Film Director Josef Fares who can be found here...
The game is a single player, story driven, short puzzle adventure game. It will take you somewhere between 2-5 hrs to complete all up. A lot of people claim that this is the first game where you’re required to control two characters at the same time. Simply put this is not true. An old and genius game called 'head over heels' has claim to that privilege, but this is a very unique game which actually uses gaming apparatus (the controller) to help tell a story and convey a message. Not too many games to my knowledge have ever really explored this concept.
The game is specifically created so that you control two characters at the same time using a dual stick controller. While the game can still be played using solely the keyboard it feels rather awkward in comparison, like as if you’re trying to drive a car from the back seat while wearing a chicken suit. A lot of the time you will be shouting at the screen, "Where the hell are you going?" as you witness one of the brothers run needlessly into danger. So if you want to feel like a pro in the driver’s seat, i highly recommend playing the game as it was intended and that is with a controller. You see literally your left thumb will control one brother and your right thumb will control the other. It's this dependency that tells a great story as both brothers have unique characteristics and abilities. For instance one has a fear of water, where the other can slip into confined spaces and can piggy back you up to a higher ledge. Both brothers need to work together in harmony and with a plan if they are to get through the 8 chapters of the game.
The complete story is told using a gibberish made up language that was slightly inspired to sound like Arabic after a massive pub crawl. Hence the real story telling is completely through visuals, body language and environments. The story begins after a recent fishing accident where the mother dies and one of the brothers feels completely responsible for. Not long after they also discover that their now widowed father is also terminally ill and according to the town doctor he needs a special ingredient from a magic tree. Both brothers not wanting to have another death of their hands go out on an enthralling fantasy adventure where they will meet plenty of friends and foes.
(Spoilers below)
It shouldn't come to any surprise that not everything goes according to plan and at the end you will be seriously thinking to yourself 'what a dumb magic tree this thing is, I'm coming back here with a chainsaw!!!'. It's a sad ending which will require you to go through a whole box of tissues maybe two. The ending and the message it conveys is based on the real life feelings of the director Josef Fares who was required to bury his own brother after the Lebanon war. He did not let this death go in vain, but used it as a motivation to do great things in his own life and wanted to convey those similar sentiments in the game.
As much as he wanted to portray this it slightly fails as most of us know what guilt can do to a person and how it can truly cripple someone's joy in life. The constant nagging 'what ifs' would constantly be on the mind of those survivors. Hence any good news at the end seems extremely fleeting. I guess one moral of the story is... 'Don’t be kind to everyone it can come back and sting you!'

Governor of Poker 2 is perfect for the shy poker enthusiast that doesn't want to play online or play for money. This game is completely single-player, with hundreds of AI opponents of different levels, and the goal is to play your way up to the big boss, the Governor of Texas. The game played is no-limit Texas Hold'em.
The screen you see the most is the overhead view of the poker table. The game is also built around what happens on the table, so don't expect too much detail from the rest of the RPG elements of the game. Even so, every character on the map has something (useless) to say, so feel free to "explore." The AI is impressively diverse, and in harder cities it helps to learn how opponents play. Definitely try the demo first to see if the AI fits your standards. The player voices are entertaining (and annoying whenever they win chips), and you can turn them on and off whenever you want. You can also quit the game whenever; the game saves the state of the table when you exit.
Some small details might raise some questions, though. You cannot input exactly how much you want to bet (you bet in increments on a sliding scale), and the AIs like to make the math annoying by betting, e.g., $37 when the blinds are $10 and $20. Also, you are unable to choose whether to muck your hand during the showdown.
Overall, GoP2 is a great follow-up to the first GoP and definitely worth a look.

It's got very high production value, you can see the budget that was put into this game before your very eyes, and there are some neat, fun touches in the single player campaign like Michael calling you when you rocket his house as trevor, but none of that matters when the game itself is actually quite boring.
I thought about not leaving a review since steam only has upvotes and downvotes because this game is a solid 5/10. Like, flashy visuals, good character acting and large amounts of high tier development technology are appreciated and do contribute to making a game better but they still ultimately don't make a good game since they're all surface level quality. Just because you have a lot of things to do in a campaign doesn't mean they're all fun. In fact I think all of the animation budget they put into the game has actually affected the gameplay, since despite good somewhat punchy firearm sound design weapons feel floaty to use likely as compensation for the fact that there is a delay for turning thanks to the animation and controls focusing on realism first and responsive gameplay second. This is alleviated by going first person mode for the most part, but still very noticeable.
In reality GTAV is somewhat of a slog. GTA Online seems deliberately grindy to get you to buy shark cards. The community is the worst one you'll ever see at times. The game gets old fast. But I could still leave a thumbs up despite all of that, were it not for mods being outlawed. This sets a dangerous precedent that should never be put in place.

Don't buy this. The PC port was appreciated even if it was 2 years late, but appreciating something doesn't mean you can't be critical of it.

The easiest way to sum up Spelunky is to call it Indiana Jones:  The videogame.  There are other games with similar premise (La-Mulana, for instance) but none that quite capture the sense of whimsy and danger, the risk/reward appeal, of diving into the unknown in the hopes of finding glorious riches.
I don't think I have ever been less enraged getting the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of me by a game.  I can't pinpoint why exactly, but dying in Spelunky doesn't cause the outrage most games do.  Perhaps because, like Dark Souls, most of your deaths will be a result of user error and not cheesiness.  If an obstacle seems particularly challenging, look harder.  There's usually a trick to getting past hard parts and traps.
Your starting loadout of bombs and rope are a lot more useful than they first appear.  In most of your early runs, you will fail to utilize these affectively due to magpie syndrome.  However, it will quickly become apparent that your health is your most valuable resource.  You'll become a lot more stingy with your hearts than you are with your equipment.  I know this seems self explanatory, but it is very easy to have a great run end because you got lazy and missed the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bat or the hidden arrow trap.
I say "great run" because, like many mainstays in the (ugh) rogue-like genre, you will gather items and powerups that can give you an edge.  Most of these are bought, some of them are found, but all of them are a godsend.  Small things, like being able to scale sheer walls insead of having to use one of your hooks, increase your chances of survival by much more than it would seem on the outside looking in.
After a good 5 or 6 hours of Spelunky, I'm still a little undecided on how I feel about it.  It's not really the type of game that you'll sit and grind on for hours, it's more of a pick up and play type thing.  It requires a lot of attention, so your time with the game will likely turn into a quality over quantity affair.  It is very challenging, but not intensely so.  Advancing in the game requires strong attention to very minute details, but rarely will you feel an abundance of pressure.  These seemingly conflicting concepts are very much the heart of Spelunky, and it deserves a look if only to experience it's unique flavor.

Honestly while I have had like 3 good times in GTA Online, and the game has an FPS mode that is really immersive thanks to some really well designed first person animations and a complete change in subtle control scheme to make it work great, the game is an unbalanced mess. It's got very high production value, you can see the budget that was put into this game before your very eyes, and there are some neat, fun touches in the single player campaign like Michael calling you when you rocket his house as trevor, but none of that matters when the game itself is actually quite boring.
I thought about not leaving a review since steam only has upvotes and downvotes because this game is a solid 5/10. Like, flashy visuals, good character acting and large amounts of high tier development technology are appreciated and do contribute to making a game better but they still ultimately don't make a good game since they're all surface level quality. Just because you have a lot of things to do in a campaign doesn't mean they're all fun. In fact I think all of the animation budget they put into the game has actually affected the gameplay, since despite good somewhat punchy firearm sound design weapons feel floaty to use likely as compensation for the fact that there is a delay for turning thanks to the animation and controls focusing on realism first and responsive gameplay second. This is alleviated by going first person mode for the most part, but still very noticeable.
In reality GTAV is somewhat of a slog. GTA Online seems deliberately grindy to get you to buy shark cards. The community is the worst one you'll ever see at times. The game gets old fast. I'm writing this review assuming you've played Frog Fractions 1. If you haven't... go play Frog Fractions 1, it's a far better game than this one and it's free.
After having loved the original Frog Fractions very dearly, I am sad to say this game does not live up to the original. The original Frog Fractions took about 5 minutes to really "start" - meanwhile depending on your luck with RNG as to where a door spawns, you could spend 10-30 minutes in the fake Fairy Game before getting to the actual game.
Additionally, while Frog Fractions kept bombarding you with new thing after new thing and witty, clever jokes - in Frog fractions 2 these "new things" are very sporadically hidden in a TEXT RPG world that is equal parts tedious, confusing, and just plain unfun. In order to get to the gameplay changes, you have to find very well-hidden doors that can sometimes be hidden behind an HOUR of puzzle solving.
Worse still, a lot of the game seems to have been made tedious for no reason other than to emulate how tedious old ASCI games were. You get TWO different upgrades, roller skates and a sword, which both make your character control WORSE - one can only be removed if you have a certain item, and another is required for progress. So your character controls their best and the very onset of the game and control worse and worse as the game goes on, so that doesn't feel great.
Imagine working a mundane data entry job, but once every 20-30 minutes someone cracks a half-decent joke. That's frog fractions 2 - a boring, frustrating, soul-crushing job that is OCCASIONALLY funny. I speak with no sarcasm or joking tone when i say that you are just better off playing Frog Fractions 1, or replaying it, than buying this game.

I'm just awful at the rapid fire FPS games, the sniper "wait and plan" motif here is a great alternative. On the plus side you have plenty of places to hide, frame your shot, sometimes wait for masking sounds, then focus and pull the trigger - exactly what a sniper game should let you do. There's also plenty of reason for sneaking around and silently disposing of some troublemakers to get into position.
However realism isn't the strong suit here. Granted, I tend to play on the easier levels since I'm much more casual but much of the game involves the bad guys having a nice chat. Then I blow off Fred's head and they all start trying to find me. I run away 50 meters and in a minute or two they just say, "Oh well, we didn't like Fred that much anyway." Repeat the process with George a few minutes later until you've cleared the board. Add to that mostly linear levels (some things I can climb, others I can't) and the bullet-cam, while a useful way to know how your shot went, can be distracting and you've got some negatives to overcome.
I would like to see more rewards for targeted, stealthy hits - but on the other hand I can set my own goals of one-shotting the gas can to blow up the barrels to disable the cannon instead of taking out everyone and just waiting between kills.  I can certainly see myself replaying levels with harder physics and personal goals to scratch those murderous itches we all get from time to time. Despite the shortcomings, I'd give this nine out of ten stars.

The killcam is disturbingly detailed and only happens if the shot is worthwhile to see.  The enemies WILL hunt down and kill you if you're not careful enough.  The vast open-world gameplay offers both mandatory and optional objectives so it's entirely up to you on how to complete the missions.  The random ambient noises in certain environments give you chances to take the long shots without revealing your position.  Otherwise, you could rely on your silenced pistol or melee skills to kill your enemies up close and personal.  Team up with your friend or a random person online for coop missions and survival.  One players provides sniper cover while the other infiltrates bases, plants explosives and guns down enemy soldiers up close.
On the other hand, the campaign's story and character voices are lame, but the gameplay makes up for those shortcomings.  There's too much paid DLC in my opinion.  If you want them, you should probably get the season pass for a lot cheaper in the long run.  In game, sometimes when you're behind cover and trying to shoot someone, the scope is pointed at the enemy, but you keep hitting your cover!  Sometimes, you can't shoot at all and have to be at a certain position behind the cover!  Cover system is somewhat janky and not quite optimized for keyboard and mouse configuration.
Overall, it's a satisfying long and short-ranged shooter that can only be complete with a season pass (but that's entirely up to you) and still has room for improvement mechanics wise.  It is a worthwhile experience, especially its coop mode, but just be careful about when and where to shoot your rifle or submachine gun.

aka GTA Mars
This is the best controller rumble I have ever played with, everything has force feedback. All vehicle types handle differently, you can feel individual tires as they traverse the terrain such as a light weight, skinny 3 wheeled speeder compared to the larger hulking mining rigs. The feeling of weight is done extremely precise and that is always at your fingertips due to the awesome power of our main charachter's sledgehammer. The Red Faction series has always catered with hard scifi elements and that tradition carries on with weapon familiarity from past games, and to see it now in an openworld tends to showcase the technology's unique reactivity to the environment. Inspect the structural integrity of a building and then figure out how you want to bring it down and with what weapons.  The physics in particular tries to steal the show although gravity here seems to be a bit lighter than our own, as vehicles tend to float a bit. The story holds the game together with the strength of kindergarden glue and the theme/setting is forced to handle the extreme plot deprivation with the weight of that 5 story building that you just razed. Plot is a barren, skeletal framework for the missions. As far as missions go, it is sabotage, industrial terrorism, extraction and outright mayhem. It seems they came up with some good solid fun gameplay device and then just copied it over to all the territories, but that is not such a terrible thing considering each environment offers  sharp contrast to the previous, that fits into it's futuristic realism. The setting is based upon a corrupt political regime and money/power hungry corporates determined to exploit the planet and its citizens. Mars may be red but it is a blue collar planet, workers rights and oppression are main idealogies here. The musical score is once again underrated, ranging from cinematic orchestral to apocalyptic electronica, I recommend turning the music volume up, it is captivating! As far as the sound effects go, they are very noticeable thoughout, like the rat-a-tat of assault rifles or vibrato of plasma guns, it is difficult to find somthing sounding dull and mundane, I especially relished the magnitude of certain tensile and monstrous demolition sounds. Voice acting is superb for the main players with top quality talent providing the personalities. Dx11 makes everything look crisp and sweet with the sand swirling effects, the glaring sun rays and lots of rocky picturesque textures. For what it has to work with in a dry dusty planet, the graphical fidelity and design  coexist agreeably each taking their one half the effort for eye candy. Explosions are fast, loud and dynamic and may be over too soon, leaving in their wake a stunned world that gives birth to a new pile of debris, then goes back about its normal business, if you let it. The key is to keep it up and in return for major destruction you are rewarded with guerilla recruits that follow you around and fight for a little while. Guerilla is difficult on normal settings, it will pay off to explore the gameplay and approach missions differently. It is even possible, but very hard to stealth through some segments, expect many failed missions reloads. Red Faction Guerilla has been a pleasure to get to know, and is definetely worthy of its namesake. I would not say it is ahead of it's time, but covers all the bases of an old school quality masterpiece and what it does so well is allows the freedom to explore the intracities even though never gives a hint. Red Faction Armeggedon is better but is also a completely different shooter and had access to SYFY channels audio library and a more focused story. I would like to see the franchise rejuvenated again.

TL:DR Red Faction Guerilla has really fun destruction physics and gives you loads of buildings to destroy. A great game if you want to cause some mindless destruction
Red Faction Guerilla is basically a big destruction sandbox. You play as Alec Mason, a recent arrival to Mars, who ends up joining the Red Faction who are a rebel movement on Mars fighting for independence from Earth.
The big feature of this game is its destruction physics that let you blow up and destroy almost any building you come across on the open world map. The game gives you plenty of weapons and tools to help you do this and it's a lot of fun. Bombing a building and seeing it collapse in on itself after is immensely enjoyable.
There's also story missions as well as side missions to complete to get scrap, which you use for currency, and to reduce enemy control of the different sectors on the map. The mapis dotted with enemy installations to destroy which require a bit more planning and heavy weaponry as they're heavily guarded. Destroying these also reduces enemy control.
The steam edition also gives you the bonus DLC campaign which lets you play as the marauders giving you some new weapons and vehicles. It's a fairly disappointing campaign being quite short and the map is mostly claustrophobic canyons which feels quite restrictive compared to the main campaign.
Overall this is a fun game. If you want some fun Michael Bay style destruction this game is for you.
Good points:
- brilliant destruction physics with plenty of buildings to destroy.
-theres a good variety of fun weapons that gives you plenty of options for causing destruction
- Wrecking Crew mode is pretty fun. It puts you in a small map full of buildings and gives you different challenges to destroy the buildings in a time limit. You get a score based on the amount of destruction you can cause.
Bad points:
- this game hasnt aged well graphically.
- The bonus campaign DLC isnt very good
-the game has a multiplayer mode but its completely dead

I feel as though there should be two separate entries here for a review; seeing as the single and multi player aspects of this game have been such different experiences.
The single player is nothing short of incredible. San andreas was always my favourite GTA game to this point, constantly making the player feel as though they were the centrepiece of their own action flick. GTA5 is a continuation of this trend; supplemented with the return of RPG-esque character stat progression that has profound impacts on not just the gameplay mechanics, but even the narrative as NPCs respond to changes to your character’s various proficiencies. The environments are spectacular and varied, the world is bustling and reactive to player actions…this is a genuinely excellent single player game. Thoroughly recommend.
Now for the multiplayer. After I finished the single-player story, I enjoyed carrying out heists and missions with a few friends. This is the best way to go about such things, as communication is critical for many objectives and attempting to go at it with a random player will have you beating your head against a brick wall. The character progression allows players to access more weapons and customisation options as they reach higher levels from gaining experience – namely by participating in world events, competing in races, and completing heists and missions. The online support is also *usually* exceptional. I lost a few items in-game due to bugs and had them restored within minutes of raising a support ticket.
This was fine up to a point, but having spent just over 100 hours in multiplayer alone, I completed a heist last thing at night with the intention of purchasing a new in-game property. I woke up the following morning to discovered I’d been banned for 4 weeks with no reason given whatsoever.
Here’s the *fun* part: a ban resets your character progress. Your stats, in-game currency and property are all nullified. This includes any in-game currency you’ve purchased with their shark-card system.
I attempted to raise a ticket with their online support, with no answer at all. I contacted them via twitter and had no response. The only time I finally had someone respond was by finding a helpdesk number and contacting them, querying why I had been banned and whether I would receive the in-game currency I HAD PAID FOR or whether I could expect a refund.
The lady politely informed me that due to my breaching of the “terms and conditions” I had been banned, and that I would not be able to receive my purchased in-game currency, and that I would not be able to get a refund. She reassured me that if I was to avoid contravening the “terms and conditions” in future, then I would not be banned again.
“but how am I meant to not do something that I do not know I have done”, I said.
She stuck to her script, reiterating that I just had to ensure I never did the terrible thing (that neither of us knew I did) again.
I said this was ridiculous, and asked to both raise a ticket and speak to her supervisor. She hung up.
So yeah. I’ve taken my research with a pinch of salt, but essentially it appears *anything* that hooks into the game executable whilst it’s running has the potentially to get you banned. This includes performance overlays such as FRAPS or MSI afterburner. In my case, I was using radeonpro as opposed to the standard AMD software.
So enjoy the game (it is excellent), but don’t invest a single penny in the micro-transaction system unless you have a fresh install of windows with nothing other than Steam, GTAV and GPU drivers installed. I can't recommend this on the basis that the support staff were rude and unhelpful, and whatever anti-cheat system they run caused me to lose over 100 hours of character progress for no apparent reason whatsoever.

I completed Brothers in one sitting, and I have to say that that's probably the best way to go about it, provided you have 3 hours to spare.
Brothers is very much a story driven game, which is both impressive and odd considering that there's no actual dialogue since the characters speak what I assume is gibberish with no subtitles. If that seems like an odd choice I assure you that you'll be sold on it after a few minutes.
If you haven't somehow been clued in yet, you control both characters simultaneously with the left and right joystick. I never had any problems with the controls mechanically but for some reason I could hardly keep focused on which Brother I was controlling when they criss-crossed accross the screen a lot. Not a game flaw, I just couldn't make my brain do the work. I had to constantly make sure the right stick brother was always on the right side of the screen and the left stick brother on the left to avoid this brain-f*ckery.
Anyway, on with the review. The majority of the time you'll spend solving "puzzles" which are more just like simple (and fun) obstacles. There's no part of brothers that could be considered "hard" but the game is simply enjoyable to play through and figure out as you go along so it's not disappointing that the puzzles don't cause any head-scratching.
The art style is just beautiful and I may just do another playthrough just to get some screenshots.
There's been a lot of talk about the story and while it's not exactly mind blowing, it's just the unique way that it's told that makes it a worthwhile experience. I feel like it could easily be a Pixar style short, but some of the impact that actually controlling the characters has on the story would probably be lost.
Good stuff, easy recommendation.

People say don't read a book by its cover... which can be acquainted with only a few minutes of gameplay in a game... but rarely does a game make this kind of impression.
This is an art and puzzle game that is best played in tandem with 1 other player. There are no comprehensible words; just gibberish conveyed with emotion and hand gestures that one can easily infer what is being communicated.
One person controls via WASD and Space whilst the other plays via the arrow keys and right control.
If you’re like me, someone who enjoys Steam In Home Streaming, then I advise playing next to each other with 1 computer running the audio, and streaming the game to another computer (or simply hooking up a secondary keyboard to the computer, but there is something to be said about having your own screen and not having to crowd each other out). I suppose since part so the game take so long (at least in the first few minutes (and not due to lack of comprehension for gameplay mechanics, but rather it just takes forever to turn a crank or push/pull a cart).
So if you have a in depth conversation to be had with a friend or someone otherwise and your hanging out together, this is a great game to play whilst doing that.
If you are playing by yourself, well you could watch the game, or you could watch TV... but you'll have both hands tied up and have to have some comprehensive skills to control 2 units on a "2D" plane (3d game and camera rotation, and the terrain is far from flat, just you do not have conceptualize moving up and down for the game will take care of that for you) whilst doing puzzles and moving with each other’s controls at times being inverted (due to their positioning relative to one another).
Do not get me wrong, I advocate this game and it probably won’t force you to play it slowly later on, but I felt the mechanics of it lent itself to be a 2 player game, and the sheer quality to start was enough to advocate for it… if you like cathartic games.
Once I finally get around to playign through this game I will update the review... but I am already predisposed to be in its' favor.

For an arcade style air combat game, this game is fun. Setting is also unique as the game is set in the battlefront of China-Burma-India, there's a campaign, about the "Flying Tigers", a squadron formed the American volunteers who were there to defend China against Imperial Japan. We don't see many games about the battles there, most of the time the WW2 video games are set in either European theater or Pacific.
Gameplay is solid enough, it has stuff that an arcade dogfighting game should have, simple controls(by simple I mean you just need a few buttons to control your aircraft). Though you may need some time to get used to it, like, you gotta center your mouse after you make a turn. Still, it's still easy to control your plane and shoot down a bandit, especially when you don't have to aim precisely to hit a bandit, just lead the target and fire away, shoot until the enemy's health drop to zero. I also like the easy to do evasive maneuvers, you just tap a button and your plane will do a loop or roll, looks really cool.
Graphics looks nice even on lower settings, it looks like something from the bigger devs out there to be honest, so, really nice.
And finally, music and sounds. I've got nothing to say, because it's really good, mostly the music. What's with the accent of the Indian guy though, it's a bit too silly.
And overall, fun game, worth the money, and get the deluxe edition for extra goodies with much cheaper price if you wish.

I could sum this sim up in two words -- with many more to follow :) -- Amazing and Aggravating. It amazes me that devs who triumph on detailing trains (some more than others) and environments, are also derailing on vital areas.
E.g.... During "Arrival of the Thunderheads" the speed limit drops *without warning* from 45 to 20, then shortly afterward posts a speed limit of 35 below the HUD, but the limit in the HUD remains at 20. The unsuspecting driver is then penalized for speeding for anything above 20.9 mph. Another example: in the Canadian Mountain scenarios, if I overshoot a switching point in a trainyard, my loco won't stop unless I reverse the engine while in forward motion, or apply the emergency brake (which requires an additional minute to recover from). Another time, the control tower radioed me that they were putting me on a siding to allow another train to pass, but when I got there the switch wasn't thrown.
This is incredibly aggravating for anal people like me who strive for gold star performances. So the key is... Save often! (But only your latest save is retained). Do this especially when approching signals or switches. However, when I resumed the Thunderheads scenario, the stormy weather I was experiencing vanished.
When the scenarios aren't broken, I enjoy Train Simulator 2015 VERY much. Driving the Challenger through Sherman Hill is incredible, as are many other trips. The mixed reviews are perfect. In my humble observations, the devs seem more focused on us spending great deals of money on new scenarios and locos than on fixing the faulty ones. Don't they play test these things?!  But as you see, I still recommend it -- on sale.

I wasn't too interested in Glittermitten Grove when it was first released, mostly because I assumed it was going to be more lowest-common-denominator shovelware like so many other resource-management and dirt-digger games. I thought the tutorial was lacking, but the remainder of the game is full of nice surprises.
With a lot of this sort of city-building sim, your progress in the early game paints you into a corner and you eventually have to start demolishing your early work to make room for more efficient progress. In this game, your settlement is built in trees, and the natural growth of the trees affects the utility of the things you build. There's sort of a fog-of-war component, and you actually have to construct objects to extend the borders of your field of vision. As your tree grows, it carries the vision object upward, so if you're not efficient enough, you won't be able to operate at ground-level.
Within the tree zone, you can only construct buildings and objects at the point at which a tree limb divides into two. There are obviously more of these joints the farther you get from the trunk, but too much weight will break the limb.
The thing that really sets GMG apart from similar games is the sunlight. Each tree (or bush, or vine, or whatever) needs direct access to sunlight in order to survive and grow. Trees shade other trees, which can make it tricky to get the most out of a tall tree without putting your comparatively-shorter food supply bushes in jeopardy.
You can instruct your population to chop sections of a tree, either to harvest the wood for building or to remove obstructions to allow sunlight to reach a lower area. It can be very tricky to cut the right branch in the areas with lots of small overlapping limbs, but you usually won't have too much built out there, so there's not so much danger. Beware, though: chopped or fallen wood will "expire" if it's not collected quickly enough; if you have to cut large amounts of wood, you should either have extra woodsheds or have other building projects in progress so none of the wood goes to waste.
There is also an underground area. One of your resources can be spent on fireworks, which blast holes through the ground. The digging system is pretty clever: fireworks are like multi-stage rockets, and you can tell each stage what shape to dig out. Choosing a narrower path will result in a longer tunnel for travel, but blasting out a large cavern (and letting some sunlight in) can actually allow you to plant seeds down below. The nice thing about the underground area is that you can construct a torch-holder anywhere in your influence, expanding your field of vision without having to rely on plant growth. While it's important to keep your tree-area construction moving along, the real treasure is hidden underground.
It might take a few tries before you get the hang of planning out your resources. Basically, if any of your resources are close to full, you should be spending them right away.
The art is cute and vibrant, and Ryan Ike provides a charming soundtrack. The guest artists also add some quirkiness; I've never been much of a Korn fan, but there are also a few tracks by Ben Prunty & Danny B.

Glittermitten Grove is a very short game. One can experience most of it in 3 hours. But is it good? Yes it is. If you can pick this game up on sale for $5 or so, I would certainly say it's a worthy purchase. Now, there is a game within a game going on here (Frog Factions 2, to be precise) and it is obvious it's the main game here as it is much longer and deeper experience than Glittermitten Grove, but I will not be taking that into consideration is this review. As to why, it is because it is a vastly different experience to Glittermitten Grove, the game that is being advertised here, and the developer has gone on to say that Frog Factions 2 is merely a bonus to Glittermitten Grove.
Anyways, on to the review.
Glittermitten Grove is a real-time strategy game where you are trying to expand your land and small group of fairies. There is no tutorial, save a few suggestions, so there will be a lot of figuring things out on your own as you go. And the concept itself is rather simple, so there really isn't a need for one. You build houses, manage resources, expand your land and collect more resources. The world is small, and is presented to you in it's entirety at the beginning of the game, albeit shrouded in darkness. Expanding you land merely consists of building light posts and torches to increase your line of sight.
The way Glittermitten Grove does things, though, is a little novel. There are 4 resources in this game; food, wood, crystals and sparkles. Wood and food comes from trees and bushes, crystals from the ground, and sparkles from the sunlight (in which you need to build a device to collect it). Now the interesting part of the game is that with the limited amount of space, you need to manage the trees and bushes growing above ground. All trees and bushes need sunlight and adequate room to grow, and if a bigger tree blocks their sunlight, they will eventually die. So you kind of have to play this balancing game where you are trimming trees and giving fertilizer to other trees to help them grow and ahve more access to sunlight. It was quite fun and added a nice layer to the game.
And that's pretty much it. There's really no goal in the game, other than perhaps building the palace, which isn't difficult. The developer definitely could have expanded on the game, as it is enjoyable. But it's obvious their resources went elsewhere. By my positive review, I certaily don't regret getting the game, but that's mainly because I got it for $3. I truly wish Glittermitten Grove was a bigger game so that I could recommend it at it's current price, but I can't.

FF2 was a disjointed mess of an ascii overworld with intentionally terrible game design that stopped being funny after the second time I had to deal with a sword tha blocks movement and skates that hijack it at the same time.  There was no sense of progress, story, connection, anything between the minigames and the overworld unlike the original FF which for all its absurdity managed to tell a cohesive story and tie even the most disparate elements together in a neat package.
GG on the other hand was surprisingly fun.  Having to manage light as a resource was a really cool mechanic as was managing weight on branches.  I would have probably payed 20 bucks for GG if the developer had spent less time making an unfun sequal to the amazing FF and had instead focused on refining the sim game elements of GG to a much more substantial game.  In the end I just siply can't recommend this game, either for the illusion or for the actual game hidden within.  But if the developer ever wanted to flesh out GG and rip out FF I'd say it might just be a game worth getting.

This is a surprisingly engaging poker sim!  It mixes heads-up, cash, small (8 player), and large (80 player) tournament play well enough to help you procrastinate and (astonishingly) develop some useful poker skills.
The AI is decent - not impressively smart, but overtly stupid, either.  On the whole, I didn't really notice trends or styles particularly to AI opponents, but their play was varied enough to keep you on your toes and make the challenge feel relatively real.  They bluff, slow-play, etc.  Real tournament players would probably be a touch more conservative, but the AI was skilled enough to make winning the bigger tournaments genuinely difficult.
I struggled a bit at first, but gradually became smarter about playing conservatively early in tournaments, then opening up the throttle once I'd secured a spot in the money.  I also became much better at learning how and when to effectively bully opponents with shorter stacks.  Let's be honest, a video game won't make you a pro, but this game does force you turn off any casual poker instincts you might have and learn to play competitively.
Whether you want to put in the hours to fully beat the game or just take part in an occasional AI tourney, this game is worth picking up, particularly if you're patient enough to wait for it go on sale.  I played here and there initially, then more obsessively as the tournaments got bigger.  Definitely worth whatever beans I traded for the bundle it was in.
Arguably the best poker game on steam currently, would highly recommend!

Playing cards with friends is convivial.  Gambling with meaningful stakes is tense and (to some) exhilirating.  Playing cards against a machine for imaginary money is neither.  To make up for that deficiency, a computer poker game needs to add a lot of bells and whistles.  Governor of Poker 2 tried to do that with an investment mechanic and hats to unlock and  a few other extra features.  For me, it still wasn't quite enough to counterbalance the tedium of slowly playing cards against a collection of uninteresting opponents represented primarily by oversized hats.

One of the best casual poker games out there and for sure the best one on Steam, at the moment, in my opinion. It's important to note tho that this game is for casual players who are not very much into serious poker strategy. I do play online poker for real money at gambling sites versus real people and I can tell you for sure that strategies applied there, even on lowest stakes against dumbest of players, won't work very often on AI in this game.
AI in this game is rather silly and most of the time plays nothing like real thinking player would. All tho you can certainly still learn how it "thinks" and use it for your advantage to predict it's behaviors. It's not like AI is completely random and doesn't make sense. But still, if you want a serious poker game where you could apply in-depth poker strategies this game is not for you. But it is excellent if you are newcomer to poker or just want to casually have fun time.

Right now this is the best Train SImulator game on the market so yes, I recommend it. If you don't believe me have a read of some of the reviews for it's closest competitor (TANE: A New Era) and compare them.
Yes, DLC is expensive in general as others have said, but there are often sales on / bundles and you can pick up a bargain if you are willing to wait for the right time to purchase.
The game isn't perfect and many others have detailed this in their reviews. However, there are some customisations you can do to make it better. For example, restrict the FPS to a set number will make the game appear smoother. Reducing shadows and draw distance will give a better FPS.
The game has many bugs and can crash quite easily, however, I have only ever encountered them in the editor and not when just driving a train. It means if you want to edit, you have to be patient and discover workarounds if you are interested in creating scenarios or routes. Scenario creation might sound like it could be easy but it's not (I won't go into the full details here). So my point is that even if the editor bugs didn't exist you would still have challenges creating working scenarios and routes.
Some people have talked about bugs in certain routes but I have never personally encountered that (probably because I don't own older routes).
The game manuals are lacking (although slowly getting better than previous years) but there some resources around if you are willing to spend some time to look for them.
Talking about this game in isloation or comparing it with some other game genre doesn't make sense to me. If you are wanting to drive a train then you'll want to scratch that itch somehow. As I said at the top of my review, I believe that this is the best Train Simulator on the market at the moment.

Squishy is a very squishy pig. This makes solving the puzzles in how to kill him rather fun, and the fun of playing a platformer that tasks you with failing is a wonderfully interesting concept that's executed fairly well. There is something inherintly satisfying in seeing the tearful porcine protagonist turn into giblets after piecing together the path to his death, and in those first few levels in particular, I was right on board.
Of course, this being a 2D platformer, Squishy couldn't stick to his guns, and began throwing "rage" levels at you where you're supposed to live and make it to the end, often times capped off with a boss at the end. No big deal in concept as it does change things up, but treading the fine line of fun difficulty with "why am I subjecting myself to this" difficulty is not something SSP does well. At all.
You see, this problem could be resolved with a simple fix. Each of these classic platforming sections do have checkpoints, and initially they represent relief. Sadly, they are one use only, and if you screw up again, you'll be sent back to the beginning and have to start all over again. The levels are never very long once you learn the ins and outs, but the lengths you have to go to see the last few challenges in the stages can be a bit repulsive when you're constantly battling Squishy's agonizingly slow movement speed, spotty hitbox detection, and equally painful jumps. Not a big deal when you're trying to find death, but when you want to escape it, you're in for a world of hurt.
This isn't helped by the fact that there are bosses that would be worlds easier if your fat little pig moved a little faster. Jesse "Boom" Coyote, the game's second boss, is the reason my hour count is as high as it is. His patterns were very basic, and the way to beat him was equally so, but the amount of cheap deaths and bugs that kept getting in the way made it impossible to the point where after many hours of near-victories followed by crushing defeat (the final hit on even normal difficulty is insanely hard to land), I discovered that there was a sort of glitch through the forums that helped get me to the last bit faster, and even then it took a good few tries. My brimming confidence even after such a cheap victory was halted by a combination of enragingly convoluted "puzzles" that were both straight forward and cruel in what they required of you. After the umpteenth box puzzle and messed up timing-restart, I was done.
All in all, Squishy definitely has promise, but the charm is quickly lost by the end of the first world. For having such a variety of ways to die, having all your creativity fleshed out within the first few minutes and then relying on frustration and boxes to keep the player interested is not good in the long run. I spent about 14 cents on it, and I only barely managed to get my money's worth. This is by no means a bad game, and it's clear that the makers had a passion here, but I can't in good faith recommend it. It does have cute sprites though.

Perhaps one of the strangest surprises of 2013 was Surgeon Simulator 2013. Starting from two guys in their basement for 48 hours coming up with an amusing, grotesque playable open heart surgery, to becoming one of the most popular inside jokes of gaming, this gem is definitely worth buying if not to play the game through, then to violently stab a man in the brain with a tomahawk, killing him instantly.
The gameplay is hilariously over the top with awkward controls that only add to the enjoyment. While it does feel like it steps over the boundaries a bit too much at times, specifically when it is overly frustrating to remove a man's kidneys while he's bleeding all over your left hand, gameplay mostly remains balanced as you take out your scalpels anywhere from space to the back of an ambulance and on anyone from the Heavy from Team Fortress 2 to an alien reminiscent of Paul. These novelties range anywhere from funny cameos to slapstick nonsense such as trying to smash TF2 characters' ribs with a bat. It's genius really, albeit somewhat old at the time of this writing.
There really isn't much to say about Surgeon Simulator 2013. It has the hilarious gameplay that is quite amusing when you first buy the game, but it slowly becomes more and more repetitive after completing at least one of the three different scenarios presented, which is why I could only muster at max 10 hours out of this game. It is certainly worth the buy, but don't expect anything serious. Kick back, relax, and stab a man in the heart for a few hours. It's sure to be a blast. 8/10

The main draw here is Frog Fractions 2, and unfortunately it is a shallow, frustrating, incoherent mess. The ASCII RPG which makes up the majority of the game is tedious, with poor controls and obtuse puzzles, and is there to very loosely tie together the mini games the first Frog Fractions was known for.
Some of these mini games show glimpses of good ideas and could have been turned into better, more fleshed out games, like the multiplayer simultaneous turn-based twist on Snake or the real time turn-less Chess, but these are the minority. Mainly they are throwaway games you often don't even have to win to progress through, and the amount of filler you have to slog through to get to them just lessens their impact.
It's also not as funny as it thinks it is, or as the first Frog Fractions was. Maybe you'll find humour in shaving the beard off of a poorly modelled Barack Obama, or playing a Flappy Bird parody (timely stuff), or seeing Dark Soul's player messaging system implemented for no gameplay reason. I just found it tedious. All the positive reviewers being coy saying you need to "DIG DEEP" (*nudge nudge*) to find the hidden "DEPTH" (*wink wink*) betray the fact that Frog Fractions 2 is more concerned with being a joke people can be "in" on rather than being a fun game in and of itself.
Perhaps the most damning thing that can be said about Frog Fractions 2 is that the shell game it is hidden inside, Glittermitten Grove, is more fun, and even It's not great by any means. It is incredibly simple, never developing its mechanics, and feels like little more than a clicker game, playing simply to see numbers go up. But it has a certain charm and priced at the sub-$10 it probably would have been before Frog Fractions 2 was bolted onto it, it would have been a passable game, but the overall package does not justify the price it is being sold for and is much less than the sum of its parts.

It's Frog Fractions 2. Well actually, no. Glittermitten Grove is better than Frog Fractions 2. Glittermitten grove is an okay game that you actually have to play for roughly half an hour before you get to Frog Fractions 2. Once you dig deep enough, you'll find a doorway that you can click on to start Frog Fractions 2.
This launches you into a clunky oldschool ASCII RPG game. It's bad. And I think it's intentionally bad, but it isn't nearly funny enough to carry the experience. Neither are the "upgrades" you can collect which make the already difficult to control character even harder to control, such as the autocorrect skates, which will cause your character to turn whenever you hit a wall.
The game itself feels like it's all about novelty and "isn't this quirky" rather than just being a solid and fun / funny game. For comparison, Barkley, Shut Up and Jam: Gaiden is successful in being as fun as it is funny. Frog Fractions 2 is not.
I looked it up and within this ASCII RPG game are all the fun minigames that made Frog Fractions great. Instead of stringing them all together linearly, and having a solid, wacky experience like the first Frog Fractions, they've decided to force you to play the awful ASCII RPG game inbetween each one.
I would really, really appreciate a "The jig is up!" option to skip Glittermitten Grove and the ASCII RPG game and just get to the enjoyable parts of Frog Fractions 2.

Governor of Poker 2 is an enjoyable poker game set in the Wild West, that offers more than just poker. There's a long campaign where you travel to different cities, play in various tournaments, encounter a variety of different opponents (including notorious ones), purchase buildings, and best of all, you get to buy new hats!
A big feature of real poker is the tells on your opponents faces, but in this game you don't see faces, just hats! In spite of this, the game does a pretty good job of giving different personalities to the characters through their voices and actions, and there are tells in the form of comments they make and other information, such as getting steamy when they lose.
A big part of the game is travelling to different cities and buying buildings, which provide you with passive income. At first you can only make money from playing poker, but once you own a reasonable number of buildings you have a steady income trickling in. The idea is to build up your reputation and take over different cities. You can borrow money from the bank if necessary, or sell buildings if you have any, and of course, you can buy new hats. New hats impart some personality to the players and allow you to enter new tournaments.
The gameplay is fairly fast paced, it's an ideal game for a quick poker fix, but I'm not sure whether the cards played are truly random and whether the AI cheats or not. Some reviews claim that it does. I'm not experienced at poker so I can't really tell, but as a casual player the gameplay seems decent to me, even though I find it pretty hard to win, even on the standard level. The Telltale poker games are a lot more fun if you want personality and banter, but for a simple poker fix, this does the job and is better than other poker games I've tried. There's no multiplayer, so look elsewhere if that's what you want, but it provides a good single player experience
The graphics are fairly basic, and low res too, but they're functional and pleasant to look at. There are free versions of this you can play on the internet but this version, the premium edition, provides more depth.
Overall I'd recommend this game for casual players, especially because of the extra interest that the campaign provides. Serious poker players may want to look elsewhere though.

Here's a review from a first time Train Simulator 2015 player but a longtime flight sim guy (FSX, DCS, Il-2, RoF). I think the best way to answer doubts and questions about this game, is by asking yourself the basics: Do you want immersion, a challenge, procedures, the feeling of being there, unpredictable factors that create in-game problems and scenarios? TS2015 does this well. In fact it's scoring system in career is excellent. Too much wheel slip, or speeding slightly and points get deducted. A nice touch and way to replay and challenge yourself (if only Flight Sim had this). I'm no train expert but controls are good and a natural heavy feeling, but you can't control every button in the virtual-cabin. Throw on Track-IR and immersion inside this cabin is fantastic. It's quite a thrill to see miles of track ahead of you along with all the lights, points, wires and stations. Weather too is well modeled and ads another layer. And the sense of speed and distance being traveled quickly is excellent.
I have no reservations recommending this sim to anyone looking for that simulator "fix". TS2015 will have you hooked. But that is where the good stuff ends. The graphics engine is outdated, the environment while well modeled is sterile and... dated. There are no birds, no planes flying overhead as you get closer to the city, towns are lifeless. There's no radio communication. No way of finding out if there's trouble ahead just a warning at the start of a scenario. You can say it's a sim, but with today's expectations and gaming possibilities, I expect more (DCS, EuroTruck, Orbx for FSX). The stand-alone game sorely lacks content. In fact I had to search forums to confirm my question about how little you actually get with the basic game. It's nice that I can buy DLC of the exact locations I would like to visit, but at $80 for just two scenarios, I am forced to hold-off until a sale.
With all the DLC and money generated from TS, I would have expected more in the way of graphics, but that is not to say the graphics are terrible. I would have expected a more generous basic game. Sure, I can learn how to operate an American giant freight loco, but I can't use one in career without purchasing DLC. I'm sure Dovetail have this dialed in financially speaking. They are business after all. I for one, want to support them. But I do feel a little hard done by with the basics.
So, if you are a simmer and love sims of all kinds then get this. It's pretty awesome in fact. Just know that it will leave you wanting more. Much much more.

So, chances are you have played a game like Torchlight II, as the game itself is very iteraitve of the tried-and-true Diablo formula.  If that is the case, when why in the world would you play Torchlight II?
Simple: Torchlight II has streamlined the experience.  It takes a lot of the annoying/boring things about the genre, and either eliminates it or makes it less time consuming.  Inventory full?  Slap it on your pet and sent it town.  Out of potions or identifying scrolls?  Your pet can pick them up for you while selling your stuff.  The fact that your town portals go away get you down?  You portals stay up indefinately and are accessable via waypoint portals.  Sick of making suicidal corpse runs everytime you die?  Not in this game, you can either respawn right where you were (for a lot of gold), at the beginning of the dungeon (for some gold) or at the nearest town (for free).
If you don't point-and-click, hack-and-lash loot games, Torchlight II isn't going to turn that opinion around.  However, if you have liked any Diablo-like game, give Torchlight II a try.

Let me just get this out there: I didn't like Torchlight 1. I always felt that the world was a bit lacking and I never really liked the character presets... Yet I came into Torchlight 2 expecting the same disappointment and now find it hard to pull myself away from it. Set in the same universe where you are a Hero sent on a quest to stop the Alchemist, yes 'that' Alchemist. From what I've played the story is very cliche to this genre which isn't a bad thing at all. The real reason I like this game is that it's action packed! The game is a click and go, ARPG that is very reminiscent of Diablo, you click to travel, gib baddies and do quests, level up and score epic loot; oh, and there will be plenty of epic loot! The action always feels meaty when you are playing it, the screen pulsates to tell you if you score criticals, swarms of enemies vanish/drop dead at your will! What makes Torchlight 2 so great is that there is diversity in playstyles, and skills. I am playing as the Outlander (think Rogues) which means there's high emphasis on ranged combat, there is many ways I could adapt my rogue to fight better with different weapons and skills, like mana consuming glaives to throw or I can improve passive skills to amp up my akimbo pistol death dealing! I recommend you think carefully about how you want to evolve your character as you can only respec the last 3 skills you add! This is a slight annoyance because it requires forward thinking before dumping points into everything. This game is also flipping hard, you can revive on the spot, at the entrance of dungeons (there are many dungeons) or back in town the first two have penalties with them. You'll find the bosses will cause most of these deaths. As another pre-warning you will be dealing with a lot of loot, you will have to dedicate a bit of time to inventory manage: to make sure you can get new loot! You do get a pet as a sidekick in Torchlight 2 which can be used as a weapon, or pack mule not much to say in that regard. If you were disappointed in Diablo 3 or just looking for a great ARPG, then I say pick this up. It's packed full of action and has an awesome artstyle! It also runs on pretty much anything! Good luck and happy looting!

You're probably going to see other people play "Getting Over It." Sure, you can grab your popcorn and watch someone fail over and over again. But honestly, the game was made to be played. So play it.
Getting Over It is surreal in nature, but its obstacles are painfully real to overcome. It's a game that rages against convention in which all of the assets are reused from other places. The narrator is painfully calm and gentle as you lose an eternity of progress with a single stupid move. It has the simplest controls imaginable, but learning to work them properly takes hours and hours, and hours, and hours.
Some people say this game is "unfair," but it's as fair as it gets: you're given a certain imperfect skill and you need to do a very-clearly-laid out task. No enemies; no bosses; no DLC. Just you and the mountain.
So why get the game? Why climb the mountain? Because it's there.

The first Wargames was pretty awesome, totally new.  The second Wargames introduced some interesting stuff, but really could be best described as "now with airplanes!"
Red Dragon of all the series is least functional.  It had a half-hearted "navy" layer added that was so comically broken that it was more or less left unchanged after it was terminally broken in the beta.  There's such a lack of focus, while there's thousands of units, only maybe a few dozen are actually relevant, and frequently they're represented by marginal quality models clearly done by the lowest bidder.  Worse, the developer itself refuses to change models that are 100% wrong, or entirely substandard quality because someone on their forums hurt their feelings once.
Please note the last statement is entirely 100% true.  They call the no-updated-models thing the "UGBEAR" policy after said poster.
In terms of gameplay it goes more or less like the following:
1. Single Player:
Terrible.  It's your more or less bog standard skirmish maps arrayed in a sequence, with a tissue paper thin "strategic" level.  The AI is frankly too moron to do anything but "drive towards things!" which it will do with gusto.  The key to any mission is successfully destroying whatever blob the AI has summoned forth before it destroys whatever much smaller blob you were allocated for the mission is destroyed.
Then pair this with some really stupid choices in terms of campaign design (Fact: Did you know South Korea's defense hinges on French and German intervention?), and just how many damned times you'll fight on the same map, doing the same thing, with the same units against the same total lack of objectives except "DESTOY TANKS," and it's really quite telling how few folks play singleplayer more than a few missions.
Which is rather a shame, the campaigns in the first Wargame were quite well put together, challenging missions with a wide variety of objectives and terrain.
Additional caveats:
a. This is the least Asian game to be set in Asia since video games were made.  You basically have two terrain types, Europe with Pagodas, or the American Southwest with Pagodas.  These two terrain types represent everything from the Russian far-east, to Tokyo.
b. Again, despite being a game oriented on events in Asia, most of the effort went into making the European countries in game larger and more full of  weirdo stuff that never actually reached service.  The Asian factions, the ones that you would think would command some attention in a game called "Red Dragon" are very poorly realized and hardly worth playing.  The Chinese forces are a curious mix of equipment China never had, and total exclusion of several key systems they used extensively, the Anzac formations are pure crap, and the North Korean force, which arguably are pretty central to a game that spends so much time in Korea are....terrible.  Not gameplay terrible, but poorly researched, poorly realized, and ultimately best skipped.
2. Multiplayer
The best way to describe it is whatever broken cheesy tactic of the month on a loop.  MRLS type rockets are powerful this week?  STANDBY FOR ROCKET SWARMS ALL MATCH AND NOTHING ELSE.  Super-cheap planes spammed out?  It's going to be raining planes for a few days.  Somehow crappy bottom tier infantry becomes way too cost effective?  Waves of mans for forever.
You'll note a recoccuring theme.  It's not even like "the heavy tank shuffle!" or some other weird tactic just works really well.  From the first Wargame, to the last most of your games start with a spammy spam rush or artillery spam and end with same.
It's all right if you're playing with a friend, or folks you know aren't douches.  But public matches are an exercise in pulling your own teeth out.
Which ties into a few subtopics on multiplayer:
a. There's only a handful of "good" maps, which is to say, ones that are not broken/unbalanced etc.  And you'll play on all those maps within the first day of playing the game more than once.  It gets old, fast.
b. Many of the maps are...boring.  Like imagine a flat open field.  Put a river through it.  Add some trees.  CONGRATS!  I just described several of the maps you'll be playing on.
3. Eugen is a terrible company.
Here's things they do okay:
+You do not have to pay for any of their DLC.
+Wargames EE was pretty good!
+As far as I can tell, none of them are terrorists.
Here's things that make them marginal
-They do not deliver on promised features, and then lie/have really bad excuses why it's your fault those features do not exist.  Examples:
a. Red Dragon was promised to have sufficent ships to fully flesh out the smaller combatants of all the factions that had Navies.  This is several times over not the case.  If you want to play Naval stuff (which you shouldn't do anyway because its pretty terrible), as NATO your force is an all nations dreamteam of Japanese, French....and really skip the American and British stuff because it's not like either of those countries had Navies anyway (and are represented by a bad frigate and a not really used in number missile boat, and a terrible frigate respectively).
b. A map pack was promised with the last major patch.  It was claimed the maps were being withheld because...well either to give the dev team more time to work on fixing a HUGE exploit that went more or less un-fixed for a month or so, or because we're sinners and don't deserve maps I guess?  Either way the maps have never showed up, and asking about them on the game's forums will get you either banned, or at the least the thread locked without comment.
c. Think of it like this.  You know those Twilight Zone episodes, where the guy finds a Genie in a lamp, and he gets his wishes, but the wishes are some jacked up terrible version of what he wished for?  That's Eugen in a nutshell.  Folks who played mostly US forces were concerned that oddly enough, despite the USAF being the largest air force in the world, is having some major issues with air to air combat.  Eugen's fix to this was to add in the PATRIOT missile system, which did not fix the US's lackluster air to air capabilities, but did totally break the rest of the air force part of the game as now there was a SAM site that could shoot down things over half the map.  Broken part broken, and new game breaking element added in for giggles.
-Their community manager is pretty much the biggest troll on their forums.  You have a problem with how things are balanced? Honhonhon, you watch too many movies.  You say something unkind about France?  He's going to be insulting as he can get away with, and then get you banned if you say so much as anything but stating a devout love of froglegs and terrible movies full of ennui.
- Things stay broken for reasons known only to God.  You can shoot down helicopters in this game with artillery.  Like seriously, here's Mr. Helicopter hovering along, and OH NO INDIRECT FIRE! helicopter is dead.  This is stupid.  This is also the reality of the game since the first one.  This has never been fixed, or addressed.  This is also but one of several brokey broke features that have remained with Wargames since 2011 or so.  You get some vague answer about "the engine cannot handle it" but that's a bit like saying the Ford Pinto is designed in a way that causes it to catch fire, so drive safe! vs fixing it when you make a new one.
I really could go on.  I'm still annoyed enough when I see this game on my list though to finally write this review.  This really is not the game for you.  If you want a good RTS, there's plenty of better ones out there.  If you want a good cold war game?  God avoid this mess, it's pretty much like if Tom Clancy was french and mildly mentally handicapped version of the cold war.  If you want realism, this game is just as much not for you.
Perhaps you could instead try a nice game of chess?

In twenty-five years, when you think of classic video games, you'll think Spelunky. It is a fusion of the genre defining games of yester years, with mechanics and visuals that will stand the test of time. It's a simple concept. Get your character to the end of a level. What happens in between your starting point and exit are the moments that will have you yearning for just one more attempt. At first, the game is presented as a deep mystery, but after many trial and errors, you will slowly become the master of it's secrets.
What initally feels like clumsy controls, and unfair gameplay eventually reveals itself to be much more than that. At your peak, you'll find yourself exploring the worlds randomly generated caves with precision, all well collecting gems as if you were pac-man. Completing the game is a hurdle in itself. But once you do, you'll only discover that there are more mysteries in the world of Spelunky.
This games magnum opus though comes from what at first glance seems to be unappealing and daunting. The daily challenge. Every player is given the same random world, with only one chance. Even once you've grown comfortable with Adventure mode and your skills as a spelunker, you suddenly have an audience, and your every move counts. There will be times you make mistakes from the desire of the seven sins, but you'll always have tomorrow to prove yourself again.
There is no real way to explain Spelunky's tragicomedy nature, you just have to discover it for yourself. It is definitely the type of game you need to invest yourself in, or you'll find yourself empty handed and frustrated. There aren't many games that are collectively considered one of the greatest. Spelunky without a doubt, is one of them.

Pleast keep in mind this is an EARLY ACCESS review, and most of the gripes is content based which can change.
There are great things to be said about this game, which many other reviewers hit upon, so I'm focusing on the reasons why I'm not going to touch it again until it gets some patches.
In order of most annoying to not-so-bad:
-There is no Custom Battle Editor.  The "DogFight" mode is only You Vs. up to 10 enemies (or a survival thing).  You can't make large furballs like in many other flight games.  You also can only pick one type of plane for you, and one type of plane for all the opponents.  Having agile fighters support heavy attack planes or protecting bombers is not here.
Will it be?  I don't know.  But I feel like the potential is there, which is why I'm not going to refund the title.
-Controls are ...wonky.  If you have a Joystick or a Gamepad and set them up right that helps a lot. But trying to use Mouse+Keyboard with the arcade settings is a great way to get a headache.
-Graphics can cause serious framerate drops.  On max the graphics are pretty good, but are a crazy drop on performance for what they are.  However you can turn them down, still look great, and run much more smoothly.
-Camera - The bomb camera needs to let you zoom out more.  It's not game-breaking though. Other players have had other complaints about the camera, but I'll only speak to my own issues.  Besides the bomb camera I thought it worked well.
Otherwise a lot of potential, and I look forward to clicking the Thumb's Up button at a later time for this game, but as a service to other players thinking of buying this as Early Access, you need to be warned.

This is one of the best train simulators out on the market. The graphics are nice, the sounds are pretty good, the driving is realistic. For me, what makes this one of the best is that it's the most realistic railroad simulators available to the public.
But with everything nice about the game, there is also a dark side to it. The number one thing that I really dislike about the game is the abundancy of payware. If you don't want just the couple of routes to drive and/or crash trains on, you have to pay hefty prices on some routes. Even though you do have to pay $5 or $6 for the cheapest route (Game of Gnomes), some of the routes make up for the price by adding new locos, rolling stock, and other stuff (Cajon Pass for $18). I really also don't like the amount of freeware assets that rely on the overpriced loco addons, such as Blue Peter ($20).
All in all, even with its major dark side, I like the game and enjoy driving trains and building routes in this simulator. I recommend this game to people who like the more realistic simulators and to rail fans everywhere across the world.

After the fantastic adventures I had years back with Grand Theft Auto III, I purchased Grand Theft Auto IV and found myself in a highly-realistic world that had massive potential for letting me simulate whatever chaos my imagination could bring about. With the discovery of modding, I was able to customize my single player experience to a level I couldn't have dreamed of--playing as all sorts of various monsters, beasts and men, flying, shooting, driving, being a villain, being a vigilante, being a superhero--the experience of a game that let me do realistic things that I wanted in a sandbox that had potential, to being able to do ANYTHING I wanted to do in a sandbox that had realized its potential, was absolutely fantastic. There are many memories I will not forget, from that game.
With Grand Theft Auto V, I was quite content to enjoy the game as-is when it was finally released on PC. The expansiveness of the world, the slight reduction of realism in favor of fun and relaxed gameplay that still had its challenge and intense moments, I found to be wonderfully balanced. I didn't touch much of GTA Online, preferring to stick to Single Player. After time went by and more and more mods were developed for Grand Theft Auto V, I immediately set about creating a personalized, customized world that spoke to me, my interests, and what I wanted out of the game. The time I spent on it was always positive, always fun, and always enjoyable.
Now, after a decade of being able to enjoy that personalized content, the developers have decided to lash out through legal means against all that a gaming community stands for. Mods are something that is part of a community venture; without community, there wouldn't be mods, and without mods, the community that does exist will never reach its full potential. Because of that, Grand Theft Auto V, a game which for me has had immense value, no longer has any standing in comparison with other titles that allow for such freedom, customization, and personalized experiences.
I cannot recommend Grand Theft Auto V until the lawsuit is reversed in favor of rendering mods legal once more. Buying this game at this point, is nothing more than donating money to a cause which seeks to tear apart communities, strip players of their freedom, and take away the singular experiences that you can create for yourself through the free, open modding tools that have been out for years.

I have to say this game has one of the most bizzare plots I've ever seen. "Squishy the Suicidal Pig" is a game about a little pig who's parents have been taken to the slaughter house to be made in to bacon. Squishy decides he wants to join them in piggy heaven so commits suicide. Instead of going to heaven, he goes to hell where the devil makes him an offer and gives him a second chance to go to heaven.
In every level, Squishy has to complete puzzles and find ways to kill himself at the end of each one before progressing onto the next. I can't tell you how the game ends (because I haven't completed it yet), but I am very much looking forward to doing so. Let me just get this out there: I didn't like Torchlight 1. I always felt that the world was a bit lacking and I never really liked the character presets... Yet I came into Torchlight 2 expecting the same disappointment and now find it hard to pull myself away from it. Set in the same universe where you are a Hero sent on a quest to stop the Alchemist, yes 'that' Alchemist. From what I've played the story is very cliche to this genre which isn't a bad thing at all. The real reason I like this game is that it's action packed! The game is a click and go, ARPG that is very reminiscent of Diablo, you click to travel, gib baddies and do quests, level up and score epic loot; oh, and there will be plenty of epic loot! The action always feels meaty when you are playing it, the screen pulsates to tell you if you score criticals, swarms of enemies vanish/drop dead at your will! What makes Torchlight 2 so great is that there is diversity in playstyles, and skills. I am playing as the Outlander (think Rogues) which means there's high emphasis on ranged combat, there is many ways I could adapt my rogue to fight better with different weapons and skills, like mana consuming glaives to throw or I can improve passive skills to amp up my akimbo pistol death dealing! I recommend you think carefully about how you want to evolve your character as you can only respec the last 3 skills you add! This is a slight annoyance because it requires forward thinking before dumping points into everything. This game is also flipping hard, you can revive on the spot, at the entrance of dungeons (there are many dungeons) or back in town the first two have penalties with them. You'll find the bosses will cause most of these deaths. As another pre-warning you will be dealing with a lot of loot, you will have to dedicate a bit of time to inventory manage: to make sure you can get new loot! You do get a pet as a sidekick in Torchlight 2 which can be used as a weapon, or pack mule not much to say in that regard. If you were disappointed in Diablo 3 or just looking for a great ARPG, then I say pick this up. It's packed full of action and has an awesome artstyle! It also runs on pretty much anything! Good luck and happy looting!
