One review of this game read "it's as easy to love as it is to hate", which I think sums it up better than anything else. Visually it's wonderful to look at with crisp, distinctive artwork, and the music is a fantastic, but the difficulty - oh my god.
It's not the fact that you die that bothers me - in a game where you can die literally seconds out of the gate, that'd be a critical tolerance to lack -  it's the fact that you can play for hours, die hundreds of times, and still feel like you're never getting anywhere. I've only gotten past the mines (the first of the locales) twice, never finished the first level of the second locale, and unlocked exactly nothing in nearly 10 hours of play. Perhaps I just suck that much, but as well-made as this game is, the punishing gameplay is making the experience feel repetitive. It claims to be a throwback to the difficulty of the first home-console platformers, but at least back then they gave you a number of lives and therefore more than one razor-thin opportunity to progress before erasing all your work and starting you back at the start.
In saying that, I recommend this game to those with patience and no desire for instant gratification because it is quite well-made, and, if nothing else, a stubborn desire to see what the game has to offer keeps me playing. Also, after playing this game, The Binding of Isaac seems like a leisurely walk in the park by comparison. However, if you like to feel like you are making headway each time you play, this probably is not the one for you.
Do not get this game unless you want countless hours sucked away from your life.

Introduction:
This game in my opinion should be titled, "The Dark Souls of Platformers". Spelunky was inspired by the Nintendo Entertainment System's Spelunker (which you can get on the 3DS eShop or the HD remake on Playstation Network). The two games are completely different games, but sort of have the same play style, except in my personal experience this game is way more difficult. Spelunky is a very charming little Platform title with some gourgeous character designs. The music doesn't feel out of place for each area that you go to.
Verdict:
As mentioned before this game is difficult, but not impossible! This game requires patience and well thought out strategies. There's a saying that you shouldn't blame the player, but the game instead; however, in this case it's the opposite! This game's controls are beyond amazing for a platformer, so you're going to want to not have a fit when you yourself are the cause of your own death! This game is harsh! When you die you have to restart all the way to Area 1 - 1... No save states! This game is an endurance test to see how far you can go before beating the final boss. Now, the game offers you a different set of items that you can play around with, so if you're damn good at this game and just so happen to beat it with ease, then consider trying out different play styles to challenge yourself! The only complaint I have is that this game doesn't have 'Online Multiplayer', but happens to offer players 'Local Co-op'; not that it needs it. Another complaint is that the shop keeper gets angry way to easily for things that you personally haven't commited against him. I don't like telling people what do spend their money on, but for $15 this isn't a bad deal if you're looking for a challenging and rewarding game.
Extra: Oh! There are also a few unlockable stuff in this game that you should probably go collect if you happen to buy the game. You can get the free version somewhere on the internet, but just note it's not exactly the same version of the game; a bit more pixelated.

This has been a very disappointing title for me.  I wish the Flying Tigers got more attention and recognition for what they did, but this game falls very wide of the mark.
First off, it is not a flight sim.  That deserves being said although it should be obvious looking at the screen shots.  econdly it is still in early access, so a lot can change and I hope it does.
The first thing you notice when the game starts is that it looks like ti should be running on an iPad or something.  Representations of pilots appear suddenly on the screen with little "whoosh" noises.  Then the music starts, which is about as wrong for a squadron of mostly US pilots flying in China in 1940 as I can imagine.
Next, you might discover that the menus don't work, constantly scrolling up or down.   Stop the game, unplug all your flight controls including the rudder pedals (irony!) because at this stage of development the game doesn't know how to interpret or at least ignore them.
Once in the game, the combat and flying is pretty arcadish, which is probably what a buyer expects, but the missions seem canned.  You fail and refly or pass and go on to the next mission.  There are no squadron management elements or strategic decisions to be made about what raids to intercept or how - things that were crucial to the FlyingTigers' success.
With no immersion, the game doesn't really inspire the player to find out what happens next.

I hadn't realised I missed this type of game quite so much until I started playing this.
Lovely, evocative visuals (with some gorgeous optional filters for that "vintage" look if you so desire), brilliantly booming sound effects and an anachronistic but strangely appropriate soundtrack all combine to make what is pretty much Ace Combat: WWII Edition.
It would be nice to have a bit more personality in the campaign in the form of more named characters/wingmen a la Strike Commander/Pacific Strike, but the campaign itself is suitably atmospheric and strikes a good balance between "I'M FLYING A PLANE!" joy and the sheer terror of machine gun bullets rattling around your ears as you struggle to shake off a bandit on your six.
The package is rounded out nicely with some fun challenge modes with online leaderboards and a multiplayer component (which I'm yet to try at the time of writing), making this altogether one of the most competent, polished Early Access titles I've had the pleasure of checking out to date. Will be very interested to see what the devs have in store for the updates leading up to 1.0.

After the fantastic adventures I had years back with Grand Theft Auto III, I purchased Grand Theft Auto IV and found myself in a highly-realistic world that had massive potential for letting me simulate whatever chaos my imagination could bring about. With the discovery of modding, I was able to customize my single player experience to a level I couldn't have dreamed of--playing as all sorts of various monsters, beasts and men, flying, shooting, driving, being a villain, being a vigilante, being a superhero--the experience of a game that let me do realistic things that I wanted in a sandbox that had potential, to being able to do ANYTHING I wanted to do in a sandbox that had realized its potential, was absolutely fantastic. There are many memories I will not forget, from that game.
With Grand Theft Auto V, I was quite content to enjoy the game as-is when it was finally released on PC. The expansiveness of the world, the slight reduction of realism in favor of fun and relaxed gameplay that still had its challenge and intense moments, I found to be wonderfully balanced. I didn't touch much of GTA Online, preferring to stick to Single Player. After time went by and more and more mods were developed for Grand Theft Auto V, I immediately set about creating a personalized, customized world that spoke to me, my interests, and what I wanted out of the game. The time I spent on it was always positive, always fun, and always enjoyable.
Now, after a decade of being able to enjoy that personalized content, the developers have decided to lash out through legal means against all that a gaming community stands for. Mods are something that is part of a community venture; without community, there wouldn't be mods, and without mods, the community that does exist will never reach its full potential. Because of that, Grand Theft Auto V, a game which for me has had immense value, no longer has any standing in comparison with other titles that allow for such freedom, customization, and personalized experiences.
I cannot recommend Grand Theft Auto V until the lawsuit is reversed in favor of rendering mods legal once more. Buying this game at this point, is nothing more than donating money to a cause which seeks to tear apart communities, strip players of their freedom, and take away the singular experiences that you can create for yourself through the free, open modding tools that have been out for years.

Pilots cost a fortune (8 pilots, 3 cost about $10 CAD, 5 cost about $20), and you NEED to spend an enormous amount on crates to get skills just to be even viable or you're stuck with very, very weak default skill kits. It's also worth noting you have to use their stupid Feds currency that doesn't even remotely math out properly.
I'm unsure if it's different in different currencies, but for CAD I can buy 360, 720, 1600, 4800, 11200 Fed packages.
Crates cost 169 feds, units cost 499 and 999. What in the hell kind of arbitrary number bullcrap is this?
Very bizarre, and also very expensive. Starting at $7 for the 360 package which as I said is slightly less than $3.50 a crate that gives 1 drop.
Ignoring all the P2W crap, 1v1 where you control all 3 pilots is far and above the best mode. However it's pretty lacking in variety. It's a very simple map and you either farm the same enemies over and over for cores, capture vision nodes, or harrass your opponent. It's kinda fun for a while but it does feel very lacking once you've gotten over learning to control 3 characters at once.
3v3 is a write-off where you only control 1 pilot and it's just a very, very bland uninteresting MOBA that is crushed by the giants HOTS, DOTA2 and LoL. There's just no comparison. But I guess it's there for variety. Modes where you have 2-3 people per team controlling 3 pilots would be much more interesting and hectic.
Overall just not worth it. It's kinda fun but requires either hundreds of hours of sub-optimal play to be viable, or hundreds of $. Neither of which is very good in a MOBA environment.

So first of all let's get this out of the way, I think it's way better than the more linear SE V2, but I think It's not as fun as the first. Let's start:
-Graphics: They are alot better than V2, textures are better and more crisp and what I like the most is that the color pallete is much richer than the grays and blacks of V2. There are yellows, blues, reds, greens and etc. To sum it up much better than V2
-Enviroment: SE3 is set in Africa, where the grass is green and the Jerries are pretty. No but seriously as I said in the graphics section, Rebellion made the game alot better looking. I really liked the fifth mission's beggining stage where you crawl through a field/oasis and then you approach a big desert town. I found that a very good contrast.
-Map design: This is where the last game flopped, V2 was very linear and only one path to go through, this game has alot more open levels with several paths to go through but the general path is the same. To sum it up better than V2 but could be more open.
-Gameplay: Preety much the same as V2 but now stealth is possible. You can go through an entire level and not alert anyone. Sniping is as great as it was in the last game, it feels superb.
-Sound: I can't comment on this because I dont pay much attention to the background sound, but the guns sound excelent.
-Campaign: A lacking plot in which you - Karl Fairburne seem to dismantle the entire Afrika Korps and the Royal Italian Army stationed in Africa in search of a Nazi prototype tank wonder-weapon called the Ratte P1000. The voice acting is honestly comedic and bad, so in summary ignore the plot. The one in V2 was better. Which brings me to the missions. They are long but there are only 8 of them. The campaign will take you about 16 hours, and also not very replayable unless you are going for the collectibles.
-Multiplayer: After the campaign you can play the much improved multiplayer. Unlike V2 where it was very campy and it was essencially a free-for-all, here spotting is more encouraged and when you are on a killstreak you are encouraged to relocate to get extra points per kill. The ranking system is cumulative through campaign and multiplayer so you can rank up faster in multiplayer after you finish the campaign. However I miss "Bombing Run" :(
-Co-op: You can play through the campaign with a buddy, and also you can play the great Overwatch mode in which one guy is a operative on the ground and another one is the sniper. It is incredibly engrosing and extremely fun.
So that sums up Sniper Elite 3, much improved over Sniper Elite V2 but the plot could be alot better. Overall not worth 40 euros, so buy it on a sale and after that enjoy. I rate it 8.5 out of 10

I keep seeing negative reviews for this game, saying that this game shouldn't be played for some reason or another. Granted, there are definitely some flaws, but there are also a lot upsides to this game.
I keep seeing negative comments about how this game only has 4 rifles. I personally don't see why this is an issue. Yes, if you want more, you need to buy DLC, but I have never felt the need to. The 4 rifles cover all your bases. A long range, slow firing rifle, a short range, faster firing rifle, a medium range rifle with a better scope and so forth. There is also a good amount of pistols, including the default silenced pistol. I have never felt that this is limiting me in anyway. Maybe if you're used to CoD, or FarCry, you might think there aren't that many guns, but for this game, mainly being a sniping based game, I feel like it works.
The other negative comment I see a lot is that there are several DLCs already out for it. I can see why that might be a little bit annoying, but I wouldn't let it turn you away from this game. As stated prior, I have never felt the need to buy any other guns, so that already opts out the gun DLCs. As far as other DLCs, I havn't played them. I have not needed to. The campaign has kept me quite sated, and the other modes, as well as competetive online, also keep you busy.
Everything in the game works well as well. I have not encountered anything game breaking or that unappealing. If the game is too easy, there is a mode that makes all bullet ballistics and physics 100% realistic, which believe me, makes the game MUCH harder. The AI wasn't anything spectacular, but nothing horrible either; it got the job done. I feel like there was a good mix of sniping and stealth, combined with "going loud" action. Voice acting was a little cheesy, but it fits the theme and time of the game.
I have had a blast playing through this campaign with friends co-op, and doing the spotter/sniper missions co-op. Decent replay value with all the modes and online, plus it's fun to try and play at higher difficulties.
Overall I'd give this game a 7/10. Worth the money, and I still come back to it often enough.

Train Simulator 2017. Master your Machines. Pfffffffffffft.
The game play is driving a train from A to B, as the title suggests. There are lots of different trains and routes but the thing you do is to drive from A to B.
The base game.
Pretty cheap for what it offers. The 3 routes and trains are all pretty good. While the UK route is a re-hash of a previous route, made in 2014, it is a decent package.
However, in order to get a full experience of the game, you will need to buy some of the mountains of Train Simulator DLC.
That in itself is a bore.
The next thing you find is that the base game and a few of the collections are actually value for money, the rest is daylight robbery. For the British stuff (which I'm focusing on, I'm not that clued-up on the other countries), all the sounds are terrible except the Class 395. If you've never heard a train before, the sounds are great but otherwise you should go to Armstrong Powerhouse and buy the Sound Packs. Well worth the fiver.
There are also many annoing bugs. There are the trivial ones which involve cars going through trains at some level crossings and some bridges blocking the track which you just drive through but there are the ones which are annoying.
The game is very unstable on many very good systems meaning crashes happen quite frequently. Sometimes trains will derail even when you are well within the speed limit or just stopped; the game will come up with the error "Game over due to consist tilt" and you will be chucked back to the menu.
Once you actually get into this simulator, you will realise that Dovetail Games treat the players not like customers but like walking wallets which they can dip their hands into whenever they have not made enough profit.
You will also notice once you get into the franchise a bit more that everything is re-used. A lot of the British rolling stock have the default 455 sounds, which are poor anyway. The re-using of appauling sounds is normal, and something you will have to get used to, I'm afraid. Then there's the routes. They are usually decent, if a bit short, but tend to come with trains that are already in the game. The Midland Main Line is an example of this because it comes with the 66 and 319, both already in the game. Trains that could have been included that are not in the game are the 222 and 387. This is repeated with the Munich to Rosenhiem (101 and 423) and various other add-ons. While I can see this happening if only 2 trains run on the routes, many of them have multiple trains on them, which instead of filling some very large gaps in the game, DTG recycle. And recycle. And recycle. This means various people have to fill the gap.
At some point, this game is going to crash because people are going to get fed-up with what DTG are doing. It has been getting worse recently and there are no signs that this is going to improve any time soon. Before you used to get a free upgrade to the next Train Simulator (even though it is just a patch with a new title) but TS2016 was sold as an entirely new game because it had "so many new features" that it warrants everyone paying for a game they already have! Well, it didn't. It had a small extra funciton that helped (like a patch) and a mode that is completly redundant as it's unofficially been in the game for a long time now. So it did not. You will get used to this constant overhyping and mis-selling of content if you get into this game. So don't.
The developers keep saying "We are aware of our standard and are trying to improve it" and "we do care [about what you want]". To pick up on the first point, we are yet to see any evidence of this. And to pick up on that last point, the things that we have been asking for for a long time such as a Eurostar route and better default sounds have not happened. Even when they do, it is usually not 100% of what was requested. For example, the Midland Main Line route for train sim only goes from St Pancras to Bedford although originally Elephant and Castle to Bedford was requested. And to pick up on the first point: nice try but nothing has happened yet. Additionally, once a route is finished, there is no chance it will be updated. Gravesend, Finsbury Park, Peterborough, London Bridge and many other stations are in old models which, as a community, we know will never be fixed by DTG. Instead we wait for people to do this stuff for free while DTG sit back and rake the cash in. A combination of "can't be bothered" and "we need to make loads of money" attitudes mean this game is on a downward curve. If nothing is done, it will crash. Hard.
It must be said that new members of the game get good value for money when joining. But this changes the moment you dip your toe into the game. DTG will exploit your desire to have your favorite train or route in the game and so you will pay the full price for it (£12 per train, £25 per route with some exceptions). This in nearly all cases is not value for money at all. It must be said that if you know a train very well, you will realise that DTG make good trains rarely. As far as I know, only 1 actually good train exists, that being the class 395, which comes with the very linear London to Faversham High Speed route.
So if you want a very realistic train simulator that gets everything right, this is the only one around. Although it doesn't get nearly everything right, as outlined above. But be prepared to spend thousands of pounds. And I mean thousands. There's more than £3,000 worth of DLC for you to waste your money on.
Form your own opinion.

Flying Tigers, funnily enough, isn't actually the name of a game about literal flying tigers; as fun as that may be/sound. In actual fact, it's the developers take on the flying tiger’s volunteer group that was apparent during World War 2, and this game makes sure to allow you the chance to play some of those pivotal moments in history for a squadron of fighters you might not know about.
As you can probably tell by looking at the screenshots, Flying Tigers is a flying game, with a heavy focus on dogfighting. Unfortunately, with flying games their control systems tend to be a touch hit and miss every now and again and it makes things bloody difficult when you're trying to figure out what you're doing. After a good couple of hours in the title, I'm happy to report that the controls for the game as a whole do their job, and they do it nicely. When you first start off in the skies, at least in regards to the "Arcade" controls, you've got a lot of room for manoeuvrability; without it being overly complicated.
For instance, if you need to have your plane head off in a certain direction or keep on an enemy target, then following it with your mouse is pretty much all that's required of you; providing that's the control scheme you're using. There is an option for you to complicate the controls exponentially, but those are recommended for individuals that either like a real challenge or know what they're doing.
Now, from a non-gameplay perspective, I appreciate the fact that I'm learning about extra areas of World War 2 that I hadn't ever heard of before. I do like a bit of history, so knowing that the game reveals little fragments of this group almost everywhere you look; it's a nice addition to the game and makes it that much better, overall.
Visuals, providing that your computer can run it, you'll be in for a pleasant experience. Obviously, you can play this under a shorter framework for graphics to improve the performance of your computer if it can't deal with it; but if it can manage having everything on max settings, then you'll certainly be in for a visual treat. Considering that this is an indie game and the models for the planes and the environments themselves look as good as they do; you have to give props to the developer for putting in the extra effort.
No game is perfect; with Flying Tigers following that particular rule. I haven't seen many issues, and even then they are minor ones, but they're worth mentioning; at the very least just to make sure that the developer knows what could do with a little tweaking. First of all, there's the small issue that appears when you have v-sync off, because if you do, then you're more than likely going to be witnessing some strange little black lines that follow along the plane, possibly in regards to its hit box - I don't know. For that very reason, it's probably for the best you keep that setting on, unless for one reason or another you NEED it turned off.
The other problem that I've seen crop up a couple of times has nothing to do with actual gameplay, but more down to some nit-pickiness on my part; yet nonetheless, it shouldn't be ignored. At times, I've seen instances where there have either been grammar or punctuation mistakes. As you can probably gather, that's not a big issue, because it isn't something that is all that prominent across the whole game, but considering you do notice it every once in a long while; it doesn't hurt to point this particular fault out.
Audio for Flying Tigers, pretty much all the way throughout is solid; there is no other way to put that. Regardless of whether you’re listening to the background music in the main menu or firing a myriad of bullets at enemy planes, the audio that you’ll be treated to is a great touch to the overall game.
Overall, Flying Tigers: Shadows over China takes a stance of World War 2 that you probably might not know much about and make it interesting, all within a fun and engaging setting for the player. Just like every other game ever, there are a couple of issues here and there, but when you add every single little thing that the game has going for it, it’s almost impossible not to recommend this game; whether you enjoy flying games or not.

Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China is quite an enjoyable air-combat action game. Those who are hungry for a dosage of adventure or are in the mood of giving their adrenaline levels an upward push, should definitely try this game out. It is a great tool for killing your boredom. If you have harbored the dream of being a fighter pilot, but could not accomplish it due to some reason or the other, you could, at least, derive some sort of solace from this lively game.
With a wide array of peppy and funky avatars, the game is obviously going to catch the attention of the youngsters at the outset. The game is set against the backdrop of the devastative Pearl Harbor carnage by the Japanese forces against the United States of America, which impelled the then US President Franklin Delano Roosevelt to wage a nearly all-out war against Japan. This masterpiece allows you to step into the shoes of an American Secret Volunteer Squadron and bask into the thrill of combating airborne in many places in the South-East Asian region, including India, China, Burma and Thailand. The experience of reigning over the skies over the towering mountains of the Himalayas or the sublime Indian Ocean would render you speechless, especially if you adore the sights and scenes of nature.
The motions of the aircraft, especially the victory roll, which would show up normally after a successful firing, are really sensational to say the least. The sound effects are pretty dynamic; whenever you drop a bomb successfully or demolish your opponent’s aircrafts, it almost feels like music to your ears. The realistic weather effects, be it the gloomy clouds in the sky or the subtle wind movements, add a whole new dimension to the game’s visual appeal.
The single-player campaign, with all its missions concerning the 2nd World War, has all the ingredients to awaken the action-oriented soul in you. Moreover, you can even immerse yourself in the vibrant multiplayer mode, where you can play with 15 more people. “Traizertime,” which is very much like a bullet-time mode, enables you to fire with a greater degree of precision by slowing down everything.
One of the most striking features of the game is its impressive graphics. The breathtaking visuals sometimes could make you feel as if all the action is taking place for real. However, one disappointing aspect of the game is the fact that your gaming device needs to be equipped with a great deal of horsepower. For instance, if you are utilizing a computer, a 1 GB discrete graphics card is recommended to squeeze the full juice out of this game. Apart from this, it is certainly a revelation and will be etched in our hearts for ages to come.

I can't remember where (or why) I decided to buy this game, but I think it was "it looked like fun".
And it is, and I keep coming back to it.
A pretty straightforward top down driving game (think "the original GTA" style) but filled with zombies and a whole lot of power ups and vehicle weapons, and you have it.   Some games are more 'in depth' and take a long time to play or finish, this one is one of my classic "Friday night Pizza and Beer" type games, where I just want to have a blast and turn my brain off after work.  It fits the bill.
It's simple and you can go as vanilla as you like (just "do the mission objectives they ask you to and nothing else") or, just before you're about to complete it, maybe go back outside the safe zone and rack up some more kills in the most imaginative ways you can think of.  Handbrake turn and kill a zombie ?  Tick.  Light them on fire with a nitro boost ?  Yes.  How about driving backwards and making a raspberry jam smear ?  Can do.
Levelling up allows you to unlock (and customise) even more cars, all with their different strengths and weaknesses, e.g. the bus carries a lot of survivors, but is slower than others.
Again, my 'go to' measure is 'how many beers would this game cost me ?'.  At $10, I'd go 'happy hour' and buy it on sale, but that's just me...RECOMMENDED in any case.

Excellent game. The 1v1 mode is exciting and fairly deep, especially with the fully customizable rig system. It's still in early access so there are some bugs and incomplete features, but even with them the game is still very enjoyable, and I anticipate it being even better come full release.
It's not really a MOBA or an RTS. It kind of takes the objective system from HotS and combines it with the multi-tasking and control scheme of Starcraft, then throws in its own twists with the customizability and score system.

If Starcraft, Heroes of the Storm, and Mechwarrior somehow got together and made a game baby this is it! If you are learning the game the 3v3 game mode is perfect for learning mechanics and what equips do what. Then as soon as you are ready, the 1v1 is where it's at. Challenging as hell yet very fun and addicting. My only negative about the game currently is that I find myself playing the same players over and over again in the Unranked 1v1 queue. It's even gone as far as hour long queues which is rather disappointing.
The customization part of the game is wonderful. 4 Classes of fighters but you can equip a ton of different weapons and pieces that make the game real interesting. Most of the time if you run into someone playing the same character as you it'll still feel cool because they aren't likely running the same setup as you. It all depends on your playstyle. Deathball, Poke, Split Pusher, and more are available and it is all up to your creativity in the garage.
The gameplay itself is great as well. Scary at first of course since you may not know the weapons and abilities but you'll learn as you go along. What is nice about the battles is that it is at a slower pace. Most fights can last 30secs or more depending on your movement and targeting. There are also no surprise 100% - 0% insta death combos in this game. Every crowd control effect and big nuke ability can also be out spaced or dodged leaving lots of opprotunity for outplays and really letting your skill show.
Also the objective based scoring makes it real interesting. Getting the cores uploaded in the heat of battle is intense at times. Then at the beginning of every game 3 bonus objectives that give multiple points that can be game changing. Things like killing bosses, getting first blood, controlling all view towers at once, and more.

The game itself features two ways of playing. 1 v 1 and 3 v 3 and there is also a fun horde/ survival mode.
1 v 1 is where I believe pro play will be the most fun to watch as it requires alot of macro decision making and micro skill and unit management from the players. You control 3 rigs at the same time and it combines gameplay from RTS games like starcraft really well with the character differences and purposes of a MOBA.
3 v 3 is the a bit more like other MOBAs where you can play with friends or randoms and every player controls a single rig. Coordination is key here and if you find yourself not on the same page as your allys it can quickly mean game over (as quick as 15 minutes can be :P).
What I also found to be very pleasant is that the game doesnt have a big paywall at the moment. Pilots and chests are okay priced compared to how much currency you get for playing. As of time of this review I have played 14.4 hours but spent at least a quarter of that with theorycrafting and still made enough cash to buy 10 crates and a pilot.
The game still has some bugs going on such as finished games not dropping currency or daily quests not properly updating once you finished the task/ one of the tasks and sometimes the pathfinding acts up a bit, however gameplay itself and the rig designing is already really nice and I find myself enjoying Dropzone alot more than I expected. It has definitly the potential to be one of the best MOBAs on the market if the developer doesnt abandon the game and keeps fresh content/ updates/ fixes coming and doesnt go the pay to win way.
Looking forward to spent more time in this game!

Things to keep in mind before we move on:
- Game is in early access, but not in the "still buggy and rough around the edges" kind. It's a stable and smooth ride, barely any crashes (maybe 1 every 15 hours). There are still balance issues, but nothing major. The biggest issue is the low quatity of maps available and the general lack of diversity and cosmetics, but at this point the dev have such a fine product it's easily forgivable.
- It's free-to-play, so yes you can expect some grind.
That being said:
It looks like a MOBA, and indeed you can play it like one. But there's a bit more to it, since you can play by yourself and control every units (3) on the map. It needs quite a bit of micro-managing, but if you lose, you won't be able to blame your teammates. Right now the ranking system is limited to this 1v1 mode, but there are talks of adding a ranking system for the 3v3 mode as well.
The grind is real, as I said earlier, but you can pay to bypass it. That doesn't, in any way, make this game a Pay-to-Win cashgrab. I actually regret buying (with in-game currency, I haven't spent a single real dollar yet) some "higher"-tier pilots since they were actually weaker than the starting ones according to my playstyle. So some of them just sit there, barely used... So yeah, if you can pay to buy new pilots and gear, go ahead, but you may still lose every match. What makes the difference really is the player, there's no way around that in this game.
The customization is also interesting and very much complete. You can build your rigs (the mechs you control) taking into account each pilots' strenght and really adapt it to your style and the way YOU want to play the game. Nothing forces you into a rigid set and there's nothing like "use this combo or you lose" here. So it's really a try-and-adapt experience where you just go with the flow.
So in conclusion: just install and try it out, if you think you may like it. Discover for yourself. There really is nothing to lose here, after all!

TL;DR This is a very unique game, from gameplay to the whole focus of the narative for the game. This game is not for the easily frustrated, or deterred. You need immense patience in order to complete the game. This game is extremely unforgiving, however extremely rewarding if you do make it through the game. A very nice little game, a great time waster, and all in all a very zen game. 8/10
Getting over it is a game where you are playing as a guy inside of a pot, and you have to get over a mountain of found objects using only a hammer, which you move around with your mouse cursor. It is narrated over by the very relaxing voice of Bennett Foddy. No matter how far you get in the game, a mistake could send you all the way back to the beginning; no amount of progress is set in stone. This game requires a lot of patience. I am only a couple hours in right now and I have only made it to maybe halfway through and then I fell all the way back to the beginning. Whenever you fall down, Bennett will quote someone famous taking about failure, or start playing a song about losing or starting over. As you progress through the game, Bennett remarkes on the inspirations for the game, and talks about different things in society. It is pretty interesting to listen to, and adds a nice touch to the game.
The gameplay is very simple, you just move your mouse around, and that moves your hammer. That's it. You eventually figure out different ways to move in order to get higher jumps, or better lift, etc. However the basic movement is very simple. The controls are a little frusterating to play with, but that seems intentional. It adds to the atmosphere of the game being extremely unforgiving. It is a great game, but it is very frusterating to play, so you have to keep that in mind. While I would say $7.99 is a bit much for this game, the experience and time it takes to actual beat the game justifies it. If you are hesitent to get it , maybe wait until it is on sale. However if you aren't I would 100% recommend this game, if you are into this type of unforgiving difficulty.

While the game can be fun and satisfying, there are issues on some DLC that ruin it:
- trains tilting the wrong way in corners
- wrong displayed speed limit (25 mph allowed, but fined when over 20 mph)
- no tutorials for special systems like cruise control, SIFA, LZB, PZB90, ... (only mentioned in the manual)
- FPS drops
- glitches like signals remaining red or even AI trains getting stuck.
- unachievable or too easy schedules (sometimes you can be 5 minutes early, sometimes you will be late, not matter what)
- no keyboard rebindings
These bugs are in the standard game career scenarios for more than a year, so it seams that DTG isn't planning to fix them.I find it very strange that they keep pushing out new DLC when the DLC included in the base game still has problems like this. It almost seems they want to discourage new players from buying more DLC.
EDIT: I would like to point out that the workshop contains fixed versions of some of the scenario's
In conclusion I would say that you should only buy this game when it's on sale and you really like to drive trains. Also make sure to read about DLC before buying, because some of it is just not good quality.

Rewriting review because of update on OpenIV situation and some things I had wrong in the previous review.
Singleplayer:
OpenIV is now legal again! Along with that, ScriptHookV was updated! This game has so much you can do to the single player with mods, and the mod loaders (such as OpenIV and ScriptHookV) actively prevent you from going online, so nobody using said loaders can mess with other people! The story is great, and mods let you do SO MUCH MORE once you've completed the single player!
Multiplayer:
It's a really, REALLY long grind to get stuff, unless you buy shark cards (don't... just don't. It's not worth it). Once you get to higher levels and get a lot of money, it's a lot easier to get what you want and to get new cars/weapons as they're added to the game. That being said, there is a major problem with cheaters in online (note: this is not due to OpenIV or ScriptHookV, as those mods prevent you from going online if they are installed). This wouldn't be a huge deal if R* didn't ban some users for picking up money cheaters drop and leaving others alone (including the cheaters :/). People also care VERY LITTLE about you and your vehicles in public lobbies. In private or friend-only lobbies though, online is pretty enjoyable! Had some funny things happen in a friend only lobby that I doubt would happen in a public lobby.
Overall, GTA V has an amazing single player that is infinitely expandable with mods, and a multiplayer that is pretty grindy, but lots of fun once you get yourself going.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a fairly original game where you control two brothers simultaneously, one with each joystick on your controller. Given its incredibly high Metacritic rating and uniqueness, one would think this would be a good game. Sadly, it is not.
Story
The story of this game is supposed to be one of its big draws. It is, essentially, the quintessential sad story. The brothers' mother drowns, their father gets sick, and it falls to the two of them to go through the world, overcoming challenges to get the cure for him. The story, as it were, is very sparse; there's a few moments where the brothers help out each other, such as the big brother diving in to help the younger one throughout one level, and then at the end of the game, when the big brother gets hurt, it is the little brother's turn to help out.
It ends with the older brother dying just before the cure gets to him, the brother returning home with the cure for his father, and them kneeling before the mother's and brother's graves.
The characters all speak in simlish, and ultimately communicate via gestures. Unfortunately, the net effect of this was to make me not care about them at all; I understood their personalities to some extent, but I never connected to them as people, and thus I didn't ever really care about them. Indeed, the very nature of the game - using the two brothers as pieces to solve the puzzles - really divorced me from caring about them.
Gameplay
This game is interesting by being simultaneously innovative and mediocre. The underlying idea behind the game is clever - you control two characters and you have to use them to overcome various puzzles and challenges. There are times when you have to be moving both characters around at the same time, and times when one character stands there and holds a lever down (or just waits) for the other brother to do stuff.
The game is at its best when you need to use both brothers at once to do stuff, but unfortunately, while the gameplay mechanic sounds really neat, it actually gets pretty old after a while; most of the puzzles are fundamentally fairly similar, and while you do various actions, none of the puzzles are particularly difficult or challenging. It generally is very obvious what you are supposed to do, which sounds like a good thing until you realize that it means that the game is more or less leading you by the nose throughout its length. There's only a few points at which the mechanics are all that interesting; for much of the rest of the game, after the beginning, you're more or less repeating yourself, with the odd new puzzle added in.
The game did do something fairly clever at the end, though; after the older brother dies, the younger brother is left on his own. Throughout the rest of the game, the younger brother has been afraid of swimming, having to cling to his older brother for support when in the water. At the very end of the game, he is faced with no choice but to swim, and the controller vibrates as you push up to the edge of the water; only by using the older brother's action button can you swim across it. You also have to summon his strength again to pull down a lever which previously only he could move.
Unfortunately, while this was clever, it wasn't very deep, and that's the trouble with the whole game - it is very shallow.
Graphics
The graphics of the game are okay but not amazing; the characters are all cartoony, but they aren't quite high polygon enough to really look as good as they should. There are some moments in the game where things are very pretty looking, but on the whole, it isn't nearly so nice looking.
Final Summary
Brothers has an interesting central mechanic, but unfortunately the overall game is very shallow. It is pretty short - clocking in at about 4 hours in length for 100% completion, less if you don't explore all the areas fully - but even in that time it gets repetitive. It is not worth your time.

“I’m flying a bomber, the Japanese are on my six and I’ve taken a lot of damage, the tail gunner has shoot few of them down but the plane took a lot of damage, we may not make it.” That is just a page out of my journal while playing “Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China”. I was making my escape after I just bombed the enemy base.
I’m not into flight games, but this one really played a number at me. FTSOC its plays nicely the World War II front in China, the team got the atmosphere of and the immensity of the war theatre just right and I got myself really immerse in the game. The events are tied to a story-line, while nice, it just holds the action together and gives you a purpose and that is just fine. Not that you really need anything more. The gameplay is amazing, you really feel like you fly the plane, while keeping things simple. It might look a bit hard at the beginning but once you get the hang of it then you’re having a huge amount of fun.
The missions are really diverse, none looks like the other in both objectives and setting. You chase enemy fighter, break bombers formation, you bomb bases and destroy bridges. You even get to be the tail gunner. Nice! Some are a bit too difficult even on the casual difficulty, especially when you have to keep the flight formation. The controls are good, there is no confusion as to which button to push and you get the hand of it easily and works well with an Xbox Controller.
The weather is also diverse, in some mission it rains, in some it snows or maybe it’s just plain sunny. The graphics look nice, the level of detail is just enough to keep you on track. Another place where the games shines is the soundtrack. It binds nicely with the overall atmosphere. The explosions and machine guns really give the WWII feeling
FTSOC also haves other game modes such as Dogfighter, Challenge and Free Flight. In Dogfighter you chose your plane and fight other planes controlled by the AI which provides a good enough opponent on normal difficulty. While a human opponent surely could provide a far better challenge, I had little luck in finding other people to play with. And I could not enter the one room I ever saw because the game kept telling me I had an older version, which was not true.
Despite being in early access, I’ve encountered only one bug, the enemy fighter didn’t take damage but restarting the mission seems to have solved it. There were no fps spikes or anything to bother me while playing which is surprisingly good.
Bottom-line Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China is a very good game, immersive and fun to play with a good soundtrack and diverse mission. Could totally compete with an AAA title an even beat it to a pulp. Hopefully at the release there would be more people getting into multiplayer.

Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China is a great dogfight game that deserves your time.
Coming from someone who doesn't frequently play flight simulators, this game is a breeze to play.  Thanks to some presets in the controls, and the "arcade" style controls, handling your mechanical death bird is intuitive and fun.  There's a decently long campaign to be explored, which adds some great context amongst the dogfighting.
There's also some pretty tough challenges to take on.  These truly test your ability to control your plane and engage in combat seamlessly.  There's also some online multiplayer, and I didn't experience much lag when playing.
As an icing on this air combat cake, the game looks great.  Even when you drop from "Cinematic" to "High" presets, the game still runs beautifully and looks grand.  The amount of different planes and visual style shows there was a decent amount of passion behind the design.  If anything, Flying Tigers is a great entry point for newcomers who want to shoot stuff out of the sky.  There's a great amount of content to reinforce that initial itch.
I wholly recommend it.

It's kinda hard for me to review dropzone, since I don't really have another standard to review it by.
The proper thing to call Dropzone would probably be a MOBA-RTS hybrid (a kind of ridiculous moniker, but it's accurate I guess). Instead of controlling an army, like in an RTS, or a single hero, like a MOBA, in dropzone each player controls 3 customizable mechs. Additionally the objectives you accomplish around the map would be familiar to any RTS player-taking out your opponent's units, capturing objectives to gain vision, etc. But you also kill or farm AI controlled units for exp to level up your characters, like a MOBA. On top of this you score in each game by taking "cores" from AI controlled nests and bringing them to the middle of the map, while making sure your opponent doesn't steal the core you're trying to take mid.
Frankly, as you can tell from the above paragraph, it's hard to explain Dropzone. This isn't because the game is overly complicated or awkward-it actually makes a fair amount of sense once you get into, assuming you've played games in either of the genres Dropzone descends from. It's just not a game that has any easy frame of reference to fit into-it's completely novel.
It's tempting for me to call Dropzone a novelty competitive game, but really I think it has potential beyond that. The customization component adds a surprising amount of depth, and watching matches almost reminds me of watching old SC2 vods. I can't exactly explain why I enjoy Dropzone, but I can definitely tell you it's worth checking out.

I'll give this game a thumbs-up. Its heart is in the right place, and it carries a poignant message about patience and resilience. I won't say this game is poorly made; if anything, it's given me a new respect for Bennett Foddy as a game designer.
But, JEEZ, this game is hard. The statements in the game description aren't playful exaggeration; this game is designed to be incredibly frustrating. It's designed to make forward progress as hard as possible-- and erasing your progress as easy as possible. Do not download this game expecting a semi-tough, but quickly surmountable challange. Get this game only if you have a lot of time to lose.
Messages aside, every aspect of this game's gameplay is fine-tuned to be an annoyance-- intentionally, I'm sure. As other reviews have pointed out, the controls are pretty unintuitive. For instance, the distance you swing your hammer is based more on the SPEED of your mouse movements than the actual distance you move the mouse. If you move your mouse an inch, slowly, you might swing it a few degrees. If you move the same distance quickly, you'll swing your hammer 180 degrees, smash it into the floor, and send yourself vaulting off a cliff back to the start of the game. Inconsistency plagues this game, especially with friction: whether or not your hammer will hold fast to a surface is based on so many subtle factors (like hammer speed, angle of contact, barometric pressure, or Bennett Foddy's current mood) that climbing can sometimes feel like rolling dice.
I get that this game is supposed to be hard. That's why I gave it a thumbs-up. But the purpose of a game review is to tell people what the game is like, from a player's perspective. And, from a player's perspective, this game is insanely frustrating.
This game isn't like, say, Cuphead. In Cuphead, the focus of the game is the exhilirating combat, and extreme difficulty is just a side effect of the combat. In Getting Over It, the extreme difficulty IS the game. And it's got plenty of difficulty to go around.

Visually it doesn't work.  Don't trust the stuff on the store page; the sky will be pitch black, the snow a bright white.  So much so that the worlds feel very empty and artificial.  Snow and light reflectivity are hard to nail down, sure.  But it isn't necessarily an excuse considering SSX had it down over ten years ago.  Textures and obstacles pop in at distances that will commonly end your perfect run, your character is the only thing on the map with sufficient polygons to represent an entity, and you'll often find things missing in locations you'd expect them to be.  You'll also be shocked at how comically bad the physics seem to be.
Audio is also odd.  There seems to be 3-4 tracks of calm, soothing electronic music that will get on my nerves after 20 minutes in game.  Considering the only way you level up is by doing "rad" tricks, the music doesn't fit what you're doing either.  It's like a gunfight to smooth jazz - it's unsettling how much it doesn't work.
There isn't a progression system.  There is no story.  You level up (extremely slowly) by sinking hours into the infinity park, crashing (often intentionally to avoid the awful interface for getting back to the top of the lift) and repeating to earn next-level rewards.  Only those rewards are every 10 levels.  And experience isn't linear.  And the rewards aren't enough to get anything.  It's free to play for a reason - because that's the only way hardcore fans will support the game.  This means they're cutting off people who want to play by boring them with a really poorly implemented progression system.  It's too slow for me, and likely for anyone else with under 4 hours on the game.  There are events, which don't feel challenging and bore me to tears.
That being said, there's essentially no character customization either.  Gear is outrageously pricey.  Considering I earned about 10 credits for reaching level 10, that's a tenth of anything on the store.  So I'd need to get to level 100 for a helmet, which would probably take a month of gameplay.  You're going to see a lot of other players with the same boring blue jacket and helmet as you if you play online, which speaks volumes of how few people are willing to pay the astronomical prices to acquire in-game cosmetics.  From what I understand before it was FTP, everything was unlocked, and I would be able to equip anything I fancied.  That was for $15, but now the store would cost significantly more.  What's worse is that players who paid for the game before it was FTP got robbed essentially, with all of their gear being locked behind a paywall.  It's as if the devs didn't think it through when going FTP.
All in all:
This game has been released on Steam Early-Access for 3 years, FTP for 1.  What you see now is likely what you'll get: Shallow and broken at it's fundamental levels.  I think the devs tried to make something that would be revolutionary for skiing on PC, but ultimately fell short and tried a new business model that screwed themselves over.  This game isn't worth more than an hour of your time.  There simply isn't more of an hour's worth of content, and after a few more hours, I was able to confirm that.
3/10

This is not really a game but a piece of artwork (but I did not say it was a master piece), what would be a collector tool for train fans, and also for people who like to travel just to watch at the scenery. As a driving simulator it is just ok but not so great.
This game has received a lot of critical review mainly because of some inaccuracies in the driving simulation and the overpriced DLC. It must agree to that, but nonetheless I think that the qualities of the games are unique and slightly outweight its flaws.
Mainly, this is the only game ever (of which I am aware of) to provide such a complete and detailed scenery of a real actual routes. I'm still looking in vain for such level of variety and realism in the scenary in car simulations, and I think this is why it is so expensive. Every mile is unique, every factory and nearly all buildings are not clones and most are appearing only once, or at least they seem to be.
I was also nicely surprised to see that a scenario (a free one) proposed a complete shunting yard operation including connecting and diconnecting cars and switching lanes.
The game has to be improved (and see the many other reviews for a complete list of flaws), and probably the developer should offer much more discount prices for buying several DLCs, since thaving an extensive collection of the trains and routes is simply unaffordable for most people, therefore I don't see the point in maintaining such high prices.
So despite its flaws, I love the scenery of this game and it deserves a good note. My strategy would be to play the base game as much as I can. I say the base game, but I had a total of 3 routes with it, including Donner Pass) As a matter of fact, it is worth approximately 40 hours of play, which is not much but just enough for the price. Maybe later I will choose carefully one or two DLC for which there are free additional content available in the workshop.
Also, I must say that I was disappointed by the career mode. Two of the routes offered balanced challenges, but the Donner Pass presented impossible timetables that were NEVER corrected by the developers despite being reported several times. Therefore, you have a nice table to put your medals but one of the boards will remain blank forever, what a waste of pleasure!
And finally, the routes are not all equal regarding quality. Probabky different people are managing the production of each route and that is visible on the result. The two European routes I own (one in Germany and one in England) are very good visually, especially the German one with a lot of details. Some station scenery with all the wires, the buildings, the factories are a jewel. But the Donner Pass (in the mountains) is just deceiving, pine trees and rocks are bland and not much varied, while textures are low quality and repetitive.

This is a game created by a famous Swedish film director, called Josef Fares ("Kopps" and "Farsan" are his most famous movies). You follow two brothers on their journey to find some plants to save their dying father. They meet all kinds of danger, everything from trolls to big spiders.
An interesting thing with this game is that you play two characters simultaneously (You need a controller to play this game, as far as I'm aware), you control one character with the left part of your controller and the other one with the right part of your controller. At first I was a bit sceptic to that mechanic, but then I tried it out, and oh man it works good! To complete the game it takes about 3 hours (at least it took 3 hours for me). It has some REALLY amazing puzzles where you need to control both brothers to continue. You can use a PlayStation 3 controller by downloading some programs (NOTE: You need to plug in the controller into an USB port).
I would give this 10/10, as I haven't find any major bugs or glitches.

Now where this game truly stands out for me is the community, for the most part the people you will meet are polite, helpful, and just fun to play with. Most servers have rules against racism, vulger language, and exploits, those rules are ENFORCED! It all adds up to a great community to play with and once you get into the rhythm the hours will fly on by. I found myself spending hours completing challenges just so I could get a cool looking skin for my M24.
Only drawback for me was that I was hoping for a more diverse selection of weapons but IT IS A FREE GAME, so I cannot complain too much.

Review: Flying Tigers
What do you get?
In modern day gaming, it is all too common for you to pay top dollar for AAA games, expecting weeks of exciting new content with pitch perfect gameplay. And more often than less, getting disappointed with rushed and unpolished gameplay and content, and you feeling like you got robbed of your money and time.
It is a breath of fresh air to play games like Flying Tigers. It is one of those games where the price you pay and the experience you get are perfectly matched and every minute play is time well spent. It is these type of games that makes me excited for the gaming community.
My System:
I ran Flying Tigers on my Windows Desktop with the following:
•	GeForce GTX 960 4gb
•	Intel Core i5-4440 @ 3.1GHz
•	16gb of DDR3 RAM
The Basics:
Performance - With my rig, with maxed out graphics, at 1080p, I got solid and stable 60 frames per second with frames dropping slightly during high content instances during campaign but nothing visually noticeable.
Joystick needed?? - Yes. Or at least a console remote. Keyboard and mouse inputs are not bad, and definitely playable, but I found myself on numerous occasions overshooting the target, flying in circles around ground targets and getting frustrated over simple controls.
Graphics - Well-polished and surprisingly on par graphics even compared to some AAA games. It is nothing ground-breaking and certainly won’t stand out as something different. But from small details on the plane to the massive open worlds filled with contest, they get it right.
Audio - To put it clear and simple, from machine guns blasting to numerous different characters and accents, the quality is excellent and coincides with the game perfectly. Even the main menu soundtrack sets the mood for the action packed gameplay.
General Gameplay - The game runs smoothly, looks great, sounds great and plays great. With almost no bugs or crashes, this type of gameplay is what every other gaming studio should strive to achieve at launch date.
Single Player:
Single player consists of of:
Campaign
Dogfight
Select Challenge
Free Flight
The Campaign consists out of 12 mission, which have huge variety in where you play, the type of mission, planes and weaponry. It is both entertaining and well written. But the progression from mission to mission does not flow from one to the next well enough as to keep you wanting to play one more. Yet it adds something new to the WW2 series as you play in locations set in China-Burma-India, which is accompanied with excellent voice acting, realistic gameplay and outcomes.
Dogfight and Select challenge are basically the Campaign without the voice acting and missing introduction, but add a couple of hours of extra flying fun to the mix.
Multiplayer:
Multiplayer consists of:
Join Online Battle
Host Online Battle
Steam Leader boards
Pilot Record
At the moment, there are minimal players online as it is almost impossible to find a match. But as the game is in early release, I expect the number of players to exponentially increase.
Something to think about:
You are getting what you are paying for here. This is a WW2 aerial combat game. And that’s it. There is a Single player and a Multiplayer and it follows the usual old recipe of flying around trying to shoot down as many enemy planes or destroying ground targets. It’s nothing new or revolutionary, but it doesn’t have to be. It’s a well polish game that delivers much than what you expect. It reminds me of the good old days when games use to be simpler and more to the point. And that’s exactly what Flying Tiger’s is.
Will I play it for more than a week?
At the moment no. As it stands any average PC gamer will be able to complete the Campaign and other single player elements in under a week, BUT when the multiplayer segment gets up and running I am sure that countless more hours will be spent flying over the beautiful China-Burma-India landscapes trying to gun down opponents.

I purchased, and played through the full Campgain. My review is based on the game at this time, however, I know, and so should others, that this game is an "Early Access Game," and as such, changes, patches, possibly more content, etc., are expected to occur.
Pros:
1. Works well with an XBOX One Gamepad.
2. The graphics are decent.  Planes seem to look decent. Explosions are nice.
3. Control schemes can be anywhere from simplistic (push button for maneuvers, auto-rudder control), to medium (giving more control, such as controlling Rudder, and Roll, etc.).
4. No detected FPS or Stuttering issues. (smooth)
5. There are Gunner positions in the aircraft that have Machineguns.
6. The Campaign has a variation of different missions, including Dogfights, Bombing, Torpedo, Bomber protection/escort, etc.
7. There is the classic/standard "track your target" ability, to keep better eye on your prey during a Dogfight.
8. The control-binding and re-binding works well.
9. Personal Pro - I enjoyed the Campaign, and enjoy the game in general.
Cons:
1. Main campaign seems short to me.
2. Free-flight Maps seem confined/small (though not ridiculously small).
3. There is no Cockpit view, and the two main views are both from the external and behind your aircraft.  To me, it is a "con," though to others it may not be (Unless I missed the option during view-change to select cockpit).
Early Access - So I expect some issues/bugs, and changes (though i'm not detecting any discernable issues/bugs).
Game is Early Access. It is also a simplistic game. I believe it is meant to be. It is one of those games you quickly hop into, if you want a quick Dogfight, or to drop some quick bombs, play a game against some other people in WWII-style fighter aircraft. It is not meant to be a "photo-realistic" "Simulator." For what it seems to be trying to be...it seems to be, and does a good job at being.
For the most part, 95%, if you are looking for what I described, I'd say I recommend it. Just expect there to be changes, possible bugs, added content, etc., since the game is still in its infancy.

I'm born in '93 eastern europe...so i grew up with crappy PC's and old jems like Age of empires..warcraft 1 & 2 & 3..Tiberian sun..all that ♥♥♥♥. Then i went gradually to MOBA's with dota 1...for like 6 years till LoL came into being, then i played LoL for 5 years as my main game. I played any MOBA created, from Paladins to some strange viking moba :))

Anyway, the idea is, if you played these kinds of games, you WILL like this !
I am not a strong SciFi fan myself, i do love warhammer 40k tho; but this game has a nice aesthetic ( comic book art ) and feel to it. Lore already exists, each mech mod you get being made by different manufacturing corporations.
You get these crates, you know, like in many other games. Here, they drop mods, practically different "spells" that are available at a certain level in-match. This thing makes sure you cannot EFFICIENTLY use the most op stuff.
I mean, technically, you can, but they become usable at lvl 4-5 which is kinda late game here. So you need to mix match stuff and it gets really creative, like others here have said.
Best thing about these mods is: you actually SEE them ! I know it may not be much for some people, but i really hate games without any visual customization. I just find it lame for everybody to look the same.
So here, you put this spell and that spell, and you look different. Most people you will see look different from you, even if same class.
Definitely NOT p2w. I mean, you get either crates or cosmetics. Crates are still random, and u get them by lvling up anyway + blueprints..which are just other mods you craft by "melting" other extra copies of mods you get, cuz it can happen.
STRATEGY !!!
We gamers must admit most game do not really NEED it, and rely on other shady mechanics to sort out the winners.
Here, i find the matches extremely balanced, and it is clearly visible what are the reasons behind a win/loss. In other words, you see easily when people suck, and that is why they lose. I did not encounter a single OP mech either some extremely OP combo of mechs...it is just strategy vs strategy...and you can actualyl spend some time in the garage and build your mechs, thinking ahead.
Then there is strategy in-match. You can drop the cores with D, so  then you can think of leaving cores in base, actually stealing cores from enemy base since here, you do not die instantly when entering enemy base, some tanks can stay in enemy base for 10 + seconds.
All in all, great customization, great art, fluid gameplay, lots of room for strategizing ways to rek yer enemy.

3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I bought this game on PS3 back in the day. It was an amazing game with so much scope and possiblity.
The online world was brutal and consisted of drive bys with pistols and smaller smgs.
The missions were tough on hard mode, but offered ok rewards.
The cars were fun to drive and the customisation was amazing.
Then you had other vehicals you could call in and drive but not customise. Things like military trucks, busses, tanks.
You would make friends and play through missions, find the most efficient missions to farm xp then go hunting again when the devs patched them. These were not massive exploits since you actually had to complete the mission.
So progress was pretty much the same for everyone. You would play more to earn more.
It was great apart from consitantly overheating my PS3, internet issues, long loading times, among other things.
One of the big things that i disliked adamantly was the fact that you could not sell your supercars. You could buy them, customise them, but when you went to sell them you were unable. But why not? Could the devs be trying to make you throw 2m down the drain? No! i cried, look at this game it is amazing. Why would they want that? Oh right they have Microtransactions. There was a large outcry and finally in later versions (after a substantial amount of time) you could sell your supers.
There are a lot of examples where GTA online overprices its content in order to make you earn more in-game, yet they consistantly make it harder (or even just keep it the same) to get more money. Resulting in you having to spend more and more time in the game in order to get the items.
If you love the online experience and have friends to game with then you are not going to have much of an issue with that, but do understand the grind will get bigger and bigger.

You play as 3 guys who are all a bit psycho in their own way and who are all interesting characters.

And then, the biggest thing, is the giant, and i mean giant, modding community. You can mod anything from new maps to new player models. New guns, cars, planes, physics.
It is all simple to put in once you get the hang of it.
The singleplayer content is ok, but once you have done it all you may want to make it your own. This is where modding comes in.
The only issue is that you have to keep updating your mods because you are not allowed to not update the game.

I recommend Train Simulator, but only with qualifications:
First of all, I am only interested in North American Content; I do not own content based on the U.K., Africa, or Asia, so I cannot comment on them.  Becuase of this, my comments will only deal with North American Content.
This game can be fun, but I find it hard to enjoy when there is so much buggy content, especially DLC in the Steam Marketplace.  There are a few third party distributors who are peerless in their production of quality content; for Steam Locomotives it is Smokebox, for diesels it is Virtual Rail Creations, and for routes is is VNHRR and GTrax Simulations. The quality and attention to detail that these artists put into their work is unmatched and I wish that other content creators would take notice.  Furthermore, the quality of these products prove that Train Simulator could be so much more if Dovetail Games would only put the time into developing it to its fullest potential.
Unfortunately, Dovetail Games does not take the same care with its releases (DTG/Kuju/RSC); these DLC add-ons are poorly done and buggy, and it seems that Dovetail has no interest in bug-fixing or updating their releases with up to date features.  As an example, I will note the Santa Fe EMD SD75.  This locomotive was produced in house by Dovetail (I believe it is an RSC model) and is indicative of the lack of attention to detail, lack of bug testing, and the general attitude of "it's good enough", that Dovetail Games gets away with.  The locomotive lacks functioning headlights; they turn on but they do not illuminate the track! This is the same with the ditch lights.  Numberboards, cab lights, step-lights, and instrument lights do not work.  DLC released by Digital Train Model at the same time or earlier had these features, so why couldn't Dovetail Games do it? Additional problems with the SD75 include spongy couplers which cause coupler slack to rapidly run in and out, causing derailments no matter how you handle the brakes.  Lack of realistic braking physics and locomotive weight and tractive effort/horsepower curves ensure unrealistic performance that destroys any sense of realism and immersion.  Windows and doors do not open (other producer's DLC has this elementary feature), and the locomotive lacks snow FX (when choosing a winter scenario, there is no snow on the locomotive walkways and hoods, and snow chunks do not blow out from the trucks).  Locomotive and rolling stock lack air hoses for the automatic brake system. The locomotive has poor sound effects and rolling stock has poor or no sound effects to simulate the rumbling sounds of heavy rolling stock, the click-clack of wheels rolling over track joints, the sound of random flat-spots on wheels, or the 'whoosh' of air escaping the train line as rolling stock is uncoupled.  There are poor/no sound effects for coupling and upcoupling.  Passenger cars and cabooses mostly lack furnished interior views with multiple camera angles and working interior and exterior lighting.  I could go on, but this is only a brief summary of the probems with associated with Dovetail Games Locomotive DLC.
Problems continue with Dovetails Route DLC:  The best example I can think of would be the Pennsylvania Rail Road Horseshoe Curve route.  This route was supposed to be set circa 1958 at the very end of steam locomotive operations on the Pennsy.  The problem is that all of the steam locomotive servicing facilities are missing!  There should be 2-3 roundhouses; the main engine roundhouse, a passenger car roudhouse, and a machine shop roundhouse where running repairs were made. All are missing.  Likewise with coaling towers (there are one or two incomplete models with all of their hardware missing), water towers, stand-pipes, and track-pans.  Either Dovetail Games didn't do their research on the route and time period, or they simply didn't care.
By the way, the user interface is buggy, laggy, and prone to crashes; ditto for the route/scenario editor.  Sometimes when booting the game, it will freeze and crash, causing my computer to completely lock up, necessitating a hard shut down to unlock my brand new computer.  This points to a profound lack of optimization as well as an abscence of well thought out and user friendly U.I.
To summarize, Train Simulator has potential to be fantastic, as evidenced by the work of Smokebox, Virtual Rail Creations, VNHRR and GTrax Simulations, but it is drowning becuase of the apathy and (to my mind) the anti-consumer practices of Dovetail Games.
Make of it what you will, but realize that Dovetail is unlikely to support this game any longer as they are moving on to their shiny new farce,  Train Sim World.  Don't expect DTG to fix any bugs or update any features for Train Simulator.   Unfortunately, the same lack of attention to detail and bug fixing is now manifesting itself in Train Sim World so it would seem that Dovetail Games is continuing it's crappy business practices with it's new franchise, but that is a review for another time.

The only chance of you having a remotely hack free experience is by playing the servers that use the ACI on top of PB as these servers actually ban for not producing screen shots and actively administrate their servers.
The game doesn't allow the players to vote kick any player anymore since it's been "abused" in the past. And when you do come across someone blatantly hacking there is nothing you can do, other then trying to teamkill and even then you'll get sent to Leavenworth and be banned from the server for 5 or so minutes. The game literally doesn't give you any means of fighting against it.
For those who'd like to tell me to "git gud" thinking I was probably owned by some very experienced players who know these maps in and out, save your breath. When he was being flashed and teamkilled once people realized he cheated he'd leave, change his name and come back.

2 - The viewmodel and crosshair. If you played CS:GO before, you will love them. They just feel and look so good, you don't have your weapon shoved in your face, and the crosshair is nice and clean, excellent.

The only complaints i have:
-Not many people playing, i sometimes can't find a server close to me with players on it.

In conclusion, it's a game really worth trying out!

Do you remember the days of playing Ace Combat on the Playstation console? Do you miss GOOD aerial dogfights and heartpounding action in a fighter plane game?  Well I believe Flying Tigers: Shadows Over China (FT:SOC) to be the game you've been pining for.
Essentially FT:SOC comes across as an arcade flight game where you pilot various World War 2 aircraft that took place during various missions around China. It is worth noting that the developer coded their own game engine (SkyLight3D) just to make this game the way they wanted, so immediate kudos goes to them for that.
It's actually a great looking game, for the cost I fully expected it to not have much detail in the textures and be more focused on the gameplay but the developers seem to have got the balance right between the two.  I play this on full cinematic graphic settings at 1080p and it runs smooth as a hot knife through butter, even when recording/streaming gameplay it rarely gets even a whisker close to 40fps and stays around 60+ fairly regularly. (FYI I'm running an AMD 8 core, 8Gb ram, 2Gb R9 380 PC)
The solo campaign is pretty good so far, I'm currently 4 missions in and although I'm no history buff, I get the feeling that the missions have been crafted with quite a considerable amount of detail and thus far they have been great fun, trying the different variants of planes helps keep things very fresh.
Multiplayer however is currently a little bit lacking due to slow traffic, I did try and host a game for a while but sadly nobody dropped in but it definately works and I feel this would be a killer game to play with a bunch of friends!
The settings are really feature filled too with nearly every option avaliable either in the pre-game config loader or in-game via the keybindings where you can even attach a proper fightstick to give better control to your plane.
Overall this game is definately worth buying and if you are a fan of this sort of game I recommend you buy into it, especially as it's only in early access right now and the developers are planning to put in more content.
