At the moment the Game features a campaign where you can learn all the basics, the story and all everything is covered in awesome soundtrack. Every dialog is full dubbed and that’s very professional. With the cinematic artwork it brings a lot of immersion. The graphics are great, the game looks very, very good, even the landscape is very detailed. In one moment you cross a huge grassland and in the moment you see a nice modelled city.
The Story is special, because it is based on the real world Fighter Group in WW2, they defended China against the Japanese Forces and their Planes got a special shark-mouth paintwork. You can re-enactment their legacy!
The second Game mode is the Free Flight Mode. In this mode you can try every plane and there are more than 20 at the Moment! More airplanes are coming soon. You can also choose between a varieties of decals.
The third Single player-Mode is the Dog-Fight, in this mode you can train your skills in a premade one-on-one. That’s pretty intense and the overall difficulty is pretty high (maybe I am bad in aviation). This Mode is good to calibrate your mouse, I self-explanatory how important it is, that you have full control over your fighter or bomber.
I am sure that the multiplayer gets more Players, which is what I am looking for. Multiplayer mode are Capture the Flag, Team-Dogfight and a Deathmatch like Mode – named Master of the Skies. A huge reason is that, the game features NO Pay2Win or Micro transaction. So everything is on the line and you can get it without spending additional money to look good in multi-player.
It’s a good game, it features a lot of great air-combat action. I always like when the Dev’s are listening in Forums where you can ask questions and they provide a lot of information. This is huge point, for a game while the Game is in Early-Access Access. Everybody can help to make a better Game. They also update the game very regularly, another important reason to choose an Early-Access Product.

I recommend Train Simulator, but only with qualifications:
First of all, I am only interested in North American Content; I do not own content based on the U.K., Africa, or Asia, so I cannot comment on them.  Becuase of this, my comments will only deal with North American Content.
This game can be fun, but I find it hard to enjoy when there is so much buggy content, especially DLC in the Steam Marketplace.  There are a few third party distributors who are peerless in their production of quality content; for Steam Locomotives it is Smokebox, for diesels it is Virtual Rail Creations, and for routes is is VNHRR and GTrax Simulations. The quality and attention to detail that these artists put into their work is unmatched and I wish that other content creators would take notice.  Furthermore, the quality of these products prove that Train Simulator could be so much more if Dovetail Games would only put the time into developing it to its fullest potential.
Unfortunately, Dovetail Games does not take the same care with its releases (DTG/Kuju/RSC); these DLC add-ons are poorly done and buggy, and it seems that Dovetail has no interest in bug-fixing or updating their releases with up to date features.  As an example, I will note the Santa Fe EMD SD75.  This locomotive was produced in house by Dovetail (I believe it is an RSC model) and is indicative of the lack of attention to detail, lack of bug testing, and the general attitude of "it's good enough", that Dovetail Games gets away with.  The locomotive lacks functioning headlights; they turn on but they do not illuminate the track! This is the same with the ditch lights.  Numberboards, cab lights, step-lights, and instrument lights do not work.  DLC released by Digital Train Model at the same time or earlier had these features, so why couldn't Dovetail Games do it? Additional problems with the SD75 include spongy couplers which cause coupler slack to rapidly run in and out, causing derailments no matter how you handle the brakes.  Lack of realistic braking physics and locomotive weight and tractive effort/horsepower curves ensure unrealistic performance that destroys any sense of realism and immersion.  Windows and doors do not open (other producer's DLC has this elementary feature), and the locomotive lacks snow FX (when choosing a winter scenario, there is no snow on the locomotive walkways and hoods, and snow chunks do not blow out from the trucks).  Locomotive and rolling stock lack air hoses for the automatic brake system. The locomotive has poor sound effects and rolling stock has poor or no sound effects to simulate the rumbling sounds of heavy rolling stock, the click-clack of wheels rolling over track joints, the sound of random flat-spots on wheels, or the 'whoosh' of air escaping the train line as rolling stock is uncoupled.  There are poor/no sound effects for coupling and upcoupling.  Passenger cars and cabooses mostly lack furnished interior views with multiple camera angles and working interior and exterior lighting.  I could go on, but this is only a brief summary of the probems with associated with Dovetail Games Locomotive DLC.
Problems continue with Dovetails Route DLC:  The best example I can think of would be the Pennsylvania Rail Road Horseshoe Curve route.  This route was supposed to be set circa 1958 at the very end of steam locomotive operations on the Pennsy.  The problem is that all of the steam locomotive servicing facilities are missing!  There should be 2-3 roundhouses; the main engine roundhouse, a passenger car roudhouse, and a machine shop roundhouse where running repairs were made. All are missing.  Likewise with coaling towers (there are one or two incomplete models with all of their hardware missing), water towers, stand-pipes, and track-pans.  Either Dovetail Games didn't do their research on the route and time period, or they simply didn't care.
By the way, the user interface is buggy, laggy, and prone to crashes; ditto for the route/scenario editor.  Sometimes when booting the game, it will freeze and crash, causing my computer to completely lock up, necessitating a hard shut down to unlock my brand new computer.  This points to a profound lack of optimization as well as an abscence of well thought out and user friendly U.I.
To summarize, Train Simulator has potential to be fantastic, as evidenced by the work of Smokebox, Virtual Rail Creations, VNHRR and GTrax Simulations, but it is drowning becuase of the apathy and (to my mind) the anti-consumer practices of Dovetail Games.
Make of it what you will, but realize that Dovetail is unlikely to support this game any longer as they are moving on to their shiny new farce,  Train Sim World.  Don't expect DTG to fix any bugs or update any features for Train Simulator.   Unfortunately, the same lack of attention to detail and bug fixing is now manifesting itself in Train Sim World so it would seem that Dovetail Games is continuing it's crappy business practices with it's new franchise, but that is a review for another time.

Gameplay 4/5 - If you have played environmental puzzle games then the puzzles in this really shouldn't give you too much trouble. None-the-less, the puzzles are beautifully done; I never tired of them; the developers use the controls and mechanics with incredible diversity. Still, I give 4/5 because during the stretches when you are running from place to place, not performing a puzzle, are difficult. If you aren't paying attention someone will inevitably be running aimlessly. This is almost more of a player issue, but dividing your brain into two tasks takes some focus. Essentially, the controls aren't hard but they are difficult in a way that even toward the end of the game you will make the same errors.
Music 5/5 - I bought the soundtrack: enough said. But seriously, the music is simply gorgeous. I am not a musical theorist, so I cannot say if the compositions are subpar or stellar, but I think they suit the moods of each area and scene perfectly while being able to stand alone as gorgeous scores.

Find the benches, sit on them, and dream. I feel that there may have been a scattering of moments when the camera was a detriment...but I can't remember them. Years ago, I used to play the original Zombie Driver, a funny if somewhat lackluster action-driving game. The HD "remaster" is a huge improvement in every aspect compared to the original.
New missions and mission types, special assignments with mission-specific vehicles (such as tanks, bulldozers or military trucks), revamped graphics and destruction physics, and a much-needed gameplay rebalance (e.g. a better flow of cash after gore-mayhem-and-destruction, and more frequent powerup placement on the game map) make the HD version the definite experience of the game. The besieged city is more atmospheric and alive (?) thanks to the extra cutscenes and the zombie-killing military allies, the new spawnnests and minibosses spice up the enemy variety well enough, while the new weather conditions (fog, bloom, rain, and night missions) also spice up the flow of simple, yet fun missions.
Besides the main story mode, there is also a Carmageddon-esque Blood Race mode and the obligatory Survival gameplay as well - none of which were present in the original game, and which also add some longevity to the overall experience.
In short, the game is a perfect no-brainer (pun intended) destruction-based top-down shooter, as simple as you might expect by its title. Missions may be repetitive in the long run, voice acting is a bit annoying, and the unskippable cutscenes do more harm than good for the gameplay, but these do not really detract from the overall experience. I really recommend it if you are looking for a simple, yet fun destruction-based vehicle shooter.

NOTE:  I received a key explicitly for reviewing Flying Tigers: Shadows over China. How I perceived this game whether it’s positively or negatively is entirely up to me.
Flying Tigers: Shadows over China is an Early Access Flying combat simulator that sets on Asia during World War II where Axis and Allies are contesting on air superiority control. There are many planes to choose from in Dogfight and Free Flight mode.
PROS
-The Arcade Gameplay it what makes the game good. There not much Arcade combat simulator nowadays and this game did it flawlessly.
-The Campaign offers different mission in different countries which you are tasked to do different thing like bomb an airfield, hunt down enemy bombers, and defend your bombing run with your machinegun against enemy fighters.
-The Sounds in the game are very well done, from the engine sound to the whirring mounted machine gun sounds really great.
-The Controls are optimized on the M+KB but it’s much better if Joystick is used while playing this game. I tried using M+KB for a while then I switched to Joystick and I had a blast using the Joystick.
-The Visual are superb for an Early Access Game and the UI is also well done.
-Optimization of the game is just great, I have 100+FPS and never have any issues at the game.
-No Microtransactions. The developers didn’t went full EA/SEGA/Ubisoft that alone makes this game 12/10
CONS
-No Cockpit view. I know it’s an Arcade flying simulator but having a cockpit view should make this game much better.
-Multiplayer is non-existent currently. I hope many people can buy this game so it will be filled with dogfights everywhere.
-The game have many contents right now, but let’s hope that more planes and places will be available as Early Access continues.
Overall
I miss going to arcade and play these kind of games and this one did delivered my childhood memories
I recommend buying it even at full price as the developer are actually delivering contents with each update. I rate it 8.5/10

Red Faction: Guerrilla is a game developed by Volition Studios and originally published by the now defunct company THQ, now published by THQ Nordic (or Nordic Games) and is also the third game in the Red Faction series
Red Faction: Guerrilla is an action packed third person shooter which follows up from the previous Red Faction II game and continues the Red Faction story line
However, this time the game moves from a linear gameplay and goes open world which was my least favourite gameplay change in the Red Faction series
The gameplay is pretty standard, but lots of fun and you also have a new nifty magnet gun and some powers with the Nano Forge
Once again the highlight of the Red Faction series is blowing stuff up, and you can blow up all the structures and also repair things since enemies will often be attacking you and stairs and other things you need to access will be gone
Overall, this game is a lot of fun and for what it is - you'll have a blast playing by blowing things up and fighting off evil cultists and aliens

Glittermitten Grove is on the surface a pretty standard town planning sim mechanically similar to "Towns" or "Dwarf Fortress". The games core concepts are based around a balancing act of resource management whilst keeping your fairys happy & contented however when you get deeper into the game and penetrate beyond the surface gameplay you'll find yourself in a much richer world than you first imagined.
Glittermitten Grove's strongest area is its rich storytelling with both memorable characters and a deep and thrilling plot you'll end up quite emotionally involved in how the story plays out. I won’t talk about the plot in order not to spoil it, however it is certainly worth getting into.
I feel the weakest part of Glittermitten Grove is the early game; with a slower introduction than might be expected and no long term goals yet introduced. My advice for the early game is to rush sparkles and fireworks. Another point of disappointment is the reduced mathematical complexity of the game, while the in-depth toasting mechanics where quite nice I found there where not as many fractions as I was expecting.
Glittermitten Grove is set apart from other similar games is its mechanical depth. The game introduces many twists to the classic building placement setup e.g. a sunlight & shade trade off, and an interesting weight distribution system. The added complexity of these systems really spices up the game play.

In conclusion I would feel comfortable recommending this game and would rate it a firm 10/10 Glitter Sparkles.

Glittermitten grove is, in and of itself, a very simply fun game with a shallow learning curve and an immediately apparent reward for learning the game's fairly simple mechanics. It's nice to look at, it's original, and it's a worthwhile time-waster if you're into building bases and managing resources. There's not really an endgame and the depth leaves quite a bit to be desired, but we all know that's not the game you want to hear about.
Frog Fractions 2, or TXT World as it's called in-game, does not measure up to its predecessor. I'll admit, it's got a very unique sort of charm, and the minigames that are unlocked are funny enough; the glaring issue is that the game utterly lacks the spirit and sense of absurdism and unpredictable over-the-top progression that, in my opinion, made the original Frog Fractions great. The game is interesting and engaging to a point, the difficulty is tough but fair and easy to adjust to, but rather than an imaginative journey from humble beginnings through a goofy and nonsensical plot that retains cohesion with interesting -- if consistently silly -- writing; TXT World serves as a sort of ascii hub through which to access games that feel like in-jokes and collectibles that reward you with cheap nonsense meant to make one laugh through its randomness and reference to pop culture. The entire time I was playing, I was left wondering, "When does the real game start?" to which the game replied, "Never." If you're a die-hard Frog Fractions fan and want to see what the developers did with the kickstarter money they raised, then you can spend $20 on a nifty resource manager and a collection of game jam titles, and hopefully prove my feelings about this game wrong. As it stands, however; I cannot reccomend this game. I was disappointed and saddened by this title, and while I don't regret purchasing it, I couldn't encourage any of my friends to spend their money on this end product. Maybe wait for it to go on sale? I don't know.

Pretty good game on multiple levels.
It does what it is trying to do really well.
People looking for more enthralling 'gameplay' might be disappointed though.
Art style is homely, simple and ties in with the audio nicely to ensure we can focus on the interactions between the brothers as well as their development over the course of the game. That being said, this game is largely focused on the relationship between the brothers, and how they handle situations differently, the gameplay is simple enough to ensure the player won't get stuck (once the controls are under harness anyhow), and the engagement with characters remains fluid.
All around the story is pretty great. Without the use of a recognizable language, the characters are quite emotive both visually and audibly to get the story across to the player, which ties in really well considering the story is pinned around their interactions with each other.
The plot however is a pretty basic fetch-quest at its heart, the duo basically proceed through a series of linear environments to acquire an item they need, people looking for more may be disappointed. This is a game that really drives home the idea of the Journey being much more than the destination, often the player is forced to traverse slowly through an environment so they can take a moment to enjoy the setting, or reflect on the struggles of the characters.
Only minor faults throughout the game are some random textures that are linked to lights they shouldn't be, such as brightly lit rock in a dark caves, or patch of grass recieving full-black shadows in a softly-lit environment. This recurred a few times in pretty much every chapter from memory (except maybe prologue?).

There's also PVE modes and spectator modes. Oh, and 2v2. I'm not sure if I'm forgetting anything...
What sets this apart from other arena-style games is each player is a laner and a jungler. To win matches you have to destroy aliens to level up and harvest their resources (cores), AND upload them via the center of the map (like capture the flag, you have to defend your rig while it uploads the alien core), all the while fending off and killing the enemy. It adds a new layer of depth to the genre.
It's a polished, great looking take on the genre, edging itself into it's own little niche too. It didn't feel too much like a regular arena/moba game either. It felt like its own game.

Heroes and Generals is ,genuinely, an amazing project and provides a decent gaming expererience, trading the realism of WW2 battles for an arcade-like session. Overall, the game caught my attention since I'm a big fan of historical based games.
After spending more than 50 hours on this game, I can easily draw a couple of conclusions.
The game provides an enjoyable and easy to learn playstyle, keeping the realistic factor in designing the 3 factions ( Germany, USA and the USSR ) and rendering their equipment. There are realistic and highly detailed tank and rifle models and reality inspired maps featuring tactical points and objectives.
HOWEVER, unless you spend a few hundread dollars, you will act as cannon fodder. Labelled as a "free to play" game , H&G requires a long grind to afford a decent weapon setup. I spent 40 hours to grind the MP-40. Then, there are several balancing and matchmaking issues. For example, there is a clear bias favouring the US. Take a look at each starter tank : The American M2A2 destroyes a Panzer I without even wasting a full ammo clip and cannot be destroyed even by 3 Pz1.s firing at the same time. The Chaffee is equiped with a 75mm gun and its most powerful german counterpart has only a 37 one. I prefer not to talk about the russian tanks....
What may I say about the graphics ? They are amazing ! If you have GTX1080, yeah, they are spectacular ! But if you have an older, but still decent graphics card and processor, you can barely hit 25 fps at the lowest settings. The game is so poorly optimized and the graphic settings can really hinder your game style. For example, on the lowest graphical presets, the rendering distance is so poor, that I have serious issues aiming with the iron sights at distances exceeding 50m.
Now, don't get me wrong, the game itself is nice and I had some really funny and good moments while playing it. It's up to you if you decide whether or not to download it, but you could take this analysis into account

In Getting Over It you play as a guy in pot. Your goal is to reach the top of a mountain and the only tool you are given for this task is a hammer that is controlled by your mouse movement. There are different ways to utilize your hammer to overcome different obstacles, the game never really explains how you should approach things though. It dumps you at the foot of the mountain and from there you are on your own.
Getting Over It is a game to test your patience, determination and ability to handle setbacks like not many other. The game is designed in a way that, at almost any point, there is a risk to fall back down and lose a lot of progress.  It can be heartbreaking to get to a certain part after hours of work and to lose all of that with a single mistake. You will notice however, that once you know how to approach an obstacle, parts that first seemed impossible become almost trivial.
While some people hate the concept of no guaranteed progress, exactly those moments of frustration when you fall down make the feeling of accomplishment, once you reach the top of the mountain, as great as it is. This game is pretty much a life lesson in game form on how to deal with setbacks and I very much appreciate the idea and concept behind it.
I also have to add that I really enjoyed the narration, which was done by Bennett Foddy himself. Having to listen to some motivational quotes after falling down certainly helped,

Despite the actual game being pretty short, "Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is a simply-put emotive adventure alongside it's beautiful visuals.
=STORY=
Shortly after their mother's death, the two brothers' (Naiee and Naia) father has non-specifically fallen ill. After they bring him to the village's doctor, it is revealed to them that the only way to cure their father is by collecting water from the "Tree of Life". And right then and there, the brothers begin to embark on a long journey (and dangerous at times) to save the only parent that they have left.
=GAMEPLAY=
You are in control of the two brothers: Naiee (young) and Naia (eldest). Despite the fact that this game requires the Xbox 360 controller for the better experience, I used the PC keyboard personally. To be honest, it was a bit iffy to get used to, but then it wasn't such a big deal for me. The brothers will interact with others that they come across on their journey, solve puzzles in order to advance, and do what brothers should always be doing: Working together.
=VISUALS/ART=
Visually speaking, I love it. Seeing the amazing areas around you while you're traveling to the Tree of Life is breathtaking, making you want to appreciate the outdoors much more with praise. There are also moments in the game where you can sit on a bench that are on the edges of various areas, high in elevation, showing the beautifully looking environment that surrounds you. Once again...breathtaking.
=MUSIC=
Musically speaking, it's great. I really adore the parts of the soundtrack that are so calm and peaceful to listen to, and the parts that make you feel like you are embarking on an amazing journey, much like the two brothers themselves
=FINAL VERDICT=
A simple, beautiful story that comes with amazing visuals and a really adventurous soundtrack certainly does make up for the short length of the game.
On a scale of liver to chocolate, I give this game: A "Nutella" rating.

In ZDHD, you are Joe Citizen who, for reasons unknown and never really explained, has been recruited by the military to conduct a series of combat, scouting, and search-and-rescue missions. The first ten or so story missions of Zombie Driver HD were fun and the last twenty-one generally vacillated somewhere between tedium and entertainment, with a couple of teeth-grinding exceptions. Most of the components of a good game are here, but none of them stand out in any way, which makes the whole more-or-less precisely the sum of its parts: a mediocre story, weak voice-acting, decent but not remarkable gameplay, nice car models and destructible terrain, and some value-added game modes.
Your missions start with briefings, like the one shown above, after which you select a vehicle and buy any upgrades that you can afford based on what you’ve unlocked so far and how much cash you’ve earned from completing objectives or finding money stashes. ZDHD is one of those top-down games where you never get out of your car. The variety of vehicles, ranging from your starter car, a taxicab, to a giant armored vehicle with a 10-passenger capacity, is fairly impressive, but when you dig into the game you’ll find that you’re really only using one or two of the vehicles in your garage, generally a compromise between carrying capacity (most of your missions involve rescuing scientists, first responders, or civilians with special skills such as pilots) and durability.
What story there is in the campaign unfolds largely through the mission briefings and monologues by survivors that you pick up and bring back to base. No explanation for what caused this breakout of zombie-ism is forthcoming although it’s evidently some kind of bio-toxin, and the military has you picking up various groups of folks to assist in containment and control efforts. Many of these groups will question (as you, the player, no doubt will) why the military is sending a lone, untrained civilian to perform these dangerous tasks and some will hint that the military is somehow behind the zombie plague, but whether these are the ravings of a paranoid few or glimpses of the truth is never made clear.
If you like top-down driving games and hate zombies, you may enjoy
. It’s not a great game but it’s not a terrible game and that’s about the best faint praise I can give it.

This comes from someone who has little experience with MOBAs, is terrible at RTSes, and is still very, very new to this.
I really like it!
What I've enjoyed about Dropzone so far is its commitment to bringing more RTS into the MOBA genre. Managing a small team of 3 rigs (heroes) at once, and as the sole player for your side, the pace of a match becomes far more reliant on your ability to micro and macro-manage on the fly. I love this idea in concept, even if in practice I'm really poor at it!
Yet that's the compelling part to Dropzone. Where I'd quit a normal RTS for being far too overwhelming, this strikes a kind of positive-frustration in my brain. I feel like if I just play a match every other night, I get a little better. Not like, MLG Pro status, but better than I was a week ago.
While I can't comment too much on the lineup (still working on the first 3 people I picked), I do like that individual characters only seem to influence ults. Other abilities are based on that character's class, and are interchangable with a wide array of class-specific unlockables. This means you can taylor a team to your liking and, even if you have the same characters as your opponent, may still end up playing differently from each other.
I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who likes competitive games, moreso to those who are deeply familiar with either RTSes or MOBAs. And bonus, I've seen that it's going free to play soon! If you're unsure, you could always wait until 4/12 to give it a shot!

I'm personally a big fan of micro-managing, so this game is right up my alley. If you don't like micro-managing though, there's a mode to play a normal 3v3 where everyone controls one character, just like with another MOBA.
The "customize your characters" part of the game is pretty lackluster. Every class currently has 3 pilots each, and each pilot can pick between a set of skills for their class; 2 different tank pilots can pick between the same active abilities, but a mechanic can't pick the same active abilities as a tank.

The game is super addicting and fun to play! I really recommend it for anyone who likes their MOBAs. All of the characters are unique in their mechanisms and playstyles (and the art is fantastic). It's a game that you will want to be a part of during their early access state and see how the game grows!

I have put 29 hours into this game so far, and still going strong. I personally love this game, and it has scratched the RTS itch I have been stuck with for sometime now. It combines my two favourite genre's and creates a replayable competitive experience.
The playerbase is currently quite small, but I do not have any issues getting a game (EU) during peak hours.
Simply, it's a top down moba, with RTS elements. You control 3 rigs (all with abilities you choose and unique passive/"ultimate" ability.
You try and put 3 Rigs together, that will give you the best synergy and then you farm nests for core, and dunk them in the middle, whilst putting pressure on your opponent to slow them down. There are also 3 "optional" objectives that give you points, if you are the first to complete them.
I.e capture all vision points.
I would like to note, this is a multiplayer, competitive game. This does not contain a campaign mode.
Games are either:
1v1 or 2v2.
There is an infestation mode, which is basically survival mode. Survive against waves of enemies.
To begin with, the game offers you a lot of options.
You have up to 4 classes:
Mechanic (Support)
Gunner (DPS)
Tank
Summoner (Utility)
Each class has 3 rigs with a unique ultimate and passive ability.
Each class also has a "bank" of abilities and passives, which you can fit to any rig within that class. Just to make it clear, you can run 2 mechanics and they can be outfitted exactly the same, only difference being their ultimate and main passive abilities.
The game feels overwhelming in the first couple of hours, but after a few rounds (15 minutes each) and a good read through the different abilities, you very quickly learn what works and what doesn't.
The Gameplay itself has depth, specifically around your decisions in game.
It's very Micro intensive.
Setting up your "Rigs" or "Squad" however is lacking a bit of depth. There is a very clear meta at high level play at the moment, but the developers will be adding more gear/abilities and a new class over the course of the Early Access, along with balance changes so I do expect this to change.

FLYING TIGERS: SHADOWS OVER CHINA is one of many World War 2 flying simulators on Steam. So why should you buy this game instead of playing other Early Access flying sims?
First off is the early good signs of polish, even with Early Access, the planes and environment look fantastic and meticulously designed. The bullets and bombs feel like they have destructive impact. When enemy planes are damaged, they show debris falling off and die in spectacular explosions. The polished voice acting will make you feel like you're fighting and flying among the Allies. There are rarely games that take the fight to the Japanese and Flying Tigers helps break the hold on Europe-centric WW2 games.
A handy life bar is present for every enemy, indicating how much you have to do to bring down the enemy. It takes a bit to get used to the controls, but who said piloting and fighting against the Axis was easy? You even get slow-mo to line up your shots and acrobatic moves to evade fire.
If you're tired of the single player, the other modes, including dogfights, multiplayer, and free flying will give you flight sim goodness. Face off in custom planes against an enemy to practice dogfighting skills.
The best part, even with all the content for only $9.99, the game is still in Early Access, meaning there's still MUCH more free content to come! More planes are very visibly seen to be coming in the selection screen, so at half price this game is a steal!

At this point you can tell I love me some "Roguelikes" (I put it in quotes now cause the term has shifted in definition to these types of games), but this one is probably the hardest of them all. I feel luck > skill in this game purely due to the game mechanics.
My main problem is getting stunned: if you take a hard hit, or a hard fall, you get stunned; which puts you out for a few seconds and in later levels that's pretty much death.
My second problem is how easy it is to♥♥♥♥♥♥off shop keepers (happens to me off screen generally cause of something I threw or a missed bomb), accidentally attack one and every single one from then on will be out to get you. They jump around a lot and pack shotguns, which if don't kill you right out, they'll stun you. They can pick you up and throw you, which stuns. It's ruthless and unforgiving. And there will be one waiting at the end of every stage. I honestly wouldn't mind if it weren't so easy to trigger accidentally.
My third problem is that it's way too easy to cling to ledges (and walls if you get the sticky glove thing), which often hurts me more than helps. I'd prefer if you could hold or tap jump again to cling, rather than it automatically happening.
Other than that I enjoy the game. It's brutal, danger at every turn past 1-1 pretty much and you're forced to manage a steady pace, as taking too long in a stage (I wanna say you have about 3 minutes?) summons a large, but slow moving ghost and if it touches you, it instantly kills you. There's also some nice random events that can happen and hidden stages you can find. Get as many goodies as you can, get the girl if you can and haul♥♥♥♥♥

I am really happy with this game. All the small details have been thought out. It runs and works well on both a PC and a laptop (with tracker pad). I tried it with both and I actually preferred it on the laptop. If you're a laptop gamer give this a try and make the most of your tracker pad.
The controls all make sense. There's nothing clunky about them. There's nothing new to adjust to as other games I have played use the same keyboard controls. There are multiple ways to fly so you can choose what is right for you.
There has been a lot of work put into each and every one of the planes and there's plenty of planes to choose from.
I would say that ground detail could be improved on but I understand if there has been a sacrifice made as the maps are expansive and in the end, this is a sky based game focused on dog fights.
I was sad to not find any online players but I'm glad that online has been made an option. With dedicated servers being and option you can have great fun with your friends. Although when I played there weren't any online players, there was a server there for anyone to hang out in.
There is a great well thought out campaign which covers everything so where online is lacking players you can still have fun on your own.
Small details make this game and I love it. It's really well done and I can't wait to see this come out of development stages. Despite it being in development stages is feels very well done.

A WW2 flight sim game, basing itself around the Japanese attacks by US fighter's and bringing back memories of the 'Blazing Angels' series and 'Battlestation's : Midway' with that type of gameplay and difficulty (If you loved Blazing Angels, you'll love this!).
The game consist's of plenty of singleplayer mission's containing a campaign mode, dogfights and multiplayer for everyone to try out.
Relive historical air-battles with the same heart-pumping adrenaline that the pilot's experienced!.
This game is still in early access and it's a wonder to see such a good game with improvement's still being added! (I really didn't feel as if I was playing a early access game!).
Pro's:-
Great graphic's (with comic stlye art) and fantastic effect's.
Has good/fun gameplay element's (Blazing Angels style).
Good voice acting and fantastic campaign, also contains multiplayer.
Great to play using a joystick! (really capture's the feel of combat).
Awesome soundtrack.
Very polished experience.
Con's:-
KB+Mouse controls are 'meh', they just don't work very well (Vontroller/joystick needed).
Ran into some minor lags during gameplay nothing much, just could use a bit more optimization for near perfect experience!.
I did find the 'simulation' tag misleading just a bit, this game is more of a fast paced, arcade-style combat game.
Multiplayer is not this game's strong suit.
Overall I'd recommend this game to anyone who's played and enjoyed any of the Blazing Angels game's since this game has quite a lot of polish and near perfect experience!
I'm pretty sure the dev's will add more stuff before it leaves early access and it's already great as it is at this stage.

FLYING TIGERS: SHADOWS OVER CHINA is a WWll fighter pilot game, with arcade-style combat, based around fighting Japan as the US, during the war. It has plenty of singleplayer options and a few multiplayer options to cater to everyone here.  Get ready to relive historical air-battles such as the Japanese Christmas-raids on Rangoon in 1941, the Flying Tigers’ first combat over Kunming in China, and the Battle of the Salween Gorge.
Overall, I would recommend this game to any fans that enjoy playing in the WWII era and gamers that like to fly airplanes and engage in dogfights. This game is already ahead of what we see from most Early Access games in terms of progress, it looks pretty well done, and I can't wait to see when multiplayer starts filling up!

I don't really understand why there are a lot of negative reviews about this game. Aside from the slow progression, and pay-to-wins with tanks, (Or just people in general who have put more time into the game and are now unstoppable with their tanks and crudd) I quite honestly enjoy this game. Heck, I will go out on a limb and even say this game is better than Call of Duty: World at War! *Braces for angry mob*
So now, more about the game itself. You have 3 characters that you start out with, each representing the "factions." You got an American, a Russian, and a German. You can select which to play as, then go into battle. You got silver coins, and gold coins, either of which to use to buy things like guns, upgrades, and vehicles, things like that. (You can also select to "auto refill" ammo and the like, so it takes a little coin out to automatically refill things) Though keep in mind you have to unlock practically everything.
As you progress, there are certain careers you can choose from. You automatically start out as an infantryman....but you can later select tank crewman, plane pilot, and paratrooper. (Probably not actual names, but you get the idea) Though once you select one, keep in mind if you ever want to go back, it costs coins. (All "coins" and such are in game, so it's all still free, don't worry!) I had chosen to be a tank person once....but you start out with a tank that only has machine guns, and work your way from there. I just couldn't do it anymore. It was taking forever, and I wasn't that good with it to even progress to eventually unlocking the cannon, so I said "screw it" and went back to infantryman. Of which is probably the best to play as. You can still have vehicles to choose whether or not to spawn with....but no tanks or anything special like that.
All in all, a very great and fun game. I highly recommend getting this if you're looking for a shooter that is not only fun and takes place in World War II......BUT IT'S FREE!!!!! What do you got to lose??

Not a game you want to just throw your troops at the enemy, You need to think, addapt and cooperate to win.
It features a good amount of different countries to fight with and against, devided in Blue and Red, blue being NATO or those allied with it in some way and Red being Warsaw Pact with those that would Ally with them, China, North korea ...
each countries troops have similarties to each other and also big differences, in what they can use as material for example. for example West Germany has Leopard2A5 and the French have the Leclerc.
the interesting part about this game, for me, is that you make a 'deck' of troops (think like making a deck in a card game)
before you enter a battle, in the battle you have a certain amount of points that you can spend to 'place' these troops on the battlefield or later during the battle, call them in as reinforcements. Each troop has a certain amount of points cost, for example: early tanks that are not that good will be cheaper than the best of the line and last produced tanks.
You also have a fixed amount of troops you have to your disposal,for example you can only call in 12 leopards2a1. so using them wisely and being carefull when and where to use them makes a difference. Not only in the fact taht you have a limited amount of troops usually the games goal is to destroy a certain amount of 'points' of the enemy team. for example destroy 1000 points of enemy troops to win. so destryoing a tank that costs the enemy 180 points is great, compared to only a tank of 20 points. vice versa the lose is also worse if it's a good, expensive tank.
You can have all sorts of troops in the game. ranging from infantry and tanks, to airplanes, ships and logistical units, which is to say that logistical units are a very important part of the game. you will need to ressuply your troops with ammo, fuel and repairs. Although this seems like a hassle, it's actually done in an easy, straightforward way, that yet keeps the tactical and strategical importance of logistics inside the game.
there's a lot more to be said about this game. Id say go watch a let's play to get a better understanding of it, it's easy yet has depth to it.

Oh boy. Where can I start with this one.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a small Adventure game based on two brothers, who after losing their mother, must go on a quest to retrieve something to help their sick father. A usually simple premise.
However, the gameplay is unique in that it's co-op... with yourself. You control both brothers; with a controller, the analog sticks and triggers are dedicated to each brother, while if playing via keyboard, the WASD keys control one and the arrow keys control the other. There is very much a sense of trying to pat your head and rub your stomach at the same time, using these controls. At first, while travelling the world is relatively easy, you may struggle but soon you get used to it.
The world itself is beautiful to wander around. It looks like an oil painting come to life, with many inhabitants and objects available to interact with in both humerous and very moving ways. They breathe a certain kind of life in this game that only few games actually achieve. The landscapes become more and more epic as you progress. One certain area (and how you manoeuvre this area) left my mouth agape for it's entirety. You'll know which one this is.
Although it starts out almost child-like, the themes become very dark, quite quickly. You'll stumble across some helpless individuals, which require assistance. The story-telling of these, even though the dialogue is not a known language, can be an emotional experience.
And emotions run very high in this game. I completed this in one 3 hour setting (recommended), and 3 days later, it is still sitting with me. Towards the end, you might even find it hard to continue due to it's emotionally draining circumstances.
Definitely one of the best Indie games I've played.

Glittermitten Grove is a game that doesn't really look like anything special on the surface, but when you dig down deeper it really opens up. The village-building mechanics are simple but fun, and the mechanics of having to balance structures on your fairy trees to make sure they don't snap from the weight or making sure you don't plant trees that block the light of other trees make things interesting. It starts out easy, but once you hit your first winter you can tell that the game's looks can be deceiving. The interface for planting trees can sometimes be annoying, though, and the game doesn't give you much room to go anywhere but down, leading to a situation where eventually your entire area will be scorched earth with trees hanging by threads after the ashes of fireworks burn away the ground. It looks a little expensive for what it is, but give it some time and Glittermitten Grove might really surprise you.

Sim Players are passionate when it comes to driving, flying or even riding the vehicles that have either thrilled and amazed us during our childhood even still do today which is why we take time out to write great reviews .. so I’d just like to add something to that ……
It’s always a shame to read about the disappointments that a fellow Sim Player has experienced instead of reading about their delights as they have taken the controls of their favourite consist and proudly taken passengers or goods from their chosen station, port or yard and delivered them on time having faced realistic challenges of schedules, other transport or sometimes signal failures and adverse weather conditions - that inner sense of achievement (and self-pride) is all we really seek - Yes they may be after all only simulations of real modes of transport –BUT…. be it an incredible landing of a fully laden 300 ton Boeing 747-400 on a real time flight from Singapore to Heathrow - Microsoft Flight Simulator perhaps -  where you take care of the Jumbo's flight deck and using the array of true to life switches, levers and dials as you descend gently down to terra firma – EGLL runway 21 to be exact to the [imagined] sounds of cheers and applause of your satisfied passengers and crew. Or that inner voice that says 'yees!' when we finally arrive at the depot and park up our Flexi-Bus for the day OMSI 2– its late, the sun has set, both outside our windows (if we care to look!) and within the Sim… but we don’t care.. We’ve driven with diligence and skill, we’ve hit n hurt no one and managed to pick up and drop off everyone without a hitch… that’s what matters.. That’s why we play these Simulators –
That’s what Sims do for us! - They fulfil our innermost desire to be a part of something that we admire, to take control of the very vehicles that we venerate and are in awe of – Hours of our lives are spent recreating the paths taken by Road, Rail, Air and Sea in order that we may share the experience in some intangible way of that of the Driver, Pilot, Captain, Fireman, Soldier and Doctor? within us all – all this achieved speedily at the flick of a mouse button and without the arduous years of universities, specialist training and professional advice and preparation, we will not suffer any loss of limb if we make mistakes as we learn the art of take-off and landing, nor will we face litigation and inevitable imprisonment from the families of the loved ones that we lost at sea due to our lack of experience of sailing cruise ships, or even suffer from docked wages from South West Trains for continued late arrivals at London Victoria… Friends our desire and task is a simple one … to Simulate through our chosen modes … without the Wind, Rain, Ice, Snow or Insurance Costs ever affecting or view of our chosen destination -
To Dream the Impossible is what drives the human spirit – But to deny someone of that dream is to deny them of the very lust for life ….. So keep dreaming keep ‘Simming’ and whether it’s by Air, Sea or Land may your journeys be filled with fun, passion and excitement –

Dropzone:
~~~~~~~~

This is the 22nd century and the combat arenas are brutal and explosive. These battles are fought with hi-tech rigs (Mechs). Can you find the right combination of rigs to take down your opponents and the Kavash (Aliens) in these arenas? But more importantly, do you dare to fight in the Dropzone?
Dropzone is an Action / Strategy/ MOBA game where you control three rigs in a battle, choosing to play against an online opponent, an AI opponent, or 2 versus 2. The aim is to upload more cores in the uplink than your opponent in order to win. There is a third mode where you have to eliminate waves of aliens and defend a reactor, which is located in the middle of the arena.
Before you begin, make sure to play all three available tutorials; they will give you a very good understanding of how to fight, and also how to develop and build more efficient rigs. There are four types of rigs to choose from: Gunners (offensive units that inflict heavy damage), Tanks (your frontline units as they have better armour and very good weapons), Mechanics (great units to have with you as they can repair other rigs and also fight), Summoners (the weakest units but they have unusual abilities, one of which is to turn an enemy unit against its own team for a short time). Now it’s time to choose your three units; if you’re not quite sure how they will work together in the arena, you can test them in the practice arena against the Alien.
A match goes for fifteen minutes and so far I have played in a couple of different arenas. The map features one uplink (which is in the middle of the arena), four vision points, several Alien hives and two Alien bosses. The hive will have a large number of Aliens to eliminate. Each hive will regenerate itself three times. The first time you destroy a hive, one core will appear next to it; the second time two cores and the third time three cores. Pick them up and go to the uplink to score a point. You will need to capture the vision points to see the map from that corner (lift the fog of war) and if you manage to capture all of them, you will get an additional point, which is very handy especially if you are locked on the same number of points (cores uploaded). If you fancy a fight with one or two of these big Alien bosses and win, an electrical icon will appear which will give you extra damage points for a short time when you pick it up. To return to the uplink, you can carry only one core per rig.  It will take about twenty seconds to upload the core and the unit will not be able to defend itself during this process. Make sure that you have two other Mechs close by to protect the unit.  When one of your units is destroyed, it will take thirty seconds to respawn on your starting point.
Each rig has specific gears which you can change before starting a game. The gears have numbers on them, which means that your unit needs to reach a certain level of experience during the battle to be able to use it. You might have a weapon with the number three on it, which means that your unit needs to level up three times to use it. How do you do that, you might ask? Very simple - each time you kill an Alien you receive an experience point, which will go towards a gauge; when the gauge is full you can level up one of your three units. The funny part is that the next gauge will need more experience points in order to be filled, and so on and so forth. Imperatibe to choose the right gears before battling.
If you are victorious at the end of the round, you will receive Jovians (game currency), crates and even blueprints if one of your rigs levels up. You can buy additional crates with your jovians and when you open them, you’ll receive additional gears.
Dropzone has good graphics and runs very well for an early access game. The controls are very responsive but it will take you a while to get use to them.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Plenty of gears to choose for your rigs
-	Four difficulty levels against the AI
-	Fun and challenging game
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~

-	Needs more arenas (layout)
-	Difficult to find an online game
It will take some time to learn this game and to set your rigs up properly for your style of fighting.
7/10

This is difficult. I enjoyed my time with Glittermitten Grove, but I can't honestly recommend it. You may have played the spiritual predecessor, and come in with some expectations. Unfortunately, this game has issues.
Unlike the first game, which followed a single character over a long period of time and many adventures, this game lacks a throughline (or really any characters at all). Other than the advisor from your starting town, and a long-running reference joke about Korn, there is nothing connecting the disparate parts of the game to each other. Each diversion is a well-executed miniature game, but lacks substance, and are completely interchangeable with each other. Their sense of humor made me laugh at times, but it's all Family-Guy-style reference comedy. The situations, while absurd, aren't particularly clever, don't have any underlying meaning, and are essentially fluffy time-wasters.
Spoilers ahead:
TXT World is the game. That's it. The rest are just time-gates you need to sit through before being allowed to progress. Half of them, you don't even need to win at to get the item you need--you'll be awarded with the prize and kicked out win or lose.
TXT World itself is only a middling ZZT-clone. It has some clever ideas and more than a few funny gags, but it never develops much, and has less than 20 rooms. The mechanics of TXT World are designed to annoy, and as the game ended, all I could think is, "Is that it?" The game opens up for the player once you leave Glittermitten Grove, and I kept hoping it would continue to unfold. All I found though, were WarioWare-style diversions and throw-away reference jokes.
This game really opens up into something entirely different after a few hours of play. It's almost like an entirely different game is buried inside this game.

In this moba/rts mixture you have the control over three pilots, each of them has their personal rig (mechwarrior) with unique skills based upon their class.
At the moment there are four different classes (tanks, summoners, mechanics, gunners) and one more is coming soon. Each class has different pilots with their own rigs that differ visually from one another. Classes differ in shape, pilots/rigs in color and textures and changing gearparts will make them look different aswell. So visually its very well made and interesting to watch.
You play in a 15 minutes timeframe in 1vs1 and 2vs2 modes. each player has 3 rigs so in a 2v2 its gonna be 6 vs 6 rigs.
Maps ain't got no lanes. All you gotta do is farming hives and the monsters that spawn out of them (pretty much similar to zergs from starcraft) and collect cores that will appear when they're destroyed. These cores need to be uploaded in the center of the map by both sides, so here's where the combat is happening most of the time. Fighting and interrupting each other during uploads.
Each game has three more options to collect points. Besides 1 core out of a hive gives you 1 point, you can take control over all 4 vision points, kill 100 kavash (the units that spawn out of hives) as first, kill 9 alpha kavash or 3 bosses. So there's a lot to control and a lot to think about when it comes to strategy and gameplay.
Each map has 2 bosses, each of them is on top and bottom of the map that wil grant the player a damage buff by killing it for a short time. Every time you destroy a hive, the next time it will be spawning as a tier 2 hive and 3 and so on. then it comes to the alpha kavash spawn that are minibosses coming out of hives, so it gets difficult with every minute of the game.
The similarity to league of legends or heroes of the storm is noticable, especially with the levelsystem. By killing hives you gain experience and level up. everytime y ou level up you can decide which pilot gets to the next level, so depending on the abilities/gearparts you chose before the match that are reliable on a specific level you have to think about which one to level up first or what level u need on which pilot to be efficient enough to win the game.
So its not about leveling up your abilities to make them stronger, you unlock your abilities by gaining the level it needs to use them, and then they're scaling in dps most of the time.
There's already a leaderboard up in this game with hidden points. So the more u win you raise in your personal rank. Ranked queue is currently still in working progress, which will be the new matchmaking. Until then you have to use "quick play".
A third mode is "infestation" where you defend the center of a map against spawning kavash that are coming at you. So get together with 3 friends or fill up with some AI bots and kill.
More gamemodes are in developement.
Positive:
+ No 45ish minutes to spend in a single match like it is in league of legends
+ no need to carry in a team since its 1v1 with 3 mechwarriors / Rigs at a time
+ a huge variety of gear, classes and pilots/rigs where everything but the passives are visually recognizeable
+ a lot of different setups to tryout and currently nothings really that OP, matches are very close if each player got skill
Negative:
- the fact that you got to control 3 pilots at once will make the learning curve very long
- sometimes you have to wait a few more minutes before finding an opponent which could be the same over and over again (solution: switch regions between north america, europe and oceania in options / takes about 5seconds)
- losing in this game can be very frustrating
So this game costs 20€ and will be free to play after early access. I'd say its absolutely worth it and maybe think about getting the commander edition that gives you all pilots and gearparts that exist and will ever be released. Because ingame you level up your pilots to unlock abilities and receive coins to purchase new pilots in an ingame shop.

Review: America's Army: Proving Grounds for the PC.
America's Army: Proving Grounds is the cautiously-anticipated sequel from some unknown, but is it any good?
It's tough to be a third party games publisher these days, and games like America's Army: Proving Grounds are a good example of why.
You already know what to expect from America's Army: Proving Grounds after the last game in the series, and the United States Army doesn't disappoint. There's some new stuff, some irratiting bugs have been ironed out, and a new storyline bolted on to make everything look welcoming for newcomers.
America's Army: Proving Grounds tries to seperate itself from the pack with interesting features. The online support for multiplayer is mostly robust, but some infrequent lag mars an otherwise competent experience. You'll find your experience of the online will closely match the quality of your internet connection, and how well the flaky matchmaking system connects you to nearby players. Enemy AI is for training only, but come on, who plays solo these days? Multiplayer is a breeze to get going, and playing against another human is always a far sight more challenging than your PC could ever be.
Co-op features heavily in the game, but it's a shame there's no support for 40 players at once on the same couch.
The graphics are a mixed bag. Some things look really nice and the frame rate is a solid 15 frames per second.
While the exteriors are nicely presented the characters already look a bit dated and fall short of the sublime photorealism we were promised by Unknown.
The 3D world of America's Army: Proving Grounds comes to life in a realistic way, which is nice if you're a fan of the genre.The visuals represent the objects they represent well.
Performance is best on a ATI system, and you'll need at least a 5500 card to be able to run the game at the now-standard 1366 by 780 resolution with full AA and trilinear mimap interpolation. Stability issues were sometimes a problem. It's a shame you can still see some UI compromises that were made for the console ports of this game.
America's Army: Proving Grounds just doesn't come together in the end, and will leave FPS afficianados wanting more.

Wargame: Red Dragon takes the overall franchise to its highest point with the addition of sea units and battles, as well as amphibious units and an expanded role for air and artillery units. Unfortunately, while the sea action side of things is one of the main things originally billed as a major draw, the actual sea dynamics are quite quirky and not especially groundbreaking or terribly well done. While the ground and air units seem to be fairly well created and designed, the sea units are quite lackluster-a fact shown out in the multiplayer where a majority of maps often used don't utilize the sea portion at all.
Additionally, the single-player tends to be typical of what you'd come to expect from a Eugen game. It's scripted and challenging, but not necessarily great by any means. The AI follows the same patterns and the "difficulty" level for the campaigns is more controlled by the "starting battle units" or "morale" than by actual strategy and capability. What the single-player turns into is more of a "How well can I micromanage my units without losing too many points?" than an actual strategy situation.
The multiplayer is where this game gets its strength. The customizability of the decks is great, the different perks are awesome, and Eugen is constantly adding, tweaking, and balancing units for the multiplayer (at the expense of any additions to single player). Not until the fix the artillery in this game. If you play redfor all you need is 1 - 3 players (depending on game size) to roll a support deck and you win. REDFOR artillery is about 30x as lethal as BLUFOR artillery. Mostly because of rockets, but even their tubed artillery is better. They don't even need to try and in most games can arty random cap points to destroy your command vehicle and usually get in 1-2 hits. Pretty dumb.
Edit: Have continued to play this game for months in the hopes it will get better and still wish I could get my money back. The bottom line is that this is very much a game. if you play it hoping to get some kind of wargame simulation out of it you're absolutely wasting your money. The units in most cases are accurate to real life (with exceptions to range for gameplay purposes) but there are some glaring inaccuracies and gameplay balance issues that kind of ruin the game in my opinion.
1) The game in GENERAL revolves around a "quality" vs "quantity" concept. For example, if you're NATO you can expect to get a few REALLY good super units but very low quantity. If you're pact, you can expect to get some good units and a few super units but with exceptionally more availability. From a "gameplay" perspective this might make sense but the reality is it scews a lot of things in favor of pact. Bottom line is if you can kill a few of the NATO "super" units you're almost guaranteed a win unless you're just an idiot. This also ties into the "balance vs realism" that I post below because the reality is the USSR could field more infantry and artillery than NATO but not more helicopters, fixed wing or tanks. However in this game they can.... by a lot.
2) Balance vs realism. Bottom line this is not a realistic game. There are a few combos that are near unbeatable in certain situations. For example, NATO patriot missle can snipe red air from miles with little risk even to SEAD. On the other side, russian spetsnatz + VDV combo in a forest is unbeatable by land units. Only chance to win vs that is bombs/napalm/artillery. There are no NATO infantry or vehicles that can defeat that combo unless you want to lose at a roughly 6 to 1 ratio. Combine that with the fact that US basically does not have infantry and you have a very "gimmicky" game. I say that the US basically does not have infantry because for the sake of "balance" their stats are so horrible that they're actually useless in most cases. The only reason to use US infantry is for their bradley which is barely decent vehicle. The infantry themselves are very close to useless. Combine that with the fact that Delta Force is also the worst SF unit in the game and can kill almost nothing then you will start to see what i mean.
Potential: The game has a lot of potential but there are some glaring flaws that still ruin it for a lot of people like myself. Artillery is still a game ruiner, not just a game changer. In low point games it's not really an issue (because no one can afford it). But anything from 3v3 up with a decent amount of points and you can expect to get shelled all game. This is made particularly worse by "Smerching" which i reference in my earlier version of my post. This is basically when a player brings multiple cards of rocket artillery and picks a spot on the map where he believes enemy units are and simply hits fire and wipes everything out. This can be gamebreaking particularly early on since the maps use a lot of choke points so you HAVE to go certain ways to get to the front. This makes sniping in early games easy and can essentially end what should be a 40 minute game in the first 40 seconds.
Bottom line: Eugen has a lot of work to do with this game before it deserves anyone elses money.

Zombie Driver is a top-down racing & shooting game in a modern setting with zombie invasion. You mostly get missions to either rescue someone, destroy or deliver something, while shooting or ramming tons of zombies on the way.
The story is quite simple, as it is with most zombie influenced games. The devs tried to implement some story "twists" but they are too obvious, so that it is quite clear how the game gonna end right early in the beginning. The story is told by mission descriptions that you receive and some minor dialogs with survivors. The gameplay is quite simple - select a car fitting the missions, fulfill the objectives and try to get secondary objective for some extra cash. The more zombies you destroy on the way, the more bonus cash you will get. Besides the story mode the game offers some survival and tournaments against KI.
Playing this game casually I did not encounter any serious challange, neither in story mode nor in tournament or survival. It is quite easy to finish the game in short time aswell win every race in tournament mode and reach golden medals in survival. The combat in Zombie Driver is consisting of mostly holding two butons down - firing your weapon and driving forward, well, with steering left and right from time to time. The weapons have limited ammo but once you upgrade them, it becomes really easy to finish the objectives on almost any car.
The graphics are nothing special, but do fit the game style. There are not many details to look at, mostly you just watch a red/green mass of squashed zombies. The interface is simplistic aswell, just showing you the most needed information to fulfill your mission.
Progress is fairly quick and simple in this game. Since it does not take long to finish the game, you wont get bored to also enjoy some tournaments or try yourself in the survival. Tournament mode receives some extra points for having different race types (destruction, race, time survival, etc.). This delivers a nice change to the game.
The weapon sound and music fit the game, are nothing special though. It is nice that they voice the mission description and dialogs, give a bit better immersion in the game. The world does feel apocalyptic especialy in later stages of the game, but it clearly does not let you dive too deep in the city of Zombie Driver.
Zombie Driver can be considered a casual top-down zombie shooter, even if you race in a car instead of running. You will get fairly quick through the story and other modes, so even though the game is nothing special, you most like wont get bored in the short time invested.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

TL;DR DOWN BELOW
I find this game fun. And that is what's important; it is fun. Mowing down countless zombies for minutes on end is a great way to pass the time, especially with the game's straightforward run over and shoot mechanics. While other games such as Civ V or Stardew may eat your time away just as much (or perhaps more), those games need the player to think rather heavily, To some of us, having to use our heads can be a deterent into enjoying something. This is where Zombie Driver shines, it is a game of pure, mind numbing fun.
That being said, its base price tag of $8-10~ isn't really justified, considering that I can spend  just as much for other titles that have more interesting gameplay mechanics, better writing, and better visuals while being capable of maintaining the same amount of enjoyment I can get from Zombie Driver. The game's current price is a bit too much for me, it feels like a $5 game even with the "Complete Edition" (which only adds in two maps for its "Slaughter" mode, a racing game mode, and some really lackluster car customization additions).
Zombie Driver's most glaring issues are its lack of a free roam mode, shallow car customization (both gameplay upgrades and aesthetic options), and while it isnt really the focus of the game, -its writing. I really wish this game had free roam. Its Slaughter mode is kind of there but it's not enough as it limits you with getting a high score until your car is destroyed. This affects its replayability but not so much that I would turn my head away from this game. As the game progresses, the zombies get more and more harder to kill and thus an upgrade system was added but all the upgrades and car options seem so pointless and feels like padding when I ended up only using the Auroch truck with full upgrades due to its high health bar and stable handling. With the latter being almost crucial with all the cramped corners in the sub-urban areas. I tried my best in paying attention to the storyline but it was so generic and badly written that I ended up skipping dialogue to just go on ahead and play.
I recommend this game. past that whole paragraph I just wrote, I still think the game is nice. But only if it's on sale. (I got its complete edition for more or less a dollar).
TL;DR :
Zombie Driver is fun at its purest form. it just has a price tag that you'd be better off spending on something more justified for $10. That, and its lacking car customization, story, and no free-roam. But don't let that stop you from getting it with even the smallest of price reductions.

While Starbreeze has enjoyed acclaim from it's previous releases, the studio hasn't exactly built it's reputation on creating whimsical worlds with moving narratives. Both Chronicles of Riddick and The Darkness gave their players dark and gritty worlds to explore and some unique gameplay twists to hook players. With such a pedigree Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons stands out as being wholly against type. It's the video game equivalent of Martin Scorsese’s Hugo, stepping away from subject matter reserved for mature audiences to deliver a memorable experience that can be enjoyed by audiences both young and old. While seemingly stepping out of the comfort zone established by their track record, Brothers stands out as one of 2013's best, and most surprising, releases.

While the setting and tone of Brothers is a departure from Starbreeze's previous titles, they have maintained their fine tradition of offering refreshing gameplay mechanics. Each brother's ability to move is mapped to a joystick and each trigger acts as an interaction button for the corresponding brother. While some games have you changing between multiple characters to solve puzzles, Brothers allows you to control both characters simultaneously reducing the tedium of having to switch between characters or deliver commands to AI companions. Initially, this control setup may seem a bit clumsy but after taking a few moments to acclimate yourself to the setup it becomes natural. The brothers will face numerous challenges and all of them can be overcome with a bit of teamwork. Having the older, stronger brother boost his young sibling up to high ledges so that he can drop a rope is a small example in a long list of ways in which the boys can join forces to overcome the obstacles in their way. Starbreeze deserves high praise for finding so many unique ways to test players and make the most of the brother's teamwork. This is a major reason that A Tale of Two Sons succeeds. Throughout the three hour game, players will shift the brother's weight to steer a glider, use a rope that tethers the boys together to swing to far away ledges, distract a pesky dog with one brother so that the other brother can pass through an area safely and so on. In spite of how many different challenges players will face, it's not difficult to figure out what to do next. Unfortunately, this reprieve from frustration is complicated by a nasty side effect: Brothers is way too easy. Most players will feel completely untested by the puzzles and proceed almost entirely unopposed.

While it's ease means most players may not recall any of the specific challenges that make up Brother's campaign after completing it, they will almost undoubtedly remember the game's tone and narrative. The plot is simple, the boy's father falls ill and after taking him to the town doctor they are told to go in search of a cure. This is a terrible blow to the brothers since they have already lost their mother after she drowned; the younger brother in particular is scarred by her loss as he witnessed her struggle before she succumbed to the depths. Their willingness to undertake such a perilous journey is indicative how important it is to them not to loose anyone else with grief and loss becoming a central theme. While the plot is simple, it benefits from the fact that it's telling forgoes the use of dialogue. The characters speak in a made up unsubtitled language allowing players to hone in on the their inflections and gestures. This emphasis on feeling rather than exposition allows the events to soak in without being burdened by anything superfluous or disruptive to the experience. Further enriching the experience is the fact that dozens of objects and people can be interacted with that are wholly non-essential to progressing in the game and each brother interacts with these people or objects differently. The younger brother comes off as quite ornery and mischievous while his big brother is a well behaved and serious. Discovering these traits instead of having them force fed to players is far more rewarding.

Rounding out Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons as more of an experience than simply a game is it's stunning art direction and score. The fantasy world in A Tale of Two Sons is rendered in bright colors and it's texture work has an almost hand-painted quality. The home of the title characters is on the coast, near a sleepy village. This humble setting gradually gives way to more wondrous settings with picturesque mountain ranges, crystal clear bodies of water and vertigo inducing cliff sides. The studio relishes the game's aesthetics by placing benches around the world that the boys can sit on, allowing the camera to zoom in and create a post card worthy view of the game world. The colorful Disney-esque landscapes do eventually give way to some areas that have darker motifs adding a bit of gravity to the boys' trek as well as giving the world a story of it's own. While the environments are fantastic but the boys can appear a bit bland with their cartoon character skin textures and average NPC villager outerwear.

The soundtrack is haunting and nuanced, giving the proceedings a bit of dramatic flair without being too intrusive or overbearing. The somber flutes, strings and chanting that make up the bulk of what tickles player's ear drums has a unique sonic signature that adds a layer of personality to a game that, due to it's fantasy setting, has some derivative subject matter.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons may very well be this generation's Ico. It's seems that the Playstation 2's companion based cult classic was an inspiration for Starbreeze's game. Emphasizing emotion over raw exposition and dialogue, A Tale of Two Sons carves a space in players memories to reside long term. The plethora of puzzles prevents players from feeling burdened by tedious and stale routines and some darker moments later in the game remind players of the seriousness of their quest lest they get lost in the game's stunning, fantasy world. Were it more challenging, Brothers could have provided an almost flawless experience. While the gameplay may not give you a sense of accomplishment, the narrative payoff is significant enough to make A Tale of Two Sons a mandatory buy for any serious gamer.

This game is freakin' amazing. The mountain has about a hundred different lines, and you unlock even more as you play. And yes, this game is free. The only paid elements are cosmetics, and the free cosmetics do not scream "I am new and lame" like they do in most free to play games. It's also really well optimized. The only problem I've found so far is that a lot of the multiplayer servers have a pretty high ping, but it hasn't been enough to really even frustrate me.
SNOW really reminded me of the days when I played Tony Hawk's Pro Skater as a kid, and the lines you can follow in SNOW are really reminiscient of that series of game. In terms of gameplay mechanics, the worst part are the rails, which are really hard to grind on, but it's not a big issue for two reasons. One, even if you land it perfectly, you don't miss out on much. Even perfect rail grinds aren't amazing. And two, if you miss the rail, it's funny watching the engine try to decide if you're wallriding on the side of the rail or not.
So play this game! There's literally no risk! Give it a try and get hooked.

I have never written a review for a game up and till now, so this is telling in and of its self. I refuse to recommend this game on several reasons that I will list in a quick and consise manner.
The Goods:
-Interesting progression system that initially had me wanting more and more.
-Accurate WW2 Shooter
-Decent Maps
-Tons of side progressions for weapons, unsure about vehicles though as I never bought one
The Bads:
-Long Queue. Sometimes you can get into a game within 3-4 minutes. Relatively long in modern standards, but not bad. I would estimate that my average was around 7 minutes though, and my longest was an excruciating 14 minutes.
-Matchmaking will pit you against lop-sided teams, and my FAVORITE*sarcasm*, put you in a match that literally has 2 seconds left...after wating 5 minutes in queue. Joy
The Uglys:
-Some of the community is toxic. Literally. I can't even put some of the things I have read in "Support Chat" here.
-Hackers. I have seen games plagued with hackers and this one takes the cake.
All and all, a waste of my time and a waste of yours. I love the idea of "MMOFPS"(it really isn't one.) set in WW2, unfortunately this isn't the answer to that dream. I beg you, please do not waste your time like I have.
OH! A final note, they have the audacity to ask you to give a favorable review for this game in Steam. PFFT!
