Aside from the many bad reviews involving poor customer service and wrongful banning, H&G has another reason to kind of be on the fence about starting. It's not so much pay to win, it's pay to break even. This game is not for the casual gamer. It is in fact extremely difficult to start out, as the way matchmaking is. There are alot of maps where infantry takes on large amounts of tank class and snipers. This could be coincidence and trust me when I say I am no expert at this game nor will I ever be. There's a large group of elite players in this game that have it down to a science, and they already don't like you because of your score. As far as a massive shooter like this, you better have a bit of money to spend right off the bat to advance your ribbons till you unlock better weapons and utilities. If you want a fair game right off the bat, play Planetside 2 instead.
Also note: This is an "early access review" on a game that has been in beta for almost 3 years. It still has many changes to go through.

In this review, I will try to do things a bit different. Since there are hundreds of reviewers praising and glorifying this game, if you're STILL not convinced by their almost-religious following, I'll give a glimpse of how a below-average player would play this incredible game just up until the first death. I'd do three, but honestly, this game is so epic, I'd just roll over the word limit in my second go.
I start my journey in a well lit mine, with a few pots down below. Careful not to fall down and break my neck, I descend to the pots. I pick one of them up and slam it to the wall with all my might. Spiders hiding in pots, man, gotta be careful. The first pot was empty. The second pot is also slammed, containing an extremely small gold nugget. A hundred bucks, score! Even though a hundred bucks is basically a dollar at a Ford dealership, you gotta start somewhere! I then find an arrow trap right in front of me a tile below. Arrow traps are nasty things - they shoot a bolt at the first thing that moves in front of it. I would be super careful around it, but I see there's a yellow utility box right in front of it! Yay, I can jump in front of the trap and the box will stop the arrow!
I have never been so wrong in my life.
Pierced through my stomach, I roll on the ground, dizzy from the pain and the bloodloss. From 4 hearts to 2 in a second, yipee... Hey, at least the yellow box broke and threw some grapling rope out! Well, you get some, you lose some. Near the trap I find a ladder with a blue sapphire at the top. I hastily climb the brown ladder, snatch the sapphire and see a pushable stone blocking my path. I can either push the rock down the crevice or throw a bomb, eliminating any need to push whatsoever. But hey, what kind of an idiot would waste a perfectly good bomb! I start pushing the block, pushing, pushing until I see a bat just behind the block. There is only a litte shove left to push the block down. I can either finish pushing the block and hope to whip the bat fast enough for me not to get damaged, OR just throw a bomb, destroying both the block and the bat. But bombs are valuable, man. So, I push the block down, only to see my face mutilated by the bat's claws. I immediately whip the bat, abolishing it into tiny blood circles. Speaking of blood, I only have one heart left. Any hit from anything will kill me. Seeing as a yet another pushable stone blocks my path I decide to play it safe and carefully shove it little by little in hopes of not disturbing the local vampire, I mean, bat population. I push the block all the way through and jump down a little hole to see myself surrounded by two least dangerous static enemies in the game. A spider hanging on the ceiling in my left and an arrow trap down below on my right.
Since going right will only throw me in front of an unpassable wall, I decide to go left. The spider hangs on the ceiling and drops down whenever an unlucky spelunker like me passes by. It would kill me instantly, since I have only one life. Obviously, I could try to RUN past the spider, but if I am too sluggish, I drop dead from the spider bite. Yea, better not risk it, better to jump slightly and whip the spider dead. Remember, good spelunkers are always careful. Careful, careful, careful. Careful, as touching the spider would also kill me, I slightly jump in front of it and whip. My whip was an inch too short.
Well, gotta climb a few blocks and try again! I jump up them in haste, trying to get revenge on the arachnid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Time for round 2, spider. I jump up, slightly more now, whip and...
...still too short. Damn, gotta get up again. I start jumping up the blocks two at a time now, I REALLY want to kill the spider this time.
Except that I jumped too high on the last block, fell down the pit to my right, got shot in the head by an arrow trap and was lying down in a pool of blood, dead, with an arrow in my eye.
My incredibly stupid adventure, full of mistakes in my life took me about fourty seconds, but was the most fun I had in a while. I really laughed out loud while playing and writing this review (which I actually did at the same time) for my idiotic mistakes and quickly pressed the "Play again" button.
9/10.
Recommended to buy.

I will be totally honest here. In my opinion this simulator needs a third thumbs rating. One that is somewhere between thumbs up and down. I shall explain why.
Firstly if you get the base game then you are not getting a full game. It will have scenarios, some tracks, locos and stock. Dovetail have always made their money from the DLC's they bring out for TS. When not on sale I find the base game and its various add ons as a bit on the pricey side. My advice is wait for a sale (as seems to happen a lot with TS).  Also read up on the various DLC's and loco add ons. You will find they are a mixed bag so research the ones you may like and then get them in a sale. Do these things and then you will end up with a half decent train sim. The game is not perfect though and is still plagued by various bugs and odd glitches. I am however happy with the level of detail put into the trains and tracks. One of them I know very well and can confirm the route is a pretty good re-creation of the real thing.
Sadly there are not many good (and far from perfect) train sims out there. TS 2015 is an expensive option if you want all the DLC's. There are older trains sims out there that had a community creating content for them but although most were free the problem was with bugs and not having the various dependecies that were required to run them.
At least so far TS has always given the players a free upgrade of the base game when new versions are released. Who knows, maybe they will finally get it right in a future version.
The game itself is a fairly relaxing way to past the time and offers various scenarios of varying difficulty. You can also choose to free roam a track if you feel like taking a no pressure ride in your favourite loco. Sounds are a bit hit and miss. Sometimes they work well, sometimes not so well.
For anyone wanting to drive a train, there is nothing better out there.  This is a fantastic simulator game, and highly recommend it.

Recieved the game from GeForce Experience Giveaway. So far I am extremely impressed, game client and UI are clean, intuitive and excellent. Tutorial was amazing, very easy to watch other players play live games, lots of content it seems. There is a ton of depth in customizing pilots, weapons and gear. Think Moba RTS; LoL or DotA but you control 3 characters of your choice, the twist in dropzone is that not only do you choose your 3 pilots, you explicitly customize both which skills and weapons each character gets as they progress from lvl 1 -> Endgame in each "match". 1 2 3 to choose which player, 4 to select all (or drag and select like standard RTS) while each character has "qwert" type skills. Games are very quick 10-15, and enjoyable seeming to take a lot of good features from other existing games and genres. There is room for improvement and I'd love to see more pilots, but honestly, dropzone has blown me away.
Had a starcraft-type feel about it, combined with other fun games I've played over the years.

I really like this game! ive had alot of fun playing it with friends. lots of customization, and overall good maps!
you can play 3v3, or 1v1. in 1v1 you face off against eachother, each controlling 3 rigs. and in 3v3, your on a team where each player controlls 1. i really like both, and 1v1 is a great, and while its difficult to controll 3 rigs at once, and keep them all doing seperate things, the payoff is great, for 1v1 can deliver some of the most intense fights immaginable, and quite often as well! i havn't had as many really close fights with 3v3, but i havn't played it nearly as much, and it can be really fun to work towards a common goal with friends.
(also theres 2v2 where each person controlls 3 rigs.)
the goal is to upload as many cores as possible, while also completing objectives. the team that has the most points at the end of 15 minutes wins!
Also, customization!
Its awesome.
but hard.
but  still awesome.
essentially you earn gear from playing rounds, and use this to compile rigs that can be effective in battle when used together. (or effective with a team you and your friends have assembled, or diverse in skills in order to help out better with randomely matched teamates)
Its really fun and ive had a blast customizing my rigs!
Overall its a really well rounded and fun early access game, but there were a few things that just personally bugged me, and i thought i might as well mention.
so, first of all, the maps are Really good and well thought out, exept for juggernaught.
Its not really a BAD map, as much as its an unneventfull one. i will admit that i have grown to not mind it that much overtime, but i just feel like theres a bit of missed pottential with it.
second, the total vision objective is in every match. and i hate it.
essentially the total vision objective is one in which you have to capture four vision towers, and then you are rewarded with 2 points.
in my oppinion its the least fun objective, and i have to deal with it every time. i mean it makes sense, as it gets you to go out and capture towers, but i feel like theres got to be a better way to do that. partially because after total vision is captured, nobody really cares unless they're actually a skilled player, and it tends to take up the first 1 or 2 minutes of a match just fighting over the towers, and in a reletively bland way. this happens especially when your knew to the game and are just figuring out the mechanics. I mean, the towers are placed right in from of you, it makes sense to go for that objective. it sounds pretty easy and like it will quickly get you ahead, but what ive found is that its better to just go for cores, because by the time they get total vision, you already could have uploaded far more cores than they would be rewarded with.
and finally, the game will give you a heart attack with how freaking intense the rounds are.
I mean, this COULD be a possative but, uh yeah.

I am a huge fan of traditional RTS games and the new wave of MOBA games. This is a great mix of both genres. I can't really say this is a 'true-to-form' RTS or MOBA, which is what makes this game so cool. Why try and make a game that is either when the market is over saturated already... Spankypants delivers a new style of game that both RTS and MOBA players will enjoy.
Tips:
- Waste absolutely NO time. Every second some unit should be doing something.
- Split your squad up whenever possible. You won't win sticking together all the time.
- LEARN THE KEYBOARD SHORTCUTS.
- Play a hefty amount of single player before venturing online... You'll get pwned, trust me.
PROS:
- Fastpaced, non-stop gameplay (literally EVERY second counts)
- Easy to pick up and play (but hard to master)
- Unlimited customization for you team and individual rigs
- Already has a pretty large community, so it's easy to start games. I have yet to wait more than 3 minutes.
- Environments, effects and characters are beautiful and detailed
CONS:
- I lose a lot... There are TONS of awesome players.
- I don't have enough time in the day to play more :)
In all seriousness, this game is awesome and for $20-40, depending on which bundle you get, you're getting an amazing game for a low cost. I have bought more expensive games that have offered less than Dropzone does.
Note: My play time is low due to most of my hours logged before Dropzone hit Steam.

The Jig Is Up, and people are either here knowing what they're looking at or a quick google search can lead them into what this game really is about. So I'm not going to play along with the fake review shtick, and review the game for what it actually is.
Frog Fractions 3 (this game) and Frog Fractions 2 (the arg leading up to this game) are both extremely ambitious, and Jim Crawford deserves my money for the effort and love he put into the project alone. So is the game actually fun to play?
Well, Frog Fractions 2 is over. You can read about it here:
I'm not somebody who does ARGs or even keeps up to date on them while they're happening, but looking back now, it's clear that Jim was dedicated and resourceful and ended up creating one of the most in depth ARGs to date. The Eye Sigil ARG even spanned across random games including QWOP and Crypt Of The Necrodancer, and the creators of those games had no idea what they were for when they were asked to put them in and didn't know who was asking (disguised as somebody named the "Sigil Master"). I gotta give mad props to Jim for this.
But how is Frog Fractions 3? Well to be honest, a majority of my playtime I found myself just not having much fun. I think the main problem is the length. Frog Fractions 1 was around 30 minutes, and didnt stay on one focus too long. Frog Fractions 3 revolves around a game called "TXT WORLD!" and lasts around 4-5ish hours, maybe more if you want to dig into all the secrets. There's a lot of good game design jokes in this game, but each one lingers for way too long to the point where it stops being a joke and starts just being bad game design added onto the game. Some are handled better than others, but some last almost the entire 5 hours.
For example, at one point you obtain a sword which you can spin around your character (to clarify, this is a top down ascii game, think old roguelikes) which is cool but also is blocked by walls. Meaning now your character is two spaces big and you constantly have to rotate and fidget with your sword to get past one wide pathways. At first I was laughing at the sheer ridiculousness of it, but when I realized that 3 hours in I was still using the sword it just made me swear at the screen every time I had to navigate mazelike rooms. Even earlier on you discover "Gems", which look like currency so you pick them up. You quickly realize when you gem counter is full you can't pick up any more gems, meaning that now every single coin on the floor is an impassable object. Again, another funny joke, but becomes tedious when you have to deal with it for the rest of the game (luckily this one is not as bad, you can find a secret to increase it to 50 and every time you beat a minigame it resets down to 0). There are tons more including a bridge and autocorrect skates but I won't delve into every single one of these as I'd be here forever.
So if TXT World is 65% of the game, how is the other 35%? Well, pretty standard and what you'd expect from Frog Fractions. The wacky minigames feel like they have way more production value now, and actually feel like they could all be real games somewhere if they didn't just last a short while. I think it's kind of funny that in the end, this is actually an educational game- FF3 has you scouring the internet for information on the Meiji Restoration, sparknotes for all the levels of hell in Dante's Divine Comedy, and old derogatory slang words. I'm glad Jim tried something different with anchoring the game around TXT world and not just making a 5 hour ADD trip, but the minigames where you're not frustrated at a smiling ascii face are the true shiners of this collection.
And how is Glittermitten Grove? Actually, pretty amazing. I think if it wasn't designed just to funnel you into FF3 and actually had a progression into lategame with more to do I'd be playing it more than the "actual game". It has a pretty genius light mechanic that makes it so you have to be careful of how you grow the trees you live in, as taller ones can kill smaller ones. You also need to manage food, but your fairies leaving is pretty penalty free because you can't lose all of them and more crawl back as food is available. But like I said, there's not much to do other than to keep expanding infinitely with your small selection of buildings until you eventually discover the door to FF3.
The ending is pretty climactic and fitting to the build up of the game, but happens kind of abruptly. I guess you know it's coming since there's literally no more rooms in the game to explore.
Anyways, this review is kind of going all over the place, but I guess that's the nature of Frog Fractions. The long and short of it is that I don't think I wasted my money because I'm giving money to an Indie dev who is massively dedicated and passionate, but I also don't feel like I had much fun. I guess buy it if you love the idea? But if you're somebody who doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the developer's intentions and just want a good end product, I think you might not like it.

I don't want to spoil anything here, but be warned that I will spoil that this game is certainly much more than what you see in the screenshots.
My experience with Glittermitten Grove started with an ARG that was for a totally (seemingly) different game.  The eventual discovery of what I believe is the most well-done examples of the genre EVER almost changed my life.
I heavlily implore you to check out the Youtuber NitroRad.  I watched him play this game live when it was first released, and his video of it is still up.  It is probably the only live stream I've ever watched and been totally and completely enamored with for that long.  An 8 hour stream, I was glued to it.  I even went back a few months later to rewatch the ENTIRE thing.
A lot of salty folk like to argue and lament the existence of ARGs especially when they weren't initially "in" on the ploy.  I understand their frustration- especially if they paid the asking price for Glittermitten having no clue what lurked within it.  That being said, I don't really see the average person just immediately dropping full-price on a game that, on the surface, and by all accounts pitched on the Steam storefront, looks like any random game on the Play Store.
Glittermitten Grove is absolutely, beyond any shadow of a doubt, a contender for my "top 10 games of the last 5 years" list.  The grain of salt being that it came with a heavy investment of emotional endearment.  I guess you really would have needed to be there for not only the first game in the "series" but for the build up that came when the sequel was esoterically pitched on Kickstarter.
Sentimentally, there hasn't been a "videogame as art" that has moved me even a fraction of the way Glittermitten Grove did.  Most of the sentiment and nostalgia I feel now comes from experiencing most of the game and the atmosphere outside of the typical videogame environment, and then instead of playing it for myself the first time, I watched an 8 hour Lets Play.
So how would I recommend this to someone who had the whole thing spoiled to them?  I would first tell them to watch the entire 8 hour video on Nitrorad's channel, because that in itself is an amazing experience- his interaction with the game and the Twitch chat was so candid and intimate, it really felt like this giant community formed out of nowhere and everyone involved got to discover all the little stuff together, so the whole thing was a crowd effort.
If you have a soft spot for "games as art" and appreciate oldschool adventure games, I can assure you this is your jam right here.  The Fairy game really could be its own thing, and maybe I do wish they'd invest a little more time on an update that would flesh it out just a little more, if not for the sake of just appeasing people who want to hate on the developer because they feel left out.  At any rate, the experience alone was worth the full asking price for me, and not counting the amount of time I put into this game (offline unfortunately) I at least got 16 hours of watching someone else play it and that itself is a testament to how tranformative I feel Glittermitten Grove is.
Hell, the possibility of there being another entry in this series alone, just hanging out waiting to be discovered, that's enough to persuade me to buy this game and gift it to as many other people as I can.  I NEED MORE, and frankly, the game industry needs more of Frog Frac- I mean Glittermitten Grove.

Cons:

The fractions that many of you are aiming to see, I can gladly say you won't be very disappointed, although I heavily encourage you not spoil yourself at all, this game in conjunction with the base game should feel like a full and non-spoiled to the gamer.
(Things that will be probably be patched in updates after this review)
At the time of writing there are no steam cards or achievements, for a game costing ZAR 206.00 it is very strange but I'm sure is mainly for the hidden aspects of this game.
Conclusion:
I heavily employ you all to play this relaxing, minimalistic game, although pricey, it is two full games, both equally enjoyable and are both worth your time.

This game series has turned out to be one of my favorite RTS games as it depicts "almost realistic" modern warfare with things sacrificed for the sake of gameplay. But, never the less. It's complex gameplay makes up for a hard learning curve, so at the start of your playing of wargames, you will get obliterated by other players in online matches. Deck system and no traditional basebuilding, Every unit has their strenghts & weaknesses and everything has a counter. These reasons help this game to stand out from the rest. To be really good at this game, you just have to learn constantly about the mistakes you make in your past games, so you know what not to do the next time you wind up in a match again.
Naval combat was advertised for this game a lot, but it winded up to be a big disappointment. It's all about who has more  anti-ship missiles or CIWS. But where this game shines is the land combat. No one really plays naval on multiplayer for that exact reason.
You really don't want to play in the 10vs10 servers, because it is usually, in my experience very inconsistent. I had a thing going on for 10vs10 games, but it just winded up too many loses for my profile, often due to other players leaving too soon or after deploying their sovre without any escort to the sea and ragequitting when it gets killed by anti-ship missiles. So you really just get sick of it. So stick to the usual matches, 3vs3 etc.
But, it's positive sides really outweight the negatives.
So I really really recommend this game to any RTS fans out there, it's an very solid RTS game optimized for PC gaming.

Video version of this review:
This game begins with an explosion of some chemical plant that turns people into zombies, and your character escapes in a taxi car. Does this guy work for the taxi company, or did he just steal it because it was the closest means of escape? I don’t know, but who cares? The point is, you are hired by the military to mow down zombies, rescue survivors, and upgrade your vehicle.
With each zombie you kill, you earn money, which you use to purchase upgrades for your car. You can also get money by picking it up off the ground, or completing the secondary missions. You get multiple different upgrades for your vehicles, like weapons and abilities. Each car has different stats, such as how far upgraded the abilities are when you get the vehicle, as well as how many passengers that particular vehicle can carry. So you better choose wisely for your next mission.
There are some vehicles you can drive but you cannot unlock, because you can only drive them on certain missions, like a truck, a tank, a bulldozer, and a firetruck. Unfortunately, these vehicles cannot be upgraded with weapons and abilities, so you’re gonna need to keep an eye out for health. I really love the tank, because you got the big gun, which is great for destroying clusters of zombies.
And of course, like any other zombie video game, there are different kinds of zombies. The regular walkers, who apparently can throw stuff at you. Rude! And there are some bigger guys who are stronger, and more difficult to run over. It’s best to use your boost on these guys because they actually slow your car down. And what would a zombie game be without an exploding zombie? I don’t think I need to explain these ones. They just explode when you get near them. And the dogs go without saying. They just run at you and attack, and are faster than the human zombies.
You also have to fight bosses as well; giant mutant creatures that throw goo at you, spray toxic... blood or whatever at you, and are extremely ugly.
The game is a ton of fun... when you’re not constantly driving straight into an exploding zombie. It’s probably just because I suck at video game driving, but after a while, it just gets kinda ridiculous. And there seem to be times when health can be scarce, most likely because I’ve just been looking in the wrong places. But honestly, I’ve driven for several blocks through alleyways, and not seen a speck of health when I desperately need it. And it’s kind of annoying when you hit something and your vehicle ends up spinning out of control. It tends to turn me the opposite direction of where I want to go, or flip me on my side, and I have to respawn in a place where I’m surrounded by zombies who kill me instantly because of my LOW HEALTH!
I was a little disappointed with the ending. I don’t know if this counts as a spoiler, because characters have been talking about it throughout the entire game. Plus, it’s kinda something pretty much anyone would half expect from a zombie game. They keep saying the military is up to something, but I don’t remember seeing anything indicating what or why.
But all of my problems aside, this is actually a good game, and I totally recommend you check it out.

The first rogue-like game I've gotten into, and still the best. Spelunky does a great job of randomly creating unique and interesting obstacles. On top of that, it gives you a collection of versatile tools to overcome them, including bombs that can be used to create your own path in the enviroment and a wide assortment of items to buy from the game's vendors that change your gameplay style immensely. This means that not only does the game ensure that every playthrough is different, but you also have plenty of room for creativity and improvisation in how you approach it's designs.
Don't let my hours counter fool you, I've put well over a hundred hours into this game on my xbox. It just so happens the game is so good I felt compelled to get a copy on my computer now that the 360 generation is coming to a close.

This game is very addicting; it sometimes feels like a slot machine: it feels like that next great cave run is just around the corner even though I just got killed by a giant spider. The graphics are very pretty, but I wish there was the option to use the original pixel art, which was also quite beautiful.

A vibrant downgrade. If the controls and character response of the original was mediocre, than the sequel is downright combative. You'll find your character desperately clinging to every ledge within sight, unless you keep the down button depressed at all times. The whip now has a slightly shorter range, meaning you can no longer be teetering over a 1 block wide pit and kill the monster on the other side. Picking up an item quickly is nearly impossible, as you have to be fully crouched before pressing the action button. This means no more hitting them both at the same time, you have to actually consciously crouch first. As a person who has died well over a thousand times in the original, I find this game simply too clunky to play.
On top of that, they made the boulder from the boulder trap several times more powerful. It's kind of fun to see the boulder fly back and forth across the screen, but you can't really steal idols unless you've checked the whole map to make sure there aren't any shopkeepers. And that really isn't an option, because you no longer have the 30 seconds of warning music before the time runs out, it's been shortened to zero.
An additional but admittedly minor gripe: the scene between levels is terrible. If you want to see your loot and kills piled up, you'll have to wait nearly a full minute to see it happen. It's horribly slow; this should have been caught immediately after playtesting started. And it doesn't pile everything up, it flashes each piece of loot once. Not a huge deal, but it certainly takes away the fun of that brief level recap that the original had.
On the plus side, you now buy items and go through doors with the space bar, allowing one to avoid the pain of prematurely leaving a level. Also, the new music isn't bad. 
I would strongly recommend playing the original game before playing this one. Playing this version first will leave an impression of mediocrity on you unbefitting of the famous Spelunky.

Another hit by LGM! Warlords is sleek, friendly, and down right fun. The game allows players to manage an small faction and turn it into an empire. Add and upgrade additions to your HQ, set up infrastructure, and build huge fleets to conquer and defend territory!
The game blends the adventure that the Starpoint Gemini games already do so well, with the tactical thoughfulness of a 4x, and does so without becoming daunting and tedious. The two genre's elements play very well together, and really do feel seamless. Managing your empire is very easy and intuitive. There are various upgrades to your HQ itself, your infrastructure (mining facilities, guardposts, etc), as well as to your civilian ships and of course, to your military ships. Building military fleets is easy and fun, and you have complete control over both your civilian and military fleets. Civilian fleets can be assigned to gather resources, and military fleets can be told to move anywhere you want, to merge with other friendly fleets, or to follow the player, all in real time.
What fleets do is all totally visible, allowing you to assist any fleets that are in combat and lemme just say, taking the helm and charging into combat surrounded by a fleet of ships, is maybe one of the most satisfying feelings I've ever had in gaming. It looks stunning, and nothing makes me quite as giddy as when as barrage just erupts from around me into the enemy fleet. There are also heroes you can recruit, that sort of "lead" your fleets in a way. They have skills like the player does, and their ships upgrade over time, also like the player. Heroes have no control over the fleet itself, but they do provide the "face" of the fleet, and tend to lead the charge alongside the player.
There's also a light diplomacy system, where you can negotiate peace, go to war, or otherwise aid other factions. It isn't too fleshed out compared to the other mechanics, but it's still impactful, and feels like a good step up from the reputation system of the last game, and definitely fits the bill of this game better. Being peaceful is totally an option though. And with that, so is trading! Trading is arguably a little more dangerous in this game compared to SPG2, but with the ability to assign your fleets to follow you, you can travel with some guards.
As for the adventure aspect: you start in a small gunship, but can work your way up to some towering monsters. Coupled with that, your character can gain experiend and level up, allowing you to take skills, which are the abilities you activate, and perks, which are your passive buffs. Gaining both experience and money can come from engaging in combat and selling the spoils, or taking missions from job boards on planets and stations. Progression feels solid, and at no point have I felt like I was falling behind or my gain was decreasing, as the game's general difficulty scales with the player's level. Lastly there's exploring, which is a blast in and of itself because the game is truly just gorgeous (there's a pinned screenshots thread if you wanna see for yourself). The map is plenty large too, even if it may not look it at first sight, so there's plenty to see!
All around it's a wonderful game and LGM really outdid themselves this time. Even if you've never played a Starpoint Gemini game, this is worth a gander for sure. Anyone who has played an SPG game will find themselves perfectly at home in Warlords though!

TL;DR: Absolutely loved this game.

Don't mind reviewers who only played the game for 5 minutes then wrote a negative review - the game opens up after about 30 minutes to an hour. You go from a "contained tutorial" where the game teaches you the basics while giving you missions. It isn't until after a significant event the game really unleashes what's available to you. Believe me when I say the game really unleashes on you - it's almost a whole new game. Without spoiling anything, you go from getting assistance from allied ships in the tutorial part of the game, to commanding those allied ships (that you've specifically built and assigned to fleets) to either carry out your orders and/or follow you across the space plane.
I'm not big on the Pros/Cons type listing, but I'll spout some stuff off: the controls in the beginning can be really annoying, especially if you've played other M+KB vessel games like War Thunder, but you'll either get used to it or be smart and change the controls yourself. The atmospheric graphics are incredible and immersive, but the craft themselves can be a little lacking. The GUI and some other aspects scream "Indie," but you know what? Those have been my favorite games.
It's OK that this game doesn't have AAA aspects, because 1) it isn't priced at AAA prices, 2) Indie games have their own charm (this gem is full of it), and 3) Dev support - just take a look on the steam forums for this game and you'll see the Devs responding and contributing to tons of converstations. This is quite possibly my favorite game of all-time. The game is an RTS in the same sense as the latest C&C4 (No real Base-building) Except it doesn't arbitrarily limit the number of units you can have. Maps are gigantic, battles are huge, and there are some aspects of it that everyone just loves. That being said, there are a few limitations that might drive some away. I'll address them below.
Good:
-Battles are gigantic
-Amazing variety of Units
-Free DLC
-Large Map Replayability
-Wide variety of countries available
-Land, Air, and Sea combat
-Immense experimentation possible
-Challenging Campaigns
-Multiplayer battles (TO THE MAX)
Bad:
-Sea is kind of half-baked and does not work realistically
-Otomatic was never sold to Denmark (Hehe)
-NO GOOD TUTORIAL!!!!
I know a lot of people complain about this one, but to be honest there's really nothing there! The in-game tutorial explains what each value means, but it never really explains how to play the game well. Many people just come in without any knowledge whatsoever and pick units arbitrarily. It requires some pretty intensive effort from experienced players (Like myself) to actually help these new guys and give them a hand. There are plenty of resources available for them on steam, but it's not always obvious where to find these.
-Planes are unrealistic as well
-SPAAG ground range is arbitrarily set at 1050m (Except for otomatic which is 2100, down from 2275)
-Tank Range maxxes out at 2275M (for no real reason)
-Ships don't fire KE/AP Rounds!!! (like they do IRL!)
Overall, I absolutely adore this game. The dings I gave it above are things most regular players won't care about or really notice. If you like RTS, you couldn't go wrong with purchasing this game and having a blast. Please read the tutorials after you do, and check out a guide or two! If you're still confused, ask someone like me who knows how to play the game well for advice! We're happy to train you new guys!

This is an under-rated game.
It definitely is a little less on the production quality than some RTS games, and is certainly not a game with a vast number of players.
But it is a RTS game with a slower pace and more mechanics at play than usual for RTS games. This is a welcome thing for those of us who are no longer in their teens and get less of a kick from being in a mad rush all match long. Plus, the slower pace opens the door to mechanics like supply and recon. Units eventually use up all their ammo and need to resupply, while recon needs to be conducted before sending other types of units into an area of the map.
It's not a perfect game, and it does suffer from sort of repetative map design and fairly inconsistent AI. But multiplayer is the meat of the game, and aside from some latency issues that crop up from time to time, the multiplayer is pretty good and allows for more thinking than reacting, which for a RTS is a breath of fresh air.
Again, by no means a perfect game, and definitely not overly polished in terms of music and UI, but certainly a game worth having for strategy gamers, particularly those who prefer a bit more though and a bit less reflexes.
This is the best RTS series ever, if you're a huge military buff then this game is for you.

Frankly, when I first bought this game I was just taking a stab in the dark, giving a random indie game a chance and boy did it pay off. Really, this game turned out to be a lot better than what I was expecting, personally I like how the game just dives right in without explaining much. Originally, this was how all games were, with only the instruction manual to help you if you had any questions, the little tips in the game kinda replace that, it's this sorta "figure it out yourself" attitude that I like to see in games that you don't really see as much in the AAA industry.
Getting back to the review after that little tangent, this game has a lot more to it than what you might get from the trailer or screenshots. First of all, all of your actions have some sort of consequence for later on. Rationally figuring out where to place things is important since trees can block sunlight for other trees later on. Accurately predicting when to store up on resources is also useful since there are seasons where getting resources is more difficult (ex. almost impossible to get food in winter). Curiously, the mechanic used for mining involves shooting fireworks into the ground. Truthfully, I actually think it's clever because the different splits of fireworks you can use provide a large amount of possible strategies to use. In my opinion, anyone can play this game since it's difficulty is lenient enough that even novice players could get along in the game while advanced players will have more than enough tools to mess around with.
Of course, $20 is quite an amount to spend for many, but if you're willing to take a chance you won't be disappointed. Nearly all the other games I've played this year can't even compare to GlitterMitten Grove. Surely this game deserves an award for it's outstanding performance, but it's relatively unpopular at the moment, so I can only hope it  gets more publicity in the future. 2 hours in and I already couldn't put it down, that's how I knew this one was gonna be one of my faves.

The setting and plot provide you with just enough context for the missions that they don't feel out of place or lacking in purpose, it's the other way around, even if you're not into the story or characters, completing the missions and conquering bases feels very rewarding because there is a sense of progression as you conquer new areas in the map and push back the enemy forces.
My only complaint so far is the main character's revenge plot device is pretty run of the mill...the way it's presented just isn't that convincing. I don't even remember the protagonist's name so that alone says something about how poorly developed he is.
That aside, the game is a TON of FUN and that's what it all boils down to.

What a name. A name like that makes a game sound so generic and dull, yet this one is tons of fun. It's basically 3 games in one, in the sense that some mechanics are shared between them but the rules are quite different, like Kirby Air Ride. On that note, let's start with...
The story of Zombie Driver HD involves a chemical outbreak
that turns most of the population into zombies (obviously) except for one man in a taxi, who ends up working with the military to help save as many people as possible. Ok, now that the synopsis is out of the way, this mode is the weakest one in my opinion. The mission variety is pretty good, with a couple boss fights and some special vehicle missions (the tank ones are a blast) breaking up the monotony of having to drive to ANOTHER location across the city to rescue people. It's not like the rescue missions are bad, it's just that most of the story mode is rescuing people and it can get repetitive after a while. The story, though, is so cliché it drags things down.
Mostly fun missions and bosses, lame and predictable story. I score it 3 bad voice acting jobs out of 5.
This mode is practically Twisted Metal meets Burnout, but top down. For what was originally a free update for the original game, Blood Race is pretty great. It's not just races either; Elimination events are basically deathmatch races (as crazy as that sounds, it actually works) and Endurance events are where the zombies really get involved, where you have to try and keep killing them while also destroying roadside obstacles to extend your time limit. If it wasn't for the ridiculous rubber-banding by the AI in the races (they literally have super tire grip and do not have to slow down in corners at all, and then they slow down to a snail's pace when they pass you) this mode would have been perfect but as is, it's just very solid. 4/5 stars easy.
Easily the best part of Zombie Driver HD, the Slaughter Mode is an endless horde mode where you drive a car around a moderately sized arena of your choice (there's quite a few to pick from) and try to stay alive as long as possible. After a set amount of kills, an upgrade drops which may give you access to sporadic weapon drops or turbo, and there are health pickups to help make the surviving a little easier. There isn't much else to say here because not much else needs to be said; Great stress relief and highly replayable for score seekers, 5 stars.
(3 + 4 + 5) / 3 = ...ah, forget it, no need for math here. Weak story and absurd race rubber-banding aside, Zombie Driver HD is a fantastic top-down action racing game. If I had to score it: ★★★★½ (the extra half star because of how much fun the whole thing is. No, really.)

All summed up, Train Simulator 2016 is a wonderfully detailed large scale train simulator.
Firstly, I bought Train Simulator 2016 when it was known as Railworks 3 (Train Simulator 2012) and mainly referred to as "Railworks" but automatically upgraded to Train Simulator 2013. Train Simulator has gone through many, many changes through the years. Train Simulator 2016, as it is now, has one of the best shadow engines or systems in any sort of video game or simulator I have ever seen. Locomotive, tree, buildings, and terrain shadows are beautifully represented for each time of day and type of weather whether cloudy or sunny.
Secondly, Train Simulator is somewhat like a massive texture and graphic increased Microsoft Train Simulator in terms of route size. Many DLC packs for Train Sim 2015 are very large and some routes may take you HOURS to cross the full length if following speed limits (Like 0.1% of the Train Sim 2016 community does). Pretty much every DLC route is full of accurately represented buildings, track plans, and landscapes as seen in real life. Though they are a tad bit pricey, they are totally worth the investment. The newer DLC locomotives are very nicely detailed and have pretty much all the small and large details on the model as they are like in real life.
The overall pros for Train simulator 2016 are: amazing shadows, highly detailed locomotives and routes, accurate routes, responsive and realistic physics and beautiful details also featuring lens flares from the headlights.
Now the two biggest cons that the TS series faces is the sound and route builder. Many hornsounds are recycled onto new engines and sometimes they don't even have that certain horn in real life. They have since improved on the clarity and are trying to make new horn sounds for new locomotives but the variety is a little questionable. Sure there are ways you can make your own and give the locomotive the horn its supposed to have but I think this should be done back at the developer drawing board. However, the hornsounds and whistles do sound good and the looping its nice, its just the recycling of them that bothers me. The route builder isn't really anything like lets say Trainz Simulator 12 or Trainz a New Era. There are many, many more features which the Trainz route builder could benefit from and the TS16 route builder gives you many oppurtunies with different terrain features, smoothing out land, bringing ground up to meet the track, and many many more options. The only thing is its actually a little complicated to make things like grade crossings, signaling, make straight lines of road, track, add traffic to rivers, road, etc. There are plenty of tutorials on YouTube to learn how to do these things but its not anything you can memorize and learn in a day.
Summed up, TS16 is a fantastic train simulator. The graphics are awesome, realistic physics, highly detailed and accurate locomotives, rolling stock, and routes as well. A large variety of DLC to purchase and expand your collection, Shadows are amazingly displayed, good weather and time effects, route builder with many, many features to create your own local railroad or fictional railway line, and overall Train Simulator 2016 is a must have for any railfan or train enthusiast.

I bought this game for Co-op, and am reviewing it as a co-op game.
The gameplay itself is actually quite fun, but there are two major points I have to criticize:
- The camera in the co-op mode only follows one player. The other players will quickly lose orientation and find themselves outside of the screen. This made coop a lot harder and more frustrating than singleplayer.
- The game doesn't let you take your time and explore. This forces you to rush the game even more, making the bad camera even worse. Again, this counts for co-op. The time limit is managable in singleplayer.
Another thing is fairness: This game is hard. There's nothing wrong with that. But often even small mistakes are punished by instant death. An enemy might hit you once and before your character recovers hit you again, until it's game over. This can by very frustrating, but of course the challennge can also be a plus.
My reason for not recommending this is the local coop mode. If you're playing alone anyway you might as well give it a try.

In recent times I have also jumped onto the moba band wagon and have played many hours of League as well as Heros. I do love mobas for their simplicity and focus on multiplayer strategy and skill but do find myself sometimes wishing there was more to it than controlling one hero in a team. When I heard of the concept of Dropzone I was very intrigued because it promises the fast pace no fuss multiplayer battle elements of a moba but the more intricate micro and map positioning elements of an RTS without the need to worry about macro elements of an rts. So far I have been loving this and finding the battles very fun and varied with already a good amount of mechs and lots of potential for weapon and build variations as well as map strategies! I definitely recommend this to anyone who loves RTS and moba games.

Upon launching the game, I was met with a sick CGI intro. I was already impressed. Compared to most Early Access games, it is well worth the purchase. $20 is a very fair price for this game. It is one of the few Early Access games that actually feels complete --which is surprising since it has only been in beta for like 6 months (I think I read somewhere).

The game provides a very well designed tutorial with plenty of time to read the skills/abilities and learn as you go along. There is a clear, scaffolded progression between the units and their capabilities.
The premise of the game is simple: you play a 15 minute game to score the most points. Winning, on the other hand can be quite difficult. The objectives seem pretty clear and the map is not too big, so there are plenty of opportunties for players to contest objectives. I could definitely see this game getting competitive real quick. (Also, the 15 minute timer is so appealing. I know exactly how much time my game will take, so I don't have to adjust my schedule according to how the game is going.)
The keyboard controls are also very intuitive and logical. If you have ever played a MOBA or RTS in the past, you will pick the game up very quickly.  As a player new to this genre of games, the controls are pretty clear so the only REAL struggle might be controlling multiple units at a time.
However, this struggle seems to be what makes Dropzone such a promising game. As I played the game, I realized that within the first few minutes past the tutorial, I was already beginning to form strategies. (I would have one unit scout out and distract my enemies for the most part, while the other two collect points.) With a team of three customizable "rigs" (units) at your disposal, it gives you a lot of control over the map. And by customizable, I mean that you can choose what rigs you want on your team and what skills they should have, etc. This, I think, is super cool because it allows for theorycrafting and rewards innovative players to come up with new strategies and pioneer the meta of the game.
There can be simultaneous fights occuring at different parts of the map. I was going crazy at first, and I noticed at times that I would forget a unit lingering at some distant part of the map for a while. I assume that more experienced players would always have units that are active and contributing to the overall victory of the match. My advice to new players: always make sure your rigs are doing something.
I am going to play some more and update my finds on this game~

My IGN is Rolf_Mützelburg. Its been about a year since my last review of this game. I have dumped enough money to buy 2 new computers into this game in that time. I've found other player's reviews entertaining but my old one was made back when the game was "Early Access" Not much has changed since last year, however, what has changed is that I no longer recommend wasting your time downloading this game at this point. The game has not changed at all in a years time. There has been some minor community drama not deserving of mention, and a few minor content updates of no significance. So I'm just going to quote my old review.
"Reto is a small company, and mislead by a lack of long term goals and just general incompetence. They have an awesome peace of real-estate, being one of the only WWII themed games to recently come out period. ‘H&G’ walks in the giant footsteps of ‘WWII Online’ aka ‘Battleground Europe’. Sadly, it fails miserably to measure up to the 15 year old giant.
For those who don’t know what ‘WWII Online’ aka ‘Battleground Europe’ is; I’m going to be comparing the two a lot. ‘WWII online’ is a MMO-FPS WWII simulator. The game takes place on a map ¼ the size and shape of Europe. It is a combined arms game set in 1939 onward. Its not perfect, but to be fair its 15♥♥♥♥♥♥♥years old! That being said, it has established its credentials and is in my opinion a milestone in gaming. ‘H&G’ for all it has over ‘WWII Online’ is a failure. It has incredible potential, but never lived up to any of it.
Reto released H&G in 2014, WWII online came out in 2001. Somehow WWII Online has kicked H&G’s butt in every possible measurement except graphics. Even the physics and ballistics have them beat. It is very pathetic for a game that purports itself as a free to play WWII game, to be as bad as H&G is at WWII in general. When confronted by these failures, rather than blame lack of funds, or have a logical argument, they just play word games to skirt the issue.
Word Games:
H&G is supposed to be a combined arms game, though it only represents 2 classes with any fidelity. Infantry and Tanks. There is no Navy, and the Airforce is neglected to the point where it exists in it’s current state only as a temporary place holder. The G in H&G is for Generals. The game, like WWII Online is supposed to simulate a full scale war. But unlike WWII online that is controlled by admin, H&G gives the players control of the war map, in a sort of worker’s cooperative using player controlled generals. The RTS side of H&G does not exist, and like the Navy, Reto hasn’t a clue on how if ever they can fix it.
You’d be forgiven for thinking H&G is attempting to become a WWII simulator like WWII Online, simply because of the realistic graphics and humorless style. But if you use the word “Simulator” as in; a virtual recreation of WWII, Reto will very quickly correct you in as vague and non-committal a way as possible. Common rebuttals from Reto and their sympathizers have been gems like ‘it is an “arcade” game’, or it is “Alternative history” Both of these terms are stretched miles to accommodate any BS Reto tries to push. The word “FUN” is non-objectively and condescendingly used to justify pretty much anything, as they try to tell their own players what is or is not fun. They do not recognize any of the issues the community has with the game to save face, thinking that if they just don’t give the accusations any credence they will go away, or won’t have any affect. Its sort of like the ‘hear no evil, see no evil, speak no evil’ approach to community management. The great irony of this of course is that no issues ever get resolved and the community at large laughs at berates them virtually unopposed. Any player foolish enough to try and speak up for Reto is beaten down by an almost sadistically cheerful mob who is all to eager to beat something other than the field of dead horses littering the H&G forums. As a member of this mob, I must say its actually quite cordial once your part of the cult. Beating up on Reto has become a national past time, and you can make friends and defuse pretty much any situation by just making a joke about Reto. Instant kinship!
But the H&G community for better or worst is powerless beyond their strong words, and ultimately don’t really matter. You probably are grinding you teeth waiting for me to get on with it and talk about the gameplay… Well, I can’t think of a better transition than this so…
Gameplay:
As said, the game suffers from a very unstable tone. Its realistic when it can be, but any semblance to reality is destroyed as soon as you hit a texture or physics bug. Most don’t affect gameplay but they look ugly as fk, and cause very silly situations, like getting your truck stuck on a railway tie, or flipping your vehicles driving in a straight line. And the ballistics or lack of it mean you can’t think too much or you will be very frustrated by the way the game doesn’t give a fk what you think makes sense. It follows the stereotypical Arcade style damage system. Even tanks, and vehicles take damage like its 1999. If you penetrate the tank you’re shell does x damage based off the size of the shell, and the rest is determined by dice and RNGesus. The tank like everything else has an old fashioned HP bar, and when the bar hits zero, you and your tank evaporate into a giant explosion. This sort of arcade logic is outdated as MOH, but like so many other arcade systems dragged from the dark ages into the game it reaks havoc on the game’s balance. Because the game despite Reto’s best attempts to convince us otherwise is based off a real event, using real life equipment from that period: And to keep it short, when the German engineers designed the Panzerfaust, the laws of physics didn’t state that vehicles exploded when the arbitrary battle royal meter ticked to zero. There is a bit more to weapon design and ballistics than this game can compensate for, and it translates to random and unrealistic combat statistics. This makes the combined arms part of the game a joke, as infantry can “kill” vehicles with the same efficiency as a 400lbs bomb.
So the game is unrealistic despite it trying to look like a hard core shooter. Plenty of games stretch the truth for marketing purposes. Arcade games can be good by their own right. It doesn’t have to be realistic to be “Fun”. But it’s not a good arcade game either. If you ignore all the obvious attempts to be a WWII game, and just measure it as a generic game without any of the WWII references, its nothing but a generic copy of every shooter you’ve ever played from yesteryear. It’s WWII identity is literally the only thing it has. The RTS bit as I said before is only a gimmick, and the game’s only retainer is grind.

Conclusion:
So, if that was the case a year ago and I still recommended it then, what changed to cause me to retract my recommendation? My answer is Competition: Other WWII themed games have come out that are simply so much better that H&G is obsolete. It was always mediocre, but it was the only "New" WWII shooter at the time it was released. Since then a WWII themed COD came out, and for those who like me are looking for a more authentic WWII environment "Hell Let Loose" is coming out in March, I'm already signed up for the closed Beta. I don't even like COD, but I'd recommend it to any casual gamers looking for a WWII shooter to play long before I'd suggest H&G.

I am an avid lover of stealth and brutal games. Thus, the Sniper Elite series is an excellent choice, but SE 2 is actually better in many ways. Playing through all of the missions and painfully getting into place, and getting all the sub objectives for the most part, this game took me around 11 hours to beat. Here's some pros and cons of this game.
Pros
Very time consuming, even if there are only two paths to take most of the time. Not getting caught is very time consuming, and the pay off is the classic utter destruction of their organs.
Clever AI, even on cadet. Truly a challenge, but can some times be annoying.
Cons
There are only 3-5 cut scenes in the whole game.
A blocked shot by thin air.
Everything that should be included in the game is sold as a dlc.
There are only really 6-8 missions (can't remember off the top of my head, but each mission took about 2 hours)
Fire does not set off traps? As in bombs.
The enemy does not use traps in the game?
I can only throw a body two feet in any directions? Which prevents me from quickly tossing a body over the edge to avoid detection?
Your boss fights are with a panzer and two... cars that have machine guns in front of them.
Enemy dialogue does not surpass two lines out of cutscenes. There's simply no creativity with the enemy. Even when all they're doing is standing around a fire.
Story... is existent but non-existent. It was similar to reading a journal of six entries with no cutscene or animation, and then there are the cutscenes that simply feel unifinished.
If you're looking for an indepth and rich game with hours of fast action thrilling gameplay, look somewhere else. If you're looking to kill things like a hunter and you could give two cents less about story or awe-inspiring environments, it's a good game.

Flying Tigers is a surprising difficult game for such an arcade title, and yes, I'm in rookie mode. It really makes you "earn" your kills, as well as use maneuvers to get away from enemies in dogfights. The game gets frustrating with time-limited objectives and requires some very efficient shooting.
Despite the name sake, you fly far more than just the P40's. You also fly the nearly obsolete Brewster Buffalos, Hawker Hurricanes (as the Brits) as well as the shoulder-wing fixed gear light bombers you see in some screenshots to bomb targets, Twin-engine level bombers, and more. You can fly Japanese planes in the dogfight mode, not in the campaign.
Actual flight is done in 3rd person mode, which emphasizes the "arcade" nature of the game. There's even a computed crosshair for you to aim your gun at whatever target you are aiming toward. Your crosshair pulses when your guns are about to overheat (and jam). Ammo is unlimited though.
You will do ground attacks, in dive bomb, level bomb, torpedo runs (fly LOW!) and strafing. The bombs and torpedoes auto-regenerate after certain segments, which reminds me a lot of the "Air Conflicts" series which also featured missions structured like this.
My main complaint is the game's surprisingly hard, even in rookie mode. I don't expect to like shoot down all 10 bombers by myself with one-shot kills, but in the first mission alone, defend area against Japanese bombers, I had to retry about 6 times, as I had to kill 4 bombers in limited time. And the guns are not that accurate. You can activate a temporary "Trazertime" (Matrix slo-mo) to get a bit more precise in targeting, but how that's recharged is not explained.
Also, the game also gives you "rolls" and "loops", but mapped to dangerous buttons (on the gamepad, stick tap, i.e. push) which can be jostled when maneuvering. I remember dying TWICE in the tutorial because I accidentally did a loop at too low a level. Roll helps you get away from a bad guy on your tail, but that rarely happens at least early in the campaign.
The dogfights in this game are epic, with dozen planes swirling around the sky shooting at each other. Fighters are easy to take down, but not quite so with bombers. And your wingmen will score kills, merely a lot less often than you do. Same with ground attacks.
There are occasional turret gunner segments where you need to shoot at enemy planes as a tail gunner or turret gunner from a bomber.
Some missions require you to take off (just go full throttle and gear will be retracted when you get airborne). There is at least one mission that require you to land to get a pilot who was forced down by engine trouble, but proper management of speed and gear made that actually quite simple.
The key to success in this game is proper management of speed and altitude, as in any fighter sim. You don't want to be too close to the target, and not so slow that you fall out of the sky, but if you are too far you'll overheat your gun and not achieve many hits, and you'll take too much flak.
For example, one of the missions was a night raid on a Japanese convoy, where the level bombers have to take out two transports. By properly lining up against the ships (fly directly over their path) I was able to drop multiple bombs on the ship rather than trying to come at it from the sides and score only one hit at a time, if that at all, which allowed me to take much less flak over all. Rather than having only 10% life left, I had over 80% left with my improved approach, which allowed me to survive the next stage.
Each mission typically has multiple segments, where you jump from one part of the mission to another. One would have the Brewsters Buffalows knock out the searchlights in the convoy, then the level bombers hit the convoy, only to defend itself from a Zero, then the torpedo bombers make a run at the cruiser, scoring several hits, only to run for their lives when Zeros came out to play.
If you failed one part of the mission you can resume the mission at the prior checkpoint (i.e. repeat just that one part you failed).
The graphics are good, state of the art, and in fact, probably a bit overdone as every plane that goes down seem to end in a huge fireball. Sound is good, though the chatter is a bit inane, as every dead plane seem to result in a "Wilhelm scream".
All in all, the game covered a part of WW2 that is rarely covered, with state of the arm graphics and turn-and-burn game play. If you are looking for a sim, this game is not it. It is an arcade-flyer for the turn-and-burn crowd. But if you keep that in mind, you will learn quite a bit about WW2 and have a blast.

Developer Eugen takes the RTS genre to a cold war gone hot. Gone is the concept of base building, and resource management. WG:RD introduces players to a realistic RTS unlike anything seen before. No longer will players contend with Actions Per Minute, but rather with tactics, units, and teamwork.

Players will find themselves lost in the sheer number of statiscal difference while attempting to create the perfect army. The complex task of "deck building" becomes simplifed by a restrictions and bonuses. The more you limit your military the more you have available.
Graphically speaking WG:RD shines above almost all RTSs on the market. With almost painstaking authentic detail to units it's a shame to realize they are only utulized when fully zoomed in. The games scale makes it impractical to play any attention more than what's needed.
Although WG:RD is a shining example of the RTS genere; it does fall short with it's limited maps, and often sidelined naval battles. You'll easily find yourself playing the same maps time after time. Now that the Jig has been Up for a while, I'll write my serious review:
So now we finally know what an 8 hour-ish Frog Fractions game looks like. (It might be shorter for you if you decide to travel to the main game hub instead of growing your fairy village to maximum castle size)
For a game that long, I think it would have been better to have more of the mechanics be on a better curve. Although the minigames are mercifully easy for the most part, the fact that you are jumping back and forth between such different games and in pretty much any order means you’re learning a broad range of mechanics but you don’t really have a chance to explore anything in depth. Some things do build on each other, like how the snake minigame teaches you the snake controls before letting you back in the hub with snake controls.
Likewise, the humor is constant. It’s good, IMHO, and I loved how the references stacked with each other. But I kind of would have liked an actual story this time. I know if you pay attention there’s the thing with the mindstones and the time machine, but a lot of the time it’s hard to tell what is just a random joke and what’s just a silly part of the main story. The fairy advisor acts like everything you see is actually part of the Glittermitten Grove universe and 100% normal but that’s more of a running gag than a storyline.
With that said, I absolutely prefer a game that’s so lighthearted you can’t tell when it’s being a little serious to something that’s unrelentingly dour because the creators don’t understand how to not take their own fictional universe too seriously. We have so many of the latter already.
I would have liked it even better if more of the minigames had actually built on each other, and if more of the silly plot was less obscured by seemingly-unrelated absurdidty. Maybe it wouldn’t have been Frog Fractions 2 if it was. Maybe what I really want is something mid-way between a serious game with one set of deep mechanics and this one.
Even so, I give it a solid 10 and a hearty thumbs-up. It would have been 8 or 9, but I gave extra points for having the gonads to make the main hub world in that style.

Great game, and virtually unique in it's genre due to the destructability / physics engine combination.
I know it sounds like a gimmick tacked on to yet another third-person shooter, and in a way it is. But this gimmick has been thoroughly cultivated by the developers, making it truly an integral part of the gameplay unlike, say, Red Faction II.
Most of it works exactly how you'd think it should work. Destroyed parts of a building do not give any cover. ALL weapons can have an effect on the structures, not just the 'terrain destruction' weapons. Knock out enough internal support beams and the roof will cave in. Topple a chimney onto a nearby factory and it will cut like a knife through butter.  It's so well done, you'd be forgiven for forgetting that the game boasts a cover system that works with destroyed terrain! Add in a collection of mini-games centered around this destruction mechanic, and you'll never be bored while there are structures to blow up.
Sadly, Guerilla does not avoid a pitfall associated with this freedom: in order to steer the player somewhat the developers have to resort to the terrain. The 'ever-changing landscape' is dominated by hours and hours of brown/grey/tan rocks. For every completely destructable building, there's a mile of dusty, desolate road with nothing to do. The story missions and large bonus missions do a good job of steering you to the fun stuff, but I can't help but feel that the devs could have made te terrain a bit more varied.
In the end though, the destruction facet has enough pull to derail you GTA-style into running around flattening every structure you please, in whatever way you want to. And in my book that marks Guerilla as a good sandbox game.

Red Faction: Guerrilla Steam Edition is an amazing package with the original game and includes all released DLC - including the Demons of the Past campaign and continues to receive updates and support from the developers. Finally, a true Red Faction game that utilizes the Geo-Mod destruction to the fullest potential on all structures (not on terrain like the original game)! Everything is destructible which creates amazing explosions and the desire to blow everything up. The game does a good job requiring the player to destroy buildings and other barriers in order to progress. This is the first game I have ever seen that actually allows you to raze structures to the ground and uses physics for the explosions and for the structural intergrity. It's awesome to see a building stand on one leg for a few seconds before it crumbles to the ground. The story is pretty good and there are a ton of missions available (~100). The optional missions become really repetitive so I stopped after doing about half of them. There are tons of collectibles to find as well, including mining ore locations, finding radio tags and destroying propaganda. Overall, I was able to find all the collectibles, beat the game and the DLC in about 30 hours and when you're blowing stuff up it's a ton of fun! Only negatives I can complain about is the weather/fog is way too thick sometimes impairing the player's vision and the enemy is able to shoot you through it with no issue and near the later half of the game everything feels pretty repetitive driving from point A to point B and doing the same thing over: do the same type of missions to reduce the control of the sector, blow stuff up and then do the story missions to free the sector. If you're looking for a game just to blow stuff up or wanting to try a Red Faction game, then look no further this is the game to get! Lastly, I need to mention the soundtrack in this game is awesome!

TLDR: Mount and Blade IN SPACE!!! Fly around in a big space sandbox in your own spaceship and blow up (or steal) other people's ships. Level up your character, buy bigger and better ships and weapons, build bigger and better fleets, research, mine and build to expand your empire.
This game is a great improvement on the previous entry (Starpoint Gemini 2). The biggest and most obvious improvement is the addition of 4X elements, where you now have a base that you can build up and use to build ships to protect and expand your little space empire. You collect resources from fixed mining operations that add resources to your stockpile at fixed intervals. You can also upgrade your base to give you access to new abilities (like building bigger ship classes or making mining operations more efficient). It all works well, even if it sometimes feels a bit grindy, espescially as you get higher up in the research tree (did I mention there's a small research tree?) and the resource requirements get really high.
Fortunately for the grindiness, the space combat is still pretty good. 3 types of light weapons (lasers, railguns and plasma) with different properties. And unlike the previous game, there's some reason to use the non-railgun weapons now! The class/skill system give pretty substantial bonuses and abilities to fighting up close which gives lasers and plasma a fighting chance against railgun weapons. Railguns are still the 'easier' weapon though, in that staying at long range requires less risk to use railguns in the most efficient manner, but at least you can use the other weapon types and not be at a big disadvantage.
The sandbox world is still really good. It randomly generates encounters as you travel through space so you're never bored, and this time encounters are not purely combat. There are some anomaly scanning / cargo container encounters that can lead to some interesting rewards. While not overly interesting on their own, they do add enough variety to moving around and makes the world feel bigger than just a random combat encounter generator would.
The campaign is OK, there's enough variety in the missions and the story and characters are compelling enough to get you through to the end. The one little twist at the end I really didn't expect and kept me interested to finish the game. Not quite sure the tone of the story sets up the postgame properly though (when you use the thing to blow up things and act like the evil empire the story tells you you are not). The voice acting is STILL pretty bad though, but whatever, it adds to the B-movie space charm of the entire thing.
On the bad side, the UI and the camera can be confusing at times. The camera in particular can be really confusing in your early fights, where ships move really fast and you can barely keep up as the enemy passes behind to shoot you. Fortunately there's a 'chase cam' mode which locks the camera to your current target so you can focus on steering and shooting. Unfortunately there's no tutorial on how to use this mode at all, so you'd have to figure it out yourself. There are also some little UI quirks than can be quite irritating (like the TGate menu always going to the Kokyra Gate WHEN I NEVER WANT TO GO THERE!). The game can also run sluggishly on older systems unless you turn down everything.
In all, great space sandbox game. A bit unpolished in terms of voice acting and performance, but the fights and the progression will keep you playing for hours on hours. Buy it. Play it. Don't forget to eat and shower.

Spelunky a rogue-like platformer, where the player traverses through the underground, fighting the dangerous wildlife, avoiding traps that were set up by someone and collecting gold to bring home. The game has randomly generated caves, so every time you try the game again, it will be different, with the exception of the daily, where everyone plays the same cave within 24 hours to see who gets the most gold or the fastest time.
The controls are simplistic, having a simple attack, that can be upgraded by obtaining guns. Most of the gameplay is looking for gold to spend at stores, to get better equipment and getting further down. The arsenal is pretty decent, ranging from freezing guns, to shotguns, and plasma cannons. There are also passives, like climbing gloves, jetpacks, and others.
There are 3 resources that need to be managed: Health, bombs and ropes. Ropes and bombs can be obtained by bags and crates, and health can be obtained by rescuing a damsel (that can be a girl, guy or a dog) and bringing them to the level exit. The shops usually have 4 items that you can buy or steal, considering that the shopkeeper will seek revenge through the whole game if you steal his items.
Whilst the game is extremely difficult, it is very fun and rewarding. It has great replay value and has tons of secrets that can let the player play it for around 150 hours. Definately worth it.

At first, the game seems impossible. Literally - it's tough to imagine even making it out of the first set of 4 levels on first pickup of the game. It's frustrating, and, initially, left me unimpressed with the game. But, sticking through the tough first few levels and forcing yourself to be more careful, more dilligent with your movements, and taking your time to think through the level (though not too long, lest the ghost show up!) really pays off. Spelunky seems relatively harmless and shallow at first glance, but I can honestly say that this is one of the most consistently rewarding and challenging games I've ever played. And that's not even to mention the sheer complexity of the game -- at surface level it may seem that each run will turn out similarly, but that is just not the case. Rough spots in levels will kill even the most veteran players with ease, and learning how to deal with increasingly complex death traps is a key point in the game that will take a lifetime to master given the inherent randomness of each new map.
It's an incredible game you can sink some time into. You have to be mentally present to play it and cannot just half♥♥♥♥♥your way to a victory. Buy it.

There are a few parts of this game, such as the sound effects which take some getting used to when compared to original spelunky. There is some more story, better menus, and a journal which gives a little information about each item, enemy, and other things that you find. As for spelunky itself, it is a really addicting game, and when one dies they have the urge to quickly play again. It is very unforgiving, and letting up for a moment could kill you. It changes the way you play the game a lot, and I like it. However it can be very frustrating to have your run cut abruptly short by a little snake or spike, and this can become annoying. The game is randomly generated, so the replay value is over the roof in combination with the difficulty that forces you to get better and get farther and farther in the game.
