I started my Defiance experience on the Xbox 360. After putting a considerable amount of time into it, my character had vanished. I contacted Trion support and there was nothing they could do to help me. They insisted that they do not save characters on their servers. rather they are stored locally. Upon further investigation this seems to be half true. A method that is completely unusual for an MMO, but I will talk about that in a later segment of this review.
Regardless, I stopped playing and I moved on. I migrated to PC a few years later and one day decided to pick up defiance again. At the time of this review I have about 220 hours in the game.
On Xbox I paid $60 for the game on launch day. On steam I paid $20 before it went free to play, and I bought the first $15 dollar expansion. So in total I spent over $100 to play the fairly mundane and extremely repetetive game that is defiance. Only to be disappointed twice by the poor management of the game by the developer.
Just today, the day of this review, I received a notice that I was banned from Defiance. No notice as to why, just a notice telling me I've been banned. So I emailed the support team, asking why I've been banned. They replied with an automated copy and paste statement telling me I've been banned for breaking the terms of service agreement, no information on what I've allegedly done wrong.
After looking around on the defince forums, I found many other people who have had a similar experience and recommended contacting an email specifically for appealing a ban. An email address that the launcher and the support team failed to mention. I emailed this appeal address and the only reply I got seemed to be yet another copy and paste automated message as follows,
"After reviewing pertinent logs, we have determined that the action taken against your account was correct. We will not be reversing relevant suspensions and/or notes applied to your account."
What exactly are these pertinent logs? Chat? Trades? Event Score? What was done on my account to cause this ban? This is still a question I have not received an actual substantial answer for. They refuse to tell me what went wrong and keep replying with the most broad, and most likely cut and paste answer, which leads me to beleive they have no solid evidence to ban me. If they have a real reason and have a real support team, there is no excuse to not be straight forward.
This is a small part of a big problem with Defiance and other games published and/or developed by Trion. They don't care as much about the community as they care about the money they make. In Defiance and other games by Trion, there is a steady issue with server stability. Whether it's peak hours or not, their games have frequent lag and some awful desync at times. Defiance is no exception. At times during raids, other players will completely disappear from your screen. If you need to be picked up, your fellow player wont be able to see you and vice versa. In a game with only a few hundred concurrent players, this is inexcusable. This is not a connection issue, it is how the game is actually intended to work. In an MMO, this is pathetic, inexcusable, and the lowest level of care from the developers
As a quick side note, in learning that the character data is stored locally AND on their servers it raises a hude red flag. Why are characters for an MMO stored on the players machine whatsoever? This makes cheating extremely easy. Trion claims to have client side and server side anticheat measures, but this is still counter intuitive for an MMO. Upon more investigation, this is still true at the time of making this review.
Trion's strategy as both a publisher and developer is to rush out a poorly made MMO on what seems like a yearly basis now, they've gone with the free-to-play model, but then add "starter packs" for $30 to $150 dollars, with items they claim to be exclusive to that starter pack, which are honestly no better than an equivalent item you can get in the game after playing for a few hours. Any experienced Defiance player can tell you the starter packs are an absolute ripoff.
Beyond this the game is riddled with microtransactions that purposely lead you to believe you're getting special in game items with promises of "at least one extremely rare item garunteed" while using a transitive currency in an attempt to make you spend more than you normally would, leaving you with excess currency that you can't use unless you pay more money and continue the cycle until you come full circle and end with no currency leftover.
For example: In Defiance there is a currency called "bits" which is obtained exclusively by paying real money. The lowest payment option is $5 for 400 bits. The lowest grade premium case costs 220 bits. If you buy the 220 Bit crate you're left with 180 Bits and can't buy another crate. Or if you want the next tier up which is 440 bits, $5 wont cut it. You'll have to pay $10 and still be stuck with excess bits that you cant fully utilize, which means you wasted money.
This trend continues across all of the games Trion has published on steam. Starter packs that cost upwards of $100, intentionally misleading microtransactions, and poor customer support.
For this reason I do not recommend Defiance or any Trion game for that matter. In fact I recommend staying away from them. This is a greedy company that doesn't belong in the gaming industry anymore.

Overall the general feel and type of game that Starpoint Gemini Warlords 'aspires' to be is what makes it a game which I keep coming back to play. It’s definitely worth getting if you KNOW you enjoy these types of games. However, it feels as though it's half cooked. It has bugs coming out of its ears and the developers clearly lack a project implementation review board because they haven't addressed basic issues. I'll not start on the various elements of the game that I could criticise because you'll be reading for hours but despite that, it’s still very enjoyable to play. The mashup of RPG elements like class skills and perks with fleet management from strategy games means there will be something that suits everyone. You also aren't limited to one style of play either. You can be an economic miner or an aggressive pirate swashbuckling marauder.
Another positive note is that it appears the developers are still making lots of changes rapidly to address the inadequacies of the game. With time most bugs at least will be systematically removed. Game GUI both in the menu and in game might take longer (if at all) for them to fix.
With substantial bug fixes combined with a complete overhaul of the information display system for EACH aspect of the game so people don't have to look into game files or forums for basic game mechanic info, this game would be amazing. Through in some more content and diversity as well then this game would be a solid nine out of ten. However it isn't. Currently it’s about a 6.5/10 if ten is perfection and everyone loves the game and one is just pure excrement.

Question: Does the idea of piloting your own ship around a HUGE galaxy making money from tasks like bounty hunting, convoy raiding, mining etc. sound like fun?
Second Question: Does the idea of building a galactic empire through the build up of a huge fleet to conquer space stations and eventually planets appeal to you?
If the answer to both questions is yes, then go ahead and buy this game.
What I like:
- Freedom to explore the Gemini galaxy at my own pace. Outside of the campaign there is no artificial time limit to finish a scenario so I can mine, scavenge, look for bounties etc. as and when I feel like it.
- Dynamic spaceship combat. Whether I'm alone or in command of a fleet, there's no such thing as simply sitting back and letting the game play itself out.
- The visuals are an improvement over the previous game in the franchise.
- The developers are active on the game forums and try to help players with technical or gameplay problems.
What I don't like:
- This is a game heavily dependent on scripts and the game has grown to the point where it's acquired a mind of its own. The developers seem to be one or two steps behind when it comes to keeping the game free of bugs, crashes and glitches.
- Some features from Starpoint Gemini 2 didn't make it into this game (dynamic trading system, faction side-quests with unique storylines)
- The game needs a game cache verification or 2-3 minutes to run and load up the first time I play it after switching on my PC. The former means having to reset my settings each and every time while the latter risks the game crashing halfway through the process. Once this "teething" problem on my PC is done, the game loads and runs very smoothly.

NOTE: This review is specifically for Train Simulator 2015 Summer Edition. I realized that, when the game updates, it keeps all of the older reviews. Hope this clears up any potential confusion.
This sounds like such a dull game. Simulate driving trains...pshhh. So this is what? The digital equivalent of model railways for people who are too lazy to actually build model railways?
It SOUNDS like such a dull game. That is, until you actually play with it. It took me watching some YouTube videos by Nerd^3 to decide to buy the game, and I don't regret it, because while it DOES sound dull, it's anything but. If you have even the least bit of a passing interest in rail transport of any kind, there's much to love with Train Simulator. I found myself starting out just by intentionally crashing the trains, seeing how fast I could push them before they derailed and such, and was quite tickled with that facet. Eventually, though, I began to take on a genuine interest in learning how the trains all functioned, what made them different, what all the different signs and lights meant... and what I discovered was that the world of the locomotive engineer is a complex and fascinating place that Train Simulator replicates in a very detailed fashion. In a word, it does one thing that other modern "simulators" rarely do in the past few years: successfully simulates what it claims to simulate. I feel that this program could actually be used as a training aid in learning how to drive locomotives.
Some general features of the game include the ability to drive the trains with an XBOX 360 controller (or, presumably, any other USB controller), a scenario editor that will allow you to create your own scenarios including any content you own (more on content later), extremely detailed control environments that allow you to interact with all important train controls, and many secondary ones, a pretty decent career mode that scores your performance, a quick drive mode where you just pick a loco and a route and drive on a clear line to wherever you like, futzing about with whatever you like as you go, and a rock-solid community that is extremely supportive when you inevitably have questions.
There is a pretty steep learning curve with some facets of the game, particularly when it comes to how signals work. However, the tutorials largely do a good job of covering it all, providing you take the time to do them. This is a bit of a task, as there are many, especially if you have the Academy add-on.
Full disclosure, I bought the Summer Edition, which includes quite a bit of DLC, and here-in lies my one serious critique of the game. Having spent the money for the highest-tier edition of the game, I still notice that I have only one Steam Loco to drive. There's also one for the academy, but it seems like you cannot use it outside of the academy. Even with the most expensive edition of the game, it feels like the game is kinda light on content. I can only imagine how sparse the base game is, as I don't believe it comes with the excellent Academy. Looking through the DLC store for TS15 shows a laundry list of content: Locomotives, Routes, Liveries, and Scenery packs. The most important content is obviously the Locos and Routes, as these are the things you actually play with in the game... and the cost A METRIC BUTTLOAD OF CASH. The average cost of a loco is $20, and the average route seems to be $40. To top this off, most Locos are designed to work with a specific route, and nearly all of them are DLC routes, while the Routes include scenarios that are mostly specific to one to three DLC locos. Meaning, if you want to buy 1 DLC, to get all of the content actually available to that DLC, you would really need to buy AT LEAST two, and up to FOUR DLCs, at an average of about $100 total. This is unacceptable, and really makes an excellent game look a lot like a shoddy cash grab. Why on EARTH are the Route DLCs more expensive than the base game?? Who thought this up??
My recommendation is this: IF you are interested in the game, buy it on sale, and ONLY buy the highest-tier version available. The Summer Edition was $57 when I bought it, which is actually an excellent value, considering it comes with about $300 worth of DLC (though sadly, seems to be missing the "Steam Edition Exclusive" locos). Then, figure out which DLC you want, do your homework on exactly what you need for bang-for-your-buck, and buy those when they are on deep discount as well. The game is definitely worth your time and money, but it's worth your time and money after doing a bit of homework to get the most content at the lowest price you can. I honestly wish they offered some kind of season pass for each iteration for about $100. You would ultimately save money, if you actually play with the content available. Lastly, I have to mention that the game doesn't work particularly well with laptops. I've got a 2.8GHz Core 2 Duo with 4GB RAM and a nVidia card, and I have to play at the lowest resolution with all the gfx settings turned to minimum, and even then, there are times when it hangs loading a scenario. On my Asus G53SW laptop, it runs great at full resolution and full detail, but don't expect much on any laptop that isn't designed specifically for gaming.

many people like this game. It has reviews around 90. I dont understand why.
I love Rogue-Likes and I love difficult games, so what could go wrong with a 90 rated game? A lot. Here is what my problems with Spelunky are (sorry if my english is not the best):
1. People say its a Rogue-Like, but I dont agree at all, at least its a really bad one. First of all in a Rogue-Like I want a lot of items, and with a lot, I mean A LOT. Then those items should be combinenable in some way. In Isaac you get a lot of items, some synergize well, others dont. In FTL you must find a good combination of the weapons you can carry and find a good tactic. In Spelunky, well, you have one "active" item and then some very little passive items. The game doesnt change that much with the items, unless you get something like a shotgun, then you are OP.
Also what a Rogue-Like needs is not just randomized items, but randomized levels, the thing is, the levels in Spelunky feel waay to random. No level has anything special about it. There are just random blocks, one time you go this, next time you go that way. What I want though is random events (there are some, but very little and not really game changing), and I want extremes. What I mean by that is, that it should feel random, yet you should be able to remember some cool randomized levels you got. Or like in Isaac where you have A LOT of room/enemy combinations. Also the enemys in this game are very boring and per Stage there are only like 4 types.
2. Lets get to the Jump´n´Run part. It has classic controls, you cant jump of walls, but you can grab on cliffs. Also with ropes you can make "ladders" and whats really cool is, that the whole enviroment is destructible (which sometimes can lead to frustrating moments). You can jump on enemys to kill or hit them with your melee weapon. It feels good, and it controls precisely. The only thing is, sometimes you cant see what is down from you, and you just have to jump and risk death, that can be VERY frustrating if you were in the 4th level of a stage(after 4th level you always come to the tunnelman, where you can make checkpoints).
3. The music is okay, it has a lot of tracks. The music is not awesome or something, but also not bad.
4. Graphics-style is terrible in my opinion, why it looks so childish? Actually I have no problem with childish, Rayman Legends looks childish too, but Rayman Legends looks BEAUTIFUL. Spelunky just looks very cheap and ugly. This is actually my biggest problem with the game, I dont know why I bought it, I could see the graphics before of course.
5. Difficulty. Okay, I like challenging games. The thing is, Spelunky is at times unfair in my opinion, and also when you completed a level, you dont feel like you have achieved something at all. In other games, you have a big boss fight, fight very hard, and then he explodes, you finally beat him and get rewarded with something. In Spelunky there is NOTHING. There arent even much shops were you can spend your money.
About money: In my opinion you should be able to get overpowered in Rogue-Likes. Really. In Isaac with luck and skill, you can later have so awesome combinations of Items, those playthroughs are really unique and make hell of fun. The feeling in FTL when you one shot the final boss is just awesome. But that should happen really rare. The thing is, Spelunky doesnt want you to become strong, because it has a pretty big design issue. It is not designed like other Rogue Likes, where you can play through the whole game in 1-2h and then replay all the time. But here you have to play and play, and unlock new stages and continue until you finish (I didnt finished the game, became too boring). So if you would become overpowered, you could rush through all levels and you would beat the game in 1 hour and never play again.
An other way to do it is like Rogue Legacy, where you lvl your character and get stronger all the time until you are too overpowered for one area, and go to the next, where you have NEW and harder enemys. But lets not talk about Rogue Legacy, thats a really special way of doing a rogue-like.
Conclusion:
Now why you should buy this game? There is no reason in my opinion. If you are a fan of Rogue-Likes, buy "The Binding of Isaac", "FTL", "Rogue Legacy", hell even "Legend of Dungeon" is better. If you like plattformers, buy "Rayman Origins" or "Rayman Legends" or some other plattformers. Spelunky has no unique thing in any of its gameplay elements, its not special to me at all. It just feels like a random game (dont understand this wrong xD).
I payed 7€ for this game on a Sale and it was not worth it at all. Maybe for 2-3€ I would like it, but I dont recommend it TO ANYONE!
I think there is also an iOS version, not sure, maybe as a handheld game it is better.
Just buy it FFS.

-WAY TOO MANY BOMB ZOMBIES TOWARDS THE END, felt like I had to follow the speed limits not to hit them and lose the whole mission from doing the one thing the game is designed for...PLOWING DOWN ZOMBIES WITH MY MURDERCAR!
-Weapons only face forwards so bossfights mostly just involve standing there firing, then driving to the health pickup a thousand times.
-At the end of a mission, regardless of difficulty, distance, or health remaining you have to drive back to base which is pointless if you aren't rescuing anyone because the next mission just sends you out again immediately.
-MY BIGGEST PROBLEM: as long as zombies wander into the mission zones, they aren't complete, so you may have to spend minutes just waiting for zombies to stop wandering from the world into the mission area so you can continue, and there's always the chance you'll pull more if you drive out to kill them. I know the point of the game is to kill zombies, but if you play this for more than an hour straight it becomes more about the missions than the zombies, which feel like more of an inconvenience than a fun challenge.
Summary:
I had fun with the first 2 hours of my 7 hour playtime, but once you've done one of the two truck and two tank missions, you've seen everything the game has to offer minus a few hours of driving and cleaning zombie guts off the windshield...
P.S. Way to make a plot pun out of your game name, if it wasn't for the fact that it started at the middle of the game and every rescue mentioned it, it would almost be a funny surprise at the end.

What a surprisingly fun little faerie simulation!
In Glittermitten Grove, you control a group of faeries in order to build your neighborhood. There aren't any real goals to the game aside from collecting enough shine (basically harvested sunlight), gems, wood, and food to build out your village, while keeping your faeries happy. The main components you have to worry about include how to expand your neighborhood as your village continues to grow, since all buildings need to be placed on trees and the larger your trees get, the more sunlight they take up. This can create situations where you need to trim and distribute more weight on one part of a tree in order to give a smaller tree the room to grow, so you can harvest more resources down the line. The other main component involves shooting fireworks to dig deeper underground to find gems and treasure chests.
While it is a fairly simple game in terms of the number of systems you have to focus on, it is a pleasant sim game with enough tasks for you to focus on, but not too many where you start to stress out over too many responsibilities and objectives. If you are looking for a palate cleanser or a game that is more serene and calming, I would give Glittermitten Grove a shot.

Red Faction: Guerrilla is a game about blowing things up on Mars.  There's a plot involving ancient artifacts, "liberation", and a race of people taken straight out of Mad Max, but in general: you are a guy whose job it is to blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and there are a bunch of enemies armed with weapons and vehicles stationed there to stop you from doing so.  Each main mission does a decent job of giving you enough buildings to destroy or baddies to press mouse1 at, although they don't come without their problems.  First off, Guerrilla does not have the sheer map size or number of destructible objects seen in similar free-roam "blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up" games (read:  Just Cause 2), although it makes up for it in the physics engine.  In Just Cause 2, destructable objects in the environment basically had two modes:  "not yet blown up" and "blown up".  Guerrilla takes the more "realistic" and computationally intensive approach of having structures collapse into bits of wall and support beams as you deal residual damage until the entire building becomes too unstable to hold itself up--in theory.  In practice, the stability of a building does not seem to take into account the weight of the rest of the structure it's supporting, and as a result, the fastest way to destroy a building is usually to attack the walls and ceiling of the top floor rather than the support beams on the ground floor.  However, despite the flaws in the building destruction, it does a good enough job at what it needs to be for the game itself to remain fun, with one caveat:  remember how I called the building destruction "computationally intensive"?  By that, I mean that even with a GTX 1060 and an i5-6400, this game will happily drop from 120+ fps to below 30 until the dust settles, even if you're looking away.  I doubt this can be chalked down to a bad port (since the game runs perfectly fine for the most part), although there is still some evidence for that.  At one point, about halfway through the game, you are given control of a bipedal rocket-launching mech.  Sounds cool, until you realize that it has a limited turning speed and you're using a mouse to look around, so you'll constantly have to recenter your mouse in order to aim anywhere (not to mention it also has a huge view bob, but that's kind of expected.)  Oh, and there's also a lack of♥♥♥♥♥♥to blow up before the final mission of the game, although there's a chance that's just due to me blowing up whatever I saw on the map until I saw nothing left.  Whoops.
With that over and done, let me say that Red Faction: Guerrilla is a fun, albeit flawed, game that is worth your time.  Definitely the kind of game that deserves an even better sequel...  we'll see about that, though.

Train simulator 2016 has been released a few months ago and so it is time to give it a proper review
First things first, this review will not be about prices, I can't give a rats♥♥♥♥♥about the price of either the game or the DLC. This game is mainly sold on Steam as is the official DLC and Steam has enough sales each year that the price of a game or DLC means diddlysquat. You find the prices to high, wait a few weeks and chances are they drop 50 to 80% for a few days. You are never more than 3 months away from a good deal.
The good
The current incarnation of Train Simulator is Train Simulator 2016. Personally I think it is one of the best yearly updates I have seen for those that bought the new edition. It has some very nice content coming with it, the new menu look is great, the new search works finally like a search should work and the content I played so far is of the better quality. My personal favorite in this years edition is the Union Pacific Gas Turbine also known as the GTEL. The new DB BR155 is a nice German engine as well and the new Riviera in the fifties route with its 5 Steam engines is one of the better route add ons I have seen in a long time. Ok, Sherman Hill and Cologne to Koblenz are reruns but if you didn't already own them they are two good additions for your collection. the Steam edition also packs the Norfolk Southern Coal District and the SD60M. The last one was added a bit later to the pack but everyone that bought the game got the engine regardless.
Also good is the TS rewards that are new this year. If you updated/upgraded to TS2016 you got a pop in after first launch where you could sign up for a newsletter which also signed you up for these rewards. Officially the first rewards are for TS2016 related content but the first reward was given to everyone that signed up even if they had the free update and it was a rather nice yellow boxcar. as extra bonus they added a 20% off coupon for the game for those that had not bought the new addition. The boxcar looks nice and imo stands out from the normal rolling stock you see but I couldn't resist making a reskin for it (as well as for the GTEL) and making a bit of fun with the yellow theme it has. You can find the reskins at
The new support system. Not really a TS2016 addition as it is in place for a few months now but my recent dealings with this new system and the people have been... satisfactory. Ok it took you long enough to actually post the correct info on
and the Steam support topics but I think it is an improvement over the email system you had
The community:  Simply an amazing bunch of people. You will find them on Steam and on several "fan sites" like railworksamerica, UKTS, Railsim.de and many other country related sites. they are providing the players with first line support, reskins, fixes, mods etc. Do visit the sites, get involved, have fun
The bad
Yes, the bad. Let's start with the fact DTG managed to ruin the update once again especially for those that did the free update. First there was no loading screen which made many players think their game had frozen and/or just didn't work anymore and when a hotfix was released it resulted in people not even being able to start the game at all. This somehow affected the free update only so I think personally that it had something to do with the fact that the new menu is now a DLC pack just like the academy for example. Yes it is part of the game but at the same time it is not. I think it is a wrong move by DTG, you want a new menu look, fine (it looks great) but release it for everyone as part of the core and not as a paid feature. It is ridiculous and doesn't make sense at all
Bugs ... it wouldn't be a DTG release if it didn't have at least a few bugs. The new drivers assist function for Steam engines for example does not work like it should. I have tried it and the tips it gives do not make any sense. It resulted several times in me running out of water, it told me to give more on the reverser and followed that up (after you followed the advice)  with less reverser, and more, and less, and so on. It basically made me nuts and ditch the use as quick as I could while having the idea it was at least tried out properly by me to give an opinion on it. Mind you, the driver assist only works (for now) on the new Riviera in the fifties Steam engines. I consider this a work in progress for DTG and it should not have been added yet
Railfan mode....... really DTG? you dare to call that a "new feature" ? ok, I give you that you added an option in the editor to set points along the track for this railfanning but common, this is for the rest just a career scenario without a player train. It can be fun for a few times but a new feature?  maybe you guys should check the workshop and see how many of your talented players have created very nice railfan scenarios without the need of a "railfan" marker. Take with that, that the Sherman Hill, Sherman Hill  railfan scenario is broken, not bugged... broken and I rest my case, what a useless addition that is
The Ugly
You thought I was done? HAH no no my friends, there is "the ugly" as well and boy oh boy it is ugly
BigBoy: You decided in your "wisdom" to repack the bigboy (and the challenger) in the Ap file compression format. In itself not a bad idea, it makes for less 'clutter" on your system although reskinners and modders are less thrilled that they have again another ap to unpack thus adding to the size of their installs but.... YOU FORGOT TO PACK THE SOUNDS.... and... you completely miscoded a bin file that has the references to said sound files as well (a fix can be found at
, you are most welcome) Which numskull has been responsible for that? how on earth can you forget a part of the setup of an engine. Worst thing though is the fact that there is still NO OFFICIAL PATCH, excuse me? it took me half a night and I am not even a game developer to get it fixed (again, you are welcome, see the link I posted, grab it, pack it and make the people happy, you are even allowed to take credit if you wish)
BNSF: Do I have to go there? hell yes I have to go there. HOW has it been able to come to this, HOW could you not see this coming. You were ordered by BNSF about a year ago to remove all BNSF content and what do you do? you remove all content that have BNSF in the name, leave the rest in place, don't inform your players of what is happening and think you are done. Then suddenly BNSF comes telling you they ordered you to remove BNSF content all together, you remove WITHOUT AGAIN INFORMING YOUR PLAYERS this content which by the way contains two very important routes. Refuse to replace those routes, refuse to replace the engines that are NOT BNSF in the other removed packs, basically flip the finger to your non US player base and when I take action and rally the community you play the innocent and one of your devs even sends me an angry mail on how I dare to talk about DTG, a certain site and "question his integrity"? Brothers is a game in the recent tradition of (mainly indie) games that seeks to move games into the realm of artistic expression through  a particular type of minimalism. These games e.g. Limbo, Flow, Journey, Don't Look Back, and innumerable flash games in the same vein diespense with mechanics to try to convey a sense of presence instead of a prescriptive story. Each of these succeeds to differing degrees depending on the temperment of the person playing them.
Unlike some of these other games, Brothers has a variety of atmospheres and shows us a variety of scenes where characters communicate and relate to each other. This probably takes a certain boldness. Nevertheless, being so up front and literal with your story- filling it with characters who undertake a literal journey- is a lot like turning all the lights on in the Pirates of the Carribean. You can see how fake the anamatronics look.
The biggest problem isn't just how literally the story is framed and the characters interact with eachother. It is how transparent the game is on a mechanical level. That is, it has virtually no mechanics or mechanical difficulty. When your characters are being chased, you know that you cannot be caught because there isn't any way to avoid being caught. Every "puzzle" has an obvious solution. This was so bad that I felt annoyed at how slowly the characters implimented the solution in comparison to how long it took to solve it.
Of course, that is framing Brothers as a puzzle game which it isn't. It is hardly a game at all, just a transparent framing device to show us some slightly imaginitive environments.
Framed as a game, it was far too simple-minded and easy. Framed as a story, it was too literal, too taken with caricature.
Perhaps this is a game that could be introduced to younger kids as a stepping stone to games more rich in mechanical depth and story-telling. For anyone else, I would play the games I listed earlier (or even better: Portal (1/2), Fez, or Braid).

First thing: I got this for .99 cents so the bar for "good bargain" is very low...
That said, Zombie Driver HD is a pretty nice game: I am not even halfway through the main campaing, but between slaughters and tournaments I can't say I didn't had quite some fun, let's say 3-4E tier fun ;-)
The basics are quite simple: you drive a car with weapon mounts, and go around wrecking havoc on all zombies with the misfortune of crossing your path.
There is a campaign, where the developer feels obliged to give us a justification for shooting and running over things until they are turned into a red pulp, there is a number of tournaments with multiple disciplines, like:
* Race, where you should theoretically drive fast, but instead you end up doing everything but that, otherwise the adversaries cheat and win all the time
* Endurance, a race where you drive a car rigged to a bomb and where for balancing reasons killing zombies is more important than driving fast
* Eliminator, where you actually have to kill your adversaries to win, so at least for once you get to do what you are supposed to
and then there is the "slaughter mode", where you just run over zombies for as long as you can, for those who find the campaing and tournaments too sophisticated.
The game is not perfect: as I said, the competitors cheat all the time for balancing reasons (as in the plain races, where otherwise it would be too easy to win) or to make the game more fun (e.g. in eliminator they defy all laws of time and space, appearing first in front of you, then behind, ecc... just to offer you more targets) and the campaing is kind of meh, but it's a total win for 99c and a nice game for less than 4E, so if you get it on sale, it definitely is worth a shot.

Now as you probably have figured from other reviews posted Take Two has just basically killed and buried the GTA V modding scene, by sending a cease-and-desist letter to the (former) popular modding tool OpenIV.  The creators of OpenIV were basically forced to take down to download.
Yes, they could have taken it to court, and probably would have won the case, but to do that to restore a status quo would be a waste of their time.
So, you're probably asking what does this mean to me? If you had no intentions of modding the single-player content probably nothing, since online "mods" (aka hacks) did not have anything to do with OpenIV and OpenIV was specifically designed to only work in offline and to automatically disable online functionalities, if you had mods.
On the other hand, if you had hoped that you could do basically anything extra in offline, say bye to that, with OpenIV taken from us there will be a large migration time to another modding tool and (I think) many modders won't or can't put the time and effort to basically rebuild their mods. So at least for the time being you can't be a part of LSPD or participate in ANY other wonderful things that the modding community had made.
Lastly, I would like to thank all previous/current/future (If there will be any) modders for their wonderful efforts to make this game a better and a longer experience. The time you spent on your mods is invaluable, but rest knowing that me and many other individuals in community have enjoyed your creations.

Let me get this out of the way first:   TS2015 is the best train simulator I've ever played, and for train sim fans, it's a must-have.
I started my interest in train software fairly recently, with Trainz 2012, which is a very good sim.  But TS2015 is better in almost every way.  It's smoother, faster, more rich in detail.  The sounds and movements of the trains are very realistic, giving you a high level of immersion.
Best of all is TS's ability to make the complex world of trains accessible.  The same details are often present in Trainz but I just couldn't figure out what was going on there.  TS's presentation and organization of the material manages to clarify but not oversimplify things.  Quite the achievement.  Oh, and TS2015's tutorials are VERY CLEAR and HELPFUL.  Among the best I've ever seen.
Finally, TS2015's user forum/website appears to be quite good.  They really know what they're doing.
If you're not yet convinced... I will admit I was put off by the many negative reviews for this game.  But reading through several of them, I saw a pattern of two types of review:
1.  Some complained it was boring, consisting of hours of carefully managing the speed of heavy equipment up and down hills in the countryside.  Yes: that's the point, this is a realistic simulator after all.  So please, don't buy this if it's not the kind of thing you usually go for.
2.  Others complained at the high cost of the DLC add-on trains and routes (scenery and rail routes based on real world places).  Yes, that may be so.  But you get what you pay for:  The content is VERY HIGH QUALITY and unique.  For instance, in the Stevens Pass DLC, which I purchased because that is near where I live, I was very happy to see regionally correct scenery, houses, billboards, murals, train types, even the mix of cars--Subarus and pickup trucks--was correct.  I see the German add-ons have German-looking buildings, plants, road signs, cars, etc.  It's definitely not "one size fits all."   You can't get this much detail and depth without spending a long time creating it, and for a relatively small audience to boot.
I managed to purchase the base game and my first DLC for about 33% off during a Steam sale.  It was not that expensive.

Brothers is an adventure puzzle game played thru the actions and interactions of two young brothers as they go on a quest to save their ailing father.  A gamepad is a must for this game, each thumb stick controls one of the brothers, while the corresponding trigger causes each brother to take action.  In order to progress thru an environment you will have to traverse and interact with it, using each brother to manipulate different parts of the environment to move on.  The scheme works much better than I thought it would, rarely did controlling each brother at the same time feel cumbersome and after some practice it felt natural.
Visually the game is very pretty, you will explore different scenery like mountains and ice, and come face to face with a vast array of NPC’s in the form of animals, giants, ferries and a host of others.  The sound is appropriate to the fantasy setting, the characters speak in a made up language, so most of the story is told thru gestures and the visuals along with the musical score, it all works together to give the gaming world a unique feeling of life.  It’s a short game, clocking in at 4 hours or so, but its just long enough to feel like you went on an adventure without getting repetitive.  Brothers is imaginative, not very violent & will challenge your brain just enough to feel like you accomplished something without frustrating you, very balanced and enjoyable experience.

I have about six hours of playtime so far, haven't finished the game, but due to almost every review being about the controls, I've decided to give my honest opinion.
Honestly, this isn't a rage game where you climb a mountain. Its a pretentious narrator game with a fun, if a bit unintuitive, physics engine.
Actually trying to climb is about as fun as launching yourself around at random so falling is LITERALLY not a nuisance, unless you're a speedrunner or something. The narrator doesn't seem to get this, though, and rather smugly tries to provoke and irritate you while occasionally quoting famous peoples' words on patience. He is the ever-persistent voice telling you that this game must be completed through struggle, not played with and enjoyed.
There is no difficulty curve, really - I've only had two parts that took me more than a few minutes to figure out, one I'm still on and one I had to look up a guide and then practice an hour for. As others have said, it doesn't lend itself to a feeling of satisfaction, and I really don't think thats due to the inpermanence of your progress. I think its because the game has controls designed to be difficult to figure out that then become your plaything after a few hours combined with the fact that every challenge is either a fun little swing in the park or the kind of challenge that requires such precision and gives you infinite tries that its just not fun when you finally get through it and back to the other 99% of the gameplay.
Overall, I'd reccomend it, with the voice over turned off, but keep in mind you will hit complete roadblocks and they won't be the controls.

Sure, RFG has been rightly criticised for its boring characters and non-existent storyline, but I feel that people who over-emphasise those shortcomings are rather missing the point.
Mechanically, I believe this is one of the greatest games of all time, not just for its destruction engine, which was far ahead of its time, and remains unmatched by anything made since, but also for the way it blends seamlessly into its brilliant combat, and the quality of that combat itself. I've spent hundreds of hours raiding bases in RFG's massive and colourful sandbox world, getting into raging firefights against waves upon waves of troops, tanks and airships, with buildings crashing down as they're hammered by cannon shells and explosive charges, and plowed into by out of control vehicles.
The shooting alone is excellent. They've nailed the sense of feedback you get from firing your weapons so that every kill feels inordinately satisfying, more so than in anything else I've ever played. The high quality sound effects and music only complement the effect. You can complain about the story, but I've been playing this for years and never even bothered finishing the main missions. The moment to moment sandbox gameplay is just that good.

With "My Pet Hotel", players of all generations recieve just what they paid for: Over 300+ hours of animal-filled thrills!
With every second I sat in front of my screen monitoring the behaviour of each of my individual furry companions, I could sense a greater bond forming between myself and the creatures of the game. Over the course of many hours, and even days of gameplay, each virtual animal became more than just that. They became my true friends. My family. I return home from work at the soup kitchen every evening, perspiring with the anticipation of greeting my fictional buddies on my Personalised Computer.
What initially struck me as interesting was the strength in dialogue throughout many levels of this elaborate masterpiece. Taking into account the story lacking a proper introduction and furthermore a real tutorial to aid the transition into the role of the "Pet Hotel Manager", the script the key characters followed in most cutscenes was by far the most creative and innovative i have witnessed in the past few years. Normally I enter willingly into a virtual world such as this to be met with an immersive and heart-stopping environment, but this was something else. The next-generation game engine which "My Pet Hotel" is run on exceeds that of any engine I have ever seen before in my many decades of pet-managing.
The unique flare within each detail and development I have encountered in my 7 playthroughs has led me to understand that each twist and turn in the plot leads to even greater story development, and when you thought that the story material had exceeded its limitations then something extraordinary emerges from the depths of "My Pet Hotel" to stun the player. Delivering an emotional punch to each player in their initial journey through the mystical world, this chilling and delicious rendition of its original 1986 work of art does not fail to deliver on the reminiscent euphoria I felt myself victim to as a young lad.
With all things considered, my encounter with "My Pet Hotel" has left me personally with a greater longing for a sequel than I have felt for many releases in the past. Who knows what this untapped vein of virtual gold holds for the future of all video gaming, nay, for all mankind.

I'm gonna be really frank about this game. I did not enjoy it much at all.
TLDR: This game has potential and a good concept, just really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and annoying execution and makes you rage not because you can't figure out the puzzle, but because of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanical issues.
Even though I did not enjoy this game, there are still good parts of the game. First of all, the concept is actually really cool and refreshing. I actually enjoyed that aspect of the game being a puzzle and turned based as well as luring enemies into traps/rivers. Also the soundtrack is pretty nice, even if there really is only two.
Now time to criticize this game. Let's start with the controls. The movement keys are 12346789 and 5 is wait. I understand that you need to mvoe diagonally in this game, but holy ♥♥♥♥ing hell those are honestly the most annoying♥♥♥♥♥keys, especially for laptop players without a numpad. I was fortunate enough to have a laptop with a numpad, but those keys still♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off so much. What is worse is that I could not find for my life a "customize" your keys option.
Aside from the keys, which I actually did somewhat start to get used to but still found awkward, the game is really punishing. Messing up at the end of the level brings you all the way back to the beginning of the level and some levels you need to do a lot of movement and thinking along the way. Furthermore, if you mess up one part of the level earlier on, you may actually not be able to complete a future one. If I hadn't saved up one of my attacks, I would have not been able to pass the next level. This punishment combined with awkward keys ♥♥♥♥ed me over so many times. I'd accidently hit 4 instead of 7 or 1 instead of 4 and fall into a river at the end of the level and have to restart. I can understand the game being difficult and I appreciate myself some difficult puzzles that took me a while to figure out, but this kind of difficulty due the user playability being ♥♥♥♥♥♥ is just not good.
Another really annoying part is that sometimes the movement of the enemies seems rather WTF. So the roach couldn't move diagonally at first, then all of a sudden half the times it can move diagonally and half the times it doesn't. How is the player supposed to kite the roach correctly without knowing when it will move diagonally. I'm sure there is some formula for its movement that I just didn't figure out, but devs please, at least give us a defined movement forumla that is more easily tangible. I was able to figure out your hard puzzles but never figured out the movement formula.
Lastly, the game does not have a great save feature. There is only one save and load, else you start a new game. So if you ♥♥♥♥ed up your levels for good halfway through... well lets just say that you gotta start over. Also when you go to the menu, the game lags for a good 5 seconds and you can't do anything. Speaking about not doing anything, the achievements are crazy hard to get as well. I was not even able to get a single achievement in all the time I put in and when I looked at the global stats, only like 3% of people were able to get one fo the achievements and that was the most that people have achieved.
With all the negatives put together, this game really is lacking in refinement. Should the devs refine the user experience, then this game could be really really fun. But as of right now, I really cannot recommend this game since it is just too lacking in polishing.
Rating: 6.2/10
Recommend: Don't buy this until it is more refined OR for under $0.50 since there are trading cards

So this is a surprisingly good TBS RPG that does have a couple of issues.  Overall I enjoyed my experience.
First off, I did play the original game by this company, which was a very different style of game but set in the same world.  The store says that it continues the story of the first game but there was really almost no story in the first game.
So the game is split into two broad sections.  First there are tactical combat missions.  These are pretty fun and well done, as you move ships across the map to explore, pick up resources and blow up the bad guys.  The controls are intuitive, and the initiative system has the combat feeling very fast paced for a turn based game and there is a nice difficulty curve as you make it deeper into the game.  Like most turn based games the missions can get a little long, especially in the later game.  Still overall they are well done.  The camera can be a little janky, but the ships look good when you zoom in and there is a good variety of backgrounds through a campaign.
The second part of the game is where the real challenge seems to lie, in managing your fleet and resources.  You have to manage three different resources... one to buy ships, one to deploy ships, and one to research upgrades for ships.  You always want more of all three, which is well done, and so you are constantly making choices about what resources to collect and what to do.  In addition you can buy and equip items, more ships, and research.  The one problem in the early game is the  tech tree sort of forces you to play with just one or two ship types, although by the end of the game you have enough research to have a lot of different ships.
The missions also follow a story that is fully voice acted.  I thought the story started out very weak, but by about 10 missions in it had improved considerably, and the emotional hits late in the campaign really had some punch to them.  On balance I think the story is well done, but you should be warned that it starts off weak and ends strong.
However this is not all roses.  First off, the beginning story is weak.  This is especially true in the tutorial which is overly long.  The tutorial is really more like a manual that describes every little mechanic of the game.  I think it is better used as a reference.  I quit halfway through the tutorial and just played, and the game is intuitive enough I had no problem just jumping in and playing.
Second, the game is long, much longer than you would think.  There are two campaigns included, and each campaign plays differently, with different units, different plot and different strategy.  This really should have been split into two games.  It is impressive that a small indie game would try and put out a game with so much content, but it is really too much unless you want to spend several weeks with the game.  Just know this is not a game that you sit down and play for 10 hours.
Third, the late game can really start to bog down as you have hundreds of units going against each other.  I'm not sure the system really scales as well as they think it did.
The base game is fun but overly long.  I started off skipping the story, and then when it started to get good I was left hoping I hadn't skipped something important early.  I would have rated the game 7/10.  However, the developers have been great about listening to the community and providing patch support for bugs and balance improvements.  Due to the strong developer interaction with the community I am adding one point to the overall rating.
8/10

Often, and this in both war battles and staged battles, your game will start with 5vs6 players only (maximum is 32, which is not enough to start with!), on huge maps where therefore nothing much is happening. Regarding their development, they only make what they think is good, usually making it worse, instead of listening to their players base. 7/10 experience. The way I'd describe my experience is that I've played more than it actually deserved. As a single player game it's an alright experience. It is fun but the real gem with this game is the madness of co-op. I've never had more fun playing a randomly generated local coop platformer... but there are design decisions that always leave me upset about my experience. As a single player game, I would have no issues with the design whatsoever but the moment it turns local co-op, things get silly.
The turn-on for me with this game was the couch-party multiplayer experience that it promised and it almost came through on my expectations. But as anyone will know that has tried to play with someone else, you know that it's almost better to play without anyone to get in your way. I suppose that that was how they made it "fair" to play with co-op is that it was the same experience but the difficulty increased BECAUSE there were more people that could throw arrows into your face at any moment. That's fine if it was designed that way to keep it equal to the single-player experience except for one blaring fact: you can't progress in multi-player. You can't unlock anything unless you're by yourself. WHY!? The designers went out of their way to make the co-op and non-co-op experience feel like the same difficulty and then decided not to allow both experiences the same priveleges. The result: I will probably never unlock everything in spelunky because I just don't have much desire to play the game by myself. It's just not as much fun! I want to play this game with my friends or not really at all. So I guess I'll never really experience everything this game has to offer because it's simply not available in the format that I prefer to play.
Last thing that robs this game of full points is the fact that I have to look up what everything does in wikipedia. A game that doesn't intuitively explain how to play itself is a poorly designed. "This has to stop!" -TotalBiscuit in his WTF of Risk of Rain video when commenting on the same vagueness of what everything is or does. I agree wholeheartedly.
I still fully recommend this game despite the silly design choices. You'll have an absolute blast for the amount you pay and I have yet to play a game that has made me laugh til I cry by the stupid deaths I go through. Buy it, play it, love it. The end.

I'm having a ton of fun with Spelunky; it's definitely one of the most addictive games I've ever played. I really can't say enough good things about it! I love the art style: colorful levels, varied enemies, excellent animation, and quite possibly the cutest "damsel" to ever appear in any form of media at any point in history. The controls are really fluid and precise, although they do seem a bit touchy when you first get started. But once you get used to the ins and outs of jumping, running, etc., it all becomes second nature.
I also love the "daily challenge." It's super fun to get a unique world every day that you truly only get one shot at and where that one shot really matters. It adds a whole new level of pressure to the already intense roguelike genre.
This is sounding like 10 out of 10 material, right? Definitely! But there's one problem: I think Spelunky is just a bit too hard. Not much, mind you. It's just a hair on the side of unfair. I know that's partially the point, and it certainly is possible to practice and get better. But, unlike the Binding of Isaac, I'm finding that there really are very few character setups that "work." Isaac allows for tens if not hundreds of item combinations that can lead to victory. In Spelunky, you're basically required to have a jetpack and a shotgun if you want to have a chance at a high score. This limitation can be somewhat frustrating: no matter my skill level, the first 6 or so levels end up being a repetitious struggle to get the right (randomly-spawned) gear, and that's not always fun.
Anyway, in my estimation Spelunky is on the cusp of perfection. If only it was just a tiny bit more balanced. Maybe a difficultly select option would be the best solution: new players could go with "normal" and get an extra life or more health. Then there'd be "hardcore" mode: "The true Spelunky starts here."

I enjoyed this more than any other Red Faction game in the series. The developer is also responsible for the Saints Row series, so they know how to make a fun open world game.
The character control is very fluid and sensible, and menus are all very solid. Since they integrated it with Steam there isn't any GFWL nonsense, which is excellent.  As with the other games in the series, this one makes a point of having very destructable environments and that is a large part of what makes this game fun. Just about anything in the game can be blasted apart in the most spectacular way.
Despite the excellent controls, Mason finds it difficult to climb anything more than a moderate slope, and can sometimes get trapped in the copious amounts of debris that regularly surround him. This is really only a small frustration though.
Generally the characters are likeable and well voiced, albeit a little forgettable. The generic characters are mirrored by the generally unchanging environments, but then it is Mars after all, so what else should it look like? In fact, the designers have given different areas a slightly different look, by way of atomsphere and terrain, which is welcome.
While the single player campaign is enjoyable, it's quite linear without any real decisions to make, and side missions exist in the way of 'guerrilla actions' of which there are 5 or 6 different types. Overall it's a fun story, but once it's over there is little incentive to keep exploring.
Multiplayer is really a shame in this game. I would have loved to see the campaign playable co-op but it unfortunately isn't. There are several multiplayer modes but they are all variations of deathmatch and similar traditional game modes.
Still, it does what it does very well, and the fun to be had with destroying vast amounts of buildings overshadows most of the problems.

Influenced by the TBS of the likes of Xcom, which I have always enjoyed immensely, their isn't quite the same enamor for your ships that you develop with our Xcom team. Still, that style of turn based play is easy to engage. You start out with decent enough ships to progress but getting the big boys later on make a huge difference. The AI is a pretty good opponent though at times, they seem to have the advantage of making shots you can't make and most certainly seem have better weapons in both range and punch. However, good probing strategies with ambushing withdrawl tactics works well in this game.
It pays well to level your ships with the side missions to either level up at no damage cost regardless of what happens in game which is a nice feature. Gearing up your ships is limited to 2 slots of add ons and so far that never changes, what does change amongst the classes is the weapons that the are base outfitted with. There's some customization, but with two slots you quickly find only one or two groups of two items that fits your playing style and stick with it, so the rest is just stuff you won't use.
The mines on the playing field are challening and offer a great defensive concern and an offensive one since torpedoes in the game can be launched to clear them and anything dumb enough to get close to them. There's not much different in each of the missions that you play, the game play can get pretty boring if you are not a tactical TBS  nut. It's a small studio game and it really shows. No fancy graphics, good modeling of the ships and animations of battle, but the rest is pretty slim.
I have a love hate relationship with the hard written storyline - I don't like the character we are playing in the game and you get no personal data control - except to rename your ships. That's it. The supposed love interest between officers that "chat" with you much like an adventure story is a bit too contrived and overtly smug. Sadly though, that's the only thing that adds change to the game once you can build the big ships.  The depth of the game is about ankle deep.
It's a fun little turn based strategy and true, there is a real void in the space game genre for a game like this - I just wish that deeper pocket big company would have taken on something like this though these two guys did okay for what is a very limited budget.  I bought it, I played it, I might mess with it if they upgrade depth or dcs it. If you can afford to toss the coin it's worth a gander if your like me and have 100+ titles in your libraries. If you have to be picky about laying down coin, you might might not want to jump in just yet - unless like these authors, you really want any kind of entry into this turn on space play.

I am enjoying this game a lot!  It's a turn-based strategy game in space.  Each unit has differing amounts of moves and actions depending on the ship.  Also you can decide the order actions you take.  For example, a unit with 2 moves and 2 actions remaining, could move away from cover, fire a torpedo at an enemy ship, move back to cover and then charge shields.  There are different factions to choose from which have different ships and abilities.  As play missions, your ships level up as well.  You can purchase different ships as you go, but it looks like you can acquire ships and other personnel, for that matter, through different means.  I like the customization in the game.  You can choose which ships to deploy for the various missions, and you can choose how to upgrade different classes of ships through tech trees.  The graphics are really well done and I enjoy the music too.  Randomly, the camera does zoom in for an action shot, to give it some cinematic effect.  There are different difficulty levels, so I would reccomend this to veterans and beginners alike to this genre.

This turned out to be a nice surprise. The voice acting is not great so at first you'll think it's a cheesy game. But once you get going its a very solid, hexy, turn based space strategy game with two long campaigns.
The combat engine is gorgeous and although the rules are streamlined (no weapons arcs or ship facing) it's very satifying and allows for interesting tactics. Your forces are persistent (you keep and grow your army mission to mission) and there's a bit of a meta game with the resources. The research tree isn't deep but it's very broad with trees for each ship type.
The game is not necessarily hard in individual missions but the challenge comes from shepherding your forces throughout the full campaign (Panzer General kept popping into my head).
On the bad side the writing and acting range from bad to ok. It's not a fast game, missions can take a little while and there's a leisurly vibe to most as you clear out a small section at a time (xcom style so as not to wake other groups of enemies).
If you like traditional turn based combat on hexes you will enjoy this.

I'm having a ton of fun with Spelunky; it's definitely one of the most addictive games I've ever played. I really can't say enough good things about it! I love the art style: colorful levels, varied enemies, excellent animation, and quite possibly the cutest "damsel" to ever appear in any form of media at any point in history. The controls are really fluid and precise, although they do seem a bit touchy when you first get started. But once you get used to the ins and outs of jumping, running, etc., it all becomes second nature.
I also love the "daily challenge." It's super fun to get a unique world every day that you truly only get one shot at and where that one shot really matters. It adds a whole new level of pressure to the already intense roguelike genre.
This is sounding like 10 out of 10 material, right? Definitely! But there's one problem: I think Spelunky is just a bit too hard. Not much, mind you. It's just a hair on the side of unfair. I know that's partially the point, and it certainly is possible to practice and get better. But, unlike the Binding of Isaac, I'm finding that there really are very few character setups that "work." Isaac allows for tens if not hundreds of item combinations that can lead to victory. In Spelunky, you're basically required to have a jetpack and a shotgun if you want to have a chance at a high score. This limitation can be somewhat frustrating: no matter my skill level, the first 6 or so levels end up being a repetitious struggle to get the right (randomly-spawned) gear, and that's not always fun.
Anyway, in my estimation Spelunky is on the cusp of perfection. If only it was just a tiny bit more balanced. Maybe a difficultly select option would be the best solution: new players could go with "normal" and get an extra life or more health. Then there'd be "hardcore" mode: "The true Spelunky starts here."

Wow, this was quite the disappointing and frustrating experience.  I don't ever post reviews, but I felt compelled to with Starpoint Gemini Warlords.  It has all the makings of an excellent game, but seems to drop the ball in almost every area.
There's no real political system.  The alliances you make just don't matter.  The factions are all copies of each other essentially with a few different ship skins.  There is no economy.  You can hold every single region in the game except one enemy station, and they can still pump out an unlimited number of fleets far faster than you could.  There is no exciting conquest system.  Taking your first region is the exact same as taking your millionth region.  Once the novelty of fleet combat wears off after the first few battles, the fights are painfully tedious and long, and since the enemy has an unlimited number of fleets, the next tedious battle calls your attention by the time youre finished with the current battle.  THE ENTIRE GAME IS JUST TEDIOUS FLEET BATTLES.
I'm not exaggerating. That's it.. That's the only content they have in the game... fleet battles. The AI is so frustrating and painful.  Your own fleet is extremely incompetent.  They hardly do anything to help you, and end up just floating around, often far away from where you need them (you can't actually give orders to your fleet.. lol).  The enemy pretty much does the same thing, but seemes to be slightly more successful in staying together.  I'm having trouble coming up with an aspect of the game that was actually good.
I finally finished the campaign and started the Titans DLC, so I promised myself: if they make me do one more fleet battle in the place of actual content, I am putting down the game for good.  Lo and behold, the first two missions were just fleet battles.  I can't do it anymore.  This game is not fun for me
The takeaway here is to boycott early access games.  Even when not "abused" in the way many developers do, it still leads to a bad game.  It encourages developers to release the first version of their game that's remotely playable.  Starpoint Gemini Warlords will be an extremely forgettable game.
EDIT:  After 70 hours put into the game, I'd like to revise my review:  There are some parts of the game that I do enjoy.  Although there are only three, I really like the class system, as playing each class definitely feels different.  Your gameplay is very different between the Sharpshooter and the Marauder for example.  The huge fleet battles can be fun in small doses.  There are 100% some epic moments mechanically and visually.  However, everything else i said in my review still stands.  I can't recomment this game at its current price.

A masterpiece; that's what Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is.
It's emotionally gripping with the storytelling as you watch the two brothers bond while adventuring to find healing water for their ill father. Straight from the beginning, you can tell that this isn't exactly a game suited for kids, as you watch your mother drown to her death in flashback cutscene, when the younger son, Naiee tragically tried to save her, but isn't able to do so in time. I don't wanna spoil anything, but the game is an adventure game that is charming, creepy and lastly, heartwrenching.
The gameplay starts when Naiee and his elder brother Nyaa carry their father to a doctor, and from there the doctor has them embark on an epic quest to find the healing water. During the epic quest, you encounter folk in the village, farmers, sheep, rabbits, mountain goats; friendly trolls, evil trolls, whales, invisible monsters; giants that fought to their death, wolves, griffins, and much more.
While you don't fight any of these beings, and really, only some of them are evil, (the mean trolls, a giant spider, wolves, and some angry cultists), you avoid them by controlling the two brothers. The game plays like a twin stick fighter or shooter, but as a 3rd person, over head view, and puzzle solving, one stick for each brother, and a trigger to interact with objects.
The game really is epic with the interactions, as you climb, swim, swing, fly, use torches, use various gears and handles; there's a large number of puzzle/interacting; but it's pretty straightforward.
The graphic style is reminiscent of Fable and Ico, but in its own way, and it works well as the game is gorgeous. The audio is perfect, the music and atmosphere really add to the charm of the game, as well as to the creepiness of certain areas (like the guy who tries to hang himself and you have to choice of stopping him, or the bloody rivers where the giants fought to their death, or the children whose bodies are hanging in the forests).
I managed through the game pretty well, but I have to say that the ending is f*cking depressing. It leaves an emotional impact unlike any game I've ever played.
10/10

RFG is a very enjoyable departure for the Red Faction series. No longer a linear fps it is instead a third person open world game similar to Grand Theft Auto or the recent Far Cry games. Destruction is by far the stand out feature here as everything can be torn apart realisticly and with precision. The story is shallow and uncompelling without any specific antagonist,no central villian...you are simply combating the EDF that controls Mars,soldiers that all look the same, for the majority of the game. What will likely push you forward is the promise of new weapons and upgrades, tools to enhance your destructive prowess. The side missions range from very cool, destroying specific structures and timed demo trials, to more mundane tasks such as rescue missions or stealing specific vehicles. I enjoyed my time with RFG and am thankful it didn't outstay it's welcome. I spent 14 hours on completing the story and am nowhere near 100% complete.

This is one of the most underrated games I have ever played. The destruction mechanics shine, and the open world format is perfect for this kind of game. Destroying in-world creations using physics and geometry makes you feel like an actual demolitions expert. You're not some tanky Hyperdeath (tm) killing machine, except when you're in your exosuit. You're just an average, run of the mill engineer who happens to be thrust into the role of terrorist. The setting is great too. I've never been in a more realistic recreation of Mars. Gravity and weights are realistic. The vehicles have this 1980s sci fi futuristic look to them, and it's all really charming. I wish I could live in Red Faction's universe, and between missions, you'll wish you could too.
This game's difficulty ramps perfectly. The game keeps throwing tougher and tougher enemies and structures to dismantle. You never feel too powerful, and never feel like a weakling either. It's just right. The game's final challenge is one of the most difficult levels I have ever played in my 20+ years of video gaming, among games that are not designed to be total cockblocks.
The only downside is the storyline. It's kind of bad. It's not as bad as its sequel, but it's still really bad. I like the idea of being a freedom fighter trying to liberate Mars, but for some reason, the game doesn't write outside of its comfort zone. It prefers that the protagonist do ALL of the heavy lifting by himself. It never seems like you're part of an organization. And for some stupid reason, in Red Faction games, the women are only eye candy, not actual helpful people. It's sad. This could have had a wonderful story arc with complex characters and deep satisfying plot twists, turns, and reveals. Nope. Just a cheesy action movie.
The story doesn't destroy the game, though. It's damn good. Definitely the white sheep of the franchise, and you should pick this up anywhere below the 30 dollar price point. You won't regret it.

I've played it since initial release and it was and still is amazing.
Pros:
- vehicles (from ATVs to Trucks) with great navigation
- player customization (not only face/race but outfits/headgear too, with great variety)
- excellent weapons (from heavy machine guns to laser swords!) with visually improving mod attachments
- tv series crossover (it's really nice to meet TV heroes and fight side-by-side with them)
- great player voices and voice acting generally. Some great actors were cast in recurring roles.
I love the psycho male voice, he's like the Joker from Batman HAHAhehehihihihohohuehuehue!
- massive open world (one of the greatest parts about any videogames)
- creative enemy units (raiders, robots, insects, zombies and high-tech ninjas, they got'em all, of all sizes and shapes)
- great story/questline (and a lot of story-like maps in the lobby system)
- seamless co-op! (and great PvP for who likes this sort of thing)
- constant events and ballanced leveled up
- interesting, satisfying, colorful graphics with a solid post-apocalyptic vibe
Cons:
- can feel lonely if you don't play with a friend.
- can be difficult to get legendary item drops
- some random encounters can be overwhelming (dying a lot a lot) if you don't have enough participants to have your back.
- can be difficult to manage inventory space (I have about 4-5 legendaries I don't use but don't feel like I should drop or destroy either). but yeah, my inventory is always stacked.
- player-to-player trading can be difficult to do unless you join 3rd party sites and even then you may not have takers
- after about 300 hours or so can become repetitive, yet events can refresh the feel of it
- the new implants/perks things is a bit complicated, but after you get it, you get it.
- Story/new Content DLCs are still expensive. I'm hoping for a 7th Legion discount still :P
Bottom line: Get it! Play the hell out of it! Enjoy this awesome San Francisco Bay area and ride the wheels off of the vehicles! Also, get a sword and slam the ground! Also, get a sniper rifle :D Also, if you want legendaries, look me up!

Firstly, I definitely recomend this game.
Ok, now some back story, I used to play a game called Dust514 on the PS3 constantly and wanted to find a game that would be just as entertaining, and I found this one. I played it constantly and when I found out it was on steam, I promtly downloaded and started playing *I have a few hundred hours logged on my main account*
Pros:
Excelent graphics
Challenging PVP matches and arenas
Co-op arenas can get pretty intense
Wide diversity of weapons and makes use of the tier system
You can co-op on literally any mission and encounter in the game. It's as simple as being in the same place at the same time
Lots of in-game events to occupy one's time
Mic and full controller support
Has a very friendly user base, if you go down, 11 times out of 10 someone will help you (assuming they are around, that is)
full trading system between players (Including in-game currency and weapons)
Daily and weekly free rewards and weekly give aways
Every player sees their own weapon/item/money/ammo drops (kinda like on Diablo 3 and several other games)
New "special" weapons offered each hour and most in game venders so plenty of chances to get great weapons
con:
Can lag somtimes, especially in highly populated areas or areas with several events going on
upper tier weapon/item drops are more rare than they should be, so many players are less likely to trade or give them away.
There is no lock or restriction for lower laveled players in regards to travel so running accross higher leveled enemies is common, making co-ops a highly recomended strategy. At least three people is best.
Third person view only so FPS players may feel a little out of their element. (feels a lot like GTA in that regard)
There's basically no such thing as stealth as far as sound goes so one needs to move quickly if one needs to move close to an enemy without being attacked. If they can see you, they can attack you. Snipers fare better because they can reach enemies in a longer range than most are willing to move to attack.
Weapons are levelled, so it's pretty rare to get a dropped weapon or buy a weapon from a vendor that isn't your current level (also a pro)
Can be a bit rough with your hardware, but if you have a decent graphics card and a fair ammount of RAM you should be fine.
Ultimately though, I'm certainly in love with this game, and I recommend that people try it out and see if they like it.
