This game is a prime example of how NOT to make a free to play game.  Absolutely everything that you ever hated about every other cheap console title is present here. My list of complaints could go on for days on end, but lets try to narrow it down to what made me review it negatively shall we?
Pay To Win... Need I say more. Sure you can unlock things for free, but everything from (the few armors that look good) to weapons people obviously spent money maxing out the rarity is only going to be obtainable through your wallet book. The most despicable thing about that concept is that it effects PvE AND PvP heavily. People who cranked out the dough early on will have a significant edge over people who haven't spent a dime. You'll next to NEVER kill someone who's either spent money making their weapon gold or farming for like 90 days+   and 90 days by the way is for those who are extremely lucky with the lockboxes.
Next order of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery...  Certain enemy types.  See your armor will break the more that you take damage. Fine right?  WRONG!!! Every faction nearly has that ONE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t enemy that either has a really cheap homing attack like the bug archers who snipe your♥♥♥♥♥  The pink missile launching  Volge, or the weird robots that dig their hands into the ground and instantly hit you from wherever you stand.  Once you have a certain amount of damage done unto you, you'll be going down time and time and time and INFURIATING time again. I've never wanted to snap my controller in half more with any other game than this one right here.  There's a difference between challenging and flat out stupid.  Even MLG pro players who obviously cranked out mommy's tax returns still somehow manage to occasionally go down at the hands of end game leveled mobs.
While the game is a scifi free roam MMO shooter, (& that's a huge turn on.)  It utterly FAILS at such basic things. Collision detecting is a big thing. You could be driving along when all of a sudden the SMALLEST lips in the world completely cut off your momentum. Or your vehicle will explode having hit cover near an arkfall! Ever wanted to get COMPLETELY stopped dead in your tracks by running straight into a Stop Sign? Well this is the game for you then! Cause  of all things you would expect to be destructible (signs)  they're not, and if you hit them you come to a complete stop. The driving is just hideous and controls like a 500 lbs. bowling ball!
The voice acting and animations I've seen for this are so cheesy. At one point you'll meet a black man who's CLEARLY voiced by a white man, & its just sooo awkward! Awkward infact, is a very accurate word used to describe the campaign which fails to make you give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about. Even sad moments are just so cheesy you just end up laughing in disgust. These devs are so lazy that they actually take armor THAT YOU PAY FOR from the cash shop and re-color it and offer it to you again either for more money or the less attractive ones can be earned through some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t pursuits. And when I say pursuits I really mean like a LIST, a full blown LIST of things you have to do.  Kill 50,000 enemies? Yeah go ♥♥♥♥ yourself!  The laziness will begin to show even more so when you start side questing and you realize just how many times they re-use and recycle areas.  You'll go back and fourth from one place getting this, talking to this guy, pressing this switch and the combat isn't even enough to keep you interested for the first 10 quests let alone the HUNDREDS. I wouldn't mind fetch questing if there were simply more to do.
Arguably the only 2 things the devs did right here is these things called Incursions & Arkfalls. These things are big events you can see going on in your map. It attracts HUNDREDS of players to that area & the sheer chaos is what has kept me addicted. Nowhere ever before have I seen SO many players in one area fighting so many enemies. It's beautiful! It's some of the best war scenes you never seen in games OR movies! The epic scale warfare is so good in fact that the downfall of it all is the last thing about it that's actually positive.   Your guns are all customizable. You can put mods on, upgrade rarity, choose from a massive list of perks. The heavy detail you can go into your powers and how your gun operates is really well done. So well done that its going to show in PvP or PvE & that's the one thing I cannot stand about this game. Absolutely NOTHING amounts to skill.  It's all about your build. If you've gotta good build (which in most cases is paid for) you'll demolish. If not..... Have fun grinding away DAYS of your life trying to get good.
What upsets me the most about this game is that the focus is nowhere near where it needs to be. Why does the game have to follow or even be parallel to the events of the show? Why can't it just be a standalone game within the Defiance universe every so often showing a main character.  Instead of investing ANY time at all into a campaign they could have focused their WHOLE game around this awesome principle of uniting hundreds of players and expanded upon it. So fellow Defiance players if you're reading this... Imagine if they had included tanks, jets, or even HALF of the vehicles you SEE parked in the game.  At the very least they could've let your partner (who's riding passenger) lean our the passenger side window and shoot.  Car chases could've been a thing for fetch questing like freaking GTA!  They could've even taken it a step further and had squad leaders determine which contracts (aka quests) to complete and then raid fully detailed buildings instead of what we're left with. (Which is buildings you see.... but can never go into.)   I'm just so tired at the half♥♥♥♥♥attempt to be a free roam scifi roleplaying shooter.  I salute the devs to be one of the first games to do this next to Firefall & Borderlands, but some of the most basic things you would expect from ANY game are just absent here.  If you attempt to contact the devs stating your gripes, they'll be sure to ignore you and then nerf an exploit that you found to be helpful in your progression. Surely this is why you see ABSOLUTELY NO uploaders on YouTube still covering this game anymore.
My verdict is simple. I won't recommend it (so that explains the thumbs down) but I will say that if you're bored and have nothing else better to do with your life. This can provide you some cheap fun.  I have not a single clue why developers keep making us fight bugs (which is so dumb) but you'll encounter those, zombies, robots, raiders, aliens, religious bigots, and dozens of other poorly voiced characters and factions. It has a sure amount of diversity and the free roam with the inclusion of vehicles is very nice. Just note that this method of rinse and repeat WILL get old. And it will get old VERY quickly...   Good luck Ark Hunter.  You'll need it!

My first Sniper Elite game and the experience was pretty good.
Thanks to the bullet cam the sniping feels really satisfying, even if, looking at it from the outside, it's a pretty gruesome part of the game.
There are "only" 8 missions in the game but completing them all while looking for every War diary, Cards and secondary objectives took me 48 hours. Now, I did go a bit too far at times, reloading over and over when something didn't play out exactly like I wanted it to, like that time I wanted to kill 4 circling soldiers back to back with the silenced gun without getting found out or the corpses spotted, but I found that part of the game satisfying as well, since it helped teaching things about the enemies' behavior and the game's behavior.
I spent the whole game either sniping, or using the silenced gun/backstab kills so I don't really know how the gunblazing approach works, but I never felt the need to go in gun blazing as crouching down, sniping some and moving out to relocate somewhere else in case a corpse was found/my gunshot was heard was the most enjoyable part of the game.
Another nice aspect about Sniper Elite 3 is in the looks department. I found the game to look really well and perform just as well, even on my old 570 and on my 970 now it looks even better.
I played it with the Italian VA and I thought it was pretty good, both in the acting part as well as the sound of the voice.
All in all, a great sniping game that feels enjoyable where it counts and looks/performs well.

Another entry in the Sniper Elite franchise. And boy, it's a great one.
Story: The story might not feel very deep, but it works.
Graphics: The graphics are absolutely fantastic. Look at the beautiful enviroments of North Africa. Definatively Scenery Porn (look it up on Tv tropes). The character models also look very good. Even on low settings it's impressive.
Gameplay: The gameplay is in my opinion, improved a bit from V2. While regenerating health still exists, now it will only fill up to a certain point of your lifebar, anymore injuries than that will require bandages or medpacks to heal. The shooting still works very nice. One flaw though is that they removed the cover system from V2 (press Q), but so far it hasn't been affecting me that much. The A.I shows some improvement from V2, they will now react more to suspicious stuff, like gunfire and dead bodies. If you kill a soldier, they will start searching for you, and will find you eventually unless you relocate. You can also occasionally find weapon parts or upgrades for your weapons which can be used to modify your weapons.
Music: The music is, like V2, epic and well made. You can even occasionally hear songs from V2 on the radios in some missions.
Overall, Sniper Elite 3 is worth the money. If you liked V2, you will enjoy 3 as well.

Spelunky is probably as close to perfection as any game I've played in recent memory, a well-crafted rogue-lite platformer that offers a satisfying challenge, endless replayability, and blissful gameplay. The visual aesthetic is clean, colorful and charming, a nice contrast to the brutal and unforgiving nature of the game itself. The soundtrack is one of my favorites of the year and features some very catchy tunes. The controls are tight and completely responsive, a must for a game that relies on precise movement and actions.
Best of all, the gameplay is just superb: No fluff, no filler, just finely-tuned mechanics that require patience and force you to study patterns and learn from your mistakes in order to progress. It's a system that appears simple on the surface but features a surprising amount of depth. Even after 200+ hours I still find myself learning new things. The high degree of difficulty is sure to frustrate many, but it's a prime example of "Practice makes perfect". And while it could easily take hundreds of deaths to finally complete the game, each run is capable of offering a sense of accomplishment, no matter how small.
If I have any complaints at all it's the lack of online multi-player, although I can understand how difficult it would've been to institute in a game where any lag whatsoever creates a huge problem. A minor issue that doesn't detract from the overall package.
Overall, Spelunky is not only my sure GOTY, it's perhaps the best indie game I've ever played. A practically flawless experience that lends itself perfectly to either short 30-minute bursts or lengthy sessions into the night. If you have the patience to stick through some early growing pains, you'll be rewarded with a wonderful experience.

What kind of game is it?
It's a 2d platformer with randomized levels.  The difficulty is very high, and it is expected to die frequently and often in humorous ways.  Each run through the game is usually only about 10-15 minutes of your time.  It can run to an hour for particularly long runs, or shorter if you die quickly.  In spite of the randomness, there is enough set pieces thrown in to allow for a sort of progression and collection quest through the game
Who will like it?
Old school gamers not afraid of difficult games.  People looking for that quick game to fill in some time here and there.  People who like platformers.  People who have a game pad in addition to their keyboard.
Good:
Level design, especially for being randomized, are great.  Controls are super tight, making screwups your own. High difficulty, but never unfair difficulty.
Bad:
Keyboard controls are difficult to play with.  Difficulty is very high.

A very fun open world action game. What makes Red Faction: Guerrilla stand out is the destruction physics which are truly awe-inspiring. They are not like what you see in other games, it is much more in depth. Its very satisfying to take a hammer and reduce a building to dust, watch it crumble apart, it never really gets old. The moment I picked up the hammer and break down the first wall in the tutorial was when I knew it was cool.
One fun memory I had of this game was when I was inside a building and there was an enemy tank firing at the building and I saw the building I was in crumble around me, the building falling apart in front of your eyes, the walls would get destroyed and troops would start firing on me through them, I rush outside just in time before the building clopses completely. Another time, I had to kill some snipers on the roof, so I used the disintegrate gun to shoot the ceiling of a building and the sniper on top fell through and I hit him with my hammer. It creates a new dimension to sandbox games that you don't see in many other games and has yet to be topped to this day. Every time you pilot a tank and fire missiles into buildings, or a mech suit and rage through buildings, is awesome. Why somebody hasn't taken this technology and applied it to a pure tank or mech game is beyond me, as the missions where you pilot a tank or a mech suit were probably my fondest memories of this game and could have made a great tank or mech game with them.
Some missions did not utilize the destruction physics to their fullest potential, such as any of the driving missions which are usually really boring with floaty driving (although given the setting on Mars I suppose it makes sense), however most of them were very good. My favourite side missions were the demolition ones where you level a building or structure using limited supplies, like a puzzle almost, which were fun, and I also really enjoyed the house arrest side missions where you have to rescue fellow resistance fighters because in those missions, you have to actually be careful about which parts of the building you want to destroy as you don't want to level the building with your buddies inside it or you lose, which you don't really need to do in the rest of the game.
There were a few design flaws, such as when a fellow guerilla helps you out and gets killed and you support in that area because the AI isn't the greatest. Losing 3 support points every time you die in free roam was annoying too. Plus sometimes buildings would be held up with only one wall and wouldn't fall over, when in real life they would have. I wish this game would have gotten a real sequel that expanded upon the destruction physics and made them even better and more satisfying, it could have even been a more linear game or a level based game like Hitman because most of the actual missions in Guerrilla are quite linear themselves.
The focus is on the sandbox fun and the story is a loose framework to hang this on. I recommend skipping the cutscenes because they are pretty boring, plus it was not very clear on who the Maurauders are in the story. All you need to know is that there's an evil totalitarian government and you're out to take them down and get revenge.
Music and audio were fine. Multiplayer is pretty dead but I've heard its fun so there might be some steam groups around to play with.
Overall, definitely worth playing through, I played it years ago on console and it still holds up today. I played it on Hard this time and the difficulty was still fine, it was fun on Normal too, will play through it on Insane sometime in the future.

At its core, this game is a space flight sim with a linear storyline that brings back memories of EV-Nova, except in 3D. The main gameplay is making money (mining, missions, trading, piracy), using it to upgrade your ship, and repeating. Flying around and fighting is the best part of this game, and you upgrade ships often enough that you don't get bored. Travel times are a bit painful though, as fast travel is fairly expensive.
There is also a 4x mode, where you build a fleet, upgrade structures, and attack/capture enemy stuff. The UI of this part needs an overhaul, as it has too much unneccessary micromanagement. You can influence this part of the game by performing various tasks in your ship, as well as participating in the combat directly.
Lastly, there is a simplistic skill/leveling system, which grants active combat skills, passive combat skills, bonuses to the 4x portion of the game, and other benefits. Level also acts as a secondary limiter to prevent you from getting op ships to early, while also changing the difficulty of enemies on the map. Being able to respec at certain locations for a small fee is a great feature, though I wish the game made that option clear to me right from the start (so I wasn't hoarding points  while I figured out what builds made more sense).

As stated above there are a number of mechanics at play, the premise is to capture zones, build up your resources, research and explore and then deal with your neighbours. While i found this aspect interesting, it doesn't take that long to building up from nothing and working your way out. The combat is now more faster paced as well it is possible you will need a few tries to adapt to it. However SPGW isn't without it's issues:
- There are too many asteroid belts and not enough junk belts, in late game expansions you will be looking for junk collections quite frequently to keep building your forces, especially if you are splitting your forces to fight enemies on multiple fronts.
- Another thing i wasn't too happy with is the research of some late game things like boarding angel 2 or boarding armour 3. Some of these require so much resources that they are practically useless even in late game to acquire. Something of a nerf to these late game upgrades should be considered, from 400k gas to 200k gas for example, it's still a tall order to get at but it's not as time consuming.
- Some places you travel to require certain things which are not mentioned and certain other things that require a bit more expansion:
a. For example you need to capture a guardpost in a radiation zone, you are not told you need to upgrade the "space wolf" trait to reduce the radiation damage by 40%, so you jump in and within 2 minutes you are forced to withdraw to get some major repairs which can take a long time without repair bots. If you had the trait and it was mentioned, you could last a few minutes longer.
b. you need to lure a certain group of ships from one place to another but you get no advanced warning, so you go after them, to find all three attacking other targets and it makes your job nigh impossible to complete because you are unable to lure all three targets. if you have warning about what to expect as a hint, you'd be much closer to where these enemies come from and be able to get you targets to where you need them.
c. as for the expansion? The boarding feature, it would be nice to have a small icon on the screen somewhere that shows when your troops are ready to board another target, the current icon in the context window is rather clumsy to keep up in a fight to watch the chevrons fill up.

Final note i want to thank LGM bringing this game to Steam and letting the community get involved. It's not often you find a development team willing to mix in with their game community to the extent LGM has managed. Thank you.

A masterpiece; that's what Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is.
It's emotionally gripping with the storytelling as you watch the two brothers bond while adventuring to find healing water for their ill father. Straight from the beginning, you can tell that this isn't exactly a game suited for kids, as you watch your mother drown to her death in flashback cutscene, when the younger son, Naiee tragically tried to save her, but isn't able to do so in time. I don't wanna spoil anything, but the game is an adventure game that is charming, creepy and lastly, heartwrenching.
The gameplay starts when Naiee and his elder brother Nyaa carry their father to a doctor, and from there the doctor has them embark on an epic quest to find the healing water. During the epic quest, you encounter folk in the village, farmers, sheep, rabbits, mountain goats; friendly trolls, evil trolls, whales, invisible monsters; giants that fought to their death, wolves, griffins, and much more.
While you don't fight any of these beings, and really, only some of them are evil, (the mean trolls, a giant spider, wolves, and some angry cultists), you avoid them by controlling the two brothers. The game plays like a twin stick fighter or shooter, but as a 3rd person, over head view, and puzzle solving, one stick for each brother, and a trigger to interact with objects.
The game really is epic with the interactions, as you climb, swim, swing, fly, use torches, use various gears and handles; there's a large number of puzzle/interacting; but it's pretty straightforward.
The graphic style is reminiscent of Fable and Ico, but in its own way, and it works well as the game is gorgeous. The audio is perfect, the music and atmosphere really add to the charm of the game, as well as to the creepiness of certain areas (like the guy who tries to hang himself and you have to choice of stopping him, or the bloody rivers where the giants fought to their death, or the children whose bodies are hanging in the forests).
I managed through the game pretty well, but I have to say that the ending is f*cking depressing. It leaves an emotional impact unlike any game I've ever played.
10/10

This is more or less a twin-stick point-and-click adventure game.  You control two young boys on a fantasy quest to find a cure for their father's illness.  The game communicates interaction and feeling purely through body language and tone of voice as the people all speak nonsense words, and for the most part it works pretty well.  The game is fairly nice graphically and I felt like each locale had a good amount of aesthetic, especially toward the mid-end, and there are a lot of just-for-fun interactions you can engage in to give flavor to the characters who participate in them.  I definately appreciated a few locales.
Game mechanics-wise, I actually didn't like the control setup for the two brothers (using a controller).  It was to easy to confuse the two and send one off in the wrong direction, and controlling one at a time sort of defeats the purpose in some minor way.  It would have been nice to have an Ico-style handhold button for the two.  As with most point-and-clicks I review I will take a special point to note that there are very few locations in the game where you can enter a fail-state and it usually involves falling off a cliff while climbing.
Ending spoilers:
At a certain point fighting the monster that causes said spoiler-event, it was heavily crippled and limping, and my thought was 'This is hubris, we've torn off almost all her legs and practically killed her already.  Can I leave?', and of course the game forces you to continue the fight to its eventual conclusion. Its obviously part of the story but my agency felt a little violated so I felt like it was worth mentioning.
Overall not a bad game, but VERY short at only 3 hours so consider waiting for a sale.  You may have to use xbox360ce to get your controller to work, but that's not unusual these days.

This game is unfairly unfairly difficult. You are fighting not only the map, which is enough already, but the hammer. The hammer is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It really is. Sometimes it's extremely bouncy, sometimes it's not. Previously, on all of the rock before hand, the hammer is fine. Actually it's pretty great. It hardly ever really is an issue. Then you reach concrete and wood, where the hammer bounces the ♥♥♥♥ around on anything it touches, so you cannot grab it with any downwards momentum. This is awful. It makes the game that much more unreasonably difficult. If this was just applied in a harder difficulty setting, i'd adore it. It would be a brilliant addition to the game to have a harder mode that adds different effects. Not unheard of but great to lengthen the time this game can give. Sadly though, the hammer, and the pot you sit in, both bounce around too much on some of the terrain. Making it "unfairly unfairly" difficult.
Also, there is one more issue with the hammer. One person on a critical stream put it nicely that the hammer has a "top speed" which makes moving it fast and issue. The issue with the max speed currently is that the hammer gets really uncontrollable at fast speeds. Speed runs make it look very easy to use the hammer, but it's really not. The hammer hardly listens fast or accurate enough. The system that connects your mouse to the hammer could use a lot of polishing.
To better explain it, when you move the hammer fast, sometimes it moves in closer, and sometimes it launches out. It makes sense to a degree. If you are moving your mouse really fast, the hammer's head takes the shortest distance between the two points where your mouse just quickly moved. It decides to take a short cut and not arc fully around. That's fine honestly. What isn't fine is if you move slightly slower, the hammer will stop it's unextended state and extend outwards. So you are on the edge constantly with these hammer controls while on the edge constantly with the terrain.
It's a painful combo that works against you. In Octodad, another game with difficult controls, finishing a challenge is great. You aren't punished way too harshy for any mistake followed up by "ehhhh it's apart of the game xd" constantly. Although I have to admit, I do love the idea of quoting people everytime a big fall happens and the entire theme of it being hard and unforgiving. It is very well done, but it still gets pretentious. It's almost coming off as lazy how the controls work. He did a great job to make them work this well in the first place, but in this type of game, "great" isn't cutting it well enough for me. It can be amazing fun, but the game is nowhere consistent enough for your falls to be enough of your fault to go "that's my bad." Back to Octodad, mistakes are usually comedic. Failing is a lot of fun in that game so it's difficult controls work well. The controls are also pretty solid, with the biggest issue being the lock on for grabbing objects which can be absurdly stupid at times but you can work around it. Never does it really get in the way of the game. The hammer in Getting Over It however, is a piece of unpolished♥♥♥♥♥♥.. sometimes.
Throughout all the issues, they aren't always hitting you in the same bad ways. So it's not nearly unplayable, thank god it isn't, but it can be inconsistent. Even great speed runners have difficulties with some parts. You'll see them swing and the hammer just shrinks on them randomly or they just bounce for nearly no reason. In a game where the interesting environment should be the challenge, I shouldn't be fighting the controls so much. I wouldn't mind the hammer being bad in some ways, but I just wished it was a more solid and less bouncy system.
TL;DR - The hammer can be fairly inconsistent at times which gets in the way of this otherwise fun anger-inducing game. Of course he wants you to suffer, but it's important to reach a balance still, not slap a "this is hard lol" label on the game and not polishing it well enough. That is not saying the theme is great though, i personally loved the theme although it got pretentious at times. Speedrunning may look easy, but the controls are very weird and you can see the same issues happening to the best speedrunners too. It's still a very fun game to play that i'm going to play even more of and continue to get better at it. It's just sad that the weirdness of the hammer makes you hit an early wall for really getting good, so most of the game you don't feel like you're getting better at all.

Routes are fairly accurate in detail.
For starts, this game is spammed with DLC. And it isn't done correctly. I payed nearly twenty bucks for this thing when it was on a sale exceeding 50%. Given my tight as hell budget, that was pushing it. I hoped that it would be worth it. Wrong. For starts, you get maybe three different overall routes, about a total of a dozen senarios (not including tutorals),  a little over a half-dozen locomotives (half of which cannot be drived outside of Quick-Drive), and next to nothing in terms of passenger services. Freight, freight, frieght. Last time I checked, that was what it was like in most of the US. While I am from the US, I do wish to remind you that I live in Illinois, an area which sees a good amount of public transport being by train. And I know as far as Europe that it is practically a nessisaty.
So in order to get more content, I need to get DLC. And it isn't the $1.99 type of DLC either. I'm talking full price. If you want another route, more engines, freight, etc. and maybe 4-5 more scenarios, then expect to pay at least $20...more likely it will be above that. How many Steam engines come with this game? One. And it is in the stupid Academy paint scheme. It looks real dumb when you want to drive one, and the only way to do that is to play a quick drive and try to ignore all the electric and diesel trains that flash past you, making you look kinda stupid.
Now, with wheelslip. Is it something that people like? Hell no. But last time I checked, wheelslip is usually something that is out of a driver's control. I'm sorry I gotta start on a steep hill with a 50 car train; that light was red. But I don't think I should be forced to give next to no throttle and allow my train to slide down helplessly, or risk recieveing huge♥♥♥♥♥penalties.
Now I know you guys are not exactly aiming for a 100% realistic road simulator. I mean, that's kind of a given to me. But on the other hand, I don't think most railroad crossings have the lights going off well before the gates even go off. And I mean that your train is doing 30 miles an hour, up a steep hill, and still close to a mile from the crossing. Then on top of that, the middle of the train will still be crossing through when the gates will go up. I mean do you know how stupid it looks when that happens? And then lets have them drive through the train like it's a hologram.
The speed limit is kinda crazy. I think most people will go five over and not have much of a penalty. But when you are are triple-digit speeds, the tenth-of-a-mile in the speedometer goes away. And if you suddenly are going 12
miles an hour instead of 120, then say good-bye to your points. Also, a little hard for most trains to go down a steep as hell hill with a massive freight train, and manage to spend the entrie time at a slug-like pace of a mere 25 miles an hour. I'm sure more then one engineer have gotten bored with the sluggishness and went a little bit over on the straightaways to cut down some time. They aren't being reckless.
Derailments are horrible in terms of accuracy. I understand that you are not wanting to focus on such a thing, but face it; these things happen. That said, four railcars derailing should not make the entire 50-car train derail as well. That's kinda stupid.
It's a good game. It has potental. But poor physics, next to no content without paying hundreds of dollars, abnormally-strict rules, among other things make what could be a fantastic game into a mediocure-at-best pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥

Spelunky is a great game. A timeless one. You have two goals: Collect Money and Get Out Of There. It's up to you in what way you prioritize either of them.
The game starts out simple, and gets more and more difficult the further you progress. But never with a steep step, always with a curve. At times a sharp curve, but always a curve. When you reach the next section of the game, you will most likely die the first few times. But each death will also teach you a way to deal with the new environment, enemies and traps.
So you go on and on and on. Collecting Experience along with Money and Progress.
It's not an easy game.
But it's a FAIR game, even though it's randomized. It never truly cheats you out of success. There's ALWAYS a chance to beat a level and escape.
There's just not always a chance to do so in the most opttimal way. And there's not always a chance to get ahold of one of the game's many secrets.
But realizing this, and discovering those secrets, is another mark of progression towards mastery of this game.
If you like challenging, tough, fun platofrmers... Give Spelunky a chance.

Spelunky is a very difficult game that is based in gradual advancement in platforming skills across randomly generated levels. The game forces players to quickly adapt to changing situations and throws a variety of expertly crafted and balanced enemies and traps at the player at all times. Though the game is very difficult, it's never very frustrating likely do to the fantastic controls  that never cheat the player or a presentation that features some great tunes and really cute characters.
Depending on how you will play the game, the Steam version of the game is likely the definitive version for most players and introduces a new mechanic known as the Daily Challenge that allows all players to enjoy the same seeded layout of the game while shooting for high scores on the in-game leaderboards. The only real knock against the game is the exclusion of online multiplayer and being forced into using the same camera during local multiplayer matches. The camera restriction can be removed by purchasing and playing the game on PlayStation Vita and PlayStation 3 on PlayStation Network, but many gamers will still prefer the Steam version of the game that also features plenty of ways to mod the characters and items contained in the game as well.

Axe, Bow & Staff comes from a small team who used to make mobile and social games and while you can certainly see those inspirations all over it, don't be put off by it. This game has some design and technical flaws but it's got some cool ideas and can be a lot of fun, especially with friends.
The core mechanics are a combination of a level-based runner game and a light RPG. You have 3 characters who specialise in melee (Axe), range (Bow) and teleporting enemies out of the way (Staff.) Each have additional traversal abilities and in single player, you have to juggle between them in order to get through the levels, which get pretty tough pretty fast. In multiplayer, you can have up to two other human players control the different classes exclusively. If you're playing alone, any players you aren't controlling at that moment will be managed by the AI, which can sometimes hold its own pretty well and other times, it dumb as a rock and will get itself wrecked in short order. Each level has checkpoints that will fully heal your party and revive any downed companions but if you all go down, you'll start back at that point.
You'll have enemies of various types to deal with, as well as environmental hazards you'll have to clear, many of which can only be handled by one class. Every character can take multiple hits but the hazards pile up quick, especially in later levels and will demand quick thinking and reflexes. You can bring up to three recovery items with you that you can trigger at any time during a level and these will become vital later on.
In between each level, there's a shop where you can buy and sell additional recovery items and upgrade your weapons, which you'll have to do frequently. Your characters also have a skill tree that unlocks additional tiers at certain level points and you can respec at any time.
While you can definitely beat Axe, Bow & Staff by yourself, multiplayer is clearly what this game was made for. If playing locally, you can divide players between the keyboard and multiple game pads. You can also play online but it's marked as beta and when researching the game, I only ever got connected to a high ping server in Japan and no one ever joined me. It has a fantastic pixel art style and a great 8-bit soundtrack but there are technical issues. I had some stutters and crashes and many of the sound effects are overmixed, drowning out the music and clipping unexpectedly, which is particularly bad if you're wearing headphones.
I enjoyed Axe, Bow & Staff but unless you want a steep challenge, I'd only recommend this if you have a local group to play with. It also has frustrating technical glitches but nothing that couldn't be fixed with small updates that I hope are coming. It's a unique blending of genres and a good time with the right group.

+ The gameplay is unique. Essentially there is 3 lanes with various obstacles and enemies. You have a party of 3 characters, and can swap between lanes or spread out. Each character in your party has unique abilities, so you have to swap between them to pass the obstacles. The game auto scrolls, so if you get too far behind or stuck behind something you will end up getting pushed off the screen and dying.
+ Visually the game looks great some very cute looking colorful sprites with a bit of a retro appeal
+ The boss fights are pretty interesting
+ Fantastic soundtrack
- The AI controlled companions are a bit dumb, and sometimes run into obstacles and get themselves killed when they could have easily moved.
- Playing solo was not very fun...mainly because the AI controlled characters generally play the game for you without you having to do much of anything besides watch your lane. I really feel like this game was intended to be played with 3 people locally or online.
- Not sure if this was a bug, but what of the early levels did not have any music which felt very dull.
- Each level felt a bit too long and dragged out
Overall, i'm not too sure about this game. It's not bad, but I didn't have the best time playing solo, so I'd suggest having a friend to play with locally or online.

From a newcomer with no experience with the prior games, but one who has been obsessing with this one for the past 3 days or so: Wargame is an amazing endeavour and is one of the most in-depth RTS's on Steam.
The Wargame series is heavily influenced by World In Crisis, another WWIII RTS, and if you've played that game, you'll be familiar with the broad strokes. The biggest difference is one of scale. In WiC, an armored commander will end up controlling maybe 3-4 heavy tanks and a couple other random units once he's maxxed out. In Wargame, a player with an armored deck (more on decks in a minute) will *start* the game with maybe 8 heavy tanks, or else mass hordes off lesser or obsolete tanks, in addition to support... and it goes up from there. The maps are also truly massive, with even the smaller ones roughly 100km by 100km and going up from there -- the scale is more in line with the first Supreme Commander. Within that vast distance, even specialized commanders must jostle with multiple control groups of their frontline guys, recon, supply/logistics (this is a big one), air defense, and so forth.
Like WiC, the game is built around hard counters, with even the mightiest unit reduced to scrap in seconds if it meets its counter. The key is recon, to know what the enemy has and where, so that you may counter it. Are they sending in mass hordes of tanks? If your recon spots it in time, you can counter with helis or Maverick-armed AT planes. Does the enemy have an assload of AA? Keep your helis/planes far away, and charge your own armor or light vehicles in. Do they have a bioball of massed infantry in a town? Time for your arty to step up -- or even better, napalm-equipped units. All of this depends on having good recon to know what counter you need to bring onto the field.
As far as the much-derired naval content goes: Yes, I'm sure the pure-navy maps suck. But coastline maps are where your navy shines. You do not command capital ships in this game -- think more along the lines of patrol boats. And every deck gets free naval units the player may build if he chooses. Completely ignoring the water parts of these maps is a valid strategy, letting you concentrate everything on your land and air; but on the other hand, owning the water denies the shoreline to the enemy, and the heavy AA of most ships gives you an excellent no-fly zone.
I mentioned supply and logistics. All units have only limited ammo, some more limited than others; all units besides infantry also have fuel; and, naturally, units need healing after taking damage in combat. Supply units take care of all these needs, but the supply units are all vulnerable and die if an enemy even looks at them wrong. This adds an extra dimension to combat not found in most of these games.
The graphics are servicable, and are mostly enjoyed in replays. In-game, you will be too busy to enjoy them, similar to Supreme Commander: you're zoomed-out, dealing with icons. Sounds are also basic and servicable; unit prompts are always in the unit's tongue.
As far as decks go: this is one of the greatest innovations of the game. A deck is the selection of units you bring into a match. Decks can be generalist, or (in the spirit of WiC) focused on armored, air, etc; focused decks give you bonuses to focused units at the expense of reduced options everywhere else. You can draw units from the entirety of your faction (NATO + Japan/S.Korea, or else WarPac + China/N.Korea), or you can limit yourself to just a few or even one nation for further bonuses at the cost of, again, reduced options. (Want to play as Denmark fighting against the Soviet Union? This game has your back!) You can and will spend hours simply building various "decks" you can bring into a game.
The AI is servicable, but limited. It will keep a new player on their toes, but its quirks will soon be learned by even the novice. It "fast moves" on roads too much; it never buys ships on coastal maps; it seems confused on what to do with infantry. On the other hand, it can build a mean armored column that will take you by surprise and back it up with gunships and AA. If you want the AI fighting at its best, give it a more armored and support-focused deck that neglects infantry.
On that note, it should be mentioned that the multiplayer community of this game is filled with racists and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. You are better off with people you know IRL.
Anyway, if you are looking for an incredibly deep RTS with a steep learning curve, yet one that eschews the APM-centric style of most RTS's, you've come to the right place.

Ancient Frontier is a turn-based, semi-RPG tactical fleet space combat game which takes place on hexagonal maps - but you can tell more or less that from the store page. What you can't tell from the store page is how slickly done it all is, especially for a game from a very small company, or that it's fairly addicting and has some nice replay value.
Things that stand out to me as positive:
-Fleet development. Building up my fleet, losing ships permanently (think X-COM in space), researching the upgrades I want for the ships I like to use most - this means I get to play my way, and that every decision (e.g., whether to go on one more optional mission) has meaningful risk to it. I tend to fall into "just one more mission" mode, which is a good feeling.
-Graphics/sound/music. The game looks and sounds very good, closer to a game from a more established developer. It runs well on multiple machines (one pretty new, one six years old and getting a bit ragged) for me.
-Story. This may surprise you if you read a few reviews mentioning cheesy dialogue and voice acting. Yes, it's true - the early missions are lightweight, focusing on slightly saccharine relationships between a few characters. Ignore that. Blow past it. Once the real shooting starts, the story gets much richer, the enemies get more fun, and there's far more at stake.
Things that stand out less positive:
-FIXED by patch, 9/27.
-It's possible on certain escort/protect the civilians missions to lose on turn 1 before you can do much to save them. This is mostly a matter of bad luck, and it should be infrequent, but is a little annoying when it happens. Edit: Should happen less due to patch, 9/27.
Other notes:
- The two campaigns really play differently from the start. Strikingly so. Tactics that work with the Alliance don't work with the Federation, and vice versa.
- Small balance and quality of life changes and patching seems to be happening quickly right now (less than a week since release). Obviously that can't continue indefinitely, but it's nice to see things that needed a quick fix get it.

Turn-based tactical goodness... in SPACE!
For a game out of nowhere, Ancient Frontier offered me a highly pleasant surprise. Good turn-based tactical games are not overly abundant to start with, so I decided to bite the bullet and buy on a whim. Something I rarely do, but boy am I glad to have done so.
The game is all about the tactical missions. There are two main campaigns, which apparnetly can take around 100 hours to play through. No multiplayer or skirmish mode.
Missions bring you varying quantity of one of the three main resources ("material," "fuel," and "research"). The first allows is used to buy new ships or components and repair battle damage. Aside from being required as well to purchase new ships, the second resource is an all-important balancing mechanism. Since each ship class (and modifier components) alter the cost of deployment for each mission. Take too many expensive ships too often on missions, and you will run out... which will probably end your playthrough. The last allows investing in upgrades to each ship class, or to research new and more efficient modifier components.
There are five ship types to start with for both campaigns, with more unlocked as the game progresses. All the ships, for both factions, have their unique niches and abilities. While in general "bigger is better," if only from survivability point of view, the deployment costs favor using lighter ships if you are comfortable in their handling and performace. There is certainly plenty to pick from, as you will likely end up being able to afford much heavier force than what can be reasonably supplied with "fuel."
The ships themselves can be further modified by equipping additional components, though I have yet to find use for anything other than shield upgrades. The drawbacks to other equipment types seem counterproductive to my style of playing.
The missions are varied and randomized enough not to be overly repetitive, although there does not feel to be too many types of side missions. Luckily, all the campaign main missions are hand-crafted as to avoid tedium. I do have to agree with something another player pointed out - the side missions actually do detract from the pacing of the campaign. On the other hand, you will need the resources they bring... as long as you can afford the deployment costs.
In the end, it's all about the combat. Ships move in a semi-randomized order based on their Initiative. Unfortunately, as of my writing this review, there is no option to delay the use of a specific ship. It is a minor thing, but something that would have come in handy a few times.
The gameplay is fluid and entertaining. The small scale engagements mean each mission does not take too long to complete, which makes for a handly downtime title for work days evenings.
The graphics are crisp and readable, the sound is GREAT (excellent VO artists, and a kickass soundtrack along with plenty of satisfying combat sounds), and the gameplay engaging, with sufficient difficulty curve on Veteran to make things challenging.
Definitely recommended for anybody with a tactical space itch to scratch.
Edit 10.01.17- The most recent patch introduced manual save option, so the above no longer applies.

There need to be much more Quality of Life Improvents for the game, before it can compete with bigger titles like Red Orchestra or Battlefield. And the game easily could compete, but the potential and great ideas, update after update, are buried under a thick layer of Pay2Progress.
Although the newest Furness Update did elevate some of the tedious player progression, it is still jarring to see, that the fun and heart of the game gets halted and blocked by the lack of awareness of the developers.
My main gripes of the game (furness update included):
- The Meat of the game and what is advertised in trailers and videos is the "War" mode, where you get assigned to squads that have to defend or attack a specific position on the huge european war map. But you have to reach level 10 to even get access. An average player will only earn around 150-300 EXP (sometimes less) points per match. Arriving at level 10 will take at least 10.000 EXP points, so you can guess that getting there takes time. To much time.
- Losing a match reduces your progression and currency multiplier. No matter how well you do on your team, the game punishes you for losing the match. Unlike games like Red Orchestra, where, no matter the side you are on, you get the same points for every action regardeless. Not so in H&G. The rewards you make when losing seem to be extremely reduced, so much so, that what you get won't even replenish your grenades.
And since most matches in the early game - the experience that should show you if you can like the game or not - don't have a time limit, you can spend an hour on a match and get gutted when returning to the score screen, discovering that you got conned.
- Which brings me to the next problem. The progression and weapon progression aren't organic. You can instantly make out why they are built the way they are. To get people to pay money. Grenades are overly expensive. Weapon upgrades as well. This game could benefit so much from a pay2play model. 30€ for the base game and a natural and satisfying progression would help Heroes and Generals step out from the free to play shadows of games like Blacklight or Warface.
- Tied in to the points mentioned before. Weapons are underpowered and unless you have a upgraded smg, they don't have any stopping power to them whatsoever. Especially frustrating with rifles like the Kar98, which needs a confirmed headshot to do the required damage. Otherwise you can spend 3 bodyshots and still haven't downed the enemy player you are aiming at.
And since money and progression are depending on how good your team and you as a player are, aquiring weapon upgrades can be a matter of weeks or months, at least as an everyday player with limited time on their hands.
- Wait times of over 2-3 minutes after you died in a match, just because the game balance needs 1-3 people to die first so you can spawn again, all while your squadmates are playing and dying on the field.
- Spawning however can't be done on squadmates, for some unclear reason, unless I missed a tutorial hint.
- There are no support classes (for the early game). Although there are ammunition and medic crates placed throughout the map, unless you are capturing a point or killing other players, there are not much ways to gain EXP. A game on such a massive scale should at least have one support class to help the players that do worse with a rifle on the frontlines.
It's been years and what promise was shown in the earliest trailers has vanished completely. The promise of a fair, fun and satisfying team based game on a massive scale in the WW2 era. But sadly, the developers don't seem to recognize their own games potential or are held back by either a publisher or higher ups that are more concerned of how to pressure players into paying for an experience that should be found in the game right now, but is not.

I'm glad this Kotaku's review was the first video I saw of the game. If you're still not sure, that video is a neat summary. I bought it immediately, because I love physics games, and I like Bennett Foddy's work. This is a masterpiece, and it's not even awfully long, except that it is because of the difficulty. Is it worth $8? Probably. Even if you don't like trial-and-error in games, this game has a unique way of helping you to not get too angry, and get over it. It's just a game. Come back to it tomorrow; your brain will probably have sorted it out without you evein knowing.
I personally enjoyed learning the weird controls, and they are far better than those of QWOP or GIRP. "Getting Over It" actually gives you more concrete control than those games. The friction on the hammer and the pot is so high, and the guy's arms are so strong, that the character generally goes where you expect them to, as long as you're careful; you should flail the hammer about, but in a controlled way, hard enough to leap upwards but not so hard that you accidentally launch yourself away from the cliff or something.
You would think the intermittent voice lines and quotes would be sarcastic and mean (like so many games which take after Portal's GLaDOS), but they aren't like GLaDOS at all. They geniunely helped me calm down, along with calming music. It's a wonderful exercise in self control, since getting angry at the game causes those little slip-ups that are so catastrophic. I found it to be incredibly zen. If you can get in the right mental place, and be zen about it, this game is relaxing. If you can't, then it's going to make you furious. Either way, you can probably enjoy the absurdity of it for a while.

Having played all the games in the series, I'd have to say the ratings are as follows: 3>1>2. 1 was incredible for the time and a unique playing experience with many huge levels to experiment in. On the highest difficulties it was a demanding experience that rewarded patience, good planning, and accuracy. 2 was a step down from 1 in the level design department,  having far too many close quarter battles in claustrophobic small levels. It's still a great 7/10 game, but it has issues. 3 is where they really hit the sweet spot, combining technical improvements over the last two games and fantastic level design. Although the amount of levels may seem sparse, each level is it's own massive sniper sandbox, allowing many numerous different approaches to each objective. The campaign took me 9 hours to beat on Sniper Elite difficulty and I only really did 50%ish of the secondary objectives, not to mention all the little collectibles scattered about each mission. In short, I highly recommend you check out Sniper Elite 3.

tl;dr: What X3 should have been, albeit a bit on the light side trading & simulation wise.
This is a space game that offers a huge variety of things to do and things to become.
You can be trader, not participating much in the politics of the universe.
Or a bounty hunter with a fully upgraded killing machine of a ship.
Or a diplomatic so-so pilot with a large fleet backing you up.
Or a miner with a vast network of facilities.
Or...
And in contrast to X 3, for example, you are also given a pretty thorough tutorial (that actually works and doesn't bug out) in the form of the campaign.
Besides the main campaign, there are also other play modes such as complete free play, conquest or challenge campaign. Within these campaigns, you also have some customizations available (such as difficulty)
As I said, there is a lot to do here, loads of content and huge amounts of replayability.
The sound is... spacey. Some 80s vibes going on here with the occasional guitars that might rub some people the wrong way.
The game also isn't purely simulationist. There are small RPG elements in that you have a class and abilities to put points in on level-up. These abilities are borderline magic, such as a space "shotgun", becoming a gravity beacon or exploding in a vast "electricity cloud" dealing huge amounts of damage.
While trading and dealing with fleets of your own is definitely possible (and fun!), it is somewhat shallow compared to X3 or EVE. The trading and resource management just isn't super deep.
So for those looking for a space trade simulation, this one probably isn't for them.

Train Simulator gets some things right, but too many things wrong. You play for a while and kinda get interested, but it doesn't take long until you see the massive amount of flaws and disgusting customer service it has. I've now uninstalled it and I certainly won't be buying any additional content ever again.
First, what does it get right?
+ Lots of DLC which means a huge amount of content to play with (see cons though)
+ Fairly easy to understand and get into
+ Steam workshop expands the playtime hugely
So what does it get wrong?
- Physics are terrid, and in no way represent any sort of realism
- This is not really a simulator since there is only about 5 buttons in the cab that work..
- Crap optimisation. Framerate dips below 20 sometimes. Probably due to lack of multi-core support.
- Tile loading system. This means the game micro-freezes each time it loads a new tile.
- Sounds are often inaccurate and poor quality, and they copy and paste them from train to train.
- Way too many bugs that they won't fix.
- DLC is overpriced. Where do they get these prices from?
- They reskin a train, call it a new one and sell it for another £11.99..
- Graphics are OKAY in areas, but horrid in others.
- Level of quality is inconsistent.
- They force advertising of their next DLC down your throat any chance they get. On the menu, on the loading screen..
- Customer support just ignores you or gives you false promises.
Could go on for a while. It's a game that has a lot of potential, but the devs are too busy concentrating on treating their customers like cattle and chugging out new DLC rather than patching the game, and fixing existing DLC.

The title of this game basically tells you all you need to know about the gameplay: run over zombies with your selected vehicle. You run over zombies or kill them with weapons attached to the vehicle while completing primary and secondary objectives in the story mode.
The story mode has a basic plot that is very typical for zombie based games, not ground breaking. It looks like another apocalypse. Your mission begins with a briefing from General Blofeld that you must clear out an area filled with zombies or rescue certain people who are being overwhelmed by zombies. As you go about your mission, you run over zombies while your vehicle gets covered in blood and earn combo bonuses. These combo bonuses continue to multiply if you continue to mow down zombies in a bloody mess, something like chaining your matches in Audiosurf. The top-down perspective looks like the first 2 Grand Theft Auto games and the action looks like the Carmageddon series since you are constantly causing a bloody good time around town.
The weapons are scattered around town and all are pretty useful. They include flamethrowers, machine guns, railguns, rocket launchers, and nitro. All weapons can be upgraded using the cash you earn from each mission completed. The nitro really speeds up your car and helps you reach your destination faster, but it is also useful in getting out of a tight situation when being overwhelmed by large numbers of pedestrians that could potentially make your car explode.
Vehicles are varied and range from taxis to buses. Some vehicles are more useful than others in some missions. The military may ask you to rescue 8 people in a given mission, so the best vehicle could be the bus because it has a carrying capacity of 48 people. All vehicles can be upgraded for more speed and better ramming ability. Even with the variety of weapons at your disposal, ramming zombies with power slides and using nitro to go full speed ahead is still more common than shooting.
The zombies range from regular zombies to exploding zombies. The regular zombies are small or medium in size and there are many zombie dogs run over. The real challenge comes in the form of exploding zombies. Exploding zombies are the fat zombies who can detonate themselves when they get near your vehicle. You can be earning great combos while killing 300+ zombies, only to be ruined by a group of 3-4 exploding zombies who commit suicide next to your vehicle, causing it to explode.
There are a few bosses to battle in the game. These bosses can only be defeated with enough firepower using the various weapons in town. It is also necessary to use defense by running away from them when they are ready to attack. A lack of defensive moves will lead to certain death. In addition, the zombies will never leave you alone during boss battles. So, while you are running away to restock ammo the zombies are chasing you. When you are firing away at the bosses the zombies are still attacking you.
There are other modes in the game that add to the zombie splattering fun. There is the blood race mode and the slaughter mode. The blood race mode is about tournaments that require you to compete in different events such as races, eliminator, and endurance and have bronze, silver, and gold medals available. Races require you to finish 1st for gold and you can destroy vehicles by ramming them or with your weapons. Eliminator events require you to cause as many wrecks as possible while going through checkpoints to increase the time remaining. Endurance events require you to drive around with a bomb stuck to your vehicle going through checkpoints to increase the time remaining. The trick in Endurance events is to kill zombies and destroy as many objects as possible to contribute to the time remaining. The slaughter mode is a good old fashioned zombie killing, splattering entertainment. It is all about killing as many zombies as possible from one wave to the next until your vehicle explodes.
The graphics are decent and, while not dazzling, they provide a well-detailed environment. The death animations look cool and make you feel like it is so much fun making your vehicle all red in blood and guts. You can hear the zombies writhe in pain very loudly when you splatter them all over your vehicle or when you blow them away with your weapons.
The vehicles handle well, as the physics feel realistic during the times you have to turn and perform power slides. They also feel realistic according to the type of vehicle. The muscle car feels very fast whereas the bus feels slow, but very powerful for ramming zombies. The super car feels like it is both fast and powerful since it combines all the great attributes of speed and power.
Some may be disappointed by the fact the Zombie Driver HD has no multiplayer. True, there is more replay value after playing the story mode because of the blood race and slaughter modes. However, those who love multiplayer action will not have any opportunity to compete in multiplayer mode.
I think Zombie Driver HD is a lot of fun to play. The story mode feels a little bit short in length, but it is still entertaining enough. The blood race and slaughter modes provide more entertainment and replay value for a low price of $9.99. All the zombie crushing and splattering fun makes this game worth your purchase.
My Score: 7.5/10

Right, let's try this again. I had to delete my original review, because I think I was a bit too harsh with it. That being said, I only have a strong enough opinion of the game to write a review after it's frustrated the living jelly out of me.
The destruction physics are great and there are plenty of tools to enjoy them with. That being said, your maximum ammo capacity is pitiful. Pair that with your absurdly tiny health bar and the harsh difficulty and you're not going to have much fun before either dying or having to run back to base to ammo up or shake off the cops.
I am really disappointed with this game, not because of what I paid for it, but because it could have been so much more fun. The same people who made this game also made Saints Row 2, but they must have been on a tight, tight leash with this project.
Set somewhere with less bland environment, with the difficulty scaled back, and more enjoyable missions and this game could be rival SR2 as my favorite game of all time. As it stands, all it has is destruction physics that come dangerously close to making me bust a nut. Sadly, however, I'm only left with a painful case of blue balls and a sense of wonder of what could have been.

I think I have the same problem with Brothers as I did with Limbo.
I'd never really heard much about either, and when I heard they were good, I made a conscious effort to
hearing about them until I could play them for myself. Largely I was going in with a blank slate and hoping for the best. And to respect that I'll keep my issues to ones where I can keep spoilers to a minimum.
Thematically the game feels as if it's supposed to be telling an emotional journey as your characters move through a hostile world, having to do what they must to survive and continue on their quest to save their father.
The problem I have is that the game feels like it's trying to make me believe in a deeper story and characterisation than it actually presents, with 'emotional' moments being overlaid with intrusive (and slightly annoying) wailing music to tragic (and happy) events that don't have enough context to give them meaning, and can frequently feel random as a result.
As a game it feels largely like a sequence of unconnected set-pieces (which is not in itself a bad thing) that are trying to get you emotionally attached to your characters and their struggle and journey. But the parts where the game tries to make you feel emotional don't really feel
to me, I could basically take them or leave them. I felt the manner in which the story was handled could have been more effective in characterising these two, their father and their mother, and giving some real emotional heft to the proceedings. But without that context the events just felt like a sequence of random events happening to characters I was kind of but not really interested in in themselves. They're far better than most game characters. I feel like there is something there
develop, I just don't think the game went the extra steps that could have taken it into 'truly memorable' territory.
I realise that most people seemed to have found this game to be affecting, so fact that I wasn't affected made me question whether I'm just too jaded, especially after my very similar experience with Limbo. But games like The Walking Dead, Spec Ops: The Line and heck, even Bastion have all had a hefty emotional impact on me, things that to greater or lesser degree are memorable and that I doubt I'll ever forget.
It's a hard game to talk about whether I would recommend or not, especially since so many others seem to have taken away more from it than I did. The most helpful thing I can say is that if you enjoyed games like Limbo, this may be for you as well. For me? I can't recommend it. On some level, I'm glad that games of this style are
, but I think it could have been done better, and might have achieved its objectives if it had.
Touching. Make an emotional impact on me. I recommend it to everyone.

For an indie developer this game has high production value with crisp graphics, peaceful music, voice acting and clear instructions with tooltips for everything.  Play is fluid and you can fully rotate the map.  Each unit only has a set number of abilities to use in each quest - ship repairs, boosts, missiles - so your tactics are important.  This title is very enjoyable to play through and makes a great turn-based space combat sim.

It's.... okay...
At it's core you have a hex based turn based space combat game and that isn't too bad. Your different types of ships handle differently. Some fighter class ships for example get given three move actions during their turn, allowing them to race in, shoot with admittedly small guns, and then use the last move actions to run away again. Bigger ships may have only one move action, meaning that once they move during their turn they are committed.
Nice enough game mechanic and once you get your head around it you can develop some very effective tactics around this.
The battles are linked by a perma death campaign system which I believe defaults to Iron Man. If you want to scum save go play Life is Strange. You play your battles, collect the three base currenties of 'material' (for repairing and building ships), 'fuel' (which allows you to send your ships out on missions) and 'Data' (which you spend to unlock the tech tree). Your ships also slowly level up. This gives each ships a minor boast to their stats each level but there is not individual skill tree.
So all that is relatively straight forward and the big love/hate thing is the storyline missions. There are two campaigns where you follow either the 'Empire' or the 'Rebels'. Each side gets different ships to select and has different characters to follow, each of which is voice acted.
So... the voice acting and the plot... Yeah... It is either deliberately ironically cheesey to play up to the tropes, or it is just cheesy bad. There may originally have been an intention to animate the characters in proper cut scenes but instead with get portraits with dialogue boxes, broken up with what seems to be the original direction notes from the shooting script. If you like playing visual novels/dating simulators you might enjoy it more but having pages of dull dialogue broken up with [he turned and closed the door behind him] directions every single time you start a story mission can get grating.
As for the actual story? Dunno. Something is happening which the story is building up to but the pace is pretty slow. Normally between each story mission you get the option to do 'bounty missions' to gain loot and skill up your crews, but this is capped at three missions before you have to get back to the plot. The problem is you do a plot mission which hints that 'Mysterious Plot Things' are happening, you finish the mission and bang, straight back to the 'bounty missions' screen with no story based cut scene to tease and tempt you as to what actually just happened. In some ways the story is not as much unfolding as suddenly waving itself in your face just when you start to get settled into some good old space ships thumping. I am not sure if as the story progresses you are given more freedom to plan your stragetic moves but the first five or so story missions are strictly scripted and linear.
The other problem is you are given a 'hero' ship which nominally contains your 'main character'. This hero doesn't go on the 'bounty missions' which means he levels up a lot slower and also when he does turn up you have no real emotional attachment to him.
So... it's not a great game. It's not bad enough for me to give it a thumbs down but I can see myself forgetting I even have this installed within a couple of days and never going back to it.
So yeah, it's 'okay'.

Ancient Frontier is a well polished and pretty straightforward addition to the turn-based strategy genre.  There are two different campaigns to play through, each with story missions, bonus missions, and training missions to choose from.  The story missions are fully voiced with a lot of flavor in the banter between the different characters.  Even the tutorial (which is completely optional and can be skipped entirely) is fully voiced and sets up the characters nicely.
The game offers three difficulty modes so it can appeal to veterans of the genre and newbies alike.  I don't play many tactical turn-based games, so it's nice to see that I can ease into the game on easy mode while veterans can dive right in without having to wade through loads of too-simplistic missions from the get-go.  The game does not have a manual save function, however, so any mistakes I make in a campaign I have to live with, without the safety net of a redo.
The story missions drive the campaigns forward, but players can choose up to two bonus or training missions inbetween each story mission to gain additional experience or resources.  Training missions do not award any resources, but they will not have any lasting negative effects (like loss of ships) should they turn out poorly, and are useful for gaining experience.
There are plenty of ship types for players to choose for their fleet: some with high firepower, some with scouting abilities and little firepower, etc.  Selecting the appropriate ship types to purchase and deploy is vital to the success of the missions.  There is also equipment to add onto ships for further customization and better tactics.
The meat of the gameplay is pretty standard for a space map, turn-based strategy game with a few exceptions.  Instead of the player taking a turn with all of his ships in whatever order he chooses and then the computer AI taking a turn with all of its ships, each individual ship gets its own turn in a randomized line-up each phase.  The player can only act with the currently active ship, and the active ship rotation is different every turn.  This adds an extra level of strategy required because the optimal turn line-up of a player's fleet probably isn't going to be an option.  Also, space terrain (asteroids and the like) play an important roll in the strategy as positioning a ship near an asteroid for cover can be a key tactic in defeating an enemy fleet or become a hazard which can destroy a ship unit.
All in all, this is a nice solid entry in the tactical turn-based genre.  There are plenty of choices for players to customize different strategies with.  The game is well polished with detailed graphics and great voice work.  And yet there are some key differences with other titles in the genre giving this game a unique feel all of its own to gameplay.  It's more of the same great turn-based tactics, without just being more of the same.

Not as in banning everyone or deleting tons of threads bad (though some were deleted before it was noted that Valve and Steam Community Moderators can see EVERYTHING deleted) and the developer did play it fair in that regard afterwards.
What happened was actually worse, pushing towards felony material.
First it had started with review fraud by an account from the game's Greenlight submission page along with a known artist for the game.
The artist immediately apologized and took down their reviews, conforming to both Valve's rules and consumer law regarding proper disclosure in review. They had changed their reviews to preserve them, claiming that they were a moderator once upon a time and no longer had ties to the developer.

They may not have understood fully what they were doing, but they tried to cover up review fraud (which usually faces many thousands USD in fines depending upon state and even federal laws) by claiming misrepresentation fraud to make people think the company was larger to entice buyers (which is a felony in most states and even on a federal level IIRC).
The developer had to be saved from themselves and shown why this was bad before it got even worse.
A Google Cache result exposing their alt account was shown, upon which the developer removed all fraudulent reviews and issued an apology.

This game deserves to have an overall "Very Positive" review. I have played many games over the last 30 years and this is one that I actually played all the way through. This is not a bad game, there are some substance and challenge, but it is a bit rough around the edges for a commercial game, and I think there are a number of better and more polished games in the crowded Tower Defense genre.
The game production is quite ambitious and certainly above many mobile TD ports. but  unfortunately it lacks polish in several areas. In particular when there are many enemies on screen the action become confuse and it is sometimes hard to place a tower where you want because there are always an enemy on the tile were you want to built hence the game display an enemy info box instead of the build pop-up just because you can't access the empty tile with your mouse pointer. Here a simple keyboard shorcut for building would have helped.
Then there are occasional fram rate drops or even a few of CTDs (though not during action proper but rather when navigating through menu).
Also annoying is the fact that the game doesn't properly save your highscore and on occasion I also had my progress reset to zero.
The campaign map is not very convenient, either to navigate or to inform you on the exact map #ID and your progress so far, here many TDs do a much better job.
Also the game lack a proper manual and a Towers and Ennemies cyclopedia.
Besides these annoying issues, there is some challenges so it might be worthwhile on sale. Though I would recommend other TDs over this one

Hydraulic Empire is a good tower defense game, and it's also a big mess.
It's hard to get beyond the first bad impression. The presentation is terrible. Lack of Menus, Lack of tutorials, Royalty free Elevator Music, Poor Graphics, everything has "Mobile port" written all over.
And that said, if you manage to get beyond your initial reaction and start playing, you will notice it's actually a very competent hex tile based tower defense game.
The gameplay is spot on. There is no major innovation in the system and the stages and enemies are just varied enough, but the mechanics are solid and the challenge level is just about right.
Be warned that there is a serious difficulty spike for the last few missions, but it's not impossible. To be frank I found the balance perfect. You will not succeed if you try the same things over and over again and just sit back and grind, like a lot of other tower defense game out there.
Hydraulic Empire encourages trying different tactics out after you fail.
But you must get past your first impression. Boy this game is shoddy! The controls can get fiddly when the map is cluttered, and so can finding your hero be. There are even some upgrade menus that are never explained, you just find them by clicking around random stuff and wonder what in the hell you've just opened and what it does.
If you can live with these issues, and know your way around TD games, you won't be dissapointed.

NOTE: This is a review of Train Simulator overall by Dovedail Games. The review is NOT specific to the 2015 edition.
Hands down this is the best train simulator out there. I am going to state that right now. If you are looking for the best, it's here. However, beware as this game can be very expensive. There is a ton of content, but almost all of it costs extra. You start out with only one or two routes, and a couple trains.
There are a few glitches in the game, mostly with the signal system on the tracks, however if your a train fan like I am, and don't mind the cost, I definitely recommend it to you. You can also build your own routes, however that can take a LOT of time, and I haven't really messed around with that.
It is also worth noting that some train interiors are more polished than others. I have around 20-25 locomotives, and some are very polished, others could use a few more buttons/features to interact with.
Rating:
Overall 7/10
Mechanics/Engine 10/10 for realism
Graphics 10/10
Signaling System 6/10 (sometimes is great, other times not)
Cost 6/10 (routes and trains are expensive, but they put a lot of work into them)
I recommend using an Xbox 360 or Xbox One controller for easier controls. Alternativly you could buy the RailDriver train controller for $200 which I don't have, however it seems pretty cool.
