I love this game but it is difficult to recommend. Here's my longest review ever.
First, a description. Defiance is an MMO with a strong single-player plot to get you through quite a few hours. The story is interesting enough and the voice acting is great! This plot acts as an extended introduction to the game world. After that, you will need to find various public happenings (seiges, arkfalls, etc.) in which to help and compete with other players. There are also instances that spawn self-contained worlds. Some of these are PvP, others are cooperative. You also have daily and weekly missions to fulfill. All in all, similar to other MMOs. You get a cool game world and then comes the endless grind.
The game is very much a glass half-full thing. First, I love the look, which is post-apocalyptic without being too dark and beige. Enemies are varied and interesting. But over the long haul you get used to them. No further mobs have been introduced. (Not strictly the case, but they are variations on the tried and true.)
Your own character is rendered nicely and you can dress up in different outfits, if that's your thing. Though this consists only of changing two articles of clothing. You start the game by choosing one of four classes and one of four main EGO powers, which becomes your special ability. Over time you fill out other passives, actives, and gain all four EGO powers. Then you are just the same as everyone else. Yep, everyone has the same attributes! The classes don't matter either, and races are purely cosmetic... and look similar enough. As do (most) of the costumes. You can spend real cash on stuff that is just a different colour from what you already have. Ho hum.
The gunplay is very good. In fact, though I haven't played them all, combat in Defiance is the best of all MMOs. Though it is third-person, it has the feeling of a FPS, which I love. You can get and modify different guns as you go on, though to a large extent there is not much difference between these either. Until you get to end-game, when you can no longer level (increase EGO), the most important thing is the EGO of your gun. Even 100 EGO matters and that's over a scale of 6000.
The game is free to play, though you will need to spend money. First, buy all the DLC by way of the Season's Pass. Really, once you discover you actually do want to play, just buy this, or you will be restricted in several annoying ways. Besides, then you get to use swords! (Not an optimal strategy and kind of orphaned, but fun anyway.)
Second, you will need more inventory slots, a lot more. Third, you will need more key capacity, or you will not be able to unlock the better random gear boxes. Overall, however, you won't need to spend too much.
Several things in Defiance completely suck, the main one being that the number of sucky things has been steadily increasing. So what was a decent and fun game when I started is being squeezed out of existence by Trion. To the point that I will NEVER buy another one of their games.
OK, let me list the sucky things.
As mentioned, classes and races DO NOT MATTER. This is not an RPG at all. Which is a wasted opportunity.
Swords don't matter, they are just fun for a while. Vehicles don't really matter, since they are almost all the same. A lot of guns, likewise.

Defiance could have been so much more. It could have been Godlike!! But stupid punitive decisions on the part of Trion have ruined it. Nonetheless, it's still the MMO with the best combat system, so I play it.

This game is awesome, simply put. I put off playing it for a long time because I had played it on the 360 in its beta stages, and although i liked it, when it released i never bought it.
I heard it went free to play but still never played it when finally bordom got the better of me and i sifted through the free to play library over and over, constantly seeing defiance. I downloaded, creeated my account and hopped in. The first thing i noticed was that for an old (ish) game the graphics were still very pleasing. Sure theres some rough edges but thats to be expected. I played about 10 hours into the story, and somehow this game had not only hooked me, but got me immersed into the worlds story, and history. It made me do something i've never doen before, and that's watch a programme ;p
I sat down and watched the first season of Defiance (the show) and oh my I was impressed. Whenever I watched the show I wanted to go play the game and vice versa. Both entities complimented each other, and whenever I had watched an episode when I went in game I felt more involved, like I had a reason why I was trying to save the planet.
Never has an mmo hooked me into its world, I mean even ESO didn't achieve that for me, so I appluad Trion.
Now onto the gameplay. Its a great third person shooter in short. You have acces to a wide variety of weaponry, smgs, assault rifles, shotguns, snipers, rocket launchers... You name it. Unlocking some dlcs brings even more flavour to the show, which I have done and which I highly recomend, while its on sale after all. If you have watched any of the show you wll be happy to know that the charge blade makes an appearance, and to obtain it you must comoplete a series of very fun arenas in my honest opinion. It opens a whole new play style as you can now effectivley play as a melee player.
Other fun weapons such as infectors (shoots bugs) projectile based weaponry and charge up weapons all make this packaged all the more exciting.
You also have to use cover,  A LOT. This is what makes this mmo a lot more fun for me, you need to be aware of your surroundings and you can't just stand still and spam your gun/abilities. There's a dodge mechanic, that can put you out of harms way from bullets and selected enemy charge up attacks, and it is also used to put out any negative effect on your character quicker, such as being set on fire or being slowed down by something.
Onto the world. from what I have explored, big, 3 continant type areas and a smaller area (i think is dlc i have not been there yet) Some areas are bleak looking and some are full of life, yes some areas look a bit empty but for the most part the world is fun to explore. Data recorders are spread throughout the map in hidden and out of reach areas so if you are into that type of thing you will feel right at home.
What brings the world to life though are the dynamic events, you will find many random encounters where you must complete a series of objectives to gain a reward. Save some prisoners, disable this, collect that etc. These are fun and a good time waster, but its the arkfalls that seal the deal. All players can see the icons on the map so going to one is normally chaotic. These really are one of the (sadly) few end game events however I was playing them at the start of my game, any one can play them and make a difference. These can be very fun and rewarding and make for a great time.
Accesing the world is very easy. You can fast travel to any hub area you have already traveled to and (which suprised me) you gain access to a vehicle VERY early on, which isn't really seen in many mmos. Time trails are present for the avid driver and driving mechanics are fun, they arnt just slapepd into the game like they dont belong, all the vehicles have different handling and whats great is you can buy the fastest ones with ingame currency.
IS IT F2P OR P2W?
f2p for sure, you can buy inventory slots etc and suppl cases with real money but you can buy the same cases with in game currency so no one is at a disadvantage.
Trion got a lot of flak for this game and I don't know why. It's solid, great fun and if you find a clan, very rewarding.

This game is best described as a platformer, with randomly generated levels and permadeath (if you die, you need to start from the beginning). It's one of the most challenging games I've ever seen. Not because it is difficult, which it is (a lot), but because there's always a harder challenge waiting for everyone.
Don't let your first deaths discourage you. This game is about dying 10 seconds into the game, and dying, and dying, until your lives begin to last longer, and longer, and longer... and then you reach the second level, and then you aim for the jungle. And then your goal is to get to the ice caves, and then the temple. And then you will curse all the game developers' ancestors because damn, that♥♥♥♥♥♥is hard. And then, after beating the temple, you have to defeat Olmec, the game final boss.
But finishing the game is not all. There are a lot of secrets, and the scariest of all is that Olmec is not even the final boss. There's even a harder way to finish the game.
If I had to single out the best feature of this game I would definitely say: replayability. There's always something to do. I'm almost 80 hours into the game and I'm still trying to get the "low scorer" (beating the game without collecting any treasure) and "speedlunky" (finishing the game in under 8 minutes) achievements.
10/10

Spelunky is the perfect game.
I say this because it is so carefully crafted, and so well designed that there seem to be no flaws.
The game is absolutely brutal and unforgiving, but every time you die, you know it is YOUR fault. It is YOUR fault you didn't see the Arrow Trap, it is YOUR fault that you angered that shop keeper, it is YOUR fault that you fell on those spikes. And it feels that way because everything in the game plays by the exact same rule set, you just need to learn it by trying.
As you play, you become better, more conservative as you play. Drop a rock here to trigger traps, hang off the ledge before you jump to see if the area below is safe, throw pots away from  you, etc, etc.
Take all this, throw in random generation, secrets, and daily challenges, and you have a perfect game. And if you aren't sold yet, the old "non HD" version is still and will always be free.

It has been a very long time since a game managed to make me cry... this one had me sobbing.
Prepare yourself for this emotional rollercoaster - this game is both as beautiful and atmospheric as it is heartwrenching. Having just lost their mother to drowning at sea, and now on the verge of losing their gravely ill father, the two titular brothers set off on a surreal journey to obtain the one thing able to cure him. The story unfolds without words (at least, not words that are comprehensible), using body language, music and nuance in a manner that is masterfully handled and pulls you straight in.
Gameplay, unfortunately, is where Brothers suffers. Firstly, you NEED to use an Xbox 360 controller. Each brother is controlled individually with each control stick, proving to have a steep learning curve. This essentially gives an illusion of co-op, which while visually interesting and making both of their movements feel organic (rather than an NPC programmed to follow you), it proves to be quite frustrating at first as you frequently lose track of which stick controls which brother. Another downside is that it's also quite short and can be finished in only a few hours.
Atmosphere, story and visuals are this game's bread and butter. Despite the frustrating gameplay, if you're fond of games strong on story that tug at your heartstrings and leave you thinking long after the credits have rolled, I can't recommend this highly enough.

My thoughts on Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons:
What an amazingly beautiful game! I picked this up quite a while a go during a sale and only because I heard YouTube personality TotalBisquit say this was his favourite game.
After playing (and finishing) it, I can understand why.
You follow the two Brothers on their quest to find a rare medicine to cure their father and help them climb mountains, fly across valleys, make their way through villages and castles, across devastaded battlefields and frozen rivers. The level design is just awesome and so beautiful I couldn't help but wish to be living there. The soundtrack too is great and fits the game and the mood perfectly.
While it takes some time to really get used to the controls (Xbox controller is required) - you control both brothers at once, using both sticks - it never gets frustrating or annoying as the game helps you out a lot and never really is too hard to be blamed on the controls.
There are no fights or puzzles, just some smal objectives like having to pull a lever with one brother while hangling across a pit with the other, in order to create a path for the big brother once you reached the other side. May sound boring, but the landscapes and the characters somehow get you entertained anyway. Plus, the game is easily beatable in under two hours, so there isn't much time to get bored anyway.
Biggest highlight of the game however is how it makes you like the characters in a way only few other games do, and the ending deserves a special mention too as it is just beautiful and really really really well made. Did I already mention how beautiful the landscapes are?
Highly recommended for anyone, especially during a sale!
Also, vote for it as best game to make you cry!

Hydraulic Empire is a tower defense game with enough new wrinkles to it to make it worthwhile to play, especially at its low price.
There are a dozen towers in the game, including a mud slinger (to slow down enemies), a bomber, a tesla tower, a gattling gun, a netter (to knock down flying enemies), and more.  However, you can only take five of these towers with you into a level.
The enemies are fun.  They're robots, and while most just simply try to make their way to the exit, others spawn more robots, or repair destroyed robots (so they get back up and start heading for the exit again), or carry smaller robots on their back, or disable your towers, or more.
There are 21 levels.  Each level is made up of a hex grid, with start and end points, and possibly some rally points that the enemies also have to visit.  Enemies travel on and you build on the hexes, and since enemies can't travel through most of your towers, you can create a circuitous path for them to follow.  If you've played Defense Grid (which I'd recommend over this), then it's the same sort of idea.
Each time you complete a level (even if you lose), you earn cogs, which you can use to upgrade your towers.  You can grind cogs if you want, or try out extra difficulty settings for extra cogs, but it's not really necessary.  I completed the campaign only repeating a few levels.
You can upgrade your towers, both inside and outside the levels.  The outside upgrading is sort of confusing, and it isn't explained well in the tutorial.  On the "factory" screen (where you upgrade individual towers), you get 14 hexes.  On one hex you have to place a tower, but then around it you can place upgrades.  That means you can't upgrade all of the towers.  You can only pick out like four and give them 2-3 upgrades each.
You build towers using your Keeper.  You have to move your Keeper to the hex where you want to build a tower, which can get tricky because your Keeper can also damage enemies and improve the capabilities of nearby towers, so there are usually 2-3 places where you'd like him to be at once.  Along with cogs, after each level your Keeper also earns some experience, which leads to levels and upgrade points.  So you can improve your Keeper as well as the towers.
The only problem I had with the game is that it stopped recording my progress.  It unlocked new levels properly, so I was able to complete the campaign, but it stopped saving my scores, which means it currently doesn't think I've completed most of the levels (and the levels where it did record a score, it recorded the wrong score).  So it's not giving me credit for completing the campaign, which is annoying.
But overall, Hydraulic Empire is fun enough.  I got it for $2, and it was more than worthwhile at that price.

There really needs to be a 'meh' option for games like this.
Look, this game is good.  It's not great, but it's good.  It handles everything you want in a tower defense well.  I played for about an hour so far and I just came across with a great feeling of 'it's all right' at the end of it.  All the classic tower tropes you'd expect are there.  Starting chain gun tower (arrow tower) that can hit land or air and fires fast but weak attacks.  The next upgrade is your bomb tower which has land only but does splash damage.  Then you get the flak cannon, which fires fast, but can only attack air....
Gee I wonder what is coming next, maybe a slow firing single target tower?  YEUP, called that one before I saw it.
Ok, so the towers are uninspired, but they work.  How about the special abilities your commander can use?  Lets see... acid rain in a hex for DoT damage, a bomb for AE damage, a slow, a sniper shot.... *YAWN*   Again, they work for the game, but... just... meh.
Well maybe this fancy upgrade system....
Pretty underwhelming, what you'd expect, increase damage, range, or speed of towers.  Upgrade your commander abilities.  I feel like I've done this before.
Now the graphics... well... they aren't bad, but they just feel... very... dated.  They would have been mind blowing ten years ago, and they look fine for 2016, but that's it, just fine.
Now the one thing I did have a problem with was the sound.  The sound REALLY begins to grate on your nerves very quickly.  The sound of my minigun towers seemed to drill into my very brain and cause my spine to itch.  I couldn't turn the sound down quickly enough after only a few minutes of playing.  The music is also pretty lack luster.
Look, overall, if you want a tower defense game to play, and this is on sale, go ahead and grab it.  It's not BAD.... it's just not really that good either.  It's a standard TD, executed well, that unfortunately feels like it's about 7-10 years too late to the party.

Train Simulator 2015 did exactly what I wanted. It simulates trains to a reasonably high quality, provides decent sounds and somewhat realistic physics. Although there are bugs and lag spikes, it still runs well and provides me hours of enjoyment. The menu hasn't changed in the update to 2016, it can still be a little annoying but it's relatively easy to navigate and use.
The 2016 version comes with a few routes, and I think the 50s Riviera line is probably the best, coming with 5 nicely modelled locomotives and a decent run from Exeter to Kingswear via the stunning Dawlish Sea Wall. All the locos modelled are reasonably easy to drive and they can all battle the gradients pretty well. The American Gas Turbine is a fun locomotive to play with on Sherman Hill, packing a lot of power. However do be cautious when driving it, it behaves a lot like locomotives with tap changers (such as the included DB BR 155 or some of the possible DLC such as the BR Class 86) and can be a bit unwieldy. The final route Cologne-Koblenz is also enjoyable with it's plethora of German electric locomotives, including the previously mentioned 155. There is the option of first class editions for the three countries, and each would probably suit a different person. The Steam edition also comes with Norfolk Southern Coal District.
Another thing that Train Simulator prides itself in is it's capability of making routes and scenarios. However, the tools can be unwieldy and sometimes quite tricky, and you will most likely have to resort to a guide. There are plenty of created scenarios on the workshop however, and people are also devoted to creating some further routes not available via DLC. Overall the scenario/route creator tool is fantastic to have, but is a little tricky to use and can be irritating sometimes due to randomised errors.
2016 also brought a whole mode devoted to taking screenshots of your favourite rolling stock. This is Railfan mode. Instead of controlling a paticular locomotive, you are placed in a location and given almost free movement around the close by area, taking snapshots and watching trains go by. Is it good? Yes, and you get a few railfan scenarios to start off with. The tricky part is making your own session. Finding a spot on your favourite route can be tricky, and to somebody who hasn't got the hang of the route/scenario maker it can be a chore. You can always try and find some in the workshop, but they might be rare or even non-existent.
Now obviously the hot topic. The DLC. There is a lot of it, and it costs quite a lot. Obviously, some people will reccommend different routes and different locomotives. But the overall total for all of the DLC right now is nearly £3500. That's rather a lot. And more comes out every year, so that total will rise. The only thing I can suggest is find the items you want for yourself, and try and catch a few of the sales. Make sure you read the reviews, they can tell you a lot about each item.
There is also another thing I should bring up: Entities not spawning. I have found that in a few routes, if you're running the game on anything less than maximum settings, some of the entities in a route such as overbridges and even station platforms will not spawn in. This is something that does need addressing, not everyone has access to a decent gaming PC or Laptop that has the capabilities of managing maximum settings, and even if you do, you can get enormous lag spikes on certain routes, and often the FPS will drop to 15.
Otherwise, the game is reasonably well polished, if still not needing a few fixes here and there. The DLC is probably the biggest downside to this game; possibly because for each stunner you see released you can get one or two duds. I originally gave it an 8.5/10 when it was TS2015. I'd say now a 7.8/10. It's good overall, but it has issues that need to be addressed. It's still worth being picked up when on sale, as it can reach as low as £7. Even with the base package or one of the first class editions, there's still at least a few hours of fun to be got out of it.
Final Score: 7.8/10

I have to admit, Wargame is something that requires patience, a high toleration of frustration and even more practice to master, but once you got to a point where you understand what to do and what not, it is pretty amazing.
It requires so much micromanagement to successfully overwhelm your enemy (assuming he's human, that is) that you won't even have time to grab a sip of coffee. It really teaches you to actually read the description of a unit and use common sense. Spamming 20 Tanks will cause your enemy to either ambush them with AT Infantry or call in an airstrike - and you can kiss these tanks goodbye.
In StarCraft or CnC, it wouldn't matter - but here? If your Leopard is gone, it's gone. The crew is dead, the vehicle destroyed, and they won't come back.
Sometimes, you feel so desperate but turn it around, sometimes you are so full of yourself that a single mistake will cause the deaths of all of your soldiers.

WARNING! DO NOT expect this game to be like any other RTS game. If you are expecting this to be similar to Total War, Company of Heroes, World in Conflict, or Men of War: Assault Squad 2, this game is not for you. This RTS is a very serious tactical and strategic game. Every mistake you make and misstep in preparation will cost you dearly. Though, in contrast, every successful push made may very well change the tide of battle. It has a large learning curve, but after some determination, it's worth it.
I tried out European Escalation and Airland Battles in the past. I sucked at it horribly and couldn't finish the campaign. Yet, I still enjoyed its unique gameplay. I bought Red Dragon because it was on sale and I was interested in trying out the additional gameplay content. Knowing the basics of how to play from EE and ALB already, I jumped straight into campaign thinking that my experience from TW, CoH, WiC, and MoW: AS2 would surely have improved my skills compared to my first time in Wargame... I couldn't have been more wrong... My forces were obliterated within the first minute of the match... Lost to an easy AI on the very first mission of the easy campaign.
This time, I wasn't going to give up on a game I couldn't win. I watched a few battles to see the tactics and strategies players used to win against both AI and human opponents from their deployment patterns to mid-battle decision making. I was also lucky enough to find a veteran player willing to give me tips on deck building, guide me through some basic combat techniques, and invite me to his group of other veteran players who would advise me on how to play. After a little more practice, everything changed. I started to win more than lose and do an efficient job.
In total, I only found two cons in this game. The minor one would be the naval battles which are just clunky and follow a last-one-standing-wins rule rather than the tactical combat that is regular land battles. The most negative con I find would be the rather newbie-unfriendly community of veteran players. I'm not saying all veterans are unwelcoming, but if you're new, you're very likely to run into matches where you're kicked for being too low ranked. You have a better chance of finding a match by joining a very large match like 10vs10 because they don't bother to check everyone's levels. Though with inexperience, you wouldn't contribute much to the team in such a match. The best way to gain early experience is by creating a server of your own and title it "Newbies only."
9.5/10 Would learn how to play rather than do college homework again.

Movement section
Pitch up - Arrow Key Up
Pitch down - Arrow Key Down
Turn left - Arrow Key Left
Turn right - Arrow Key Right
Roll Left - A
Roll Right - D
Accelerate - W
Decelerate - S
Full Stop - X
Combat section
Fire heavy weapon - E
View section
Camera zoom in - Mouse scroll up
Camera zoom out - Mouse scroll down
Commands section
Fire at will - Q
Power to engines - Left Shift

Update: A developer responded to my review and updated the game based on the feedback. I have not had time to play through it again, but I appreciate their effort. If you read the original review below and are on the fence about Hydraulic Empire, you might consider giving it a chance. My intention was not to be the bad review that killed their business; I was genuinely frustrated at the time. I don't know if it's better, but they seem to be honestly trying, which is commendable. Original review follows:
Well, I just uninstalled this one, having decided it was no longer worth the effort. Another good example of a game with an interesting concept but poor execution. Also, a good example of why you should always check the global achievement stats: less than 1.5% of people who own this game even finished it.
I am starting to get the impression that most reviewers just sample games and base their reviews on a fun initial impression, imagining the possibilities - they do not complete the games and they do not have a complete picture of what they are talking about. Would you trust someone who read a book halfway through and just told you their general impressions?  Many games just end up becoming repetitive and run out of ideas about halfway through. At that point you get the sense the developers are working to fill time and hard drive space. Guess which type of game Hydraulic Empire is.
That's right! Hydraulic Empire is a tower defense game but it's also a puzzle game in that many of the levels are only completeable if you build out a path the correct way. No amount of upgrading or leveling towers will save you if you have not made the path correctly. So although it may seem like you have a lot of options to play with, there is usually one strategy you must take to beat certain levels. By far the easier levels are those in which you don't have to think too much about your path building. Some may call it poor game design, others may call it having nothing better to do on a Saturday afternoon.
You can build upgrades for both your overall game and for individual towers - the difference being that the individual tower upgrades give higher stat bonuses, that is, they give not completely useless stat bonuses. This is all done on two grids (one for overall, one for towers) and so there are a limited number of slots for each upgrade. The overall upgrades are generally so weak that you would need to create 3 - 6 fully upgraded attack (or speed or range or whatever) upgrades to see a noticeable difference.
So for about halfway through the game as you are collecting gems (cogs?) to be able to buy these upgrades you get the impression that the upgrades aren't really doing much, and by the end of the game you simply think about how much worse you would be losing had you not had a fully upgraded grid. This game plays that much with the margins of those power ups and will not let you expand once you fill up your grid that for some there will most likely be no way to complete the game. After playing through what I presumed was the last level on Normal difficulty something like 20 times, I decided I was one of those people because there are other things to do on a Saturday afternoon.
Oh you also have a robot guy with special abilities, who shoots at enemies, and can power up your towers. He too has a max level cap that seems frustratingly low (25) at the end of the game. Why not give the option for a player who is having difficulty completing the game grind his way through so he can feel like all those little doggie hoops he was jumping through were not for naught? No, the developers decided that the last hoop would be a ring of fire and no matter how many times you try to leap through it your fur and skin will become singed and burned off in small bits every time until you have neither hair nor patience left.
Of all the tower defense games I own, this one is one of the worst, once you get past the first 3 or 4 towns, the game is impossible to play, needless to say I would not recommend this game, sorry.

Ability to specialise your player character for various roles, allowing a couple of different styles of play.
Difficulty levels, four so far, and reasonably steep progression.
Some stability problems have been reported, I haven't seen them. Graphics are nice, not too complex. Storyline is simple, but I don't play for that :)
This is a good game for when you only have a 30 min spare, but it's easy to get sucked in and try another level, or a harder difficulty, or go back and try that early one with the new tower you unlocked... so you can easily spend quite a while on it.
A terribly addictive feature is the scoreboards, for each level and difficulty. There's always the temptation to try to get to the top... just one more try... I can do it with less towers and score better than that guy...
This is still a work in progress, but given the care and attention paid by the developers, I think it looks very promising.

Wow it's the QWOP guy with a new game. A 2D platformer with a strange control scheme, but instead of feeling too unweildy and confusing, you've merely got high difficulty this time around. Took a brief glance through Foddy's reviews and he pointed out enjoying a game for the sense of gaining expertise and Getting Over It is no different from that.
You'll fall frequently, but if you stick with the game, you'll notice more and more of the game becoming easier and easier. While the mountain is certainly a pile of garbage, it's been arranged in a way to present challenge and a real sense of tension. Some areas are intensely difficult, but it has been divided up into defacto levels that function as natural checkpoints.
It's definitely not as punishing as a Kaizo game or IWBTG sorts of games, but I think where the frustration really comes from is having to pay so much attention to how you're controlling the hammer. It demands keen awareness of your cauldron's position, the hammer's position, the speed you handle it, the angles you are interacting with. It's a different sort of difficulty. It demands a level of precision that is fluid, and not naturally accessible as traditional platformers.
But that is the core of the fun. After spending nearly 15 hours on my first loop through the game, it's quite incredible to see that time drop down below an hour for a second loop.
Also, a bit meta, but don't look at speedruns of this game. Save that for after completing a play or two.
Lastly, the game made me gasp and move my body, as though moving my limbs would will the digital man to reach out just a little further.

My thoughts on Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons:
What an amazingly beautiful game! I picked this up quite a while a go during a sale and only because I heard YouTube personality TotalBisquit say this was his favourite game.
After playing (and finishing) it, I can understand why.
You follow the two Brothers on their quest to find a rare medicine to cure their father and help them climb mountains, fly across valleys, make their way through villages and castles, across devastaded battlefields and frozen rivers. The level design is just awesome and so beautiful I couldn't help but wish to be living there. The soundtrack too is great and fits the game and the mood perfectly.
While it takes some time to really get used to the controls (Xbox controller is required) - you control both brothers at once, using both sticks - it never gets frustrating or annoying as the game helps you out a lot and never really is too hard to be blamed on the controls.
There are no fights or puzzles, just some smal objectives like having to pull a lever with one brother while hangling across a pit with the other, in order to create a path for the big brother once you reached the other side. May sound boring, but the landscapes and the characters somehow get you entertained anyway. Plus, the game is easily beatable in under two hours, so there isn't much time to get bored anyway.
Biggest highlight of the game however is how it makes you like the characters in a way only few other games do, and the ending deserves a special mention too as it is just beautiful and really really really well made. Did I already mention how beautiful the landscapes are?
Highly recommended for anyone, especially during a sale!
Also, vote for it as best game to make you cry!

There are two fundamental flaws with this game...
1) It's not multiplayer. I say flaw because if this game was multiplayer, I am pretty confident none of us would ever play another game ever again except this one. Explosions, endless bullet spray, flames...flames at the corner of my brain, fodder, more flames and a laser which basically just punches a hole through an entire city block. Now all that control in one mans hands is fun, place it in three, have a timer and endless enemy spawns and you have a pixelated armageddon catering for an endless maniacal laughter.
2) There is a scientific equation law here which is never broken. The equation is this... Zombie + Speeding Car = Tomato Sauce. Problem is not everyone likes tomato sauce. Some like Bbq, others go for mayonaise, some like wasabi and some boring people dont want any sauce at all. Since the developer/s do not want to limit their audience they should really provide an option in game where you can either change color of sauce, or even have the option of 'no sauce'.
Maybe modders can come to the developers rescue on the second point since the game has been completely opened up for them to run mayhem. Personally i like to place several sauces at the same time on my fodder, so give me white, red, green, in fact even make a rainbow sauce please so i can really paint the town.
Basically the story mode is rather linear in the way it plays out like carmageddon, so that you run over various zombies picking up people from various locations in the city. Each time you pick someone up you get treated to a small dialogue of the story which more often than not pokes a bit of fun at itself and the zombie game genre providing some laugh out loud moments. But it does become a bit stale after a while because most of the levels are basically the same thing over and over. You just grind away making money so you can buy more cars and upgrades.
Most of the zombies really do the same thing, they just cause your car's health meter to go down when they hit it while your standing still or if they throw a projectile at it. It doesnt take much intelligence to find the zombie spawn points which are usually a converted zombie bus, or a massive zombie hive and blow it up first. There is one zombie which really is a major pain though and thats the fat zombie, which is somewhat parroted from the 'boomer' in 'left for dead' if he gets close enough to your car he will explode causing massive health damage to your car if your still within his blast radius.
The HD graphics in this game are TRULY AMAZING. I found myself a number of times just parking and looking at the beauty around the place regardless to the fact that I was being pounded into the concrete. I just had to look at the houses and green houses and go 'isnt that pretty, go away zombie leave me alone i'm admiring this flowering bush'...
The other grand mention of this game are the two other modes. This is where the game REALLY shines.
First there is a Slaughter mode where its your job to last as long as possible driving around a small map collecting upgrades and money as the waves of zombie spawns slowly get worse each round. There is an achievement to last for 30 waves. This is really challenging and more often than not personally found that my car was exploding into tiny debri even around wave 10. Place this mode in multiplayer and it would be awesome.
Second there is a tournament mode. The tournament caters three events.
1) Blood race. Race around a track against challenging ai racers poling for first position.
2) Endurance mode. Race around a track by yourself, trying to hit the checkpoints in time against a devilish timer.
3) Elimination mode. Race and blow up as many AI cars as possible.
Again if all this was in multiplayer it would bring back the feeling of the good old days of 'rock and roll racing' google it.
Seriously enjoyed the graphics and the fun of the modes, just really, really wish it was multi player and could turn off that damn red color and change it to pretty rainbows. Still recommend, but if you don't like tomato sauce I would give this one a miss until modders or devs give more options.

The game is actually a lot better than I had it would've been.
First its PROS:
-Large world. Not the biggest, but it is still a fairly large Open World Free Realm, and I enjoy that in games.
-Wide range of weapons to choose from. I've noticed that a lot of would-be good Shooters aren't good due to the fact that they have few weapons. Defiance has a large Range of main weapons, and then sup weapons that branch from their, and then you can even mod the weapons with sights, stocks, mags, and barrels, and not to mention the synergy which is like a passive buff u can have on weapons.
-Missions. There are main missions, side missions, and episode missions. And even challenges so you really can't run out of anything to do. And to add on that, there are side events like Arkfalls, Incursions, and other stuff that happen often for a constant stream of gameplay.
-Classes. There are no classes to choose from technically. This may seem bad but its actually not. You pick a main skill, unlock perks for it, and bam, done. But, if you ever get board of that abillity, or if you're like me and have more than one playstyle per character, you can eventually unlock all the abillities. There is no limitation saying you can't do something like the ever popular, "Your mage is too weak to carry the battle axe. Only a warrior class can carry this." If you want to have an overpower abillity, long distance, sniper rifle with a heavy machine gun than you can do it.
-Leveling. You have your main level, your EGO, and then sub levels, like weapon leveling. My main character has a lvl 9 Bolt rifle, a lvl 7 Simi Auto Rifle, and lvl 4 Pistol (And a few more gun lvls i couldn't care less about), with a EGO of about 400. 400 May seem like a lot, but leveling is super easy in this game. But not so easy to. You level you EGO lvl crazy fast, but each unlock you get from your EGO lvl is very spaced apart. For instance, in order to get your second loadout, you need to be lv. 50. Your 3rd is like 100 or something. Your 4th is 250 i belive, and so on so forth. It's rewarding and easy, but also engaging and challenging.
-Co Op. It isn't required that you have a party and play with people, because if any one is in the mission area you are in, they can help, and recives awards as if they were in a party with you, without doing anything more then showing up, do the objectives, and walk away. I enjoy this as a solo player. I can't stand partys, squads, or really too many people really (sterotypical NEET gamer here XD), so it helps that i can recive help with having to vitually sociallize with avatars.
CONS:
-Co Op. I said before, this co op was really good because you dont need to join any thing to get help, but that means there is a slim chance you can do a mission %100 solo.. I wish to do so, to test my strenghts, and while it isn't impossible, it is fairly difficult.
-PVP. There is pvp, and unlike archeage, you can't just PK (player Kill) Anywhere you want. Which is good. instead they have Shadow Wars, which are like team deathmatch or capture and hold the point wars. They are clear and easy, and you don't have to do them if you don't want to, BUT there isn't much balancing in it. All they do is raise your EGO score a little, to help balance the match up. But that doesn't do much when the one shot you with a weak pistol and you have to shoot them like 6 times in the head with Crit and Dam Buffs with a strong (or as strong as you can get) Rifle.

MEH:
-Character customization. It has more customization than some MMO's, but less than others. It is still there though, so it really isn't a pro or con.

-Bear vs. Dragon [Player - China]
-Pearl of the Orient [Player - UK]
-Climb Mount Narodnaia
-Second Korean War [Player - BLUFOR Forces]
Each of those campaigns host a different style and strategy of gameplay which the player must adapt to and stand on the winning platform.
The developers weren't lying when they said there were over a 1,000+ units in the game,they can all be found in the 'Deck Create' option in the Main Menu.
In Multiplayer, the player can also select from a variety of gameplay modes to play from,
- Destruction
- Conquest
- Siege
- Vox Populi
Each of these gamemodes host a different kind of objective, for example, in Destruction mode the player has to destroy a certain amount of units which depletes their "Objective Points" for each kill, let's say that the enemy has 1,000 points. The player must then destroy units which points are equivalent to the number of "Objective Points" that they have.
There isn't many flaws in the game and I can say that the game has never once crashed on me or shown me a bug, It's a great game overall, if you don't mind paying $39.00 to play it.

I bought Red Dragon when it was 75% off thinking, "Wow, what a deal!" And I guess it was. I wouldn't pay more than $10 for this game, and you shouldn't either, assuming you want to buy it at all.
Wargame: Red Dragon is probably a step under AAA. Why would someone not recommend it?
Red Dragon is the third installment in the Wargame series, following European Escalation and Airland Battle. In Airland Battle, air units were added, and in Red Dragon, naval units. The air game seemed to fit decently into the meta, but the naval game...is a mess. Eugen's love for dice rolling comes out in a real nasty way, and any semblence of either realistic or tactical naval gameplay is set aside for blobbing up your units and praying that your anti-missile equipment holds out longer than the other guy's.
So far as graphics go, yeah, it's a pretty game. It'll take your nice gaming rig and make things look real nice, or you can play it just fine on a potato like mine (just...don't go into those 10v10s if that's a problem).
But where this game really drops the ball is in the single player. The campaigns are actually decently-structured---on paper. Consider the "Medium" difficulty campaign, Bear vs. Dragon, where you've got your Chinese/N.Korea army in 1979 facing 1984 T-80s and experimental units. This wouldn't be too big of an issue if you just fought a small number of them, but Eugen's AI compensates for certain shortcomings in AI programming by having it both be omniscient and have several factors more deployment points than it has any right to at the start of a match.
This is a huge problem in naval games, where the enemy can deploy its 500 point flagships with an entire supporting navy *and* air support while you're lucky to get out a few frigates and some meager anti-ship missile defenses. And because, as we've already established, maneuvering and tactical combat gets one nowhere in the game, particularly against the AI, who fields a vastly superior force bar none, every game, what was a problem becomes a gamebreaking flaw.
The ironic thing is, the sort of naval warfare that it looks like Eugen was going for would do great in a WWII setting. But by pushing in the opposite direction, I fear Eugen jumped the shark with Airland Battle, and it's all downhill from there.
While I like the idea of taking regiments and attaching battalions and companies to them to make your force much more than ALB's "here, have an army and let's tag team it up" campaign, you're still woefully underequipped to deal with most of what the enemy will throw at you unless you specifically pick out the one little hard counter company, which often means having prior knowledge about what you're going to be facing several turns in advance.
A common motif in Red Dragon is the necessity of recon. Unfortunately, while map sizes seem larger, point compensation wasn't considered, meaning the maps are now far too spread out for your unit visibility. This is again a compounded issue when you remember that the AI is omniscient. I've always felt that all units could use a visibility increase (both recon and normal units), but I know that's an argument made in vain, because that's a core mechanic to the game. But the amount of times I've had a recon unit one-shot the moment he spotted an enemy vehicle leads me to believe something funny is going on, and it just leaves me with a bad taste.
In brief: the only reason I would recommend buying Red Dragon would be because you have friends that play it, or want to get into the multiplayer scene. But for the love of all that is holy, stay off the chat. It's unmodded, so if you think you can walk in and make a few friends, you've got another thing coming. If you're entirely new to the Wargame series and want to try it out, I would highly recommend ALB over Red Dragon. Yes, the AI still cheats there, but there's far less units to dig through, and the campaigns there are a bit more friendly. The single-player modes look great on paper, but Eugen's AI makes them a horrible experience, and the modding support simply isn't there to fix it.

When I witnessed this game flood Steamgifts, I had to investigate and saw that it was on sale for pennies. I had to roll my eyes - yet another trashy indie game using cheap sales/mass giveaway stunts to get into as many hands as possible after getting raked over the coals. Saying that it was from the developers of Hero Siege meant little to me - I had never played that game. And yet, Squishy looked kind of interesting. A puzzle/platformer where you have to kill yourself? It was dirt cheap, I could give it a chance.
Squishy was good. Surprisingly good!
Squishy's parents were slaughtered, and the little piggy kills himself in an attempt to reunite with them in Heaven. His suicide sends him to Hell instead, but luckily the devil is bored and offers him a challenge that can get him into Heaven: cross four worlds and find ways to kill himself. Easier said than done!
Each level is a puzzle you have to navigate to open the way to your intended death, which can be anything from finding a level to open a trap door over a bottomless pit or launching a box to crush yourself. The puzzles are clever and sometimes ask you think outside of the box. The game also switches things up with boss fights and key races where you have to navigate and obtain a key quickly, both of which are scenarios where you
want to die. The visuals are good, though the music is a bit quiet, and there are collectable apples and other challenges for the completionists. If you like puzzle platformers, you can't really go wrong here.

So, you want to learn about the colour brown? You've come to the right place. Shades of Brown Simulator will show you pretty much every shade of brown you could ever wish for, and then some more on top. You want brown, they got brown, buckets of the stuff.
I remember first playing Red Faction Guerrilla quite a few years ago when it was ... infected ... with Games for Windows Live. Given that, I can't remember how it got into my Steam account (although saying that, the GWFL Batman's were there too). Anyway, just like Batman, I was very glad to see the GFWL removed with the “Steam Edition”.
On playing this new and improved version, I had a blast. Erm, literally too. Not too many games offer destructible environments (even if it only relates to structures), and those that do have a habit of reverting the destruction as soon as you leave the area. Not so RFG. Blow up a building or a bridge and it stays blown up – and in the manner you choose, not some scripted destruction. Fully physics driven, you can poke a hole in a wall, or take a sledgehammer to supports and watch it crumble. Aside from the odd improbable physics such as the entire second story of a fairly large building being held up by tiny metal pole, this is generally well done, and it's very satisfying planting charges around a tall structure and watching it implode.
Give that RFG takes place on Mars and all the tropes that involves, the terrain is very barren. And brown - not sure if I mentioned that already? As a result, the game feels really bare and outside of the small towns there's bugger all to see except brown, brown and brown! OK, there's the odd radio tag and crystal structure to hit if you're so inclined. And crates. Lots and lots of crates. (But no crowbars). Graphically however, RFG isn't the best.
There is a reasonable variety of vehicles to drive, and the civilian vehicles change with each new zone you enter, and a reasonable array of weapons too, although I ended up just sticking with the same 4 throughout the whole campaign. As well as the primary missions there are various secondary missions (get this vehicle from A to B as fast as, eliminate the enemy, blow up a building using a limited toolset) which were all fun. The main mission story is as clichéd as the setting, but it was all good fun.
Overall a pretty enjoyable game, especially if you like breaking things. Or running down dudes with various Big Guns and smacking them with a hammer. Oh yes.
I recommend this video game. I consider it a classic.

I'll have to keep editing this review as the game has been growing on me. The devs are still at work with it as well, and many of the initial issues I had with the title are being adressed.
It's a fairly simple tower defense game, with a few twists in that it both allows for building mazes for the mobs to pass through, as well as having a controllable hero/builder that can do a lot of the work himself. Also, there's a talent system for your builder to expand upon in between missions, even if it's not all that advanced, and you can upgrade towers as well to become more effecient.
The pros so far:
- Building mazes. It's always nice to be able and change the path of attacking mobs, as it adds another layer to any tower defense out there.
- A hero that's both building towers and can be used to attack the mobs with various abilities.
- Interaction between mobs! This may be the big one that makes the game most enjoyable. Many of the mobs can boost each other in various ways, and even ride- or merge with each other as they go. This feature is also well done graphically, which makes it all the more interesting.
The cons:
- There's still a few bugs in the game, as of v.1.02, though I know they're being adressed by the devs.
- Sadly, a lot of the graphic interaction between mobs is a bit lost on me, as too many mobs in the same area at once will make for quite a mess...
- The story, and the presentation of it, isn't much to write home about really. It's a tower defense game with a bunch of unique levels and a score board to compare your skills with other players, and sometimes you happen to notice that there's some kind of reason to why your hero is building all those towers...
- Just like the story, it's also difficult to see what exactly those talents / upgrades you can choose between missions will actually do for you in the game. You can upgrade damage, speed, range and lower the cost of your towers, but there's very little information to what they actually do for you.
In all it's not a bad game, and will provide with a few hours of fun trying to beat each level and possibly make it to the top of the highscore boards. More updates and content should make it more recommendable.

Few games (or products in general) get me to write a review, so that should say something off the bat.
Hydraulic Empire takes a fun genre (tower defense) and adds what it has often been lacking: main player interactivity.
I like that the difficulty ramps up as you go - this aspect, plus the RPG components, makes me feel like I'm playing an old school, "easy to play, hard to master" game.
Two thumbs up, and I'd love to see this develpoer explore other genres with this kind of a fresh perspective.

At the hard levels which I elected to play, it's absolutely critical that you micromanage your builder, towers, scrap, etc. For players that want the TD with RPG feel, this is it. There are skill trees for you builder, upgrades for towers, and just a unique way to build and maze.
One of the harder things in this game is that there's a good amount of problem solving. There are tool tips for the new items and towers you unlock but there are a good amount of features where clicking will help (leaving this vague so to keep the excitement haha).
Overall, my ratings look something like:
Design: 7/10
Gameplay: Moderate-Moderately Difficult
If you're looking for something new, definitely try this game out! You won't be disapponted!

Spelunky is endlessly engaging, replayable, and the perfect mix of skill and luck. Spelunky works so well because of it's unparraleled design. No death ever feels like your fault, it is always consistant to the rules it sets and deaths are always because you weren't able to deal with the situation set in place. When you die, it really is your fault and you can feel the consiquences. However, the moments where you succeed and overcome adversity are where Spleunky really shines. Only rouge-likes can really truly offer these accomplishments, and Spelunky a great embodiment of this. Spelunky is very difficult from when you first start out, however there is a really good sense of progression even with the great randomly generated levels. When you first make it out of the mines, you feel like a king, yet you die to a tiki trap one level in to the forest. It works very well, especially when player goals are met in a single beautiful run only to have yourself die and set new goals to meet. The decision to make the presentation cartoony and vibrant really also works well to create a good juxtaposition to this difficulty and it really makes you want to keep playing. Lastly, Spelunky should be commended on it's game feel. Everything looks and feels smooth and tactile; whipping has impact, enemy deaths feel satisfying, and taking damage has a real soulcrushing effect. It all leads back to the fact that Spelunky knows how a rouge-like should be designed. It has great adveristy for the player to over come, feels fresh and rewarding, and is simply a blast to play, regardless if you are doing terrible or terrific. Overall, Spelunky is likely the best rouge-like ever made and I greatly recommend it to fans of the genre and anyone even remotely intrested in it.

Spelunky is an insanely compelling 2d platformer with random level generation. It’s a brilliantly designed game that offers a great deal of depth from some fairly simple mechanics. The rules of the world are all consistent, it’s the kind of game where you learn through failure and the challenge feels fair. Before long you’ll find yourself learning all of its intricacies and achieving a great sense of mastery.
In the standard adventure mode there are no permanent unlocks other than characters and yet you’ll find yourself going from not being able to clear the first world to consistently reaching the end which is a really satisfying progression.
In the ingenious daily challenge everyone’s random level generation is seeded the same so everyone’s playing through the same set of levels for that day. You have 1 life to get as far as you can and your progress is registered on a leaderboard so you can compare your score with friends.
The game also supports local co-op which suddenly makes the game a way more chaotic experience as you try to stay together without whipping each other into spikes. There’s also a multiplayer deathmatch mode which is surprisingly brilliant, capturing the frantic party atmosphere of games like bomberman.
Overall this is one of the purest, best gaming experiences I’ve had and I can’t recommend it enough.

In the world of video game most zombie games are in first, third or isometric view. You take control over some human, but in how many you can drive a car and slaughter zombies? Not many. This is the thing that intrigue me here. And the game is properly named – Zombie Driver.
The game have a lot of video option. Except resolution you can find clouds, bloom, FXAA, fog, V-sync, SSAO, fullscreen and shadow type. Despite all those settings and the HD in the name, the game is not that good looking. It's not ugly, just okay. But to be honest most of the times you won't even notice the graphics quality, because there is a danger to be surrounded by zombies and you will drive all the time. The bad texture mostly noticeble when the game stop you to show something.
You play as a nameless character, a taxi driver, that is caught in a city during a zombie outbreak. He now have to do the military's job. Why? No one knows. Even in the game is mentioned that. To story is the worst thing here. It's not worth paying attention. You do few things here to progress it – save someone, clear a place to move the base, kill something that spawns zombies, plant a gas sparying device and the game is over. Some of the people that you save are saying things that are making hints for something deeper, but ultimately the story goes nowhere. Do some missions and get out of the city.
I don't mind a bad story if the gameplay is good. Here it's just that. The controls are fine. I try controller, but I end up playing with mouse and keyboard. With them it's much more fun. You start with a your taxi and by doing missions you will unlock more vehicles and get money. The cash can be also earned by driving through zombies and break what can be break in the world. With the money you will upgrade your cars and weapons. The upgrades for all straightforward – more ammo, bigger explosions, faster car etc. So pretty much that's it. You drive around, kill zombies, get cash, upgrade vehicle. You don't have all the weapons in all the time. They are on the ground spread around the level and you have drive through them. And all are useful. The thing I found is you need a truck that can take a lot of damage and have good ramming points. After that other vehicles are useless, at least to me. I played with Auroch through most of the game and the only time I change it is when I need to save more than 10 people. For those cases I used a bus, which is pretty decent. The speed of both vehicles is fast enough. The map don't have many places that you can drive really fast. The vehicles have the tendency to fly in the air when you hit a wall. So for me there is no point of using some of sport cars. They can be destroyd easily.
From time to time the army gives you a different vehicle – tank or a bulldozer or a truck. This is a neat idea to change a little bit the gameplay. Beside the main objective you have a secondary. It's wise to do them, because you get more money or car or something else. But ultimately the missions are as I mention above – kill, save or destroy.
There three bosses in the game and all are fun. They have some similar attack and you circle around them and shoot them. Near all the bosses have those places that spawn zombies constantly and it's wise to destroy them first.
The world is really great. It's not a huge map, but it's big enough. It's very diverse – train stations, houses, industrial zone, suburban area and so on. There are a lot of shorcuts that can be found and it's helpful know them in situations where you are in a hurry. Almost all objectives have some sort of time limit.
Sound design is okay. Shooting, engines, explosions and other effects are good, but the music is not memorable. It adds a little bit tension, it's fast paced, it's sometimes orchestral, it uses a lot of drums and guitars. It kinda remind me of Resident Evil the movie soundtrack and Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2. It's a game about shooting zombies and I don't excpect creepy music. I want high octane tracks and that's what i've got. But it's there somewhere in the background. Sadly I can't point one track that stands out above the other.
Voice acting is bad, especially the people you save. They are all steriotypes you can think of – gamer, scared scientist, obnoxious  politician and so on. I know, the focus of the game is the gameplay, but the problem is you can't skip any dialog.
It seem so far that I dislike the game, but actually I don't. I'm just a little bit disappointed The game for me is just okay. I really like to run over zombies or to blast them to pieces, but the main campaign gets kinda repetetive, but thankfuly it's not that long. I took me around 4 hours the finish it. There is too many minor things that annoy me. Beside the campaign I have problems also with the weapons. They are only four. Don't get me wrong they are all great, especially when you upgrade the rockets and railgun, but they are only four. When you combine all this with the bad voice acting, the repetition, it's brings the game down for me. But there is one saving grace – the Blood  Race. It racing with other cars and zombies on the road. I had so much fun shooting other vehicles. There are 3 different type of races and I like all of them, especially the Eliminator. Here you have to destroy certain number of cars for a limited time. You can shoot them, you can ram them or combination of both. As a conclusion I would say I recommend the game, but on sale.

Easiest way to explain this game series is Total War in the modern ages, or Company of Heroes: The Cold War, with a dynamic campaign meta map. That is a complete over simplification of course, but the game basically takes place in turn based campaign maps with realistic real time battles on fixed maps during the late Cold War era.Graphics are great, sound is amazing, and the campaigns are really informed alt history ideas presented with enticing old school "news reel" videos. Simple, but fun and effective presenation. Quality wise these games are very well made, with a few bugs here and there, and UI "quirks" that take a little getting used to. The Wargame games are also constantly being patched and improved, and with a set of FreeLC at your disposal.
This one adds in naval combat as well to the series, so if you haven't bought a Wargame title yet and are wondering which one to go for first, I'd say this one for the simple fact it has all the bells and whistles of the past with the above and I'm sure a few more improvements I haven't really noticed being a bit of a noob with the franchise.
Only real consumer down side if your weighing this agaisnt something like CoH2, if you can call it that, is they have a very steep learning curve. Once you get past that first layer of learning however it becomes a very intuitive game engine. Online is a very steep curve to get used to as well difficulty wise, but I've run into a fair amount of like minded noobs to learn with. From my experience the existing old guard player base is a healthy, helpful community as well even when they're wiping the floor with you're army online lol.

Red Faction Guerilla is the sequel to Red Faction (at least a true sequel, unlike Red Faction II). In the aftermath of the first game's events, it seems the EDF are treating everyone the miners like trash, so it's up to Alec Mason to lead the "guerilla" (There's barely any mention of quick runs, you mostly destroy everything without so much as a hint of subtlety) rebellion against their tyrannical overlords...
other than blowing the unliving parts of every building ever.
May the Masons strike me down with their almighty hammers, but I think this game is average at best, with some nifty building destruction that lands on you every once in a while. The vehicle time challenges in this game is infuriating, and the GPS is worthless in those. Perhaps it's just those darn vehicle challenges that soured my experience, but I feel it's a bit overrated just becaue of the GeoMod alone (Guess I'm not the destruction enthusiast I thought I was). It's however, better than/not Red Faction II, so great work for that.

Red Faction Guerrilla is good for what it is, but it is starting to show its age.
The building destruction mechanics are awesome, and there still aren't really any games that compare to how satisfying and detailed the destruction of buildings is. Sadly, the insides of buildings feel very lifeless compared to the sculpted mountains and hills of Mars. Add the fact that you can raze the entire building with a mis-click, it adds to the lifelessness of buildings, and the world feels somewhat better without them. 90% of the buildings don't ever respawn, which means once you enjoy the destruction of everything on Mars once, you won't be able to do it again on the same save file. Also, having good building destruction kind of pales in comparison to the terrain deformation from the original Red Faction, and it is a shame that they couldn't somehow implement that as well.
The combat is the usual stale third person shooter type, similar to Watchdogs. The melee with things like hammers is pretty satisfying against enemies, though it is very risky on harder difficulties since enemies will take out half of your health with great accuracy while running up to them. The driving is OK, a little stiff, but solid. Smashing a truck through an outpost is great, and really highlights the great destruction engine.
The graphics are fast becoming very dated. The cutscenes look almost like something from a PS2 game, the human models look kind of chunky, like action figures, and I don't know if it's just me but the sound files for voice acting sound really compressed and garbage sounding, as if they were from a game from 2002. Mars looks fine, it looks like Mars.
The game is pretty unbalanced on the hard difficulty. Enemies empty magazines into you with very little inaccuracy, and because the health regeneration takes such a long time to begin, the sheer amount of enemies that start chasing you will kill you. The enemies also take a huge amount of damage. It helps make the EDF feel more like armoured bad guys, but it's very annoying using all of your ammo on only 3 normal bad guys, especially when there are 12 more around the corner. The sheer randomness of the physics system also takes part in causing much frustration. Sometimes getting hit in the head with a fallen turbine blade will only give you some damage and won't knock you down. Sometimes a stray hand-railing will knock you down, take out a quarter of your health, and pin you under a nearby walkway making you a sitting duck for enemy soldiers while you wait for the standing up animation to happen. I don't know what a remedy could be for something like this, because it makes sense to die from a bulding landing on your head. But sometimes the physics are just too random.
Overall, the game is good. It's just kind of showing it's age with some other problems from the time. If you are in the mood for games like GTA, Watchdogs, or other third-person drivey-shooty games, then this game will fit the bill with some added cathartic destruction.

I love this kind of game, but I was hoping for a game engine update, and a UI redesign. Additionally, the game interrupts the action with story instead of enhancing it with story. I want to get the story via voice - preferably while I'm at sublight - and if a part of the story is important enough to write dialogue about, then it is important enough to voice. What puts this as a firm "do not recommend" though is frequent bugs with the campaign. They didn't even create a new game engine, so the least they could do before repackaging the same game is give it some QA.
The UI feels like it was designed by someone who has never studied this before - not even a quick Youtube tutorial. For example, the galaxy map should center on you (not the center of the galaxy even when you are at the rim) and automatically zoom out enough to include your mission waypoint. Instead, every mission starts with a wide zoom-out and then a hunt for the star-point to click on. What would be even better is if in boring repetitive easy situations like that, we could just be prompted by our crew with a single button press question - should we head toward the objective?
Additionally, the UI for buying/selling, upgrading gear, etc. is unecessarily small and spread out. When we are in these screens, they have the player's full focus, so use the full screen to show all the information with high visibility and reduce the number of tabs we have to navigate to get to the thing we want to do.
I'd just go freeroam as most of the bugs I've encountered so far have been in the campaign, but I need the tutorial for fleet/force management and I'd like to know a little more abou the game/universe. . .  still, I think this may just go on the back burner. The well-made, user-friendly space sim of modern PC gaming should be something that is acheivable without creating just a space flight-sim like Elite:Dangerous or a boondoggle like Space Citizen, but unfortunately Starpoint Gemini Warlords is not it. . .   and yet, it is the closest thing to it for now, so I'm keeping it, and I suggest that other people who want a Freelancer/Privateer-esque space sim get it too. Maybe they'll make a sequel with a better game engine, better QA, and the UI designer will spend an hour researching his job on Youtube.

I'm no rail expert, but I'd like if someone could explain to me that if you stop a heavy train in a hill with the train brake, apply the loco brake, apply full power forwards and release the train brake, the train actually goes backwards. I could understand that if the wheel friction from the loco was to little to hold the train by itself, BUT the wheels are not slipping, AND if you release the loco brake the train starts moving forward. There are other things as well, like how the compressed air from the brake cylinders seems to move back into the reservoir when you release the brakes and more. Making a train simulator is by itself on the limit of what is reasonable, because most of the time it's simply boring to "play". If you choose to do so however, you SHOULD get the very few things that come into play, like engine and brakes, right!
While I like the idea of the academy, I don't think the devs ever actally tried it, it has bugs and won't always complete if you follow the instructions, and some of the "lessions" are: load for ages - press one button - finished. Graphics is dated, cars run through trains, sounds are looped, and all in all it gives the impression of an alpha release. Yet, every little thing costs a lot of money. The "base pack" is nothing more than a ticket to the DLC shop. DLC's are overly expensive.

This is one of the only games I've ever played where switching control schemes has improved it so drastically that I've gone back and altered my previous review.
Long story short: Play this game with a gamepad. Analog sticks are absolutely essential, the M/K controls are complete sewage, but you could probably guess that.
Apart from that, the game is a really fun, fast-paced, and generally intuitive skiing sim. Combos require enough skill in timing to be genuinely satisfying to pull off, the maps are absolutely gorgeous (CryEngine ain't no slouch in the visual department) and there are very few other games that so accurately recreate the feeling of flying through a forest at breakneck pace. It makes the moments of triumph all the more fun to achieve when they're punctuated by your character inevitably crashing into a tree and his ragdoll shooting into space.
On that note, the game can get frustrating at times. The camera is angled slightly downward by default, and the way the maps are laid out makes it very difficult to actually see past bigger inclines. That means that if you're going for the biggest jumps (and why would you not be?) you're taking massive leaps of faith every time, and it's almost impossible to predict whether your angle is going to send you into a fluffy patch of snow for a perfect landing or into a rock so your character can make another trip into space. Meanwhile, the combo system gives out points for tricks and penalizes mistakes, but the amount it penalizes doesn't seem to have any correlation to the severity of the mistake you made. At one junction, I had just pulled off a cork 1440, earning 80 points in the process, and had landed right next to a row of trees, so I had to do a little weaving to avoid a crash. I didn't quite get out of the way of a slight incline in the ground, though, and my character tripped up on it, so I rewinded about 20 feet to turn a little harder left and avoid it, for which the game penalized me 120 points. So my net profit for one of the biggest jumps and longest combos I pulled off in the game was -40 points. I don't know how it calculates those penalties, but that formula needs an overhaul before this game finishes its Early Access run.
Tokens are ridiculously hard to earn without microtransactions, but that much was predictable just from the fact that the game has microtransactions at all. Of course they're difficult to earn without paying, that's the whole point. But what bewilders me about the microtransactions is that the only things currently available in the store are a paltry handful of challenges and cosmetic bonuses, neither of which really seem enticing when the game already comes with six maps and a bunch of unlockables. Mind you, only one of the maps that comes with the base game (Sialia) is actually an open world for exploration and the rest are just challenge runs with one or two jumps in their entirety. It's not like I expected Skyrim for the asking price, but when the game sells itself as an open-world skiing experience I would like a change of scenery every now and again. I was never a fan of jump events even back when I was on a ski team in real life, and exploring giant mountains at high speed has always been my favorite part of the sport. It's not a deal-breaker, because Sialia is a pretty good map with a lot of places to explore, but I'd definitely like the game more if it had more open areas like that. Moreover, it wouldn't make the store itself feel completely vestigial.
So in short, it's a little bit buggy and a little bit of a cash grab, but I can't really begrudge it because the core experience is still rock-solid as far as skiing games go. Definitely feels like an Early Access title, but it's at least got me interested enough to hold out until the full release. Make of that what you will.

I suppose gameplay is interesting enough, with fun stealth and FPS done reasonably well. But in summary the reason I can't stand this game is that they heavily advertise the "realistic ballistics" in the sniping, when, in fact, this game has the worst ballistics I have ever seen. It not only ruins the gameplay, but also puts them squarely under the category of blatantly lying. So if you don't care about reallistic ballistics, then you might have fun. But this was certainly a game ruiner for me.
Now for the details.
It's time for a quick physics lesson. The bullet from an M1 Garand travels at about 850m/s. Over a shot distance of 70m, that results in a time of flight of 0.082 seconds. In that time, the bullet should drop a grand total of 3.2cm. So if I aim for the back of his head, I should hit a 3.2cm lower spot on the back of his head. In this game, I aim for the back of the guy's head 70m away, and I hit his kidney. After some rough estimates, I find that this requires a time of flight right around .35 seconds, giving a muzzle velocity a bit over 200m/s. Realistic ballistics?
It gets better, cause I then went to long range and did some time of flight estimates. I ended up with a bullet velocity of ~750m/s. So their muzzle velocity isn't off, it's their gravity. A quick calculation later shows that their gravity strength is roughly 13*g, well above the point at which everyone would black out. Also, I would weight 2,500lbs.
So in short, when they say "realistic ballistics," they are simply lying.
Add to that, 100m shots are not sniper shots. Their entire maps aren't big enough from one end to the other for decent sniper shots. So they've compressed the distances and increased bullet drop to the point where even close range shots are practically impossible without using their cheating help reticle.
And if your entire game is stealth based, don't make it easier for me just to run through the whole map shooting up the place. Punish the player for not being sneaky.
