This is my first, and likely to be my only ever Steam review of a game, but given current events I felt it necessary to say something.
First things first, GTA V is a good game, all in all. It provides for hours of hijinks and entertainment, but can easily become monotonous. GTA Online had the potential to be a repreive from this monotony, but was handeled with such greed and a complete and blatant disregard for its audiance that it's frankly insulting.
The "gameplay" offered by GTA Online is based entirely around a grind for cash and RP for leveling, and many gameplay elements are blocked out to the player unless they have enough cash or a high enough level. This not only serves to prolong this feeling of monotony, but also stips the gameplay of any of the fun that could be acheived in the singleplayer.
This is only worsened by the games use of microtransactions, "graciously" allowing players to skip the ridicilous and unnecessary grind by rewarding the player with cash and RP in exchange for ridicilous amounts of real money. For instance, the price of a yacht in in-game currency is $8,00,000 which translates to either dozens of hours spent in-game grinding, or $100 in real world currency.
GTA Online is also completely hostile to new players; new players, lacking the necessary level or cash to have access to any decent vehicles, weaponry, armor, housing, and vehicle storage have no way to combat the more experienced players or those who chose to pay for their levels and cash. This makes it nearly impossible for new players to advance in the game without having to waste their money on microtransactions, as they will not be able to compete with the other players.
This monotony could, and was, eliminated through the use of mods, giving the player a potentially indefinite amount of hours of hijinks and entertainment through the hard work of dedicated modders. Unfortunately, and what I find has proven to be the nail in this games coffin, the game's publisher Take-Two issued a cease-and-desist to OpenIV, one of the major modding tools of GTA V, used by most of the better mods.
Now, I am no lawyer so I could be completely off base, but from my limited understanding this cease-and-desist has no actual basis, but instead is just an assualt on the modding community and on the fans. Unfortunately, independent modders don't have the funds necessary to challenge a multi-million publishing company in court, so instead they've been allowed to get away with this frankly disgusting behavior.
Without mods, I cannot honnestly recommend this game, nor would I want to, and I'd recommend that potential buyers avoid this game for the time being, if for nothing more than to send a message to the publishers that we will not tolerate such greed and disgusting, underhanded business practices.
On another note, the keyboard controls or terrible, but the game has controller support, so it's not that much of an inconvenience.
TL;DR
Avoid this game unless the publishers go back on their current practices and begin to, at the very least, tollerate the existance of mods.

One thing I want to make clear straight off the bat is that this game gets a positive review from me solely because it is more than worth it's current price of a whopping nine pence. That being said, given that I would probably purchase an empty wrapper that used to contain a chocolate bar and still has some hint of the fragrance for the same price, that's no indication of the game's quality, and to be blunt you can sum up the biggest strength and greatest weakness of the game in one word. Cheap. In both senses of the word.
I don't want to make it sound as if the game is bad - it isn't - but this is an instance where you get what you pay for. Despite the original sounding concept - you need to kill yourself in every level rather than avoid death - it plays ostensibly the same as any other puzzle-platformer; push some boxes, activate some switches, and get to the end. The only difference is that the end of the level is a pit of spikes rather than a princess in a castle.
The controls are simple and not too shabby. Aside from moving and jumping, there's nothing to do. Sure you can walk up to a switch or push a box, but you only need buttons for left, right, and jump. Around 80% of the time the levels are surprisingly decent, showing a good understanding of level design given that your character has barely any abilities. One thing I would improve is the jumping mechanic, as I've died more than a few times due to an unclear cooldown period after jumping during which you can't jump again. That reminds me - every few levels the 'You're trying to die' mechanic is eschewed in favour of finding a key or chasing something, so there are moments when the game loses the biggest asset that was keeping it original.
The other 20% of levels present a pretty big problem though. Some of the levels are ridiculously unclear and downright stupid, and on these levels you won't fail because you lack skill, you'll fail because the game is withholding information you would need to beat it. On one level - and I don't feel the slightest bit guilty about spoiling this - there's a row of pits and two boxes, and the game somehow expects you to figure out that you need to push boxes into pits 4 and 6. There is no indication of this whatsoever, and the closest I could find was a note in the dirt reading 'A-N T-G'. There's leaving things to the player's imagination and then there's just taking liberties.
I'm currently on the Boss of World 2 and I can safely say that as someone who has finished around 75 Steam games, it is the worst boss I've faced in any of them. The arena is small and the boss throws six bombs down, which cover half of the arena. The bombs have a blast radius that is a little over twice their size. Do the math. It doesn't help that to win the battle you need to avoid this attack EIGHTEEN TIMES in a row. That pretty much sums up the worst parts of the game - 10% skill, 90% hoping the random number generator lets you win.
Overall, despite what I've said, this guy is well worth the price. The graphics are pleasant, there's a bit of humour and variety, and although it's hit and miss, there are more hits than misses by far. But bear in mind that if it was priced at say, £5 or more, this would definitely be a negative review. It's fun, but approach with caution.

Mount & Blade: Warband is an action RPG from TaleWorlds Entertainment.
The Good
I don’t even know where to begin with this game. I’ve clocked close to 100 hours into this game and I will, undoubtedly, be clocking a hundred or so more in the coming months. Let me just talk about what kinds of things you can do in this game.
Explore the world (which is quite large in the vanilla game, but can be made far larger through mods).
Become a bandit and pillage the countryside.
Become a complete menace and attack everything in sight (and probably get annihilated doing so).
Become a lord in the service of a monarch and wage war on multiple fronts.
Betray said monarch and try to wrest control of the kingdom for yourself.
Switch sides, join an opposing monarch, and fight against all your old comrades.
Raid defenseless villages and slaughter their populations.
Steal all the cattle from a village, slaughter them, and leave the meat to rot.
Become a trader and travel from settlement to settlement selling  your goods.
Become a slave trader and sell helpless villagers into slavery.
Get an entire army of cavalry and wreak havoc in open combat.
Get wrecked with your entire army of cavalry when your try to siege a castle while dismounted.
Demand that you be able to ride your steed up the siege tower/ladder and into the enemy castle.
Hurl javelins/axes at the enemy from the relative safety of the siege tower.
And much, much more.
Woo fair maidens.
Participate in tournaments and feel the pain that is the terrible lance controls for jousting.
I don’t really think anything else needs to be said here.
The Bad
What? Bad stuff? What are you talking about? Get out of here.
The Meh
The graphics aren’t outstanding, but it makes it so you can have battles with hundreds of people on both sides. And, you know what? I’m perfectly willing to make that trade off.
Verdict: Yea
Honestly, if you don’t have this game already, I don’t know why you haven’t already bought it. Seriously. Stop reading and go buy it right now.

So I just beat this game, and can say without a doubt it filled the void in my life for the last 50 hours. I am not finished yet either, as I have the DLC to do still as well as conquering the rest of the system(I own about half). I learned about this game from the Starpoint Gemini 2 forums, which was my first game made by Little Green Men. I liked it as well, but this game expands on that one and is much funner and thus I am getting way more hours of play out of this one. Warlords is a sandbox game with a campaign to play through in the sandbox. You can just play with the sandbox as well and disable the campaign when starting a new game. I guess I will just go over the main categories most reviews do briefly.
The graphics are good, but not the best either. Most other newer space games like Elite Dangerous do beat it down a bit. But they do a fantastic job with the art direction and nebulas here. There is not much more to write about here as you can view screenshots. Audio is pretty good as well, but again not state of the art or anything. Some of the campaign is voiced as well(but not a lot of it unfortunately).
The gameplay is fantastic, and where this game shines. It has a tactical based combat system. You try to manage your ships shields as you aim your turrets at the opposing ships. You can manually aim, but you will mostly just use the "fire at will" command for the AI to do it, as you need to focus on rotating your ship and using skills. The main complaint I have against this system would be the lack of balance for missiles. I found my self ignoring missiles(the heavy weapons of the game), as they barely do anymore damage than your main guns and have limited ammo. The boarding is done well, and I am not sure that I would want much changed about it. Your marines have to progress from room to room after you grapple a ship and send in your boarding party. Once the ship is yours(which you can increase your chances with perks and research) you may then choose to either sell it, keep it, or send it towards research if you don't have access to that ship yet. Besides the campaign you have mining, side missions, salvaging, bounty hunting, trading(which I almost didn't mention the economy is static) and conquering the map. You may build a fleet of ships that you can have follow you, or you can have them help defend some outpost. I mostly only saw the need to have them follow me though, and just get a death fleet to go around and conquer. This leads me to another complaint about the late game. While you are conquering and doing missions you have to micro-manage the crap out of your civilian fleet. This consists of every few minutes having to open up your map, and scroll around looking for stuff for your civilian fleet to do(this is seperate from the combat fleet that follows you). It is very annoying having to click on each allied station to see what they are trading. It would be nice if there was a window of some sort that popped up and showed you all of this information and you could choose to send your fleet from that screen instead. Or even allowing wasd movement on the map would help alot.
The story of the campaign is alright, but nothing to write home about. It is pretty well done, but there is way to many fetch type quests IMHO. It could as well use more cinematics to tie everything together and have fully voiced dialogue throughout it. This would make it much more immersive and interesting. I sort of lost interest halfway through for a while and just ran from point a to b without reading the story. However towards the end it gets much more interesting as you start working on the end game.
Overall this game was a lot of fun, and well worth the money I spent on it. I can safely recommend this game to anyone interested in sci-fi, space, RPG, empire building, or tactical combat as it has all of these elements going for it. I can see myself playing this quite a bit longer with the dlc(titans!), and trying to conquer the rest of my map. If they add other playable factions then it will add tremendous replayability to the game as well(hint hint!).

Very mixed feeling.  I really would like to see more narrative-focus adventure games being made, but Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons just didn't feel like a game - more like an interactive film (more so the fact it's so short), and not a very good one at that.
Visual and audio directions are amazing.  That plus the emotional ride mentioned by other positive reviews kept me playing.  Unfortunately the adventure didn't live up to its hype.  The control scheme is interesting but felt it wasn't fully explored in puzzle design.  Puzzles, if you can call it that, are way too easy and feel more like a distraction.
There are a lot of interesting places and characters, but the game never give opportunity to explore and learn more about them.  So the adventure ended up feeling like a dream.  It's emotional at times but like a dream it's so random and moves so fast that in the end you weren't sure if it was a good dream or bad dream, but it leaves you feeling melancholy.
If you like that sort of feeling, definitely play this game.  Otherwise I wouldn't recommend it.

At first, I thought the developers were just too lazy to make an AI, so they had the player control both brothers. I could have not been more wrong, and I should have known better! Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is all about the masterful storytelling from beginning to end
. The game is set in a rich and vibrant world that's full of people, animals and breathtaking scenery bringing it all to life. The gameplay is always interesting and very good at motivating the player to move forward at the perfect pace to progress the story; meanwhile, you're also accompanied by a swooping soundtrack on this emotional journey. However, it's not the most keyboard-friendly game, so I recommend playing with a controller if possible - and you still might get a little confused from time to time with one. Regardless, this polished gem is a fine example of storytelling at its best; there are certain interactions present, a depth, which can only be reached and expressed in the form of a video game. I simply can not recommend this experience enough.

Spelunky is an exquisitely designed hybrid roguelike/platformer that is simple to learn, but very difficult to master. Often a single mistake from certain death, you must depend on your own skills and knowledge to progress through the procedurally generated caves, uncovering the treasures and secrets that lie below. Death comes often, especially to newcomers, but every death is a learning experience that improves your chances of survival in subsequent attempts.
Spelunky is a game that is simultaneously merciless and fair. Even with multitude of threats you'll face, almost every death you experience is preventable and the result of poor judgment or a lack of skill. All of Spelunky's mechanics and enemies follow a persistent and predictable logic, each element a tiny cog in a massive interlocking machine. Learning about the inner workings of Spelunky's world is necessary to venture into the deeper reaches of the caves.
Those that are looking for an easy game to breeze through should look elsewhere, but those that desire a game that will test their skills as well as the speed and accuracy of their decision-making will likely enjoy Spelunky. Like many roguelikes, the initial difficulty is very high, and may be offputting to some, but those that persevere will be rewarded with an incredibly satisfying game that has nigh-infinite replay value and keeps even experienced players on their toes.
Below is a short story inspired by Spelunky, which may give a potential player an idea of how the game plays and what I find so appealing about it.
/----After carrying both the valuable golden idol and the defenseless pug to the exit, I turned back to recover the shotgun that I had left on a perch high above, but partway through my journey, I felt a shiver run down my spine, and the air grew cold. It seemed that I had overstayed my welcome. Seconds later, I spotted the translucent spectre effortlessly slipping through solid wall, approaching me with single-minded determination. Having dealt with this ghost many times before, I was undeterred. I grabbed my shotgun and nimbly weaved my way through the twisted caverns as the sluggish spirit fell behind. However, as I neared the exit, something caught my eye: a lone supply crate sat at the end of a corridor, begging for its contents to be revealed. My desire for treasures overwhelming my senses, I made a dash for the crate, and within it I found a parachute. “Hardly worth the effort”, I muttered as I turned towards the exit, but as soon as I began to make my way back, I realized what a terrible mistake I had made. My unnecessary detour had allowed the ghost I had previously danced around with such confidence to corner me. I scrambled to blow open an escape route, but the walls that surrounded me were too thick, and the fuses on my bombs too long. Realizing the inevitability of my fate, I turned to face the approaching phantom and awaited its deadly embrace...
...And as quickly as I felt my life being sucked away, I woke up at the cave entrance, no worse for wear. After taking note of my own death in a dusty old journal and etching another tally mark into the nearby stone wall, I journeyed yet again into the mysterious caves below, tightening the grip on my trusty whip as the surrounding rocks and dirt shifted under my feet. “This is the one” I assured myself as I entered an abandoned mine with renewed determination and a newfound respect for the ghost that haunts the caves below. “I just know it.”----/

At core, this is a game about upgrading your ship, exploring a huge galaxy, trading, and blowing things up. If that's enough for you, you'll have a good time with SPGW. It looks good, the ships are cool, and the mechanics are solid, if on the repetitive side.
There's some problems though. The campaign is pretty poorly done. The much-vaunted RTS element is... meh. You can create these huge fleets and send them into battle, but your AI ships die frustratingly easily, so it's never as satisfying or efficient as just doing the thing yourself. You can take over vast swaths of the galaxy over many hours to get resources, but one lucky boarding run on a carrier in a random mission will get you FAR more. I felt like these aspects were bolted on and dispensable.
The difficulty curve is also a bit silly. Low-yield random missions and encounters will kill you with alarming regularity, up to the point where you have a Dreadnought and top-tier enhancements -- at which point you can solo a friggin planet with minimal issues. It tends to be frustrating until it's boring, with a preciously slim window in between the two.
But again, that core gameplay is there, and it's pretty choice. So overall it has to be a thumbs up.

Despite a few rocky points, Starpoint Gemini Warlords is absolutely worth picking up.
I played Eve Online for many years, and there is a familiar feeling if it's more Eve "Offline", and in a good way for the most part. It can definitely feel empty without other people to chat with, but there's NPCs roaming around, various factions squabbling over turf, and you're free to make friends and enemies as you see fit.
I started with the Campaign, and while the story is pretty mild with plot twists, it was not the worst story. Most of it felt like a dragged out tutorial, and some of it even your character seemed to make some snarky remarks that mirrored my own thoughts. It did set the tone for the game, and there were some dialogue options if you had the right perks, which made some parts easier to complete.
Most of your time will be spent actually roaming about, where there is a fair amount of things to do. From boarding ships, to just mining, you can do just about whatever you choose to do. Most of it can get repetitive, so having a lot to do at least keeps it refreshing for awhile.
There's a decent variety of ships in the game, as different areas have offered different ships for sale, and some that can only be acquired from boarding actions. Ships range from small Gunships to a massive Titan (Note, there is only one Titan without the DLC). Different factions have different aesthetics, as well as different stats. I personally flew the ships that I liked over the "best" stat ships, and never felt it hindered my gameplay. Getting the larger ships can feel a little grindy, while some of the ships you can only capture put you at the mercy of RNG, even with really good stats/perks.
The map feels pretty large, and it takes some time to get around without the use of T-Gates. At first, the map did not look all that large fully zoomed out, until I started panning around. Once I only used my sublight drive to go from one corner to the other, and it took me a fair amount of time ignoring everything along the way.
Combat takes a little getting used to, and after a while it gets fairly repetitive, especially once you have the larger ships where it's more of a slugging match, rather than a dogfighting spiral (though the larger ships is similar, but slower). You can also go into a "turret mode" to keep your guns trained on an enemy ship, or have your ship "fire at will". While you might have some turrets blocked depending on ship design, you might also be able to deliver a nasty broadside!
The boarding mechanic is more or less spending points to move from room to room, and spending points to pillage/capture. Larger ships are far harder to capture, so don't expect to successfully board a battleship early on, and even with a fully kitted out capital, boarding a ship to capture isn't a guarantee. You can choose to keep these ships, sell them, research them (so your HQ can build them for your warfleet), or scrap them for materials.
This brings me to the strategy portion, which for some will seem overly simplistic, and for others a chore. Obviously, to build a warfleet capable of taking over the map (or to get through the campaign), you'll have to build mining stations for ore, gas collectors for gas, junk collectors for "materials", and of course credits. These 4 resources are needed to buy/build ships, build/upgrade structures, and perform research. You will also get access to "civilian fleets" which can be assigned to projects on the map as you see fit. Every "week" you will get resources, and the more territory you own, the more you get.
Taking over territories will require you to battle stations/outposts to gain control. The other factions will have fleets they have patrolling to help defend their own turf, as well as to attack rivals. Destroying these fleets, capturing the stations and outposts will queue a battle, with a meter to see if you're winning/losing. If you leave the fleets to NPCs to fight it out, they'll have a timer until the battle is "won", but if you as a player intervene the timer goes away. To win these fights, you basically have to destroy all the marked targets, but the player can tip the balance in lopsided fights, and early on this is more important. By the "end" I was just letting my fleets attack on their own, while I attacked something else.
Overall, I am really happy to have picked this up, and it scratches that itch of flying around in space blowing stuff up, or just trading between stations to afford the really big ships. I haven't picked up the DLC yet, but still have about 1/2 the map left to conquer, so definitely got my money's worth.

I have several train simulators including Trainz: A New Era and all four World of Subways games, but Train Simulator 2015 is fast becoming my favourite. Lots of interesting and challenging driving scenarios, wonderful scenery, a good variety of locomotives and very realistic controls that can be managed either via the actual engine controls or the HUD make this a train buff's dream!
If I have one complaint, it's that the add-ons are prohibitively expensive. However, you can buy "collections" that include several routes and locos at once, and I would recommend this as a way to save some money. There are also sales with big discounts now and again. Within the game, the long ad at the very start gets rather tedious, as do the promos when scenarios are loading. Thankfully, it is possible to get rid of the introductory video by unchecking a box in the Settings. Also, there are times when the HUD doesn't always show speed changes, and I have been caught out on more than one occasion by these "hidden" speed limits. That all depends on the specific scenario though - some scenarios are near flawless, while others can be somewhat buggy.
But these minor gripes aside, I think this is a superb game and arguably the best train simulator currently available. It has more variety than the World of Subways games (which can get a bit monotonous after you've completed all the missions), and its controls are more user-friendly than in the Trainz series of games. Also, its bugs can generally be worked around, whereas the ones in T:ANE cause you no end of exasperation and ruin your gaming experience. So I am only too pleased to highly recommend Train Simulator 2015!

First time doing these, so take it easy on any replies (if any). I have not bothered to play the English adaptation nor do I intend to.
Story: The tale revolves around the sword with the power to destroy the eponymous Tsukumogami, objects which have gained sentience after long years of use. The protagonist loses her mother and her father goes missing after the Tsukumogami raid the capital city, leaving her to grow up and learn swordsmanship under foster care. Her destiny is then intertwined with the sword. How the tale is resolved is then up to the choices made by the player over the course of the game.
Setting: Early medieval/medieval Japan with magic and the supernatural weaved into the fabric of society. The Tsukumogami are based on the Hyakki Yakou legends and the paintings associated with them over the ages.
Characters: Hayabusa's characterisation is quite standard, trained to wield the sword and seeking vengeance against the Tsukumogami responsible for taking her parents away from her. Over the course of the journey, she does change perceptibly and is given a more human side to her. The people and deities she interacts with have their own personalities, players should not have trouble distinguishing one character from another due to distinctive character designs and the personalities given to each character.
Art: Very distinctive designs for each character as well as the Tsukumogami enemies themselves. Highly reminiscent of the old paintings of Japanese scenery and the supernatural mostly found in museums.
Music: Traditional Japanese melodies with a heavy emphasis on the piano for the slower tracks. Players who like the music can purchase the soundtrack as an extra on the store page, but it is purely a matter of personal preference and budgetary constraints.
Gameplay mechanics: This game is built on the KiriKiri engine which has been a workhorse for Japanese games for over a decade. The interface is simple and requires players to move from one end of the playing field to the other whilst defeating enemies which stand in the way.
The combat system in this game is both a strength and a weakness. It is unique as it requires players to identify the opposing enemy before it can be exorcised or captured (reflecting traditional East Asian perceptions on malignant spirits). Unfortunately the novelty of the combat system will wear off once players become accustomed to the mechanics and discover they cannot breeze through regular enemies in a matter of seconds.
The "RPG" aspect of this game is reflected in the spirit capturing mechanic and upgrades to the sword. After a certain point in the game, players are given the option of capturing spirits in order to exploit their abilities instead of simply exorcising them. There is a wide range of abilities to choose from as each spirit offers two abilities when captured into service, most abilities provide a useful boost to players with a small minority strong enough to upset game balance. To simplify the process of grinding, the sword can be upgraded very early on in the game with points granted upon each level-up. A fully-upgraded sword significantly shortens the time required to defeat regular enemies, but the time investment required from players might be off-putting for many.
Game stability: The version provided by Steam is 1.10, however it is not completely bug-proof as certain enemies or combination of enemies will crash the game forcing a reset to the main menu. Hence it is strongly recommended players save before and after significant milestones in the game to minimise disruption.
Recommended Japanese proficiency: There is no English in this game (that's why this game only comes bundled together with 99 spirits). Players are expected to be familiar with the Japanese syllable table and to associate the various Kanji which emerge when using the sword's spirit identification function with the objects the Tsukumogami relate to. There will be quite a number of occasions when players need to manually input the correct syllables to unmask the identity of the enemy in question (with at least one very annoying phase in which the syllable table is scrambled) but most of the time the enemies can be identified using the handy master scroll of enemies which is filled in upon discovery or purchase of new scroll parts.
The dialogue and exposition in the game doesn't utilise complex grammatical structures, but some of the vocabulary used isn't common for non-native speakers. Anyone interested in playing the game through without a full-blown walkthrough should have JLPT N2 or N3 with a good grounding in Japanese mythology and culture. Either way, having a good Japanese dictionary on hand (hard copy or online) is extremely handy.
The developer Toraiki does have a blog page with tables listing the characteristics, locations and abilities of the Tsukumogami enemies so those who can read Japanese can consult the tables to save time.
Conclusion: For a debut work, this is a decent attempt with a coherent storyline, unique if eventually tedious mechanics and characters which leave an impression long after the game is completed. Thanks to Steam's decision to bundle this game with the English adaptation, more players can experience the Japanese doujin market which is more popular than ever thanks to English translations of games like Recettear. Highly recommended for anyone looking to improve their Japanese vocabulary while having fun at the same time.

I bought Mount and Blade in August of 2012, I have to say it’s one of my favorite games. I've logged over 350 hours on this game between the three official versions and mods. The graphics are a bit dated at this time, there are many total conversion mods for this game so in reality the replay value is great. You can find most mods for this game on ModDB or simply through a Google search. Most mods are pretty simple to install and upon installation, they are available from the launch screen.
Now, when you start a new game you'll see the intro screen, pretty basic click and progress, you'll pick a gender, then a short back story. The back story creates your stats based on the choices you make. When you're done with this it'll take you to your stats page, where you will pick the difficulty you want: Realistic (No quitting without saving) or where you can quit the game without saving. Set your stats as you like, there's plenty of choices to pick from. Tooltips will pop up in the top right corner to give a short description of the choices. Fill in your stats and create a name.
Once you're done with that it's off to creating the likeness of your character. Creating a character requires you choosing your hair and facial structure. Essentially much what you'd expect from a RPG. Once you've confirmed your character, you basically pick a place to begin your adventure.
The game begins and you find yourself in an alley facing a random enemy, either defeat them or do your best. You'll then go through a short tutorial quest which will teach you the basics of the game. When you've finished that you're pretty much on your own.
Once you’re on the campaign map there's a multitude of things to do in Calradia. You can become a mercenary with your own band of troops, recruiting them from the local villages or finding mercenaries who want a bit of coin to fight for you. Train your recruits to become the best of the best. Fight your way to victory, eventually leading to the becoming a vassal of one of the 5 or 6 factions depending on if you're playing Warband or the original.
You’ll soon find yourself in a battle of some kind. You’ll begin with your troops on one side of a map, the enemy on the other. Based on your difficulty settings the AI will react accordingly. I find the base game AI to be kind of predictable, there’s mods to remedy that. Either way your troops will begin charging, you’ll either want to continue, or you can order your troops with the function keys on your keyboard. You can organize your troops by troop types, and then put them as you want and order them as you see fit. The control scheme for orders seems to get a bit muddled once you find yourself in combat.
The combat is fairly basic, you’ll block and swing your weapon. It can get repetitive quickly. This is one of the shortcomings of the game. There’s a lot of fighting in this game so if you’re into a lot of first or third person close quarters combat this is a good choice. There’s not any fancy animations for killing blows or that sort of thing. Riding your horse into combat is the main focus of the game, hence the title.
You’ll constantly find yourself being attacked by bandit groups at the start of the game because you have few troops and you’re a low level. The beginning of the game can be a challenge at times and sometimes frustrating. Try to fight smaller groups of bandits, loot the best gear, sell the worst gear, and buy the best you can afford. Your troops will equip themselves so all you have to do for them is pay them and upgrade them when they earn enough xp to become better warriors. There’s a plethora of different troop types. Though I do have to say that I favor the Khergits. They are very much like the Mongolians, mostly mounted troops. They have excellent horse archers and decent knights. Your play style may vary. I’ve logged countless hours and have yet to play the game the same way twice.
You can start a new game and do a completely different path. Instead of fighting for the Swadians you can fight for the Nords. You can become a merchant and trade your way to riches by buying low and selling high across the lands. There’s also the option to become a champion fighter in the various tournaments across Calradia, you go to city and join a tournament or you can go to the arena and find the closest one. Keep doing those and you’ll earn renown and maybe a vassalage or a chance to marry a noble’s daughter.
The game also features quite a few companions, some of whom get along with one another and others that completely detest one another. You will need to pick and choose your companions. Balance them between liking one another and their skills. As you progress in the game and gain levels and higher stats so do your companions. They’ll have the option to upgrade as recommended or you can pick what they learn. You’ll also be tasked with outfitting them with their gear in the same way that you equip yourself.
The idea is to get enough renown and enough respect from the various factions in the game you can create your own kingdom. Once you’ve done that your next goal is basically to unite Calradia under your banner, mostly through force and getting lords from other nations to fight for you. You’ll create a kingdom by attacking a castle or city, conquering it, and naming your kingdom. In my experience, you’ll likely wind up having to fight all of the other nations and beating them into submission by battling constantly until you’ve won enough battles that they sue for peace or you conquer them entirely.
The management system for lords and vassals when owning your own kingdom could use some work, I’m sure there’s mods to revamp the entire UI for it to provide a better overview of what you currently control.
Overall despite the game’s graphics being dated, and the playability being repetitive in combat. There’s a lot going on in the background of this game, between stats and the players attributes. You’ll definitely get hours of enjoyment and probably some frustration depending on your difficulty settings. This game can be a challenge. If you want a game at a fair price that entertains for a long time, this game is worth the money in my opinion.

Torchlight 2 is a Loot-Driven Action Roleplaying Game, very similar to the legendary Diablo franchise.
It's also very fitting that some of the people that developed it are some of the old Diablo devs and even the soundtrack is made by the same person that did the soundtrack to Diablo series.
The gameplay is pretty standard, click on the enemies, they die, you get loot, rinse and repeat until you level up and spec your points into stats and skills. Basically it's just like any other "Diablo-like". You choose from one of 4 classes, which can use any type of weapon and armor in the game, excluding some legendary/unique class specific items. Even though you only have 4 classes, they can be build into several diferent roles. For example, an Outlander can be your standard "Ranger" type class or you can spec it to be a summoner or a even crititcal dealing assasin. You also have tons of variety when it comes to items, as the monsters and chests are very generous into sharing it with you.
The game looks gorgeous, not due to any "HD 4K Textures" or some nifty effects like "HBAO+" and "Sunshafts", the game has none of that. What it does have are some nice simple textures and an awesome visual style. The game runs great on both low end PC/Laptops, to the very high end SLI/Crossfire machines.
In addition to all of that, the game's community is still very active to this day and thanks to the mod tools provided by the devs, the game has plenty of mods to choose from.
In general, it plays great, it looks great and it performs great. If you like games such as Diablo, Titan Quest, Path of Exile and Sacred, you'll love Torchlight II.

Red Faction Guerrilla doesn't hold up graphically to recent RPGs, but the destruction elements and open world missions make up for the visual side of things. The story itself is pretty mediocre although there were a few stand-out tasks. The physics engine is suprisingly powerful for a 2009 game, and it alows you to approach different missions in different ways. For example, if you need to destroy a power generator, you can either ram your car through the front gates and take a direct route, or use your jetpack to fly over the defensive walls to get to the target. You can even plant shaped charges to blow your way through the back of the complex/fort. These "up against the world" sorts of moments make the game have a very positive and curious energy, although it can be repetitive.
Overall, if you are looking for an incredible story, look elsewhere. If you are searching for a Mass-Effect style third person shooter, look elsewhere. However, if you want to sink some hours into creative destruction challenges, and experiment with the physics engine's gameplay elements, this would be the game for you.

This is one of the best shmups I've played so far. Everything is great about it: stages, bosses, voice acting, soundtrack... and it's much better than the first game.
In the game, there are 7 stages (the final one is divided into two parts) and the main gameplay element is polarity switching which is also present in Ikaruga. Additionally, the game has difficulty scaling (the difficulty changes according to the player's skill) and chaining which grants bonus points and that's very useful for quickly getting extra lives.
The boss fights are very good because of the (mostly) epic music and the voice acting (most bosses say something according to your progress in the fight), which made the fights really cool at times.
The soundtrack is perfect because the songs are fitting for the given situation and they are top-notch.
My favorite part of the game would be the 7th stage because it's fun and it gets better towards the end.
I would recommend this game for those who are interested in shmups.

Awesome game, haven't got to play it a lot but I do love it. I played it quite a while when it was in early access. If you like the previous games you will really like this game.

The good:
A lot of fun to be had with this game. This is the best space game I played in a very very long time. Quite a few spacecrafts to choose from, a relatively extensive (yet a bit too simple) research system and also a couple of different playstyles (and I don't mean the three 'classes', but more like strategies) to choose from. But one thing tops them all: everywhere I look on the fora on here on Steam the developers are really committed to the community and take suggestions very serious (and implement them in the game!). I really like that about this game and I think other developers should take note because this is how I would like to see all games being developed :-). This for me really is an example for how it should be done!
The bad:
The optimalization is quite bad. So bad that I am unable to get normal frame rates even though I have a really fast quad core with either a AMD R9 390 or Nvidia GTX 1070 (I use both in different PC's), SSD and 16/32GB of RAM. I tried every suggestion in practically every post or issue I could find about performance issues, but none work. Now I play the game with every setting on the lowest/least demanding setting and I get between 20-30 FPS (even less at large battles), which is really terrible. The worst part is that the CPU and GPU are not doing that much (quite the opposit)when the game is running. I don't get it and would really love a fix so I can play the game normally.
Other bad stuff: I think the minigame with the civilian fleets is rubbish. It's a stupid mechanism that isn't that rewarding to begin with and only seems to exist to extend the game time or something. In its current state, it should be automated (maybe after research?) or be thrown out of the game asap :-). Your mate back on the station is running most of everything anyway, why can't he sent a couple of civilian fleets to pick up some materials every now and then? Short and sweet:  The new mechanics in SE3 is an improvement over V2 and I quite enjoyed it, but it does get old.
Recommend for sniping action, but wait to pick it up on a sale.
Cavaet:  I did not play the multiplayer SE3, this review will only be concerned with the single-player/co-op campaign.
The new shoot-and-hide mechanics really enhance the sniper feel of this game.  Couple that with the really big, open levels and you will have a lot of fun running around setting traps and sniping people.  I like it, it's a step in the right direction.
The down side?  SE3 makes sniping, dare I say it, boring.  I found that, about halfway through the campaign, that I abandoned the snipe-and-hide mechanic and went with isolated, silent kills using my knife or my Welrod.  I found that more challenging than an enemy which will hear dozens of loud gun shots but won't call for backups or do more thorough searches.
Shoot an enemy with your loud rifle, everybody ducks under cover, and in ten seconds they're out of cover and acting as if nothing had happened.  Sure, enemies will react if they see the body of their dead compatriots, but only to engage in an alert mode that will wear off shortly.  And it never seems to re-engage or expand in scope, once someone has seen a body once, they only react once.  It's silly to see Wehrmacht patrolling right past a pile of dead bodies of their fellow soldiers.  So why bother hiding the bodies?
Worse, there's only a limited amount of targets per level, and no matter how much of a ruckus you make, they never receive re-enforcements.  Couple that with a slow-to-react AI (even at the highest difficult level), and the game isn't all that challenging once you understand the snipe-and-hide mechanic.
In fact, I rarely died by enemy action while playing SE3.  %90 of my save reloads were regarding some trap that failed horribly or blowing myself up accidently with a nearby barrel. :)
The levels themselves are quite nice and I had a lot of fun setting traps for soldiers, doing isolated kills, and so on.  I much prefer the wide-open level design of SE3 versus V2.   The final level, however, is a rather big let down.  You don't have the chance for a real boss battle and the final baddie is so easy to take out, it just feels like you are curb stomping a six month old.
Pick this up if you like sniping, particularly since it does support real honest co-op play through the campaign (and we know how rare that is).  But I recommend only picking it up if it's on sale.

A fun stealth-shooter with iconic cinematic gore-porn. Sneak up on enemy bases, study their movements and either eliminate or avoid - your call. Knife or silenced pistol for up close, a variety of scoped rifles for far away, a few other guns for everything in-between, and even some anti-tank stuff.
It's military-esque, but don't expect a military simulator - the 3rd person perspective should tip you off to that right away. But it's a fun shooter with lots of achievements and gameplay that you can do however you want. Not too much hand-holding, but was designed primarily for slow and sneaky.
Maps/chapters are big, varied, and well-done, but there aren't as many as I thought there would be - in other words, the game feels a bit short and inconclusive. Expect to complete it in 8-10 hours or so. Has some replay value - owing to the huge maps and open gameplay choice. The DLC was obviously left out of the main game at launch so they could squeeze more money out of you for it. Some physics bugs (clipping, invisible walls, etc.) in spots can be annoying, but not game-breaking. Plays very well with keyboard and mouse.

I got this game at release, and despite my main interest being the co-op mode, I started by playing through it alone. I loved it. Its relocation mechanic makes for a very different kind of stealth, which really comes into its own with the wide open levels that are full of alternative paths, places to hide, and elevated sniper positions. The controls are responsive and the weapons are satisfying.
Unfortunately the net code is atrocious. I have been unable to finish most of the levels in co-op because it randomly kicks me or my partner. Not even necessarily when something interesting happens, we'll be in the middle of doing something and the game kicks us both back to the main menu. In very long missions this can be a tremendous waste of time, as we can sometimes play for half an hour before we get kicked, and it won't let us wait for our partner to rejoin or even just load a savegame. "Maybe it's your connection", I hear you say. Nope, we were on Skype the whole time and the call never dropped.
There are other issues in multiplayer. Sometimes when I start a game in co-op, I have no scope reticle (making sniping somewhat difficult). On one occasion, I was playing the Survival mode and we'd made it to the last round - my friend went down, and when I revived him, he got stuck in spectator mode. His character was just lying there uselessly looking around.
If you want to play this game in singleplayer, buy it. It's a fairly long game - 9 missions including the tutorial, but each is easily an hour long, probably more. Worth the asking price for sure. If you're buying it for co-op, give it a miss. You probably won't be able to.

The difference between this title and it's predecessor is astonishing.
Where eXceed 1st barely functioned, and was subpar even when it did, eXceed 2nd... EXCEEDS it in every way!
In all seriousness though, after the terror of the first game, I expected this one to be similarly terrible, but my fears were quickly quelled.  For starters, eXceed 2nd actually has some resolution options and can be played windowed.  Granted - it doesn't feature as great a breadth of options as I would have liked, but there is actually some choice this time around.  The game also doesn't immediately crash when minimized, so it has that going on for it too.
The story is still incoherantly silly - but at least it's actually translated this time, and I sure hope you're not playing a shmup for it's gripping narrative anyways.  The visuals are still nothing to write home about, but they've been significantly upgraded - especially in the character sprite department.  Another big upgrade goes to the soundtrack.  While I probably won't listen to it outside of the game, it's a much, much better offering than the looped samples of the first title.
As for the only truly important part of a shmup - how it plays.  I'm pleased to say that eXceed 2nd is a fantastic bullet hell game.  It uses the Ikaruga system where you can switch between two colors and absorb same-colored dots, but die to opposite colored dots.  While Ikaruga is much more visually striking, I'd go so far as to argue that eXceed 2nd has far more interesting bullet patterns and is overall a more challenging and enjoyable experience.  This title also features a dynamic difficulty system - the longer you survive the higher it goes, and the more points you earn, but after dying you lose a skill level.
I would even go so far as to say this game is fantastically balanced difficulty wise.  It's entirely possible for a complete novice to get through the levels using stage select on easy mode, yet it will be a monumental challenge for someone to 1-life the game - especially while keeping it on the higher difficulty settings.
All in all I heavily recommend this title to anyone who is a fan of shmups, or wants to try to sink their teeth into a more "core" title.  It's also super cheap, goes on discount, and has steam trading cards..!

eXceed 2nd - Vampire REX, the sequel to Gun Bullet Children, has everything that the 1st one lacked: Astonishing graphics, a soundtrack you'll want to own, and tight gameplay.
The game is story-wise a sequel to Gun Bullet Children, but this time you'll side with the vampires against the Church and their Gun Bullet Children. You play as Ria File, a half-human, half-vampire (aka a deviant bloodline). She has the ability to shift polarity: switch elements to absorb bullets of the same element while the other type becomes fatal. This is a mechanic that shouldn't be unknown to Ikaruga players. The game also has a dynamic difficulty implemented, whereas long survival and scoring gets you in a higher difficulty while playing, and dying reduces the difficulty. The overal difficulty of the game is okay. It might be tricky at first for newer people, but you'll get the hang of it quickly.
Although there isn't much to the story in most danmaku shooters, this one had a story i liked. The game references characters from the previous game as well. Just like the previous game, the characters have voicing in Japanese, and unlike Gun Bullet Children, this one has an official translation in the game.
The soundtrack was made by Saitama Saishu Heiki and Shibayan, well known names in the doujin world, and this soundtrack delivers, just like their other works. The boss music fits rather well with the bosses' personalities or significance in the story, whereas the stage music either takes it a bit easier or just gets really tense to prepare you for your next big challenge.
This game is just fantastic and is among my favourite danmaku shooters now. They really outdid Gun Bullet children by far. You can get it for 6 EUR, but i'd be willing to pay double price for this game.

This game was fantastic.  Great story, lots of feels, and the gameplay just felt right for this type of story telling game.

First, the bad.  This game has no dialog, and I did not find that artistic, different, or at all engaging.  The lack of real language did not bring me "closer to the emotion" or any such thing.  It was just plain annoying and brought the level of the whole game down to a more cartoony, childish experience.  A little time spent on some sparse voice acting would have done wonders for Brothers.  I did not really develop an attachment to the characters, and without giving anything away let me say.. the ending scenes would have been much more effective at drawing out emotion if the two brothers were not so flat, and maybe a verbal que existed to tell me what the heck I was supposed to do..
Now, the good.  The scenes were very well done, and although a lot was left unexplained that is not necessarily a bad thing.  A richly detailed world fiction describing past battles and current world politics is something that would likely be ignored by most players (myself included) anyway.  Creating huge, dramatic scenes and leaving me to wonder what the heck is going on around the two brothers just made those scenes more interesting and drove my imagination.  Everything was beautiful to look at and the story was charming, at least what can be pieced together without dialog.  Level design was always interesting and I was never bored.  Some of the extra things you can do on the side were also pretty neat and unexpected.  I really liked the disparity between the two brothers' personalities, how they interact with things differently.
I would not hesitate to pick this game up on sale.  I did, and I don't regret it.  However, if I had paid full price I would have been disappointed.

I bought this game years back after i saw it on a thread in the DF forums. I didn't have much expectations, the developer was unknown with just 1 simple game as the only sample of its work. I was pleasantly suprised thou, the game was a cute mix of tower defense, terraria and colony management, it had some nasty pathfinding bugs and a few issues, it definately wasn't a DF wannabe or even trying. It was its own thing.
It has a progression system that ties research to crafting. Crafting also is tiered by mats, from wood to mithril. There are 4 worlds, i believe its 1 small, 1medium and 2 large. Each world has its own biome and challenges, such as an ice world or a desert world where you have to get creative with water sources. Monsters, fauna and flora are also unique to each biome.
You unlock the worlds by defeating certain bosses and crafting the portal parts. Every night undead will rise and attack your dwarfs, every 45 mns portals to the netherworld will open and hordes with bosses will come out, these get progressively harder. To fight them, you build towers, doors, traps and terraform your environment around you. The blocks you can build are extensive as well, allowing for some pretty impressive designs. But no wall or tower will keep the hordes away forever, your main defense will likely always be your dwarves.
Your dwarves have needs (sleep/hunger) and can learn up to 3 skills. They always come with at least 1 and books drop while mining/harvesting that you can use to teach a skill or improve it if they already know it. You can also equip your dwarves. They have a armor(head/chest/feet), weapon, pickaxe, axe, 2 utility slots. There are 3 combat classes you can assign your dwarves as, archer, warrior and mage. Mages get 2 dmg spells a polymorph that turns your enemies to chickens. There is also several crafting related skills as well as utility ones such as swimming and climbing.
As you explore the map looking for resources and secret boss rooms you will find other secrets below. And you get to build mine carts and elevators (which they've completely changed and fixed since release thankfuly).
There is also a quirky sense of humor to the game that i enjoy. Its a perfect game to relax on a weekend afternoon.
Now, years later, this game is still installed. The developer hasn't stopped adding things to it, its gotten better and better, i just covered the surface of all of it. It's been polished and tightened squeaky clean, this game oozes with details.  After over 100hrs, albeit on and off, I can't recommend it enough and its definately staying installed.

Like it's predecessor Exceed 2 is a bullethell shmup, but is a lot better. The game is translated, has controller support, dialog can be turned off and you can choose settings like resolution. You can still only select 1600x900 as highest resolution, but you can choose to play it windowed.
New is the polarity mechanic it borrows from Ikaruga. Only bullets of an opposite polarity can kill the player. Same-color bullets are absorbed and converted into energy for special weapon. Switching the polarity also changes the color of your bullets, and shooting an enemy using opposite-polarity bullets will cause double damage. The game only forgets to tell you that it uses this system.
For a bullethell shmup it's quite oke. Main issue that puts me off is the anime art style and setting. I'm just not a fan of that and prefer I'm something like a ship in shmups. I already find bullethell shmups a genre hard to enjoy and this makes it even harder. So I can't recommend it to most people.

Arguably one of the best space sims out today. Starpoint Gemini Warlords is a space sim that combines RPG elements, base building, and RTS for conquering other regions. If you are fan of any of these elements, consider Starpoint Gemini Warlords.
There is quite a learning curve but once conquered this is an excwptionally fun and challenging game.

In 2013 I wrote a series of forum posts on the SPG2 forums detailing exactly what I wanted to see in a single player space RPG/sim game. The result of this development team's incredible attentiveness to the community and years of development is SPG Warlords, and I feel that this game is such a winner because of how closely they have matched their community's expectations.
I can't thank LGM enough for going the extra mile to satisfy so many community requests and make this such a fun, diverse and interesting game -- they even continue to exceed my expectations with more interesting content in the DLCs that I wasn't expecting to see.

Pros: Challenging but rewarding. Extremely detailed graphics and units. Red Dragon seamlessly integrates air and sea combat into the foundation laid by European Escalation. You will lose days of your life, because the game will engross you. Like, seriously, pack a lunch if you plan on playing a match, because it's going to last a while (I love that). The only Cold War force missing is Cuba, and knowing Eugen, it's probably in the works.
Cons: Lack of depth in naval units; the game only has twenty or so naval units out of maybe two or three hundred, but it leads you to believe there are more. Wish there was, frankly. There is a learning curve and it is steep; the game is unforgiving, and if you make a mistake you *will* pay for it. The game could use some video tutorials. As an addendum to that last, it's in game tutorials are woefully inadequate. There's a feeling that the developer expects you to muddle through, and this game is not forgiving enough for that. If Starcraft I/II are go fish, Red Dragon is a world championship chess match. Red Dragon is if anything more forgiving than it's predecessors, but it is definitely not easy to just pick up and play.
TL;DNR (?): This game isn't for everyone, but if you're looking for beautiful graphics, glorious depth, realism, and a challenge, I highly commend it. If you just want simple RTS to play casually, RUN AWAY FOR THE LOVE OF ALL THAT IS HOLY. That said? Omigyad I love this game.

TL;DR: Take the fun of Carmageddon, the viewing angle from GTA (the original ones) and strap weapons on your taxi and you're good to go on a quest to save the city.
In Zombie Driver (HD) you are some dude who drives a taxi. Military ("if they even are the military", says the random hippie) enlists you to save a bunch of civilians in a zombie infested city. Mow those zombies! Mayor will pay you a bonus for their smashed bodies! Gruesome, silly kind of humour is cultured in the overly dramatized monologues everyone else gets to give you when you meet them.
Zombie driving gets a lot more fun once they strap a machine gun to your car. Later, you'll get equipped with flamethrowers, rocket launchers and even experimental rail guns that shoot blue, helical rays of mass destruction. Not to forget, a tongue-in-cheek car game wouldn't be complete without a turbo booster. Between missions you get to upgrade your cars (new ones unlocked every few missions) and weapons.
There are no surprises in the zombie varieties: in addition to the regular, shambling corpses, there are legions of zombie dogs, wailing slingers of industrial junk, bloated monsters of the exploding variety and of course the hulk. Naturally, it is more difficult to ram the bigger ones and especially in large groups.
Story mode has two kinds of basic missions: 1) taxi missions: go and save people from buildings around the town (usually with generous time limits), and 2) slaughter missions: go somewhere and kill everything. Here,
includes the zombie spawners (introduced by the HD version): enormous Jabba the Hut creatures that blurt out more of the monsters (it figures that these are not your average zombies after all). In addition, there are the awesome cleaning and destroying special missions where you get to drive e.g. tanks, with infinite ammo of course. HD version also has a couple of bosses that add nicely into the game's limited lore.
Story wasn't the strong part of the original Zombie Driver and it has only been patched partly by the HD upgrade. It ends abrubtly but rather appropriately although leaving your contribution vague: it is unfortunately never explained why the army (or whatever they are) needed a random taxi driver to sort their mess.
Two other game modes are more like what the game was designed for: there's the copy of Death Rally called Blood Race (though you can't destroy your opponents permanently) with several different tournaments and challenge missions. Unfortunately, career mode is missing. You'll get money for winning races and can then buy limited upgrades to your car. On the other hand, Slaughter mode is an endless killing spree of perpetually spawning zombies for higher points to show off in the leaderboards. Here only death ends the level.
Game is fun and pretty awesome. However, it is easy to get stuck in corners and sometimes it is not clear what items can be driven through resulting in further stuckiness. Mob spawning can be ruthless and illogical, especially in Slaughter mode: zombies tend not to walk as fast (or at all?) when you are not seeing them in front of you in the camera and the game considers it fair to spawn a group of exploding zombies right behind you when you are reversing.
Despite the few complaints, I can give it thumbs up. Graphics are nice, sounds are not irritating and gameplay is very nice (I used keyboard and mouse). Also, the improvements from the original Zombie Driver are very welcome: e.g. they made booster a separate item from weapons, added a map and made the story mode more interesting with the zombie spawners, bosses and special vehicles. If you have doubts but are interested, you can also grab it on sale for 2 euros or less.

EXceed 2nd is the complete opposite of the 1st.  First, you’re a half vampire trying to prevent your kind from being wiped out by humanity.  Second, it’s good instead of being terrible.  Finally, they spent the hour or so to use Google translate to localize the subtitles so I can understand the story (I still don't understand the story.  I guess I should've read the comic book... I'm sorry Manga.)
The graphics are vastly improved and the soundtrack is still solid.  The player’s sprite and enemy bosses have some pretty good looking animation.  The bullets are no longer monochromatic blobs.  The backgrounds look nice.  The run of the mill enemies are still pretty bland, though.  Overall it’s a huge improvement from eXceed 1.
The game play is what really stands out.  The enemies’ attacks are either light or dark.  The player has a ‘polarity’, which means you can absorb one type of bullet to power up while you are vulnerable to the other.  The game play is tough without feeling cheap and the difficulty curve is well balanced.  Most importantly, you can move diagonally with your gamepads analog stick.
In conclusion, this game is as good as the first one was bad.  If you’re only going to play one game in the series (which is what I’d recommend) this is the one.

Exceed 2nd is a bullet hell shooter that lifts its main gameplay mechanic from Ikaruga. All bullets/enemies come in two colors, and you can switch your own color to absorb same colored bullets (which recharges your invulnerable laser) while being vulnerable to opposite colored bullets. You also do more damage to opposite colored enemies, though it's often riskier to do so.
Exceed 2nd is more of a traditional twitch/reflex game than the puzzle shooter Ikaruga though. You can still apply strategy to the stages and bullet patterns to get better at them, but it has a lot more flexibility and room for improvisation.
The game also has a lot of aggression. You're encouraged to get close to enemies to melee them, and use your laser as soon as it recharges to kill bosses faster. It gives a great sense of risk/reward to the boss fights, since you can choose whether to try and kill them as soon as possible, or save your laser to protect you later. Combine this with how you damage bosses faster by staying close with the opposite color, and you have a very aggressive, up-close-and-personal game.
The level designs and bullet patterns are really solid, though maybe not as intricate or perfect as a Cave shooter. But they are fast paced and have a lot of intense moments. Overall the game is really, really fun, and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys shmups. It's the best Exceed game imo, and probably one of the best shmups on Steam if not the best as of this writing.

I think this is my first review, first let me say how disappointed I am that there are so many negative reviews for such a beautiful, enchanting and absolutely delightful game to play. I note that many of the negative reviews are from those with just a few hours of game play, yes it can be a stressful learning curve, but stick with it, once you know how to survive it just grows on you. The graphics and attention to detail are awesome, and it's bug free. With four distinctly different levels, and campaign or custom for each that's 8 games in one!
A few tips to help you get started. (not a walk through - this is how I play, once you learn the basics you may form your own strategy)
1. Choose your start point - start the game and have a quick look round to locate the shop, resources and lay out, if it's not to your liking restart the game.
2. Make good use of the portal spell, much quicker than having your dwarves walk everywhere!
3. Mine lots of stone and build stone walls and a roof up and over your stockpile, it's your safe haven to run to if the pesky monsters start to overwhelm you.
4. Don't worry about it looking pretty, and don't leave any gaps for a door or hatch, enter and leave via your portal spell, you can easily add doors and make it pretty later.
5. Chop a few trees and make simple clubs as weapons and a few ladders, then dig a very basic house and place your first totem.
6. Now your house is complete you can add a few beds, dwarves need to sleep to recover from injury.
7. Tools, food, tables, ornament's etc. can be added later, these are low priority at the start, prioritise building a very basic shelter and your stress level and blood pressure will reduce.
A. Once you start to produce tools wait until you have enough axes and picks to give all your little peeps one each, otherwise those without just keep nagging you for the right tools.
B. Personally I don't use Warriors, they get too close in combat and take a beating, Mage's and Archers will step back from the enemy to fight. (Elixir of Obliteration makes them forget the Warrior skill, then use the Mage or Archer book to teach a new fighting skill)
C. Use your first gold coins to buy health elixir, soon as you hear the 'low health' alarm pause the game with the 'equip' button (bottom right of the screen) then click through each dwarf and give those in need a swig of elixir.
D. Add a couple of pets as soon as you can (Frogolisk or Owlcat) they help defend your house when it's attacked.
E. Oh! one final tip, don't try to kill the 5 guardians of the portal blueprints too early, work around them and wait untill your peeps have good armour, weapons and skill levels, only then should you attempt to bring them down.
Again - this is not a walk through, just a few basics to get you 'addicted'

A good relaxing game with some great ideas, but unfortunatly falls a little bit short due to bad AI which massively slows down progression.
You start with just a few dwarves, building a basic shelter to sleep in (sleeping heals hurt dwarves). You give orders to your dwarves by simply marking a block you wish to be mined, an animal that you wish be hunted, an enemy you wish to be killed ect. and a random dwarf (usually one of a class suited for it) will follow the order. Or in the instance of an attack order on an enemy, all of your forces will head toward the marked enemy target.
You can manually control a dwarf yourself, which is one of the only ways to get around some of the bad AI in the game. But it only helps in a few of the situations. Often you may mark a tunnel to be mined out, each reachable block will get one dwarf assigned to it. But if only the 1 block can be reached, a single dwarf will head there and dig out the whole tunnel alone and they may randomly swap tasks with each other, causing the frontmost dwarf to head back while you wait for the replacing dwarf to arrive and perform the task. They won't work together in mining or hunting. Even in building tasks, if they are not able to reach the place you want them to build, they won't bother. So only one dwarf will go out and place a background block, only then will another dwarf will head out to place the foreground block, then another dwarf will head out to place the next section and so forth. They won't go out in a group, prepared with the materials they need to construct what you want.
You also can't designate priority tasks to specific dwarves. For example, you can't tell a dwarf to prioritize smithing and continue smithing above all other oders until your smithing queue is finished. Dwarves will immediately stop smithing, training. cooking, building, mining or sleeping when you issue an attack order and will not drop an order when you make a new one that is suited to thier class. So if your smith is off hunting for example, then you add something to your smithing queue it will not call the smith back to do it. It will hand it to another class. It could have sent any other class out to do it, mage, warrior, archer, miner ect. but it sent the crafting class instead.
When you have attacks coming from both sides of your base, you set an attack marker on an enemy from each side, but the dwarves flock to the first one you marked. They will not defend both sides of the base or split up among multiple marked enemies. So there is little to no control over where you want your forces to split during combat. It could have divided a portion of your dwarves per attack marker, allowing you to set how many should go to each combat area but it doesn't.
The tech progression in the game comes from unlocking a set of 6 items which include, decorations, materials, traps, armor, weapons, spells or crafting stations and then the next tier is unlocked by using the spells or building those items. There are 3 paths to follow in tech unlocks, but sometimes they cross over requiring 2 paths to be unlocked in order to proceed. It works ok but is probably around 70% decorations as opposed to necessary items to make you stronger. It seems to progress slowly, but I suspect that this is more due to the AI and the way it often only efficiently sets 1 dwarf on a task instead of finding a way to use 6 of your twelve (for good example). There are ways the game could have worked around the limitations when waiting on the first dwarf before other dwarves can help, but the devs didn't seem to bother working it out. This makes the progress of completing tasks/research very slow.
There is a survival aspect to the game where it seems to get harder the longer you survive, enemies do a large attack about once every 45 minutes during the night. There is also some multiplayer component which I have not explored yet. Something to do with invading multiplayer games through a special portal if you build it. I typically avoid MP with survival games unless it is co-operative, but it may well be worth checking out for those who are interested in PvP.
I'd give the game a 3/5 stars but if the AI was better implemented to make the game flow faster and feel more responsive with your orders, I'd easily give it a 4.5. So just consider how patient you are, if you can handle waiting 5-10 minutes to complete a task that really could have been done in 1 minute or less if the AI was somewhat efficient, then you will enjoy the game. If you are the impatient sort that is easily frustrated by stupid AI, maybe give it a miss.
