I bought Mount and Blade in August of 2012, I have to say it’s one of my favorite games. I've logged over 350 hours on this game between the three official versions and mods. The graphics are a bit dated at this time, there are many total conversion mods for this game so in reality the replay value is great. You can find most mods for this game on ModDB or simply through a Google search. Most mods are pretty simple to install and upon installation, they are available from the launch screen.
Now, when you start a new game you'll see the intro screen, pretty basic click and progress, you'll pick a gender, then a short back story. The back story creates your stats based on the choices you make. When you're done with this it'll take you to your stats page, where you will pick the difficulty you want: Realistic (No quitting without saving) or where you can quit the game without saving. Set your stats as you like, there's plenty of choices to pick from. Tooltips will pop up in the top right corner to give a short description of the choices. Fill in your stats and create a name.
Once you're done with that it's off to creating the likeness of your character. Creating a character requires you choosing your hair and facial structure. Essentially much what you'd expect from a RPG. Once you've confirmed your character, you basically pick a place to begin your adventure.
The game begins and you find yourself in an alley facing a random enemy, either defeat them or do your best. You'll then go through a short tutorial quest which will teach you the basics of the game. When you've finished that you're pretty much on your own.
Once you’re on the campaign map there's a multitude of things to do in Calradia. You can become a mercenary with your own band of troops, recruiting them from the local villages or finding mercenaries who want a bit of coin to fight for you. Train your recruits to become the best of the best. Fight your way to victory, eventually leading to the becoming a vassal of one of the 5 or 6 factions depending on if you're playing Warband or the original.
You’ll soon find yourself in a battle of some kind. You’ll begin with your troops on one side of a map, the enemy on the other. Based on your difficulty settings the AI will react accordingly. I find the base game AI to be kind of predictable, there’s mods to remedy that. Either way your troops will begin charging, you’ll either want to continue, or you can order your troops with the function keys on your keyboard. You can organize your troops by troop types, and then put them as you want and order them as you see fit. The control scheme for orders seems to get a bit muddled once you find yourself in combat.
The combat is fairly basic, you’ll block and swing your weapon. It can get repetitive quickly. This is one of the shortcomings of the game. There’s a lot of fighting in this game so if you’re into a lot of first or third person close quarters combat this is a good choice. There’s not any fancy animations for killing blows or that sort of thing. Riding your horse into combat is the main focus of the game, hence the title.
You’ll constantly find yourself being attacked by bandit groups at the start of the game because you have few troops and you’re a low level. The beginning of the game can be a challenge at times and sometimes frustrating. Try to fight smaller groups of bandits, loot the best gear, sell the worst gear, and buy the best you can afford. Your troops will equip themselves so all you have to do for them is pay them and upgrade them when they earn enough xp to become better warriors. There’s a plethora of different troop types. Though I do have to say that I favor the Khergits. They are very much like the Mongolians, mostly mounted troops. They have excellent horse archers and decent knights. Your play style may vary. I’ve logged countless hours and have yet to play the game the same way twice.
You can start a new game and do a completely different path. Instead of fighting for the Swadians you can fight for the Nords. You can become a merchant and trade your way to riches by buying low and selling high across the lands. There’s also the option to become a champion fighter in the various tournaments across Calradia, you go to city and join a tournament or you can go to the arena and find the closest one. Keep doing those and you’ll earn renown and maybe a vassalage or a chance to marry a noble’s daughter.
The game also features quite a few companions, some of whom get along with one another and others that completely detest one another. You will need to pick and choose your companions. Balance them between liking one another and their skills. As you progress in the game and gain levels and higher stats so do your companions. They’ll have the option to upgrade as recommended or you can pick what they learn. You’ll also be tasked with outfitting them with their gear in the same way that you equip yourself.
The idea is to get enough renown and enough respect from the various factions in the game you can create your own kingdom. Once you’ve done that your next goal is basically to unite Calradia under your banner, mostly through force and getting lords from other nations to fight for you. You’ll create a kingdom by attacking a castle or city, conquering it, and naming your kingdom. In my experience, you’ll likely wind up having to fight all of the other nations and beating them into submission by battling constantly until you’ve won enough battles that they sue for peace or you conquer them entirely.
The management system for lords and vassals when owning your own kingdom could use some work, I’m sure there’s mods to revamp the entire UI for it to provide a better overview of what you currently control.
Overall despite the game’s graphics being dated, and the playability being repetitive in combat. There’s a lot going on in the background of this game, between stats and the players attributes. You’ll definitely get hours of enjoyment and probably some frustration depending on your difficulty settings. This game can be a challenge. If you want a game at a fair price that entertains for a long time, this game is worth the money in my opinion.

Torchlight II is easily one of the best Action RPGs that you can play right now and that has been released in recent years. It also happens to be one of my all-time favorite games. With the FREE play event going on now through Sunday 1PM PST, you owe it to yourself to play this great Runic game and see why its so highly rated. One awesome feature is that you can play this game in Offline Mode, a great way to pass time when having internet issues. It contains great character classes, very fun skills to use, and so much shiny loot to pick up that your head will explode. Also don't forget about the fishing. :)
It just gets better with the addition of Steam Workshop now that there is a great amount of content that has been converted and updated using this format. While it does suck that you can only run the game with a total of ten active mods, you can have steam workshop track and auto-update fifty mods in total.
Thankfully, skilled users have become quite successful at releasing compilations that help bypass this limit and enhance your gaming experience with lots of active mods such as the fantastic work done by Bandit in his "Combine Them All" mod. :)
Another great feature Runic added is that the game separates your original-stock and workshop-mod characters into different save folders and cloud saves. This makes it very easy for you to play your high level stock characters online with others for those purist out there. Then you restart your game in mod mode and play with your friends online using your modded characters. If you're modded toons are like mine, they will be custom classes such as "Necromancer" and "Warlock" from the SynergiesMOD by Salan or "Ninja" and "Ronin" from the Far East Pack by Zyph.
I can recommend a nice list of workshop mods that play very well together and enhance your game even further once you have beaten the standard version of the game. It's what I use when playing online or offline to help me relax, unwind, and clear my head from design fatigue. One of these days I'll get around to posting them as a Collection in the Steam Workshop when I have more free-time between designing games.
TIP: I highly recommend that if you play modded games on-line with your friends that you synch your game mods and the order they are loaded beforehand to eliminate most on-line problems. The easiest way we found to do this was share a zip file of all the mods we would use with a text file listing the mods priority when loading them if anybody joining didn't have them. We would not include large and popular mods such as SynergiesMOD, Far East Pack, and Enhanced Retex, but we would note the version number in the text file. There are a few mods that don't work well together or on-line, but we've been able to play the majority of them in different combinations as long as we followed this tip.
TIP: While the Steam Cloud synch tends to do a good job overall, sometimes it can fail and override your local copy of your saved game with an outdated one from the Steam Cloud. What I've done is keep a secondary backup of my saved games so when that happens, I can easily replace the cloud copy with my current local backup. The default location for the Torchlight II saved games is at "My Documents\My Games\Runic Games\Torchlight 2\". You want to backup the "save" and "modsave" folders regularly especially if you play the game frequently in offline mode.
Hopefully someday we will get a remastered HD version of the game but I will settle for Torchlight III. =)

I played this game for a fair bit some time ago. Eventually it just wore me down with repetitive, uninteresting quests that dragged out way too long.
It just doesn't know when to stop spawning in yet another wave of identical trash mobs for the quests. I could maybe live with killing a couple waves of baddies, maybe disable a couple turrets, maybe another few baddies show up, and that was that. But no. The game won't be satisfied until you've killed 100 or 200 identical raiders or hellbugs for that one quest.
I just don't feel like some badass space cowboy Ark Hunter.. I feel like an overworked janitor being told yet another kid puked in the halls and I have to go clean it up.
I suppose some of these quests are meant to be approached as a world co-op event, but it doesn't account for there only being one player in the area. It just keeps throwing trash mobs at you. And given that as I write this there are only 574 players in-game, you might want to get used to being one of the (very) few players around.
Also I just tried playing it again today to decide whether I'd keep it installed on my library or not, and I was having absolutely horrible texture pop in issues, or it might be more accurate to say whole-buildings-right-next-to-me pop in issues. Massive objects in the world would just flicker in-and-out of existance. (Running on a GTX 970)
And I was just asked to kill a few too many of the Infinite Raider Clone Army. So my final verdict is that no, I will not be keeping this game installed. Here's to 15GB of free space in my hard drive.
As to whether I would recommend it? Well.. the game is free, and it did kill a few hours for me. So it's hard to say no, although I don't really think it's a particularly good game. If you've got nothing better to do and don't mind a decently large download.. check it out I guess. But tbh you can probably find something better. I wish there was a shrug icon next to the thumbs up or down, but if I'm pressed for a yay or nay.. I vote nay.

I could type up a complete list of items that need to be rectified and/or added but I have better things to be doing.  A short list would be little details like the whistle posts on the CP Mountain Sub are diamond shape, not square.  Approach signals are usually staggered and display proper sequences, for example: not clear to slow then medium to stop.  Train braking physics are way off as well.  Do not pay full price for this game, wait for it to go on sale first.  @Steam, if you read this, I am very sure there are some experienced Locomotive Engineers that are using Train Simulator that would be more than happy to give you input for improvements, I know I would offer advice.

I grabbed this ages ago on hefty Steam discounts... And, that's honestly where the value is.
+ 2015 version has great UI
+ Fun to drive trains
+ Interesting tutorials
+ lots of workshop content
+ started with 2013 edition, free upgrade to 2015
+ some free DLC (known as Classic Routes in the workshop)
+ career system seems interesting so far
- some tutorials need better explanations (ie: when breaking, explaining what wheel slippage is and why it happens would be nice.. or the right time to start slowing down when a speed limit is changed, etc)
- even with beefy spec'ed machine I still lagged out in certain areas
- graphics could be plenty better or at least better polish
- riddled with bugs
- insane base price
- insane DLC prices
My positive and negative bullet points basically sum it all up. It's a neat game, and there's a lot of great stuff here. But is it worth $60CAD? Heck no, not compared to so many other titles out there. Why is that? Because for AAA prices, I don't want to see "ID Not Found" when trying to create my profile. I don't want to see lag or framerate drops on my high-spec'ed machine every time I pass through a town - and all the other little bugs. This is further worsened by the DLC prices - when they are priced the same as full-version titles, and I can read about how they have the same craftsmanship (aka riddled with bugs), I'm just not going to take the chance at getting burned.
And that is disapointing, because I like sinking my teeth in detailed sims; and I'm not afraid of opening my wallet and investing considerable sums into a game to support it... But when the title is riddled with bugs, the content (such as the tutorials) need further ironing out and so on, you cannot justify these prices - no matter how niche-market the title is.
I guess I can conclude this all by saying that in the end, I am enjoying it. A) because I did get the base copy and some DLC for cheap, and B) because my base copy keeps getting updated for free; so it's hard to really feel ripped off. So I am enjoying it - but I'm disappointed because I feel like my replay value is going to be capped until I can get some more DLC for cheap; because I won't be paying their regular price that's for sure.
I wish I could say maybe on the reccomendation... but it has to come down to this: until they drop their base prices for the game and the dlc to something more fitting the quality of the game you're getting right now, my reccomendation has to be no.
tl;dr; Great Steam Sale buy if it's dirt cheap (60-70% off or more I'd say). Game is nice, but buggy. Insane DLC prices will likely hurt replay value.. but I'm still enjoying it (since I did get it cheap ages ago) so far.

While I wasn't the least bit impressed with the first eXceed, Vampire REX is on a whole other level, so much as to completely eclipse its predecessor! Borrowing Ikaruga's color swapping mechanic, eXceed 2nd is a much more strategic and engaging game full of intricate bullet patterns and impressive boss battles, that demands concentration and forces you to use all your abilities in quick succession if you want to survive.
Even though it lacks anything truly original (besides the nonsensical and thankfully entirely optional dialog), and the frame rate is still liable to fluctuate at times, eXceed 2nd has greatly improved on all fronts and is a great bullet-hell shooter in its own right. Tight controls, crazy amounts of action, a hefty challenge, and an incredible soundtrack; there's little more I could ask for, which makes Vampire REX an easy recommendation for any fan of the genre!

The second entry in the eXceed series, Vampire REX changes the formula up quite a bit while keeping the same narative style and character boss battles. This time you're playing as the opposite side that you were in the first game. There is only one playable character this time, a half vampire girl. The main draw of this game however is the light and dark bullet mechanic. You can switch from light to dark and back at any time. Being in one form makes you immune to bullets of that type and deals extra damage to enemies of the opposite type. This is the exact same system employed in Ikaruga. So if you like Ikaruga, you will most likely enjoy this game.

One of my most favorite replayable crafting/building/digging games. What I love about it is that it is simplified enough, with a clear goal to finish the level, or you can stay and build your fortress, whatever rocks your boat. Plus a clear, functional and easy enough tech tree, crafting system, skills and progress. No need to memorize any recipies either, which is often a pain in the *** for me. You have a nice little book that shows you all what you need. No random guessing involved either. There are few worlds which all behave a bit different, and a multiplayer stage which you can access through the single player game and train your dwarves for it.
While games like Terraria are brilliant and awesome, the crafting system alone in them can overwhelm me, so much that if I have a long break it's a rather deep curve to get back on. This one is more like riding a bike.
The developers also are still at it, which is a-ma-zing. I think I've had the game couple years at least now, and yet another update just rolled out (and not just bug fixes either).
Don't get me wrong; the dwarves be dumb!! haha. So much so that I can see how it frustrates a lot of players way too much. You really do not have direct control over them and they can seem to act quite randomly at times, it is rather different in this sense than lot of other games - which is part of the fun. You gotta play with their rules and needs and adjust to it. You have skills and items too to help them out when they go stubbornly walk the other way and run into bunch of baddies etc. It's like herding a bunch of cats. ...Stubby, grunting, super clumsy dumb cats that die easy.. And like beer. Lots of beer.
All in all a great little gem!
Fun, even in solo but a pain to progress!

This game is kind of similar to Terraria. You craft the world with your little dwarfs, create new items, increase your tech, build a base, and defend your base in the mean time against waves of enemy incursions. It is very fun initiailly, after which it becomes slightly repetitive (more details below). Still, it is very satisfying to craft a nice looking aesthetic home.
Even though I recommend it and I have so far quite loved it, I have a few suggestions for the devs as the game does have some small issues:
1. The campaign really should have a sense of progression. After finishing chapter 1 with mihtril technology going back to wooden clubs and zero technology in level 2 seems really redundant. It becomes sort of a 'chore' to reach that stage once again. My suggestion is that level 1 of the campaign should be completable with say silver weapons, and the tech-tree should end there, level 2 could increase the tech cap and so on.
2. I think the combat aspect of the game becomes a bit tiresome after a while. I just want to craft a really nice looking peaceful base for myself, but I have to keep building tesla towers and arming my dwarfs etc for the constantly growing wave of timed zombie raids.
3. There are some nice ideas, such as the train system, but it comes near the very end of the tech tree, and with that kind of tech you have probably already (or nearly) defeated the guardians and opened the portal. All of that tech is somewhat wasted -> as I said, I think the tech-tree needs a careful revamp.
4. I do not think zombies should be able to climb ladders.
5. The item collection algorithm should prioritize closer dwarfs and definitely not send 5 dwarfs for 5 items, when 1 dwarf can carry all of that stuff. I have noticed that the game has a certain system to prevent such stuff, but it does not seem to function at all times. The same can be said with digging activity, if there is an idle dwarf CLOSER to the target block to be dug, he should be the one who receives the job, not somebody all the way over in the base.

There's a bit of a learning curve when it comes to the controls, but it's well worth it to learn how to command your destructive battleship in the heat of a massive battle.
You start off a with a single ship, build yourself up and eventually you'll own a station, then another, then more ships, and then before you know it you've got yourself a whole little fleet and you're combating other factions that you used to take missions from to earn a living.
It's a blast; literally and figuratively. It's pretty ingenius and the developers did a great job making it a game you can easily sink lots of time in to. If I had more time and less other games to play I would have put a lot more time into this, and once I have more time I know I will be. It's well worth it.
The only downside is the voice acting sounds like a couple friends got together, had a few drinks (a couple of them had a few too many) and recorded a couple of lines and went "Yeah, alright, good enough". But that's okay; you can't expect a game to be perfect.

Torchlight II is easily one of the best Action RPGs that you can play right now and that has been released in recent years. It also happens to be one of my all-time favorite games. With the FREE play event going on now through Sunday 1PM PST, you owe it to yourself to play this great Runic game and see why its so highly rated. One awesome feature is that you can play this game in Offline Mode, a great way to pass time when having internet issues. It contains great character classes, very fun skills to use, and so much shiny loot to pick up that your head will explode. Also don't forget about the fishing. :)
It just gets better with the addition of Steam Workshop now that there is a great amount of content that has been converted and updated using this format. While it does suck that you can only run the game with a total of ten active mods, you can have steam workshop track and auto-update fifty mods in total.
Thankfully, skilled users have become quite successful at releasing compilations that help bypass this limit and enhance your gaming experience with lots of active mods such as the fantastic work done by Bandit in his "Combine Them All" mod. :)
Another great feature Runic added is that the game separates your original-stock and workshop-mod characters into different save folders and cloud saves. This makes it very easy for you to play your high level stock characters online with others for those purist out there. Then you restart your game in mod mode and play with your friends online using your modded characters. If you're modded toons are like mine, they will be custom classes such as "Necromancer" and "Warlock" from the SynergiesMOD by Salan or "Ninja" and "Ronin" from the Far East Pack by Zyph.
I can recommend a nice list of workshop mods that play very well together and enhance your game even further once you have beaten the standard version of the game. It's what I use when playing online or offline to help me relax, unwind, and clear my head from design fatigue. One of these days I'll get around to posting them as a Collection in the Steam Workshop when I have more free-time between designing games.
TIP: I highly recommend that if you play modded games on-line with your friends that you synch your game mods and the order they are loaded beforehand to eliminate most on-line problems. The easiest way we found to do this was share a zip file of all the mods we would use with a text file listing the mods priority when loading them if anybody joining didn't have them. We would not include large and popular mods such as SynergiesMOD, Far East Pack, and Enhanced Retex, but we would note the version number in the text file. There are a few mods that don't work well together or on-line, but we've been able to play the majority of them in different combinations as long as we followed this tip.
TIP: While the Steam Cloud synch tends to do a good job overall, sometimes it can fail and override your local copy of your saved game with an outdated one from the Steam Cloud. What I've done is keep a secondary backup of my saved games so when that happens, I can easily replace the cloud copy with my current local backup. The default location for the Torchlight II saved games is at "My Documents\My Games\Runic Games\Torchlight 2\". You want to backup the "save" and "modsave" folders regularly especially if you play the game frequently in offline mode.
Hopefully someday we will get a remastered HD version of the game but I will settle for Torchlight III. =)

This is a lengthy review, so if you would rather see the pros and cons, just skip to the bottom.
For those new to the series, Wargame: Red Dragon is the 3rd game in the series. It differs from the first two in that the battles and campaigns take place in Asia, mostly the Korean peninsula, instead of Central and Western Europe. It also differs from the first two in that naval combat is present in this game, but more on that below. Now onto the review.
Graphics and Sound
This is first thing most people see when watching the trailer. They don't dissapoint. All three games in the series have amazing graphics, and Red Dragon is no exception. Watch in amazement as dozens of rockets, shells, and rounds pound the enemy and the ground. Craters are left, forest burned down, and entire neighbourhoods destroyed as you fight for control of the strategic sectors scattered around the map. Sounds are also well done. Not only will you see that 500 pound bomb hit the ground, you'll hear it loud and clear. Some explosions can even be heared clear across the map!
Campaigns and Skirmish Mode
Singleplayer consists of two game modes: campaigns and skirmish mode. Skirmish mode has stayed the same from the previous games. Not much to say about it, pick your army deck, your enemy, and your map and fight it out. The campaigns are where things have changed. There are currently five campaigns:  Busan Pocket, Bear vs. Dragon, Pearl of the Orient, Climb Mount Narodnaia, and 2nd Korean War(DLC). So far I've tired Bear vs. Dragon and Pearl of the Orient, which are pretty challenging. I've more or less played through Busan Pocket and 2nd Korean War, each of which play well and are pretty balanced.
The main addition to the campaigns is the seperation of units. Unlike Wargame: AirLand Battle where each division had reccon units, tanks, planes, ect., Red Dragon seperates units into armored divisions, infantry divisions and squadrons. I found this an interesting addition, and I think it adds to the game. You'll now have to decide who gets air support, who gets armored units and even who gets proper supply lines. There are drawbacks however. I noticed that there are little or no random events and the strategic options such as commando raids and air reccon arn't present either. While they didn't really affect the campaign overall, I did miss the air reccon.
Naval Battles and Gameplay
For my last trick, I'll talk about the long awaited naval battles! From what I gathered, these were a long awaited addition to the game. Let me just say that if your buying this on account of the naval battles, don't. To be honest, they're harder than the ground battles, and not really in a fun way. If you play as NATO, you'll find yourself massing your fleet of two destroyers and seven PT boats together to avoid the rain of anti-ship missels being thrown at you by the Soviet-Chinease fleet, which is made up of one or two large destroyers, and dozens of light ships. I suppose it could just be me(I didn't really try to conquer the sectors to get more points), but it feels unbalanced. It also felt unrealistic because the larger ships can't fire over obstacles or even very far. If your like me, and your playing this more for the land battles, then you'll enjoy it. The navel aspect means some vehicles can cross rivers, and the PT boats are fun to use on the smaller rivers. Reinforcements can also come by sea in landing craft.
One thing I did notice from all this is the AI has been downgraded a bit from AirLand Battle. I find that the AI is constantly massing units together and rushing me. This usually ends in 90% of the AI's army being destroyed at bridges or other choke points. It did ambush me a few times when I was on the offensive, but overall it seems dumber. Another slightly annoying thing is that when your making custom decks, your now limmited to a certain amount of transports. So if I want to build an airborne army consisting of Huey helicopters, I can only select five units before I have use a different helicopter. Again, It's not a game breaker, but it is a little annoying. I suppose it does challenge you, though, as you'll have to decide who will get the best transports.
So overall, here's what I see:
Pros:
Excellent graphics
Great Sounds
Good campaigns
Lots of new units and new nations
F-86 Sabres with rocket pods!
New naval combat units for you to rule the coastal maps with
Cons
New naval battles a little out of wack
AI seems a little dumber
Deck building a little more complicated
No random events or strategic options
Overall, I've really enjoyed this game, and despite it's few problems, I still reccomend it. It's a good addition to the series and it is a lot of fun. If your on the fence, or still want it for the naval combat, then I'd wait untill it's on sale.

Wargame: Red Dragon is a PC Wargame/Real-time Tactics hybrid. It is the most realistic, stratigic combat simulator I have played in all my years of gaming. It has enough unit diversity to satisfy and, indeed, surpass my unit diversity comfort zone. If you like fast-paced, click-faster-to-win games then skip this title. But, if you enjoy real, tactical combat, then this is the game for you.
Graphics: 9/10. Very realistic units and landscape, and, oddly enough, no lag.
Balance: 8/10. There seems to be a strong balance between the game's armies, but, as I have not played it for as long as some (i.e, 34 hours), I have not looked into the balance factor.
Performance: 10/10. I have a 6 GB Ram computer with an I3 intel core and it runs better than any other game I have.
Sound: 7/10. Music is medicore (some tracks I have heard in other game franchises), and the gun-fire seems a little muted but it does provide an acceptable atmosphere.
Gameplay: 8/10. Realistic armour and damage, which I enjoy because I am a history fan. The Aircraft are also extremly innovative and fun, is somewhat fragile.
AI: 7.5/10. The AI is not a very enjoyable opponent, as it always either charges head-on or does nothing.
Campaign: 7/10. Campaign mode is the only place I seem to experience lag. It does also seem shallow and gets tire-some very quickly. However, it does provide a larger perspective on 70s/80s warfare and tactics.
Verdict: A somewhat challanging game with it's fair share of cons, but, it does simulate real warfare better than almost any other stratagy game.
Final Score: 8.5/10
Certainly worth looking at if you are intrested in modern or semi-modern stratigic warfare.

This game has a great premise and decent mechanics but doesn't deliver.
The premise of this game is that you're playing a "campaign" where your dwarves are teleported to a new world, presumably to escape demons from a previous world, but they aren't far behind. You need to build shelter, feed and defend your dwarves and reach a high enough level of technology to construct the portal to teleport away to the next world before you're overrun by demons.
Really cool premise, right?  Well, the delivery could be better.
For starters, the AI of the dwarves is pretty mediocre.  They'll often get confused and lose their pathing, sometimes in an endless loop that requires you to restart the game. They aren't smart enough to do a lot of basic quality of life tasks. Found a juicy pach of ore you want to mine? Well, if it's taller than 2 blocks, they'll likely just dig out the bottom of the patch first (rather than the top) and be stuck, unable to reach further than one block above themselves.  So you're constantly constructing and deconstructing ladders to let them reach every single damn thing out of range of their stubby fingers.  This is especially obnoxious for decorating your home.  The game punishes you with tedium if you want the rooms of your home to be taller than 2 blocks.
Then, there's the pacing of each level.  In your constant research of technology, you'll often be given access to some recipes that you can't build because they require recipes that get unlocked far later in the tech tree.  It's not fun to not be able to use your unlocks until you unlock 10 more things.
Each "world" takes around 20-40 hours to beat.  When you finally find the portal room with it's final guardian that you need to beat to move on to the next world, you're then requried to basically dig around the entire map to find 4 more of the exact same room to beat the exact same guardian.  By the time you reach the first guardian, you've already reached the end of the tech tree, so this isn't a new challenge, it's just an additional 4 hours of busywork.
So you FINALLY reach the new world? Great, it's time for almost the exact same thing.  You start from scratch, with 1 dwarf and no researched technology, with the exact same quests, exact same technology to research, and maybe 1 or 2 new challenges (an extra couple types of enemies, bigger waves of enemies, and maybe a new weather type).
It's a good premise, but ends up being a lot of repetetive busywork. 6/10
TLDR; Buy Kingdoms: New Lands instead. Very similar premise, much less building but a much tighter experience. This game barely feels like it's about the crafting and building and more about the fighting, survival and tower defense, which Kingdoms does far better.

It's the best all-around simulator out there, currently, full stop.
If you like trains, you will love this game.  However, it is not a cheap date.  Like collecting trains and tracks and so on for model train enthusiasts, you will spend $$$ building your collection.  If you can approach it that way, instead of having to own the entire model train shop from the beginning, you will like the game.  If you can't deal with not having "all of the assets", probably ever, and don't want, or can't, approach it like a model train collector does, you will be frustrated by the business model -- so know yourself and your own approach beforehand.
The game itself offers several modes.
Quick drive permits you to pick a route and a locomotive (a loco), set your destination, and just drive freely without other goals or timetables.  It's a great casual mode, and also great for trying out new locos, and learning new routes.
Standard mode provides scenarios (tasks, like running a commuter train according to a timetable, or running freight or what have you) in a pre-packaged scenario.  You can pick the loco you want for the task, provided it fits the route.
Career mode is the "game" mode of the simulator.  It provides preset scenarios, with preset locos, which vary in difficulty from relatively easy (still easy to mess up for a beginner) to quite challenging -- both for passenger and freight train work.  You are scored based on a number of factors, and can gain medals and levels and so on.  It's the challenging mode of the game, when you are up for a challenge or just want something a bit more serious.
Free Drive mode is also available, which allows you to explore certain routes with certain locos.
There is a huge number of locos available (for purchase, again as a train collection), as well as a substantial number of routes.  Dovetail is UK-based, and there are more trains and routes in the UK than anywhere else (and there are some fantastic trains and routes for the UK available), but there are also great locos and routes for Germany and North America, with some of the most iconic routes and locos represented for each.
In all, if you love trains, you will love this game, but you have to approach it like you would a model train hobby and not expect to own every train and track in the hobby store in one visit.  If you can manage that, this game will provide hours and hours of great train fun, which will be even more enjoyable for you if you like either the British or German rail systems (I am a fan of both, and so it is great fun for me).

Do you like racing games where you get to shoot guns? How about running over hordes of squishy enemies? You can do both these things in Zombie Driver HD. This is the re-release of a 2009 game with improved graphics and additional content, and while the game seems to have mediocre meta ratings, the user review scores on Steam are very positive (in the 90’s). The game was released on consoles like Xbox 360 and Playstation 3, but the Steam version seems to have a lot more achievements than the console ones (more than 100).
The game’s story is actually very rudimentary, where all you know is that some sort of disaster has occurred, creating zombies all over the city. The opening and closing animations are like motion comics, where they just kind of zoom around on a single painting (not really movies). This means that you mostly pick up the plot from the intros to each level, where your commanding officer gives you your orders. It’s worth noting here that the voice acting is pretty bad, and has some grammatical errors and misplaced emphases. It’s not that big a deal since the game is mostly zombie squishing, and the story is just for adding flavor.
Zombie Driver is a top down car shooter where you drive around a large city map infested with thousands of zombies. There are about 30 levels in total, and the game “world” resets between each mission so you can grind for money or achievements if you want. There are only 4 different types of weapon (machine gun, flame thrower, rocket launcher, and rail gun) and the ammo is scarce enough that you can’t just drive around firing wildly. Fortunately, most of your kills will probably be from squashing ♥♥♥♥♥es with your ride. Things like ammunition and repair kits respawn every few minutes so if you take your time, the game is actually pretty easy. There’s no way to change the difficulty, by the way. By completing side objectives during certain missions, you can unlock different cars to drive, each with different stats for speed, armor, and ramming power. If you have the DLC, the best car for most of the game is the Auroch truck. Vehicle upgrades are separate for each car, so you don’t want to spend all your money upgrading your early cars, but the weapon unlocks/upgrades carry over for all cars.
As for the enemies you’ll be facing, most of them are weak shambling zombies that barely slow you down as you trample over them, but after the first few missions you’ll meet the guy that makes you drive cautiously all the way to the end of the game – the exploding fat zombie. He’s pretty much the only enemy you try not to run over, and this prevents you from just holding down the nitro and boosting around the map. There are also a few bosses to fight, but they’re basically all the same in gameplay (rooted to the ground throwing stuff at you). Since health and ammo pickups respawn on the map, you can use hit and run tactics on bosses, and run away to heal if you’re about to die.
Pros:
+Very nice gruesome graphics for such a small game. I think it was about 1gb to download.
+Fun for casual zombie squashing, and if you want, you can replay levels you’ve already beaten (but these don’t “save” meaning your main campaign save file doesn’t keep the money found or cars unlocked from level replays). That means the only real reason to replay levels is to unlock achievements.
+I enjoy games where you can (but don’t have to) grind for money to buy persistent upgrades. I originally thought this game was like the Alien Shooter / Zombie Shooter games, and it kind of is similar in the way you take extra time on each level just to look for extra money to buy upgrades.
Cons:
-The game gets repetitive by the middle of the campaign. Every mission is basically the same (clear out the zombies in a particular area) and it all takes place on the same map. The enemies don’t get any stronger, just more numerous. At least the map is big and you’re constantly upgrading your cars.
-The game camera swings wildly at times since it seems to be on a slight delay. This means you can do a sharp skidding turn, and a second later the camera rotates 180 degrees. I didn’t get a headache playing the game, but I can see how it would bother some players. There’s also a bug (possibly intentional) where it’s possible for you to get “stuck” on certain obstructions. Despite being a top down game, you can still make small jumps if you’re going fast enough (like hitting a wall at full turbo speed). This means once in a while you’ll get stuck on a wall or a fence and need to restart the level. It’s really annoying if you’ve already completed the mission objectives and are just running around looking for money before ending the stage, suddenly you get stuck and have to start all over again.
-The “story” is pretty generic and predictable, so don’t play it for the story.
Overall Zombie Driver HD is a great game if you enjoy top down shooters and mowing down massive hordes of weak enemies. Seriously, by the last level you probably can’t go half a screen without running over a dozen zombies. If you’re just playing for the Steam achievements, I can tell you that about half of them are pretty easy to acquire, but the other half require a lot of grinding (kill 10,000 zombies each with machine gun/rockets/fire, etc.).  If you have half an hour to kill (literally), you can beat one story mission at a time until you finish the campaign and move on to the other 2 game modes: Blood Race and Slaughter. Blood Race is an actual racing mode, unlike the main game where it’s just you vs zombies. Think of it as a top down version of Rage racing, with machine guns and missiles. Slaughter mode is a survival game where you try to live through rounds against increasingly dangerous waves of zombies (more fat exploders).

TLDR: don't buy yet, only if it's around 5bucks. bugged, still a console game with small closed totally linear maps, huge open maps and new tactical gameplay is a blatant lie, shooting feel got worse, missions are sometimes annoying, relocation mechanics ruin the immersion and are very annoying, AI is worse then V2, the sound masking finally makes some sense and works, game looks better and real pretty, pre-scripted chain reaction explosions are fun to trigger and watch.
Just like others said before me, this is in almost no way better then v2 was.
The most basic problem with the previous game was, that it was a console game, which made it play more like an on-rails shooter than an open world game. Small enviroments, a maximum of 2-3 paths to take on each map. It is still the case.
The pros:
- it looks better
- more stealth options, like hiding in bushes, and now most things that go bang loud enough will hide your shots, like broken generators or explosions
- chain explosions: you don't have to place bombs to take out every hard target you come across. This is the one and only freedom of choice you get during the missions. Place explosives/throw grenades, or find the right "explosive tank of gas/ammo" and shoot it, thus starting a chain explosion that takes out the target.
The cons:
- you are forced to move after every third shot you take, it doesn't matter that the nearest enemy is over 300 meters away, or 20. They will always instantly pinpoint your exact location, and start attacking you. So you must use the "innovative, awesome, super new Relocation system". It's a cheap and blatantly stupid way to save time and money on coding a proper AI, which in this case is worse than it was in the 90's. This means you cannot use any sniper hidout in the game for more than two shots, regardless of concealment, distance, and so on.
- again this relocation system means, that if you run far enough without being spotted, which is like 30 meters, they stop searching for you. At least the game sais that it's all clear after about 30 seconds pass. This is a fail in itself. There is no pressure, you just need to have a rock a couple of meters back the way to hide behind.
- But, when the game tells you it's all clear, sometimes it doesn't tell the AI this. A random soldier out of the dozens that was after you, stays in pursuit and keeps running towards your now supposedly unknown location, will find you no matter what, and will try to gun you down. So its a total fail.
- There are a bunch of unlocks and upgrades in the game, they are all 100% useless and doesn't worth your time. They may change the scope wobble a bit, but lose the zoom on the scope, and such trade-offs make every choice a bad choice. Get another rifle, although all 4 works about the same, some are just more annoying to aim with than the others.
- "Sniper's Nests" are thrown around the maps, basically telling you where to go and shoot from. You are encuraged by the game every time to visit and use these. The problem is, that these spots are totally useless, as you cannot shoot more than twice from them, because relocation...
- first day DLC (I own it I think, because I was stupid enough to pre-purchase. I would not do it again though)
- AI is as bad as it was, magic aim with machine pistols from a 100 meters, more accurate than your sniper rifle. It's really just a way to force you to "use more stealth". To put it bluntly, all the "features" in this game are there to make you play the game in the exact way the creators want you to.  So that you wouldn't notice the abyssmal AI, the total lack of open world and freedom of choice they promised. See, that's the deffiniton of an "on-rails shooter". The exact opposite of open world/multiple choice.
-  the missions are a mess. For example, the very first mission after the tutorials. SPOILER ALERT: You are supposed to kill 4 officers, loot them, then a fifth a one pops up out of nowhere on a halftrack and you must blow it up. You are in the worst possible place, but the mission text and your character tells you that no worries, you have time to prepare. That is, actually, about 15 seconds, before the halftrack turns the corner and spots you. Once you are spotted, it's mission failed. If you hide, the truck simply leaves through the gates which takes about another 15 mintues. It's a quicktime event, which you can only solve if you have prepared for it, before you knew it existed. Clever, ehh? So after you figure it out, that the game autosaved before! you looted the last officer and started the event, you make the "open world" decision to use the mines and dynamite you found right before the autosave, to blow the hell out of the truck. It's no challange at all once you know that you need to place a single, otherwise useless, mine on the one and only road. See, that's the complex tactical and strategic "decision" you are allowed to make.
The LIES:
- Large open maps: The maps may be a little bit bigger, but this is still a last-gen console game. Everything is cramped into small valleys or obscured by hills and fog so you may not see farther than your avarage console shooter. And they are most certainly far from open. Every map is made out of "zones" like the city squares in v2. You have these small, little bit "open spaces", connected by valleys formed by walls of sand, rock, buildings...
- Tactical gameplay: See mission example above. Where there is some more open space, the enemys won't load up, until you get close enough. This makes it impossible to properly plan an attack, because they will pop up in places where you wouldn't expect them. It's like we are back in 2000. At least in V2 it wasn't as annoying, because the narrow streets kept the pop-in hidden, and by the time you turned the corner onto the next street, most of them were in position, ready to receive their headshots. This time around, even when they load in, their hitboxes are bugged. Sometimes, although you should most definetly hit them according to the built-in "aim bot diamond", it still won't register as a hit on the target, because it's too far away for the game to handle. The hitboxes of enemies are generally bugged. You can only perform heart shots by aiming at the middle of their backs. A seemingly perfect hearth shot from the front will never kill.
The Simply Disappointing:

Well, so much for modding in singleplayer. I may have not bought the game since it first came out on PC, but I've seen things. Take-Two's "cease and desist" of the only possbile way to actually mod the game in singleplayer has really put them in deep water. But they don't care. All they cared about was money. Yes, I understand that they (Take-Two and Rockstar) are trying to fix the cheater problem that's been going on ever since GTA Online started and that Rockstar is NOT the cause for the problem, but OpenIV was never used for modding in multiplayer. It was in OpenIV's policy that it was not for multiplayer use, and never was, as well as their intent specifially stating that. Besides, the game would not let you play Online if you modified anything within the game files (ScriptHook would disallow such as well). And Rockstar enouraged the use of singleplayer mods (with OpenIV being the only way to do so), and they were fine with that. I personally have not used OpenIV in a long while, but now I am resonably sure GTA IV is not moddable either due to it also being the only way to mod the game. People may have to resort to SparkIV for GTA IV, unless Take-Two has taken care of that already...
I understand other players' anger and frustration (and I admit, I am one of them too). This however, isn't going to stop me from playing singleplayer/multiplayer as a result of Take-Two's recent action against the modding community. Something tells me that if this gets worse, we are going to have another FROMSOFT developer team, where changing anything (anything at all, even if its just a harmless texture) will result in a ban (it is an odd comparision, but if you played any of the Dark Souls games on PC, you would understand). GTA V had that problem a long time ago, where it was banning players that were using mods in singleplayer, and I wouldn't be suprised if they re-integrate that again.
In my honest opinion, I actually really do like this game, both singleplayer and multiplayer (as you might be able to tell with the amount of hours I put into it), with the majority being multiplayer. Finished the game, missing a few things here and there, and pleased with the new Gunrunning update that was released a couple days ago (when this review was posted). I'm happy to say that I have never bought a shark card for Online, and doing pretty well in multiplayer (doing Criminal Mastermind with my crew certainly helped with that :p).
In conclusion, I woudn't be suprised if this ongoing problem would turn for the worse, but regardless, it is not going to stop me from playing the game. I like the game, I like the crew that I am a part of, and despite the large pool of cheaters that still exist to this day, multiplayer isn't that half-bad. The only thing I am concerned about is how badly this will turn against the players and the overall playerbase. Each playerbase is seperate (Xbox 1, PS4, PC, etc.). They don't cross-platform. I fear that this action (and its subsequent actions and consequences) might end up crippling the entire PC playerbase for good.
TL;DR: Game is good, multiplayer isn't half-bad, Take-Two is shooting itself in the foot (in my opinion) and might become the second FROMSOFT (if you play any Dark Souls you understand). I'm fearing for what might happen in the future due to this action, but isn't stopping me from playing multiplayer, and RIP singleplayer modding. You will be missed. :(

I could describe it as pure and utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ however that would mean at some point it was ingestable.  That is had some delicious content you actually enjoyed consuming.  That it was good, it was something you liked, and would want more of.
No, it's more like...it's garbage - pure trash.  Like the other content he wants to so flippantly bash on, Bennett Foddy fails to realize his own game is also on that same trash heap mountain.  It reminds me of those games you saw mass produced in the 90's, that would sit on a store shelf for days, weeks, months, years.  Maybe once in a while someone would buy it, maybe someone would even wrestle through the awful gameplay and controls, and beat it.  (Daikatana, anyone?)  However, more often than not, these games lived a brief and painful life, ending up where they belonged: in the trash.
Much like a similar game from what to us gamers was eons ago, there was a reason why the ET game on the original Atari ended up being buried, by the thousands, in a desert somewhere.  This game has the potential to be good, even great, but is wasted.  Bennett himself even thinks (though the more I play I believe he is/was incapable) of greating a good game.  With good controls, and your character doing what you expect and want them to do, climbing this nigh-impossible mountain would have felt like an achievement, an undertaking that if finished, would make you feel accomplisehd, as though you had mastered its controls.
No, however.  It is random, as random as can be.  I imagine if the mouse and WASD keys were swapped for movement of this game, it would be as if the WASD keys had been popped off, and swapped randomly whenever you played the game, or even attepted to move at all.  Sometimes, your hammer grips onto a surface, and you are able to drag it.  Others, not.  Other times still, your character will shoot the hammer outwards, and cause you to fly at warp speed in a direction you never intended, with all but the gentlest of mouse movements.
As a gamer, or rather, a great gamer, I'm known among my circle of friends as someone who just plays, and beats hard games.  On my Steam profile right now, I have 3 perfect games, and over 1000 achievements.  You could say, I've beaten hard games before.  Ninja Gaiden Black.  Mike Tyson's Punch Out.  Street Fighter II turbo.  This game however, is not difficult.  The issue is in a garbage design, an inherently fatal flaw in mechanics that makes you, as the player, not feeling empowered.  More as though, you're playing a Grand Theft Auto game, and you speed your car off a cliff, and then attempt to steer while flying through the air.  Pro tip: cars are not airplanes, and can't fly.
As of this writing, I have over ten hours into the game.  It really lost any enjoyment or fun after the very first hour.  If you feel inclined to ever purchase this trash, just don't.  Watch a YouTuber like Markiplier play it, and see how intensely frustrated he gets.  That's what it's like.  Don't waste time, money, energy or effort on this.
Or, if you really want an amazing, incredible, fun game to play, try Hell Yeah!  It's about a rabbit, who rides around a giant murderous wheel-machine, to get his porn collection back from The Devil.
Now, doesn't that sound so much more awesome than the Adventures of Pot Man?

This game looked alright and was less than 4$ so I picked it up.  I then spent 30 hours of the next two days playing it somehow...
Summary:
Really addicting fusion of Terraria + Dwarf Sim.  Instead of controlling a character yourself, you send out a group of dwarves to mine, craft, attack, etc. for you.  You create a shelter for them and decorate it with tons of furniture and customization options.  At night your house gets attacked and bigger "monster portal" waves also attack every ~45 minutes. Everything gives XP and as you level up you get more dwarves to control.  Each has their own skills and equipment so as you unlock better gear you slowly upgrade all of them.
The goal is to find the five bosses underground that drop recipes for one of five pieces of a portal while protecting your shelter and taking care of your dwarves.  Once you have all the recipes you craft the portal and beat the level.
Pros:
-High quality 2D graphics
-Lots of decoration options
-Lots of resources and stuff to do
-Weather effects and biomes increase the challenge by changing the resources that are easily accessible
-Fun!
Cons:
-Tech tree doesn't always make sense, you have to build furniture to unlock high end armor?
-Dwarf AI is good but can be derp sometimes (ex. complains it can't pick up an item in a chamber with monsters, travels half way across the map to pick up a leaf, lets a portal vanish so ends up stranded)

The second in the eXceed series, Vampire REX (the updated version of Vampire) is a bullet hell shooter brought to us by FLAT/Tennen-Sozai. What makes this game "unique" is its mechanic of swapping polarities to absorb either blue or red bullets. If this sounds familiar that's because it is - this is the same mechanic that Ikaruga used famously to great effect. The series as a whole was created by a dōjin circle, similar to the Touhou project and, while not as good in my oppinion, eXceed is still a lot of fun and definitely gets your heart pounding. I beat the first game, but it was pretty generic and I would not recommend it; however, the second - Vampire REX - is a lot of fun and worth playing if you like these types of games. While Ikaruga is hands down the better game, Vampire REX is short, fast, fun, and really scratches the bullet-hell itch I've had for awhile. It doesn't have a lot of fancy options like leaderboard support but it does have minimal controller support, replays, high scores, and an arcade mode to skip dialogue. The story isn't very good, but that's to be expected, and the all important soundtrack is enjoyable and varies from Gothic choir music to hard techno - each boss even has its own theme. It was pretty easy after you figure out the mechanics of the game: collect one type of bullet to build your "bomb" and dodge the other color, you do double damage to the unit opposite your current polarity (the difficulty also increases while you play if you're doing well, which was cool), and while not the be-all-end all of bullet-hell shooters, eXceed is a worthwhile series to play and you're not going to find much like it on Steam, so I recommend this title, but not the first. We'll see if the third is as enjoyable as Vampire REX.

As you descend down the depths of the mining tunnel, one thought keeps creeping back into your mind: "What if this is dangerous?" - But too late to wonder about this, because you're already dead, bitten by a snake and then ravaged by an angry spider.
Next try, with your basic knowledge of the underground wildlife you make a second daring attempt for treasure - of which you spot some behind an obstacle. Time to use your bombs - well, you shouldn't have because you are dead. Blew yourself up in your carelessness.
Three time's the charm, so down with you again, using your bombs and ropes sparingly, you now know every inch of level 1-1 by heart. Or do you? The levels generate randomly, so each attempt is slightly different. Bad for you, because you're dead. Fell down a pit that wasn't there before and landed on some spikes.
If you played the old Spelunky, this experience may sound familiar. It is very much a game about trial-and-error at first, then later it is all about honing your spelunking-skills, hurling rocks with great precision and knowing when to use bombs or ropes, when to buy what you need from the shops or just simply killing the shopkeeper. Spelunky is a somewhat unique 2D platformer, with randomly generated levels made out of blocks and treasure to be found everywhere. This game excels at testing your will, playing cruel tricks on you but only making you try harder every time you hit that "restart"-button. The learning-curve is steep and you do get that sense of nostalgia, taking you back to arcade-times. Only now you won't have to insert coins for each run.
Spelunky has you run, jump and climb through various styles of levels (tunnels, jungle, iceworld and hell just to name a few) in pursuit of riches - driving you to take your highscore to the limit.
Multiplayer is possible as well, with up to four spelunkers at the same time.
Spelunky is a great little game to have if you need to sink a bit of time, but cannot be bothered to fire up one of the big boys. While being a rather simple game, the difficulty is absolutely unforgiving, and you yourself are your best mentor, getting further and further with each attempt. Many secrets also lie buried in this devil of a game and trying challenge after challenge should keep you interested for a good while. I would recommend playing this game with a controller (ideally an XBox-controller), with it originally being an XBLA-title.

This is a pure classic, must-buy.
You play an Indiana Jones figure, hat and whip included, equipped with a few climbing ropes and bombs. You explore caves filled with treasures and monsters, in increasingly rewarding and difficult environments. The controls are simple but extremely tight.
At first it feels a little spare. The same elements crop up repeatedly: snakes prowling along the ground, rocks to throw, arrow traps that shoot anything that moves, damsels to rescue.
Then you begin to feel puzzled, because in the face of these simple elements and easy to learn patterns, you die. You fall on inconveniently placed spikes and are impaled. You forget to look down and take a little fall damage. You throw a rock up to trip an arrow trap, then the rock bounces and hits you in the head. You take a running jump and barely miss the edge. You have trouble whipping things in time.
The elements combine into emergent situations. A skeleton gets stuck in a web that lies across the easiest passage through the level. To kill him, you would have to wake a gigantic spider. So you decide whether to waste a bomb on a fragile, motionless enemy, or risk whipping the skeleton and getting stuck in the web as the spider approaches.
Like many roguelike-likes, a lot of the pleasure comes from peeling the onion yourself, discovering all the interesting strategies and layers the game holds. You also get a great source of stories and screenshots, as the RNG strikes again and again.

SPG: Warlords improves a lot on where SPG2 fell flat. If you are a fan of the series, especially SPG2, you'll feel right at home here as Warlords at its core, still plays and feels much like SPG2 with some basic 4X RTS elements thrown into the mix.
One of my biggest gripes with SPG2 was how shallow the game felt overall, with little to do or incentive to explore after the first few hours. Warlords improves upon that formula by offering even more ships, better armed ships (The dreadnaught Formidable allows you to do 30 turret broadsides!), more missions/job boards with varying objectives and the biggest change and theme of the game, the fleet system. This is no Civ by any means. It's basic as basic gets, but it ties into everything smoothly and it works and unlike SPG2 you'll have plenty of tough encounters to actually utilize your ships offensive and defensive powers to test your setups.
Though not all is perfect. LGM is a small studio so expectations should equal such. One of the biggest downsides to Warlords is the Campaign story. To me if felt rushed and unpolished. It was basically doing one mission, then go level up till in a new class of ship which will then unlock the next story mission. rinse and repeat. On top of that the story is just boring and predictable. I couldn't connect with any of the 'characters' and just wanted to be done with it so I could focus on taking over sectors and building massive fleets, which let's be honest that's all you will really care about anyway.
To sum up the Pros and Cons with Warlords;
+More challenging
+More stuff to do
+Fleet/Upgrade/Research system
+Beefier ships
+Improved visuals over SPG2
-No Titans
-Lack of upgrades/customization for Warmasters and their ships
-Forgettable story and cast
-AI too passive
Warlords is a good game and worth the price. If you liked SPG2, but just felt like it needed something more, Warlords is your answer. It is made only better by the hordes of workshop mods.

This is a really hard negative recommendation for me, I paid the full £26ish price for it and I've definitely gotten more than an hour per £ in playtime.
Have I enjoyed it? Kinda, yeah. There's some wonderful beauty to the game, and I've been honestly stunned using the camera angles to appreciate battles, or simply flying through space. Commanding fleets of massive capital ships and being able to fly in any direction you like Is lovely, and god it looks beautiful.
The issue is flying the 'Gunship' class (smallest ship class, essentialy a massive fighter) feels exactly the same as flying a heavy Cruiser (first big capital ship you get) with smaller guns and quicker turning, but even with the smallest ship class you're still setting your weapons to auto-fire and largely waiting for them to kill things or deciding you're not strong enough yet.
I also (largely the reason I've bought the game, and why I've tried to stick with it) found this game referred to as Mount and Blade in space. It certainly looks so, at least in the sense that there's other factions reacting to your actions and your ability to create and expand an empire, conducting military actions as a single combatant leading from the front (if you so choose).
The problem with the two previous points, is that in Mount and Blade I can see my troops, see what they look like, their weapons, how they look in combat, and how the whole battle looks. In Warlords all I've ever felt like I'm doing is getting into combat, pointing the right part of my ship at a target, and waiting until it dies.
Similarly to M&B there's also RPG elements, as in ability to customise your pilot, your ships, your loadout (though I've mostly found myself equipping whatever is the most expensive items I can find and doing brilliantly doing so), it's there and my character specialising in boarding (and stealing ships) definitely got good at that quickly. Though I can't really think of any major penalties I had from choosing to specialise only in boarding out of about 30-40 different options (though admittedly, I've only played the one game for an entire 24 hours, which might not be enough to see these choices be meaningful?)
There's strategy, in that you have an area to defend and need to make sure when the trouble starts you can either bring yourself and/fleet(s) to help. Mostly I noticed anything smaller than a destroyer was in danger of being blown to hell in any late-game fight so I stopped building anything other than battlecruisers and seemed to win fights easily after than point.
There's also the 4X (eXpand, eXchange, eXplore, eXterminate) element to the massive world map with so many other factions and things to explore. My next point covers this bit anyway so I wont say more here.
So, why am I giving a negative review? Ignoring how unbelievably beautiful it is, the game just feels empty, stale, and like I'm enjoying myself less than I'm simply going through the motions, trying to advance my empire. There is so much more for me to explore, vistas to see, factions to meet, bigger fleets to build, but I'm bored.
I can't control my fleets directly, I can't even assign a ship to my fleets and choose to use it for myself (literally, for some reason you have to buy empire ships with one type of resource, and purchase ships for yourself using money, I had 2 battlecruisers while I was still piloting a damn frigate!)
It doesn't matter what ship I'm flying, they all fight the same, I can use a mouse button to shoot but what's the point when every enemy looks pea-sized and everything auto-locks-and-fires at the push of a button?
Every fight is basically a slugging match between the biggest ships while the smaller ships try not to die from auto-fire (tactical advice, big ships soak damage, send those in first, then smaller ones for more DPS)
I think I hoped for a more beautiful X3: Terran Conflict (or the Albion Prelude expansion) but somehow the old, glitchy game with barely any global impact from your decisions makes me feel far more depth than SPG: Warlords, and even though the world is smaller and I can't even conquer it with mods.
Actually thats the major issue, the fact you could start out in actual fighter and make your way up to a super-heavy was a huge part of the game, but not the requirement. X3s interfact was a painful learning curve, but jesus it was good, comprehensive, and gave you genuine, total, real-time tactical control of your fleets (be it huge militaries, small traders, or just a couple of scout-fighters)
You can play as a gunship in Warlords and support your big fleets, but there's absolutely no point. Any ship in your fleet cannot be flown by you, any ship in your garage cannot be used in your fleet. You can outift your garage ships in the most badass way possible, but your fleet ships will do whatever they want. If you're not using auto-fire on all your guns you're stupid, and outside of that the only combat depth is "I need to mark THIS target so my turrets/other nearby ships focus on it, and repeatedly hit the X button so my missles will also hit it - OR - I will move THIS fleet in now, and use THIS one for something else.
There's so much more I could say on this, but really the thing which makes me sad is Warlords feels like an absolutely gorgeous Mobile Turret Platform Simulator in space. There's plenty of other potential depth, but it feels gated behind increasing difficulties of combat that require steadily more numerous and powerful Mobile Turret Platforms.
Personally? I wish I could see the beauty of this game and it's true sector takeover mechanics in X3, then I'd be seeing something magical.
Sorry for the harsh review, I think the devs have worked really hard on something lovely, it just can't truly grip me due to too many things.

I have trouble recommending this game. On one hand it is 4X strategy RPG with both direct ship control as well as fleet control? Sign me up! But every part of this game's design screams “Make them grind so they don’t notice how little content we have!”
The game is big but empty. Everything you do seems simple and boring. The most efficient way to fight space combat is basically just hold the pitch up key and turn on auto fire. Then you just circle the enemy ship for 30-60 seconds waiting for it to blow up. Oh yeah, and you can click a class power button every 10-15 seconds which will reduce the wait a little bit. Super exciting. Similarly the most efficient way to make money in the game is to spend 5 minutes figuring out what the best trade item is to sell between two nearby planet/stations and then just make that trade run a hundred times.
You can also do side missions to get money but the break down into two categories. Fetch quests, and kill quests. Neither option pays out nearly as much as trading does and the kill quests are very likely to kill you and your very expensive fleet. These side missions have no story attached to them so the end up taking more time, without providing any extra fun, and reward you with less resources.
And everything is expensive. Your average side mission pays about 300,000 credits and takes about 3-4 minutes. One of the early level ships, a corvette costs 900,000, so that's not too bad, about 9 minutes to get into that. But now let's assume you want to put some decent weapons in it. I go for the level 3 rippers which cost 1,200,000 each, and there are 3 slots for them so now we are up to 42 minutes. And that's just weapons. For the next level ship its 2,000,000 and another 3 slots so have fun grinding for another hour. And it just goes up from there. And the missions never seem to pay out any more. 90% of them are in the 300,000 credit range. I did see one search and destroy mission that was for 1,200,000 that was around my level but when I took my maxed out frigate along with a fleet of 4 other corvettes I got completely wiped. It's like the game was saying, no no, grinding only.
Then there is the materials resource. A separate resource from credits. It is needed to do just about everything in your empire, upgrade your space station, build fleets, do research, and build mining posts. Literally every action you could take to improve your empire requires this resource, and it is super scarce. It can only be earned through fleet actions (one off tasks you can tell frendly ships to do) or by salvaging. Material salvaging can only be done by salvaging stations. Which of course take material to build. So the whole thing breaks down into a long and boring waiting game where you wait to have enough materials so you can build things to get materials faster, and while you wait you can either do boring fetch quests, or boring trading routes.
And according to at least one of the devs, this is not an accident, as you can read in this quote “Materials is the most important resource, it determines your fleets which determine your faction strength so idea is that it is the most scarce resource unless you work on it. And there is, of course, a choice if you want to rush your economy. You will have have to focus Ore and Gas instead of materials to optimize gains.” (post #11 here:
In that same post, the dev in question also talks about maybe allowing fast travel for free. Because yes, currently it costs 35,000 credits to buy a fast travel or T-Drive. But using a T-Drive doesn’t guarantee you get where you’re going. First off, they have a limited range, so if you want to get any reasonable distance expect to use 3-4 of them. Additionally, story and side missions will sometimes force you out of warp, halving your distance but not refunding you’re very expensive T-Drives.
As much as you can fly space ships, fight space battles, build space stations, and expand your space empire, I feel like there is nothing to actually do. Now I will admit, at this point I think I am still early in the campaign. I just unlocked and upgraded the frigate class. So maybe the game has yet to open up for me. But I am also 7 hours in and wondering when I am going to be allowed to start having fun instead of grinding non-stop to keep up with the ridiculous difficulty and upgrade cost ramp.

There is a ton of room for meaningful build customization, combat is smooth and rewarding, the art style is appealing, orchestral soundtrack is wonderful, and, honestly, this is what Diablo III should have been. Co-op, the dungeon generator, and modding tools make this game even better, and it's definitely worthy of your time and money.

Apogees Duke Nukem Death Rally meets Rockstars Classic Grand Theft Auto.
Top down car driving gun blazing zombie killing goodness.
Played the original a what seem like 6 ish years ago ?, and to be honest didn't give it much thought, it was ok but found it fiddly with a keyboard and mouse. Skip forward to 2015 and I picked up the ZD HD complete pack for just over £2 and have been playing it nearly 5 days now, this time however with an xbox controller.
In short the game visualy looks very nice, easily some of the best "indie" game graphics available even against 2014/15 offerings. SFX compliment the game well nice solid sounding guns and squishy zombie splatter under the tires. Heavy Metal BGM during the survival mini games gets your adrenalin pumping but is less suited perhaps to the missions of the main game, it is good but can become repetative. Voice acting ... well at least there is some, lets just say it doesnt add nor detract from the game, and I've defo heard a lot lot worse.
Game can be tricky to control with kyb and mouse and is definatly easier to be prescise with a stick controller like xbox/ps3 controller.
Main game offers 31 missions each taking between 3-10 mins to complete on your first play through, each with highscore tables and secondary optional missions offering limited replay value but atleast it has. These can be replayed in any order, using any car you have unlocked with ay upgrades you have unlocked making a replay easier to obtain a better score or to do secondary missions.
Survival mode offers erm.... 7 ish arena maps with the aim to survive as long as possible with waves or increasing numbers and toughness of mobs, earning upgrades each wave to assist you and random weapon and bonus score drops. each map having its own high score tables. This is easily the most fun mode and will keep you playing for significant time after having completed the main game. To be fair some of these maps can feel a little small or tight to move around and can feel like you are just driving in a circle, but most are nice arenas with multiple paths to manouvre around.
Race mode, this is somewhat similar to a classic game Death Rally from the 90s, I havent played much of this so far but is a series of tournaments made up of a set number of events, such as race, checkpoint and elimination. This can be a little frustrating as it is very easy to get stitched up right at the end of an event after leading 95% of a race. This mode seems to be 75% player skill and 25% luck.
Money spent on car and weapon upgrades from the main game are for the main game only, in the main game new cars are unlocked through playthrough. In survival upgrades  are earned in each game for that game only by completing waves cars are unlocked in this mode by unlocking them in the main game. In race mode cars have to be unlocked with money, money earned and spent on cars and upgrades in race mode is for race mode only.
I can not comment of the race mode achievements, however achievements for the main game are not difficult to obtain. There is one that you should be aware of before starting your first playthrough which if missed will require a full 2nd replay.... which is probably best as it will be easier with some experience having played the game, and one that will require a little skill and luck and several play throughs requiring to complete last mission with less than 10% health. The survial achievements are easily obtainable and fun to boot. With my limited time spent of race mode, I do not think they will be too hard just frustrating needing several replays that will take time, depending on skill or rather luck.
Perhaps the best thing about ZD HD is whether you have 5 mins to play a game or 4 hours, it will keep you entertained and survival mode will always suck you in for just one more try.
If your paying full price just pickup the main game and the Apocalypse pack well worth the money. If its on sale then buy the complete edition, either way this game is easily a must buy for your collection.
***EDIT***
Just a quick note, system specs are i7 4500HQ, 16gb, R9 265x and game runs fine at max settings 1080p, a little slowdown ( just dips below 30fps ) at points in a couple of the later missions, no slow down on survival or race modes. Accidently run with onboard 4600HD for the first couple of missions and would be fair to say it handled max settings well around 28-38 fps but would be fair to say later missions would pose a problem given the 265x diped below 30 at times, should be ok on HD or HD+ however with 4600HD.
