This is to Jonny Moseley Mad Trix as Skate 3 is to the Tony Hawk Pro Skater series.
If the goal of sport-simulation games are to recreate the emotions and emulate the motions from their target, SNOW is taking the right steps toward that goal.
From the start, I'm most immediately impressed with the visuals and aurals. The UI, models, and mountain itself with all its parts are gorgeous even on the lowest settings, which still beat up my GPU/CPU - no complaints as I'm using some older gear. There's a radio-style soundtrack that plays some great stuff that I want to get in my library - sorta electronica styled, I heard some vocal tracks, too. Reminds me of Chairlift or Bloc Party. The swoosh of skis and - though I haven't grinded rails or pulled off crazy jumps - the grinds sound real and constant enough to immersify me.
As a cross-country and downhill skiier of 8 years, the game targets my demographic of speed-seekers - but I can see the appeal to anyone who likes an open world where you can choose your fun. Meditatively ski from point A to B, gazing across the valley - or shred hard and fast off-piste taking opportune upward slopes to show off your aerial skills. I'm eager to virtually ski again, eager to get better gear to play full-screen on high graphics, eager to see every patch of SNOW there is to be seen.

You like Insurgency, Squad, Red Orchestra, or any other tactical/realistic FPS? Then you'll like this game. (NOTE: I only have a few hours in this game, so this is more like a first impressions review)
Gameplay: All around very solid. You can take two, maybe three bullets depending on where you get shot at, and bandaging stops you from bleeding out (a faded portion on your health that depletes. If you bandage it gives back whatever amount it has dwindled to). All the guns feel good, and this game has one of the best dual rendered scopes that I've ever seen.
Sounds: Amazing sounds. Each crack of a gun sounds simple, yet very menacing.
Content/Customization: There aren't that many guns, but that being said, there doesn't need to be. As you play, you accumulate kills with each weapon, which unlocks different camos for that specific weapon. You can also change the camo of your character and what gear (doesn't affect gameplay) is on him.
Gamemodes: There are only two, technically, but there are varients of those two modes, so it feels like there are more modes. There's also a good selection of maps that fit the different gamemodes.
VOIP: There is a team, and a public chat. This may be a gateway for trash talking, but it suprisingly isn't because the community isn't really toxic. There may be the one player here and there, but with playing against and with over 100 people so far, I've only really encountered one or two toxic players.
All in all, this is a good game. If I had to give it a numbered review, I'd say 8.5/10. The reason for this is that I prefer to play Insurgency or Red Orchestra, but this is a free to play game that is just as good, gameplay wise, as those two games. You should give this game a shot, especially since it is completely free.

This game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Make no mistake about that.
However, you need not fret, for not only is this strangely addicting, but it is also chock-full of people that are both willing and able to help you play better and understand why what you are doing is failing completely. Soon, not only will you enjoy being beaten (who doesn't love to see a massive Soviet army assault helpless French soldiers?) you will also find yourself slowing down the game to watch turrets rotate, artillery fly through the air, helicopters slow down their rotors, and infantry fire tracers in a hellmarch to their enemy. You'll enjoy losing because you found a new way to be beaten. You found a new tactic you had never seen before, saw units used in a completely innovative way (there's SAS
) and laughed like a moron because your army was shredded by a superior foe, despite all of your attempts to stop the bleeding and hold the line.
Eventually, after careful study and lots of reviewing, you will one day be the one who is doing the beating. You'll lead your own massive Soviet motorized regiments across small towns, infiltrate enemy lines with elite Korean special forces, set entire forests ablaze with your planes, and send missiles crashing into the hulls of the opposing fleet. You'll be unstoppable...until someone better than you comes along and shoots up your transports, swats your planes out of the sky, annihilates your special forces, and sinks your fleet before it can even leave home. Then the cycle continues.
All of that being said, this game will also kick your computer's♥♥♥♥♥- weak cooling systems need not apply. You may get frustrated because the computer cheats. Tutorials are non-existant. You learn by doing, and this is an evolutionary battlefield - live or die. Throw whatever you know about other wargames out the window, because this will not play by rules like you would see in R.U.S.E. or a Tom Clancy game.
If, however, you feel that you can overcome those obstacles and still have a desire to see a Chinese mechanized division square off against French Marines, then this is your game.
Has a steep learning curve, and demands you forget some of your typical strategy game habits in favour of real world tactics, but great fun once you get the hang of it.

Long story short: Squishy: The Suicidal pig is a brilliant puzzle-platformer with brain-crunching puzzles during it's best moments, but a horribly frustrating mess with bad controls during it's worst.
This game promises to be a 2D puzzle-platformer with an exciting twist: instead of trying to stay alive, like you do in most games, you must help the depressed pig Squishy to commit suicide. That sounds a lot easier than it actually is. There are multiple ways of taking your own life, varying from jumping into spikes all the way to building complex traps in order to drop wooden crates on yourself. What's consistent throughout the game, however, is that you have to solve increasingly difficult puzzles in order to be able to commit suicide. And some of those puzzles are really well made.
Especially during the earlier parts of the game you'll be playing levels that initially look impossible, but slowly unravel themselves as having very simple (but not so obvious) solutions. I really enjoy the solving the problems that are presented to Squishy. All elements in these levels have a function and those stages are some of the best parts of Squishy: The Suicidal pigs. Somehwat more common than those well-thought out levels, however, are levels that are purely made to frustrate, with many elements that don't seem to have a function and solutions that are so far-fetched that they take much of the fun out of the game. They're still kind of nice to play, but they feel unsatisfactory if you know how beautifully this game shines during it's better parts.
Much, much worse are the platforming levels (luckily there aren't many of them). Instead of trying to kill yourself like you do in the 'regular' levels, here you have to find a key in order to pass through a gate. Most of these levels are very difficult, not because of the well thought-out puzzles but because of the careful timing that's required. That wouldn't be much of a problem if it weren't for Squishy: The Suicidal Pig's sloppy controls. During the puzzle levels, you hardly notice the significant delay between your input and Squishy's reaction, but it becomes terribly frustrating during the platforming parts. To make things even worse, you sometimes have to finish these already difficult level in a (very) limited amount of time.
What's also kind of disappointing is the unpolished nature of this game. While the graphics are pixelated, I think they're quite charming and I don't really have much to say about it. However, the soundtrack of this game is just plain bad. It sounds like a MIDI-file and I turned it off after the first level. What really disappointed me is how lazily the devs have ported this game. The game constantly refers to console buttons that you can't use on your keyboard and you can't use your mouse. Well, actually you can use your mouse, but not in a way that's intended; you can teleport to about everywhere by right-clicking. I think it's a debugging feature that they forgot to remove and it isn't much of an issue if you have to discipline to resist abusing it, but it's still disappoingting that the devs were too lazy to remove it.
Luckily, Squishy: The Suicidal Pig is a really decent game when you look past the platforming levels and it's unpolished nature. The game offers some nice gimmicks besides the main campaign as well. These are a gamemode called "Battle" (Two players fight with each other using different parts of the same keyboard. It can be funny at times, but gets old really quick.), a gamemode called "Impossible Level" (It isn't impossible, just insanely hard. Too hard to be fun, actually.) and my personal favourite, "Survival". Here you must avoid crates that drop from the sky for as long as possible while you are dodging a spiky ball that rolls through the stage. The time you survived is saved and because there are leaderboards (both personal and global), improving your time can be really fun.
I paid only €0,14 for it and at that price it's a really fun game. I even dare to say that the game is worth it's full price as well. Just don't expect to buy a masterpiece when you click on the "Add to Cart"-button.

Game sequels are suppose to improve on the mistakes made in the previous games, and offer enough new content to keep everyone hooked. Sniper Elite 3 does exactly this. I feel like theres a lot of game sequels nowadays that either really suck and make people think 'What Happened?' or don't do much new thinks to keep people interested. Sniper Elite 3 gave us new open evnironments with multiple pathways and the ability to complete your objectives in any order you chose. This is true to a certain point, there are some parts of some mission where you must reach a certain area, or collect a piece of data etc. However the game offers you many ways to complete said task. The ai is definitley improved from v2 however there is still minor problems, sometimes two ai overlap each other or simple glitch while walking, although the new relocation mechanic fits them well, and the whole WW2 authenticity as a whole. Since there were no suppressors in WW2 you need to rely on relocating, when taking a shot the enemy will become alerted and search, so, you need to move away from your current position and shoot somewhere else. I think this is the best addition to the game seeing as it adds some authenticity and challenge. For the ai as a whole, I still play on the hardest difficulty, I feel the ai is now kind of too easy, when you get caught the ai does some querky reload animation like they didnt♥♥♥♥♥♥their gun, I feel playing the game on the hardest dificulty makes the ai more of a threat and makes the game a better challenge for me. The multiplayer had improved, theres not a lot of camping anymore which is wierd, i didnt think just putting the relocation mechanic in multiplayer would fix the problem. I would of like to see something like giving everyone low amount of ammo to force them to move out of cover and find ammo, but if the relocation has fixed the problem then thats good. Granted there are still some campers, buts its minimized A LOT since v2. As for the xray bullet cam, i dont need to say anything, we all love it. The dlc, I do think its pretty readiculous, but, I dont plan on buying them anyway so not a problem to me at all, although having 3 (or was it 4?) day one dlcs is kind of stupid when they couldve just put it in the game anyway. The only real problem I see is I feel like the ballistics system is kind of screwy, and for 50 bucks there doesnt seem much in terms of content considering the guns and campaign, nonetheless im still loving what I have.
Sniper Elite 3 improves on the the things that put Sniper Elite v2 down, exatly how a sequel should be. It has some glitches but nothing that cant be fixed by some minor patches. The massive amounts of dlc may turn some people off, but remember; no one said you had to buy the dlc. Also the fact that in terms of campaign and guns the game comes up a bit short, but IMHO i think I didnt waste 50 bucks, sniper elite 3 is a fun game in my book that improves on everything from the last game. Sniper Elite 3: 9/10

Where do I start? Well, if you've played the first Torchlight, and any part of you enjoyed it, you should give this one a go. Where as the first one was an enjoyable yet repeatitive grind through a single dungeon, this game features a randomly generated and ever changing open world to explore. Nearly every aspect of the original was improved upon. Graphics, story, world building, modability (there's workshop support, and free modding tools), and the all important gameplay were all improved. Combat is smooth, fast, and satisfying; which is the meat of any Diablo like HnS RPG. There is multiplayer for up to 6 (8 if you install an official Runic Games mod), and the loot and gold litteraly explodes out of chests, objects, and enemies before you. In fact, there are constant explosions. Gorey enemy explosions, chests gushing out loot, and even some of your skills create a bit of havoc. It's all great fun and excitement to go with your dungeon crawling. So if you enjoy the Diablo style of gameplay, or even if you don't because you find it too slow. Give this a go. It doesn't innovate, but it perfects. And it does so with a more than reasonable price tag for the content.

Review from no experience w/ early access POV - 1 star out of 5
Long time SPG fan and played ~400+ hours of SPG2 - vanilla and modded. Loved it and eagerly awaited SPGW launch.
However, I decided to wait until full launch and did not partake any part of early access. Therefore, this review is from the pov of someone familiar with the SPG franchise, but no knowledge or prior impressions from EA.
TLDR is SPGW in my mind is one massive fail - not because of lack of potential. I concede it could certainly live up to surpass SPG2, but at the moment the devs have shot themselves in both legs and don't seem to know it.
Critique #1 - lack of basic information that is absolutely essential
A) Fair minded people should be able to agree if a player can't even earn (1) single ore, gas, or material - and the game never mentions anywhere how to correct this 'bug' or lack of progression, it puts a giant roadblock to continue playing more than a few hours.
And the early hours, the first impressions, is what makes people abandon or keep playing a game. Apparently, after many google searches (almost all of which involved search results re: how to efficiently obtain or grow your resource income but absolutely nothing about why the entire station building was locked out and zero resources were obtainable, I found a buried post that shared the info so minor by the devs they didn't include it anywhere in the 1st campaign tutorial mission, or any obvious place the user would naturally find it via regular game experience or UI.
To wit, that unless the player proceeds past certain phase of the campaign missions, the entire ability to even collect (1) single ore, gas, or material is locked out.
The UI offers completely contradictory or misleading hints however in that it makes user think if they put a point into the skill for collecting - to get more gas, or mining to get more resources mined, that they should then finally start getting some ore, gas, etc.
But no. It is hard locked and coded by the devs, with zero notice what to do to unlock it (zero mentions in the manual either). If the campaign missions were easier, then to some degree this would be mitigated by players zooming through the campaign missions and accidentally unlocking without knowing it the station building and resource collecting ability. But no........
Critique #2
B) The campaign missions are silly difficult - not difficult from an absolute point of mind, but from a relative point of view where brand new player starts. Keeping in mind I've played and had extensive SPG2 combat experience, it wasn't basic mistakes making the campaign missions hard but the lack of progression before I took them on.
What do I mean? I mean that mission #1 is basically the glorified basic tutorial to move your ship, etc. Ship power/ performance of your starter gunship is 100% irrelevant. So fair enough - and all players finish this mission with no obstacle to complete.
Mission #2 though was a brick wall for me. Yes I still had the starter gunship with zero new enhancements. But I had just finished the prior mission as a glorified hello mission. The devs should not put in mission scaling where it goes from 0 difficulty to 10 (relatively speaking). It should scale in reasonable curve, so you are hinted to need to upgrade.
Despite knowing about weapons fire angles, ship maneuvers to close or hold ranges while firing within the arc my weapons can cover, etc - all the stuff learned from hundreds of hours in SPG2, I just could not kill even barely 1 enemy ship before the ship I was to defend dies, and therefore mission fails.
Now - combnine #1 with #2 - I am frustrated that I apparently can't seem to unlock any part of station building or collecting even a single resource the UI tells me by obvious means (e.g. any game that shows at top screen the basic 'currencies' of the game is directly telling you that a core part of the game is going out and getting those 'currencies)
And that trying to do what progression I can until I mysteriously learn how or what unlocks this leads into a giant stone wall where the 2nd campaign mission is scaled so hard you need actual new ship or upgrades to the starter gunship.
I am sure, and I entirely concede, there has to be players that got past campaign mission #2 with just their starter gunship. But I also say that can't be the norm if someone like me who has extensively played and familiar with SPG2 combat mechanics can't get past this silly bugger.
Now, I could have decided to farm for awhile, do some freelance missions, trade between station and planet to earn better ship or upgrade gunship significantly. But I was burned out by then. I had already spent nearly first 10 hours of my brand new experience to this new venture in SPG-verse by doing many, many asteroid ore runs --- followed by gas collecting attempts -- followed by exploring and fighting enemies I met in other areas.
Which by the way was successful enough I captured 2 enemy ships, one of which was a convenient freighter to start trading in more bulk if I desired.
But by then I had zero desire. Why? Because to add insult to injury, when I captured those ships, the options to salvage the ships for materials was greyed out, along with all other options other than sell it for credits, it buy into my garage.
So my little starter gunship is just fine to capture 2 enemy ships, but not fine to do even the second mission. The devs failed miserably in the campaign scaling but more importantly, in the brain dead decision to lock all progression out without telling the user in big, huge font 60 size disclaimer when starting the game.
They lead the user to squander what good will they may have and just build pent up frustration they are going nowhere with zero explanation AND when the user still manages to progress a little bit (e.g. capture some ships) ----> they kick the guy in the nuts and basically tell the guy might as well uninstall and write a scathing steam review of the pile of garbage they just jumped into.
I concede and will honestly admit the game has good potential. But somewhere along the line, perhaps due to tidbits here and there trickled out in early access or constant updating and 'being in the know' via forum as the game evolved through early access, both the devs and EA player base completely forgot how a brand new user would experience the game - knowing nothing other than what the campaign info, tutorial, or game manual says.
And yes, I RTFM. The devs obviously did not.
If I could give the review on steam any lower grade, I would

There's three games to the Wargame series, and in my opinion this is the best. A lot of people will disagree with me, and say that the 2nd; Air Land Battle was the best. However, this one here adds a completely new realm to the series; naval combat. I've played the second, and to this, this is much better. Not because of naval combat, but "stuff".
The Red Dragon version is just into "stuff". You load up the game in some sort of military command room lit with ominous red lights and given 16,000 units to chose from. Yes. Sixteen thousand! Now, a lot of the units are just different units with different weapons, but I'd say 75% of them are completely modeled, textured, for their roll. Now, the issue I had when I loaded this up was to understand the difference between a "USA Marine Stinger" and a "USA Marine Igla" was. The two weapons are anti-air, have the same strength and so on. And you'll realize how confusing it is when you are juggling tons of units.
The game play is completely different to all other RTS. You really need to coordinate with your team. Tell them to flank here or there, smoke a certain position to cover retreating units, send recon helicopters behind enemy lines near a mountain top and spot what ever they're doing. Don't expect to walk into a game and win. You'll either lose the ones you play, or just be carried by some amazing commander.
The Campaign is lack luster. Not amazing. It's good for starting out, mainly for practice. But I would rather do skirmish battles. They're a little more fun, and you have more freedom. There isn't even a story so to speek.
Would I reccomend this? Yes. It's a great game. I don't have much hours because I don't really have someone I can trust in a battle to protect me from getting flanked. And that's an issue you'll run into. Many unskilled players. So you either learn quickly, or dominate the other team.
I'd get this if you want a change to most generic military RTS's out there. Just get ready for the incredable learning curve this game offers.

PROS:
- good game if you are a train enthusiast.
- intro video is neat
- i really cant say much. just too much wrong with this game
CONS:
- game is very unpolished. things like the narration dialog boxes feel cheap and the additional hud controls seem like they can be so much better.
- train horns suck. you can hear the looping, which is dead obvious on certain engines, and it doesnt even play back as you intend most of the time.
- zoom mechanism is very shoddy when in 3rd person. if you 'ram' the camera down into the car behind the engine in focus, it'll push the camera location out and away. yet when you scroll, it basically crops and zooms the visible area of the camera without actually moving it TO the engine in focus.
- - not only 3rd person, but it really needs to be improved in general. it seems too constricted to pre-set areas. especially when going through tunnels and such.
- the headlights seem nearly ineffective. like the only thing it's doing is giving the engine a lit up look.
- and my biggest complaint: so much expensive DLC yet every one i've tried has an issue with it. things like a train coming at you head on whenever you get to a certain point, with no way to avoid it or complete the scenario. or improperly set timings. or random unmarked speed zones which slaughter your points, forcing you to restart if you want to make gold. or any metal for that matter.
- objectives seem unclear or confusing at times
- just general bugs, inconsistencies, problems, unpolish.
CONCLUSION:
dont buy this game unless you mind the bugs, unpolish, and are willing to research good packs that dont have any issues.
OTHER THOUGHTS: most companies release software (not just games) on a 2 step cycle: new features, then bug fixes. they push out new features one update, then fix all the bugs the next. rinse and repeat. this company fails to do so. they're more worried about pushing out content as fast as possible than they are about giving us a quality game. its a shame this is the best train sim that's out there. sure, they updated to *better* menus and looks a few times. but its still confusing to navigate. it took me forever to find the community content section within the game, and i wouldnt be able to remember off hand from not playing it for a while.

Okay, so I went into this game following the big hype that predated it. In some aspects it was fullfilled, in others it fell flat on its belly.
For the good parts: The world it's made in is beautiful. From the very beginning to the very end, the areas you go through are amazing. It reminded me of the Trine and Ico series, for some odd reason and the just felt good. Another up-side is that the game is extremely short, you can easily finish in 3 hours and maybe one extra if you want all the achievements. This is normally a bad side, but for this game it was good, since it didn't mince and draw the story out so long it becomes stale. You can interact with heaps of stuff in the world with either brother or sometimes with both, leading to events that better explore their personalities.
For the bad parts: The controls are strange. You can play without a controlled but be ready to hear a lot of beeping. The characters are kind of, I don't know, lacklustre? The made up language they talk in doesn't help you connect to them at all. The story is very basic and predictable.
Neutral parts: The puzzles weren't challanging. I feel this to be neither a good nor a bad part, since it's a game of atmosphere and scenery. The mid part of the game was truly gruesome, starting from chapter 3 to about 6 or so, it's very nasty. To me it only added to the atmosphere, but it was still Zeno Clash-level strange.
All in all, I would recommend a playthrough of this, if you are ever in the mood to watch an adventure/fantasy movie on Netflix, you could spend the few Dollars on this game and play it through in about the same amount of time and be left with an overall pleasant experience. It doesn't cost a lot, it's even cheaper on holiday sales.
Buy this game if :
You are looking for a genuine adventure. (Those are rare to find these days)
You would like to see a different, highly rich fantasy world.
You are in the mood to waste a little time.
You liked Trine and Trine 2.
You liked Ico and Shadow of the Colossus.
Don't buy this game if:
You are looking for a challenge (there isn't one)
You are looking for innovative puzzles (there are a couple, but they are not even remotely challanging to any skill level)
You are looking for a game heavy in action.
You are allergic to basic/stale storylines with predictable plots.
You want big bang for your buck. This is a game that has very little replayability, and it extremely short, treat it as an adventure movie.

This game is a really great new twist on a classic style of game.  The old game series where you'd fly a helicopter around, saving guys with your ladder and fighting enemies all over the map as you did little missions.
It's like those old games but with a slightly customizable car selection and zombies.  Grab it if you like zombies and see it on sale, it's a very fun smaller title.

Simple premise - zombies have resulted from a large explosion at a corporation trying to cure cancer, and everyone is infected. You are a talented driver (I guess) and you are recruited to help out the army as they try to evaculate or establish a base. Missions are fun, fast and filled with satisfying gibbing of zombies everywhere. Typical mission is going to pick up a few specific survivors to help build the base (Doctors, Shipcrew, etc) or going to defend a specific objective. There are secondary objectives, and the game does a good job of mixing up the mission objectives.
Simply put, this is a great game to sit back and relax with, slamming into a billion zombies. I have only played the Campaign so far, but there is two additional modes to the game! Really excited to dive in further. Absolutely worth the price paid.
TLDR; Fantastic fun arcade driver game, in the vein of Carmageedon and others. Splatter zombies, equip and upgrade vehicles. 8/10

Well, so much for modding in singleplayer. I may have not bought the game since it first came out on PC, but I've seen things. Take-Two's "cease and desist" of the only possbile way to actually mod the game in singleplayer has really put them in deep water. But they don't care. All they cared about was money. Yes, I understand that they (Take-Two and Rockstar) are trying to fix the cheater problem that's been going on ever since GTA Online started and that Rockstar is NOT the cause for the problem, but OpenIV was never used for modding in multiplayer. It was in OpenIV's policy that it was not for multiplayer use, and never was, as well as their intent specifially stating that. Besides, the game would not let you play Online if you modified anything within the game files (ScriptHook would disallow such as well). And Rockstar enouraged the use of singleplayer mods (with OpenIV being the only way to do so), and they were fine with that. I personally have not used OpenIV in a long while, but now I am resonably sure GTA IV is not moddable either due to it also being the only way to mod the game. People may have to resort to SparkIV for GTA IV, unless Take-Two has taken care of that already...
I understand other players' anger and frustration (and I admit, I am one of them too). This however, isn't going to stop me from playing singleplayer/multiplayer as a result of Take-Two's recent action against the modding community. Something tells me that if this gets worse, we are going to have another FROMSOFT developer team, where changing anything (anything at all, even if its just a harmless texture) will result in a ban (it is an odd comparision, but if you played any of the Dark Souls games on PC, you would understand). GTA V had that problem a long time ago, where it was banning players that were using mods in singleplayer, and I wouldn't be suprised if they re-integrate that again.
In my honest opinion, I actually really do like this game, both singleplayer and multiplayer (as you might be able to tell with the amount of hours I put into it), with the majority being multiplayer. Finished the game, missing a few things here and there, and pleased with the new Gunrunning update that was released a couple days ago (when this review was posted). I'm happy to say that I have never bought a shark card for Online, and doing pretty well in multiplayer (doing Criminal Mastermind with my crew certainly helped with that :p).
In conclusion, I woudn't be suprised if this ongoing problem would turn for the worse, but regardless, it is not going to stop me from playing the game. I like the game, I like the crew that I am a part of, and despite the large pool of cheaters that still exist to this day, multiplayer isn't that half-bad. The only thing I am concerned about is how badly this will turn against the players and the overall playerbase. Each playerbase is seperate (Xbox 1, PS4, PC, etc.). They don't cross-platform. I fear that this action (and its subsequent actions and consequences) might end up crippling the entire PC playerbase for good.
TL;DR: Game is good, multiplayer isn't half-bad, Take-Two is shooting itself in the foot (in my opinion) and might become the second FROMSOFT (if you play any Dark Souls you understand). I'm fearing for what might happen in the future due to this action, but isn't stopping me from playing multiplayer, and RIP singleplayer modding. You will be missed. :(

This is quite lengthy but I've basically split it into FAQs which I see new players often ask in the game chat (this is mainly for people who have never played any of the Wargame series before instead of people coming to this from EE and ALB):
Yes and no. It's easy to learn how to play; it's very hard to learn how to play
(which in my opinion is where a lot of the fun lies).
It was for me, and I think that can be what puts some people off this game before they've really gotten into it. The huge number of units is quite scary if you've never played any of the Wargame series before (I hadn't). Perseverance is key at the start, but once you get used to the game, you'll find this a joy rather than something to be afraid of.
There are actually no playable tutorials in RD. The tutorials are basically just text with instructions on what to do. It is worth giving these a read to start with, but I appreciate that this is likely to be quite boring for some players (although if you really dislike this idea, I'm not sure if this is really the game for you).
. There are plenty of people who have made Youtube vids to give you instruction not only on the mechanics of the game but also on deck-building (which is important to this game but not something you need to spend tonnes of time on if you don't want to). I can highly recommend ICBMRaptor (I love his tutorials and other Wargame vids, it's worth watching them if you're new since watching someone else play multiplayer games can be a good way of learning), Bubblebox (nice, clear explanantions of stuff), Boltsauce and VulcanHDGaming.
When I first started out and was resorting to the general chat for questions, my experience was pretty good (and I maintain that the community is better than a fair number of other multiplayer games I've played).
, recently the game has obviously been on sale and it seems that lots of people have picked it up while it's cheap. This has led to quite a few - how can I put this - "not-so-nice/mature" people entering the game and general chat. My mute list has been filling up a bit recently :( (prepare for spam sometimes)
On the upside, two things: 1)  you can just close the chat window if you don't want to see this, and 2) a lot of the people who helped me and people who are good players are still around and willing to help out :)
Sometimes intense, sometimes slow-paced. It depends who you're playing against and what your opponent's play style is like. I won't say a lot more than that because it is quite hard to generalise due to the vast amount of unit combos/deck types you can have combined with the different play styles of different people.
However, one thing I will add:
. If you enter a lobby and you see 3 people on, say, the BLUFOR team and RED is empty, check their stats immediately. This will help you decide whether these are just 3 friends who want to play together (and maybe aren't that good) or if they're 3 pro players who want to ROFL-stomp some newbies.
Spammers can also be an issue, especially in 10 v 10 or 20 v 20 games. Some players will just chuck tonnes of helos/artillery at you, which can be frustrating if you're not ready for it and they crush you. However, if you and your team are ready for it - and act accordingly (i.e. making sure you deploy enough AA to keep yourselves covered and not taking predictable routes to avoid arty, as well as coordinating) - the boot will be on the other foot when you smash their spam and then utterly wreck them ;)
In general, it's fine. Sometimes it will do smart things (i.e. try to flank you, change its attack approach according to what you bring against it, especially if you thwart it once, etc.) but often it will also do some stupid things (e.g. advance infantry across open ground towards tanks).
I would always recommend when starting out that you go into Skirmish mode and play lots of games against the CPU, as this will let you become familiar with the various maps and gameplay. The CPU will punish you if you make mistakes, so this will also teach you some good if basic things to be aware of when playing and basic tactics.
- you will likely just get frustrated unless you learn the game mechanics in Skirmish mode first.
I have spent a lot of hours in this game just playing against the CPU because it is good fun :) if you find it boring by yourself, team up with a friend and go comp-stomping. If you have general chat open, you might see some good players also opening comp-stomp lobbies for games vs the CPU.
Yes. As far as I know, Easy mode AI gets the same number of deployment points as you (you'll learn what these are when you start the game) but it gets a slight bonus to how fast it receives them during a battle. Medium gets more of a bonus to this and gets c. 1,000 extra points to start with (don't quote me on that, I just remember seeing it somewhere), and so on. This might put some people off playing against the CPU.
However, it really isn't that bad for the most part. The CPU, while making mistakes, is sensible and plays well enough that it can be a challenge, even without resorting to spam (which it can do on higher difficulties). It can also be fun sometimes to face off against a vastly superior force than you and be able to defeat them with the right defensive tactics (or offensive if you're particularly good/bold/brave/stupid :P).
There are definitely some issues with it. It isn't as varied as land combat, that's for sure. However, saying it "sucks" would be too harsh. Naval combat is fun, especially on maps with mixed land/naval action! Playing against the CPU can prevent issues with spam which may occur when facing players - otherwise I actually enjoy it and don't find it "imbalanced" as some say

Well, I've been meaning to write one of these for a while now so going on 200 hours I'd say I've pretty much seen most of everything this game has to offer.
I really like H&G. I genuinely enjoy playing it. It's fun, an original and innovative take on an FPS game with a strategy element mixed into it. But it of course does have its drawbacks, though. Snipers, campers, and machine guns rule the battlefield. It makes it hard for anyone who isn't one of those to enjoy the game. There are some matches where it's really close, well balanced, and really fun. Unfortunately, however, these matches are few in far inbetween because of the horrendous matchmaking system the game uses.
The developers claim it's the most accurate and realistic WW2 game out there, but then also claiming that it's also the well balanced. Well, sorry, no. You can't have realistic and balanced. It literally cannot happen, especially in a game like this. This is most evident in the fact that any old shmuck can run right up to any tank, place three bombs on it, and it blows up with no way of defending itself or seeing its attacker (who gets tons of money for doing so). It's evident in the fact that someone with a machine gun can run around hipfiring and getting headshots with zero weapon sway, then proceed to snipe infantry from anywhere from 50-100 meters. It's evident in the fact that the penetration, damage, and deflection of tank shots is seemingly totally random with no regards to actual factors.
Despite all this, there is a fun game with lots of potential buried underneath the absolute mess it is right now. More than half of the games you play you'll get frustrated, angry, or otherwise rage. You'll come off of a game and think to yourself "I never want to play this again". I do it all the time - I'll stop playing for a couple days, maybe a week or so, then pick the game back up and have a couple good games, get back into it, then have some bad ones and rinse and repeat.
It's entirely possible that you're either just that good or that lucky that every game you have will be a good one. In that case, good for you. If not, if you find yourself liking the game at its core but hating the unfairness of the matches or the loss, set a goal. Pick out a certain thing to buy, whether it be a gun or vehicle, and work towards it. H&G is basically pay/grind2win, so it'll take a while if you don't have the real-life funds necessary to buy gold. But every time you get frustrated, every time you rage, tell yourself "I can achieve my goal." "I'm almost to the next ribbon." "I've almost got enough credits." "I'm not even halfway yet, but with a couple more games I'll be close." "That was a good game, just need to keep it up."
I believe that having goals, things to work towards, in this game is integral to having fun. You aren't penalized for doing bad because you get a base salary and the only thing that affects that are the good things you do in the game. Without something to look forward to, after a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game you'll be sitting there thinking "Why am I dying over and over and over for no reason?" Well, you're pretty much right there. You're just dying, earning your base salary, for no reason. Nothing to look forward to. So I'll say it one last time - have a goal. If you get frustrated and don't want to play anymore, you can always come back to it later. You'll still have your goal, or maybe you'll find a new one.
To wrap this all up, and in sort of a TL;DR way (this was pretty long), despite having more cons than pros, this game has fun at its core and I do recommend it.

whenever I wasn't setting up a shot, emptying my lungs, and pumping a sharp metal bullet through the thick skull of an unsuspecting enemy soldier, I was frustrated with Sniper Elite III. Not because the surrounding mechanics are broken or the levels are poorly structured, as the subsidiary elements of this third-person shooter are, for the most part, serviceable. However, every action building up to you actually pulling the trigger of a rifle feels more like a chore than an interesting setup for the perfect shot. There's an undeniable satisfaction that stems from the glorious slow-motion kills that abound in Sniper Elite III, but missions tend to promote stealthy, silent takedowns rather than the grotesque headshots it does so well.
Fortunately, what the game does best is on full display early on. The level design in Sniper Elite III is more open than previous games in the series, often encouraging shots being fired from more than 300 meters away. Instead of funneling you down a straight path, each of the eight locations in the campaign presents you with a sniping sandbox where creativity leads to better shooting and stronger positioning. Bullishly rushing headfirst into enemy territory is always an option, but the grizzled protagonist crumples to the dirt after just a pair of well-placed shots. Silent steps often lead to better vantage points, and with so many routes to choose from in any given level, the method by which the objective is completed is up to you.
That doesn't make this an open-world game, though. There are various side objectives like shutting down search lights or sabotaging the enemy's explosives supply, but there's still a clear path to completion within every mission. An ever-present objective marker reminds you that just 200 meters away lies a folder of intel that could greatly benefit the Allied forces, and all you need to do to collect it is pick off whatever patrolling soldiers stand in the way.
You're not required to kill everything with a heartbeat in order to progress, but the innate satisfaction that comes with long-range marksmanship is almost too great to pass up. After perching atop a sniper nest and locating a viable target, you have the option of steadying your breath and adding an additional red reticle that illustrates exactly where your bullet will drop. Once you fire off that perfect shot, the camera ignores the man behind the rifle and instead follows the round as it leisurely approaches its mark. It's a remarkable scene that all but erases auxiliary threats, letting you enjoy the slow-motion mayhem. The crack of your barrel will likely alert anything with a heartbeat nearby, but in that very moment, all that matters is the journey of a single bullet.

Not having played any of the predecessors of this game, I cannot judge the quality of this title compared to the others. Having said that, I tremendously enjoy this game. Four difficulty settings to choose from depending on how confident a sniper you feel, this title gets hold of you and doesn't let go until you are through with it. You can choose the style that most suits you or combine them in different levels - sneaky, silent, explosive, heads-on (...) Whatever you choose, there are plenty of achievements and challenges to take on. Your actions/kills/achievements are rated in points and added to a grand total which moves you up in the rank awarded. This enables you to use different and more sophisticated weaponry and equipment, which again gives you the edge for other levels and makes it possible for you to choose a different way of "handling" events :-)
I can definitely recommend this one, both for gameplay AND the graphics. The only drawback is probably the strangely monotone design of campaign levels and environment. But hey, then again, you can engage in co-op and multiplayer as well. The campaign is there to give you the initial feel. And it works well!

This game scratched a particular itch for me.  I wanted to fly capital ships.  Some of the other titles in the genre like Elite Dangerous are pretty and fun but you never fly stuff much bigger than a fighter or a frigate.  I wanted a dreadnought.  And I got what I wanted.  There are some minor issues with the controls and UI, but they don't detract from the experience.  There's low-level 4X elements which I enjoyed and thoroughly took advantage of, but if you're looking for heavy interplanetary resource management, diplomacy, culture wars, etc, this is NOT the game for you.  Ship design is pretty cool, each manufacturer has a distinct look and feel across their entire line.  Everything meshes well into a fun overall romp around the galaxy.
Level progression is pretty well paced, though some might feel it's too fast.  There's a bit of a disconnect when you get into larger ships as smaller ships become utterly pointless fodder.  The costs of research, upgrades, ship and base construction become astronomically high late in the game, to the point that doing the farming yourself, even through lucrative freelance missions, becomes largely pointless.  You eventually just run the missions to farm credits while you let your mining facilities, junk collectors and gas collectors pour the resources in every few minutes, which does makes total sense when you're controlling an interplanetary faction in a galactic conflict.  But when you use those credits and resources to fund your massively upgraded dreadnought, your warmasters' ships, and the four or five other capital ships in your fleet rolling into battle and utterly decimating rival sectors, all the little nitpicks fall away to a devastating chorus of railgun fire and ships breaking apart.
Interactive devs, a decent modding community, and a fairly robust set of tools that continues to be expanded mean players should have fun with this for a good while to come.  Easily worth the price.
Campaign *nonspecific spoilers*
You begin as a gunship pilot (one of three player 'classes' that grant abilities) and progress from there to frigate, destroyer, cruiser, battleship, and finally dreadnoughts and carriers.  The story stays pretty close to home and centers around your faction and a rival rogue faction despite the dozens of other occupied worlds and sectors in the galaxy.  It stays pretty tame until mid-late game when your faction ups the ante by beginning construction of a superweapon.  The final few missions are hectic, stressful, and challenging.  All told it took me about 30 hours to play through the campaign, upgrade and research nearly every part of my headquarters and take over every hostile sector on my side of the map.  I'm sure some players could do it much faster.
Campaign missions are commonly gated behind something, such as moving up to the next class of ship or getting a fleet power score of a certain amount.  They're never more than a few freelance missions away, except for the final few missions that require an immense amount of resources to be collected.  Those do necessarily take quite a bit of time and by that point my infrastructure was robust enough to support it.
Besides the campaign missions (which I believe there are 19), dock at any spaceport or planet in the galaxy and there is a Jobs Board for freelance missions, covering things as tame as mining/repair/scanning missions or as dangerous as devastating a rival faction's forward base, or gathering up a fleet and taking down a 'Warmaster.'  These are NPCs that have the same/similar abilities as you, the same items to use, and routinely have a fleet of their own.  Never try to take these guys solo.
Controls
There's a definite learning curve.  Much of the controls in space are via a context menu depending on what you have selected, and that menu is accessed via the mouse wheel click.  You need both left and right mouse buttons in the default scheme, though.  It takes some getting used to but becomes second nature after a few missions.  Capturing vessels while in combat is unwieldy but worthwhile.  Troops board a rival vessel and your radar is replaced with a progress UI of sorts.  You click a button to pull your troops out, pillage in the area of the ship they're in, or keep pushing to the command center.  This is fine by itself, but doing it while also fighting multiple dreadnoughts is problematic, particularly because this interface blocks your ability to modify your energy output between engines, shields, and weapons for the duration of the boarding.  But capturing ships is immensely lucrative, and I found myself dumping tons of resources and perks into elements that boost my capture chances.
Most of the menus when docked at a station or planet are straight forward, and they have instructions for specific functions on the galaxy map.  Repairing your ship and restocking your heavy weapon ammo is a one button click similar to a 'repair all' button in any MMO.
Effects/Sound
They get the job done.  Weapons sound appropriate.  The music is nice ambient stuff that feels right in the environment. My one nitpick is you better get used to the 'incoming missile' warning alarm.  It will basically play nonstop in combat.  Every combat.  There's a mod that changes the sound if needed, though I managed to tune it out.
Ships
Ship design is varied and pretty cool.  Each manufacturer has a distinct look and feel, and each ship class is significantly larger in size than before.  Each ship has different weapon placements, different strengths and weaknesses.  Firing arcs are something to consider, but there's no element to show them when purchasing a new ship.  I found myself gravitating towards ships with more turret placements or larger arcs rather than looks, but you can learn to optimally position yourself for any ship to capitalize on your weaponry.  Bigger/More is always better.  Exception:  Dreadnoughts at the time of this writing are significantly stronger than Carriers.
4X "lite"
There's only four main resources to deal with - Credits, Ore, Gas, and "Materials."  You need all of them in abundance, but I found myself lacking ore for most of the game.  Trade deals with rival factions are one-shot deals.  I found myself not even bothering to talk to ambassadors, I didn't bother with peace treaties.  Reputation with other factions was peaking and tanking as I blew up ships in the campaign.  Most resource gathering in late game is single clicking on 'construct' at specific sites on the map that generate resources over time.  Mining Facilities, gas harvesters, etc.  These can eventually be upgraded to produce more.  Your base can be upgraded, some upgrades required for the campaign.
Fleet management is point and click.  You only control your ship.  Ships in your personal fleet are AI controlled, though if you go Sub-Light or TDrive (Hyperspace jump) out, they'll follow.  Outside of your own private fleet you can build and assemble other fleets to patrol and defend your sectors.  Enemy fleets will try to attack your outposts, and any ships in place will fight along with the defenses of the specific outpost/station.  When this happens, a HUD element informs you there is an attack, and a timer and a battle progress indicator will show the relative strengths of each force.  You can choose to let the AI fight it out, or you can do your best to get there in time to save the day.  Expect there to be some back and forth on sector control.
I liked the light 4x elements.  Just enough there to break up the combat, and just enough there for me to worry about without getting overwhelming or time-consuming.

Red Faction Guerilla is the third Red Faction game and a big departure from the previous titles. While Red faction 1 & 2 were first person shooters, Guerilla is a third person open world action game. Destruction has always been the symbol of the series and this 3rd installment really delivers on that front!
I found it extremy hard to care about the plot because it plays super seriously while the gameplay is just a hilarious chaos. In the cutscenes everything is gloomy and about these ragged freedom fighters who are just fighting for survival and whatnot. The actual gameplay is about stealing walker, shooting a way through enemy base and leaving literally dozens of corpes and millions in damage behind. I skipped though all the cutscenes and at no point felt like i missed anything.
The destrucion engine in Guerilla is unsurpassed to this day and looks amazing even while the game is already 7 years old. Buildings can be destroyed bit by bit or simply driven through with a tank. Explosions are really satisfying and destroying supporting elements of a structure can make large parts of a building collapse. All the debris is handled by physics engine and can be walked on or knock the player down. There are games with prettier explosions but there simply isn't many games with this kind of destruction.Terrain on the other hand cannot be destroyed in any way and since it's Mars there is not much foliage or trees.
While everything explosion related is a load of fun, less can be said about shooting. Enemies take load of bullets and guns just don't have any impact on anything. Same goes for the main character and the best way to handle things is just run around throwing satchel charges without paying any attetion to the enemy soldiers. Tank or a walker is practically a god mode for a while and it's super fun. Unfortunately there are no flying vehicles for player to pilot and sometimes driving to a destination can be tedious.
There are only a handful of mission types and all of them are relatively identical. In raid missions the player takes a few npc guerillas and goes to destroy a building. In house arrest the player has to rescue few guerillas from a building. Destruction missions are all about causing damage either on rails or with a pilotable vehicle. The most distinct mission type is a timed race which does say a lot about variation. There are lot of buildings to destroy when not on a mission but since in the missions you get the chance to destroy most of them anyway, hunting them while not on a mission is just filler. Story missions follow the same pattern most of the time though there are some exeptions here and there.
Destroying stuff gives scrap which can be used for upgrades. Unfortunately there are not that many upgrades to choose from and don't really add much to the game. Some of them basically have to be acquired and are priced really cheaply. Other cost more but are not interesting. Completing challenges opens up cheats that can be activated in the menu, but using them disables saving and achievements. Most of the cheats are like "unlimited jetpack" and such which could have been straight upgrades. I would have preferred better upgrades without the cheats.
It took me 17 hours to finish the game on normal difficulty. I played with a controller since this game doesn't require any finesse and it was fine. As an older title Red Faction Guerilla runs extreme well even with ridiculous amount of action on screen and i didn't encounter any crashes. Some glitching here and there but with this kind of physics going on it's amazing how well everything works! I couldn't find a multiplayer match but it's no suprise with older titles.
Red Faction: Guerilla isn't intellectual or thoughtful experience. It's about blowing stuff up and it works wonderfully well. Plot is forgettable and as the game is often on sale it's something that can be played for just a few hours for the action and still get enough bang for the buck. Recommended.

Spelunky is an amazing 2D roguelike platformer.
In Spelunky, you have to delve deep into caves, jungles, ice caves, temples, and even hell, all the while collecting items to help you and gold to determine your endgame score. The game's platforming is very comfortable, and once you've got the hang of it, it gives you a very organic feel that makes it easy to control where your character goes.
The levels are all randomly generated. This includes the structures of the levels, the monsters, the items, the gold/ treasures.. Basically, every aspect is changed every time you play it. Sometimes you'll get a good run where you found some great items like the Jetpack, and sometimes you'll get a bad run where you're slightly off game and you've had bad luck finding good items.
Spelunky is a 2D platformer, but don't let it's simplicity fool you, because it is VERY easy to die in Spelunky, even if you're having an amazing run. You could suddenly fall on some spikes, and those 20 hearts you collected won't matter one bit. You can break a pot that a snake was hiding in, get bit by the snake, fall down some ledges, have a Yeti pick you up and then endlessly toss your body against a wall until death. What I'm trying to say is; this game is very challenging at times (But if you like ultra-hard games such as Dark Souls or Binding of Isaac, you'll have a great time).
As mentioned earlier, the basic goal of Spelunky is to get to the end of the game with the highest amount of gold as possible. Sometimes you'll finish a run with just over 150,000 gold, by quickly skimming through the levels. Sometimes, you will finish a run with over 200,000 gold, by scavenging every nook and cranny in the game for gold bars, treasure chests, and jewels... And finally, sometimes, you will finish a run with over a million gold, by utilizing hard game tactics such as "Ghosting" (You will know what this with experience). And with the Daily Challenge, every Spelunky player has 1 chance to play the exact same level as the last guy to compete for the highest score.
The art style is also quite superb. Spelunky's bright and cartoonish colors are staple identifiers of the game, and in itself, are staple identifiers of where you are in the game (For example, it's very easy to tell just by the color scheme that you're delving through the mines, in an underground jungle, or in a blistering cold cave of ice).
Overall, Spelunky is a tough-as-nails 2D platformer with roguelike elements that tie the game together very nicely. Albeit hard, the game is a great deal of fun, and with it's many random combinations and synergies, you can expect to sink hundreds of hours into this game, as the experience is different everytime.

Octopus Patties or Burgers
1 beach caught octopus
Light olive oil
3/4 cup red onion, small dice
1/2 cup celery, small dice
1/2 cup carrot, small dice
3/4 cup red, green and yellow bell pepper, small dice
Sea salt and black pepper
Cook partially skinned octopus in plenty of water in large pot (keep the suckers on to add color). It takes one and a half hours to cook octopus until tender. Cool until it's safe to handle. Cut in small pieces, small enough to fit in grinder. Grind using the smallest grinding blade. Set aside.
Save a few teaspoons each diced vegetable, set aside for salad. Heat 2 tablespoons oil in sauté pan; add onion, celery, carrot and bell peppers. Cook until translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add mix to ground octopus, mix well. Add sea salt and pepper to taste. Use an ice cream scoop to measure burgers.
Heat additional 1-2 tablespoons oil in same sauté pan.
Add octopus burgers, cook until browned on both sides.
Serve with Sea Lettuce salad and Sesame Rice Wine Vinaigrette.
Sea Lettuce and Sesame Rice Wine Vinaigrette
4-6 pieces cleaned and dried sea lettuce, sliced in ½ inch pieces
2 teaspoons sesame oil
1/4 cup rice wine vinegar
2 teaspoons red onion, fine dice
2 teaspoons carrot, fine dice
2 teaspoons red, yellow and green bell pepper, fine dice
1-2 teaspoons honey
Wash and dry sea lettuce with paper towels. Make vinaigrette by mixing vinegar and honey. Add sesame oil. Mix well. Add diced raw vegetables. Pour over sea lettuce, toss well. Season with sea salt and pepper to taste. Serve with octopus burgers.

I bought this game on the 360 back when it first came out and loved it, so when I switched to a PC I bought this so I could add some more replayability through mods. Now Take Two has spit in the face of its consumers with its cease and desist order against the Open IV (a fantastic modding tool used primarily for single player mods, mods for which Rockstar has expressed support) team and other notable single-player mod developers.
The game still has a fantastic single player experience that I wish I could recommend to anyone, but the company that owns the game doesn't deserve our support. The online multiplayer is toxic and so fueled by microtransactions that it takes hours of painful grinding in a community filled with trolls and hackers to get anything special, or you could buy it with your own real-world money like so many of its annoying pipsqueak players who have nothing better to do with their allowance. Add that to the infamously bad customer support and the equally bad anti-cheat system which has auto-banned players for using services such as teamspeak while actual cheats get off scott free, and it's apparent where the decision-makers' priorities lie - and it's not the gamers.
Mods made the game worth it for me after all these years, since I lost interest in the multiplayer ages ago, but now that they're cracking down on them, I'd recommend you go spend your money elsewhere, with a company that really respects you as its consumers.

This game is by-far one of the best Platformers out there. Well refined, great art-style, but it is hard to control with a Keyboard. I suggest using a Gamepad.
There are a few improvements I would suggest, otherwise this game would only get like a 75 from me:
The difficulty can jump rapidly from floor to floor, and game to game. Perhaps selection for difficulty, each with their own leaderboards, could suffice. But what would also be great is if they used some kind of progressive-skill system like there is in The Binding of Isaac.
I really feel that either this game has siginificant balance in the games favor, or just a really high yet still varying skill-cieling.
The way the game is set up, it's significantly hard to play any other way but cautious and slow. Thus, it can drive at least me away for a few hours, or even a few days, before picking it back up again.
Some floor-types are very unfair, such as dark levels. It's very hard to look ahead of yourself to see if there are any dangers, and the primary way of doing so puts you in significant danger. Again, making a varying skill-cieling.
The only differences that can be seen in peoples play-styles is what items they like, and if they kill Shop Keepers or not. I feel if there were some more options here, there could be a much broader community for this game.

Spelunky is one of those greate games which, in spite of its simple controls and gameplay, grows more interesting with each death (which can take anywhere from 5 seconds to a few hours).  This means that, while being quick to learn and quick to play, it's got a long shelf life - I feel I'll be coming back to this game for many years to come.  That's not the only dichotomy this game displays: Spelunky has its roots in two seeminly opposite genres.  The side scrolling console games of old have had their static levels and limited player abilities replaced with the roguelike's randomly generated maps and ever expanding weapons and tools.  For people who are intregued by the promise of roguelikes, but who are put off by their steep learning curve, ASCI graphics, and long intruction manuals, Spelunky is perfect.  For people who miss the platformers of old, Spelunky is perfect.  For people who want a quick but interesting pick-me-up on their lunch break at work, Spelunky is perfect.  I love Spelunky!
NOTE: while this game can be played with a keyboard just fine, I really recommend using a controller.  Logitech's PC controller (modeled on the X-Box's) at Best Buy is a cheaper and better alternative to Microsoft's own X-Box controller.

I am new to the Starpoint Gemini series so this review will be based off of what I have experienced over the last 15+ hours.
Starpoint Gemini is a combat oriented space simulation game where you build an empire from the ground up.  The campaign walks you through much of the mechanics as you complete the missions with minimal grinding necessary to get the next bigger ship.  When considering ships, you can buy ships from several different places, each with their own unique look.  You can also board and takeover ships as well as raid the contents of enemy ships should you so choose.
With the building portion, you can upgrade various parts of your main station while upgrading the smaller outposts that can generate materials or serve as a defense peremiter against an enemy fleet.  As you grow in size, your territory will eventually also expand.  Taking out stations and other areas expands your territory, resource gain, and total capacity in fleets.  So far, I have maintained a large fleet for myself while keeping minimal presences in my remote sectors that I cannot easily warp to.
Trading, mining, scavenging, scanning containers, etc., are all part of the game.  While this isn't a 4X game like the X series, you can still look up prices for items in your cargo hold to get the best price.  Honestly, I feel this is a nice touch but its easier for my to just head back to base and sell everything.  The missions end up providing more of a bonus to credits.
Speaking of credits, there are 4 primary resources in the game.  Credits, as already discussed, materials which are used for construction, gas, and ore.  Each of these are used in various ways to construction, research, and trading.  You will find some things in the game you cannot do without proper upgrades and resources on hand.  This is where things can get tedious if you are not utilizing trade routes with your T gate (warp gate).  Getting these resources can be a grueling process manually and through civilian fleet operations that you can use.  Civilian fleets basically do all of the non-combat related stuff for you but you have to micro these missions.  Once they are done, you have to send them somewhere else, which gets annoying.  I would have liked a way to prioritize which kinds of missions they take automatically, but, after the beginning of the game, the returns on the fleet missions are negligible anyways.
With combat, you fly your ship and use firing arcs to hit the enemy.  Front, aft, port, and starboard guns with a configurable amount of turrets each help you decimate your enemy.  You cannot configure your AI fleet, as they go in with whatever ship type you built and assigned and help you.  While this might seem like a drawback, I have never seen the need to outfit them with anything other than what they get.  Plus, with research, you can get better variants of the same ships.
As combat continues, you have light weapons.  These are weapons such as rail guns, lasers, plasma cannons, etc.  Each having a specific effect on the enemy.  Rail guns are generally better for hull damage while lasers are better for shields.  Plasma weapons are middle of the line and what I usually stick with.  Researching other weapons gives you a vast amount fo choices.  Your other weapon type is a heavy weapon.  These are the weapons that do more damage upon impact and can easily wax a ship in a matter of seconds if you have researched the best stuff and loaded up while continuing to fire everything full blast.  While I feel they could be stronger, I think for now, they are sufficient to not be a waste in their basic form.
For every ship you get, each has its own speed, agility, weapon mounting points, possible  fighters that you can launch (the bigger ships have these), hill, and shield capacity.  Obviously, the bigger you go, the slower you go.  I haven't found much of a reason to stick with the smaller ships, when you go up against a dreadnaught, you don't want to be in a measily corvette or frigate class ship, that's asking to get waxed.
Outside of that, so far, I am probably about 70% done with the campaign and it is fairly decent.  I wouldn't say its the games strongpoint but it does get you going and pick up after the first 3 or 4 hours.  Things get serious quick and the crap goes down.
Overall, I think there is some room for improvement with the resource gathering.  The AI seems to be drunk when they fly in formation with you, often times ramming you dealing no damage.  Load times, even on a M.2 SSD, Ryzen 1700x, and  32 GB DDR4 RAM can be sometimes around the 10 second mark, or more.  This isn't common but does happen.  With all of that being said, if you like the Mount and Blade series, wanted more out of X Rebirth, and enjoy star trek simulation games like Star Trek Legacy, this might be a good game to try.  I enjoy it, despite some of its flaws, I think its great.  The developers launch DLC with actual content at a small price and add other features to the game for free that they think should either be part of the original game or simply want to add without a price tag.  Give it a shot, after 2 hours you don't like it, refund it.

I want to like this game. I really do. It really does look good, the characters and the world. But it just feels empty, and that's saying something considering that there are events happening every 50 meters. When I say "empty," I don't mean lack of content, but rather lack of substance. As for content, the game is close to being 99% arena-style, run-n-gun combat, which puts it squarely in the arcade game category, where the primary objective is to get a high score.
As for the Arkfalls, they can be fun and hectic, especially when you have a large group of people. But then the run-n-gun becomes a duck shoot. Climbing a tower to use the sniper rifle works for a few minutes, but ultimately, the npcs group up underneath the platform, so that you have to get down and run-n-gun them anyway.
There are some broken features of the game. Server lag hits often, creating a latency of 2-4 seconds, which spells ruin in the middle of the run-n-gun combat. Textures don't fully load, so I'll find myself driving over a white plane with some world objects scattered about. The phasing also malfunctions, so that a location with two missions will bounce back-n-forth, meaning enemies will phase in and out as they fire at you, so that you're taking damage, but can't see them or hear them.
The weapons look good and are varied, so the combat itself has some diversity, which can lessen the tedium slightly. You can switch loadouts, so go from a sniper/lmg to a shotgun/rocket launcher setup. Episodes have a little bit of backstory with some cutscenes for extra drama. A few of the characters have interesting personalities.
But the encounters themselves are just tedious and boring. You have wave after wave of npcs coming at you, where they spawn from bunkers, back of vehicles, and out of doors. If you have a companion or two with you, they're useless, going down quickly and staying on the ground while you run around doing all the work. You can't revive them until you get the numbers down or have some cover, because to revive them you have to hold the E key down for about five seconds, and enemies can shoot you and disrupt you. Basically, encounters with tougher enemies last a long time, because all you can do is run-n-gun and chip away at their HPs.
I've only played this game for a while, having almost reached 1000 Ego Pts (6000 is the cap), and I just don't know if I can push ahead. Shoot, I'd even spend some money on the game if it had more to offer other than arena combat. I'd certainly pick up some clothing and vehicles, but the clothing in the store looks unappealing. Ultimately, I really want to like the game, but frustrations abound and have peaked. The Defiance universe is definitely interesting, but the game needs something more.

Sniper Elite 3 is the highly anticipated entry in the Sniper Elite franchise. I am a big fan of this series, and I even enjoyed the somewhat repetitive Zombie Army titles. I was hoping for an enjoyable romp through a slightly larger world with improvements to the stealth and sniping mechanics. Rebellion certainly doesn't disappoint.
You play as Karl Fairburne, a US Sniper dropped into Africa during World War II to combat the Afrika Korps stationed there. You'll navigate through gorgeous rendered canyons, valleys and deserts to complete your objectives, and Rebellion has done an excellent job in the graphics department. I was never once disappointed by the visuals in this game, and was wowed at every opportunity.
The levels are also quite large, and there are also optional objectives to complete during a main mission. These include tasks such as assassinating a visiting colonel, sabotaging a German fuel depot and eliminating enemy tanks. While not particularly original, these objectives are fun to complete and provide a nice XP boost.
Gameplay has a number of mechanics designed to create a good sniper game. You have items such as stones and flint that you can use to distract enemy soldiers, as well as a silenced pistol to kill enemies discreetly. You can loot these corpses for items before moving their corpse to another location, which is a relatively unseen feature in modern shooters. Another stealth mechanic is the ability to create noise with other items so you can fire your rifle without being detected.
On the subject of sniper mechanics, this game excels. The gory x-ray kills are back, and you can witness your bullet shattering bones and puncturing organs in fantastic HD glory. Bullet drop and wind speeds are an added factor to sniping, which makes each kill that more satisfying.
Despite being a solid game overrall, Sniper Elite 3 has a number of flaws. Enemy AI is fairly inconsistent, and will go from spotting you easily to being blind to your movements and visible corpses. The amount of bugs in this game is quite baffling, but most have been fixed due to frequent patches. Not a game breaker, but definitely frustrating if you're not a fan of bugs and glitches.
Overall, Sniper Elite 3 is a solid entry in a solid series. It improves over its predecessor, but still has the dull story and characters retained in the series. Despite this, I'd recommend this game for the huge levels and enjoyable mechanics. 8 / 10

Rebellion clearly had good intentions. Sniper Elite 3 is far more open-ended, and offers a much wider variety of playstyles than what V2 did. It’s only too bad then that the end product just doesn’t feel competent enough to satisfy its own ambition. It has all the features required to make the ultimate sniping game. But not enough time and effort was given to iron out and polish up each of these features to the levels that would make the game shine. Let’s hope Rebellion take everything they’ve learned so far, and turns the next sequel into what this game was so close to becoming, had it only been in development for a little longer; the benchmark that all future sniping games will be measured against. For its retail price, I can really only recommend it to those with a serious fetish for sniping. At a good discount or with some heavy patches ironing out all the issues, I would have less of a problem recommending it to anyone out for a good time shooting Nazis. Because although it’s not saying much, Sniper Elite 3 is currently the best game entirely devoted to sniping that we’ve gotten so far.
