Okay, first this is a great game and you should play it.
But which version?
If you have friends who like to visit your physical house, then you should buy this version or the XBox version so that you can make use of the local multiplayer. No doubt the shenanigans can only make this game even more awesome.
But if you don't have local friends, I'd suggest checking out the dev's website. There he distributes for free an earlier version of Spelunky which is fairly much the same game. Most of the mechanics are the same between versions and the largest differences are the change in artstyle and the addition of several new types of enemy and a (few?) level(s).
That said the transition between the new and old versions isn't completely plain sailing. There are slight quibbles with both that keep them on par. For example, the shopkeepers in the old version pause when they leave the screen making them supremely exploitable, whereas in the new version they do not. Likewise in the new version arrow traps fire horizontally, which makes them far less fun and far more gotcha than the arcing arrow traps that the older version uses which will not catch you off guard if you accidentally run at them from off-screen.
So overall, if have friends, buy this great platformer, grab some controllers and have fun. If don't have friends, play the game for free until you wisk to pay the dev some money for being awesome (and increase the difficulty marginally).
Just in case you're not convinced this is a great game, it's a very strong platformer, with the focus on going fast and jumping accurately so you can traverse the level and collect all the gold before it launches a heat-seeking kill ghost after you. And even that you can out platform.
The rest of the game relies on many interlocking subsystems that work brilliantly together, and it's a matter of learning what you can pull off when that determines how well you do beyond the simple jump puzzle. For example, you can jump on most enemies to defeat them. But a couple will punish you for jumping on them. But as soon as you pick up some spike boots, at least one of the enemies no longer retaliates due to the spiky death. So there's this constant game of "I have these items so these strategies are open to me" that keeps discovery fresh, and makes this game very replayable.
So 5/5. Just don't expect to win very frequently if you anger all the shopkeepers consistently (like I do).

I decided to wait until I got over it with Bennet just once before coming to make a review.
This game, whether you want it to or not, will evoke real emotion from you.  You will wince, scream, laugh, curse, and sigh throughout your entire journey that Bennet has laid out for you without your avatar muttering anything more than the occasional "...no."  The only thing that is a constant in this game in order to complete it is a resolve to not let it beat you, which it will unabashedly try to do to you time and again, both through the game and through your ego.
While fairly sensitive, the control system is fair and responsive for something that only uses mouse movement.  If you're thinking about playing, I sincerely implore you throw your keyboard to the side and get a large/multiple mousepad/s, lest you lose control of your character because your soft drink got in the way.
The only critique I will make is that I felt when you reached certain points on the mountain it started to bear down harder on my graphics card and would occasionally skip frames, particularly at the toilet around 45% in and at the shopping cart after ice mountain at nearly 90% the way through. It may just be signs I need to tidy up my hard drive again, but finding why the gpu spikes in those areas and possibly addressing them in the future are the only quality of life touches I would like done to the game. I would prefer not to accidentally push myself 300 meters left just because Diogeness decided to teleport his hammer to the right side.
I won't babble about the gameplay too much, as it's fairly simple.  Get to the top of a mountain with a hammer.  The controls will throw you every which way when you first learn how to wield your giant toothpick and then the rest is up to you.
Remember that this game is about the process and journey.  Getting over the mountain itself is nice, but learning how to do it is just as much of the game as completing it.  It's a digital Rubik's Cube, more than it is a modern game, and that can be both refreshing and exhausting. Sincerely listen to the narrator's advice, and take a break when you need to. Lest you end up like some less graceful youtuber throwing office furniture.

I received this game as a gift from someone, and I probably would've bought it myself if I knew how much fun it was going to be. I only have about two hours put in to it, but that's certanily enough time to figure out what this game is all about. Picture a mashup of the early Grand Theft Auto titles and your run of the mill zombie destruction game.
That really sums it up, but being able to upgrade your car and play around with different weapons is interesting. You will find yourself rolling around, running things over, and picking up health a good bit (or maybe I'm just bad at the game and tend to play recklessly.)
It's not something I can see myself sticking with through endgame, but it IS a fun time waster for those who are looking for something to fill the slot while they decide which next big AAA title they want to go after. I'm a big fan of indie games for this reason, they usually have a simple purpose, are easy to play, and offer enough challenges to stay interesting. We're at a point now that they can no longer espouse graphical beauty as an aid to actual gameplay or "fun factor" - graphics just don't make a game more fun. A game can be beautiful to an extreme degree and still be boring. This, however, is not boring. It's fast paced, interesting, and an oddity in the world of indie games in that it stands out by being a unique combination of largely overdone concepts.
Easily a 9/10, and definitely playable and enjoyable in small doses. You aren't, however, likely to pour 80 hours of your life in to it.

A few notes before the review -
This game is still heavy in EA and dev mode (he is a solo developer)
Second, just had a very interesting stream - which you can watch back on
(past broadcasts)
*interesting stream =* for about the last hour  or so TIm (Nitrous Butterfly) the dev came on my stream so consider it a semi playthrough/*interview with the dev*
=================================================================
SO the review -
First impressions:
Might be completely biased here as i love these kind of *3d civ/sim/mining* games i mean i was a teen when Dungeon Keeper came out and that started the love of the entire genre for me.
Ok - the GOOD
GFX - amazing i guess? Very stable (0 fps drops on OBS)
SIZE (game world) - 60 x 60 is too small IMO - 80 x 80 is *ok... i guess* 100 x 100 *now ya talking!*
ASTHETICS - Aamazing (i do not mind doing a 24 hour hour stream of this game) and easy on the eyes
FUN - Expect hours of fun in this game (and more to come) - but this is a personal opinion thing
Neutral:
CONTENT - Great (for the current state of dev) i thought i would end up getting bored after 45 mins (i watched a youtube video) i was so so wrong! the fun kept up all the way through. - But the content does need more to it (dev said more is going to be added as he updates - this is OFC obvious)
A.I - *Priorities* - this can be very confusing to get used to as a nub, but Tim tells me the secret is - the prioity order depends upon what was placed/queued FIRST and then whether or not they have the materials to do the job in question - although personally it still seems *somewhat* lacking (once again Tim said priorities are planed in the next? Update)
BAD -
BUGS - yes yes... bugs are always bad, however the few i experienced on my stream were still limited enough that i still had a ton of fun, also Tim and myself worked through some of these as i noticed them on stream (they WILL be fixed!)
PRICE - *?* not really a good or bad thing... personally - just because it is VERY EA i would say it could do with a SMALL discount - but as i say - solo dev + needs money to continue, so its a personal thing i guess... if you want to support a great dev with an amazing idea for a great game? Then go for it! If you have the EA blues/Fears like most do, (in general i mean)  then stay away for now until later!
CONCLUSION -
I like the game, i hope it does well and i hope Tim continues with the dev - but as i say he is currently solo so with that in mind apart from the above (and crashes ofc) this game can be a lot of fun if you like the genre and don't expect too much - otherwise as said, wait until it has been developed a bit more - i was happy to take the risk

The dizzying array of units to choose from is enough to keep you occupied for thousands of hours.  Game runs smoothly, player base is active, sounds are satisfactory, music a little repetitive, and pathing is fair enough.  You will remain a noob for many scores of hours if you're totally new to the Wargame franchise.  I can't say whether that should dishearten or encourage you.  It's a steep learning curve, but one worth testing regardless.

I decided to step out of my mainly-indie gaming to see if a pre-cloud game developer has modernized well. The concept behind Red Faction: Guerrilla seemed like a pretty interesting one, for a big-budget studio at least, in that it's centered around destructible buildings and mildly strategic combat.
After the player completes the tutorial, they'll see that familiar GTA3+ style of gameplay: there's an open world with a clearly defined map pointing you to the missions and other objectives. It also has a number of "challenge" objectives -- for those who are into that sort of thing.
After a short while, whether through tearing down buildings or getting into skirmishes, the gameplay reminds one of Mercenaries: you start off outnumbered without much support, but as you fight (and blow stuff up) more people become willing to help.
While they tried to make it seem like crafting, though, their upgrade system is a simple progress-capped shop using salvage as currency. Nothing groundbreaking. Also, with the effort they put into dismantling buildings I feel they could have lived up to their M rating better and applied it to gore effects as well. With proper physics it could remain fairly subtle but make the weapons feel like they're actually lethal.
All in all, it's a decent game. Worth a play, but I wouldn't say it's a must-see.

Spelunky is one of my favorite games of all time and I can't recommend it enough. It is one of few soul crushingly difficult games where your deaths come with very little frustration, and with every death you get a better understanding of the game, and the better your understanding of the game becomes, the less frustration there is to be had. And that is a huge feat given that the game is randomly generated and features perma-death. There is so much depth to the mechanics in place and so much you can do with them and the way in which they can work together to screw you over in glorious fashion is more often than not hilarious. You'll laugh at an absurd (but well deserved) death when one tiny mistake spirals off into a rube goldberg-like chain of f#ckery, even if you're on the brink of progressing past a point you've never reached before.
There's so many things to learn and it can be overwhelming at first, but it is so worth it. The accomplishments you'll make along the way, big or small, feel so incredibly satisfying, from just making it past the mines, to finding the black market, to killing Old Bitey, beating Olmec, unlocking the city of gold, getting to hell, successfully robbing a shop, ghost mining, speedrunning, and so much more. The skill ceiling is incredibly high, but you don't have to be a god at the game to enjoy yourself, and you're always getting better, a failed run is a new lesson learned in how to approach whatever it was that screwed you over the last time. Mastering Spelunky was one of the most rewarding experiences I've had with a game, and I can only hope to play something as good as it again.
Thanks to Derek Yu & Andy Hull for their amazing work.

From Dekovir Entertainment, tunnels from under, Craft the World, A Steam Greenlit game. CtW is a sidescrolling survival game where you play god, and manage a bunch of Dwarves (who are apparently all white, and also male without the DLC).  The idea is similar to other games that popped up in recent years like Terraria and Starbound, but this is the first where I’ve seen the player control AI instead of a singular character.  CtW appears to be the dev’s only notable game on PC while the rest of their games are mobile.
Craft the World runs at a solid 60 frames per second without many dips, even while zooming in and out, or having tons of dwarves fighting and mining in the background.  Unlike most side scrolling resource games, the art style in CtW retains its own cute little aesthetic, instead of a pixel artstyle.  Colors are bold, and details are not always extreme, keeping each design pretty basic like a cartoon.  The music also pretty much matches the whole style of the game, reminding me of The Sims tracks, minus the Simlish.
The game suffers from tons of AI pathing bugs.  One issue I encountered many times involves dwarfs crossing a bridge after it has rained.  Water accumulates on top of the bridge, but becomes connected to the water resource below.  I’ve found countless dwarves swimming in place, stuck between the small layer of water and the bridge below.  Compared to the amount of bugs to the amount of content, I’m going to have to say the game is worth the hassle.  The UI is pretty well thought out, with all inventory connecting to each other in one big menu, and different tabs.  In terms of design, the game feels pretty polished.  There is even a Bestiary Book that was illustrated to show the different enemies throughout the game with a little bio.  To get up through the Tech Tree, you must grind-build items you may or may not need to get higher in the Tech Tree.  I’m 11 hours in and only half way through.
Yes the pathing bugs are annoying, but there are workarounds.  Since I took a hiatus from writing, the devs added in more bug fixes and a few new features like resource detection (with little icons when zoomed out), visual paths the dwarf will take, and more.  I also have concerns about the female Dwarves behind a paywall, and so are additional multiplayer options, but like most of us, we don’t know what’s going on at their studio.  This may have been the only reasonable way to make a profit.  I will eventually review those DLC packs so keep an eye out and start minin!

Mercury Fallen is the debut title from indie developer, Nitrous Butterfly. It's a
In Mercury Fallen, you control the survivors of a malfunctioning Mercury Facility from Infinity Corp. Placed in stasis capsules countless years ago and sent across space to colonise a new planet, you wake to find that the underground facility that was built by autonomous robots while you slept has failed to wake your colonists at the designated time. Unknown decades have now passed -- years in which the facility has slowly degraded.
All is not lost, though. You still have a working mining robot and a handful of survivors alive in their capsules, whom you need only to wake and they will be eager to get to work restoring the facility and carving out a life in the underground surroundings.
The graphics in Mercury Fallen are really rather good.
The game has a nice sort of high-tech underground feel to it, with neon-like 'mood' lighting (you can even select the colours for placed lights) and relatively dim, but not annoying, ambient light. Characters all wear Star Trek - like jump suits -- again, you can choose the colours -- and move about well, with nice animation loops. There's free camera panning and rotating about the relatively small maps, and zooming covers a fairly wide range, though a bit more zoom out would be nice. Character models when zoomed in to the maximum look a little weird, with no discernible facial characteristics, but rather than being creepy or lacking, it actually looks quite good.
The interface is a little bit wonky in places. It shouldn't be hard to use, but I always find myself opening the wrong menus when I want to build things. I think it's because of the icons used for the menus. There are also a number of spelling and grammar errors, and the tutorial tooltips don't fit properly: "Click on a stasis capsule and ...".
Graphics options are very limited and there's no vsync, so my video card fan tried to levitate my laptop while playing. The performance seems mostly very good, with only a couple of small hiccups when rotating the camera on occasion. Given the large number (thousands) of elements on the floor once I'd cleared the map, I was actually quite impressed; the prefabs work well.
Sound is extremely lacking at the moment.
There's no music at all, beyond a few resounding notes on the title screen.
Sound effects, too, are minimal, with sporadic mining laser sounds seeming to be the only in-game sounds. The interface gives some auditory feedback, but other than the video card fan, the game is very quiet.
There are no voices.
Mercury Fallen plays essentially like any other colony simulator. You move the camera about with mouse and keyboard, place blueprints and assign roles to indirectly control your minions -- er, colonists -- and gradually unlock new and better things to build to make your colony more productive / self-sustaining / profitable / whatever.
However, in everything in Mercury Fallen is currently very limited, like a proof of concept or demo. Research, in the form of data recovered by computer from the Mercury Facility's archives, is limited to six items, which you can gain in under an hour of play. There are only two crop types: hemp for plastic and potatoes for eating. Potatoes can be eaten raw or, with the appropriate research completed and cooking items built, cooked into mashed potatoes, but they're the only two items that colonists can eat; they must be suffering from some pretty intense vitamin deficiencies.
Colonists have three basic numeric characteristics: smarts, muscles, and athletics. These don't really matter, though. Similarly with the individual traits that colonists can have; you'll probably not even notice any difference unless you really try. I also didn't notice any difference to my colonists' mood or performance once I added medical cabinets, plants, and lights. Even beds aren't really a necessity.
Within about two hours of directed play you will have seen everything the game currently has to offer. I left it running at top speed for an extra half an hour while my colonist mined the rest of the map, and as expected all I found were a few more scattered powered-down robots and sealed stasis chambers. I ended up with a bigger population, but still nothing to do.
There are no set maps. Instead, everything is procedurally generated based on a human-readable seed string that you can specify or randomly generate from a pre-defined list. In theory this should provide essentially unlimited replayability, but in practice the game currently has so few elements that every map plays out basically the same as every other one, with only the availability and distance to resources making much of a difference.
There are no challenges: no game-changing events, no enemies, and ultimately no real exploration. That may all be coming in the future -- I hope so -- but at the moment the game only offers a couple of hours of interest. After playing the excellent RimWorld, Mercury Fallen just feels a bit lacking.
One expects Early Access games to have a few issues and Mercury Fallen is no exception, but it is pretty stable. So far I've only found a few annoying issues, such as WASD-based panning of the camera becoming stuck after pressing ESC to close a window (you need to right-click the mouse instead); water being stated as reducing movement speed by -55%, but actually colonists and robots can't cross it at all; saving and loading remembering production queues, but forgetting selected mining areas; and a relatively large number of grammar and spelling errors. The "Comm Officer" colonist role is also not explained and, I assume, not yet implemented.
Other issues that are not really bugs, but which could do with some attention, include the elevator (not yet implemented); colonist management, which would be much better with individual priorities rather than the simple enable/disable options currently available; power and water routing, which doesn't seem to work quite right with multiple sources, and really needs an on-screen indicator of maximum range -- and also a way to remove conduits once built; and informational messages explaining why things aren't happening as you expect. For example, I couldn't work out for ages why no one would use the ore refinery to make the steel to build my cloning chamber and refridgerator (sic). It turned out that I didn't have the plastic required for the construction; once my next hemp crop was ready a colonist harvested it and turned it into plastic, and then finally another colonist started using the ore refinery to make the steel and built the devices.
Pros:
+ Lovely graphics
+ Good start
Cons:
- Not enough content
- Some interface issues
- Minimal sound and music
I would love to recommend Mercury Fallen, but I can't right now. The game is a great start, and I expect it to be fleshed out further in the coming months, but at the moment there's just not enough here to justify the price. If you enjoy colony simulations then you should definitely keep an eye on this one, but until there's a lot more to do it can only provide a couple of hours of moderately fun distraction.

If you enjoyed SPG2, you will likely appreciate the fixes in this title. Basically, this took a lot of what was good at slowing your progress down in the last title and updated it to match user's input. Engine seems to have been greatly overhauled as well. Things seem smoother running and details are sharper overall. Those fixes include improvements to trading. I can now rack up 2 million credits per round trip run in a captured Heimdall freightliner just between the initial station and planet of the campaign, hauling fertilizer, hydroponics pods, envirosuits and thrusters one way, and medical kits and surgical supplies the other way. Basically, I run a few dozen trips while I manage the civilian fleets out harvesting for me and I can afford the next class of warship for the campaign.
The story is a major change, too. You may not appreciate it much if you haven't played Starpoint Gemini or Starpoint Gemini 2, (or just buy the Origins DLC for SPG2), but for those of us who have been playing along it's a refreshing change. In the first title you played as the rebel Gemini League, the second had you as a freelancer continuing the League's work, now you're an Imperial Refugee. Ever played Starwars as the Empire? Similar deal here. Everyone in the system has a grudge against you, and sometimes you just gotta fly the black flag and start slitting throats to buy yourself a little breathing room.
The game is incredibly customizable this go-round as well. For instance, default behavior is for everything to keep running while you navigate menus, view the map, etc. But the options menu allows you to set up the game to pause whenever you view a context menu or open the map to give it a feel somewhat similar to an RTS like Civilization. If it feels like everything is moving too fast, you can thus slow it down as you need to. Or you can let everything run itself while you focus on the stuff you actually care about. Also, turning on fire at will doesn't doom you to the questionable targetting choices of your crew.  Now you can manually hold down the mouse button to fire at a specific ship for awhile, and your gunners will take back over as soon as you release the button.
Warmasters are available that add fleet commanders with special ships and player skills to the map. You'll start with one, win a second in the gladiator event in your home system, and pick up a third during early part of the campaign. I've done fleet assaults with my warmasters that see them using the Ramming skill to take down enemy capital ships, etc. So, when I do actually want to focus on missions or trading, I can park a warmaster with a support fleet at a particular border chokepoint and actually assume they'll handle it while I'm away.
Finally, my character's perks actually feel like they matter in this go around. I picked up hacker 1 and 2 and noticed on my last mission that I could now access additional options in the mission dialogue with an NPC. Where formerly I was just hoping my comms officer would hack the channel so I could follow the enemy ship, I could now additionally hack the stations comms channel to steal 350k credits and their navigational logs. An early mission made similar use of the fixer and tactical perks to bluff my way through a conversation. I'm realizing the dialogue tree has a lot of depth to it with a few perk choices.
Overall, it's a really nice update to the series. I'm curious about the bounty DLC, though I have enough of them to play with in the initial game that I'm not really hurting for boss hunts. (In addition to The Liberated bounties, ever station I land on seems to have a few normal, veteran or warmaster hunting bounties to play with).
One bit of caution however, is that both boarding and salvaging have been reworked since the last title. While they're less overpowering than they were, it can take some getting used to before you figure out how to make good use of each. It's much harder to capture ships larger than you are, but much easier to capture smaller ships especially after you invest in a few boarding upgrades.

I would give Wargame: Red Dragon 9/10, 8 for the overall playing experience, and 1 for the superb support and constant maintanence to this game provided by Eugen.
I am no stranger to the RTS franchises and I must say that Wargame: Red Dragon has one of the harder learning curves of its rank. With about 150 hours of playing, I still don't have a firm grip of the intricate parts of the gameplays and mechanics. Though Wargame: Red Dragon is an impressive game overall, it is difficult for the new players to become the part of the active community due to its time consuming learning curve.
This is the first Wargame franchise I have played and I found lack of guidance in early experience of the game. It is necessary for the new player to spend hours on solo campaign/skirmish without much guidance to try and feel the every bits of the game. Also the overwhelming amounts of information in deck building/armory panel did not help in simplifying the experience.
As for the playing experience, Wargame: Red Dragon has many immersive battlefield system such as terrain, morale, logistics, garrisons, flying altitude, stealth/reconaissance that will keep you well occupied through the match. Each engagement requires careful examination and preparational positioning and only then, will you can gain the upperhand advantage.
If Eugen gives more friendly guidance for newcomers, I know many more players will be hooked on Wargame: Red Dragon rather than 'veteran players' from previeous franchises dominating the community. As of now, in my opinion, Wargame: Red Dragon is mostly dependent on its hardcore fan base to keep it a relevant community.

I love the concept of Real Time Strategy games, but am too damned old to play StarCraft or any RTS that comes close to the APM needed to keep up. Wargame delivers a beautiful RTS, at a pace I can keep up with, using units that I grew up reading about as a Cold War kid. What more could I ask for?

Are you on the edge of considering a purchase? Just buy it, you won't regret it, *if* you heed this one piece of advice:
Learn how to use your recon units first and foremost. Most people get frustrated because they never see the enemy before their units start to die. This is because they can't see the enemy, because they're not using their Recon units appropriately. Playing recon takes a little getting used to, but once you have it down, it opens up the rest of the game.

This game is way overrated.  The charater designs are very generic, as are most of the environments. The controls, while novel, are used to solve the same kinds of puzzles over and over.  It is totally linear.  There is no music.  So why all the high scores?  I suppose its because the the mommy dies, and that makes it emotionally deep or something.  I am am sorry, but you're not going to emotionally blackmail me to recommend a game with such blatant shortcomings.  This game has a couple of cool levels, and the mommy drowning is sad, but that's not enought to justify the universal praise for this 3.5 hour game, or its price when it's not on sale.
The ending is sad too, btw.  If you don't cry, or rate this game highly, you must be a monster.
But what's saddest of all is that the gaming press is so easily manipulated into giving a game a high score because it tugs on a few heartstrings.

This game really gives you that warm feeling. The two brothers help each other (controlling them simultaneously sometimes starts to feel like playing a both-handed instrument, but once you get the hang of it, it starts feeling natural) and one can easily see that they're very connected, because when one of them gets further away from the other, they start calling each other. Each one of them has their own personality, the little brother being more playful and jolly, and the older one being more mature and serious. The scenery is absolutely beautiful and it feels like going for a walk in real world with beautiful nature. One starts to feel that serenity within and the game proves to be a real relaxation from everyday stress. Now that the game is on sale, you should absolutely get it. Maybe I'd just mention that it might not suit everybody; do not buy it if you're not into puzzles or co-op. If it helps, I'd say that this game in a way resemles Trine because you simply cannot get some tasks done without using both brothers. Additionally, there's a warning that one needs a controller in order to play, but I've managed just fine using only my keyboard.
